# Clinical Diagnosis — A Practical Manual for History, Examination and Differential Reasoning

This manual is about the part of medicine that no machine performs: working out what is
wrong with the patient in front of you. It begins with how a history is taken and ends
with how a diagnosis is reviewed, taught and, when it turns out to be wrong, disclosed.
On the way it describes how each part of the body is examined and what each sign means,
what the common complaints of clinical practice are, how the sick patient is recognized
in the first minute, and how all of it is done when the laboratory is closed, the
radiograph is a day's journey away, and the only instruments are a stethoscope, a
thermometer, a torch and a pair of hands.

Every subject is treated at two levels. First the principle: why the question is asked,
why the sign appears, what the finding does to the probability of disease, and what the
listener should be thinking while the patient is talking or the hand is on the abdomen.
Then the practice: what is actually said, done, looked for and written down, in a
well-resourced hospital and again in a clinic that has almost nothing. The comparison is
deliberate, because the same diagnostic problem is solved with very different tools
depending on where the patient lies, and the reasoning is what travels between those two
places.

It is written to be listened to rather than read. Nothing can be looked up or underlined,
and no diagram can be consulted. Where a chart, a table or a photograph would help on a
page, this book describes the thing in words precisely enough that the listener can see
it: the shape of a rash, the sound of a murmur, the feel of a liver edge, the look of the
patient who is about to deteriorate. Numbers appear as illustrations of reasoning, and
every one of them must be checked against the current guideline and the protocol of the
institution where the patient is being seen.

The seventy-seven chapters are organized in ten parts, followed by five appendices: the
foundations of clinical reasoning, the clinical encounter, examination skills by system,
diagnosis by presenting complaint, the recognition of the sick patient, the common
diseases of each system, special populations, investigations, decision tools, and the
practice of clinical judgment over a working life. The appendices are examination
checklists by system, differential diagnosis tables by symptom, normal values and
reference ranges, red-flag summary cards, and a glossary. The book is meant to be heard
in order once and returned to chapter by chapter afterwards.

This is educational material. It is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is
not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is
actually with the patient. Every appendix repeats that caution, and so does the first
chapter. What the book offers is the reasoning that lets a student, a house officer, a
clinical officer in a district hospital or a nurse practitioner in a clinic ask the right
questions in the right order, notice what the examination is showing, and know which of
the possibilities on the list will kill the patient first if it is missed.

# Chapter 1 — How Diagnosis Works

Diagnosis is not a test result, and it is not a list of diseases learned by heart. It is a cognitive act performed under uncertainty, in which a clinician assembles fragments of a story, a body, and a few measurements into a working explanation of what is wrong with this person at this moment. Before anything else, this book must say plainly what it is. It is educational material only; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is actually with the patient. Nothing spoken here should be used to decide the care of a real person without that judgment, and without the local rules and the current guideline that govern your setting. With that established, we can turn to the reasoning itself.

Clinical thought moves in two modes, and most teaching introduces only one of them. The fast mode is pattern recognition, in which the experienced eye takes in the whole scene at once and an answer arrives before the reasoning can be inspected. The slow mode is hypothetico-deductive, in which a hypothesis is proposed, its consequences are worked out, and findings are sought that would support it or defeat it. Neither mode is the correct one, and neither is a beginner's error or an expert's shortcut. What separates a mature clinician from a merely competent one is not the possession of one mode but the ability to notice which mode is running and to change it on purpose.

The experienced clinician slides between the two modes without ceremony. A familiar story at the start of a clinic is recognized within seconds, and the rest of the encounter becomes a search for the small deviations that would make the familiar answer wrong. A strange story, or a familiar story in an unfamiliar patient, stops the fast mode and forces the slower one to take over. The signal to switch is a kind of discomfort, the nagging sense that something does not quite fit, that the pattern is almost right but not right enough. That discomfort is not weakness, and it deserves to be trained, because it is the only warning the fast mode gives before it misleads you.

Pattern recognition is powerful because it compresses years of experience into an instant. It works because disease does often present in recognizable shapes, and because the human mind is remarkably good at detecting those shapes from incomplete information. The clinician who recognizes a stroke, a measles rash, or a tension pneumothorax in the first seconds has gained time that no laboratory can return. This speed matters most where it is least available, in a crowded clinic or an understaffed emergency department. Yet the same mechanism that produces the instant answer also produces the confident wrong answer, and it does so silently.

The most common way the fast mode fails is not that the pattern is false but that the patient is atypical. Frail older people, infants, pregnant women, and people whose immune defenses are suppressed often present in shapes the textbook did not draw. A constructed illustration makes the point: an older patient with a perforated ulcer whose only complaint is mild indigestion, whose abdomen is soft, and whose temperature is normal, may be recognized as a classic case of nothing at all until the clinician deliberately looks for the signs of peritonitis and shock. The finding that saves this patient is not a memory but a habit, the habit of asking what dangerous thing could hide behind a bland story. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is treated as a fever in some protocols and not in others, so confirm what your own service calls a fever against the current guideline and the local protocol before you rest any reasoning on it.

Pattern recognition also fails when the clinician stops thinking too early. The first plausible explanation tends to close the search, and every later finding is then bent to fit it. This is not stupidity; it is how a mind conserves effort. The remedy is procedural rather than moral: name the working diagnosis out loud, then ask what findings would prove it wrong, and go looking for at least one of them. A clinician who never tries to break his own hypothesis is not being decisive, he is being unprotected.

The alternative to the instant answer is a loop, and the loop is the engine of the whole book. A hypothesis is formed from the story and the first observations. From that hypothesis, a predicted finding is derived: if this is the disease, then this sign or this result should be present. The prediction is tested by examining the patient or by ordering a test, and the hypothesis is then revised in the light of what was found. The loop repeats until the explanation is good enough to act on, or until the clinician decides that it cannot be resolved with the tools at hand.

The discipline of the loop lies in making the prediction before looking. If the clinician examines first and interprets afterwards, the finding is free to mean anything, and it will usually mean whatever the clinician already believed. A prediction made in advance is a small act of self-binding, and it converts an examination into evidence rather than decoration. This is also why a finding that was not predicted is so valuable: it is the one piece of information least contaminated by hope.

Revision is not failure, and a diagnosis that survives contact with new information is stronger for it. When a predicted finding appears, the hypothesis gains support but is not proved, because other diseases can produce the same sign. When the predicted finding is absent, the hypothesis loses support but is not always dead, because the test may have been performed badly or the disease may be early. The clinician who treats every negative as a refutation will abandon true diagnoses, and the clinician who treats every negative as an accident will keep false ones. Judgment lives in between those two errors.

Time is itself a diagnostic instrument, and it is the one that is always available. Many conditions declare themselves not in a single examination but in their trajectory, so a finding that is equivocal now becomes decisive when it is repeated in a few hours. The patient who looks slightly unwell and is unchanged after observation is a different patient from the one who is quietly deteriorating. This is why the interval between observations matters, and why the clinician should record not only what was found but when it was found and what had changed since the last look.

Probability enters the reasoning in plain language rather than in arithmetic. When a clinician says that a diagnosis is likely, unlikely, or possible but must be excluded, he is speaking about how much of the available evidence points that way. The listener does not need to calculate anything; the listener needs to hear that probability is a property of the whole clinical picture and not of any single symptom. A symptom that seems dramatic may be common and harmless, while a quiet detail may be the one that changes everything. Thinking in probabilities means holding several explanations at once and letting the balance move as the evidence accumulates.

Pre-test probability is the name for the estimate a clinician makes before a particular piece of evidence arrives. It comes from the patient's age and sex, the setting, the season, the duration of the complaint, and the clinician's experience of similar patients. A finding never enters an empty mind; it enters a mind that already has a prior, and the same finding moves different priors by different amounts. This is why two clinicians can examine the same abdomen, find the same tenderness, and reach different conclusions, and why the disagreement is often about the prior rather than about the finding.

The prior is heavily shaped by where the patient is sitting. A district clinic, an emergency department, and a referral hospital each admit a different mixture of illness, and the same complaint carries a different weight in each. Chest pain that arises from a strained muscle in a young person in a general clinic may be produced by a clot in the lung in the same young person brought to an emergency department after a long flight. The symptom has not changed; the population has. Diagnosis is therefore always local, and a rule that was derived in one setting must be re-examined before it is trusted in another.

Prevalence is the word for how common a condition is in the group being considered, and it is the single most powerful influence on what a finding means. If a disease is common, a suggestive finding raises its probability a great deal; if the disease is rare, the same finding may leave it rare. In a general clinic, chest pain from a common and benign cause may occur in 1 in 4 people who present that way, while a dangerous cause may be far less frequent. That proportion is an illustration, so confirm the figure for your own population against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the composition of every clinic differs.

The mathematics is usually hidden, but the movement it describes is simple. A pre-test probability can be turned into pre-test odds, and a finding then multiplies those odds by a factor that describes how much the finding shifts belief. The result is post-test odds, which can be turned back into a probability if anyone needs one. The clinician who never performs this calculation still performs the movement, because the whole encounter is a sequence of such multiplications. What matters is knowing the direction and the rough size of each shift, not the arithmetic that formalizes it.

A likelihood ratio is the name for that factor, and it can be understood without a single computation. It answers one question: how much more often is this finding seen in people who have the disease than in people who do not. A finding with a large ratio moves belief strongly towards the disease, a finding with a ratio near one moves it hardly at all, and a finding that is more common in health than in disease moves belief away. The listener who remembers those three sentences has everything the arithmetic would have given, and will use it more often because it costs nothing to recall.

The counter-intuitive case deserves special attention because it misleads so many. A finding can be present in most people with a disease and still be nearly useless, if it is equally present in people without it. A red rash may accompany a serious infection in almost every case, but if the same rash is common in healthy people in the same ward, its appearance changes very little. The question is never whether a sign is common in the disease, but whether it is more common in the disease than in the alternative explanations.

The same logic governs the language of test performance. A test that is positive in nearly everyone with the disease is good at ruling the disease out when it is negative, and a test that is negative in nearly everyone without the disease is good at ruling the disease in when it is positive. Neither property survives a change of population unchanged, which is why a result that is decisive in a referral hospital may be almost meaningless in a screening clinic. The number that describes the test is not a property of the test alone; it is a property of the test in a particular kind of patient.

A test result is not a diagnosis, and a laboratory does not think. It measures, counts, or images something, and it returns a number or a picture to be interpreted in the light of the whole picture. The interpretation is where error enters: a normal result in a patient who is dangerously ill may mean the test was too early, or too insensitive, or performed on the wrong sample. The clinician who orders a test to settle a question must first decide what each possible result would change, and if nothing would change, the test should not be ordered at all.

A diagnosis made at the bedside and a diagnosis confirmed in a laboratory are two different achievements, and both are legitimate. The bedside diagnosis is built from the history and the examination, and it is often accurate enough to start the right decision immediately. The confirmed diagnosis waits for evidence that is independent of the clinician's senses, and it is what allows a disease to be named with confidence, recorded, and communicated. The two are not rivals; the bedside diagnosis decides what to do now, and the confirmation decides what is true.

Confirmation has limits that are easy to forget. A laboratory can only answer the question it was asked, on the sample it was given, at the moment it was taken, and its answer depends on the quality of the whole chain that produced it. A result can be falsely reassuring when the disease is early, and falsely alarming when the patient is not representative of the group in which the test was studied. The clinician who understands this treats results as evidence to be weighed, not as verdicts to be obeyed.

The question is therefore not only what disease is most likely but what disease is most dangerous. The two answers are frequently different, and the difference is where patients are harmed. A common benign explanation may be the most probable, while a rare lethal one is the most consequential, and both must be carried in mind at once. This is why a differential diagnosis is ranked twice, once by likelihood and once by danger, and why the dangerous end of the list is examined first.

Naming the dangerous possibility early is a rule of safety rather than a symptom of anxiety. In chest pain the possibility of a torn aorta or a clot in the lung must be considered alongside the far more common muscular cause, and the finding that would reveal it must be sought deliberately. In headache the possibility of bleeding around the brain must be weighed against tension headache, and in back pain the possibility of compression of the spinal cord against a strained muscle. The clinician who asks what would kill this patient first is not being pessimistic, he is ordering the search correctly.

Red flags are the practical form of that priority. They are findings that, when present, change the acceptable pace of the encounter and sometimes the place of care. Their value is not that they prove a dangerous disease but that they prevent the clinician from relaxing too early. A patient who has no red flags after a deliberate search is in a very different position from a patient who was never asked the questions that would have found them.

The history is the most powerful diagnostic instrument in medicine, and it is available everywhere. It carries more information per minute than any test, and it is the only instrument that can tell the clinician what the patient is afraid of, what has changed, and what the patient has already tried. A history taken well narrows the field before the patient is touched, so that the examination becomes a set of targeted questions rather than a ritual tour of the body. The examiner who listens first examines better.

The examination is applied reasoning, not a checklist performed for its own sake. Each maneuver exists because some disease produces a sign that can be elicited in a particular way, and the clinician who knows the reason will notice the sign and understand its absence. A sign that is sought without a question behind it is easily missed, because the eye sees what the mind is prepared to recognize. The examination should therefore be performed with a short list of hypotheses in mind and a clear idea of what each finding would do to them. This is why the order of the examination can be reorganized around the leading question without losing anything essential.

Single signs are usually weaker than the pattern they belong to. One finding may be suggestive, but several findings that point the same way, or a finding combined with the right history, are far more convincing. This is why a diagnosis assembled from a constellation is more robust than one resting on a memorable detail. It is also why a clinician should be suspicious of a diagnosis that depends entirely on one striking sign.

None of the examples in this book describe a real patient. Where a case is used, it is a constructed illustration built to make a piece of reasoning visible, and it should be read as a teaching device rather than a record. Real patients are messier, more variable, and more surprising than any illustration, and the listener should expect that. The purpose of an illustration is to fix a habit of thought, not to supply a portrait of a disease.

Reasoning with limited resources is not a lesser version of reasoning with many. It is the same reasoning, asked to work with fewer inputs, and it exposes the logic more clearly because nothing can be hidden behind a machine. In a clinic with a stethoscope, a thermometer, and a torch, the clinician must decide which question matters most, which sign is worth the time, and what to do when the answer remains uncertain. Those decisions are the essence of diagnosis, and they are made in every setting, with or without a laboratory. A duration such as 3 days may mark one condition as acute and another as chronic, but the interval that separates them is not fixed, so check the current guideline and the local protocol rather than trusting a remembered figure. The clinician who reasons well with little is not improvising; he is doing exactly what the hospital clinician does, with fewer distractions.

In a well-resourced hospital the clinician can reach for imaging, for a laboratory, and for colleagues. In the clinic at the end of the road the same clinician reaches for a careful history, a systematic examination, and the courage to name uncertainty. The tools differ, and the decisions about referral differ with them, but the questions are identical. A clinician who can diagnose without equipment is not a relic; he is the proof that the method is sound.

The book therefore works on two levels throughout. The first is the principle: why the question is asked, why the sign appears, and what the finding does to the probability of disease. The second is the practice: what is said, done, looked for, and written down, in a hospital with every resource and again in a clinic with almost none. The principle is what makes the practice portable, and the practice is what keeps the principle honest. Listening for both is what allows one book to be useful in two very different rooms.

What transfers between those rooms is reasoning, not equipment. A clinician who has learned to form a hypothesis, predict a finding, test it, and revise is not disabled by the absence of a scanner, because the method does not depend on the scanner. Equipment extends the senses, but it does not supply the questions, the priorities, or the judgment about what the answer means. That is why a good clinician with few tools so often outperforms a poor clinician with many.

Vital signs are the cheapest evidence available at the bedside, and they are often the first thing to contradict a reassuring story. A pulse of 110 beats per minute may be fear, fever, or blood loss, and the rate that should alarm you must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol because it shifts with age, pregnancy, and fitness. A systolic pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury means something different in a trained athlete and in a patient who is normally hypertensive, so treat it as an illustration and confirm the threshold that matters against the current guideline and the local protocol. A respiratory rate that has climbed since the last observation may be the most sensitive sign of all, precisely because it is the one most often estimated rather than counted. The point is not the individual figure but the direction in which the figures are moving.

Equipment can also create a false sense of completeness. A normal computed tomography, or CT, scan of the head does not remove the possibility of a bleed that has not yet declared itself, and a normal blood count does not remove the possibility of serious infection. In the same way, an electrocardiogram, or ECG, may be normal between episodes of a rhythm disturbance, and the intensive care unit, or ICU, with all its monitoring, still relies on a person noticing that the patient looks worse. Machines report what they measure, and the clinician must still decide what the measurement means.

Uncertainty is the medium in which diagnosis is performed, and tolerance of it is a skill. Some clinicians reduce uncertainty by ordering more tests, which often replaces one kind of uncertainty with several new ones. Others reduce it by deciding early, which feels decisive and can be equally expensive for the patient. The mature response is to hold the question open for exactly as long as it needs to be open, and to act decisively when the decision can no longer wait.

Calibration is the name for knowing how much to trust your own judgment. A clinician who is right nine times out of ten when he feels certain, and wrong half the time when he feels uncertain, has useful self-knowledge and can act on it. A clinician whose confidence is unrelated to his accuracy will be dangerous in both directions, because he will neither check what he should nor defer when he should. Calibration is learned from feedback, which is why follow-up and the review of outcomes are part of diagnosis and not an administrative extra.

The patient's own account is the beginning and the correction of every hypothesis. Patients describe their illness in the language they have, and the clinician's first task is to understand what the words point to rather than to translate them too quickly into a diagnosis. Time and again the decisive information arrives in an aside, a hesitation, or a detail the clinician did not ask for. The habit of listening past the first answer is one of the most valuable things a clinician can cultivate.

Documentation is reasoning made visible. What is written down should show not only what was found but what was considered and what was excluded, so that the next clinician can pick up the thread. A record that lists findings without the thinking behind them forces the next reader to start again, and a record that states a diagnosis without the evidence leaves no way to challenge it. The written note is therefore part of the diagnostic process, not a report filed after it.

Safety-netting is the acknowledgment that a diagnosis is a statement about the present, made with imperfect information. The clinician who is not certain must tell the patient what to watch for, where to return if it appears, and when the picture should be reviewed. This is not a substitute for a decision; it is a second decision layered on the first, and it protects the patient when the first decision turns out to be wrong. It is also the point at which the reasoning meets the patient's own judgment and daily life.

The same method that diagnoses a patient also teaches a clinician. Each encounter is an experiment in which a prediction was made and an outcome followed, and the clinician who notices the gap between the two improves. Reflection on cases, including the ones that went well, is how the fast mode is built and how its errors are found. The listener who is studying rather than practising can use the same loop, predicting what a described case will show before the explanation is given, and learning from the difference.

To summarize, diagnosis is a loop of hypothesis, prediction, test, and revision, run in two modes and always in the presence of uncertainty. It asks not only what is most likely but what is most dangerous, and it ranks findings by how much they change belief rather than by how dramatic they seem. Every number, score, cut-off, and reference range that this book mentions is an illustration only, and each must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol before it influences any real decision. This book is educational material, it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient. If a patient is deteriorating, the reasoning pauses and the patient is treated, because no hypothesis is worth the delay of someone who is becoming more ill.

# Chapter 2 — Cognitive Biases and Diagnostic Error

Diagnostic error is not the same thing as ignorance, and the difference matters more than any list of mistakes. Ignorance is the absence of knowledge, and it is cured slowly by study. Error is the failure of a process that worked well enough to feel correct, which is why it survives study and returns in a new shape. A clinician who knows the sign, looks for it, finds it and still reaches the wrong conclusion has failed in reasoning, and will repeat that failure until the reasoning itself is examined. This book is written for that second failure, because it is the one that follows the experienced clinician home.

The beginner and the expert do not fail in the same way, and the difference is not simply one of degree. The beginner fails through absence, because the wrong question is not asked, the relevant history is not taken, and the finding is not sought. The expert fails through the very patterns that made the expert, because a mind that has seen many patients recognizes a shape quickly and then arranges the evidence around it. Both are errors, but only the expert's arrives with a feeling of certainty attached.

Anchoring is the name for the moment when a first impression becomes the frame inside which every later fact is placed. The anchor is often reasonable, because the common disease is common and the first version of the story usually points somewhere sensible. The trouble is what happens next, because once the anchor is set the questions that follow are no longer neutral. The clinician asks about the features that fit the anchor and skips the features that would break it, and the examination drifts toward the parts of the body the anchor has already chosen. By the end of the encounter the record looks like careful work and reads as a single argument for the first idea.

An early label given by someone else is even more powerful, because it arrives with authority and without the reasoning that produced it. A referral that opens with the word pneumonia tells the receiving clinician where to listen, what to look for and which alternative to leave unexamined. The patient also learns the label and begins to describe the illness in its language, so the original guess returns to the clinician as independent confirmation. A constructed illustration makes the shape of it clear: a man is sent to hospital with a note saying gastritis, and for the next several shifts nobody asks about the chest pain that comes with effort, because the note has settled the question.

Premature closure is the moment the search stops because a plausible answer has arrived. Plausible is the operative word, since the answer need not be probable, only satisfying. A diagnosis that explains the main symptom and fits the patient's age and habits can feel complete long before the dangerous alternative has been considered. The remedy is not more knowledge but a deliberate refusal to close while a lethal possibility remains unexcluded, which is an act of discipline rather than of memory.

Every presentation carries at least one diagnosis that must be excluded before the comfortable one is accepted, and the experienced clinician names it early rather than late. In a patient with chest discomfort the possibility that must be excluded is a problem in the heart or the great vessels, and the finding that would reveal it is sought in the first minutes rather than after the ward round. In a patient with headache the possibilities that must be excluded are bleeding and infection inside the head, and the questions about sudden onset, fever and neck stiffness belong at the start. It means that the comfortable diagnosis is accepted only after the uncomfortable one has been looked for and not found.

Availability is the tendency to judge how likely a diagnosis is by how easily an example comes to mind. Memory is not a fair sample of disease, and it does not try to be, because it keeps what was vivid, recent, frightening or personally costly. A clinician who has just cared for a patient with a rare clot in the lung will see that clot in the next several breathless patients, and a clinician who has just been humiliated by a missed infection will over-investigate the next patient with a fever. The last dramatic patient therefore distorts the next ordinary one.

A constructed illustration of this is easy to picture. A clinic spends a difficult week with several patients who turn out to have a serious tropical infection, and by the following week every patient with a fever is being assessed for it. Meanwhile the ordinary bacterial infection that is far more common in that place and season is treated late, because it has become uninteresting to the person doing the thinking. Availability is not corrected by resolving to be fairer, because the clinician cannot feel the cases that are missing. It is corrected by looking at what the local data actually show, and by asking what an ordinary week in this clinic usually contains.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek and to notice the evidence that supports the leading hypothesis while passing lightly over the evidence that threatens it. It operates in the questions and in the observation at the same time. The clinician asks about weight loss because the leading hypothesis predicts weight loss, and forgets to ask about the night sweats that would point elsewhere. On examination, the finding that fits is written down and the finding that does not is described as equivocal, or simply not recorded. This is why the same patient can be examined by different competent clinicians and yield sets of findings that are each internally consistent.

The remedy for confirmation bias is to look deliberately for the finding that would make the leading hypothesis wrong. This is a different habit from looking for more support, and it feels uncomfortable because it works against the momentum of the encounter. If the leading hypothesis is an infection of the urinary tract, the clinician should ask what would be found if the truth were something else entirely, and then check that. If the leading hypothesis is a benign headache, the clinician should ask which single feature, if present, would change the plan, and then hunt for that feature specifically. This is not doubt for its own sake; it is the cheapest form of safety available at the bedside.

Search satisficing is the failure to keep looking once the first abnormality has been found. A patient falls, a fracture is seen on the image, and the search stops there, though a fall in an older person often has a second explanation and the fracture may be the consequence rather than the cause. A patient has one abnormal laboratory value that explains the presentation, and the other abnormal values on the same report are never examined. After finding the first abnormality, the clinician should look once more through the whole of the available information before deciding that the search is complete.

Base-rate neglect is the tendency to weigh the impressive features of a case more heavily than the ordinary frequency of the disease in the population in front of the clinician. The rare diagnosis is more interesting, more memorable and more flattering to the person who makes it, and none of those qualities has anything to do with probability. A student who has just learned about an uncommon disease will see it everywhere, and a clinician working where a common infection is rampant may still reach first for the exotic explanation. The common disease in an unusual dress is far more frequent than the rare disease in its classical dress. The first question about any presentation is not what could cause it, but what usually causes it here, in this season, in this patient.

A constructed illustration of base-rate neglect is worth carrying in mind. Consider a pair of patients who arrive with the same ordinary complaint of fever and cough. One is diagnosed with a rare tropical infection because the clinician has just read about it, and the other is diagnosed with the common respiratory infection that is going around the ward. If the rare disease occurs in a very small number of people each year in that district and the common one in a very large number, then the unimpressive diagnosis is the more likely one in almost every patient who walks through the door. This does not excuse missing the rare disease, but it means the rare diagnosis must be sought for a reason found in the patient rather than in the clinician's reading.

Framing is the effect of the words in which the problem arrives. The same set of facts, described as a patient who is anxious and breathing quickly, leads the next clinician toward one set of questions and away from another; described as a patient with sudden shortness of breath and a fast pulse, it leads elsewhere. The referral letter chooses the frame, sometimes deliberately and usually not, because the person writing it has already performed an act of diagnosis and can only report what that act produced. Handover does the same thing in speech, and a tired clinician at the end of a shift transmits a summary rather than a set of raw findings. The practical response is to ask for the observations behind the label, and to look at the patient before reading the note.

Framing is not corrected by ignoring the referral, because the referral contains real information and the person who wrote it has usually seen more of the patient than the receiver will. It is corrected by separating what was observed from what was concluded. When a colleague says that a patient looks septic, the useful question is which findings produced that impression, and when a note says that the chest is clear, the useful question is who examined it and how. The frame is then kept as one opinion among several rather than as the shape of the whole case.

Overconfidence is the mismatch between the certainty a clinician feels and the accuracy actually achieved. Certainty is a feeling and not a measurement, and it is generated by fluency, because a diagnosis that comes to mind easily feels true while one that has to be assembled feels doubtful. Clinicians are usually better at ranking possibilities than at estimating probabilities, and they are often worse at estimating their own error rate than at estimating anything else. The dangerous zone is not the case that feels difficult, since a difficult case summons care, but the case that feels easy and is not. Calibration, the habit of comparing confidence with outcomes, is learned only by looking back at what actually happened.

The absence of feedback is one of the deepest problems in clinical reasoning, because a wrong conclusion that is never corrected is stored as a right one. A clinician who discharges a patient with a benign diagnosis and never learns that the patient returned with something serious will continue to feel that the original judgment was sound. This is why units that track their own errors and review their own misses improve, while units that do not, do not, even when the individuals within them are equally able. Every clinician should therefore know how a patient who was sent home actually fared, and should make it easy for that information to arrive. A system that hides the outcome is manufacturing overconfidence one patient at a time.

Hindsight bias is the tendency, after an outcome is known, to believe that the outcome was visible all along and that any competent person would have seen it. The record is read backwards, and findings that were ambiguous at the time become obvious warnings, while the alternatives that were reasonable then are quietly forgotten. The clinician who missed the diagnosis is judged by a standard that nobody could have met at the bedside, with the answer in hand and unlimited time. The defense is to review decisions in the order the information actually arrived, and to ask what a reasonable clinician could have known at each point.

Not every diagnostic failure is a cognitive error, and the distinction decides what should be fixed. A result that was never returned, a message that was never delivered, a handover interrupted before the important sentence, a chart that cannot be read and a patient moved between wards without the notes are failures of the system, and the clinician may have reasoned perfectly inside a process that lost the information. The clinician who reasons well inside a system that leaks information will still produce a wrong diagnosis, and no amount of personal vigilance will repair the leak. Judging the two together is how units end up punishing individuals for the failures of their tools.

Blaming the individual alone fixes nothing, and often makes the next error more likely. If the response to a missed result is a reprimand, then the next clinician will be slower to report a near miss, and the unit will lose the information it needs. Punishment drives error underground, where it cannot be studied, and it teaches everyone to protect themselves rather than the patient. A just response separates the person from the process, holding people accountable for concealment and for reckless disregard while treating ordinary human fallibility as a property of the system to be designed around. The question after an error is not who is at fault but what made this outcome possible and what would make it less likely next time.

The first debiasing move available at the bedside is to generate alternatives deliberately, before the leading hypothesis has hardened. This is not the same as listing every disease that could cause the symptom, which is an exercise in memory rather than in reasoning. It means producing more than one plausible alternative with different consequences, so that the plan must accommodate more than one world. The list should be made before the tests are ordered, because a test ordered after the decision is usually a test chosen to protect the decision. A list of possibilities built in this way is short, ranked and useful, and it can be revised without embarrassment.

The question that does most of the work is the plain one: what else could this be? It is worth asking aloud, and worth asking early, because it changes the clinician's posture from defending an answer to testing one. The next question is which of the alternatives would be most dangerous if it were true, and whether anything has yet been done to exclude it. In a patient with abdominal pain, for example, the dangerous alternatives include a perforated bowel, a vascular emergency and a pregnancy outside the uterus, and each of these has a question or a finding that speaks to it. The purpose is not to investigate all of them, but to know which ones have been considered and to have a reason for setting each one aside.

The previous question becomes operational through a pair of habits. The first is the search for the finding that would disprove the leading hypothesis, which requires the clinician to name in advance what would change the plan. The second is the diagnostic time-out, a deliberate pause before the decision is committed, in which the case is restated from the beginning as though it had just arrived. A time-out costs little and is best performed aloud, because speech exposes gaps that silent review smooths over. Done properly, it asks a short set of questions: what is the leading diagnosis, what is the greatest danger, and what would make me change my mind.

Cognitive forcing strategies are methods that make the mind slow down at the moment it would prefer to leap. One is to state the diagnosis together with the evidence that supports it and the evidence that argues against it, so that the reasoning is exposed rather than implied. Another is to consider the opposite of the first impression, asking what the patient would look like if the leading diagnosis were wrong, and then checking whether the patient looks like that. Another is to write the list of possibilities down before seeing the result of any test, so that the result is interpreted rather than obeyed. Each of these costs only the willingness to be uncomfortable for a moment, and the discomfort is the point, because a reasoning process that never feels resisted is usually not being tested.

A checklist has a place in diagnosis when a case is hard, and its value lies in what it forces the clinician to consider rather than in what it concludes. A useful diagnostic checklist is short, and it asks about the things most often omitted under pressure, including the vital signs, the full set of observations, the medicines, the allergies, the pregnancy status where relevant, the possibility of infection and the possibility of a vascular event. It should also instruct the clinician to ask what is missing from the story, and to confirm that the results which were ordered have actually been seen. Used in the right place, however, it catches the omissions that expert reasoning is most likely to make.

Asking a colleague is the most underused debiasing strategy, and often the most effective. The value is not that the colleague knows more, though sometimes that too, but that the colleague does not share the anchor. A fresh listener hears the story without the first impression, and asks the obvious question that has become invisible to the clinician who has been inside the case for hours. The request should be specific, not a general plea for help but a short statement of the leading diagnosis, the reason for doubt and the question that needs answering. No clinician should be embarrassed to ask, and units should make such conversations easy rather than heroic.

Individual habits are strongest when the system supports them, and weakest when they depend on the character of one tired person at the end of a long shift. A unit that expects a second opinion in defined situations, that schedules time for difficult cases and that treats a request for help as ordinary will get more second opinions than a unit that leaves the matter to individual courage. The same is true of the diagnostic time-out and of handover, because if they are not part of the routine they happen only when someone remembers, and someone remembers least often when the shift is worst. The design of the working day is therefore part of the reasoning, and it can be changed.

When an error has occurred, the honest disclosure of it to the patient and to the team is part of the clinical work rather than an administrative aftermath. Patients generally want to know what happened, what it means for them and what will be done now, and they are entitled to that. The conversation is difficult because it requires the clinician to say plainly that a mistake was made, without hiding behind the passive voice or behind an explanation that blames the process in order to avoid the person. Disclosure protects the patient first and the clinician second, and it is the only version of the story that can be acted upon.

An apology is not an admission of incompetence, and its absence is usually felt by the patient as a second injury. Saying that the clinician is sorry this happened, and that the patient was not treated as well as they should have been, costs nothing and repairs a great deal. It must be followed by an account of what will change, because an apology that leads to no change is heard as an attempt to close the subject. A unit that handles these matters well is one in which errors surface early, and early errors are smaller errors.

A book about reasoning has to teach the failure modes alongside the skills, because the skills are learned quickly and the failure modes are not. Every clinician is taught how to take a history, and almost none is taught how the history will be distorted by the first idea. The rules of evidence, the meaning of a sign and the interpretation of a test can all be acquired from a text and improved by practice. The biases cannot, because they are part of the equipment that does the learning, and they operate whether or not the clinician believes in them. The only reliable defense is to know their names, to recognize their arrival in the middle of an encounter, and to have a habit ready that interrupts them.

Reasoning is a craft, and every craft is taught with its failure modes attached. Medicine has been slower than others to teach its own, partly because the stakes make the errors painful to discuss and partly because they feel like personal defects rather than like properties of a mind. Naming them changes that, and turns a private shame into a shared object that a team can work on. The clinician who can say that the case was anchored, or that the search was satisfied too early, is describing a process rather than confessing a character. That vocabulary is the beginning of correction, and it is also the beginning of teaching.

The habits described here are small, and they are meant to be small, because a strategy that requires an hour will not be used in a clinic that has only a few minutes for each patient. Each of them fits into the encounter as it already happens, as a question asked aloud, a pause before the decision, a sentence written before the test is ordered, or a colleague consulted at the door. What matters is that the habit exists before the difficult case arrives, because the difficult case is exactly the one in which the clinician will not think of it. Debiasing is a practice in both senses of the word, since it is done repeatedly and it is done professionally.

Numbers enter the reasoning at every point, and each of them is local. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is called a fever in one protocol and investigated from a different value in the next, so that figure must be checked against the current edition of the guideline and against the local protocol before it decides anything. A pulse of 110 beats per minute is comfortable in a young athlete and alarming in a patient who takes a medicine that slows the heart, so the threshold has to be confirmed in the local protocol and in the current guideline that governs the ward. A systolic pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury is a decision point in some settings and an ordinary finding in others, and it too must be verified against the current guideline and the local protocol, which differ between countries, editions and hospitals.

Other measurements behave in the same way, and each belongs to the place where it was made. A fluid loss of 2 liters means one thing in a patient who is already dry and another in a patient whose kidneys are failing, and the value that prompts action varies with the guideline and the local protocol in force. A history of 3 days is a short illness in one clinic and a long one in another, depending on the local pattern of disease, so it must be read against the current local guidance rather than against a memory of a textbook. A frequency of 1 in 4 patients may be quoted for a complication in a specialist center and be much lower or higher in a district hospital, so that figure requires confirmation from the local data and the current protocol before it shapes a decision.

Reference ranges are the clearest example of a number that cannot be carried between places. A laboratory range for a blood count or a liver enzyme is derived from its own population, measured on its own machines and reported in its own units, so a value that is normal in one hospital can be abnormal in another. The clinician should therefore read the range printed beside the result rather than the range remembered from training, and should confirm it against the current reporting standard in local use. The same caution applies to any score, because a score is a formalized piece of reasoning and its cut-off is a decision about a particular population, so the score must be checked against the current guideline and against the population in which it was derived. The listener should treat every score as a question to the local source, not as an answer.

To summarize, the clinician's task is not to avoid having a mind that takes shortcuts, because no such mind exists, but to build habits that catch the shortcuts before they reach the patient. Anchor the case deliberately and then test the anchor, keep the search open until the dangerous possibilities have been excluded, generate alternatives before the tests are ordered, ask what would disprove the leading idea, pause for a time-out when the case is hard, and ask a colleague without embarrassment. Treat every number, cut-off, pressure, temperature, rate and reference range as a local fact that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it is acted upon, because these values differ between countries, editions, laboratories and wards. Separate the cognitive error from the system failure, because blaming the individual alone repairs neither, and disclose what went wrong to the patient and to the team. None of this replaces training, supervision or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient, and none of it is a licence to delay care in an emergency. The aim is a reasoning process that is honest about its own weaknesses, and a clinician who is therefore safer than confidence alone would make him or her.

# Chapter 3 — Building a Differential Diagnosis

Every diagnosis begins as a question, and a differential diagnosis is the shape of that question written down. It is not a list of every disease that could produce the patient's complaint, because such a list is both endless and useless. A differential is a working set of explanations, ordered by likelihood and by danger at the same time. The clinician who carries that set into the room behaves differently from one who carries a single hypothesis. One looks for evidence that will strengthen or weaken each possibility, while the other looks only for confirmation of a decision already made. The first is doing diagnosis, and the second is doing something else and calling it diagnosis.

When a learner first tries to be thorough, the result is usually an undifferentiated catalogue in which a common cold and a rare metabolic disease sit side by side with equal weight. The catalogue feels safe because it looks complete, yet it offers no guidance about what to do first, and a list that cannot direct action is not yet a diagnostic tool. Thoroughness in generating possibilities and discipline in ordering them are separate skills, and the second is much the harder. Generating broadly ensures that no dangerous possibility is overlooked, while narrowing spends the patient's time and the clinician's attention on what matters most. Breadth without order becomes paralysis, and order without breadth becomes error. The two must be practised together, in that sequence, at every encounter.

It helps to name the movements explicitly. The first is divergence, which asks what could possibly be going on, and at this stage the clinician should be generous, because the only cost of an idea is a moment of thought. The second is convergence, which asks which of those ideas the evidence supports, and here the clinician should be strict. Many clinicians perform both movements unconsciously and then wonder why their first impression survives, because an unexamined impression quietly becomes the whole list. Writing the divergent list down, even in shorthand, protects against that, since an idea that has been named can be examined and discarded. Breadth comes first, and the knife comes afterwards.

One of the oldest and most dependable frameworks is anatomical. The clinician begins with the structure that hurts, or whose function has failed, and works outward through the layers and neighbours that share its nerve supply, its blood supply, its drainage or its space. Pain in the right upper abdomen draws the mind through the liver and its capsule, the gallbladder, the duodenum, the colon, the diaphragm, the pleura and the rib cage, and even the heart. Each structure suggests its own mechanisms, and the framework is powerful because it forces the question of what lies next door. Anatomy also prevents the clinician from forgetting the compartment that shares a nerve root with the site of complaint, which is how hip disease presents as knee pain.

Anatomy has a second use that is easy to overlook, because it tells the clinician where to look during the examination. If the working list includes the gallbladder, the pleura and the rib cage, then the hands and the stethoscope have a route to follow, and the findings will either narrow the list or reopen its breadth. Anatomy alone, however, is a map rather than an explanation, and it traps the clinician who stops at the organ without asking what is happening inside it. A diseased structure creates a differential, but the diseases of that structure form a separate list. The anatomical frame answers where, and it must be followed at once by a frame that answers how.

The second framework asks which mechanism could produce this finding, and its categories cover almost anything a patient can bring. Obstruction narrows or blocks a tube, whether it carries bile, urine, blood, air or intestinal contents, and it announces itself through pain, distension and the signs of what has backed up. Inflammation damages tissue and recruits the body's defenses, producing pain, heat, swelling and loss of function. Infection is the invasion and multiplication of an organism, local or systemic. Ischemia starves tissue of blood and punishes delay cruelly. Bleeding removes blood from the vessels, sometimes visibly and sometimes into a cavity where nothing is seen. Metabolic disturbance corrupts the chemistry every organ depends on, and malignancy grows without regard for the controls that restrain a cell.

Running these mechanisms against the anatomical list produces a grid far richer than either framework alone, and that grid is what the experienced clinician consults. A tender swelling in the leg may be infection of the skin, a clot in a deep vein, bleeding into the muscle or a tumor, and each demands a different urgency and examination. The mechanism frame also rescues possibilities that are easy to forget because they are not local: a metabolic disturbance may present as confusion, and a malignant process as weight loss long before it produces a lump. When a presentation resists explanation, the fault is often that only one mechanism has been run.

To make that walk through the mechanisms memorable, many teachers use a mnemonic that spells a word: Vindicate. It is pronounced as an ordinary English word, and each letter stands for a family of causes, so the framework can be carried in the head and recited at the bedside. The first letter stands for vascular causes, the diseases of the blood vessels and of the flow within them. The next stands for infectious causes, from the trivial and local to the overwhelming and systemic. The next stands for neoplastic causes, both benign and malignant, and the next for degenerative causes, the slow wearing down of tissue in later life. The remaining letters stand for iatrogenic and intoxicated causes, congenital causes, autoimmune causes, traumatic causes and endocrine causes.

The strength of Vindicate is that it is exhaustive in a way that unaided memory is not. Run honestly, it surfaces the congenital anomaly present since birth, the drug reaction the patient does not think of as a medicine, the endocrine disease that explains a cluster of complaints, and the vascular event that the clinician, absorbed by the inflammation in front of him, has never considered. It is especially valuable when the presentation is vague or the obvious explanation does not fit, because it forces attention onto categories that habit skips. It also guards against the trap of the single organ, since one presentation may begin in another system. Used as a checklist for the written list, it gives the record a completeness a casual note never has.

Vindicate has a serious weakness, the weakness of every generative framework: it treats all its categories as equally available, when they are not equally likely. An honest run through the letters places a rare congenital syndrome and a common infection side by side, and a careless clinician begins to reason as though they were equally likely. The exotic diagnosis is also more memorable and more interesting than the ordinary one, and interest is a quiet bias in its favour. A framework that widens the imagination must therefore be paired with a discipline that narrows it, or the differential becomes a museum of possibilities rather than a tool. Vindicate tells the clinician what to consider, never how likely anything is.

Between the broad list and the probable list sits the can't-miss list, and it is the most important list in the exercise. These are the diagnoses that must be excluded before any other explanation is accepted, because they kill or disable quickly and the opportunity to prevent that harm is brief. The list is drawn up before the patient is examined, from the complaint itself, and kept at the front of the mind throughout. A patient with severe headache has a can't-miss list including bleeding around the brain, infection of the meninges and a rise in pressure inside the skull, and the findings that would reveal each are sought deliberately. A patient with chest pain has one including a heart attack, a torn aorta and a clot in the lung, and the early examination and tests separate those from the far commoner chest wall strain.

The habit of asking, for every patient, what would kill this person soonest is what separates safe practice from merely clever practice. It is not pessimism; it is a triage of reasoning, a decision about which hypothesis earns the first minutes of attention. The dangerous diagnosis is not always the likely one, and the point of the can't-miss list is that risk does not wait for probability to be established. Until the serious possibility is excluded, the comfortable explanation remains a hypothesis rather than a conclusion. The finding that would reveal the danger must be named in advance, because a sign that is not sought is rarely seen.

With the broad generative list, the can't-miss list and the list of what is common in hand, the clinician ranks. Ranking is done by likelihood and by danger at the same time, and those orderings disagree so often that the disagreement becomes information. Likelihood orders possibilities by how frequently they occur in patients like this one, while danger orders them by how much is lost if they are missed. The most probable diagnosis is usually benign and the most dangerous usually uncommon, so the two orderings routinely put different names first. A clinician ranking only by likelihood will miss the catastrophe, and one ranking only by danger will investigate everyone exhaustively and harm them. The skill is to act on the dangerous ranking first while keeping the likely one in view.

Likelihood is not a property of a disease in the abstract; it is a property of a disease in a particular patient in a particular place. Prevalence sets the odds before any finding is known, and the setting determines which prevalences apply. Chest pain that is usually muscular in a young person in a clinic may be usually cardiac in an older person arriving by ambulance, and the starting point must shift. A district hospital with no laboratory, a crowded camp, an urban emergency department and a private office each present a different mix of disease, and a differential imported unchanged from one to another will mislead. This is why the first question about any remembered statistic is where it came from and whether the patient in front of you belongs to that population.

A fever in a returning traveller, in a person whose immune defenses have been destroyed, in a small child and on a surgical ward after an operation are different problems, even when the measured temperature is identical. The clinician who knows the local prevalence carries a useful prior, while one who does not is guided by the most dramatic recent case, a poor substitute. Where a frequency is quoted as something like 1 in 4 in one place, that proportion is a reminder of how much the setting matters and not a number to carry unchanged elsewhere, since every such figure must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, where the numbers differ between countries, editions and the populations served. When prevalence is genuinely unknown, the honest approach is to widen the list, weight the dangerous possibilities more heavily, and use the examination to create information rather than confirm a guess.

After prevalence, the characteristics of the individual patient do the next work of ordering. Age moves whole families of diagnosis up and down: the same joint pain suggests injury or inflammatory disease in a young person and degeneration in an older one, and the same breathlessness suggests asthma in a child and heart failure in an older adult. Sex changes the prior in ways that are sometimes biological and sometimes social, and a stereotype must not stand in for a question. Background includes where the patient has lived and traveled, which infections are common there, and which diseases run in the family. Exposures include work, animals, food, water, sexual history, injected drugs, alcohol, tobacco and every medicine taken, including those bought without a prescription and those borrowed from another person.

Exposures most often convert a vague list into a short one, and they deserve to be asked about directly rather than hoped for. A cough in a person who keeps birds, a rash in a person who has walked through long grass, a fever in a person who has recently received blood, and a weakness in a person who preserves food at home all point in particular directions. None of these details is a diagnosis, and each must be weighed against the whole picture, but each raises the odds of a specific possibility enough to reorder the list. The patient's own beliefs and fears sometimes reveal an exposure the clinician would not have thought to ask about. Listening for the detail that does not fit the expected story is one of the most efficient diagnostic acts available.

A differential diagnosis is not finished on the first day; it is a living picture repainted as the illness evolves. Time is a diagnostic instrument in its own right, because the trajectory of a symptom carries information no measurement can. A pain that was constant and severe and is now settling, a fever that has traced a particular rhythm across 3 days, a weakness that ascends rather than stays still, and a confusion that fluctuates rather than deepens all tell different stories. That interval of 3 days is only an illustration of how a pattern is read, and the interval that truly matters must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such durations differ between countries, editions and wards. The clinician who writes the first list and stops looking has abandoned the most powerful tool available, the patient's own future. The findings that were absent at the beginning must be sought again at every contact, because their appearance changes everything.

A differential is closed in one of a small number of ways, and the clinician should be able to say which has been used. Exclusion means a diagnosis has been made unlikely enough by evidence to be set aside, and it is the most common way a list shrinks. Confirmation means the evidence is strong enough to name the disease, and it is the way a differential finally disappears. Watching means deliberately keeping the list open and letting time reveal which branch the illness follows, which is legitimate when the patient is stable and the dangerous possibilities have been addressed. Accepting a working diagnosis means treating the most probable explanation as the basis for action while remaining ready to revise it, and it is honest only when recorded rather than assumed.

Exclusion is harder than it sounds, because excluding a diagnosis requires more than failing to find it. The absence of a finding is informative only when the clinician knows how often that finding is absent in the disease being excluded, and only when the examination or test could have detected it. A normal examination in a patient who was not examined properly excludes nothing. Confirmation carries the opposite danger: a positive finding may belong to a different disease, or to no disease, and a clinician who stops at the first confirmation may never notice a second process running alongside the first. Both movements require the same question: what would the evidence look like if the hypothesis were false?

Watching deserves more respect than it receives, because many illnesses declare themselves only with time, and a premature label is more dangerous than a deliberate wait. A wait is not the absence of a plan; it is a plan with defined observations, a defined interval, findings that would change the decision, and a route back to care. A plan that promises review after 24 hours but names no finding to look for is not watching, and the interval chosen must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than copied from habit, because safe observation periods differ between conditions, countries and clinics. The patient must be part of that plan, because the clinician cannot watch from a distance. If the waiting patient does not know what to look for and whom to contact, the differential has not been closed but only postponed. Safe watching is written down and explained, and it names the finding that would end the wait immediately.

Accepting a working diagnosis is the everyday end of the process, and it is not a confession of uncertainty but a statement about what is probable enough to act on. The working diagnosis carries the treatment decision, the follow-up plan and the safety net, and it must be revised when the patient does not follow the expected course. The clinician who treats a probable diagnosis after actively considering the dangerous alternatives is practising well. The clinician who treats the first label that came to mind, without ever having written the list, is practising on hope. The difference is invisible in the prescription and visible in the reasoning that preceded it.

Consider a constructed illustration, invented to show the method and describing no real patient. A middle-aged person arrives with upper abdominal pain that began suddenly and has been constant for several hours, with vomiting but no diarrhea. The clinician generates broadly first: the stomach, duodenum, pancreas, gallbladder, liver, colon, aorta and heart all appear on the sheet, together with the possibility that the pain is muscular, referred or metabolic. The can't-miss list is drawn before the examination: a perforated ulcer, pancreatitis, a ruptured aortic aneurysm, a heart attack presenting as abdominal pain, and, if the patient could be pregnant, a pregnancy outside the uterus. The anatomy then directs the hands and the mechanism frame directs the questions, asking whether obstruction, inflammation, ischemia or bleeding is at work. The list is ranked, the patient is examined, and the ranking changes as the findings arrive.

A well-built differential also protects the patient from unnecessary investigation, because a test is worth doing only when its result would move the list. If two possibilities would be managed identically, the test that separates them changes nothing and exposes the patient to cost, discomfort and incidental findings. The list tells the clinician which question is actually open, and it is that open question the next test should answer. When the list is vague, tests multiply; when the list is sharp, tests become few and decisive. This is the practical reason to spend time on the differential before ordering anything, and the reason a good list saves money and harm.

At the moment of first contact, the differential is often little more than a set of dangerous possibilities and a direction of travel. The clinician may not yet have a diagnosis, but the list already tells him what to ask next, what to examine and what to observe. That early list is provisional and should be spoken as provisional, because a diagnosis announced too early is hard to take back and hard to unhear. As the history unfolds, items move up and down, and the clinician should be able to say aloud which item has moved and why. The list is the visible form of the clinician's thinking, and keeping it visible is what makes the thinking correctable.

Every framework in this book is a memory aid and not a diagnostic instrument, and that distinction matters more than it may appear. A framework cannot examine the patient, weigh a finding, know the local prevalence, or notice that this patient is unlike those in whom the rule was derived. Vindicate will produce a category for almost any complaint, but a category is not a probability and a filled-in mnemonic is not a diagnosis. Frameworks also encode the assumptions of those who built them, including the populations studied and the diseases expected, and those assumptions travel badly. The clinician who uses the structure to remember and then returns to the patient to think is safe, while the one who mistakes the structure for the answer is not.

There is a further limit that is easy to state and hard to practice: the differential belongs to the patient and not to the symptom. Two patients with the same complaint may need entirely different lists, because their age, setting, history and physiology differ, and a list copied from a textbook is a starting point rather than a conclusion. The clinician must ask whether the population behind a framework resembles the person in front of him, and must be willing to set the framework aside when the patient does not fit. Rules derived in one setting have repeatedly misled clinicians in another, and the honest response is to hold them loosely rather than discard them. Certainty that arrives too early is the commonest reason a diagnosis turns out to be wrong.

The most seductive error in this process is the diagnosis that explains everything too neatly. A pattern that fits perfectly feels like a solution, and the clinician relaxes, stops generating, and stops looking for the finding that would contradict it. Yet completeness of fit is not evidence of truth, and several diseases can produce the same pattern, so the comfortable explanation may be the one the clinician knows best. The differential is the antidote, because it keeps competing explanations alive until the evidence has separated them. A clinician who can still name the alternatives after reaching a diagnosis is far safer than one who cannot.

A differential that exists only in the clinician's head cannot be checked, taught or handed over, and much of its value comes from being spoken or written in a form someone else can examine. Saying the list aloud forces the clinician to hear which possibilities have been considered and which have been quietly ignored. A colleague who looks at the same patient can attack the reasoning rather than repeat it, and the diagnosis improves. The list should also record what would change it, so the next clinician inherits not a verdict but a working question. This matters most at handover, when the reasoning is often compressed into a single label and everything supporting it lost.

Teaching the differential is largely a matter of teaching the discipline of holding several ideas at once without committing to one. The learner should generate before evaluating, name the dangerous possibilities before the comfortable ones, and say what evidence would move each item up or down the list. A teacher who asks what else it could be, then what would prove that it is not, builds a habit that survives long after the facts are forgotten. A differential debated at the bedside, with permission, also teaches the patient that uncertainty is normal and that the reasoning is being taken seriously.

The frameworks in this book were not designed for well-equipped hospitals, and they work best where resources are fewest, because they replace tests with thought. Where there is no laboratory and no imaging, the differential must be built from the history, the examination and the passage of time, and every dangerous possibility must be identified by a sign the clinician can elicit. In that setting the can't-miss list becomes the central document, and the decision to refer or to treat rests on the findings available rather than the ideal. A framework that requires a scanner to be useful is not useful in a district clinic, and its categories must be translated into questions and hands. The discipline of the differential is portable in a way no piece of equipment can be.

Uncertainty is not a failure of the method; it is the medium in which the method works. A clinician who feels no uncertainty is usually not thinking about the alternatives, and one paralysed by it is not acting on the evidence available. The differential holds those two failures apart, because it acknowledges that the answer is not yet known while organising the next step anyway. Over time, the clinician learns which lists recur, which items are almost always benign, and which quiet possibility deserves a second look even when everything fits. That accumulated judgement is what a framework can guide but never replace.

When the vital signs are abnormal, they reorder the list before any diagnosis is named. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius, a pulse of 110 beats per minute and a systolic pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury each push infection, bleeding and circulatory failure toward the top, whatever the patient came in complaining of. Each of those thresholds is a teaching illustration rather than a universal rule, and every one of them must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, laboratories and wards. The pattern, not the number, is what travels: an abnormal vital sign is a claim on the clinician's attention that outranks the original complaint, and it should send the clinician back to the list rather than to a conclusion.

To summarize, the differential diagnosis is the ordered set of explanations that turns a complaint into a plan, built by generating broadly, framing the problem anatomically and pathophysiologically, running the Vindicate categories as a memory aid, and narrowing against a can't-miss list drawn up before the patient was examined. It is ranked by likelihood and danger at once, adjusted for prevalence, setting, age, sex, background and exposure, and repainted as findings unfold. It is closed by exclusion, by confirmation, by deliberate watching, or by an honestly recorded working diagnosis. None of this replaces seeing the patient, and no framework or remembered statistic can stand in for the examination and judgement of the clinician present. Every number here is an illustration rather than a universal rule, and any threshold must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, laboratories and wards. Educational material of this kind supports training and supervision rather than replacing them, and it is never a reason to delay care for a patient who is deteriorating.

# Chapter 4 — Using Tests Wisely

A test earns its place in the clinical encounter by changing a probability, and a changed probability has value only when it changes a decision. The commonest error is to order a test in order to confirm what the history and the examination have already made certain, which adds cost and delay without adding information. The second commonest error is to order a test without first asking what result would alter the plan, so that an unexpected answer arrives with no prepared response. Before anything is requested, the useful question is what finding would make me do something different, and if no finding would, the test should not be ordered.
