This is the reasoning that organizes the whole of this discussion, because every property of a test and every harm of testing follows from it.

The first property to understand is sensitivity, which describes the behavior of a test in people who truly have the disease. A test with high sensitivity is positive in most of the people who are ill, so it is good at finding disease and a negative result from it is reassuring. A hypothetical test might be positive in 90 per cent of people with a particular infection, and that figure is an illustration that you must check against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the real value shifts with the population, the technique and the edition of the reference you happen to be holding. Sensitivity is therefore the property that a clinician values when the danger of missing the diagnosis is high, because a sensitive test rarely lets a case slip past. It says nothing yet about the people who do not have the disease, and that is where the second property begins.

Specificity describes the behavior of the test in people who do not have the disease, and it is the property that governs how often a positive result is a mistake. A highly specific test is negative in almost everyone who is well, so a positive result from it is strong evidence that the disease is really there. If the same hypothetical test were negative in 95 per cent of healthy people, the figure is again only an illustration, and it must be confirmed against the current guidance and the practice of your own laboratory and ward before you treat it as a fact about your patient. Specificity protects the patient from the consequences of a wrong positive result, from unnecessary anxiety to unnecessary procedures. A test can be sensitive and not specific, specific and not sensitive, or good at both.

Sensitivity and specificity are usually stable properties of the test itself, at least in principle, while the predictive values belong to the patient in front of you. The positive predictive value asks what proportion of people who test positive actually have the disease, and the negative predictive value asks the same question of those who test negative. These two values depend heavily on how common the disease is in the group being tested, which is why the same test result can mean very different things in different settings. Prevalence is the word for that underlying frequency, and it is the quiet variable that most often decides whether a positive result is a genuine finding or a statistical accident.

Consider a constructed illustration of a test with a sensitivity of 90 per cent and a specificity of 95 per cent, values whose true form must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because they differ between settings and editions. Suppose the test is applied in a community where the disease affects 1 in 1000 people, an illustrative proportion that must likewise be checked against the current guidance and local practice. Among a thousand people there will be about one person with the disease, and the test will probably find that person. Yet the small proportion of healthy people who test positive, when multiplied by the large number who are healthy, produces a surprising crowd of false positive results. The positive predictive value in that setting is therefore low, and most of the people the test flags will turn out not to have the disease. This is the arithmetic that explains why screening a whole population for a rare condition produces so much anxiety and so many follow-up tests.

Now move the same test into a clinic where the patients have been selected by their symptoms and the disease affects 1 in 5 of them, a proportion that is an illustration only and that must be checked against your own setting and the current guidance. The sensitivity and the specificity have not changed, because they are properties of the test and not of the room, but the predictive values are transformed. A positive result now means that the disease is genuinely present in a large majority of those who receive it, and the test becomes a useful instrument rather than a source of noise. Nothing about the chemistry or the physics of the test has altered; only the prior probability has. This single contrast is worth more than any number of measurements, because it shows that a test cannot be judged apart from the patient and the population in which it is used.

Likelihood ratios are the bridge between the properties of the test and the probability in the patient, because they tell you how much a given result multiplies the odds of disease. A likelihood ratio close to one, a value whose exact form you should confirm in the current guideline and local protocol, leaves the odds almost where they were, so the test has told you very little and its result should not move you. A ratio of perhaps 2 to 5 raises the odds usefully without settling the question, and these illustrative values must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol if you intend to use them in arithmetic rather than as a way of thinking. A large ratio, in the region of 10 or more, can take a modest suspicion and turn it into a strong one, which is what clinicians mean when they say that a test result was decisive, though the exact figure belongs to the current guideline and your local protocol and should be confirmed there. Ratios below one work in the opposite direction, reducing the odds and supporting the exclusion of disease. The practical point is that ratios can be carried in the head and applied to the patient in front of you, whereas sensitivity and specificity alone cannot.

Every diagnostic decision has two thresholds rather than one, and they are not the same line. The first is the point at which the probability of disease has risen enough that testing becomes worthwhile, because a positive result would change management and a negative result would be meaningful. The second is the point at which the probability has risen so far that treating without waiting for a result becomes the right thing to do, because the harm of delay now exceeds the harm of treating someone who turns out not to need it. Between those two lines lies the zone of genuine uncertainty, where a test is most valuable and where its result, whatever it says, will guide the next step. Below the first line you should not test, and above the second you should act, with the test left to confirm what you have already decided.

The position of those lines depends on the disease and on the consequences of being wrong, which is why a dangerous and a trivial condition cannot share a rule. For a disease that kills quickly if it is missed, such as bacterial meningitis or a leaking aortic aneurysm, the threshold for treatment is low and the clinician may act on suspicion alone. For a self-limiting illness that will resolve whatever is done, the same probability is not worth a test or a treatment, because the harm of the intervention is now the greater risk. The same test result therefore leads to different actions in the two situations, which is a point that scores and algorithms cannot decide for you. This is also why a rule derived in one population, such as a busy emergency department, may behave badly in another, such as a quiet outpatient clinic, because the mix of disease and the cost of error are not the same.

Testing is never free of harm, and the harm is easiest to see when a test is applied to people who are unlikely to have the disease. A false positive result sends the patient down a path of repeat tests, imaging, procedures, and referral, each with its own risk and its own waiting. It also produces anxiety that does not disappear when the follow-up result is normal, because the person has now been told that something was found. In a low-prevalence population the false positives can outnumber the true positives by a wide margin, as the earlier arithmetic suggested, so the test's main output may be worry rather than diagnosis. The discipline is to ask, before ordering, whether the chance of a false positive and its consequences are acceptable for this particular person.

Beyond the false positive lies the incidental finding, the unexpected shadow on an image or the borderline value on a laboratory report that was never going to harm anyone. Such findings are common precisely because modern tests look at more than the question being asked, and each one creates a new decision that did not exist before. The cascade that follows is familiar: a small abnormality is pursued with a larger test, which finds something else, which requires a procedure, and the patient ends by carrying a diagnosis and a risk that the original complaint never justified. Overdiagnosis is the name for the detection of disease that would never have declared itself in the patient's lifetime, and it is a harm of testing rather than a benefit of early detection. This is why an unexpected result should prompt the question of whether it explains anything the patient actually has, rather than an immediate escalation.

Each unexpected result also consumes something scarce, whether it is the patient's time, the clinician's attention, or the budget of a clinic that has only a few tests to spend. In a setting with limited resources the harm is sharper still, because a test performed on a patient who cannot act on the result may take the place of a test that someone else genuinely needed. A negative result can also mislead when the prior probability was high, since a sensitive test is not a perfect one and a low-prevalence interpretation of a high-prevalence patient is a common source of error. The honest position is that tests reduce uncertainty without removing it, and a result must always be read together with the history and the examination that preceded it. When a result contradicts a strong clinical impression, the first response is to question the result rather than the patient.

Spectrum bias is the reason a test so often performs better in the textbook description than in the clinic. The people in whom a test is first studied tend to be the obvious cases and the clearly healthy controls, so the test is measured where the difference between them is largest. In real practice the same test meets mild, early, atypical, and overlapping illness, together with people who have several conditions at once, and in that mixed company its sensitivity and specificity fall. The published figures, whatever they are, come from a particular population, and their transfer to your patient requires the assumption that your patient resembles that population, an assumption that is often false. This is one reason to be cautious with any figure quoted without its setting.

The reference standard problem is deeper, because measuring the sensitivity and specificity of a test requires a way of knowing who truly has the disease, and that way is usually imperfect. If the reference standard is itself a test with its own errors, then some people are misclassified, and the new test is credited or blamed for mistakes that belong to the standard. In some conditions there is no acceptable standard at all, and the best available answer is a consensus of experts, which is an opinion rather than a measurement. A test validated against a flawed standard inherits the flaw, and the number that emerges should be held loosely. When you read a study of a test, ask what the standard was and how it was applied, because that question decides how much the result is worth.

Test characteristics are also not fixed, because a test is a procedure performed by people in places, and both of those vary. A chest radiograph read by an experienced radiologist is not the same test as the same film read at the end of a night shift by someone who rarely sees one. An ultrasound examination depends on the hand holding the probe, on the machine, on the time taken, and on the question asked, so its accuracy belongs partly to the operator rather than to the instrument. A laboratory assay depends on the sample, the transport, the reagent, and the calibration. A test that is excellent in one hospital can be mediocre in another without anyone changing the instructions. This is why the local protocol matters as much as the textbook, and why an imported accuracy figure should be treated as a hope rather than a promise.

Serial testing means performing tests one after another, and it is used to increase specificity, because a second positive result is harder to obtain by chance than a first. The arithmetic of repetition is easy to underestimate, since a test with a modest chance of a false positive at a single pass gives a low-prevalence patient an accumulating chance of a false positive with each additional test. Parallel testing means ordering several tests at once and accepting a positive result from any of them, which increases sensitivity at the price of more false positives. A repeated test that yields the same result may confirm it, but a repeated test that disagrees with the first is a signal that the test, the timing, or the patient's condition has changed. The rule to carry away is that each additional test must be justified by the decision it could change, not by the discomfort of uncertainty.

There are times when the correct decision is not to test at all, and the first of these is the situation where no result would change what is done. If the patient is already going to be admitted, treated, or referred on the basis of the clinical findings, then a confirmatory test may add cost and delay while altering nothing. If the test is being ordered for reassurance alone, it should be clear whose reassurance is being sought and whether the test can honestly provide it. The question that prevents most unnecessary testing is the same question as before: what would I do differently if this result came back positive, and what would I do differently if it came back negative.

The second situation in which testing is the wrong move is the patient who is too unwell to wait for the answer. A person in shock, with a threatened airway, or with a rapidly spreading infection may need the decision now, and the time spent obtaining a result is time spent not treating. This is not a rejection of tests but a recognition of their place in the order of events, because the unstable patient is stabilized first and the test follows when it can no longer harm. The threshold for treating without waiting falls as the danger of the untreated condition rises, which is the same reasoning that set the two thresholds earlier. If the treatment is safe and the disease is lethal, the balance tips toward acting.

The discipline that ties all of this together is the habit of stating the probability before the test and the decision that each result would trigger. A pre-test probability held in words, even loosely, turns a test from a ritual into an experiment with an expected answer. If the probability is already very low, a positive result is more likely to be an error or a coincidental finding than a diagnosis, and the test should not be ordered without a plan for that outcome. If the probability is already very high, a negative result should not overturn the clinical impression without a serious second look. The clinician who writes down the question and the possible answers before ordering has already avoided most of the harm described here.

Tests also have to be explained, because a result that the patient cannot interpret is only half a result. A word such as positive and negative sounds absolute, while the reality behind it is a probability that has moved, and the gap between those two is where fear grows. Telling the patient what the test can and cannot show, and what the next step will be if the result is unexpected, is part of using the test wisely rather than an extra courtesy. The clinician should also be honest that some results will require further tests, and that this does not necessarily mean that something serious has been found. Uncertainty managed in conversation is lighter than uncertainty discovered later.

In a clinic without a laboratory, the discipline of testing still applies, because watching the patient over time is itself a form of testing. The change in a fever, the response of a pulse, the appearance of a new sign, and the evolution of pain all carry information, and they are the observations available when no result can be obtained. What matters is that the observation is planned and interpreted in the same way a laboratory result would be, rather than treated as a vague impression. Serial examination, in this sense, is a test with a sensitivity and a specificity of its own, and it is subject to the same biases and the same limits. A clinician who has no tests is not without evidence, only without machinery.

A normal result deserves as much suspicion as an abnormal one, because a false negative can be more dangerous than a false positive. The test may have been performed too early, when the organism or the marker was not yet present, or too late, when it had already gone. It may have been taken from the wrong site, transported badly, or interpreted against the wrong reference range. A reassuring result in a patient who looks unwell should therefore be treated as a discrepancy to be explained rather than a question that has been answered. The safest response is to repeat the reasoning that led to the test, not merely the test itself.

Scores and decision rules are useful because they force the clinician to collect the same information every time and to compare it with a defined threshold. They are also dangerous when they are used as substitutes for judgment, because a score is a summary of probabilities in a population and not a verdict about a person. A rule derived in one age group, one setting, or one severity of illness may lose much of its value when applied elsewhere. The score's own numbers change with the population and with the edition of the guideline, so any figure attached to it must be verified against the current source and the local protocol before it is used to make a decision. The proper use of a rule is to sharpen a probability that the clinician has already estimated, not to replace that estimate.

Every test also has a cost that is measured in more than money, because access to testing is uneven and a diagnosis that depends on it can become a diagnosis available only to some. When a test is unavailable, the clinician must reason with the history and the examination, and that reasoning is not inferior merely because it lacks a number. When a test is available, the clinician must resist the temptation to use it because it can be used. The equity question is not separate from the diagnostic question, since a test ordered without a plan can take a place that another patient needed. Using tests wisely means using them where they change outcomes, and not using them where they only move uncertainty around.

A final constructed illustration may help to hold the pieces together, and it is invented for that purpose rather than drawn from any patient. Imagine a middle-aged person who has had a fever for 3 days, a cough, and a fast pulse of 110 beats per minute, and note that both of those figures are illustrative and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such values differ between countries, laboratories, and wards. The clinician's pre-test probability of a chest infection is moderate, neither negligible nor certain, and a chest radiograph would move it in one direction or the other. If the result were positive, the decision to treat would follow, but if it were negative the clinician would still have to decide whether the clinical picture justified treatment, because the test cannot exclude every possibility. The right order is to decide the question first, then the test, then the response to each possible answer, rather than to order the test and wait to see what it says.

Any test is an intervention, and like any intervention it must clear a bar of expected benefit over expected harm. The benefit is the change in management that follows from a more accurate probability, multiplied by the value of that change to the patient. The harm includes the discomfort of the procedure, the anxiety of the wait, the complications of the follow-up, and the possibility that the pursuit of one answer will reveal something that was better left alone. A test that is justified in a research protocol may be unjustified in a clinic, and a test that is unjustified in a screening program may be exactly right in a symptomatic patient. The judgment belongs to the clinician who knows what will be done with the result.

All of this rests on a pre-test probability that someone has to estimate, and that estimate is itself a clinical skill. It begins with the history and the examination, then adjusts for the setting, the age of the patient, and the local pattern of disease. A clinician who has not thought about the prior probability will read every result as though it were equally meaningful in every patient, which is the error that makes a screening test seem useless in one room and excellent in another. The estimate does not have to be precise, only explicit enough to be revised. Writing it down, even as a sentence, exposes the assumptions that a number would otherwise hide.

Not every test is a diagnostic test, and the properties that make a test good at one job can make it unsuitable for another. A test used to diagnose must separate people who have the disease from those who do not, which is where sensitivity and specificity matter most. A test used to monitor a known condition must instead detect change over time in the same person, so its precision and its within-patient variability matter more than its ability to classify a stranger. A test used to screen a population must be safe, cheap, acceptable, and followed by a confirmatory path, because most positive results in that setting will be false. Using a monitoring test as a diagnostic test, or a diagnostic test as a screening test, is a category error that no amount of technical accuracy can repair.

It is often useful to ask how many tests must be performed to find one case that matters, because that question exposes both the yield and the cost. When the disease is rare and the test is imperfect, the number can be large, and the clinic spends most of its effort on people who do not have the condition. When the disease is common and the test is good, the number falls and the effort is repaid. This is not an argument against testing the rare disease in a patient who has the signs of it, because the relevant probability then belongs to that patient and not to the population. It is an argument against testing everyone for everything, which is a different activity with a different arithmetic. The decision to screen a population deserves a higher standard of evidence than the decision to investigate a symptomatic person, because the first exposes many healthy people to the harms of testing while the second exposes only the person who came for help.

To summarize, a test is a tool for changing a probability and therefore a decision, and it should never be ordered to confirm what is already known or to fill a silence. Its sensitivity and specificity describe what it does in people with and without the disease, while its predictive values depend on how common the disease is in the patient in front of you. Likelihood ratios carry that information into practice, the two thresholds tell you when to test and when to act, and the harms of false positives, incidental findings, overdiagnosis, and cascades are real harms that fall on real people. Every number used in this discussion is an illustration, and each must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol before it is used, because the values differ between countries, editions, laboratories, and wards. Ask before you order what finding would make you do something different, and if no finding would, do not order the test. And remember that this is educational reasoning and not medical advice, so no test, score, or rule can replace the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient, and none of it should be applied without supervision, the local protocol, and the current guidance in hand.

# Chapter 5 — Diagnosis with Limited Resources

Diagnosis in a setting with few resources begins from a different premise, and the premise is not that the medicine is worse. The clinician who holds a torch, a thermometer and a stethoscope is not practising a degraded version of hospital medicine; that clinician is practising a different discipline, with its own instruments, its own tempo and its own particular strengths. The setting changes what can be learned, so it changes what should be looked for, and it changes the order in which the questions are asked. Where a laboratory can be summoned within the hour, the reasoning may lean on the result; where no laboratory exists, the reasoning must lean on the patient, on the examination repeated over time, and on the clinician's willingness to name uncertainty aloud. This is the first thing to understand about limited resources: they remove tests, but they do not remove evidence. The evidence simply moves back to the bedside, into the history and into the hands and eyes of the person who is present. A clinic with no imaging can still reach a correct diagnosis, and can often reach it more safely than a hurried unit that orders everything and examines nothing.

The reason the setting changes the diagnosis rather than only the treatment is that the available evidence changes, and with it the cost of being wrong. In a referral hospital, a missed diagnosis may be caught by the next scan or the next blood count, while in a district clinic the same missed diagnosis may declare itself only when the patient returns too late, or does not return at all. That asymmetry should make the clinician more cautious, not less, and it should make certain lethal possibilities the first things to exclude. The febrile child who cannot be roused or whose neck is stiff may have bacterial meningitis, and the finding that reveals it is the examination of alertness and of the neck. The woman who bleeds heavily after childbirth may be losing her circulating volume, and the finding is a uterus that stays soft and a pulse above 110 beats per minute, a rate whose exact cut-off must be confirmed in the current guideline and the local protocol because it differs between countries, editions and wards. The older patient with chest pain that radiates to the jaw and arrives with sweat and breathlessness may be having a myocardial infarction, and the finding is the pattern of the pain together with a systolic blood pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury and a tracing on the electrocardiogram, both of which must be read against the values the guidance in force defines for your machine and your ward. Each of these possibilities must be named at the bedside and named early, because in a setting without rescue technology the diagnosis is the rescue, and a number carried in the head is no substitute for the guideline on the shelf.

The history is the highest-yield instrument available anywhere, and in a clinic without a laboratory it is the instrument that carries the diagnosis. A question asked well costs nothing, harms no one, and can separate a self-limiting illness from a lethal one before the patient has taken off a coat. The duration of the fever, the order in which the symptoms arrived, the travel, the contact with a person who coughed for weeks, the pregnancy, the medicine already taken, and the family's own account of how this illness differs from previous ones, all of these are data that no machine supplies. A fever that has lasted more than 7 days, a cut-off that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because it moves with the disease and the place, changes the list of possibilities at once. The clinician who learns to listen in this setting is not settling for a lesser method; that clinician is using the method with the highest diagnostic yield that medicine has ever had. The discipline lies in asking a complete set of questions in the same order each time, so that nothing is skipped because the room is busy, and in noticing which answer does not fit the story. A history is not a formality that precedes the examination; it is the first and often the decisive test.

Examination follows the history and, where no test exists, it must be performed with more care than it would receive in a teaching hospital, not less. Certain signs are worth more than any result a clinic could obtain, because they change the diagnosis on their own. A respiratory rate above 30 breaths per minute in an adult, a value that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because age and setting move it, is one such sign. So is a capillary refill that stays slow, a chest that moves less on one side, a liver edge felt below the costal margin, a pupil that does not react, a calf that is tender and swollen, or a rash that does not fade when pressed. Each of these is a finding that a laboratory cannot produce and that no queue can replace, and each carries its meaning only when the reasoning behind it is understood. The clinician should therefore say out loud what is being looked for and what its presence would mean, because a sign sought with a question in mind is seen, while a sign passed over in a hurry is missed.

When the laboratory is missing, the examination can be repeated, and repetition is a diagnostic instrument in its own right. Time is the reagent that no clinic runs out of, and a finding that changes over 6 hours carries information that a single measurement never could, with the interval itself confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than assumed. A child who was alert at the first visit and is drowsy at the second has declared a direction of travel, and that direction may matter more than any single number the clinic could have measured. The clinician should therefore build return into the plan deliberately, deciding at the first encounter what the next observation should show if the working diagnosis is right and what it should show if it is wrong. A diagnosis that declares itself over a day or two is often the safer route, because it allows the clinician to watch the disease behave rather than to freeze a single instant and guess. Patience here is not passivity; it is a scheduled sequence of examinations with a purpose attached to each one. The question to carry between visits is simple: is the patient moving toward recovery or away from it, and does the speed of that movement fit the illness I have named?

Clinical scoring rules and syndromic management guidelines were built for exactly this kind of setting, and they are allies as long as the clinician knows what they assume. A score takes several findings that a person without a laboratory can obtain, assigns each a weight, and returns a summary that points toward a decision. Syndromic guidance does something similar for a symptom, grouping the possible causes under a named syndrome and directing the clinician along a path that covers the dangerous ones together. Both were derived from a particular population, studied at a particular time, and validated against outcomes that the authors chose, and those details travel with the rule wherever it goes. A sign that was studied where a disease is present in 1 in 10 patients carries a different meaning from the same sign studied where the disease is present in 1 in 100, and both figures must be confirmed against the epidemiology of your own district and the current guideline, because prevalence is the quiet assumption inside every rule. A rule derived where one disease is common will perform differently where a different disease dominates, and a rule that assumes a certain prevalence can mislead precisely where prevalence differs most.

Consider how the Glasgow coma scale behaves in this setting, since it appears in almost every guideline for the unwell patient. The scale formalizes three observations that any trained clinician can make without equipment: the opening of the eyes, the content of speech, and the response of the limbs to a command or a painful stimulus. Its total is often used as a threshold for referral or for a decision about the airway, and that threshold differs between the guideline that trained you and the guideline that governs the hospital you are calling, so confirm the current value with the receiving team before you let it decide the journey. Integrated management of childhood illness works in the same spirit, taking a small set of signs that a nurse or clinical officer can see and touch, and sorting children into groups that receive urgent referral, specific treatment, or advice at home. The strength of such guidance is that it is designed by people who know what a rural clinic contains, and its limit is that its categories were cut to fit the diseases of the places where it was developed. Where a different disease is common, the same signs may sort a child into the wrong group, and the clinician who understands the reasoning can notice the misfit rather than follow the chart into error.

A rule travels badly when the population changes, and the clinics with the fewest resources are often the places where the population is least like the one the rule was derived from. A scoring rule for pneumonia that was built where the disease is common in older adults may sort a child poorly, and a rule for fever that assumed malaria in every case may mislead where the same fever is now caused by something else. The clinician should ask, whenever a score is applied, what the authors studied, what they excluded, and what prevalence they assumed, because those three answers decide whether the rule applies at all. The safest posture is to use the rule to make sure nothing dangerous is overlooked, and then to reason beyond it about the patient in front of you. A pattern is a guide to probability, and the patient is the only source of truth.

When a test is unavailable, the clinician sometimes has to treat on the strength of the working diagnosis, and that decision deserves a clearer name than it usually gets. A diagnostic trial is a test whose result arrives after the decision, and it should be understood honestly as such. The logic is that if the working diagnosis is right, the patient will improve in a way that confirms it, and that if the patient does not improve, the diagnosis is wrong and must be revised. That logic is sound only when the response is unambiguous, when improvement could not have happened anyway, and when the clinician has defined in advance what a response would look like and by when. The clinician should therefore write down the expectation before starting, naming the finding that would count as a response and the interval over which it should appear, and should confirm that interval against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than trusting a remembered figure. Without that discipline, a diagnostic trial becomes a story told after the fact, in which every outcome is made to fit the original guess.

There is a second and more dangerous use of treatment, and it must be distinguished from the diagnostic trial with care. A therapeutic trial given to relieve symptoms can hide the disease it was meant to reveal, and the concealment can be permanent. The pain that settles after an analgesic may be the pain of an appendix that is about to perforate, and the fever that falls after an antipyretic may belong to a bloodstream infection that is still spreading. When a clinician treats first and observes second, the observation is contaminated by the treatment, and a later improvement no longer carries the diagnostic meaning it would otherwise have. This is why the decision to treat for a symptom must be separated from the decision to treat for a diagnosis, and why the reasoning should be recorded when the two are merged for the patient's comfort. The rule to carry is that relief is not evidence, and that a patient whose symptoms are suppressed must be watched more closely, not less.

A working diagnosis is the clinician's current best explanation, written in plain words and revised when the evidence changes. Its value lies less in the label than in the reasoning around it, and that reasoning must be recorded so that the next clinician inherits it. A note that says only the name of a disease tells the next person what was thought; a note that says which findings supported it, which findings argued against it, what was excluded and why, and what would change the opinion, tells the next person how to think. In a clinic where the same patient may be seen by several different people in a week, this record is the closest thing to continuity that exists. The working diagnosis should also be named to the patient, in language the patient can hold, because a patient who understands what is suspected can report the change that matters and can cooperate with the plan. The label should be offered as a provisional explanation, never as a verdict, and the uncertainty should be spoken rather than hidden.

Safety-netting is the central skill of the under-resourced clinic, and it is a clinical act rather than a courtesy at the end of the visit. It means telling the patient, in specific and checkable terms, what to watch for, when to return, and how to return. The instruction should name the signs that would make the illness dangerous rather than listing every possible symptom: a fever that will not settle, a breathing that becomes fast or laboured, a drowsiness that deepens, a bleeding that does not stop, a pain that moves and worsens, a swelling that spreads. It should also name the time frame in which the patient should return if things are unchanged, and the time frame in which the patient should return regardless, and those intervals, whether they are measured in 3 days or in hours, must be checked against the local guidance rather than quoted from memory. The patient should be asked to repeat the plan back, because a plan understood is the only plan that works, and the clinician should check that the patient can actually make the journey. Where the road is long, the instruction has to be made real: a named person who will bring the patient, a means of transport identified, a note carried, and a reason to return that the family believes in. If a clinic sees 1 in 4 of its patients again only when the illness is advanced, the safety net has failed, and that figure should prompt a review of how the instruction is given, with any threshold drawn from it confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Making safety-netting real when the journey is long requires the clinician to think like the family rather than like the hospital. The distance, the cost, the loss of a day's work, the care of other children, the season of the roads, and the permission of a husband or an elder can each decide whether a return visit happens. A clinician who understands these constraints can design an instruction that survives them, perhaps by setting the return around a market day, by involving a community health worker, by giving the patient a written note that carries the reasoning, or by arranging a review at a clinic closer to home. The patient who cannot return must be told what to do where they are, and the limits of that advice must be stated honestly. Safety-netting is therefore a negotiation about the future, conducted at the end of a consultation that already feels finished.

Referral thresholds exist to mark the point where the clinic's resources stop being enough, and applying them well is a diagnostic skill. The decision to send a patient away is made on the balance of danger and treatability: how likely the lethal diagnosis is, how quickly it might declare itself, and whether anything the clinic can do would change the outcome while the patient travels. Certain findings should lower the threshold sharply, among them a patient who cannot be woken, a breathing that is failing at fewer than 8 breaths per minute in an adult, a suspected obstruction or perforation, a pregnancy with bleeding or convulsion, and a child who is not feeding or not drinking. That respiratory figure, like every threshold in this chapter, is an illustration whose exact value must be confirmed in the current guideline and the local protocol, since adults, children and newborns are cut differently. A referral is not a failure of the clinic; it is a diagnosis of the clinic's limits, made in time. The clinician should also send the reasoning with the patient, so that the receiving team begins where the referring team stopped.

When a single test is available, the question is not how many times it can be used but what it could change. A test earns its place only if its result would alter a decision, and a result that alters nothing is a cost with no return. The clinician should therefore ask, before the sample is taken, what action follows a positive result and what action follows a negative one, and if the answer to both is the same, the test can be set aside. If only one test exists, it should be chosen for the hypothesis whose treatment is most dangerous to get wrong, or for the hypothesis whose exclusion would most change the plan. The test should also be performed as well as the clinic allows, because a poorly taken sample produces a confident wrong answer, and a confident wrong answer is more dangerous than no answer at all. One test used with a clear question attached is worth more than several used because they happen to be there.

The specific risks of this setting deserve to be named plainly, because they are not the same risks a hospital faces. One of these is the false reassurance of an absent result, since a test that was not done, or a result that has not returned, can quietly harden into an assumption that the disease is not there. A negative result on an imperfect test is not the absence of disease, and a test that has not been performed is not evidence of any kind. The clinician should record not only what was found but what was not looked for, so that the next reader knows the difference between an excluded diagnosis and an unexamined one. This habit protects the patient twice, once from the missed disease and once from the misplaced confidence of the clinician who inherits the note.

A further risk is the borrowed authority of a piece of equipment, which can make a weak observation feel like a strong one. A machine that prints a value invites the clinician to stop reasoning, and the value may be wrong, poorly calibrated, or right for a different patient. The stethoscope, the torch and the thermometer are tools for the senses, and they must remain subordinate to the reasoning that directs them. Another risk is the pressure of the queue, which rewards speed over completeness and punishes the clinician who spends an extra minute with the patient who most needs it. Under that pressure, the temptation is to reach a diagnosis that lets the line move, and the diagnosis that lets the line move is often the benign one. The clinician must therefore defend a small amount of time for the dangerous possibilities, and must be willing to slow down precisely when the room is fastest.

None of this means that the reasoning taught in a teaching hospital becomes obsolete when the tools are taken away, because the reasoning was never the tools. The teaching hospital teaches a method: take a history, examine the patient, assemble the findings, rank the possibilities by likelihood and danger, and let the tests change the ranking. Remove the tests and the method remains, thinner in evidence but identical in shape. What the teaching hospital sometimes forgets to teach is the confidence to act on that method alone, and what the limited setting teaches is exactly that confidence, earned by watching patients recover or deteriorate in front of you. The clinician who can reason without a laboratory is not behind the clinician who has one; that clinician is simply working with a different balance of uncertainty.

Consider a constructed illustration, assembled rather than drawn from any real patient, to see how the pieces fit together. A man walks into a clinic that has a thermometer, a torch and no laboratory, and says he has had a fever for several days and a cough that will not leave. The history reveals that he has lost weight, that the cough has lasted long enough to matter, and that a neighbour was treated for tuberculosis, so the dangerous possibility is named at the first visit rather than deferred. The examination finds him thin, with a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius, a reading that must be confirmed against the reference range used by the current guideline and the local protocol before any conclusion rests on it. The clinic has no chest radiograph and no sputum laboratory, so the working diagnosis is written as suspected tuberculosis, together with the findings that support it and the plan to refer for confirmation. The patient is told what to watch for, when to return, and how the journey will be arranged, and the note carries the reasoning so the next clinician can continue it. Nothing in this illustration is a real case, and the details serve only to show the method.

Fever is the presentation where syndromic thinking earns its keep, because the same symptom can belong to malaria, typhoid, tuberculosis, a urinary infection, a bloodstream infection, or the first sign of something the clinic will never name. The syndromic path asks the clinician to look for the signs that separate the dangerous from the self-limiting: a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade, a breathless chest, a tender abdomen, a pregnancy, a very young or very old patient, and a patient who is drowsy or confused. In a patient with human immunodeficiency virus infection, the fever may belong to an opportunistic infection that no test in the clinic can identify, and the threshold for referral should fall accordingly. Where the response is not what was expected, the working diagnosis is revised rather than repeated, and the patient is either referred or brought back for another examination. The syndromic approach is not a shortcut around reasoning; it is reasoning compressed into a form that a busy clinic can actually use, and it works only when the clinician continues to think inside the category.

Treating empirically is sometimes the only defensible choice, and it should be made with the same structure as any other diagnostic decision. The clinician names the working diagnosis, states what the treatment is expected to do, sets the interval over which a response should appear, and defines what will be done if the response does not come. The interval and the expected response must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because those are exactly the details that differ between settings and editions. If the patient does not improve, the clinician treats that as a result, and returns to the differential diagnosis rather than to the same prescription. The honesty of the trial lies in naming which of these two outcomes would count as failure before the treatment begins.

The decision that a patient must travel is easier when the clinician has thought in advance about what the local clinic can and cannot finish. The clinician should ask whether the journey itself is safe, whether the patient needs company, and whether the receiving hospital has been told to expect a patient with this problem. A referral without a reason is a transfer of uncertainty rather than of care, and it burdens the receiving team with a question that could have been framed locally. The framing is part of the diagnosis: the referring clinician should state what is suspected, what has been excluded, and what is feared. Where the nearest hospital is a long way away, the threshold for sending should be lower and the preparation more careful.

To summarize, the clinic with few resources does not practice a lesser medicine; it practises a medicine whose evidence comes from the history, the examination and time, and whose safety depends on naming the dangerous possibility early and arranging what happens next. The reasoning of the teaching hospital survives the removal of its tools, because the tools were never the method. Every number, threshold, score, interval and reference range mentioned in this chapter is an illustration of that reasoning, and none of them should be acted on until it has been confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such figures differ between countries, editions, laboratories and wards. Nothing here is medical advice, and nothing here replaces training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is actually with the patient. The clinician who works this way is not guessing; the clinician is deciding with the evidence that exists, recording the decision, and making the patient a partner in the watch that follows. Let the caution travel with the patient, and let the record carry the reasoning, because in a place without tests the reasoning is the most valuable thing the clinic can hand on.

# Chapter 6 — Taking the History

The history is the most powerful instrument a clinician owns, and it is the only one that is always available, in the teaching hospital and in the clinic at the end of the road alike. Everything that follows in this book, from the first inspection to the last laboratory result, is built on the account a patient gives before anyone touches the body. The reasoning that organizes this chapter is simple. A story is a body of evidence, and like any evidence it can be collected well or badly, in an order that preserves its meaning or in an order that destroys it. Our purpose here is to learn how to let the story arrive, how to guide it without breaking it, and how to hear the one detail that decides the diagnosis. This is educational material, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the local protocol of your own service.

The encounter begins with the chief complaint, and it should begin with the patient's own words rather than with a category the clinician supplies. A patient who says that his chest feels as though a belt is tightening around it has given information that the phrase chest pain does not contain. A patient who says that her head feels as though it is being pushed apart from inside has described an onset and a quality in one image. When the clinician rewrites that sentence immediately as possible angina or possible migraine, the translation is not wrong, but it arrives too early, and it closes the door on the words that were actually spoken. The chief complaint should therefore be recorded close to the original phrasing, because the phrasing itself is data. The word the patient chooses often points to the diagnosis the clinician has not yet considered.

Some stories contain a lethal cause so plainly that the history alone identifies it, and this is why the history must be taken before the examination rather than after it. A patient who describes a headache that reached its full intensity within seconds, like a blow to the back of the head, is describing the onset of bleeding around the brain, and the finding that reveals it is that abrupt maximal onset together with vomiting, neck stiffness, or a brief loss of consciousness described in the account. A patient who describes pain that began in the back and moved to the front, tearing from the inside, may be describing a tear in the aorta, and the revealing feature is the migration of the pain and its quality rather than its location. A patient with a fever and a rapidly spreading dark rash may be describing an infection of the blood, and the history of its speed is the warning. These are not rare curiosities to be remembered for an examination; they are the reason the first minutes of the history are treated as an emergency of listening. The clinician who waits for the examination to find them may have lost the time in which they could be treated.

The history of the present illness is built by opening the story wide before narrowing it. The first question is deliberately broad, something like what happened, or tell me about it from the beginning, and then the clinician's main task is to be quiet. Open questions produce longer answers, more unexpected detail, and more of the patient's own reasoning about what is wrong. Narrow questions produce short answers, and a patient who is asked only narrow questions will confirm whatever the clinician already suspects. The order matters as much as the content: breadth first, then depth. A clinician who has heard the whole story can narrow with purpose, because he knows which corners of it deserve pressure.

Narrowing is not forbidden, only mistimed. Once the account has run its course, the clinician narrows deliberately, using closed questions to establish the facts the story left unclear: when exactly it began, what the patient was doing at that moment, whether anything similar has happened before, and what the patient did about it. Each closed question should exist because some diagnosis depends on the answer, and not because it appears on a form. The transition from open to closed is announced in the clinician's own mind rather than in the room, and the patient barely notices it. The skill lies in knowing when the account is complete, which is usually when the patient begins to repeat himself, and in resisting the urge to cut the story short because a familiar pattern has already appeared.

Chronology is the spine of the present illness, and it is worth building in the patient's own sequence before it is reorganized. What was the first thing that was not right, what came next, and what has changed since. Onset, duration, and trajectory carry more diagnostic weight than any single feature, because they separate the illness that is still rising from the one that has already peaked and the one that is smouldering. A pain that is worse every hour has a different meaning from the same pain unchanged for a week. The patient's sense of direction, whether things are getting better or worse, is a diagnostic finding in its own right. Ask for that sense explicitly, because patients often assume the clinician can see it.

The Oldcarts framework is a way of organizing the whole illness so that nothing essential is left unasked, and it is best understood as a set of reasons rather than a script. It prompts the clinician to establish when the problem started, where it is felt, how long it has persisted, what it feels like, what makes it worse, what makes it better, how it behaves over time, and how severe it is. Each of those prompts is a hypothesis in disguise. The onset separates the sudden from the gradual, the location narrows the anatomy, the character suggests the tissue, the aggravating and relieving factors test the mechanism, the timing exposes the pattern, and the severity estimates the effect on the patient's life. A framework of this kind was assembled from the way clinicians reason in a particular tradition, so it organizes the common presentations well and can quietly miss the unusual one. The clinician should therefore use it as a net and not as a cage, returning to the patient's own words whenever the framework and the story disagree.

When the complaint is pain, the Socrates framework gives the same discipline a sharper edge. It directs the clinician to the site of the pain, its onset, its character, whether it radiates and where, what accompanies it, how it varies with time, what provokes or relieves it, and how severe it is. The reasoning behind each element is easy to state. Radiation describes the path of a shared nerve supply, so it tells the clinician which structures might be implicated together. Associated features such as sweating, nausea, or breathlessness describe the response of the whole body rather than the site alone. Timing separates the pain that is constant from the pain that comes in waves, and that distinction changes the list of causes before any test is ordered. The framework is a memory aid for the questions a careful clinician would ask anyway, and it earns its place only when the answers are heard rather than ticked.

Frameworks fail in two characteristic ways. The first is recitation, in which the clinician works through the prompts in order and the patient's story is chopped into a questionnaire, so the meaning that held the story together is lost. The second is omission, in which the clinician trusts the framework so completely that a feature the framework does not contain is never explored. Both failures come from the same mistake, which is treating a tool for organizing a story as a substitute for hearing it. It is also worth saying plainly that such frameworks were derived in particular populations and particular settings, and their usefulness elsewhere is an assumption rather than a fact. They are safe only in the hands of a clinician who remains willing to be surprised by the patient in front of him.

Silence is a diagnostic instrument, and most clinicians underuse it. After a patient finishes an answer, the temptation is to fill the pause, and the pause is frequently where the most important sentence is waiting. A patient who hesitates is usually deciding whether the next detail is worth mentioning, and a clinician who speaks first makes that decision for him, in the negative. Silence of a few seconds is not an awkward gap in the interview; it is an invitation, and patients accept it more often than clinicians expect. The clinician who can tolerate silence learns things that no question would have produced. It is one of the few diagnostic skills that costs nothing but composure.

Interruption is the opposite instrument, and it is nearly always a loss. A patient who is cut off in the opening sentence may never return to the thing he was about to say, and he will often read the interruption as a judgment that the detail was unimportant. Interrupting also teaches the patient a style of answering, so that the rest of the interview becomes a series of short replies to the clinician's agenda. This is efficient in appearance and expensive in content. A clinician who notices himself interrupting should stop, apologize briefly, and hand the floor back. The few seconds recovered by the interruption are rarely worth the information that was cancelled.

There is a particular value in the question that is asked twice, because the first answer is often a performance and the second is the truth. Asked whether he drinks alcohol, a patient may answer with the amount he believes is socially acceptable, and asked later, in a different way and with a different reason attached, he may answer more accurately. Asked whether the pain is the worst he has ever felt, a patient may say yes to convey how much it hurts, and asked again after a pause, may distinguish between the worst pain and the most frightening one. The repetition must be deliberate and unaccusing, because a patient who feels caught will close rather than open. Asking the same content in new words is also a check on the clinician's own hearing, which is fallible in a noisy room and a tired mind. A clinician should never be embarrassed to ask again; the second answer frequently changes the diagnosis.

Every question in a good history has a reason behind it, and the reason should be visible to the clinician even when it is never spoken. A question about night sweats is asked because a chronic infection or a malignant disease can announce itself at night, and the clinician who knows that will listen differently to the answer. A question about waking at night with breathlessness is asked because it points to the heart rather than to the lung. A question about a change in shoe size or hat size is asked because a slow hormonal illness enlarges the tissues. When the reason is known, the follow-up question arrives naturally. When the reason is forgotten, the answer is recorded and not used.

The line between an acute illness and a chronic one is drawn by time, and time is one of the first things the history establishes. A complaint present for 3 days invites a different list from the same complaint present for 3 months, even when the words used to describe it are identical. Treat that interval as an illustration of the reasoning rather than a rule, and confirm the figure against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the boundary between acute and chronic is drawn differently in different services. The direction of travel matters more than the label: a symptom that is stable, worsening, or improving changes the urgency of the whole encounter. The clinician should ask not only how long but what has happened during that time. A timeline that is reconstructed carefully will often exclude a diagnosis before any test is ordered.

On a quiet ward, the history can be taken in the way it deserves. The clinician sits at the same level as the patient, keeps the notes closed for the first minutes, and lets the account run without looking at a screen. The room is arranged so that the patient is not straining to be heard and the clinician is not standing over the bed. The full present illness is reconstructed, the frameworks are used quietly in the clinician's own mind, and the summary is read back before the examination begins. The examination is then planned around what the story suggested rather than performed as a fixed tour. In such a setting the clinician has time to be thorough, and the temptation is to be thorough about the wrong things: many questions, little listening.

In a crowded clinic the same work must be done inside a few minutes, and this is a different craft rather than a lesser one. Suppose that 3 minutes are all that is available for the conversation, and treat that figure as an illustration of scarcity, because what a service can permit varies between countries and between clinics, so check the local arrangement rather than a remembered figure. Within that limit the clinician still opens with an open question, because it costs almost nothing and returns the patient's own frame. What changes is the triage of attention: the dangerous possibilities are asked about first, the story is allowed to run only as far as it is productive, and the closed questions are chosen for what would change the decision. The summary read back is shortened to a single sentence. A clinician working at this speed must know in advance which questions he will never omit, and that list is personal and must be practised.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the history carries even more of the diagnostic load, because there is no laboratory to fall back on and no imaging to defer to. Here the clinician cannot order his way out of uncertainty, so the questions about duration, trajectory, exposure, and contact become the tests. A fever with a clear story of where it came from, or of who else is ill at home, may be diagnosable without a single measurement. A cough with a history that names the exposure may be named without a radiograph. The absence of equipment does not make the reasoning weaker, it makes it more visible, and the clinician who is honest about uncertainty does better than the one who pretends to a certainty he cannot reach. Where the journey back is long, the history also sets the safety net, because the patient must be told what would bring him back.

In a well-resourced hospital the opposite error is available. Because a scan or a blood test can be ordered within the hour, the history can be shortened without appearing to fail, and the machine is asked to answer a question the clinician never formulated. This is the source of a great deal of unnecessary investigation, and of the occasional diagnosis missed because nobody took the story that would have directed the scan to the right place. A computed tomography scan of the head performed on a patient whose history was never heard may be normal and irrelevant at the same time. The history is what tells the clinician which test is worth doing, in which order, and what a normal result would mean. Riches do not remove the need to think; they only make it easier to postpone.

The order of the encounter is itself a diagnostic decision. The history comes first because the hypothesis must exist before the hands arrive, and an examination performed on a mind with no question in it becomes a search for something to believe. If the clinician examines first and asks afterwards, the findings are free to be interpreted in the light of whatever the examination suggested, and the story is then bent to fit them. A prediction made from the story before the examination is a small act of honesty, and it is what makes the examination evidence rather than decoration. This is why the habit of examining while the history is still being taken, however convenient, damages the reasoning. Listen, form the question, and only then look.

A constructed illustration may make this concrete, and it is a teaching device rather than a record of any real person. A patient arrives with a fever that has lasted several days and no localizing complaint, and the examination is unremarkable. The rushed response is to order a broad set of tests, or to give a treatment and observe. The history, taken properly, asks what the patient does for a living, whether he has been in contact with anyone ill, whether he has traveled, whether an animal has bitten or scratched him, and whether he has had a procedure or an injection recently. One of those answers may name the source and change the whole plan. The examination was not wrong; it was simply silent, and the history was the only instrument that could speak.

Another constructed illustration shows the same principle in a dangerous direction. A patient describes pain in the upper abdomen that came on suddenly and has been constant, with a history of heavy alcohol use and a pulse of 110 beats per minute. The pulse supports the story but does not prove it, and the number that should quicken the clinician's questions is not fixed, so verify the rate your own service treats as abnormal against the current guideline and the local protocol. The examination may be unimpressive in the early hours, while the history of sudden onset, constant severe pain, and a background that makes a complication likely points to a diagnosis that can kill. The clinician who trusts a soft abdomen and a normal temperature in the first hours without hearing the story has been reassured by the wrong evidence. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius would be a fever in many services, and a normal reading in the same patient would not remove the concern, so check what your own protocol calls a fever rather than resting on a remembered figure.

Closing the history with a summary read back to the patient is a diagnostic test on the clinician's own understanding. The clinician states the story in a few sentences, in the patient's own terms, and asks whether it is right. The patient will correct a date, a sequence, or a severity that the clinician had assumed, and each correction is information that would otherwise have been carried forward as error. The summary also shows the patient that he has been heard, which changes what he is willing to add. It is worth leaving a deliberate pause after the summary, because the correction often arrives a moment after the agreement. A history is not finished until the patient has heard it returned.

The history has limits that should be named as clearly as its power. Memory is reconstructive, and patients under stress compress, reorder, and sometimes misattribute what happened. Fear changes what is reported, and so does the wish not to be a burden or not to seem weak. Some patients do not know the answer, because they were unconscious, very young, or living with a cognitive impairment. Others answer with what they believe the clinician wants to hear. The clinician should therefore treat the history as strong evidence and not as proof, and should look for corroboration where it exists. A history that conflicts with a reliable observation deserves to be investigated rather than dismissed in either direction.

How a symptom is expressed varies with age, language, culture, and experience, and the clinician who mistakes the expression for the disease will misjudge the severity. Pain may be described as pressure, tightness, or heat rather than as pain. Distress may be shown through the family rather than by the patient. Infants and older adults may show illness as irritability, poor feeding, or a change in behavior rather than as a named symptom. The clinician must therefore ask what the symptom prevents the patient from doing, because function is more comparable between people than vocabulary. The same question about the same complaint can mean very different things in different mouths, and the history is only as good as the clinician's awareness of that.

Numbers belong to the history as much as to the examination, and they should be heard as measurements with uncertainty rather than as verdicts. A blood pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury recorded at home may be the most important number the patient brings, and it must be interpreted against his usual value rather than against a single remembered threshold, so confirm the cut-off that matters in the current guideline and the local protocol, because the value that defines a low pressure is revised between editions. A weight that has fallen without effort is a finding, and the interval over which it fell changes its meaning. A temperature taken at home and reported as high is weaker evidence than one the clinician measures, but it is not nothing. The clinician should ask who measured the number, with what instrument, and when. A number without its context is a fact that has lost its meaning.

A history can also mislead, and the clinician should expect it to happen. Patients attribute symptoms to causes they know, so a smoker may call breathlessness age and a patient with a family history may call indigestion the family illness. A dramatic event in the recent past can capture the explanation and hide a quiet one that started earlier. The clinician who notices that the story explains only part of the picture should keep the remainder open rather than force it into the same shape. Re-asking is not a sign of a failed interview; it is part of a competent one. The best protection against a misleading history is a second account, taken later, and a willingness to revise.

Time is a resource that is allocated by systems rather than by clinicians alone, and the pressure of a full waiting room is real. The response to that pressure should be to protect the few minutes that carry the most diagnostic weight, not to abandon the method. A clinician can decide in advance which questions he will always ask, which dangerous possibilities he will always consider, and what he will say to a patient he cannot fully assess today. That decision, made calmly, is worth more than speed improvised under pressure. The clinician who names his uncertainty to the patient and arranges a way back is practising good medicine, not failing at it. Good history taking is not a luxury of well-funded systems; it is the part of medicine that travels best.

None of the frameworks, questions, or figures named in this chapter is a rule that can be applied without thought, and none of them replaces the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient. Every threshold, interval, and measurement mentioned here is an illustration of a way of thinking and must be confirmed in the current guideline and the local protocol of your own service before it influences a real decision. The account a patient gives is the beginning of diagnosis, not its end, and it is always to be weighed with the examination, the available tests, and the passage of time. This material is educational only, and it is not medical advice, not a protocol, and not a substitute for training, supervision, or local practice. Where a patient is deteriorating, the interview pauses and the patient is treated, because no question is worth the delay of someone who is becoming more ill.

To summarize, the history is the highest-yield instrument in medicine, and it is taken by opening the story wide, hearing the patient's own words, and narrowing only when the account is complete. The Socrates framework for pain and the Oldcarts framework for the present illness organize the questions, but they are scaffolds and not questionnaires, and they exclude and assume as much as they reveal. Silence earns more than interruption, the second answer is often truer than the first, and dangerous possibilities such as bleeding around the brain or a tear in the aorta announce themselves in the manner of onset. The same work is done differently on a quiet ward and in a crowded clinic where only a few minutes exist, but the questions and the priority of danger do not change. Every number, interval, and threshold in this chapter is an illustration that must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material, it is not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or local protocol, and no patient should be managed on the strength of a chapter alone.

# Chapter 7 — Past, Family, Social and Medication History

The first half of the history explains why this patient has come today; the second half explains why this patient might have this illness at all. Past illnesses and operations, the family pattern, work and its exposures, travel, animals, the sexual history, alcohol, tobacco, allergies, and the medicines actually taken set probabilities that no examination can supply. A constructed illustration shows the safety at stake. A patient who takes an anticoagulant and reports a headache may be bleeding inside the head, and the findings that reveal it are a new weakness, a change in speech, or a fall in the level of consciousness, none of which can be read without the medication history.

This part of the history is the one most often skipped, and the reason is structural rather than lazy. The presenting complaint is vivid, the examination has a visible end, and the past history sits where fatigue is greatest. A patient asked what he was in hospital for, what was removed, and what the doctor said will tell a story, while a form produces a blank. A previous event then changes the probability of a future one in three ways: a disease may recur, as a second heart attack or a second episode of a mood disorder; a disease may leave a residue that is itself the new problem, as a damaged valve leaves the patient vulnerable to infection of the valve; and the treatment of a past disease may cause the present complaint, as surgery leaves adhesions that can obstruct the bowel.

The past history should be opened with questions about events rather than diagnoses. Asking whether the patient has ever been in hospital, and what for, reaches further than asking about medical problems, because patients do not count a past admission or a broken bone as a medical problem. When a diagnosis is named, the clinician should ask how it was discovered, since labels are often assigned without explanation and then carried for years. A label of ulcer, of asthma, or of anxiety may have been a guess never tested.

What matters about a past illness is its severity, its treatment, and its ending. An admission to the intensive care unit, or ICU, marks a serious event even when the diagnosis has been forgotten. A transfusion in the past raises questions about blood-borne infections, and the tests available then were not the tests available now. A childhood illness that kept the patient in bed for weeks may have been rheumatic fever, which can leave a damaged valve, or tuberculosis, which can reactivate.

Operations deserve careful reconstruction, because a scar is a document. Was anything found that the patient was not told about, and did the wound heal slowly? A previous abdominal operation makes adhesions a leading explanation for colicky pain with vomiting and a distended abdomen, and removal of the spleen raises the lifetime risk of overwhelming infection. The clinician should look at the abdomen while listening, because the scars often correct the account.

A history of tuberculosis is among the most important items in the interview, because the disease can reactivate years later, particularly when immunity falls, as in untreated infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, or HIV. The findings that should raise suspicion are a cough lasting 3 weeks, weight loss, night sweats, or blood in the sputum. The interval that should prompt investigation is not the same everywhere, so confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than trusting a remembered figure. Household contact with a person who had tuberculosis should also be asked about, and childhood illnesses such as measles and chickenpox are usually remembered well enough to date.

The family history is not a form to be filled with yes and no; it is a pattern drawn in words. The questions that generate it are the age at which each relative became ill, the age at which each relative died, and the cause of death as the family explained it. A condition appearing at an unusually young age in a close relative carries more weight than the same condition late in a distant one. Consanguinity should be asked about plainly, because it raises the probability of recessive disease in a way that nothing else does.

The pattern that most changes management is sudden death in a young relative, because some inherited conditions that cause it can be found in the living. A young person who died suddenly, a relative who drowned unexpectedly, or a family story of a death in the night may point to an inherited disease of the heart muscle or of the heart's electrical system. The findings that reveal it are fainting during exertion, a murmur, an abnormal electrocardiogram, or ECG, and a family tree that repeats the pattern. Such a history is not a curiosity, because the risk may extend to the patient and to the patient's children.

Cancer in the family shifts the differential, but only when its details are known. Cancer of the bowel or of the womb in a close relative at a young age, or cancer of the breast or ovary in several relatives, raises the probability of an inherited susceptibility. Cancer of the lung in a relative who smoked carries less weight than the same cancer in a relative who did not, because the exposure explains the pattern. The clinician should ask about the site rather than the word cancer, since many families use the word loosely.

Family history also reaches conditions whose inheritance is diffuse rather than tidy, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, asthma, autoimmune disease, mental illness and kidney disease, each of which raises the prior probability in the patient. A patient with a strong family history of diabetes who presents with thirst and weight loss is a different diagnostic problem from the same patient without that history.
