Central cyanosis suggests a problem in the lungs, the heart, or the blood itself, and it is a finding that must be taken seriously at once. Peripheral cyanosis usually reflects poor circulation from cold, shock, or heart failure, and it improves as the extremity warms. Cyanosis is a late and insensitive sign, so its absence never rules out dangerous hypoxia, and the oxygen saturation that is judged acceptable must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the value changes with age, altitude, and the condition being assessed.

Clubbing is the painless enlargement of the soft tissue at the end of the fingers, with loss of the angle between the nail and the nail fold, and it develops over weeks or months rather than hours. The clinician looks for swelling of the fingertip, sponginess of the nail bed when pressed, and increased curvature of the nail, and asks whether the change is symmetrical across both hands. Its mechanism is not fully settled, but it accompanies chronic shortage of oxygen and certain diseases rather than any single one. Clubbing appears in lung cancer, in chronic lung disease that destroys the air spaces, in tuberculosis, in some diseases of the heart, in inflammatory bowel disease, and in disease of the liver. The dangerous possibility behind new clubbing is a lung cancer, and the finding that would reveal it is a persistent cough, weight loss, or a shadow on a chest radiograph, which must be arranged promptly rather than at leisure.

Edema is the swelling caused by fluid collecting in the tissues, and inspection establishes where it sits and whether it pits when pressed. The clinician notes whether the swelling is confined to a single leg or is present on both, whether it reaches the ankles only or extends to the thighs and the lower back, and whether the skin is tight, shiny, warm, or tender. Swelling of a single leg that is tender and warm suggests a clot in the deep veins, and the danger that follows it is a clot travelling to the lungs, which may present as sudden breathlessness or chest pain. Swelling of both legs that pits and rises as the day goes on suggests heart failure, kidney disease, or liver disease, and the accompanying examination of the jugular venous pressure, the lungs, and the abdomen helps to separate them. The pitting is tested by pressing firmly over the shin for a moment and watching how long the mark takes to refill, and what is seen is recorded in words. Any grading or duration of edema quoted in a local chart is an illustration, and it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the scales in use are not the same everywhere.

The lymph nodes are inspected before they are felt, because a visible node that the patient has not mentioned is a finding in its own right. The clinician looks for swelling in the neck, above and below the collarbones, in the armpits, and in the groin, and notes whether the overlying skin is red, whether the swelling is single or multiple, and whether it is fixed to the tissue around it. A node that is hard, painless, matted, and fixed suggests cancer, while a node that is tender, warm, and mobile suggests infection, and the way a node behaves over 2 or 3 weeks carries as much information as its size. A node above the left collarbone deserves particular attention, because it can signal disease in the abdomen or the chest rather than in the neck. Any interval used to define a persistent node must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the period that prompts investigation differs between services.

The skin as a whole is the largest organ on display, and it is inspected for color, moisture, temperature, texture, and the pattern of any eruption. The clinician looks for bruises that do not match the story, for tiny bleeding spots that do not fade when pressed, for dry scaling, for ulcers, for scars, and for the marks of injections or self-harm. A rash that does not blanch in a patient with fever is a medical emergency, because it may signal meningococcal disease, and such a patient must be treated before any test confirms the diagnosis. The distribution of a rash matters as much as its appearance, since whether it favours the trunk, the limbs, the skin folds, or the areas exposed to the sun changes the list of possibilities. Inspection of the skin is also the moment to look at the hair and the nails, which reflect nutrition, disorders of hormones, and long-standing disease. Because skin findings change, they are best examined in good light with the body exposed as far as consent and dignity allow.

No single sign in general inspection is decisive, and the value of the exercise lies in the pattern that several signs make together. Pallor with sweating and a racing pulse means something different from pallor with a slow pulse and a swollen abdomen, even though the color of the skin is the same in both. Jaundice with a mass in the upper abdomen, weight loss with a hoarse voice, and clubbing with a long-standing cough each narrow the field towards a particular set of explanations. The clinician should therefore move from the individual finding to a short list of possibilities, and then decide which of them is dangerous enough to be excluded first. The inspection ends with a sentence formed in the mind, or spoken aloud to the team, that states what the appearance suggests and what would disprove it.

In a well-lit hospital bay the sequence can be performed in a fixed order so that nothing is forgotten. The clinician stands at the foot of the bed and looks at the whole patient, then moves to the side and inspects the hands and nails, then the face, the eyes, the mouth, and the neck, then the chest wall and the abdomen, and finally the legs and the feet. Each step takes seconds, so the whole inspection is cheap in time and generous in return. The hospital setting adds tools that sharpen the eye, among them a monitor showing the oxygen saturation and the rhythm, a glucose meter that answers the question of low blood sugar almost at once, and imaging that can confirm a suspicion raised at the bedside. Those tools should be used to test the hypothesis formed by looking, not to replace it, because a clinician who watches only the monitor will miss the patient who is plainly unwell while the numbers remain reassuring.

The hospital also allows the inspection to be extended when the first look raises a specific question. A patient with new clubbing can be sent for a chest radiograph the same morning, a patient with jaundice can have liver tests and an ultrasound arranged before the next meal, and a patient with a rash that does not blanch can be moved to a resuscitation area while the blood cultures are drawn. The value of this speed is not convenience but the closing of the interval in which a dangerous diagnosis can hide. The clinician should also remember that resources create their own traps, because an incidental finding on a scan ordered for another reason can set off a cascade of further tests, and a normal result can relax a vigilance that the patient's appearance did not justify relaxing. The patient at the end of the bed remains the primary instrument in the most equipped room in the building.

In a clinic where the tools are a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same inspection is performed with whatever light is available. The clinician waits a moment for the eyes to adjust, then uses the torch at an angle rather than straight on, because side lighting reveals the relief of a rash, the depth of a wound, and the color of the conjunctivae far better than a beam shone directly into the face. Daylight through a doorway is better than any bulb for judging jaundice and cyanosis, so the patient is positioned to face the window whenever that is possible. A cold room changes the findings, because extremities turn blue and pulses become hard to feel, so the hands are warmed before judgment is passed. The patient wrapped in blankets must be uncovered enough to see the legs, the feet, and the skin the blankets have been hiding, with consent given and warmth maintained as far as it can be.

The limited clinic makes some judgments more important rather than less. A patient who is pale, sweating, and confused in a room without a laboratory may be bleeding internally, and the correct action is not a test but an urgent journey to a place where the bleeding can be found and stopped. A patient with fever and a rash that does not fade under pressure must be moved with the same urgency, and the clinician should not wait for a confirmation that will arrive too late to change anything. A thermometer, a torch, and a watch supply enough to identify these patients, provided the clinician looks at the patient rather than at the equipment. Where the road is long and the return uncertain, the inspection also decides what must be written in the referral note and what must be said to the family before the patient leaves.

A constructed illustration makes the sequence concrete. A middle-aged man is brought to a clinic with 2 days of vague tiredness and no pain; he is pale, his skin is cool and damp, his pulse feels fast and thin under the fingers, and he answers questions slowly while asking for water. The torch shows no rash, the eyes are not yellow, and there is no swelling, but the conjunctivae are strikingly pale and the abdomen is slightly distended and tender on the left. Taken alone, each of these findings is ordinary, while together they suggest blood loss from the gut, and the correct decision is urgent transfer rather than a wait for the next clinic day. This example is a teaching device built to show how inspection orders a differential diagnosis, and it is not a description of any real patient. The listener should notice that the diagnosis was available before the abdomen was examined in detail and before any test was ordered. The exact value of the pulse or the blood count does not matter here, but the direction of the reasoning does, and every figure that is later applied must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Inspection has limits that must be stated as plainly as its strengths. Color perception differs between clinicians and is affected by lighting, by the tint of the skin, and by the observer's own eyes, so a finding that is equivocal deserves a second look or a second person. The very young, the very old, the pregnant, and the immunosuppressed often look less ill than they are, and the patient with deeply pigmented skin may show jaundice and cyanosis in places that are easy to miss, such as the palate, the conjunctivae, and the nail beds. Obesity can hide wasting, blankets can hide swollen legs, and clothing can hide the rash that matters. The clinician who knows these limits looks harder in the places where the signs are usually found rather than concluding that nothing is there.

What is seen should be written down in words that another clinician could picture, because the inspection cannot be repeated by the next reader in the same light. A note that records only that the patient looked unwell is useless, whereas a note that records pallor of the conjunctivae, cool clammy skin, a pulse that felt thready, and a reluctance to lie flat transfers the reasoning to whoever reads it next. The inspection should also be repeated at intervals, because the appearance of a patient at the start of a shift and the appearance at the end of it may tell a different story, and the direction of change is often the most sensitive evidence of deterioration. The clinician should look again after every intervention and at every handover, however briefly, and should record what changed rather than only what was present.

Age changes what inspection shows and what it means. A newborn baby is inspected for color, tone, feeding, and the alertness of the cry, and a baby who is quiet when handled and difficult to rouse is not simply sleepy. An older adult may show none of the expected signs of serious illness, so a fall, a new confusion, or a loss of appetite becomes the finding that demands a search rather than a discharge. In both groups the inspection is brief, gentle, and repeated, and in both the clinician should be slow to accept a benign explanation for a change in function. The same principle applies to the patient who cannot speak, whose posture and breathing may be the only account available.

The hands repay a longer look than they usually receive. The clinician notes the warmth, the color, and the refill of the nail beds, the shape of the fingers, the presence of tremor or of a fine flap of the outstretched hands, and the stains, scars, or calluses that speak of occupation and habit. Splinter hemorrhages under the nails, small painful nodules on the finger pads, and a dusky mottling of the skin can each point towards infection of the heart or a disturbance of the circulation, and they are easily missed when the hands are examined as a formality. The palms may be sweaty in an overactive thyroid or dry and cool in an underactive one, and a fine tremor of the hands is a useful clue in the same conditions. A capillary refill that takes longer than a few seconds suggests poor perfusion, and the number of seconds that counts as delayed must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since practice and ambient temperature alter it.

General inspection is an examination like any other, so it requires consent, an explanation, and the same respect for privacy that the rest of the encounter demands. The clinician should say what will be looked at and why, offer a chaperone when the inspection will include intimate areas, and keep the patient covered except for the part being examined. On a busy ward the inspection is often done through a curtain with the patient half dressed, and the temptation to skip the feet or the back is strong, yet those are precisely the places where swelling, ulcers, and pressure damage hide. A patient who declines part of the inspection has the right to decline it, and the record should state what was not seen as clearly as what was. The order of the inspection should follow the patient's comfort as far as it can, while ensuring that nothing important is left unexamined.

The reasoning must come before the looking, or the looking becomes a ritual. Before entering the bay the clinician should already hold a short list of questions, among them whether this patient is perfusing adequately, whether this patient is oxygenating, whether this patient is losing fluid or blood, and whether there is a surface sign of a disease that has spread through the whole body. Each part of the inspection is then chosen to answer one of those questions rather than performed because it appears on a list. A finding that was not predicted is still welcome, because it is the least contaminated by expectation, and it should be written down and followed up rather than explained away. The clinician who looks with a question will see more than the clinician who looks at everything.

What transfers between the well-lit bay and the clinic at the end of the road is the sequence of questions, not the equipment. The hospital clinician who understands why the conjunctivae are inspected will still inspect them with a torch, and the clinic clinician who understands why the legs are uncovered will still ask the patient to remove the blankets. The principle is physiological, because the surface of the body reflects the volume of the circulation, the oxygen in the blood, the work of the liver and the kidney, and the activity of the immune system. Once that is understood, a finding is not a name to be memorized but a consequence to be reasoned from. The equipment changes what can be confirmed; it does not change what should be looked for.

To summarize, general inspection is the diagnostic act performed before the patient is touched, and it takes seconds while returning information that shapes every later step. It reads the work of breathing, the posture, the color, the moisture, the smell, the nutrition, the hydration, the lymph nodes, the skin, the nails, and the limbs, and it treats each of those findings as a physiological statement rather than a label. The appearance of a pale, clammy, restless patient is the finding that must never be allowed to wait, because internal bleeding can be fatal within a short interval. Every threshold, score, duration, and reference value mentioned in this chapter is an illustration only and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such numbers vary between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material; it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or local protocol, and no real patient has been described here.

# Chapter 11 — Vital Signs as Diagnostic Tools

Vital signs occupy an odd position in clinical practice, because they are recorded so routinely that they are often written down without ever being read. A pulse, a respiratory rate, a temperature, a blood pressure, and an oxygen saturation are the cheapest physiological information available at the bedside, and they are frequently the first evidence to contradict a reassuring story. This chapter treats them not as a ritual performed before the clinician arrives but as a set of instruments for reasoning, each with its own physiology, its own failure modes, and its own way of moving the probability of disease. The idea that organizes everything that follows is that a vital sign is a trend before it is a number, and that its meaning depends on the person in whom it was measured. What is said here is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the local rules of the place where you work.

One reading is a point and two readings are a direction, which is why the interval between observations is part of the measurement rather than an administrative detail. Physiology usually moves before it fails, so a value sitting at the edge of normal while drifting steadily in the wrong direction carries more warning than a value that is frankly abnormal and stable. A constructed illustration makes the reasoning visible. A young person is brought to an emergency department after a collision, and the first recording shows a blood pressure of 110 over 70 millimeters of mercury with a pulse of 110 beats per minute. Those figures look acceptable when each is read alone, yet the pulse is fast for a resting adult and the pressure is lower than one would expect in a person who is frightened and in pain, and the repeat recording an hour later shows the pressure falling while the pulse climbs again. The lethal cause to carry in mind at that moment is hemorrhage, into the abdomen or into the chest, and the bedside findings that reveal it are a rising pulse, a narrowing pulse pressure, capillary refill that has become sluggish in a cool periphery, and a patient who is increasingly restless and thirsty. Those figures are an illustration rather than a rule, and the values your own service treats as abnormal must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because reference ranges differ between countries, between editions, and between the populations from which they were derived.

Infection follows the same priority, and the dangerous possibility has to be named before the comfortable one. A fever with an obvious source, in a patient who is alert, drinking, and passing urine, may reasonably be watched, but the same fever accompanied by a climbing respiratory rate, a new confusion, a cold and mottled periphery, and a falling urine output points towards septic shock and demands immediate assessment. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is treated as a fever by some protocols and not by others, and the figure that matters is the one your own service uses, confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since definitions of fever shift with the country, the edition, and the population. The most dangerous trap is the infection that does not raise the temperature at all, because a normal or low reading allows everyone to relax. A rash that does not fade when pressed, a patient who is drowsy or difficult to rouse, and a cold periphery with a normal thermometer together suggest a severe infection of the bloodstream or of the meninges, and that combination is a reason to act rather than to observe.

The pulse is the most familiar of the signs and the one most often reduced to a single number, which wastes most of what it can say. Its rate is the first branch of the reasoning, and a fast pulse at rest has only a few broad explanations: fear or pain, fever, a failing heart, a disturbance of rhythm, a hormonal excess, or a loss of circulating volume. The clinician's task is to decide which of those the whole picture supports rather than to treat the number itself as a diagnosis. A young person with a fast pulse, warm hands, clear mentation, and no pain is very different from an older person with the same rate, cool hands, and a new confusion, even though the two recordings are identical. The pulse rate is therefore evidence about compensation, and its significance depends on whether the body is coping or beginning to fail.

Several common situations blunt or exaggerate the pulse, and the clinician who forgets them will misread the trend. A patient taking a drug that slows the heart may mount no tachycardia at all during serious illness, so a normal rate in such a patient is not reassurance. A patient with an artificial pacemaker may have a rate that is set by the device rather than by physiology. Trained athletes and healthy young adults can compensate for a long time before the pulse reveals distress, while infants and small children may compensate and then deteriorate very quickly. In each of these groups the pulse must be interpreted against what is normal for that person, and any figure taken from a textbook must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The respiratory rate is the most sensitive of the vital signs and the one most frequently recorded as an approximation rather than a count. Breathing responds early to a great many problems, including infection, metabolic disturbance, pain, anxiety, and a failing heart, so a rate that is rising may be the first sign that something serious is developing. It is neglected because it takes a full minute of quiet attention, and because the person recording it can often see the chest moving and assumes that watching is the same as counting. The assumption is dangerous, since an estimated rate tends to be pulled towards whatever number the clinician expects. Counting for a full minute, without telling the patient what is being counted, converts an impression into evidence.

Where and how the temperature is taken changes the number, and a comparison between readings taken by different routes is a comparison between different measurements. A reading taken in the mouth, in the ear, under the arm, or in the rectum will not agree exactly, and the clinician must know which route the previous recording used before deciding that a patient has improved or worsened. A normal temperature is often quoted as lying between 36 and 38 degrees Celsius, yet that range is an illustration drawn from particular populations, so confirm the range in use at your institution against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it differs between countries, editions, and methods of measurement. The most important teaching point here is negative: a normal temperature does not exclude serious infection, and it is common in older patients, in people whose immune defenses are suppressed, and in the early hours of a severe illness.

A low temperature is a danger sign rather than a comfort, and it deserves the same attention as a fever. In older adults a serious infection may present with a temperature below 35 degrees Celsius, with confusion or a fall instead of the expected symptoms, so the combination of a low reading and an altered mental state should prompt a search for infection. Cold exposure, hormonal failure, and severe metabolic disturbance can also lower the temperature, and each of those carries its own urgent decisions. That figure is an example rather than a universal definition, and the threshold that should alarm you must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Blood pressure is the vital sign most trusted by clinicians and the one most likely to be falsely reassuring. The circulation defends its pressure with several mechanisms at once, tightening the peripheral vessels, increasing the heart rate, and retaining salt and water, so a patient can lose a considerable amount of volume or develop a severe illness while the measured pressure remains within the expected range. Hypotension is a late finding in a previously healthy adult, which is why a normal blood pressure is never by itself a reason to relax. The pressure has to be read together with the pulse, the perfusion of the skin, the mental state, and the urine output, and it is the combination that identifies the patient who is compensating.

The systolic pressure is the number usually quoted, and the difference between the systolic and diastolic pressures is often more informative. A narrowing pulse pressure, in which the two figures come closer together, suggests that the heart is ejecting less with each beat while the periphery is tightly constricted, and it may appear before the systolic value itself falls. A substantial difference between the two arms, measured properly, suggests a problem in the aorta or in one of the arteries supplying an arm, and it should be sought in any patient with chest pain or an unexplained collapse. A fall in pressure on standing, accompanied by symptoms, is a clue to volume loss, to abnormal reflexes controlling the circulation, or to the effects of medication. Each of these observations is a piece of reasoning rather than a routine step, and each changes what the clinician does next.

Oxygen saturation measures how much of the hemoglobin in arterial blood is carrying oxygen, and it is a measure of binding rather than of delivery. It answers whether the blood is loaded, not whether enough blood is reaching the tissues, and not whether the tissues can use the oxygen that arrives. This distinction explains why a patient with severe anemia, a failing heart, or an inability to use oxygen at the tissue level can have a perfectly normal saturation while remaining desperately ill. Saturation is therefore an important sign and a limited one, and it must be read alongside the pulse, the pressure, the perfusion, and the mental state rather than instead of them.

The device has several well-known ways of lying, and the clinician should know them before trusting a reassuring number. Cold hands, poor blood flow to the finger, movement, and nail covering can all prevent the sensor from finding a stable signal, and a device that cannot find a signal may display a plausible value rather than an error. Skin pigmentation can affect the accuracy of some sensors, and calibration may drift across the range of saturations. The most dangerous failure is that ordinary saturation monitors cannot distinguish hemoglobin carrying oxygen from hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide, so a patient with carbon monoxide poisoning may display a normal saturation while being seriously poisoned. Whenever the reading does not fit the patient in front of you, trust the patient and seek another way to measure or another explanation.

A saturation of 94 per cent or higher at rest is often taken as adequate, but that figure is an illustration, because the target differs in pregnancy, in chronic lung disease, in children, and at altitude, so confirm the value that applies to your patient against the current guideline and the local protocol. A saturation that is normal now may also fall when the patient moves, coughs, or lies flat, so the measurement should be repeated in the position and at the activity that provokes the symptoms. Falling saturation during exertion or on lying flat is itself a diagnostic finding, because it points to the heart or to the lungs as the source of the problem. A single normal reading, taken at rest, in a comfortable position, at one moment of the day, settles very little.

The shock index exists because the pulse and the pressure compensate together, and each one can look acceptable while the relationship between them has already changed. It expresses that relationship as a single number, and it rises when the pulse increases faster than the systolic pressure holds up, which is exactly the pattern of concealed bleeding or early shock. Its value is that it draws attention to the pair rather than to either figure alone, and it can be worked out at the bedside in a clinic as easily as in a hospital. Like every index, it is a prompt rather than an answer, and it must be interpreted in the light of the patient's usual values and the rest of the examination. No index replaces the eyes, the hands, and the question of what dangerous thing might be happening.

An early warning score is a formalization of a piece of bedside wisdom, which is that several signs each a little abnormal are more alarming than one sign that is very abnormal. It works by giving points for each sign that has moved away from normal, with more points as the movement becomes larger, and then adding the points into a single figure that prompts a response. The reasoning behind it is sound, because physiology fails in a coordinated way, and the pattern of small deviations is often the earliest visible stage of a serious illness. The score also serves as a shared language, allowing one observer to communicate the seriousness of a situation to another in a way that is difficult to ignore.

The score has failure modes, and the clinician must know them or will be captured by the number. A total can hide a single extreme value, so a patient with one danger sign and several normal ones may receive a reassuring total, which is why the individual readings must still be read. Missing observations, particularly a respiratory rate that was estimated rather than counted, corrupt the total and the trend, and a score calculated in a different setting or with different equipment will not mean the same thing. A score derived in one population may also perform poorly in another, so a rule validated in one hospital should be re-examined before it is trusted in a clinic or in a different country. The score prompts a response; it does not make the diagnosis and it does not replace the examination.

The most difficult patient is the one who does not look ill enough to explain the concern, or who looks unwell while every number is within range. A patient who is compensating may maintain a normal pressure, a normal saturation, and a temperature that has not yet risen, while the respiratory rate has crept up and the manner has changed. The clinician who relies on the numbers alone will send that patient home, and the clinician who relies on the impression alone may over-investigate a patient who is merely anxious. The resolution is to use both, and to give the impression the same evidential weight as the measurement, asking what the body is doing that the instruments have not yet detected. An experienced clinician who is uneasy about a patient whose numbers are normal should treat the unease as data and arrange a review.

A constructed illustration shows how the two worlds meet. A middle-aged patient attends a clinic with a cough, a mild fever, and a pulse that is a little fast, and the clinician, pressed for time, records the numbers as satisfactory and advises a symptomatic treatment. The patient returns two days later, more breathless, with a respiratory rate that has doubled and a saturation that falls when walking, and is found to have a serious infection of the lung. The finding that should have changed the first decision was not a single abnormal number but the trend, the work of breathing, and the clinician's own sense that the story did not fit. That example is constructed to make a point and does not describe any real patient, and it is not a criticism of the clinician, because the lesson is about the limits of any single observation.

Where there is no monitor, the clinician still has four measurements that require nothing but attention, and they are the same ones that matter most in the hospital. The respiratory rate can be counted with a watch and quiet observation, the capillary refill can be timed with the eye, the mental state can be assessed by conversation, and the urine output can be followed with a bottle and a record. Those four observations detect most of the deterioration that a monitor would detect, and they detect it earlier than a single set of electronic readings, because they are repeated by a person who is looking at the patient. A stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer extend them further, allowing the clinician to listen to the chest, to look for a rash or a pale conjunctiva, and to measure the temperature directly. That is the whole examination of the unstable patient in a setting with almost nothing, and it is enough to decide who must be referred and who may be watched.

Capillary refill is the simplest test of peripheral perfusion and the most useful when it is performed consistently. The clinician presses the tip of a finger or the skin over the sternum for a few seconds, releases the pressure, and watches how quickly the color returns, with a delay beyond 3 seconds suggesting that the periphery is poorly perfused. That figure is an illustration rather than a fixed rule, and the cut-off that should concern you must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it varies with age, with ambient temperature, with the site tested, and with the lighting. The test is valuable because it changes quickly with the patient's condition and because it requires no equipment at all, but it is also easy to perform badly, and the result depends on the observer. It should be repeated at intervals and interpreted together with the respiratory rate, the mental state, and the urine output rather than alone.

The mental state is a vital sign that many clinicians forget to measure, and it is often the first to change. A patient who was alert and orientated an hour ago and who is now drowsy, agitated, or speaking nonsense has deteriorated, whatever the monitor shows, and that change requires an explanation. The causes range from low oxygen and low blood pressure through infection, metabolic disturbance, and drugs to bleeding around the brain, and the search should begin immediately rather than after the next set of observations. In older adults a new confusion may be the only sign of a serious illness, and it should never be dismissed as age or as the hospital environment. A brief, repeated assessment of attention and orientation costs seconds and can be recorded as a trend in the same way as a pulse.

Urine output is the vital sign that reports on the recent past, because it summarizes whether the kidneys have been adequately perfused over the hours that have just passed. A fall in output below about half a milliliter for each kilogram of body weight in each hour suggests that the circulation is failing to reach the kidneys, and it may precede any change in the blood pressure. That figure is an illustration and the definition of adequate output differs with age, with pregnancy, with kidney disease, and with the fluid the patient has been given, so confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol. Recorded hourly in a hospital and observed roughly in a clinic, output is one of the most reliable signs of a circulation in trouble, provided that the collection is complete and the times are accurate. It is also easily lost, because a patient who is not asked and not measured has no output to report.

In a well-resourced hospital the same assessment is performed with continuous monitoring, and the additional information is real. A continuous trace shows the rhythm rather than a single beat, an arterial line shows the pressure beat by beat and allows a sample to be taken, and a monitor that displays the respiratory rate, the saturation, and the pressure together makes the relationship between them visible. The monitor also stores the trend, so the direction of travel can be reviewed without relying on memory. Those advantages are genuine, and they are the reason such monitoring changes outcomes when it is used well. The danger is that the display becomes a substitute for the patient, so that the clinician manages the numbers and stops looking at the person.

Monitors fail in predictable ways. They produce artifacts when the patient moves, they alarm when nothing is wrong, and they fall silent when a lead has come off, and the clinician who has heard a thousand false alarms will begin to ignore the true ones. A value measured by a machine is not necessarily more accurate than one measured by hand, because the machine is calibrated, positioned, and interpreted by people. An arterial trace can read falsely high or falsely low if the transducer is at the wrong height, and a saturation reading depends on a sensor that may be cold, displaced, or poorly perfused. The monitor is an instrument, and an instrument is only as good as the person who decides what its output means.

The two worlds differ in tools and not in reasoning, and the same questions organize both. In the hospital the clinician asks whether the trend over the last hour is reassuring, and has a continuous trace with which to answer. In the clinic the clinician asks the same question and answers it with a note of the time, a counted respiratory rate, and a comparison with the previous visit. Neither setting allows the clinician to conclude that a patient is safe on the basis of a single normal set of readings, and neither permits the dangerous possibility to be set aside because the numbers look ordinary. The clinician who understands the physiology can transfer the reasoning from the monitor to the watch and the hand without losing the thread. That portability is the whole purpose of learning the principle behind the measurement.

Children and young adults deserve particular caution because their compensation is so effective and so brief. A child can maintain a normal blood pressure and a normal appearance until the circulation is close to failure, and then deteriorate very quickly, so the trends in the pulse, the respiratory rate, the perfusion, and the behavior matter more than any single figure. The normal ranges themselves differ with age, so a rate that is ordinary in an infant may be alarming in an adolescent, and any table of values must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The child who is quiet, floppy, or difficult to rouse is more concerning than the child who is screaming, because the quiet child may have stopped compensating. Watching the child interact with the parent, drink, and play is a form of monitoring that no device can replace.

The interval between observations is a clinical decision, and it depends on how uncertain and how unstable the patient is. A patient who is clearly unwell and whose diagnosis is unclear may need review every 15 minutes until the direction is established, while a patient who is improving may need only a daily check, and the figure chosen must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because practice varies between services. The interval should be shortened when a finding is unexpected, when a treatment has just been started, and when the clinician cannot explain what is happening. Whatever the interval, the recording should include the time, so that the next observer can see not only the value but how long it has been there. Repeating the measurement is one of the most powerful diagnostic acts available, because it turns a snapshot into a trajectory.

The final safeguard is the clinician's own discomfort, which is a form of evidence that no instrument records. A patient who looks unwell while the numbers are ordinary should be examined again, and the question should be what the numbers have missed rather than how to make the impression fit them. A patient whose numbers are abnormal but who looks comfortable should still be taken seriously, because the measurements describe physiology and not the person's resilience. The correct response to a discrepancy is to observe more closely, to repeat the measurement sooner, and to seek another opinion rather than to choose the more convenient interpretation. That habit, more than any device, is what prevents the deterioration that is discovered too late.

To summarize, vital signs are instruments for reasoning rather than items on a form, and they are most informative when they are read as trends in a particular person. The direction of travel, the relationship between the signs, and the impression of the patient together carry more weight than any single reading, and the dangerous possibilities must be named early so that the finding which would reveal them is deliberately sought. Every value, score, cut-off, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, and duration mentioned in this chapter is an illustration of that reasoning, and each must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. A normal set of numbers does not make a patient well, a monitor does not think, and a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer still answer most of the questions when there is nothing else. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the local protocol, and if a patient is deteriorating then the measurement stops and the patient is treated.

# Chapter 12 — Cardiovascular Examination

The cardiovascular examination is an inquiry into a pump, the pipes it feeds, and the pressures that keep fluid moving in the right direction. The reasoning that organizes it is a pair of questions asked in order: is the circulation delivering enough blood to the brain, the kidneys, and the working muscle, and is the cause of this illness one of the few that kill within hours. Those urgent causes deserve to be named before anything is touched. They are infection that has destroyed a heart valve, a tear in the wall of the aorta, fluid or blood compressing the heart so that it cannot fill, and the flooded lung of acute pulmonary edema. This chapter is educational material and nothing more; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient. Every number spoken here is an illustration of reasoning, and each must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories.

The examination is a series of small experiments rather than a fixed procession of rituals. Each maneuver is worth performing only if the clinician knows in advance what its result would change, and a sign sought without a question behind it is a sign that will be missed. The order can be rearranged around the leading hypothesis without losing anything essential, so a clinician who fears compression of the heart goes first to the neck veins and the blood pressure, while one who suspects a damaged valve listens first and then looks at the hands, the eyes, and the temperature chart. What must not be rearranged is the principle that the reason precedes the maneuver, because the reason is what makes the finding visible.

Observation begins at the end of the bed, before the patient is touched, and it costs only seconds. The clinician notes whether the patient lies flat in comfort or is propped upright and fighting for air, whether the lips and fingertips carry a blue tinge, whether the skin is pale, sweaty, or mottled, and whether the ankles are swollen. Posture is itself a finding, because a patient who cannot lie flat without gasping is telling the clinician that the heart is failing to clear the lungs. In a clinic with a torch and no monitor, this inspection is not a preliminary; it is a large part of the examination.

The hands and the face carry signs that point to the heart long before the heart is heard. The nails may be clubbed, curved and spongy at the base, which speaks of long-standing low oxygen or of infection inside the heart, and small painless red streaks may lie lengthwise under the nail plate, while the pads of the fingers may bear tender nodules that appear and fade within days. The skin may be pale, cool, and clammy, and the tongue and lips may be dark rather than pink. Fever with a new murmur and these peripheral marks is the combination that must raise the possibility of infection on a valve, which is one reason a fever is never only a fever.

The pulse is the pressure wave the heart generates, felt at the wall of an artery, and its character carries information that a number cannot. The rate, the rhythm, the volume, and the shape of the wave each answer a different question, so the pulse is examined in parts even when it is felt in a single gesture. The rate is counted for a full minute rather than a fraction of one, because an irregular rhythm makes a short count unreliable in both directions. A resting rate above 100 beats per minute in an adult may mean fever, fear, pain, anemia, or a failing heart, and the figure that should cause alarm varies with age, pregnancy, and fitness, so confirm the threshold that applies in your setting against the current guideline and the local protocol. A rate that is unusually slow may be normal in a trained athlete and dangerous in someone taking a drug that slows the heart.

Rhythm is assessed by whether the interval between beats is even and whether each beat has the same force. A regularly irregular rhythm points to a repeating pattern, such as a beat that arrives early and is followed by a pause, while an irregularly irregular rhythm with no pattern at all points to the chaotic electrical activity of atrial fibrillation. When the rhythm is irregular, the clinician compares the rate felt at the wrist with the rate heard at the heart, because some beats are too weak to reach the wrist and the difference measures how much the heart is wasting. An irregular rhythm that is also fast may reduce filling enough to drop the blood pressure and confuse the patient, so it is never a curiosity to be noted and set aside. The two wrists are compared with each other whenever an artery is suspected of being narrowed.

Volume and character are judged together, and they are learned by comparing many healthy pulses until the normal feel is stored in the hands. A pulse that is full and then collapses away from the fingers suggests that a great volume of blood is escaping backward with each beat, and a pulse that rises slowly and plateaus suggests that the outflow from the heart is obstructed. A pulse that alternates in strength from beat to beat is a serious sign that the heart muscle is failing to empty consistently, and it often accompanies a low output state. A pulse barely perceptible at the wrist while the patient is awake and talking warns that the blood pressure is being held by constricted vessels and may fall at any moment.

The pulse is sought at several places, because a pulse missing in one place and present in another localizes the problem. The carotid pulse in the neck, the brachial pulse in the arm, the radial pulse at the wrist, and the femoral pulse in the groin each represent a different segment of the arterial tree, and an absent or diminished pulse at one of them, in a patient with pain, is an emergency rather than a finding for the next clinic. A difference in the pulse or in the blood pressure between the two arms raises the possibility of a tear in the wall of the aorta, one of the lethal causes named at the start of this chapter. The finding that would reveal that tear is exactly this asymmetry, together with pain of sudden onset, and it must be sought on purpose because the patient may look deceptively stable at first. An unequal pulse in the two arms is not a variation to be attributed to technique until the dangerous explanation has been excluded.

The blood pressure converts the feel of the pulse into a number, and it is the number most often trusted more than it deserves. The cuff must fit the arm, because one that is too small reads falsely high and one that is too large reads falsely low, and the arm must be supported at the level of the heart, because an arm held low reads high and one held high reads low. The reading should be taken in both arms at least once, and repeated after the patient has stood, because a pressure that falls on standing points to a loss of the reflex that maintains it. A systolic pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury in a patient who was previously well is a warning to search for bleeding, infection, or a failing heart, but the value that should trigger action depends on the patient's usual pressure, on age, and on pregnancy, so confirm the threshold in your own service against the current guideline and the local protocol.

One pattern of blood pressure deserves separate attention because it points to a specific emergency. When the heart is surrounded by fluid or blood inside the fibrous sac that holds it, it cannot fill properly, and the pressure falls during inspiration more than it should, because the blood returning to the right side competes for space with the left side. The clinician detects this by inflating the cuff above the systolic pressure and lowering it slowly while watching the first sounds appear and disappear with breathing, and a fall of more than about 10 millimeters of mercury during inspiration is the pattern usually described, though that precise figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The same patient is likely to have a raised jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds, a low blood pressure, and a rapid pulse, and the combination is the picture of tamponade. The finding that reveals it is the falling pressure on inspiration together with the distended neck veins.

The jugular venous pressure is the height at which blood stands in the great veins of the neck, and it is a direct manometer of the pressure in the right side of the heart. The vein is observed rather than felt, because it has no valve and its level rises and falls with the pulse and with breathing, while the carotid artery beside it is felt as a single brisk thrust. The patient is propped up at an angle with the head turned slightly away, and the light is directed across the neck so that the flicker of the vein can be seen. The height is described in relation to the sternal angle, and a level more than 3 centimeters above that landmark is usually taken as raised, but that figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the reference point and the normal range differ between services. A raised jugular venous pressure points to the right side of the heart while the clinician is still at the foot of the bed.

The waveform of the jugular venous pulse carries more information than its height alone. The vein normally shows two gentle rises for each heartbeat, one produced when the atrium contracts against a closed valve and one produced as blood fills the atrium while the heart contracts, and a loss of that pulsation, so that the vein is full and still, is itself a serious finding. A very large rise in the neck with each beat suggests that blood is leaking backward through the valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle, and a rise that increases when the patient breathes in points to a heart that cannot accept the extra returning blood. Pressing gently on the right upper abdomen for a short time normally raises the venous level only slightly and briefly, and a sustained rise during that maneuver is a sign that the right side of the heart is failing to cope with the added return.

Auscultation of the heart is an exercise in timing and location, and it should never be a random tour of the chest. The first heart sound is produced by the closing of the valves between the atria and the ventricles, and it marks the beginning of the contraction that ejects blood. The second heart sound is produced by the closing of the valves at the exits of the ventricles, and the way its two components separate during breathing tells the clinician about the pressures on the two sides of the heart. The first sound is best heard at the lower left edge of the breastbone, where the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle sits, and the second sound is best heard at the upper right edge, where the aortic valve sits. The clinician who knows which sound belongs to which event can date every other sound in the cycle, and that dating is the whole of auscultation.

Extra sounds are the small additions that change the meaning of the cycle. A third heart sound, arriving a short time after the second, is a low soft thud that suggests a ventricle filling too quickly, and in an older patient it is a strong clue to a failing heart, while in a young person it may be entirely normal. A fourth heart sound, arriving just before the first, is a soft sound that suggests a stiff ventricle resisting the push of the atrium, and it is common when the blood pressure has been high for years or the heart muscle has thickened. A sharp early click after the first sound can mark a valve that is narrowed but still mobile, and the opening snap of a narrowed left-sided valve has its own early position in the cycle. Each of these sounds is meaningful only in its place in the cycle.

A murmur is the noise of turbulent blood, and it is described by four properties that must all be reported together. The timing says whether the noise occurs while the heart is ejecting, between the first and second sounds, or while it is filling, after the second sound and before the next first sound. The site says where the noise is loudest, because each valve projects its murmur to a characteristic place on the chest wall. The radiation says where the noise travels, and a murmur that travels into the neck or the armpit means something different from one that stays where it began. The response to posture and breathing says whether the turbulence changes when the heart is filled differently, because a murmur that becomes louder when the patient stands or breathes out narrows the possibilities.

The changes that posture and breathing produce are as informative as the murmur itself. When a patient stands from sitting, the heart holds less blood, and the noise of most obstructions to outflow becomes quieter, while the noise of a thickened, leaky valve may become louder. When a patient squats, the heart holds more blood, and the opposite happens. When a patient breathes in, more blood returns to the right side of the heart, which increases the noise of murmurs arising there, while a maneuver that raises the pressure in the chest reduces the return to the left side and quietens the murmurs that arise there. These are the clinician's substitute for a pressure measurement when no laboratory is available. A murmur is a product of flow, not a fixed property of a valve, and a description that omits these changes is incomplete.

The peripheral signs of heart failure are the visible consequences of a heart that cannot keep up with the blood returning to it. Swelling of the ankles and the lower legs, worse in the evening and less after a night in bed, is the commonest, and it is caused by the raised venous pressure pushing fluid into the tissues. The same pressure raises the jugular venous level, enlarges the liver so that it may be tender under the right rib margin, and can fill the abdomen with fluid. When the left side fails, the lungs fill with fluid, so the patient becomes breathless on lying flat and wakes at night fighting for air, and the clinician may hear fine crackles at the bases. Weight is the simplest measure of the fluid that accumulates, so a patient who has gained weight without eating more is retaining fluid.

Acute pulmonary edema is one of the lethal presentations named at the start, and it can be deceptive. The patient is desperately breathless, sitting bolt upright, often unable to speak in full sentences, with cool and clammy skin, and yet the chest may be surprisingly quiet, because the air spaces are so filled with fluid that little air movement remains to generate sound. The quiet chest in a breathless patient is more alarming than a loud one, and it should move the clinician to act rather than to wait for confirmation. In hospital the diagnosis is supported by the picture and by a chest radiograph, and in a clinic with only a stethoscope and a torch the same picture must carry the decision. The clinician who waits for a test before treating a patient who is drowning is making the one error that diagnosis cannot afford.

Infection on a heart valve is the second lethal possibility, and its danger lies in how ordinary it can look at first. A patient with fever, fatigue, and a murmur that has changed or appeared for the first time may have infection growing on a valve, and that infection can destroy the valve, throw infected material into the circulation, or cause an abscess in the heart. The findings that would reveal it are a new or changing murmur, a fever that does not declare its source, tender nodules on the fingers, painless streaks under the nails, small broken vessels in the eye, and an enlarged spleen. A clinician who hears a new murmur in a febrile patient should not simply record it and move on. The decision to treat rests on the combination of fever, a changing murmur, and evidence of infection in the blood, while the decision to withhold treatment rests on a clear alternative explanation for the fever and an unchanged, old murmur.

Compression of the heart and a tear in the aorta are the other lethal possibilities, and each announces itself through the pulse. In tamponade the blood pressure is low, the jugular venous pressure is high, the heart sounds are muffled, and the pulse is rapid and weak, and any one of these alone may be attributed to something benign, which is why all four must be sought together. In a tear of the aorta the pain is often described as tearing and moving, the pulses in the two arms may differ, a murmur of leaking back through the aortic valve may appear, and the patient may lose blood into the chest with very few external signs. A ruptured aneurysm of the abdominal aorta presents with pain and a pulsatile mass, and it can bleed enough to cause collapse before any laboratory result returns. In each case the absent or unequal pulse, or the pulsatile mass, is the finding that turns a vague story into an emergency.

The cardiovascular examination is also the examination of shock, and it often separates its causes. A patient with cool hands, a rapid weak pulse, a low blood pressure, and collapsed neck veins is likely to be losing volume, whether through bleeding, vomiting, or diarrhea, while a patient with cool hands, a rapid pulse, a low pressure, and distended neck veins is likely to have a heart that cannot pump or cannot fill. Warm hands with a bounding pulse and a low pressure suggest that the vessels themselves have opened wide, as they do in severe infection. The distinction is made at the bedside, with the hands and the eyes, and it changes what the clinician does next, because a failing pump and an empty circulation are treated in opposite ways. The clinician who examines the veins as carefully as the pressure will make that distinction in a minute.

These patterns were described in particular populations, and their meaning can shift with age, pregnancy, and the presence of other disease. The examination changes its shape when resources are plentiful, but not its logic. In a quiet cardiology room the clinician can listen without competing noise, repeat the blood pressure with an electronic device, ask a colleague to confirm a murmur, and send the patient for an electrocardiogram, for an echocardiogram, and for imaging of the chest. The electrocardiogram, or ECG, adds the electrical story to the mechanical one, and the echocardiogram shows the valves and the muscle directly, which is the closest thing to looking inside the heart. Even here the physical findings come first, because they decide what the test is being asked to answer, and because a normal result in a patient with a strong physical sign should prompt a repeat rather than relief.

In a noisy ward or a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same examination is performed more slowly and more carefully. The torch is used to look at the eyes for small broken vessels and at the mouth for the state of the tongue, the thermometer confirms the fever the hand suspected, and the stethoscope is used in a quiet corner because background noise hides the soft sounds that matter most. The clinician counts the pulse for a full minute, compares both arms, looks at the neck with the patient propped at an angle, and examines the ankles and the abdomen for fluid. Without an echocardiogram, the decision rests on the combination of findings, and that combination is often enough to identify the dangerous case and to arrange a referral that cannot wait. A clinic that cannot image the heart can still detect the patient who needs to be moved.

The findings must then be written so that the next clinician can use them. A pulse should be recorded with its rate, rhythm, volume, and character, and a murmur with its timing, site, radiation, and response to posture and breathing. The jugular venous pressure should be recorded with the position of the patient and the reference point used, because a bare number means nothing without them, and the blood pressure with the arm used and the position of the patient. The peripheral findings should be recorded with the side and the extent, so that a later reader can tell whether the picture is improving or worsening. The note should also show what was considered and set aside, not only what was found, because reasoning that is not written down cannot be checked by the next person.

Uncertainty is a normal finding in the cardiovascular examination, and it must be managed rather than hidden. A patient with a soft murmur, no fever, and a normal pulse may be safely watched, but the clinician must say what to watch for and when to return. A patient with chest pain, an unequal pulse, or a murmur that appeared with a fever should not be sent home with reassurance, because the dangerous causes named here progress quickly and the window for treatment is short. Where the clinician cannot be certain, the safest course is often a review in a few hours or a referral, and the reasoning for that decision should be recorded as carefully as the findings. Safety-netting protects the patient when the first decision turns out to be wrong.

A constructed illustration may make the sequence visible, and it is a teaching device rather than a record of any real person. A middle-aged patient arrives with fever and a new murmur, and the clinician, having taken the temperature and felt the pulse, looks at the hands and finds the small streaks under the nails, then examines the eyes and the spleen. Nothing about the story is dramatic, and the dangerous diagnosis is found not because the clinician was clever but because a fixed set of questions was asked in a fixed order. In another constructed illustration, a patient with sudden severe chest pain has a pressure in one arm that is 20 millimeters of mercury lower than in the other, and that single comparison moves the patient from the waiting area to the resuscitation room, though that figure is an illustration and the difference that should matter in your setting should be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The examination improves with practice, and the practice is not the memorizing of lists but the repeated comparison of what is felt and heard with what is later found to be true. Some bodies are harder to examine than others, and the difficulty should be acknowledged rather than ignored. A thick chest wall, breast tissue, or a noisy ventilator can hide a murmur and an extra sound, and in those situations the clinician must rely more openly on the history, the pulse, the blood pressure, and the visible signs. Older patients often have stiff arteries, so a pulse may feel strong while the true pressure is high, and a very fast heart rate may make murmurs impossible to time by ear alone, in which case the honest course is to note the uncertainty and arrange the test that can answer it. Describing what could not be heard is as useful as describing what was.

To summarize, the cardiovascular examination asks first whether the circulation is adequate and second whether the cause is one of the few that kill quickly, and it answers both with the hands, the eyes, and the ears before it reaches for a machine. The pulse is read in rate, rhythm, volume, and character, the jugular venous pressure is read as a manometer of the right heart, the heart sounds are dated within the cycle, and every murmur is described by its timing, its site, its radiation, and its response to posture and breathing. The peripheral signs of heart failure, the swollen ankles, the raised venous pressure, the enlarged liver, and the fine crackles at the lung bases, are the visible consequence of a heart that cannot keep up. The dangerous possibilities, infection on a valve, a tear in the aorta, compression of the heart, and the flooded lung, are sought early and deliberately, because they are the findings that change the plan within minutes. Every rate, pressure, height, and cut-off mentioned here is an illustration only, and each must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it influences a real decision. This is educational material, it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient, and where the patient is deteriorating the examination stops and the patient is treated.

# Chapter 13 — Respiratory Examination

The respiratory examination is best understood as an interrogation of a mechanical system rather than a tour of a list of diseases. The chest is a bellows, the airways are a branching set of tubes, the lungs are a pair of elastic sacs, and the whole arrangement is sealed inside a pleural space that holds each lung against the chest wall. When a patient is breathless, the fault may lie in any of those parts, and each part produces a somewhat different set of physical findings. The examination is organized to separate them, and the reasoning that drives it is the subject of this chapter.

Long before the stethoscope touches the chest, the work of breathing has already told the examiner most of what matters. The clinician who watches from the end of the bed notices the rate, the depth, the effort, and the position the body has chosen, and those observations are made in seconds. A respiratory rate that looks fast is counted rather than estimated, because the eye underestimates it consistently. The patient who sits forward with the arms braced on the knees, who uses the muscles of the neck with every breath, and who cannot finish a sentence is telling the examiner that the ventilatory reserve is nearly gone. This is the moment to look for the lethal cause rather than to continue a leisurely examination.

The lethal cause that must be named at this point is tension pneumothorax, in which air enters the pleural space and cannot leave, so that pressure builds and the lung on that side collapses while the heart and the great veins are compressed. The findings that reveal it are a sudden onset of breathlessness and chest pain, one side of the chest that moves less than the other, breath sounds that have disappeared on that side, a percussion note that is louder than the healthy side rather than dull, neck veins that are distended, and a blood pressure that is falling. The trachea may shift away from the affected side, but that sign appears late and its absence proves nothing. In this condition the decision does not wait for a chest radiograph, because the pressure is the emergency and the film is a delay.

The examination that follows has a fixed order for a reason. Inspection comes first because it is free and because it directs everything that follows. Palpation then tests the movement of the chest wall and the transmission of sound through the tissues. Percussion tests the density of what lies beneath the hand, and auscultation listens to the air itself. Each step is a question about a different layer of the system, and each finding is read against the same finding on the other side, since the patient is his own best control. A clinician who performs the steps in this order is building an argument rather than collecting sensations.

Access matters more than technique at the start. The patient should be undressed to the waist, because a vest or a gown hides asymmetry, scars, and the pattern of movement, and dignity is preserved with a blanket and a screen rather than with clothing. The examination is done in a good light, which in a well-resourced hospital means a bright room and in a remote clinic means a torch held at an angle across the chest so that the shadows reveal the shape. The back must be examined as carefully as the front, and the axillae must not be skipped, because a lesion at the apex of a lung announces itself there. The patient is asked to breathe through the mouth, since breathing through the nose makes the sounds quieter and harder to interpret.

Counting the respiratory rate is among the most useful measurements in respiratory medicine. It is counted for a full minute while the patient is unaware of being watched, because a patient who knows that the rate is being timed will alter it. A rate of 12 to 20 breaths per minute is often quoted for a resting adult, but the figure that should concern you must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the range differs with age, with pregnancy, with fever, and with the reference used by each service. The rate is least useful as a single value and most useful as a trend, so a rate that has climbed since the last set of observations carries more weight than the same number found once.

The pattern of breathing matters as much as the rate. A deep and regular pattern without distress suggests a metabolic cause rather than a mechanical one, while a shallow pattern with a fast rate suggests that the effort of each breath has become too costly. An irregular rhythm that waxes and wanes, with pauses followed by deeper breaths, points to a disturbance of the control of breathing rather than of the lung, and it is common in advanced illness and with some medicines. In an infant the signs are different and must be looked for deliberately: flaring of the nostrils, drawing in of the ribs and of the space above the sternum, and a grunting sound at the end of each breath, which is the child trying to keep the small airways open. An older patient may show almost none of this and still be dangerously short of breath, so the absence of visible distress is not reassurance.

The muscles that should be silent during quiet breathing are the ones to watch. The sternocleidomastoid muscles of the neck, the muscles between the ribs, and the muscles of the abdominal wall are recruited only when the diaphragm and the ordinary effort are insufficient. When the diaphragm is exhausted, the abdomen moves inward as the chest moves outward during inspiration, which is the reverse of the normal pattern and a sign of a failing pump. The clinician should also note whether the patient can lie flat, since a patient who must sit upright to breathe is describing a problem with the mechanics of the chest or with the heart behind it. These observations cost nothing, and they are available in a clinic with a thermometer and a torch just as they are in an intensive care unit.

Palpation begins with the movement of the chest wall. The examiner places both hands flat on the back with the thumbs meeting in the midline, asks the patient to take a deep breath, and watches how far the thumbs separate and whether they separate equally. The same maneuver can be performed on the front of the chest, and either version answers a simple question: does this side of the chest fill as well as the other. Reduced expansion on one side means that something is preventing that lung from inflating, whether pain, a collection in the pleural space, a collapsed lung, or a blocked airway. Expansion is a coarse measure and it will not detect a small lesion, but a clear asymmetry is a strong clue that directs the rest of the examination.

Tactile fremitus is the next question, and it is best understood through the physics of sound. Sound travels poorly through air and well through solid or fluid, so the vibration felt on the chest wall tells the examiner what the lung beneath the hand is made of. The examiner places the flat of the hand on the chest and asks the patient to say a short phrase in a normal voice, then compares the two sides at the same level. The vibration is increased over an area of consolidated lung, because solid tissue transmits the voice better than air does, and it is reduced over a pleural effusion, a pneumothorax, or a lung whose airway is blocked, because none of those transmits sound well. The sign is a comparison rather than a measurement, and it is more reliable in a thin chest than in a muscular one.

Percussion translates density into sound. The examiner places one finger firmly on the chest wall, strikes it with the tip of the finger of the other hand, and listens to the note that results, moving from the apex to the base and comparing the two sides at every level. Air beneath the finger gives a low, hollow, resonant note; solid lung gives a dull note; and fluid gives a note that is flatter still, often described as stony dull. The reasoning is direct, because the note reflects how much air is present in the tissue under the hand, and it therefore changes with consolidation, with collapse, with fluid, and with air in the pleural space. Percussion is difficult in a thick chest wall, it is unreliable for small collections, and its agreement between two examiners is modest, so a normal percussion note does not exclude a serious problem.

Auscultation should be performed systematically and with the patient breathing through the mouth. The examiner listens at the apex, the axilla, and the base on each side, then repeats the sequence on the back, comparing side with side at each level. The stethoscope is pressed firmly enough to make a seal but not so firmly that it hurts the chest wall, since pain alters the breathing pattern and defeats the purpose. The examiner should listen through several full breaths at each site rather than snatching one and moving on, because many abnormal sounds are intermittent. The patient should be asked to breathe a little more deeply than usual but not to the point of dizziness, since over-breathing produces misleading sounds and distress.

The normal breath sound is generated by air moving through the branching airways, and its character changes as the airways become smaller and the distance from the chest wall shortens. At the periphery, where the examiner listens over the lung, the sound is soft, low in pitch, and only slightly shorter in expiration than in inspiration, and it is described as vesicular. Over the trachea and the large airways, the sound is louder, harsher, and higher, with a clear gap between the two phases. The examiner who knows where the normal sound belongs will notice immediately when the wrong sound is heard in the wrong place. Much of respiratory auscultation is the detection of sound where it should not be.

Bronchial breathing is the name for the harsh, high-pitched sound of the large airways heard where the soft peripheral sound belongs. It appears because consolidated lung transmits sound from the airways with unusual efficiency, so the examiner hears the tube rather than the surrounding air spaces. The same quality can be heard over the top of a large pleural effusion, where the lung has been compressed against the airway, and it can be heard over the trachea in a healthy person, which is why the site matters as much as the sound. The phenomenon extends to the voice, because when the patient speaks the syllables are heard with unexpected clarity through the stethoscope over the same area, and whispered words that should be inaudible become distinct. These are among the more specific findings in the examination of the chest, and they point to solid tissue where air should be.

Crackles are the sounds produced when small airways that have closed are pulled open again as the lung inflates, or when air moves through a film of fluid in the small airways. The mechanism explains their timing. When the cause is a stiff, deflated lung that needs a high pressure to open, the crackles cluster at the end of inspiration, are fine and close together, and are heard at the bases. When the cause is fluid or secretions in larger airways, the crackles are coarser, earlier, and may shift after a cough. Crackles are therefore not a disease but a behavior of the airway, and the same sound may accompany very different processes. Their value comes from the company they keep, the history, the percussion note, and the other findings taken together.

A wheeze is the sound of air forced through a narrowed airway at speed, and its mechanism tells the examiner what it means. The narrowing may come from spasm of the muscle in the airway wall, from swelling of that wall, from secretions, or from a mass pressing on the tube, and the examination alone cannot distinguish them. A wheeze is therefore evidence that airflow is obstructed, not evidence of a particular cause. A wheeze heard without a stethoscope across a room is a loud one, and its disappearance may be alarming rather than reassuring, because it can mean that the patient is moving too little air to make a sound at all. Stridor is different, since it arises in the upper airway, is heard on inspiration, and signals a threat to the airway itself rather than to the lung.

The pleural rub is the sound of the two inflamed pleural surfaces moving against each other. It is heard in both phases of the breath, it is not altered by coughing, and it is often described as the sound of walking on fresh snow, a texture rather than a tone. The examiner finds it over a localized area, sometimes only under firm pressure of the stethoscope, and it may be the earliest physical sign of an inflamed pleura. It appears in infections of the pleura, after a clot reaches the lung, in inflammatory conditions, and in some cancers, but it is not sensitive enough that its absence excludes any of them.
