Its importance lies in the fact that it is a sign of inflammation rather than of fluid, and it therefore directs the reasoning differently from dullness or crackles.

Consolidation is the first of the three great patterns, and it means that the air spaces of part of the lung have filled with something that is not air, usually fluid or inflammatory material. The findings follow from the physics. The patient is often febrile and breathless, the rate is raised, and the cough may bring up sputum. On the affected side the chest expands less, tactile fremitus is increased, percussion is dull, and bronchial breathing is heard with crackles. The same combination is produced by pneumonia, by a part of the lung that has collapsed, and by other processes, so the pattern must be interpreted with the history. The findings are typically unilateral and localized rather than diffuse, and that distribution is itself part of the reasoning.

A pleural effusion is a collection of fluid between the lung and the chest wall, and its signs depend on how much fluid is present. A small collection may produce nothing at all, which is why the examination cannot exclude one. A larger collection reduces expansion on that side, reduces tactile fremitus, is dull to percussion, and abolishes the breath sounds below the fluid, while the lung above it may be compressed and transmit bronchial breathing with a rub or crackles. The percussion note is the most useful single sign, but its reliability at the bedside depends on the size of the collection. Fever, weight loss, and a history of exposure to tuberculosis in a patient with an effusion change the balance of causes, and the fluid must be sampled where that is possible rather than assumed.

A pneumothorax is air in the pleural space. When it is not under tension, the signs are a sudden onset of one-sided pain and breathlessness, reduced expansion on that side, a resonant or hyper-resonant percussion note where the lung should be dull or normal, and absent or greatly reduced breath sounds. The combination of hyper-resonance with absent breath sounds on the same side is the signature of air rather than fluid, and it is what separates a pneumothorax from an effusion at the bedside. The size of a pneumothorax does not map neatly onto the intensity of the signs, so a patient may be uncomfortable with little to find. In a patient with known lung disease, a small leak can become a large problem quickly, and the examination should be repeated rather than trusted once.

Tension pneumothorax is the same process with pressure behind it, and it is the emergency that this chapter names at the start. The findings that reveal it are the ones already described, and the clinician should look for them in any patient who becomes suddenly breathless and hypotensive, particularly if the patient is receiving positive pressure ventilation or has sustained a chest injury. The decision to treat does not wait for imaging, because the film takes time and the pressure is compressing the heart. The finding that would make treatment the wrong answer is a patient who is stable with a small collection and no sign of pressure, in whom the same procedure would be unnecessary. That distinction is a bedside judgment, and it must be made against the current guideline and the local protocol, which vary in how they define the unstable patient.

A large effusion that compresses the lung is dangerous for a different reason. The fluid occupies space, pushes the lung aside, and may shift the mediastinum, so that the trachea and the apex beat are displaced away from the affected side. The patient becomes breathless at rest and cannot lie flat, and the percussion note becomes stony dull over a wide area. If the fluid is blood the cause may be trauma or a cancer, and if it is infected the patient is septic, and either possibility changes the urgency rather than the physical findings. The examination cannot tell the nature of the fluid, and the reasoning must therefore include the history, the temperature, and the local capacity to sample it.

The silent chest and the exhausted respiratory effort are the third dangerous presentation, and they are recognized by an absence of noise rather than by any sound. In severe obstruction the airways are so narrow that air moves too slowly to generate a wheeze, so the examiner hears a quiet chest in a patient who is clearly working hard. The patient who is tiring may become quiet, drowsy, or confused, and the rate may fall as the effort fails, which is why a falling rate in a breathless patient is a warning rather than an improvement. The findings that demand immediate help are a diminishing level of consciousness, a weakening effort, and a chest that has gone quiet while the distress continues. This is a situation in which the examination is interrupted and help is summoned, because the next event may be respiratory arrest.

The most important limitation of the respiratory examination is that a normal result excludes very little. A clot in the lung may leave the chest entirely normal, with no crackles, no rub, and no change in the percussion note, and a patient whose only findings are breathlessness and a fast pulse may still have a dangerous obstruction of the pulmonary artery. Early pneumonia may be inaudible, and tuberculosis in its early stages may produce no findings at all. A small pneumothorax and a small effusion may both be missed by careful hands. The clinician who understands this examines the chest for the findings that are present rather than to obtain reassurance, and he uses the history, the vital signs, and the risk factors to decide how much weight a normal examination can carry.

When imaging is immediately available, the examination does not become unnecessary; it becomes the frame in which the image is read. A chest radiograph answers questions about consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax, and the size of the heart, and computed tomography, or CT, answers finer questions about the lung substance and the vessels. Ultrasound imaging at the bedside is increasingly used to find fluid and to guide its sampling, and it is often more sensitive than the radiograph for a small collection. Each of these tools was studied in a particular population and has a limit to its resolution, and none of them replaces the observation of the patient. The clinician who examines first knows what to look for in the image, and notices when the image and the patient disagree, which is the moment that needs explaining rather than dismissing.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the examination is the imaging. The clinician can identify a consolidation with reasonable confidence when the findings are unilateral and consistent, recognize a large effusion by the stony dullness and the displaced apex, and identify a pneumothorax by the hyper-resonance and the absent breath sounds. What cannot be identified at the bedside must be treated as possible and referred, and the question is not whether the patient has a disease but whether the patient can safely wait. The thermometer identifies fever, and its pattern over time is itself a diagnostic instrument, while the torch examines the throat, the tongue, and the mouth for the signs that a chest examination would otherwise miss. A clinician working this way is not practising a reduced medicine; he is performing the same reasoning with a smaller set of tools.

Pulse oximetry, where it is available, adds a number that must be interpreted rather than obeyed. A saturation of 94 per cent is often used as a threshold for concern in a healthy adult breathing room air, but the value that matters must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the target differs for a patient with chronic lung disease, for a child, and for a pregnant woman. The device is unreliable in poor perfusion, in motion, in severe anemia, and in some patients with deeply pigmented skin, in whom several devices read falsely high. A normal saturation does not exclude a clot in the lung, since that patient may maintain oxygenation while ventilation and circulation are compromised. The number is a useful trend and a poor verdict.

A constructed illustration may make the reasoning visible. Suppose an adult arrives with a fever that has lasted some days, a cough, and breathlessness that has worsened, and the examination finds a rate of 24 breaths per minute, reduced expansion at the right base, dull percussion there, increased tactile fremitus, and bronchial breathing with fine crackles over the same area. A rate of 24 breaths per minute is above the usual resting range and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, as must the local definition of a fever. The pattern is coherent, because the findings all point to the same piece of lung and the mechanism of each is explained by solid tissue where air should be. No single sign is decisive, but the constellation is strong, and the reasoning then asks whether this patient is well enough to be managed where he is.

A second constructed illustration concerns the emergency. Suppose a patient develops sudden breathlessness after a procedure on the chest, becomes restless, and has a falling blood pressure with distended neck veins and no breath sounds on one side, where percussion is louder than on the other. The finding that makes this a tension pneumothorax rather than a simple one is the combination of pressure and compromise, and the finding that would change the decision is a patient who is stable with the same physical signs and no evidence of obstruction to the return of blood to the heart. The clinician who waits for a radiograph in the first patient has misunderstood which of the two problems is urgent. The procedure is named here as a decision rather than a technique, and that decision belongs to the setting and to the local protocol.

A patient can deteriorate during the examination itself, and the clinician must be willing to stop. If the rate climbs while the chest is being examined, if the patient becomes drowsy, or if the effort visibly weakens, the examination is over and the response begins. The findings gathered so far are still useful and should be recorded, but they are no longer the priority. The clinician who completes a leisurely sequence on a patient who is failing has confused thoroughness with care, and the principle that governs every chapter of this book applies here: when the patient is becoming more ill, the reasoning pauses and the patient is treated.

To summarize, the respiratory examination is a structured interrogation of the mechanics of breathing, beginning with the observation of effort and rate before the stethoscope is applied. Inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation each ask about a different layer of the system, and the findings are read as patterns: consolidation with its dullness and bronchial breathing, effusion with its stony dullness and reduced expansion, and pneumothorax with its hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds. The tension pneumothorax, the large effusion that compresses the lung, and the silent chest of the exhausted patient are named as emergencies, and each is recognized by findings rather than by a radiograph. Every number, threshold, and reference value mentioned here is an illustration only and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. The examination is performed with a full service behind it and again with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, and it is the same reasoning in both places. It does not replace training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient, and a normal chest never excludes a dangerous cause on its own.

# Chapter 14 — Abdominal Examination

The abdomen is the part of the body where the ordinary and the lethal wear the same face, so it must be examined in a fixed sequence rather than with a hopeful hand. Indigestion and a strained muscle are common, and so are a ruptured aortic aneurysm, a perforated viscus, a strangulated hernia, and an ectopic pregnancy, and each of them can begin as a vague ache. A systematic examination makes the dangerous findings hard to miss and the common ones easy to set aside once they have been sought. This is educational material and cannot replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. What follows is reasoning to be practised under supervision, not a set of instructions to be applied alone.

Four catastrophes deserve naming at the very beginning, each with the finding that would betray it. A ruptured aortic aneurysm appears as a pulsatile, expansile upper abdominal mass, often with pain that has traveled to the back or flank, a rapid pulse, and a falling pressure. A perforated viscus produces a rigid, board-like abdomen that hurts on any movement, with bowel sounds that have gone quiet. A strangulated hernia is an irreducible, tender swelling at one of the natural orifices, and the bowel inside it is already losing its blood supply. An ectopic pregnancy presents with lower abdominal pain, a missed or unusual period, and the signs of peritoneal irritation or internal bleeding in a woman of childbearing age. The fifth danger is the abdomen that is tender but not yet rigid, because early peritonitis and mesenteric ischemia can hide behind an examination that looks almost unremarkable.

The reasoning is identical in a hospital full of machines and in a clinic whose whole equipment is a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, but the consequence of a finding differs enormously. Where a laboratory, a bedside ultrasound, computed tomography, and a surgeon are within reach, the examination decides which of those to summon and how fast. Where none of them exists, it decides whether the patient can be watched safely or must begin a journey that may take hours. The clinician who examines well with his hands will examine better when imaging exists, because he already knows which question the image must answer.

Before the hands touch the abdomen, several things must be settled, and they are part of the examination rather than a courtesy around it. The patient lies flat with the head on a single pillow, the arms at the sides rather than folded behind the head, and the knees slightly drawn up to relax the wall. The abdomen is exposed from the lower ribs to the groin, because examining through clothing hides exactly the scars, hernias, and swellings that matter. Hands and stethoscope are warmed, the space is private, and the patient is told what will happen and asked for permission. For the rectal and pelvic parts, consent is sought separately, a chaperone is offered, and a refusal is respected without pressure and recorded without judgement.

The classical order is inspection, then auscultation, then percussion, and finally palpation, and the order is not arbitrary. Listening precedes touching because palpation and percussion stir the bowel and change the sounds the stethoscope is meant to record. Palpation comes last with the painful region saved for the end, because a wall already tightened by pain hides everything beneath it. Within palpation the order runs from light to deep and from the least tender region towards the most tender. The examiner watches the face throughout, because a grimace is a finding in its own right and often more honest than the patient's account.

Inspection begins as soon as the abdomen is uncovered and continues while the patient describes the pain. The examiner notes whether the shape is flat, hollowed, or distended, and whether the distension is uniform or local. Scars are named by position and direction, since a scar is surgical history the patient may have forgotten to mention. Dilated veins, bruising around the umbilicus or in the flanks, yellowing of the skin, and small spider-like vessels on the upper trunk all point to what may be happening inside. The examiner also looks for visible peristalsis, and for any bulge at the umbilicus, the groins, or the line of an old operation.

Distension is produced by a small number of things, and the examiner works through them silently. Gas, free fluid, fat in the wall, a growing fetus, a large mass, and a full bladder can each create the same rounded shape, and the rest of the examination separates them. A visible upper abdominal pulsation matters greatly, because a normal aorta transmits its impulse forward while an aneurysm expands in every direction. The examiner therefore views the pulsation from the side, where an expansile mass seems to push the wall outward in two directions at once. A mass that merely lifts with each beat usually lies in front of the aorta, while a mass that widens with each beat is the aorta itself.

Auscultation is performed with the diaphragm laid lightly on the skin, because pressing hard creates artefacts of its own. Normal bowel sounds are irregular soft clicks and gurgles, and their complete absence means something only after the examiner has listened in several regions long enough to be sure. High-pitched rushing sounds arriving in waves suggest bowel contracting hard against an obstruction, and a tinkling quality carries the same implication. A quiet abdomen may instead mean a bowel paralysed after surgery, an inflamed peritoneum, or a disturbed electrolyte, so the sounds are always read with the rest of the picture. The examiner also listens over the epigastrium for a bruit, over the liver and spleen for a friction rub, and at the stomach for a splashing sound that suggests an organ that cannot empty. A bruit may be heard over an entirely normal aorta, but a bruit with a pulsatile expansile mass and new back pain is a different and far more urgent matter.

A common teaching is to listen for a full minute in each region before declaring the abdomen silent, but that interval is a convention rather than a law. Confirm the duration your own teachers and current guideline recommend against the local protocol, because the recommended listening time varies between settings, examiners, and editions. What matters more than the exact interval is the discipline of listening in several places and recording that the examination was quiet rather than normal. A truly silent abdomen in a patient with pain and distension is serious, and it can never be inferred from a hurried listen through clothing.

Percussion is the bridge between listening and feeling, and it answers questions palpation alone cannot. Tapping produces a tympanic note over gas and a dull note over fluid, solid organ, or stool, and the pattern of notes maps what lies beneath. The examiner percusses lightly at first, then follows the change of note that marks the edge of the liver, the spleen, a mass, or a full bladder. Percussion is used deliberately over a painful region as well, because percussion tenderness is a reliable sign of peritoneal irritation and can be elicited when deep palpation is too distressing. The technique is gentle, the movement comes from the wrist, and the examiner watches the face for the flinch that shows the spot has been found.

Free fluid is detected by looking for shifting dullness, in which the dull note over the flank moves as the patient is rolled towards one side. The test relies on fluid settling with gravity while gas-filled bowel floats, and it becomes detectable only once the collection is large enough to change the note reliably. A figure of roughly 1 liter is often taught as the volume needed, but treat that as an illustration rather than a measurement you can trust, and confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the amount differs with the patient's build and the examiner's technique. When the collection is very large a fluid thrill may be felt by flicking one flank while the flat of the other hand rests opposite, with a hand in the midline to prevent a wave of fat being mistaken for fluid. Where these signs are equivocal, the everted umbilicus and the other signs of chronic liver disease carry as much weight as the note itself.

One percussion finding points towards perforation and deserves special attention. The normal liver is dull, and free gas under the diaphragm can press against it and reduce or abolish that dullness. The finding is famous but unreliable in both directions, because a length of normal gut can lie in front of the liver and imitate the change. Where no imaging exists, a rigid abdomen, quiet bowel sounds, and a lost area of liver dullness together are enough to force the decision rather than reassure the examiner.

Palpation is performed with a warm, flat hand, beginning lightly and examining the least painful region before the worst. The examiner asks the patient to breathe gently through the mouth and to say what he feels, because tenderness is data and its location is more useful than a general impression of tightness. Light palpation surveys the whole abdomen for a mass, an area of resistance, or an unexpected fullness. Deep palpation follows in the same order, and for the liver, spleen, and kidneys a bimanual technique presses one hand towards the other in time with breathing. Every finding is described by what the examiner actually did and felt, because a note that says the abdomen was soft and non-tender means little without saying where the hands went.

Guarding is contraction of the abdominal wall, and its meaning depends on whether it is voluntary or involuntary. Voluntary guarding is the patient deliberately bracing against expected pain, and it relaxes when he is distracted or asked to breathe slowly. Involuntary guarding is generated by the spinal reflex that fires when the peritoneum is inflamed, and it does not disappear when the patient is reassured. Rigidity is the extreme of involuntary guarding, in which the wall becomes board-like and barely moves with respiration. The examiner therefore never judges on the strength of guarding alone, but asks whether the tightening can be abolished by the patient's own effort and whether it is confined to one region.

Rebound tenderness is the pain felt when the examining hand is removed after pressure, and it reflects sudden movement of an inflamed peritoneum rather than the pressure itself. It is elicited deliberately and gently, because the maneuver hurts and a rough test produces the same complaint in a patient who does not have peritonitis. Peritonism is the whole pattern: involuntary guarding, tenderness on percussion, pain on movement or coughing, quiet bowel sounds, and often a rising pulse with a falling pressure. The examiner thinks in terms of that pattern rather than one positive sign, because each sign is imperfect while the pattern is far harder to produce falsely. A patient with peritonism needs the surgical decision now, whatever the underlying cause turns out to be.

There is a particular patient who punishes the clinician, and he is the one whose abdomen is tender but not yet rigid. In the first hours of a perforated ulcer, in the early phase of a strangulated hernia, in mesenteric ischemia, and in a leaking aneurysm, the classical signs may be absent or seem mild. The pain of mesenteric ischemia is classically severe and out of proportion to a soft abdomen, and that mismatch should alarm the examiner rather than reassure him. The same holds for the older patient, the patient whose immune response is suppressed by illness or treatment, and the patient with poorly controlled diabetes. In these people the decision rests on the trajectory and the repeated examination rather than the first set of findings, and the threshold for asking for help is lower rather than higher.

Organomegaly is assessed by the character of the organ rather than by the number of fingerbreadths below the rib, and this is one of the most useful habits in the examination. A liver edge may be felt in many healthy people, especially when a high diaphragm or a distended lung has pushed it down, so its presence alone proves little. What matters is the span from the upper border percussed in the chest to the lower edge, the consistency of that edge, whether the surface is smooth or irregular, whether the organ is tender, and whether it moves with respiration. A span of roughly 12 to 15 centimeters is often quoted as normal in an adult, but treat that range as an example of the reasoning and confirm the figure against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the span changes with body size, technique, and the reference the examiner was taught from. A hard, nodular, non-tender liver means something different from a smooth, tender, soft one, even when both edges lie at the same level. The examiner therefore describes what he felt rather than how far he felt it.

The spleen is not normally palpable, and when felt it is usually the tip of an organ that has enlarged enough to travel below the left rib margin. It is identified by the way it moves downwards with inspiration towards the right lower abdomen, by a notch on its inner border, by dullness to percussion, and by the fact that the examiner cannot reach above it. The kidney behaves differently, because it moves with respiration, can be held between the two hands, is often reachable from the flank, and the examiner can usually get above it. Both kidneys are examined bimanually with one hand lifting from behind, and a kidney that is enlarged, tender, or irregular suggests obstruction, infection, or a mass. A very large spleen that crosses the midline narrows the differential towards a small set of causes.

The bladder is examined as a suprapubic dullness that extends upward when full and disappears after the patient passes urine, so a bladder still palpable after voiding suggests retention. Any mass is described by its site, its size in the examiner's own units, its shape, surface, consistency, mobility, whether it moves with respiration, and whether it is tender. A mass that pulsates, one that is hard and irregular, and one that is fixed and painless each carry their own short list of explanations. A swelling that disappears when the abdominal wall is tensed probably lies in the wall rather than within the abdomen, and describing a mass by how it behaves is more useful to the next clinician than naming the organ it might belong to.

The aorta is palpated deeply in the upper abdomen, with the examiner's hand placed along the vessel rather than across it, and the width of the pulsation is noted. In a thin patient the normal aorta may be felt to pulsate, and that alone is not an aneurysm. The finding that matters is a pulsatile mass that is expansile, that widens in two directions as the hands are placed on either side, and that is wider than about 5 centimeters across. That figure is an illustration and not a rule, so confirm the current guideline and the local protocol for your setting, because the width that triggers a decision differs between countries and editions and is influenced by the patient's size. Aortic palpation must be gentle, and the examiner should not chase the finding at the expense of everything else. A bruit heard over such a mass, or an absent femoral pulse on one side, makes the situation more urgent still, because an aneurysm in the abdomen and a blockage in the legs often travel together.

Hernias are sought at every orifice, and the search is not complete until all of them have been examined. The umbilicus, both groins, the femoral canal below the groin crease, the site of every previous operation, and the rare sites along the abdominal wall each deserve a deliberate look and feel. The patient is examined flat and standing, and asked to cough while the examiner's finger rests at the inguinal ring, because a hernia invisible at rest may appear with a rise in abdominal pressure. An umbilical hernia in an adult with a distended abdomen may be the outward sign of fluid within, and should lead back to the liver and spleen rather than being dismissed as cosmetic. A hernia with colicky pain, vomiting, and distension is an emergency until proven otherwise, and it must be looked for before the abdomen is dismissed as a medical problem.

A strangulated hernia has trapped its contents, and the bowel inside loses its blood supply while the examination is still taking place. The signs are an irreducible tender swelling, skin that may be red or warm over it, and the features of obstruction: colicky pain, vomiting, distension, and later the passage of nothing at all. The absence of a cough impulse over the swelling is ominous, because it suggests the neck of the sac is tightly closed. The patient may not volunteer the swelling, and an obese or large abdomen may conceal it from everyone. When strangulation is suspected the decision is surgical and immediate, and waiting for a clearer picture is unlikely to improve the outcome.

Bowel obstruction produces a pattern worth assembling before any image is seen. The patient has colicky pain in waves, vomiting, distension, and a failure to pass stool or gas, and the bowel sounds may be high-pitched and rushing at first and quiet later. A previous operation raises the probability of adhesions, a palpable mass raises the possibility of a tumor, and a hernia at any orifice raises the possibility of strangulation. Fever, tenderness, or a rising pulse in a patient with obstruction suggests the bowel is already compromised and the problem has become a surgical emergency. The record should say clearly which features are present and which are absent, because the next clinician will decide differently depending on the answer.

The rectal examination is quick, informative, and frequently omitted for reasons that have more to do with the examiner than the patient. It is performed with the patient on his left side and the knees drawn up after the reason is explained and consent obtained, or in any other position he finds acceptable. The examiner inspects the skin around the anus for cracks, openings, skin tags, prolapse, and external swellings, then passes a lubricated gloved finger gently through the anal canal. The finger assesses the tone of the sphincter, the contents of the rectum, the presence of blood, and the surface of the walls, and it reaches further than most beginners expect. In the male the prostate is felt through the front wall and described by size, consistency, central groove, and any nodule, while in the female a bimanual examination can be completed with the other hand on the abdomen. It must not be omitted when there is bleeding from the gut, when a pelvic or rectal mass is suspected, when weight loss or anemia is unexplained, or when a collection of pus is suspected after surgery, and it must not be performed without consent, privacy, and a chaperone.

The pelvic examination answers questions the rectal examination cannot, and it deserves the same frankness in the description. With consent and a chaperone the examiner inspects the external genitalia, passes a speculum to see the cervix and vaginal walls, and then performs a bimanual examination with one or two fingers in the vagina and the other hand on the lower abdomen. The size, position, and mobility of the uterus are noted, the structures beside it are felt for a mass or tenderness, and the cervix is moved gently to see whether that reproduces the pain, which is a sign of pelvic infection. Blood in the vagina, a discharging cervix, an ulcer, or a mass all change the differential immediately. The examination is limited to what the clinical question requires, and the patient's comfort and dignity are part of the technique rather than a concession to it.

Ectopic pregnancy is the diagnosis that makes the pelvic examination urgent, and it is named here because the cost of missing it is measured in minutes. The patient is a woman of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain, often on one side, a missed or unusual period, and sometimes slight vaginal bleeding. The examination may reveal tenderness on one side of the pelvis, a tender mass beside the uterus, and pain when the cervix is moved, while a ruptured ectopic adds the whole picture of peritoneal irritation with a rising pulse and a falling pressure. A pregnancy test changes the reasoning more than any other single step, and where no test exists the menstrual history and the signs of early pregnancy must carry the weight. The examiner who considers the possibility in every woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain will find it, and the one who assumes a gastrointestinal cause may not.

A patient who is shocked and whose abdomen is the source requires a different pace from one who is comfortable. A rapid pulse, a pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury, cool clammy skin, and a pulsatile abdominal mass together describe a leaking aneurysm, and they should move the clinician to summon help rather than to finish a leisurely examination. That pressure is an illustration of the reasoning, so confirm the figure your service treats as shock against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the value is changed by age, pregnancy, longstanding high blood pressure, and the definition being used. A falling urine output, which for an adult may be described as less than half a milliliter for each kilogram of body weight in an hour, is another sign that the circulation is failing, and that figure must likewise be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol because it is adjusted for age and illness. The abdomen may be soft in such a patient, and a soft abdomen is not a reason to wait.

When imaging is available the abdominal examination becomes the question the image is asked to answer. A bedside ultrasound can show free fluid, a distended gallbladder, a dilated aorta, a pregnancy inside the uterus or outside it, and an obstructed kidney, and it can be performed while the patient is still being examined. Computed tomography, or CT, gives a more complete picture of perforation, obstruction, inflammation of the pancreas, and masses, while magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answers particular questions in the liver and the biliary tree. The examiner decides what he expects the image to show before it is performed, so an unexpected result is recognized as a surprise rather than accepted without thought. Imaging extends the examination but does not replace the reasoning that chose it, and a normal scan in a clearly unwell patient is a reason to think again rather than a reason to relax.

Where imaging will not come, the examination must be performed more thoroughly and repeated more often, because nothing else will correct a first impression. A torch allows the skin around the anus and the hernial orifices to be examined properly, and a thermometer turns a vague sense of illness into a number that can be followed. A stethoscope brings the bowel sounds, bruits, and rubs, and a watch allows the pulse and respiratory rate to be counted rather than estimated. The urine can be inspected for color and tested if a dipstick exists, and weight, intake, and output can be recorded by hand. The decision that follows is not a diagnosis but a plan: whether the patient can be watched safely, whether treatment can begin on the clinical picture, and whether the journey must start now. The examination also has limits that should be stated honestly, since it cannot exclude an early obstruction, a small perforation, or a leaking aneurysm with confidence, and a normal examination in a worrying story is a reason to repeat it rather than a licence to discharge.

A constructed illustration may help to fix the sequence. Imagine an older man with some days of vague mid-abdominal discomfort and a new ache in the back, no fever, a soft abdomen, and the only striking findings of a rapid pulse and a pressure lower than his usual. The examination is not complete until the aorta has been palpated deliberately, and if it is expansile and unusually wide the working diagnosis changes from indigestion to a leaking aneurysm and the plan changes with it. Now imagine a young woman with lower abdominal pain and a fainting episode, in whom the examiner asks about the last period before deciding the pain is colic, and receives the answer that redirects everything. Neither patient is real and neither should be read as a portrait, for they are constructed only to show how one further question can reverse the order of a differential.

To summarize, the abdominal examination proceeds from inspection to auscultation to percussion and finally to palpation, with the painful region examined last and the hernial orifices and the rectum sought deliberately rather than hopefully. It reads guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness, and peritonism as a pattern of peritoneal irritation rather than as isolated signs, and it judges an organ by its character rather than by the number of fingerbreadths below the rib. The dangers are named at the bedside and not deferred, among them a ruptured aortic aneurysm, a perforated viscus, a strangulated hernia, an ectopic pregnancy, and the abdomen that is tender without yet being rigid, each with the finding that would reveal it and each demanding a decision. Every number in this chapter, whether a width, a span, a pressure, a rate, a temperature, a volume, or an interval, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This recording is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A tender abdomen that does not yet look peritonitic is a patient to be re-examined and discussed, never a patient to be reassured and sent away.

# Chapter 15 — Neurological Examination

The neurological examination is an exercise in localization rather than a parade of tests, and every maneuver in it answers one question about where in the nervous system the trouble lies. A finding earns its place only because it narrows that map, so a clinician who holds the map in mind examines with a purpose. This chapter describes one method in two forms, a screening round for any bedside with nothing beyond a torch, a thermometer and a stethoscope, and a focused examination for a hospital where imaging and specialist help are at hand. What follows is educational description and not a protocol, and it is no substitute for training, supervision, the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient, or the rules of the local service. Two emergencies dominate this territory and are named now so that they are carried through every step: the stroke that still has time for its blood supply to be restored, and the compression of the spinal cord that has almost none. Both are revealed by findings the examination below is designed to expose before any image is made.

Everything begins with the level of consciousness, because a patient who is not fully awake cannot be examined reliably, and because a falling level is the most sensitive sign of a nervous system that is failing. The first observations are made before any instrument is touched: whether the eyes are open, whether the patient answers, whether the answer makes sense, and whether a command is followed. The Glasgow coma scale is the standard formalization of those observations, converting eye opening, verbal response and the best motor response into a number that can be handed to the next clinician without ambiguity. The scale runs from 3 to 15, and the total is less informative than its parts, since a patient who is mute from a stroke and a patient who is deeply unconscious may reach a similar figure by different routes. That range is a convention rather than a law of nature, so confirm the version in use against the current guideline and the local protocol, and remember that a patient who is intubated, sedated, deaf or speaking another language cannot be scored fairly.

Beyond the level of consciousness lies the content of the mind, which localizes more loosely but still matters. Orientation to time, place and person, attention, short term recall and the use of language are tested within the conversation, by asking the patient to repeat three words, to count backwards, to name common objects and to obey a two step command. A patient who is alert but cannot repeat a phrase has a problem of language, while one who speaks fluently but produces nonsense has a problem of comprehension. Confusion that has developed over hours is not a psychiatric event until a metabolic and a structural cause have both been excluded, and the bedside glucose is the most useful test in that search. What the examination adds is whether a focal deficit accompanies the confusion, since that raises the probability of a structural cause and changes the speed of everything that follows.

The most reversible dangerous mimic of a neurological emergency is hypoglycemia, and the finding that reveals it is a glucose measurement made at the bedside before any other interpretation is offered. A drowsy, sweating patient who cannot give a coherent history may be labeled as having had a stroke by an examiner who does not measure glucose, and that error is tragic because the remedy is simple. A blood glucose of 3 millimoles per liter is treated as hypoglycemia in many services, but the level that matters depends on the patient, the meter and the local protocol, so verify the cut off in the current guideline and the local protocol. The same caution applies to a patient known to have diabetes who arrives with focal weakness, because both high and low glucose can produce a deficit that resolves when the level is corrected. In a clinic without a laboratory, a glucose meter is one of the few pieces of equipment worth its space, and where even that is absent the history of missed meals or recent illness must carry the suspicion.

The cranial nerves are examined in the order that follows the face from the eyes outward, and each step answers a question that a different part of the brainstem must satisfy. Pupils are inspected in a dim room with a torch, and size, symmetry and the reaction to light are recorded together, because a pupil of 3 millimeters that reacts briskly means something different from the same pupil that is fixed. Any figure for pupil size is a local convention, so the number that defines abnormality must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, and the more useful question is whether the two pupils are equal and whether each responds. A dilated pupil that does not react, especially with a drooping eyelid and an eye turned outward, points to compression of the third cranial nerve, which in a patient with a headache warns of an aneurysm or of a brain beginning to herniate. Eye movements are tested in all directions, and double vision and nystagmus are recorded for their direction and for the position that provokes them.

Visual fields are tested by confrontation, one eye at a time, and a defect that respects the vertical midline points behind the eye while one that respects the horizontal midline points to the optic nerve. The back of the eye is examined with an ophthalmoscope where one exists, because swelling of the optic disc signals raised pressure inside the head. The face is inspected at rest and then asked to move, and the distinction that matters is whether the forehead wrinkles on the weak side, since a weakness that spares the forehead suggests a lesion above the brainstem while one that includes it suggests the facial nerve itself. Hearing is screened by rubbing fingers beside each ear or by whispering, and the gag reflex and soft palate are observed in any patient who is drowsy, has swallowed badly or has a hoarse voice. Difficulty with speech, swallowing or the protection of the airway demands immediate attention because it predicts aspiration and respiratory failure.

Motor examination begins with observation, because wasting, an abnormal posture or a limb that moves less than its partner is visible before any test is performed. The patient is asked to hold both arms out with the eyes closed, and a slow downward drift of one arm with the palm turning inward is a subtle sign of an upper motor neuron lesion that is easily missed. Tone is assessed by moving each limb passively through its range, and the examiner is feeling for resistance rather than for power. Increased tone that gives way suddenly, like the closing of a clasp knife, suggests a lesion of the corticospinal pathway, while a constant resistance throughout the movement suggests the rigidity of a basal ganglia disorder. Reduced tone suggests a lower motor neuron lesion, a cerebellar lesion or the acute phase after injury to the cord, and the limb that feels different is the one that deserves the closer look.

Power is tested in each limb group, and the examiner resists the movement rather than merely asking for it, because a weak patient will often appear to move well when no load is applied. The conventional grade runs from 0, meaning no movement, to 5, meaning normal power, and the grade is useful only when it is anchored to what the patient was asked to do. These numbers are a shared shorthand rather than a measurement, and the boundaries between them must be read according to the current guideline and the local protocol, which differ between training programmes. The pattern of weakness matters more than its severity, so the examiner notes whether it is proximal or distal, whether it affects one side, both legs or one leg and one arm, and whether the face or tongue is involved. Weakness that begins in the feet and climbs, especially with reduced reflexes and lost sensation, can reach the muscles of breathing, and a record that says only that the patient is weak has thrown away the most valuable half of the finding.

The sensory examination is the most subjective part of the encounter and therefore the one where technique matters most. Light touch is tested with a wisp of cotton, pinprick with a fresh disposable pin, temperature with a cold or a warm object, vibration with a tuning fork on a bony prominence, and joint position by moving a toe or a finger slightly while the eyes are closed. The modalities travel by different pathways, so a patient with normal vibration sense may still have lost pain and temperature, and the reverse is equally possible. The examiner maps any loss by its border rather than its extent, because a sensory level across the trunk is one of the most important localizing findings in neurology, and a border that shifts with distraction suggests that the loss is not organic.

A loss of sensation in a single dermatome points to a spinal nerve root, while a loss that follows the territory of a named nerve points to the nerve itself, and a loss that begins at a level and continues downwards points to the spinal cord. A glove and stocking pattern affecting the feet and hands symmetrically suggests a length dependent process such as the damage of diabetes or of alcohol, and a patchy loss that follows no rule may point to the brain. Cortical sensory testing, in which a number is drawn on the palm or an object is placed in the hand with the eyes closed, is abnormal in lesions of the sensory cortex even when the simpler modalities are preserved. The sensory examination is unreliable in a drowsy, distracted or frightened patient, so a normal result there is weak evidence while an abnormal result in a fully alert patient is strong.

Tendon reflexes are tested with a tendon hammer where one is available and with the edge of a hand, a stethoscope or a firm finger where it is not, and the response is compared left with right. The biceps, triceps, suprapatellar and ankle jerks sample the roots of the upper and lower limbs, and the grading from 0 to 4 is a shared vocabulary whose meaning depends on the examiner and the service. A reflex that is much brisker on one side than the other suggests a lesion of the corticospinal pathway above the level of that reflex, while a reflex that is lost suggests a problem in the nerve, the root or the muscle it supplies. The plantar response is elicited by stroking the sole and watching the toes, since extension of the great toe with fanning of the others is a sign of a corticospinal lesion in an adult, and sustained clonus at the ankle is a further sign of the same pathway. The anal reflex, obtained by stroking the skin around the anus and watching for contraction, is easy to omit and carries decisive information when the spinal cord is in question, and that scale is a local convention to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The cerebellum is examined by asking for movements that require accuracy rather than strength. Finger to nose testing, first with the eyes open and then closed, reveals a tremor that worsens as the target is approached, which is the intention tremor of a cerebellar lesion. Heel to shin testing is performed on each side, and rapid alternating movements such as turning the palm up and down show a slowness and irregularity that is called dysdiadochokinesia. The signs of a cerebellar lesion appear on the same side as the lesion, unlike the signs of a cerebral lesion, and this rule alone prevents a great deal of confusion. Truncal ataxia is tested by asking the patient to sit without support, and a patient who cannot sit steadily should not be asked to walk unaided, while scanning speech and a coarse nystagmus complete the picture of a cerebellar problem.

Gait is the most informative single maneuver in the neurological examination, because it integrates power, tone, sensation, coordination and balance in one act. The patient is asked to walk a few steps while the examiner watches from the side and then the front, noting the width of the base, the length of the stride, the swing of the arms and the posture of the trunk. Walking heel to toe along a line tests balance more finely and reveals a truncal instability that a normal walk can hide, while walking on the heels tests the muscles that lift the foot and walking on the toes tests the calf. Turning is observed because a patient with a basal ganglia disorder turns in several small steps rather than in one movement, and a patient whose legs move well when lying down but not when standing may have a problem of the frontal lobes rather than of the legs. The examiner should be ready to catch the patient, and no gait test should be attempted that cannot be safely supervised.

A hemiplegic gait drags a stiff leg in a circle, with the arm held flexed and the foot scraping, while a parkinsonian gait is slow and shuffling, with small steps, a stooped posture and a reduced arm swing. An ataxic gait is wide based and unsteady, and it worsens when the eyes are closed if the cause is a loss of position sense rather than a cerebellar lesion. A steppage gait lifts the foot high because the muscles that raise the toes are weak, and a waddling gait rolls from side to side because the muscles around the hips are weak. The Romberg test separates the two great causes of unsteadiness, since a patient who is steady with the eyes open and unsteady with them closed has lost position sense, while a patient unsteady in both conditions more likely has a cerebellar or a vestibular problem.

Localization is the discipline that turns these findings into a place. A lesion of the cortex produces a deficit on the opposite side of the body, while a lesion of the brainstem produces a cranial nerve deficit on one side with weakness or sensory loss on the opposite side, and this crossing pattern is one of the most reliable signs in neurology. A lesion of the spinal cord produces a level below which sensation is altered, with weakness and brisk reflexes below that level, and a lesion of a nerve root produces pain in the territory of the root and a loss of the reflex that the root carries. A lesion of a peripheral nerve produces weakness and sensory loss in a territory that follows the nerve, with reduced reflexes and often wasting. A lesion of the muscle produces weakness that is usually symmetrical and proximal with normal sensation, and a lesion at the junction between nerve and muscle produces fatiguable weakness, often of the eyelids, the face and the muscles of swallowing.

The first of the two emergencies that must never wait is the stroke that still has time. A sudden focal deficit, whether weakness, numbness, a disturbance of speech or a loss of vision in one eye, is a stroke until another explanation is proved, so the examination should be brief, targeted and repeated rather than complete. The findings that raise concern are a new weakness of the face and arm, a new inability to understand or produce speech, a new visual field defect, and a deviation of the eyes towards the side of the lesion. The decision that matters is whether the blood supply can be restored, and it depends on the time since onset, the appearance of the imaging, and the presence of conditions that make restoration dangerous. The finding that would make restoration the right answer is a disabling deficit in a patient who is within the window set by the local protocol with imaging that shows no bleeding, while the finding that would make it wrong is hemorrhage on the scan, a deficit already resolving, or an onset that cannot be established. That window must be looked up in the current guideline and the local protocol rather than trusted from memory.

The second emergency is compression of the spinal cord, which is recognized by findings that are easy to collect and easy to overlook. The patient often has back pain that is worse when lying flat and that wakes them at night, sometimes with a history of cancer elsewhere in the body, and the examination may show a band of altered sensation around the trunk and weakness that is worse in the legs than in the arms. The findings that demand immediate action are a sensory level, a loss of the sensation of a full bladder or of urination itself, numbness around the saddle area, and a reduction or loss of the anal tone. When the compression lies below the end of the cord the same findings arise from the cauda equina, and the whole spine is the unit of interest because a second level may exist elsewhere. The decision here is not about a drug but about the speed of imaging and specialist referral, and the finding that makes immediate action right is a deficit that is still incomplete in a patient who can still be helped, while the finding that makes delay acceptable is stable mechanical pain with no neurological signs.

Infection of the nervous system belongs in the same urgent group and is recognized at the bedside by a small number of findings. Neck stiffness, an inability to touch the chin to the chest, and pain on extending the knee while the hip is flexed are the classic signs of meningeal irritation, though they are often absent in the very young, the very old and the very ill. Fever, a new headache, drowsiness, and a rash that does not fade when pressed form a picture that requires immediate action, and the finding that confirms the diagnosis is the examination of the cerebrospinal fluid obtained by lumbar puncture. That examination is itself a decision with a risk, since a swollen brain can be pushed downwards when fluid is removed, so a focal deficit, a falling level of consciousness or a seizure before the puncture is a reason to obtain imaging first where that is possible. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius may be called a fever in one service and not in another, so the definition that governs the decision must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and in a clinic without a laboratory fever with headache, neck stiffness and a change in the level of consciousness is enough to justify urgent referral.

Raised pressure inside the head is another condition in which the examination must lead the decision. The signs that warn of it are a headache that is worse in the morning or on coughing, vomiting without nausea, a falling level of consciousness, and a new weakness or a new dilation of one pupil. The combination of a rising blood pressure, a slowing pulse and an irregular breathing pattern is a late sign rather than an early one, and waiting for it is a mistake, so a patient in whom high pressure is suspected should not be laid flat and no fluid should be removed from the spine until the risk of herniation has been assessed. The finding that changes everything is the swollen optic disc seen through an ophthalmoscope, or the focal deficit that suggests a mass, since either one moves the patient from a medical to a surgical pathway. In a hospital the response is imaging and specialist help.

In the unresponsive patient the examination is reduced but not abandoned, and it is performed in a fixed order so that nothing is omitted. The airway and the breathing are assessed first, since a patient who cannot protect the airway or who is breathing abnormally needs help before any diagnosis is refined. The pupils and the eye movements are then examined, including the response to turning the head or to cold water placed in the ear where that is available, and the pattern of these responses localizes the lesion within the brainstem. The motor response is tested by pressure on a nail bed or on the sternum, and the difference between a purposeful withdrawal, an abnormal flexion and an extension response is recorded in words as well as in a number. In a clinic without imaging, the examination separates a patient who needs immediate transfer from one whose problem is metabolic, and the finding that most often changes that decision is the glucose measurement.

Where the resources are few, the neurological examination is not a diminished version of the hospital examination but the same examination with a smaller instrument tray. A clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, a thermometer and no imaging can still establish the level of consciousness, the pattern of the pupils, the symmetry of the face, the strength of the limbs, the presence of a sensory level, the reflexes, the coordination and the gait. What changes is the use of time and the threshold for referral, since a clinician who cannot image the head or the spine must decide earlier. The five minutes that a screening round is often said to take is an ambition rather than a rule, and how long an examination should last is a matter for the current guideline and the local protocol. Two habits carry the most weight here, the first being to repeat the examination at a defined interval so that a change is detected, and the second being to write down what was found in words that the next clinician can act on.

Where imaging and specialist help are available, the same examination is performed first, and the machines are used to answer a question that the examination has already framed. A computed tomography, or CT, scan of the head separates bleeding from blockage with speed, and magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answers finer questions about the cord, the brainstem and the tissues around them. Imaging does not replace the examination, and a normal scan in a patient with a convincing deficit is a reason to repeat the examination and reconsider the timing rather than a reason to relax. The specialist who is called should receive a summary that includes the level of consciousness, the focal findings, the time of onset and the question that the imaging is meant to answer. A patient who deteriorates during the wait for a scan is a patient who should have been reassessed, so the examination here is faster and better supported but not different in its logic.

Because the nervous system declares itself over time, a series of examinations is more informative than any single one. A weakness that has progressed between two observations describes a different patient from one whose weakness has not changed, and the direction of travel is often clearer than the absolute finding. The level of consciousness, the pupils, the power in the limbs and the effort of breathing are the observations worth repeating at a fixed interval, and that interval should be short enough that a change is caught before it becomes irreversible. The record should state the time of each observation, what the patient could do and what had changed, since a note that says only that the patient is stable gives the next clinician nothing to compare.

A constructed illustration makes the reasoning concrete, and it describes no real person. Consider a middle aged patient brought to a small clinic after the sudden onset of weakness of the right arm and difficulty finding words, whose glucose is normal, whose face droops on the right, and whose right leg is weaker than the left but still moves. The immediate conclusion is that this is a stroke until proved otherwise, and the clinician records the findings and the time of onset before arranging transfer. In a hospital the same patient is examined briefly, imaged quickly and assessed for whether the blood supply can be restored, and if instead the weakness had been accompanied by a band of numbness around the trunk, retention of urine and loss of the anal tone, the leading concern would be compression of the cord or of the cauda equina. The value of the illustration is the habit it builds, which is to ask first what must not be missed and then to let the examination answer.

To summarize, the neurological examination is an act of localization in which every finding is collected for the single purpose of placing the lesion, and the same reasoning serves the clinic with a torch and the hospital with a scanner. It begins with the level of consciousness and the Glasgow coma scale, proceeds through the cranial nerves, tone, power, sensation, reflexes, coordination and gait, and asks at every step what the finding says about where the trouble lies. Two presentations must never wait, the stroke that still has time for its blood supply to be restored and the compression of the spinal cord that has almost none, and both are recognized by findings that can be elicited at any bedside. Every score, grade, cut off and interval mentioned in this chapter is an illustration of reasoning rather than a universal rule, and each must be re-established from the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, between editions and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material, it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it does not replace training, supervision and the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient; if a patient is deteriorating, the examination pauses and the patient is treated.

# Chapter 16 — Musculoskeletal Examination

The musculoskeletal examination asks a question no machine answers: what does this joint do now that it did not do before, and what does that change cost the patient. A joint is examined as part of a body that walks and works, so findings are read against function from the first minute. Before any maneuver the examiner must hold the dangerous possibility in mind, because the most feared catastrophe here is an infected joint, and septic arthritis destroys cartilage quickly. The finding that reveals it is not subtle: one joint that is hot, swollen, and held rigid, hurting on the smallest passive movement, often with fever and a patient who looks unwell. That picture is examined first, and everything else is ordered around the speed it demands. This is educational material only, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the local protocol.

The history comes before the hands, because it decides what the hands should seek. The examiner asks which joints are involved, how the problem began, what makes it better and worse, and what the patient can no longer do. The pattern outweighs any single answer: a joint that flared suddenly differs from many joints that drifted into pain over a long period. Morning stiffness that lingers after waking and eases with use points toward inflammation, while pain that worsens through the day and with activity points toward mechanical wear. A prosthetic joint, a suppressed immune system, diabetes, or injected drug use raises the chance that a hot joint is infected, and a normal temperature does not remove that chance. The examiner also asks who the patient is, because a swollen knee means something different in a young runner and in an older person who has just finished treatment that weakens the immune response.

Inspection is done with both sides visible, because the patient's other limb is the best available control. The examiner looks at posture and how the limb is held, at swelling, redness, wasting, alignment, deformity, scars, and the overlying skin. Swelling of a whole joint suggests fluid or thickened lining, whereas swelling clearly outside the joint, over a bursa or tendon sheath, points elsewhere. Wasting above and below a painful joint shows the problem is not new, because wasting takes time to appear. Redness and a shiny tense skin are serious and demand that infection be excluded rather than assumed away. The examiner also notices what the patient does with the limb while talking, since a leg that is never straightened is itself a finding.

Palpation follows gently, because the aim is information and not a test of endurance. The back of the hand is used for warmth, since it senses temperature better than the fingertips, and both sides are compared in the same room and at the same moment. The examiner feels the joint line, a boggy fullness that suggests thickened lining, a fluid thrill that suggests effusion, and tenderness over bone, tendon, or ligament rather than over the joint. Sharp tenderness at one point of bone suggests fracture or infection in the bone, while tenderness in a band along the joint line suggests disease of the joint. A joint that is hot compared with its partner is the single finding that should stop the examination and redirect it toward infection. The comparison is repeated at the end, because warmth that has increased during the encounter strengthens the same conclusion.

A measured temperature adds to the hand but does not replace it, and a normal temperature does not exclude deep infection. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is often taught as the line between normal and fever, yet it varies with the site of measurement, the age of the patient, and the routine of the ward, so confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol. What matters more than the exact figure is the direction of travel: a temperature rising since the last check, with a joint that has become more painful, is a message that cannot be ignored. In a frail, elderly, or immunosuppressed patient the temperature may be normal while the joint is destroyed, so the examiner trusts the joint and the general state as much as the thermometer. A patient who is sweating, confused, or breathing quickly beside a hot joint is seriously ill and must be treated as such while the joint is assessed.

Movement is tested actively first, because this shows what the joint can do under the patient's own control and reveals pain and weakness together. Passive movement follows while the patient relaxes, and the comparison between the two is the heart of the assessment. If active movement is limited by pain but passive movement goes further, the problem is more likely in muscle, tendon, or the pain itself, whereas a joint that stops at the same point both ways has a mechanical restriction. A joint that hurts at the very start of passive movement should not be moved again until infection has been considered. The examiner notes not only how far the joint goes but what stops it: pain, spasm, a hard block, or a soft springy resistance each tells a different story. Restriction that is painless and longstanding is usually wear, while restriction that is new and painful is a reason to keep looking.

There is no single normal range, because the range of a joint varies with age, sex, build, occupation, and the population in which it was measured. The knee, for example, is commonly described as bending to about 135 degrees, but that figure is an average drawn from one group of people and should be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since published values differ between editions and populations. The wiser approach is to compare the affected side with the unaffected side in the same patient, which supplies an individual reference no table can give. The range should be recorded as the patient reaches it, not as the examiner forces it, because a range obtained by pressure measures the examiner as much as the joint. A small painless loss may matter little, while a small painful loss that is new may be the earliest sign of serious disease.

Effusion is excess fluid within the joint, detected by feel and movement rather than by looking alone. A small effusion may show only as fullness beside the joint line or as a bulge that shifts when the examiner presses one side and watches the other. A larger effusion in the knee can be felt as a tap when the examiner presses the kneecap against the bone beneath, and the sensation is unmistakable once it has been felt a few times. Crepitus is the grating felt or heard as the joint moves, and its character matters: fine crepitus in a worn joint is common and often harmless, while coarse crepitus with a sudden loss of movement may follow a fracture or a loose fragment. Neither effusion nor crepitus names a disease by itself, and both must be read with warmth, tenderness, and the general state of the patient. An effusion that appeared overnight with heat is very different from one that has been present for a long time without pain.

Special tests are the part of this examination most often taught as ritual and most often misunderstood. Each test is a question asked in a particular way, and its value lies in the question rather than the movement. A test that stretches a ligament asks whether that ligament is torn, a test that compresses a meniscus asks whether it is caught, and a test that narrows a passage asks whether a tendon is pinched. The examiner should know what each test is meant to exclude, perform it the same way each time, and record the result as positive, negative, or uncertain rather than as proof. A positive test raises the probability of its target and a negative test lowers it, but neither settles the matter, because the same test behaves differently in different populations and in different hands.

Several tests are worth describing so the listener can picture them. To test the ligaments of the knee, the examiner holds the thigh with one hand and draws the lower leg forward or pushes it back with the other, asking whether the tibia slides more than it should; the test asks about the cruciate ligaments and is unreliable in a guarding or swollen knee. To test the menisci, the examiner bends the knee, rotates the lower leg, and straightens it while watching for a click or a catch, which asks whether a torn fragment is trapped. To test the shoulder for impingement, the examiner raises the arm through an arc and looks for pain in the middle of the movement, which asks whether a tendon is compressed under the bony arch. Each test refines the history, and none is decisive; an examiner who treats a click as a diagnosis has stopped reasoning too early.

The spine is examined as a column that carries load and protects the cord, and the examination is organized by those two jobs. The examiner inspects from behind and from the side, looking at the curve of the back, the level of the shoulders and hips, the muscle bulk beside the spine, and any patch of hair or dimple over the lower back. Movement is tested in bending forward and backward, in bending to each side, and in rotation, and the examiner watches how the whole spine moves rather than only how far. Tenderness is sought along the spinous processes and in the muscles beside them, because tenderness over bone may mean infection or fracture, whereas tenderness in muscle usually means strain. The examiner also notices how the patient stands and sits, since a spine that hurts only when loaded behaves differently from one that hurts at rest.

The spine carries the most time-critical danger here after the infected joint, and it must be named where the examination is described. Compression of the spinal cord or of the nerves at its lower end can be caused by infection, tumor, or a disc, and the findings that reveal it are numbness around the saddle area, difficulty starting or stopping the flow of urine, weakness or numbness in both legs, and loss of bowel control. Any of these turns back pain from a nuisance into an emergency, and the patient must be referred without waiting for imaging, because the interval in which function can be saved is short. Infection in the spine may declare itself with fever, pain that wakes the patient at night, tenderness over a single vertebra, or pain worse on movement and unrelieved by rest. Malignancy is more likely in an older patient with a history of cancer, constant nocturnal pain, weight loss, and bone tenderness. Weight loss with night pain in an older patient is a combination that must never be followed by reassurance alone.

The sacroiliac joints sit at the base of the spine and are examined by provocation rather than direct feel, because they are deep. The examiner presses down and outward on the pelvis, or squeezes its two sides together, and asks whether pain is reproduced over the joint rather than elsewhere. The pattern that points to inflammation in these joints is pain in a younger person that begins gradually, is worst in the early morning and at rest, improves with exercise, and often wakes the patient at night. That differs from the mechanical back pain of someone who hurt the back lifting and is now better lying still. The examiner should also look for inflammation elsewhere, in the eye, the skin, the gut, and the tendons, because these joints are rarely inflamed alone.

Three patterns are held side by side, because the examination is a search for which one the patient shows. Mechanical pain is related to use, worse with activity and better with rest, localized, and unaccompanied by swelling, warmth, or systemic illness. Inflammatory pain is worse at rest and in the morning, improves with movement, often affects more than one joint, and is accompanied by lingering stiffness and sometimes by swelling of the lining. Infective pain is severe, begins quickly, is accompanied by heat, swelling, and a patient who looks unwell, and is made unbearable by any movement. These patterns overlap in real patients, and the examiner who finds features of more than one must follow the most dangerous until it is excluded. A person can have longstanding wear in a joint and then develop an infection in it, and the second problem is the one that must be recognized.

Septic arthritis deserves a closer look because delay in recognizing it causes the most harm. The joint fills with pus, cartilage and the bone beneath are damaged quickly, and the patient may become systemically unwell, so the examination aims to find it before that damage is done. The joint is usually single, most often the knee, hip, shoulder, or wrist, and it is held still because every movement hurts. The skin over it is hot and often red, the joint feels full, and the patient resists even the gentlest passive movement. Fever may be present or absent, and the white cell count may be high or normal, so neither the temperature nor a single blood test can rule the condition out. Risk is higher with a prosthetic joint, a recent joint injection or operation, a skin infection, diabetes, a suppressed immune system, or injected drug use, and a child with fever and a limp must be treated as infected until that is excluded. In a hot painful joint the decision that matters is whether to aspirate the joint fluid, and it is made on the examination rather than on a waiting result.

Gout and other crystal diseases produce a joint that is hot, red, swollen, and extremely painful, so they imitate infection closely and are among the commonest reasons a septic joint is missed. A first attack of gout often strikes the joint at the base of the big toe, reaches its worst quickly, and may bring fever and a raised inflammatory marker, which makes the two nearly indistinguishable at the bedside. The examiner should look for tophi, for previous similar attacks that settled, and for the same problem in other joints, since these favor crystals over infection. None of these features is decisive, and the only reliable way to separate the two is to examine the joint fluid, a laboratory step that may not be available where the patient sits. When the fluid cannot be examined and the joint is hot, the safe course is to treat the situation as infection until it is proved otherwise. A past history of gout must not close the question, because a person who has had gout can still develop an infected joint.

Inflammatory arthritis is recognized by its distribution and the character of the swelling rather than by any single sign. The examiner looks for the same joints on both sides being affected, for the small joints of the hands and feet, and for sparing of the joints nearest the nails, which are usually the first to wear with age. The swelling of inflammation is soft and boggy and feels like thickened lining, whereas the swelling of wear is hard and bony. Movement is often full but painful, and any crepitus is fine rather than coarse. Tendon sheaths and bursae can also be inflamed, and tenderness that follows a tendon rather than a joint line points away from the joint. The examiner should look for inflammation in other systems too, because arthritis is often the visible part of a disease that also affects the skin, eyes, lungs, or kidneys.

Wear of a joint produces a picture that is more mechanical and more local. The joint may be enlarged by bony outgrowths, the examiner may feel hard swelling at the margins, and movement is reduced with crepitus that is often coarse. Pain is worse with use and better with rest, morning stiffness is brief, and the joint is not hot or red unless something else is happening. The hands may show bony nodes at the joints nearest the nails and at the middle joints, and the knees may be bowed or the hips may lose rotation early. The presence of wear does not exclude inflammation or infection, and the examiner must ask whether the current pain has the same character as the usual pain. A joint that has grumbled for a long time and has suddenly become hot is a new problem in an old joint and should be treated as one.

Fracture is the third common possibility and the one most easily missed when the patient is calm. It shows itself through deformity, tenderness sharply localized over one point of bone, inability to bear weight or use the limb, and pain increased by any movement at the site. In an older patient with thin bones, a fracture of the hip may present with no deformity at all, and the only findings may be an inability to walk and pain when the leg is gently rotated or the heel is tapped. In a child, a fracture may be incomplete with little swelling, and the child may use the limb until the examiner tests it. The examiner should compare both sides and examine the joints above and below the injury, because a second injury may be less obvious.
