This recording is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and whether the setting is a hospital with every resource or a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same questions order the reasoning and the same obligation remains, to find the dangerous cause early, to decide whether the patient can safely travel, and to explain honestly what remains uncertain.

# Chapter 23 — Dyspnea and Cough

Breathlessness and cough are taught apart and met together, because a patient who is short of breath usually coughs and a patient who has coughed for weeks usually notices that he can no longer do what he used to do. The pairing is not a convenience of the syllabus, since the two symptoms arise from the same apparatus and often from the same disease, and a cough that has changed may be the only early evidence of a lung that is losing function. This chapter organizes them around four questions rather than around a list of diseases: what the sensation of breathlessness actually is, how its pace narrows the possibilities, how the character of a cough separates the causes, and which findings at the bedside identify the patient who cannot wait. This chapter is educational material and cannot take the place of training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which you work. What follows is reasoning to be practiced under supervision, never a set of instructions to be applied alone.

Certain presentations are dangerous enough to be named before the reasoning that surrounds them, and each is recognized by a specific finding. The patient who cannot finish a sentence and who sits upright using the muscles of the neck is in ventilatory difficulty now, and if he is also blue, drowsy, or exhausted then failure is already advanced. The patient with a silent chest is in greater danger still, because a chest that has stopped making sound during a severe attack may mean airflow too low to generate any, and the examiner who mistakes that silence for improvement has made a lethal error. A new swelling of one leg in a breathless patient points to a clot in the deep veins and a clot that has traveled to the lungs, and it is found only when the patient is undressed and both calves are compared. Coughing blood is never trivial, and it demands an explanation that includes tuberculosis, a tumor, an infection, and a clot in the lung until one of them has been excluded by the evidence rather than by hope.

Breathlessness is a sensation rather than a measurement, and it is produced by a mismatch rather than by a single sensor. The brain issues a command to breathe and receives back information about how the chest and lungs responded, and when the effort demanded and the movement achieved do not match, the patient feels short of breath. Receptors in the airways, the lung tissue, the chest wall, and the muscles of respiration all contribute, together with the chemical drive from carbon dioxide and oxygen, which is why the sensation is compounded of effort, tightness, and the feeling of not getting enough air. The practical consequence is that breathlessness and oxygen level are not the same thing, so a patient may be deeply breathless with a normal oxygen saturation while another whose carbon dioxide has risen slowly over months feels almost nothing. Anxiety, fever, anemia, and poor fitness each lower the threshold at which ordinary activity produces the sensation, and none of those is imaginary. The examiner therefore records both what the patient feels and what the body shows, and treats a disagreement between the two as information rather than as error.

The history of breathlessness is built from comparison rather than from description, because the words patients choose for the sensation vary enormously while pointing at the same thing. The useful questions are about what the patient could do before and what he can do now: how far he walks on the flat, how many stairs he climbs before stopping, whether he can carry shopping, and whether he has quietly given up something he used to enjoy. A change in exercise tolerance that the patient noticed and explained away is often the most important fact in the room, and it should be dated as precisely as he can manage. The pace of onset sorts the possibilities more sharply than any other single feature, because a collapse in the doorway and a decline across a season admit very different explanations. What the patient believes is wrong, what he has already taken, and what he fears are part of the history too, because they shape what he will accept and what he will conceal. The clinician who asks about function will learn more than the one who asks the patient to grade his breathlessness on a scale.

Two questions deserve their own place because they move the ranking so decisively. Orthopnea is breathlessness that appears when the patient lies flat and eases when he sits up, and it is often reported not as a symptom but as a habit, in the pillows that have been added over the months and the chair he now sleeps in. Paroxysmal nocturnal breathlessness is the patient waking after a period of sleep with a terrifying sense of suffocation, sitting up, and taking many minutes to recover, and it is among the most specific symptoms of a failing left ventricle. Both arise from a shared mechanism, in which lying flat returns fluid from the legs and the abdomen to the chest and a heart that cannot keep up allows it to collect in the lungs. Neither is exclusive to heart failure, since severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, obesity, an airway that collapses during sleep, and reflux can each produce a version of the story. The clinician therefore asks how the patient sleeps and not merely whether he sleeps, and listens for the pattern of the change rather than for a single detail.

Cough is first divided by how long it has been present, because duration moves the list of causes more than any other feature. A cough of less than 3 weeks is usually an infection of the upper or lower airway, and most of those settle without any diagnosis being made. A cough that lasts between 3 weeks and 8 weeks is called subacute, and its common explanations are a lingering airway infection, a cough that persists after the infection has gone, and a cough driven by the upper airway or by reflux. A cough beyond 8 weeks is chronic, and it brings in asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a drug effect, an allergy, and tuberculosis, along with a tumor in a patient whose story includes weight loss or blood. Those boundaries are a teaching convention and not a natural law, so confirm the intervals against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the divisions between acute, subacute, and chronic are drawn differently in different countries and revised between editions. What matters more than the number of weeks is whether the cough has changed, because a cough stable for years that is suddenly different deserves the same attention as a new one.

The character of the cough is the second sorting tool, and it is gathered by watching the patient cough rather than by asking him to describe the sound. A dry cough suggests irritation of the airway, an allergic trigger, a drug, or the early phase of a viral illness, while a productive cough suggests infection, chronic bronchitis, or a cavity in the lung. The sputum is examined for color, quantity, and blood, and a change from clear to yellow, green, or rusty is a fact that can be followed over time even where no laboratory exists. The sound carries information as well, since a barking cough, a whooping cough in a child, a brassy cough that suggests pressure on the windpipe, and a cough that ends in a vomit or a faint each have a short list of their own. Timing is as useful as sound, so the clinician asks about cough at night, on waking, after meals, on exertion, in cold air, and on lying down. The company the cough keeps matters too, because fever, weight loss, night sweats, chest pain, or a swelling in the neck turns a common symptom into a different problem.

Asthma is the first explanation to consider when breathlessness and cough come and go, and its defining feature is variability rather than severity. The symptoms are episodic, often worse at night and in the early morning, and they are provoked by cold air, exercise, dust, smoke, pollen, and infection in a patient who often has an allergic history. Between episodes the chest may sound entirely normal, which is why a quiet examination does not remove the diagnosis and why the history must be trusted over a single listening. During an attack the examiner finds a widespread wheeze heard on expiration, a prolonged expiratory phase, and a patient who is working hard to move air. The paradox of the silent chest belongs here, because when the attack becomes severe enough that airflow falls very low the wheeze disappears and the chest goes quiet, so a chest that has fallen silent in a deteriorating asthmatic is a sign of impending respiratory arrest rather than of recovery. A response to treatment that is repeated each time it is given, with the variability returning when treatment stops, is the pattern that supports the diagnosis, and the decision to start and to stop treatment should rest on that pattern rather than on one measurement.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presents the opposite shape, with breathlessness that is persistent and slowly progressive rather than episodic. The history usually contains many years of tobacco smoke, or of smoke from cooking and heating fires in a poorly ventilated room, and the cough is productive and chronic. The examiner sees a patient who may be barrel-chested, who breathes through pursed lips, who uses the muscles of the neck and the spaces between the ribs, and whose expiration is prolonged and quiet. Air entry is reduced everywhere, and added sounds such as wheeze or crackles come and go with exacerbations rather than defining the condition. The practical difficulty is that a patient with this disease can also develop pneumonia, a collapsed lung, a pneumothorax, or heart failure, and a sudden change in a previously stable pattern is a new problem until it is proved otherwise. The distinction from asthma rests on the history of variability, the age of onset, the exposure history, and the response to treatment over time, and no single finding at the bedside settles it alone.

Pneumonia is the most common acute explanation of fever with cough and breathlessness, and it is recognized by a pattern of focal signs. The patient is often flushed and sweating, the breathing is rapid and shallow, and the affected side of the chest moves less than the other. On the sick side the examiner finds crackles, a dull note on percussion, a change in the transmitted voice sounds, and bronchial breathing when the lung is consolidated. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or higher supports the diagnosis in a younger patient, but that figure is a teaching illustration and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since fever is defined differently in different countries, revised between editions, and measured differently by every laboratory. The older patient is the trap, because pneumonia there may present with confusion, a fall, or a general decline and almost no fever or cough, while the chest may be quiet rather than noisy. A patient who is breathing rapidly, whose oxygen saturation has fallen below 90 per cent, or who looks exhausted should be treated as seriously ill while the cause is being confirmed, and that saturation is an illustration as well, so establish the number your service acts on from the current guideline and the local protocol.

Disease of the pleura changes the examination in a way that is easy to recognize and easy to reason from. When fluid collects between the lung and the chest wall, the note over it is dull, the breath sounds are reduced or absent, the voice sounds are reduced, and the trachea and heart may be pushed away from the affected side if the collection is large. When air collects instead, as in a pneumothorax, the note is hyperresonant, the breath sounds are absent, and a large collection under pressure pushes the trachea and the heart toward the opposite side while the patient becomes shocked. The distinction between an effusion and consolidation is made at the bedside by the voice sounds, which are increased over solid lung and decreased over fluid, and by the character of the breath sounds rather than by their mere presence. A patient with sudden pleural pain and breathlessness, especially a tall thin young man or someone with known lung disease, must be examined for pneumothorax before any other explanation is accepted. Where no radiograph exists, a hyperresonant silent side of the chest with a displaced trachea in a deteriorating patient is enough to act on.

A clot that has traveled to the lungs is the diagnosis that most often hides behind a normal examination, and it must be considered in every patient with unexplained breathlessness. The presentation ranges from a sudden breathlessness with a clear chest to a collapse with a falling pressure, distended neck veins, and a heart beating very fast. Pleuritic pain, a cough, and blood in the sputum are common, and a fainting episode may be the first event. The finding that reveals it is often in the leg rather than the chest, namely a new unilateral swelling, warmth, or tenderness over the deep veins, which is why both legs are examined in every breathless patient. A heart rate greater than 110 beats per minute and a systolic pressure less than 90 millimeters of mercury mark a large clot and a patient who needs help immediately, and those two figures are illustrations of the reasoning, so establish the values your own service treats as critical from the current guideline and the local protocol, because the thresholds differ between countries and editions and are set locally by each service and laboratory. A normal electrocardiogram, or ECG, and a normal chest radiograph do not exclude it, and treating either as reassurance is a recognized cause of preventable death.

Heart failure explains breathlessness, cough, and a wheeze that is easily mistaken for asthma, and the discriminating findings are those of a circulation that is congested. The patient describes orthopnea and waking at night gasping, and reports swelling of the ankles, weight gain, and a need to sleep propped up. The examiner finds a raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound that suggests a failing ventricle, crackles at both lung bases that do not clear with coughing, and swelling of the ankles or the sacrum. The apex beat may be displaced, the pulse may be irregular, and the liver may be enlarged and tender. A cough that is worse on lying down and a wheeze that accompanies it are common, which is why heart failure is one of the classic imitators of lung disease and why the jugular venous pressure must be looked for rather than assumed. Where a laboratory exists, a blood test for the peptide released by a stretched heart muscle helps to separate the two, and the cut-off used for that test is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the value depends on age, kidney function, and the assay the laboratory uses.

Tuberculosis is the chronic infection the clinician must keep in view, because it is common in many settings this book serves and because its early symptoms are ordinary. The cough has usually lasted more than 3 weeks, it may be dry at first and productive later, and it is accompanied by blood in the sputum in a substantial minority. Night sweats, fever, loss of appetite, and weight loss of more than 5 kilograms complete the picture, and there may be a history of contact with someone already treated for the disease. The chest may sound normal, which is why the history and not the stethoscope is the instrument that raises suspicion. A patient infected with the human immunodeficiency virus, or HIV, is at much higher risk, and the combination of that infection with a chronic cough and weight loss should lower the threshold for investigation sharply. Where a laboratory exists, sputum is examined for the organism; where none exists, the same combination of history and findings justifies referral, because investigation is decided on the clinical picture while treatment is decided on the confirmed result. The interval of 3 weeks and the weight of 5 kilograms are illustrations of the reasoning, so confirm both against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the thresholds that trigger investigation differ between countries and editions and between programs.

Assembling these explanations into a ranked list is the central work of the chapter, and it is ordered twice, once by likelihood and once by how much harm a delay would do. The pace of the illness does most of the sorting, and the boundaries between an abrupt onset, a rapid course, and a gradual decline are conventions that must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because they are drawn differently in different countries and revised between editions. An abrupt onset suggests a clot in the lung, a pneumothorax, a foreign body, an allergic reaction, or sudden flooding of the lungs, and each of those is an emergency. A rapid course suggests pneumonia, an exacerbation of asthma or of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure, or a large pleural effusion. A gradual decline suggests anemia, a tumor, tuberculosis, a slowly enlarging effusion, or a neuromuscular cause, and the same long time course applies to a cough that has never settled. The setting adjusts the order again, because a young person in a rural clinic and an older person in a referral hospital do not carry the same probabilities. The ranking should be written down so that the next clinician can see what was considered and what was set aside.

Examination of the breathless patient begins before the stethoscope is lifted, because the work of breathing is visible from the door. The examiner notes whether the patient is comfortable, sitting up, or leaning forward with the arms braced, and whether he is using the muscles of the neck, the spaces between the ribs, or the abdomen to breathe. The rate is counted rather than estimated, because a rising respiratory rate is often the earliest sign that a patient is deteriorating, and the rhythm, depth, and symmetry of the movement are noted as well. The lips, tongue, and nail beds are inspected for a blue tinge, the neck veins are examined for a raised pressure, and both legs are compared for swelling. The patient is asked to speak a full sentence, and the length of that sentence is among the most useful observations in the whole encounter. Only then is the chest examined, with the examiner listening to both sides in a fixed order and describing what is heard rather than what is expected.

The chest examination is directed at four questions: whether air is moving, whether it is moving equally on both sides, whether there are added sounds, and whether the signs point to consolidation, fluid, or collapse. Air entry is compared side to side at the same level, because the difference between the two sides carries more information than the absolute quality on either. Wheezes are widespread and musical and suggest narrowed airways, crackles are discontinuous and suggest fluid or inflammation in the small airways and air sacs, and a pleural rub is a grating sound that suggests inflamed pleural surfaces. Percussion maps dullness and hyperresonance, and the voice sounds tell whether the lung beneath is solid or compressed. Where a peak flow meter or a pulse oximeter exists, the measurement adds an objective number that can be followed over time, and where neither exists the counted respiratory rate and the patient's ability to speak are the equivalents. No single one of these findings is decisive alone, and the pattern they form together is what moves the ranking.

It is as important to know what the examination can exclude as what it can confirm, because overconfidence at the bedside costs lives. A chest that sounds clear does not exclude a clot in the lung, an early pneumonia, or a small pneumothorax, and a normal oxygen saturation does not exclude serious disease. A normal chest examination in a patient with a long smoking history and a changed cough does not exclude a tumor, and a normal examination in a patient with fever and breathlessness does not exclude pneumonia in its first hours. What a careful examination can do is identify the patient who is working hard to breathe, the one with focal signs that demand a radiograph, the one with a swollen leg, and the one whose oxygen is falling despite treatment. Those findings change the pace and the place of care even when the diagnosis is still uncertain. The examination is therefore used to sort urgency first and to name a disease second, and a patient who is deteriorating is treated before the label is settled.

Where a radiograph is available, the examination becomes a set of questions that the image is asked to answer. The clinician predicts what the radiograph should show before it is taken, so that an unexpected finding is recognized as a surprise rather than accepted without thought. A plain chest radiograph separates consolidation, a pleural effusion, a pneumothorax, a collapsed lung, a mass, and an enlarged heart, and it is the single most useful image in this presentation. An electrocardiogram is recorded in almost every patient with acute breathlessness, not because it diagnoses the lung but because it identifies the rhythm and the strain on the heart that change the ranking. Imaging of the veins of the legs, an ultrasound of the heart, and a computed tomography, or CT, scan of the arteries of the lungs answer specific questions that the history has already raised. A normal radiograph in a breathless patient is not a normal patient, and it should send the clinician back to the history and to the leg examination rather than to a discharge letter.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a thermometer, and a torch, the same reasoning is performed with fewer inputs and with a greater reliance on repeated observation. The thermometer turns a vague impression of fever into a number that can be followed, the stethoscope supplies the four questions of the chest examination, and the torch allows the mouth, the throat, and the nail beds to be examined properly. A watch allows the respiratory rate and the pulse to be counted rather than guessed, which is often the most valuable information available. The decision in this setting is rarely a final diagnosis, since it is whether the patient can be watched safely where he is, whether treatment can begin on the clinical picture, and whether a journey must start and how urgently. Where a trial of treatment is used as a diagnostic test, the clinician must decide in advance what improvement would confirm the diagnosis and what failure would overturn it, and must arrange a review at a stated point rather than leaving the patient to return on his own judgment. The examination here cannot exclude a clot in the lung, a small pneumothorax, a tumor, or early tuberculosis, and that honest limit is itself a finding that shapes the plan.

A constructed illustration may make the sorting visible, and neither of the patients in it is real. Imagine a young man who has had episodes of wheeze and dry cough since childhood, worse at night and after running in cold air, whose chest is quiet between episodes and who improves when the pattern is recognized and treated as asthma. Now imagine a woman in middle age who becomes breathless across a single day, whose chest sounds clear, whose heart is fast, and whose left calf is swollen and tender. The first patient is separated from the second not by the loudness of the wheeze but by the pace of the illness, the triggers, and the state of the leg, and the second patient's clear chest is the finding that makes her situation more dangerous rather than less. A third constructed patient, an older man with a cough for months, weight loss, and blood in the sputum, is included to show how a story that sounds chronic can still demand urgent investigation. These illustrations exist only to fix a habit of thought, and real patients are more variable than any of them.

To summarize, breathlessness and cough are read together, first through the sensation and its mechanism, then through the pace of the illness, then through the character of the cough, and finally through the findings that separate a patient who can wait from one who cannot. The dangerous presentations are named where the symptom is described rather than deferred, among them the patient who cannot finish a sentence, the silent chest in a severe attack, the new unilateral leg swelling that points to a clot in the lung, and the patient coughing blood, each with the finding that reveals it. Asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pneumonia, pleural disease, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, and tuberculosis are carried as competing explanations and separated by the pattern of history and examination rather than by any single sign. Every number in this chapter, whether a temperature, a rate, a pressure, a saturation, an interval, or a weight, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This recording is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who is working hard to breathe is treated while the diagnosis is still being assembled, because no label is worth the delay of someone who is getting worse.

# Chapter 24 — Headache and Dizziness

Headache and dizziness most often mean nothing and occasionally mean everything, and the clinician must sort one from the other before the patient has finished speaking. Both are symptoms rather than diagnoses, shaped by age, setting, and speed of onset as much as by the quality of the pain. This chapter is organized by pattern and by triage rather than by a list of diseases, because a pattern tells the clinician what to do next while a label only names what has happened. It is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and what follows is a way of thinking to be practiced with a teacher rather than instructions to be applied alone.

The dangerous causes of headache must be named where the symptom is described, because each hides behind the ordinary and each is revealed by one finding. Subarachnoid hemorrhage produces a headache that reaches full intensity almost at once, often called the worst of a lifetime, sometimes with vomiting or a brief loss of consciousness. Meningitis reveals itself through fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, a rash that does not fade when pressed, and a consciousness that does not match how well the patient looks. Raised intracranial pressure betrays itself by pain worse on waking and lying flat, by vomiting without nausea, and by a swollen optic disc. Cerebral venous thrombosis is suggested by a headache that worsens steadily in a young woman who is pregnant or recently delivered. Temporal arteritis in an older patient warns through scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing, and any disturbance of vision. A stroke in the posterior circulation may present with headache together with vertigo, unsteadiness, double vision, or slurred speech rather than weakness of a limb.

The dangerous causes of dizziness deserve the same naming. A posterior circulation stroke can present with vertigo alone, especially when the patient cannot stand or walk, and a cerebellar hemorrhage can imitate a benign inner ear disturbance until the patient suddenly deteriorates. A cardiac cause is named by an irregular pulse, a murmur of narrowing in the aortic valve, or a faint during exertion rather than after it. Serious blood loss shows itself through a rapid pulse, a falling pressure, pallor, and a history of bleeding from the gut, while anemia, infection, and dehydration produce a similar complaint and are separated by simple measurements. The clinician who asks first what would kill this patient, and second what is most likely, will order the search correctly in both halves of the chapter.

Headache is read by pattern before it is read by diagnosis, and the patterns are defined mainly by time. The sudden headache arrives in an instant and demands exclusion of bleeding, while the progressive headache builds over days or weeks and points toward a mass, an infection, a venous thrombosis, or a rise in pressure within the skull. The postural headache changes with the position of the head, one kind worsening on standing and another on lying flat. The recurrent headache returns in the same shape again and again and usually means a primary headache disorder once a secondary cause has been considered, while the chronic daily headache has usually been present for months and forces a review of what the patient has been taking. The intervals separating one pattern from another are conventions rather than fixed borders, so confirm the definitions your service uses against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The sudden headache is the one that most often carries a lethal cause and must be treated as an emergency until explained. A subarachnoid hemorrhage usually produces its worst pain within seconds, and that pain may then settle, so a patient who feels better at the consultation is not thereby safe. A smaller warning bleed may occur days earlier and is easily dismissed as a strain or a migraine, so any severe and unusual recent headache deserves a direct question. The examination looks for neck stiffness, photophobia, a changed level of consciousness, and weakness of an eye movement, since a nerve supplying the eye can be compressed by blood at the base of the brain. A computed tomography, or CT, scan of the head is the first step where imaging exists, and its ability to detect fresh blood falls as time passes from the bleed. A scan in the first hours is far more likely to show blood than one after a day or more, but those intervals are illustrations rather than laws, so confirm the timing your service relies on against the current guideline and the local protocol, and if the scan is negative while the story stays suspicious, the decision about further testing belongs to a clinician with the full picture.

Meningitis and encephalitis are the infections that turn a headache into a race, and their signs are sought in every patient with fever and headache. The neck resists flexion, the light hurts the eyes, the patient may vomit, and consciousness may fall out of proportion to the fever. A rash that does not fade when pressed with clear glass or a finger should stop the consultation and start the response, because it suggests bleeding into the skin from a bloodstream infection. Kernig and Brudzinski described maneuvers that stretch the inflamed membranes around the brain and spinal cord, and though neither is reliable alone, a positive result adds weight to a picture that already concerns the clinician, and a falling consciousness, focal weakness, or seizure may mean that raised pressure must be considered before the fluid around the spinal cord is sampled. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is treated as a fever in many settings, but the figure that matters is the one your own service uses, so confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A raised pressure inside the skull produces a headache with a character of its own, and recognizing it may prevent a catastrophe. The pain is often worst on waking, worse lying flat, and worse when the patient coughs, strains, or bends forward, and vomiting may occur without preceding nausea and may briefly relieve the headache. Vision may blur, the optic disc may swell, and one eye may turn outward because the nerve that moves it is stretched along the base of the brain. The safest way to look for the swollen disc is to darken the room, ask the patient to look at a distant point, and examine the back of the eye with whatever instrument is available; a torch held at the outer corner of the eye can sometimes show enough to raise or lower suspicion. A lumbar puncture in the presence of raised pressure can cause the brain to shift, so the revealing finding is the swollen disc together with the postural pattern of the pain, and either alone is a reason to seek help rather than wait.

Cerebral venous thrombosis is most often missed because its headache looks ordinary and its first scan can look normal. It is a clot in the veins draining blood from the brain, and it occurs more often in young women, after childbirth, in dehydration, in inherited clotting conditions, and in people using hormonal contraception. The headache commonly builds gradually and may worsen on lying flat or straining, and it may come with vomiting, seizures, weakness on one side, or a change in behavior or speech, while a swollen optic disc may be seen even when the clot is invisible on a plain scan. The clinician who waits for a definitive image before considering the possibility may lose time that matters, because the treatment decision depends on recognizing the pattern and arranging the right test. When a young person has a new and progressive headache with any of these features, the question should be asked aloud and the answer sought from imaging able to show the veins as well as the brain.

Temporal arteritis is the headache emergency of the older patient, and it threatens sight rather than life. It causes a new headache in a person usually older than 50 years, and the pain may sit over the temple, may be tender to touch, and may be joined by jaw pain on chewing and by pain in the muscles of the shoulders and hips. Any disturbance of vision, whether brief blurring, double vision, or sudden loss of sight in one eye, changes the situation at once. The clinician should feel the scalp arteries, look at the back of the eye, and arrange the blood tests that reflect inflammation, but when the story is strong the decision to begin treatment may have to be made before those results return. The age of 50 years is a common teaching rather than a sharp boundary, so confirm the current guideline and the local protocol for your population instead of treating the figure as a rule, and remember that the revealing finding is the tender, thickened artery with jaw pain and visual symptoms, while the finding that makes treatment wrong is a clear alternative cause with no inflammation anywhere.

Several other secondary headaches are worth keeping in mind during a busy clinic. A sudden painful red eye with a fixed, mid-sized pupil and blurred vision suggests a rise in pressure inside the eye that can damage sight quickly and demands immediate attention. Pain over the cheek or forehead that worsens when the head bends forward, with a blocked nose and fever, suggests sinus infection, while pain beginning in the neck and spreading to the back of the head, worse on neck movement, points to the joints and muscles of the cervical spine. A headache that appears every day and is relieved by a painkiller only to return as its effect wears off suggests the treatment itself has become the cause, and the answer is a planned withdrawal rather than another tablet. Carbon monoxide poisoning causes headache with nausea and confusion that improves on leaving a building and returns on going back inside, and it should be suspected when more than one person in a household is affected. Pregnancy brings its own causes, including a rise in pressure that endangers mother and child.

The primary headaches are far more common than the dangerous ones, and the task is to recognize them without letting familiarity dull the search. Tension-type headache is usually a band-like pressure on both sides, mild to moderate, without vomiting and without worsening on ordinary movement. Migraine is often one-sided, throbbing, moderate to severe, worse with movement and light, and accompanied by nausea, and it may be preceded by a visual or sensory disturbance that spreads slowly across the vision. Cluster headache is a severe pain around one eye with redness, tearing, a drooping eyelid, and a blocked or running nose on the same side, and it comes in bouts that may wake the patient from sleep. A previous identical pattern is reassuring but not conclusive, and the trap is to attribute a new and severe headache to a familiar label, so the safeguard is to ask what is different about this attack before accepting it.

Migraine deserves more attention because it is so often both the correct answer and the wrong one. Its aura is a reversible disturbance that develops gradually, and it may take the form of flashing lights, a spreading blind spot, tingling across the face and hand, or difficulty finding words, while the headache that follows is often one-sided, throbbing, and worse with movement. A patient who has had exactly this sequence many times and is now in it again is usually having another migraine, and the clinician can be reasonably confident once the dangerous patterns have been considered. The same patient with a headache different in onset, site, severity, or accompanying features is not having a routine attack, and that difference is the finding that matters. A migraine that is new after middle age, or that comes with fever, neck stiffness, a change in consciousness, or a new weakness, requires a different search altogether.

The patient's circumstances change the probability of each cause, and the clinician should let them do so. A new headache in a person with the human immunodeficiency virus, or HIV, or with another condition weakening the immune defenses raises the possibility of an infection or a tumor behaving differently from the usual picture. A patient with known cancer may have spread to the brain or its membranes, and a patient who has had a recent fall or a spinal procedure may have bleeding or a leak of spinal fluid. Pregnancy brings a rise in blood pressure and clotting that can threaten the brain, and the period after delivery carries a particular risk of venous thrombosis. Children may not describe a headache well, and their presentation is often dominated by vomiting, irritability, or a change in behavior, so a parent's report deserves as much weight as the child's words, and an older patient may have more than one cause at once.

Dizziness is a word covering several different experiences, and the first task is to find out which one the patient is describing. Vertigo is the false sense that the world or the patient is spinning or moving, and it points toward the vestibular system, whether in the inner ear or in the brain. Presyncope is the sense of being about to faint, with dimming vision, warmth, sweating, and nausea, and it points toward the circulation. Disequilibrium is unsteadiness on the feet without a false sense of movement, and it points toward the balance system as a whole, including the feet, the joints, the eyes, and the cerebellum. The vague light-headedness that fits none of these may arise from anemia, infection, dehydration, low blood sugar, anxiety, poor sleep, or a medication, and the clinician should ask the patient to choose among these descriptions rather than accepting the single word dizziness as an answer.

Once vertigo is described, the next question is whether the cause lies in the inner ear or in the brain, because the second is the dangerous one. Vertigo of inner ear origin is usually severe, rotational, and accompanied by nausea and sweating, and it is often worse on head movement, but the patient can usually stand and walk with support. Central vertigo is more often joined by an inability to stand or walk, by double vision, slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, numbness or weakness on one side, or a headache or neck pain, and any of these shifts the balance toward the brain. The nystagmus, the rhythmic movement of the eyes, is examined by asking the patient to follow a finger and then look straight ahead, and its direction, persistence, and response to fixation all carry information. In inner ear disease the fast phase usually beats away from the affected ear and is reduced by fixation, while in brain disease the nystagmus may change direction with gaze, may be vertical, and may persist or worsen with fixation, and that difference is one of the most useful signs at the bedside.

The stroke in the posterior circulation is the diagnosis that must not be missed in a dizzy patient, and its features are assembled rather than found in any single sign. The patient may have vertigo and may also be unable to stand or walk even though the limbs are strong when tested in bed, and that inability is a serious finding. There may be double vision, slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, facial numbness, loss of coordination in one arm or leg, or a sensory change on one side of the body and the opposite side of the face. A new headache or neck pain may accompany it, and the patient may be drowsy or behave unusually. The clinician can test the reflex that stabilizes the eyes when the head is turned quickly, can look for nystagmus, and can check whether the eyes are aligned by covering one at a time while the patient looks at a target, and a combination of abnormal results raises the suspicion of a central cause. The patient who cannot walk, or who deteriorates while being observed, needs urgent help rather than watchful waiting.

The common inner ear causes each have their own pattern. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is brief and intense, brought on by a particular change of position such as rolling over in bed or looking up, and it lasts only seconds. The maneuver described by Dix and Hallpike places the patient flat with the head turned and lowered to one side, and it reproduces the vertigo after a short delay with a rotational nystagmus that fades if the position is held; the same maneuver can reposition the crystals that cause it. Vestibular neuritis is a single severe attack of vertigo developing over hours, with nausea and unsteadiness but no hearing loss, and labyrinthitis is the same picture with hearing loss or ringing. Meniere disease causes episodes of vertigo with fluctuating hearing loss and a feeling of fullness in the ear, and vestibular migraine causes episodes in a patient who also has migraines. A new one-sided hearing loss deserves particular attention, and the durations separating these attacks are taught differently in different places, so confirm the definitions used in your own service against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Presyncope is the second great category, and it is a symptom of the circulation rather than the ear. The patient feels faint, vision dims or closes in, the skin becomes warm or clammy, and there may be nausea, and the episode often ends when the patient sits or lies down. A faint during exertion, or while lying flat, is more concerning than one after standing a long time in a warm room. The examination looks for an irregular or slow pulse, a murmur suggesting narrowing of the aortic valve, a difference in the pulses of the two arms, and any sign of bleeding from the gut. The blood pressure is measured lying and then standing, and a fall of 20 millimeters of mercury in the systolic pressure or 10 millimeters of mercury in the diastolic pressure supports a postural drop, though those figures are commonly quoted illustrations, so confirm the definition your service uses against the current guideline and the local protocol. An electrocardiogram, or ECG, is essential when available, because a disturbed rhythm may be the whole explanation and may be intermittent.

Disequilibrium is the third category, and it is examined by watching the patient walk rather than by asking about spinning. The clinician asks the patient to stand with feet together and eyes open, then with eyes closed, and a marked increase in swaying when the eyes close points toward a problem with position sense from the feet and legs. Walking heel to toe, turning, and walking while the examiner watches from the side reveal a great deal, and an unsteady gait worse in the dark or on uneven ground suggests a sensory rather than a cerebellar problem. The cerebellum produces a wide-based, staggering gait with poor limb coordination, and a stroke or tumor there can present this way. Weakness of the legs, joint pain, a neuropathy from diabetes or alcohol, poor vision, and the fear of falling after a previous fall all contribute, and the gait examination is also a test of safety because the patient who is unsteady is at risk of a fracture.

The vague light-headedness that fits none of the previous categories is a diagnostic problem in its own right, and its causes are frequently outside the nervous system. Anemia reduces the oxygen carried in the blood and produces tiredness, breathlessness on effort, pallor, and a racing pulse as well as light-headedness. Infection, fever, and dehydration reduce the effective volume of the circulation and produce the same complaint, and low blood sugar produces sweating, hunger, confusion, and tremor that improve when the patient eats. Anxiety and rapid breathing can produce light-headedness, tingling in the hands and around the mouth, and a sense of unreality, and a medication that lowers the blood pressure, a sedative, or a drug affecting the inner ear can each be the cause. Poor sleep, low fitness, and a long illness also produce a persistent light-headedness that is real even though no single organ can be blamed, and the patient deserves an explanation rather than a dismissal.

The examination of the dizzy patient is a complete examination of the nervous system, the ears, the eyes, and the circulation, performed in a fixed order so that nothing is omitted. The clinician looks at the ears for discharge, scarring, or a blister-like rash in the canal that might indicate a viral infection of the nerve, and tests hearing by whispering or rubbing the fingers near each ear in turn. The eyes are examined for redness, pupil size and reaction, range of movement, and nystagmus, and the back of the eye is examined for swelling of the disc. The heart is examined for a murmur and an irregular rhythm, and the pulses in the neck and limbs are felt, because a narrowed neck artery can produce both dizziness and a stroke. The blood pressure is measured in both arms and again after standing, the temperature is taken, and the gait, coordination, and neck are examined.

In a hospital with immediate imaging, the examination decides which image is needed and how quickly. A patient with a sudden severe headache is usually scanned first without contrast, and if the story remains suspicious after a normal scan, the blood vessels or the fluid around the spinal cord may need further study. A patient with vertigo and any feature suggesting the brain is involved is imaged with magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, because it shows the back of the brain and the brainstem better than a plain scan. A patient with suspected infection may need the fluid around the spinal cord examined, but only after raised pressure has been considered, because the test can be dangerous when the pressure is high, and a patient with suspected temporal arteritis may have the artery examined by ultrasound or by a small sample sent to the laboratory. Each choice is guided by the history and examination rather than by the machine, and the clinician should state what is expected before the image is taken, so that a surprise is recognized as one.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a thermometer, and a torch, the same reasoning is performed with fewer instruments, and the decision replaces the image. The torch is used to look at the pupils, the eye movements, the back of the eye in a darkened room, the ear canal, and the throat. The thermometer turns the patient's sense of being unwell into a number, and the watch allows the pulse to be counted rather than guessed, which is essential when a faint or dizziness may be caused by a disturbed rhythm. The stethoscope reveals a murmur of narrowing in the aortic valve, an irregular heartbeat, or a bruit over the neck artery, and the cuff, if one exists, allows the pressure to be measured lying and standing. The clinician tests gait, hearing, coordination, and neck, and asks directly about rash, stiff neck, recent fall, pregnancy, and bleeding. Where no imaging exists the decision is not a diagnosis but a plan, and the clinic should state honestly that it cannot exclude a small bleed, an early stroke, or a clot in the veins of the brain, so a normal examination in a worrying story is a reason to repeat it rather than a license to send the patient home.

Fundoscopy with a simple torch is a skill worth practicing, because it is the one test that can reveal raised pressure where no other instrument exists. The patient sits in the darkest room available, looks at a distant object such as a light or a mark on the far wall, and keeps the eyes still. The examiner stands slightly to the side, holds the torch at the outer corner of the eye and shines the beam through the pupil, then looks along the beam into the back of the eye from a short distance away, moving closer as the view allows. What the examiner looks for is the pale disc where the optic nerve leaves the eye, its margins, its color compared with the other side, and the dark vessels crossing it, and a disc that is swollen, blurred at the margins, or ringed by a pale halo is the finding that matters. The torch technique is imperfect and may miss a swelling that a formal examination would find, but a swollen disc found with a torch is serious, and a normal-looking disc found with a torch does not exclude raised pressure.

To summarize, headache and dizziness are symptoms whose meaning is carried by their pattern, their speed, and the company they keep, and the clinician's first duty is to name the lethal causes before settling on the likely ones. Subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, raised intracranial pressure, cerebral venous thrombosis, a stroke in the posterior circulation, and temporal arteritis in the older patient are each revealed by a finding that can be sought in the history or at the bedside, and each changes the pace and place of care. Vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium, and vague light-headedness are separated by the patient's own words, by examination of the eyes and gait, and by a few simple measurements. Every figure in this chapter, whether an interval, an age, a pressure, a temperature, a rate, or a proportion, is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such values differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This material is educational and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen, and no patient described here is real, so when the story is worrying and the examination is reassuring, the answer is to repeat the examination and to seek help, not to relax.

# Chapter 25 — Abdominal Pain

Abdominal pain is the symptom that most often asks the clinician to choose between patience and action, because the same dull ache can be a passing indigestion or the first sign of a catastrophe inside the abdomen. The reasoning that organizes this chapter is spatial and temporal at once: where the pain began, where it has traveled, what it feels like, and what makes it better or worse, all mapped onto the structures that lie beneath the skin. Pain is not a disease but a signal, and the clinician's task is to work out which structure is signaling and how urgently it must be answered. This chapter is educational material only, and it cannot replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. Every number that appears is an illustration of the reasoning, and each must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it influences the care of a real person.

The lethal possibilities must be named before the comfortable ones, each with the finding that would betray it. A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm produces pain that bores into the back or the flank, a pulsatile and expansile upper abdominal mass, a rapid pulse, and a pressure that is falling. A perforated viscus produces a rigid, board-like abdomen that hurts on the slightest movement, with bowel sounds that have gone quiet. A strangulated bowel, whether it is trapped in a hernia or twisted on its own mesentery, gives colicky pain in waves, vomiting, distension, and a failure to pass stool or gas. An ectopic pregnancy in a woman of childbearing age gives lower abdominal pain, a missed or unusual period, and the signs of internal bleeding. Mesenteric ischemia gives pain that is severe and out of proportion to a soft abdomen, and that mismatch is the finding that should alarm rather than reassure. These are the causes that force action, and they are named here so that the search begins with them rather than arriving at them last.

The acute abdomen is a syndrome rather than a diagnosis, and it is recognized by a pattern of findings that point to irritation or compromise of the peritoneum. Involuntary guarding is a tightening of the abdominal wall that the patient cannot relax on request, and rigidity is that tightening taken to a board-like extreme. Rebound tenderness is the pain produced when the examining hand is lifted, and percussion tenderness is the same irritation elicited by a gentler tap. Quiet bowel sounds, pain on coughing or movement, a rising pulse, and a falling pressure complete the picture. The clinician who assembles the whole pattern, rather than resting on one dramatic sign, is far harder to mislead. When peritonism, rigidity, or shock is present, the diagnosis can wait and the decision cannot, because the patient needs surgical help now whatever the underlying cause turns out to be.

The same reasoning must serve in two very different rooms. In a hospital with a laboratory, a bedside ultrasound, computed tomography, and a surgeon within call, the history and examination decide which of those tools to summon and how quickly. In a district clinic whose equipment is a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same history and examination decide something else: whether the abdomen can be watched safely here, or whether the patient must begin a journey that may take hours. The questions do not change between the rooms, only the consequences of the answers. A clinician who reasons well without imaging will use imaging better when it exists, because he already knows which question the image must answer. What travels between the two settings is not the equipment but the method.

Abdominal pain is a good place to practice the diagnostic loop, because the findings arrive in a sequence and each one should change the working explanation. The clinician forms a hypothesis from the site alone, predicts what the examination should then show, and looks for it deliberately, so that the abdomen becomes a set of answers to questions rather than a general impression. The pre-test probability is set by age, sex, the setting, and the pattern of previous illness, and it is why the same tenderness means different things in a young woman and in an older man. Time is part of the instrument, because an abdomen that is equivocal now may declare itself in a few hours, and the interval between observations is information in its own right. The clinician who records the time of each examination, and what changed since the last, is using the cheapest diagnostic test that medicine possesses.

Pain from the abdominal organs travels along nerves that follow the embryological origin of the organ, and that is why the site of early pain so often differs from the site of the disease. The foregut, which includes the stomach, the first part of the small bowel, the liver, the biliary tree, and the pancreas, sends its pain to the upper abdomen around the epigastrium. The midgut, which includes the rest of the small bowel and the first half of the colon, sends its pain to the region around the umbilicus. The hindgut, which includes the remaining colon and the rectum, sends its pain to the lower abdomen. Visceral pain of this kind is usually dull, poorly localized, and accompanied by nausea or sweating, because the organs themselves are not richly supplied with the nerves that localize touch and injury. When inflammation spreads to the peritoneum that lines the wall, the pain becomes sharp, well localized, and tender to the hand, and that change is one of the most useful transitions in the whole assessment.

Location is the first filter, and the clinician should ask the patient to point with one finger to where it hurts worst and to say where it started. Epigastric pain draws attention to the stomach, the duodenum, the pancreas, the biliary tree, and the lower esophagus, but also to the heart, because pain from the heart can be felt in the upper abdomen. Right upper quadrant pain draws attention to the gallbladder, the liver, and the diaphragm, and a right lower lung infection can produce pain in exactly the same place. Right lower quadrant pain draws attention to the appendix, the terminal ileum, the right ovary and tube, the right kidney and ureter, and a hernia at the right groin. Left lower quadrant pain draws attention to the sigmoid colon, the left ovary and tube, and the left kidney and ureter. Central and suprapubic pain draws attention to the bladder, the uterus, and the pelvic organs, and to the small bowel when it is obstructed or inflamed.

The migration of pain is often more informative than its final position. The classic movement of appendicitis is from a vague ache around the umbilicus to a sharp, well localized pain in the right lower quadrant, and that shift is produced when inflammation reaches the peritoneum of the abdominal wall. The migration of pain from the epigastrium to the right lower quadrant, or from the epigastrium to the back, carries its own implications and should be asked about specifically. Pain that begins in one flank and travels toward the groin along the line of the ureter suggests a stone, while pain that begins centrally and then becomes generalized suggests that a hollow organ has perforated. A woman with lower abdominal pain should always be asked whether the pain began suddenly and whether it was first on one side and then spread. The clinician who records when the pain moved, and what the patient was doing at the time, has gathered evidence that a single snapshot of the abdomen cannot provide.

Character is the next filter, and patients describe it in words that are worth recording verbatim. Colicky pain comes in waves, builds to a peak, and then subsides, and it is typical of a hollow organ contracting against an obstruction, whether that is the bowel, the bile duct, or the ureter. Constant pain that never lets go suggests inflammation, stretching of a capsule, or ischemia, and it is the character of pancreatitis, cholecystitis, and appendicitis once the inflammation is established. Burning pain that rises into the chest suggests reflux, while a tearing or ripping pain that moves suggests a dissection of the aorta, and the word the patient chooses should be written down exactly as it was spoken. Pain that is severe beyond the appearance of the abdomen is the signature of mesenteric ischemia, and that discrepancy should change the pace of everything that follows.

What provokes the pain and what relieves it narrows the field further. Pain that is worse after a fatty meal and settles over some hours suggests the gallbladder, while pain that comes when the stomach is empty and eases with food suggests the stomach or the duodenum. Pain that worsens on movement, coughing, or jolting suggests that the peritoneum is involved, and a patient who lies very still and resists being moved is giving a physical sign rather than an answer. Pain that eases when the patient leans forward may come from the pancreas, and pain that improves when the patient lies still with the knees drawn up may come from the peritoneum. Pain related to passing urine, to menstruation, to defecation, or to intercourse points toward the urinary tract, the pelvic organs, or the bowel.

The associated symptoms make the story a whole, and each one should be asked for directly rather than left to the patient to volunteer. Vomiting that comes before the pain suggests a medical cause, while vomiting that follows the pain suggests a surgical one, and the color and content of what is brought up carry further meaning. Diarrhea, constipation, and the failure to pass gas speak to the bowel, and any blood in the stool or vomit must be asked about explicitly. Fever, sweating, and shivering suggest infection or inflammation, while weight loss, a change in appetite, and a new anemia suggest a process that has been present for longer than the pain. Urinary frequency, burning, and blood in the urine shift attention to the urinary tract, and a missed period, vaginal bleeding, or a discharge shift attention to the pelvic organs. A cough, a sore throat, or a chest pain reminds the clinician that the abdomen can be an innocent bystander in a disease of the chest.

The context in which the pain appears changes what it probably means. Age and sex set the prior before a single question is asked, because a young woman with right lower quadrant pain has a different list from an older man with the same complaint. A previous abdominal operation raises the probability of adhesions and obstruction, and a previous hernia, stone, or ulcer raises the probability of its return. Regular medication is part of the history, and steroid treatment, immune suppressing treatment, and pain relief that masks a fever can all make a serious abdomen look quieter than it is. Alcohol use raises the probability of pancreatitis, liver disease, and gastritis, and smoking and age together raise the probability of an aortic aneurysm and of a tumor. Whether the patient is pregnant must be settled in any woman of childbearing age before the reasoning is allowed to settle elsewhere.

Duration changes the meaning of the same pain. A pain that has been present for a few hours is assessed as a possible emergency, while a pain that has been present for months is assessed as a chronic problem with a different list, though neither time frame excludes the other. Recurrent pain that comes in discrete attacks suggests a stone, a peptic ulcer, or an irritable bowel, while pain that has been constant and progressive over weeks suggests inflammation, a tumor, or a chronic infection. A pain that is new in an older patient, or that has changed in character in a patient with a long history, deserves a fresh assessment rather than an old diagnosis. The clinician should ask what the pain was like the first time, what has changed since, and what treatment has already been tried, because those answers often separate a benign pattern from an evolving one.

Examination begins at the end of the bed and not at the abdomen. The pulse, the pressure, the respiratory rate, and the temperature are recorded first, because a patient with a normal abdomen and abnormal vital signs is not a patient with a normal abdomen. The abdomen is then examined in the fixed order of inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation, with the most painful region saved for last. The hernial orifices, including both groins and the umbilicus, are sought deliberately in every patient, because a hernia can be the whole cause and can hide from a hurried look. The rectum is examined when there is bleeding, a suspected mass, or an unexplained picture, and the pelvic examination is performed with consent and a chaperone when the pelvic organs are in question. In any man or boy with abdominal pain, the testicles must be examined, because a torsion can present as abdominal pain alone and will be lost if the clinician does not look.

Pain in the right upper quadrant is one of the most common problems in any clinic, and the reasoning there is a good model of how location, character, and provocation combine. Biliary colic is a steady pain that builds over minutes and lasts for hours, often after a fatty meal, and it may settle as the stone falls back. Cholecystitis adds fever, a persistent pain, and tenderness under the right rib margin that catches when the examining hand presses below it while the patient breathes in. A perforated peptic ulcer can present in the same region with a sudden onset and a rigid abdomen, and the loss of liver dullness is one of the findings that points to free gas. A right lower lung infection, a heart attack, and a kidney infection can each produce pain that the patient places in the right upper quadrant, so the chest and the urine belong in the assessment even when the abdomen is the complaint. Where the pain is right upper quadrant and the patient is jaundiced or feverish, the decision about imaging and about help should not wait for the picture to become obvious.

Epigastric pain is shared by the stomach, the pancreas, the biliary tree, the lower esophagus, and the heart, and the examination must be broad enough to hold all of them. Pancreatitis produces a steady, boring pain that often radiates to the back and eases when the patient leans forward, and it is frequently accompanied by vomiting that does not relieve the pain. A perforated ulcer produces a sudden, severe pain with a board-like abdomen, and it is one of the emergencies in which the diagnosis is made at the bedside rather than in the laboratory. A heart attack can present as epigastric pain, sweating, and nausea, and in an older patient with risk factors an electrocardiogram, or ECG, must be part of the assessment. An aortic aneurysm that is leaking or expanding produces pain that reaches the back, and the palpation of the aorta is therefore never omitted in an older patient with new epigastric or back pain.

Right lower quadrant pain assembles a list that runs from the trivial to the fatal. Appendicitis typically begins as a vague ache around the umbilicus, moves to the right lower quadrant, and is accompanied by loss of appetite, nausea, and a low fever. An ectopic pregnancy must be considered in every woman of childbearing age, and a pregnancy test changes the reasoning more than any other single step, while the signs of internal bleeding change the pace. Torsion of the right ovary produces a sudden, severe pain with vomiting and a tender mass, and it is a surgical emergency of the same order as testicular torsion. A hernia at the right groin can present with pain in the quadrant and a swelling that the patient has not noticed, so the groin is examined before the diagnosis is settled. The decision to observe, to image, or to call for surgery turns on how the findings move over the next few hours as much as on the first examination.

Left lower quadrant pain in an older adult usually raises the possibility of inflammation of the sigmoid colon, which produces a steady pain, a low fever, and a change in bowel habit. Torsion or rupture of a left ovarian cyst, a kidney stone, and a hernia at the left groin are the other frequent explanations, and constipation with a loaded colon can imitate them all. Left upper quadrant pain draws attention to the spleen, the stomach, and the tail of the pancreas, and a spleen that is enlarged and tender suggests infection or a blood disorder rather than a surgical cause. Pain that the patient describes as coming from beneath the left ribs and radiating to the left shoulder suggests irritation of the diaphragm, and that finding should send the clinician back to the chest and to the abdominal catastrophes that can leak upward. The region of the pain is a starting point, and the clinician who stops there will mistake a referred pain for a local one. Every abdominal complaint deserves the same pair of questions, which structure is most likely, and which dangerous structure could produce this same pain.

Testicular torsion deserves its own place in a chapter on abdominal pain, because it is a diagnosis that is lost when the clinician trusts the location of the complaint. The testicle develops in the abdomen and descends, and its nerve supply still reaches the abdomen, so torsion can present as lower abdominal pain with vomiting and no complaint about the scrotum at all. The finding that reveals it is a high, swollen, tender testicle that lies horizontally and hurts when it is lifted, and the absence of the cremasteric reflex on that side supports the diagnosis. The window in which the testis can be saved is short, and the clinician who examines the scrotum in every boy and man with lower abdominal pain will find the cases that others miss. This is a constructed reminder rather than a portrait of a real patient, and it exists only to fix the habit of looking beyond the site of the pain.

Pain that is generalized or that has no clear home requires a different order of thinking. Widespread peritonitis produces a rigid abdomen, quiet bowel sounds, and pain on the slightest movement, and it matters less which organ perforated than that the patient needs surgery at once. Bowel obstruction produces colicky pain in waves, vomiting, distension, and the failure to pass stool or gas, and the bowel sounds may be high-pitched and rushing at first and quiet later. A previous operation raises the probability of adhesions, a palpable mass raises the possibility of a tumor, and a hernia at any orifice raises the possibility of strangulation, which turns a mechanical problem into a dead bowel. Mesenteric ischemia produces pain that is severe and unrelenting while the abdomen remains soft and the examination looks deceptively benign, and it is one of the diagnoses most often made too late. Gastroenteritis and a viral illness can produce diffuse pain, but they are diagnoses of exclusion in a patient who is deteriorating, and they are never made at the expense of the dangerous ones.

The patient whose pain is mild or whose abdomen is soft may still be the patient in the most danger, and this is the trap that fills the surgical ward. The older patient, the patient whose immune response is suppressed by illness or treatment, and the patient with poorly controlled diabetes can all mount a blunted response, so fever, rigidity, and even tenderness may be absent while the disease advances. A woman in the later stages of pregnancy has her organs displaced and her abdominal wall stretched, so the pain and the signs may be both shifted and muted. A patient who has received pain relief may look comfortable while the peritoneum is already inflamed, and a patient who is confused or drowsy may not report pain at all. In all of these people the decision rests on the trajectory and the repeated examination rather than on the first set of findings, and the threshold for asking for help is lower rather than higher. A soft abdomen in a patient who looks unwell is a reason to examine again, not a reason to relax.

Where resources are available, the examination becomes the question that tests are asked to answer. A bedside ultrasound can show free fluid, an inflamed gallbladder, a dilated aorta, a pregnancy inside or outside the uterus, and an obstructed kidney, and it can be performed while the patient is still being examined. Computed tomography, or CT, gives a more complete picture of perforation, obstruction, pancreatitis, and masses, while magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answers particular questions in the liver and the biliary tree. A urine test, a blood count, and a pregnancy test are inexpensive and frequently decisive, and they should be chosen because their result would change a decision rather than because they are available. The clinician should say what he expects each test to show before it is performed, so that a result which contradicts the expectation is recognized as a surprise rather than absorbed without thought. A normal scan in a clearly unwell patient is a reason to think again, and never a reason to dismiss the examination that prompted it.

In a district clinic the task is not the same diagnosis but the same reasoning pushed to a sharper decision. Without imaging the clinician must rely on the history, the vital signs, the repeated examination, and the few tests that are actually within reach. A patient who is stable, whose pain is settling, and whose abdomen remains soft after a period of observation may be watched safely, provided that the plan for review is explicit and the patient can return. A patient with peritonism, rigidity, shock, a pulsatile abdominal mass, or a pain that is severe beyond the appearance of the abdomen must travel, and the decision to send should be made early rather than after a second look confirms what the first already suggested. A thermometer turns the impression of fever into a number that can be followed, a torch allows the hernial orifices and the anus to be examined properly, and a watch allows the pulse and the respiratory rate to be counted rather than estimated. The clinic's advantage is not its equipment but its continuity, and the clinician who sees the patient again in an hour may learn more than a scan would have said.

A constructed illustration may fix the reasoning. Imagine a man of about 50 with a sudden severe epigastric pain that has moved to the back, a pulse of 110 beats per minute, and a pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury. Those figures are illustrations of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the rate and the pressure that should trigger action differ with age, fitness, medication, and the definition in use. The deliberate palpation of the aorta, however, reveals an expansile mass, and the whole plan changes within a minute. Now imagine a woman of about 25 with lower abdominal pain and a fainting episode, and the clinician who asks about her last period before deciding that the pain is colic. Neither patient is real, and neither should be read as a portrait, for they are constructed only to show how one further question can reverse the order of a differential.

The pain itself is never a diagnosis, and a patient who is sent away with a label that the findings do not support is a patient at risk. The clinician should record what was found, what was considered, and what was excluded, so that the next reader can pick up the thread rather than start again. Safety netting is part of the decision, because the patient must be told which symptoms should bring him back, how quickly, and where to go, and that advice must be specific enough to be followed. A pain that has been present for a long time and is unchanged is a different problem from a pain that has appeared in the last few hours, and the tempo of a complaint is one of its most important features. The clinician who is uncertain should say so, and should convert that uncertainty into a plan for review rather than into a confident answer that the evidence does not support.

To summarize, abdominal pain is read by its site, its migration, its character, and what provokes and relieves it, and those features are then mapped onto the structures that lie beneath the skin. The acute abdomen is a syndrome rather than a diagnosis, and it is recognized by peritonism, rigidity, and shock, which demand action before the underlying cause is known. The lethal causes, among them a ruptured aortic aneurysm, a perforated viscus, a strangulated bowel, mesenteric ischemia, an ectopic pregnancy, and a testicular torsion, are named at the bedside and each carries its own revealing finding. The same reasoning is used in a hospital where imaging and surgery are at hand and in a district clinic where the task is to recognize the abdomen that must travel. Every number in this chapter, whether a rate, a pressure, a temperature, a score, or an interval, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient whose abdomen is soft but whose story is alarming is a patient to be examined again and discussed, never a patient to be reassured and sent away.

# Chapter 26 — Nausea, Vomiting, Diarrhea and Constipation

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation are taught as four separate symptoms and are usually met as one disturbance, because a gut that empties too fast and a gut that empties too slowly are answering the same questions about tone, contents and control. They also travel far beyond the abdomen, since a brain under pressure, a diabetic crisis, an infection in the blood and a medicine taken for the heart can each produce them with no lesion in the bowel at all. This chapter therefore treats the four together, reading each by its mechanism, its timing and its content before any name is attached to it. As with every section of this book, what follows is educational material and cannot replace training, supervision, clinical judgment or the protocol of your own service. Every patient mentioned here is a constructed illustration rather than a record of a real person.

Seven dangers deserve to be named before the ordinary causes are considered, each with the finding that would betray it. Bowel obstruction declares itself through colicky pain that comes in waves, abdominal distension, vomiting, and a failure to pass stool or gas, and a strangulated hernia may be the cause hiding quietly at one of the natural orifices. A perforated viscus produces a rigid, board-like abdomen with pain on any movement, quiet bowel sounds, and often a rising pulse as the peritoneum becomes inflamed. Mesenteric ischemia gives pain that is severe and continuous while the abdomen remains surprisingly soft, and that mismatch between the complaint and the finding is the alarm rather than the reassurance. The older patient and the patient whose immune defenses are suppressed may show all of these dangers through a muted version of the same story.

Severe dehydration from any cause shows itself in a rising pulse, a falling blood pressure, cool clammy skin, reduced urine, sunken eyes and a patient who is drowsy rather than merely thirsty. Invasive bacterial infection is suggested by a fever such as 38 degrees Celsius or higher, blood mixed in the stool, severe cramping, and a patient who looks far more ill than the diarrhea alone would explain, although the figure your own service treats as a fever must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the threshold shifts with age and with the site measured. Diabetic ketoacidosis presents with vomiting, deep sighing breathing, abdominal pain that can mimic a surgical abdomen, and a sweet or fruity odor on the breath. Raised intracranial pressure produces vomiting, often in the early morning, with headache, visual change and a level of consciousness that is not quite right.
