Each of these is a reason to move quickly rather than to watch, and the finding that reveals it is named here so that the search is deliberate rather than accidental.

Vomiting is a reflex with a final common pathway, and knowing its inputs explains why the same symptom points in different directions. A center in the brainstem receives signals from the gut through the vagus nerve, from the balance apparatus of the inner ear, from a zone that samples the blood, and from higher centers that carry memory, smell and expectation. Gut-driven vomiting is usually preceded by nausea, follows a meal or a pain, and relieves the discomfort for a while. Vestibular vomiting arrives with vertigo and is worse with head movement, while vomiting from a chemical or metabolic cause may come with little warning and little nausea. Vomiting driven by the brain itself often arrives without nausea and may be projectile, which is a different kind of warning.

What is vomited, and when, carries more information than the act itself. Undigested food suggests a stomach that cannot empty or an esophagus that cannot pass its contents, while bile-stained vomit means the obstruction lies below the point where the bile duct enters the gut. Fecal-smelling or fecal-looking vomit is a late and serious sign of a bowel that has been blocked long enough for its contents to stagnate, and it demands a surgical opinion rather than a symptomatic remedy. Coffee-ground material means blood altered by stomach acid, and fresh red blood means bleeding that is active, so the color of the vomit redirects the whole assessment. Vomiting long after eating points to delayed emptying, while vomiting during or immediately after a meal suggests an ulcer, a stricture or a nervous habit. Projectile vomiting in an infant is its own category and belongs to the assessment of the newborn and the young child.

Nausea without vomiting is a symptom in its own right and should not be treated as a milder version of the same thing. It can arise from the gut, from the inner ear, from a medicine, from a metabolic disturbance, from pregnancy and from anxiety, and the company it keeps is what identifies it. Nausea with early morning headache and visual change belongs to the brain, while nausea with vertigo and ringing in the ears belongs to the balance apparatus. Nausea with epigastric pain before meals belongs to the stomach, and nausea with lower abdominal pain and a missed period belongs to the pelvis. The clinician who asks what the nausea comes with, rather than how severe it is, has already narrowed the field, because tolerance varies between patients more than the diseases do.

Diarrhea is read first by duration, because the passage of time changes the list of causes almost completely. An episode of short duration is usually infective, dietary or caused by a medicine, while diarrhea that persists for weeks suggests malabsorption, inflammatory disease, a chronic infection or a tumor. The distinction is one of reasoning rather than a fixed calendar, since the interval that separates the acute from the chronic differs between sources, so confirm the limit your own service uses against the current guideline and the local protocol. The character of the stool is the second question, since watery stool points to a disturbance of absorption or secretion, fatty stool that floats and is hard to flush points to malabsorption of fat, and stool containing mucus or blood points to inflammation or invasion. Frequency and volume matter most for the risk of dehydration, while weight loss and waking at night are the features that make a chronic cause more likely.

Blood in the stool is never dismissed, because it separates illnesses that need a different pace and sometimes a different place of care. Invasive bacterial infection produces fever, cramping pain, a constant urge to pass stool, and visible blood or mucus, and it is the reason a patient with diarrhea can become seriously ill quickly. The same picture may come from an inflammatory disease of the bowel, from a parasite, from a sexually transmitted infection in the rectum or from a tumor, and the history of travel, sexual history, medicines and previous episodes is what orders them. A patient with bloody diarrhea and a fever should not be treated as a simple upset stomach, and the decision about antibiotics rests on the likely organism, the severity of the illness and the local pattern of resistance, which is a decision for the current guideline rather than for memory. The safe rule is that blood, fever and a patient who looks unwell together change the plan.

Constipation is the symptom most easily dismissed and most easily misread, because most people who report it have a habit rather than a disease. The clinician therefore asks what has changed, since a lifelong pattern of infrequent stool is a different matter from a new inability to pass anything at all. A change that has developed gradually in an older person, especially with weight loss, anemia or blood, raises the possibility of a tumor and deserves examination of the rectum and the colon. Absolute constipation, meaning that neither stool nor gas is passing, with distension, vomiting and colicky pain, is obstruction until proven otherwise. The patient's own meaning of the word should be sought, because some mean infrequency, some mean straining, and some mean a sensation of incomplete emptying.

The gut has its own nervous system and its own rhythm, and it also lies under the influence of the autonomic nerves, hormones, electrolytes and the blood supply, so a disturbance anywhere along that chain can present as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation. This is why the four symptoms so often appear together, and why one cause can produce a mixed picture, since an infection that empties the bowel quickly may be followed by a quiet, distended abdomen, while an obstruction may begin with diarrhea as the bowel empties behind the block. The medicine history belongs to the gastrointestinal history, because many common drugs alter gut motility and a symptom that began with a new prescription should be treated as linked until proven otherwise, and alcohol or its withdrawal is an easily missed cause of both vomiting and diarrhea. Diabetes can damage the nerves that control the stomach and the bowel, and a diabetic crisis itself presents with vomiting and abdominal pain, while thyroid disease, adrenal insufficiency, a high calcium level, a low sodium level and kidney failure each disturb the gut and change the whole patient. The clinician who considers the whole body before settling on a gastrointestinal cause will recognize the patient whose gut symptoms are the first sign of a metabolic problem.

The history is taken in a fixed way so that nothing important is left to chance, and the Oldcarts framework for the history of the present illness gives that structure without dictating the conversation. Onset, location, duration, character, aggravating and relieving factors, timing and severity are the questions, and applied to the gut they become asking when the symptom began, where it is felt, what it looks like, what makes it better, what makes it worse, and what comes with it. The listener should not march through the list like a form but should use it to notice the gap the patient has left. Bowel habit before the illness is the baseline against which every change is judged, and it must be asked explicitly. Diet, travel, water source, contact with others who are ill, recent antibiotics and the menstrual history in a woman of childbearing age each change the differential, and the patient's own fear about what this might be often points to the answer the clinician has not yet considered.

The examination follows the history and is aimed at the questions the history has raised. The general impression comes first, including whether the patient is alert, drowsy or confused, whether the skin is dry or clammy, whether the eyes are sunken, and whether the breathing is normal or deep and sighing. The abdomen is then examined in the sequence of inspection, auscultation, percussion and palpation, with the painful area left until last, and the hernial orifices and the rectum are examined deliberately rather than hopefully. A rectal examination is the only way to feel a low tumor, a loaded rectum or blood that has not yet appeared on the surface, so it is not omitted because the patient has not mentioned bleeding. In a woman, a pelvic examination answers related questions, and a tender mass beside the uterus or pain when the cervix is moved redirects the assessment toward the pelvis. Vital signs are repeated rather than recorded once, because the direction in which the pulse and the pressure are moving often says more than any single value.

Dehydration is assessed by signs that are available everywhere, and its severity is read from several of them together rather than from any one alone. Thirst, a dry mouth and tongue, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, a pulse of 110 beats per minute, a pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury, cool hands and feet, reduced urine and a change in alertness are the findings, and no single one of them is reliable by itself; those two figures are illustrations of the reasoning, so confirm the values your service treats as abnormal against the current guideline and the local protocol. In an infant the soft spot, the tears, the wetness of the mouth and the number of wet diapers are the practical measures, and the weight is the most objective of all when a scale exists. A loss of a few per cent of body weight is a useful gauge of fluid deficit, but that figure must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than remembered, because the threshold differs for infants, children and adults. Urine output can be measured when a container exists, and the simplest monitoring is to ask the patient or the family to record how often and how much urine is passed.

The decision to rehydrate is a reasoning decision before it is a prescribing decision. A patient who is alert, drinking, passing urine and making tears can usually be managed by mouth, with small frequent amounts of a solution whose composition follows the current guideline and the local protocol. A patient who is vomiting everything, who is drowsy, whose pulse is rising and whose pressure is falling needs fluid into a vein, and the choice of solution, the rate and the total belong to the protocol of the unit and not to this book. The finding that makes oral rehydration the right answer is a patient who can swallow and keep fluid down, and the finding that makes it the wrong answer is one who cannot, or who already shows the signs of shock. Rehydration is also a diagnostic act, because the patient who improves quickly was probably volume-depleted alone, while the patient who does not improve needs the other causes reconsidered.

Diabetic ketoacidosis sits at the front of the list whenever vomiting and abdominal pain meet a patient with diabetes, and it can appear in someone not previously known to have the disease. The findings are deep sighing breathing, a characteristic odor on the breath, drowsiness, thirst and heavy urination before the illness, and sometimes abdominal pain and tenderness severe enough to suggest a surgical abdomen. A glucose measurement changes the picture at once where a meter exists, and where it does not, the history of weight loss, thirst and passing large volumes of urine in a young person is the substitute. The patient can be profoundly dehydrated, and the dehydration and the acid disturbance together explain much of how ill they look. This is not a condition to be managed with reassurance and a wait, and recognizing the pattern is the contribution of the clinician who meets it first.

Vomiting that comes from the brain has a different shape from vomiting that comes from the gut, and the difference is worth learning because missing it is severe. It tends to occur in the early morning, it may be projectile and without preceding nausea, and it is often accompanied by headache that is worse on waking, by blurred or double vision, and by a change in consciousness or behavior. In an infant the equivalent findings are a bulging soft spot, a rapid increase in head size, and refusal to feed with irritability that does not settle. A head injury, a known tumor, a recent infection of the brain or its coverings, or the use of a blood-thinning medicine all raise the probability. The clinician who finds these features should not treat the vomiting as a stomach problem, and should look for the neurological signs and seek urgent help.

Mesenteric ischemia is the vascular catastrophe that presents through the gut, and it is named again here because it is so easily missed. The pain is typically severe, continuous and poorly localized, while the abdomen is soft and the examination seems far too benign for the complaint, and that contrast is the classic warning. The patient may be older, may have an irregular heart rhythm or a recent heart attack, may have narrowing of the arteries elsewhere, and may describe pain after meals with weight loss from fear of eating. Blood in the stool, a rising pulse and a patient who is deteriorating despite a soft abdomen make the picture more urgent. The decision is surgical and immediate, and waiting for the picture to become classical is a mistake, because by then the bowel may already be dead.

Bowel obstruction is a pattern assembled from the history and the examination before any image is seen. Colicky pain in waves, vomiting, distension and the failure to pass stool or gas are the four features, and their presence together is more convincing than any one alone. A previous operation raises the probability of adhesions, a hernia at any orifice raises the possibility of strangulation, a palpable mass raises the possibility of a tumor, and an older patient with weight loss and anemia raises it further. Bowel sounds are high-pitched and rushing early and may become quiet as the bowel tires, so a quiet abdomen does not exclude obstruction. Fever, localized tenderness and a rising pulse suggest that the bowel is already losing its blood supply and that the problem has become a surgical emergency.

A perforated viscus is recognized by the sudden onset of severe pain, a rigid abdomen, and the loss of the normal movement of the wall with breathing. The pain may begin in one region and spread as the contents of the gut irritate the whole peritoneum, and the patient often lies very still because any movement hurts. Percussion tenderness and pain on coughing are useful when deep palpation is too distressing, and the loss of liver dullness is suggestive though unreliable. The patient may be pale, sweaty and tachycardic, and the pressure may fall as inflammation and fluid loss take their toll. An ulcer, a tumor, an inflamed diverticulum and a foreign body are the usual sources, and the decision is surgical and is taken on the clinical picture rather than on a scan.

The older patient and the patient whose immune defenses are suppressed present the same diseases through a quieter channel, and both deserve a lower threshold for investigation and help. Fever may be absent or blunted, pain may be reported late or not at all, and the first sign may be confusion, a fall or a general decline that the family has noticed. Constipation in an older person can be the presenting feature of obstruction, a tumor or a metabolic disturbance, while diarrhea can be the first sign of an infection that will become serious quickly. A patient taking a blood-thinning medicine may bleed into the gut with little warning, and the resulting diarrhea or vomiting may be attributed to something else. The clinician who asks the family what has changed, and who repeats the examination rather than trusting the first one, will catch what the textbook picture hides.

Children lose fluid faster than adults and show it differently, so the assessment in a child weighs the same signs with a different emphasis. An infant with diarrhea may lose a large share of body fluid before the pulse changes noticeably, and the soft spot, the tears, the mouth, the skin and the wet diapers become the working measurements. Vomiting in a newborn that is bile-stained is a surgical emergency, and green vomit in an infant is never treated as a feeding problem until obstruction has been excluded. Projectile vomiting in a young infant, especially with poor weight gain, suggests a narrowed outlet from the stomach, and the decision is surgical rather than dietary. In an older child, vomiting with abdominal pain and a rash should raise the possibility of a serious infection, and the pattern of the rash matters as much as the gut symptoms.

Constipation that is not a habit deserves a deliberate search, guided by what makes it different from the usual complaint. A new change in bowel habit in an older person, with weight loss, anemia, a family history of bowel cancer or blood in the stool, is a reason to examine the rectum and to arrange the appropriate test according to the local protocol. Constipation alternating with diarrhea, a sensation of incomplete emptying, and a stool that has become narrow suggest a narrowing of the bowel that must be explained. Constipation with severe pain, distension, vomiting and the passage of no gas is obstruction, and constipation after abdominal surgery may mean a bowel that has not woken up or a collection of pus. A neurological cause should be considered when there is weakness, numbness or difficulty passing urine, because the bowel and the bladder travel together.

Imaging and laboratory tests are chosen to answer the questions the history has raised rather than to survey the patient. A blood count, electrolytes, kidney function, glucose and a measure of acid base balance are the common starting point, and the stool is examined when infection or blood loss is suspected. A chest radiograph is useful when aspiration, pneumonia or free gas under the diaphragm is possible, and an ultrasound can show free fluid, an obstructed kidney, gallstones or a pregnancy inside or outside the uterus. Computed tomography, or CT, answers questions about obstruction, perforation, inflammation of the pancreas and masses, and it is chosen when its result would change the plan. The clinician should decide in advance what each result would mean, because a test whose answer changes nothing is a cost, a delay and a false reassurance.

Where there is only a stethoscope, a torch and a thermometer, the same reasoning is performed with fewer instruments, and the discipline is to extract more from each. The thermometer turns a vague impression of illness into a number that can be followed, the stethoscope brings the bowel sounds and the chest, and the torch examines the mouth, the skin, the eyes, the hernial orifices and the anus. A watch allows the pulse and the respiratory rate to be counted rather than guessed, and a scale, when one exists, allows weight to be tracked and fluid loss to be estimated. The urine can be inspected for color and volume, the stool for blood, and the abdomen felt for tenderness and distension by hand alone. The decision that follows is rarely a diagnosis but a plan: whether the patient can be watched safely, whether treatment can begin on the clinical picture, and whether the journey to a hospital must start now.

A constructed illustration may fix the reasoning. Imagine an older woman who has vomited repeatedly, whose abdomen is distended and tympanic, who has passed no stool or gas, and who had an operation years before; the working diagnosis is obstruction, and the questions are whether the bowel is compromised and how quickly she must travel. Now imagine a young man with diarrhea and fever who looks well enough to be sent home, in whom blood in the stool and a pulse that has risen since the morning change the decision, so that infection with an invasive organism becomes the leading concern. Neither patient is real, and neither should be read as a portrait, for they are constructed only to show how one further finding can reverse the order of a differential. The value of the illustration is the habit it builds, not the diagnosis it displays.

The patient who is sent home needs a plan as clear as the one made for the patient who stays. The clinician states what should improve, what should prompt an immediate return, and the patient or the family repeats it back so that misunderstanding is found. The findings that should bring a patient back at once are blood in the vomit or stool, a rigid or newly painful abdomen, the passage of no gas, a fever with a patient who looks worse, a failure to keep any fluid down, reduced urine, drowsiness, and pain that is far worse than the examination suggests. The plan should name a person and a place, because advice to return if worse is useless without somewhere to return to. Follow-up is a diagnostic instrument, since the patient whose symptoms resolve confirms one hypothesis and the patient who returns with new findings corrects another, and the written record should show the reasoning and the plan so that the next clinician can continue rather than begin again.

Pregnancy changes both the list of causes and the urgency of the assessment, and vomiting in a woman of childbearing age should always include it in the reasoning. Vomiting in early pregnancy is common and usually manageable, but severe vomiting with weight loss and dehydration requires assessment and support rather than reassurance. Diarrhea and vomiting in pregnancy can also be the first sign of an infection that threatens both mother and fetus, and the threshold for seeking help is lower. Constipation is common in pregnancy and usually harmless, but abdominal pain with bleeding or a missed period raises the possibility of a pregnancy outside the uterus, which is a surgical emergency. The clinician asks about the last period before deciding that the symptom is gastrointestinal, because that one question can redirect the whole encounter.

To summarize, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation are read as one disturbance of the gut and of the whole patient, interpreted through mechanism, timing, content and duration rather than through severity alone. The dangers are named as the symptoms are met, among them bowel obstruction, a perforated viscus, mesenteric ischemia, severe dehydration, invasive bacterial infection, diabetic ketoacidosis and raised intracranial pressure, each with the finding that would reveal it and each demanding a decision rather than a wait. Every number, score, cut-off, reference range, temperature, rate, pressure, volume and interval in this chapter is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, between editions and between laboratories. Rehydration belongs to the reasoning even though its amounts belong to the protocol, and the same assessment is performed with a laboratory and with only a scale, a watch and clinical judgment. This recording is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment or the protocol of your own service. The patient who is deteriorating is treated while the reasoning continues, because no explanation is worth the delay of someone who is becoming more ill.

# Chapter 27 — Gastrointestinal Bleeding and Jaundice

Bleeding from the gut and yellowing of the skin are two of the oldest signals in medicine, and they arrive together often enough that the clinician should hold them in one frame. Both ask the same three questions, which are where the source lies, how fast the process is moving, and what dangerous thing it may turn out to be. Bleeding travels downward from a point that cannot be seen, and jaundice spreads outward from an organ buried under the ribs, so the diagnosis is assembled from indirect evidence and from the way the picture changes over hours. This chapter is educational material and cannot replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which you work. The reasoning is the same in a hospital with endoscopy and in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch and a thermometer, but the decision that follows from it is very different.

The causes that must not be missed are few, and each has a finding that betrays it. A bleed from swollen veins at the lower end of the esophagus, the variceal hemorrhage of raised pressure in the portal circulation, appears in a patient who already carries the marks of chronic liver disease and who vomits fresh blood and then turns pale, sweaty and tachycardic. A perforated peptic ulcer announces itself with sudden severe pain and a rigid, board-like abdomen, while an ulcer that bleeds without perforating may erode an artery and cause a large loss with little warning. A ruptured aortic graft presents as bleeding from the gut in anyone who has had surgery on the aorta, sometimes after a smaller warning bleed, and it is fatal when it is not recognized. Cholangitis, which is infection behind an obstruction of the biliary tree, produces fever with chills, yellowing of the skin and pain in the right upper abdomen. Obstructive jaundice in an older patient is a malignancy until it is proven otherwise, especially when it is painless and progressive and accompanied by weight loss and by a gallbladder that can be felt below the rib margin.

The first practical question in any bleed is whether the source lies above or below the junction where the duodenum becomes the jejunum, because that distinction changes the likely cause, the instrument that will find it, and the speed required. Blood from above that point usually arrives as vomited blood, fresh and bright or dark and partly digested, and it may also pass downward as black, tarry, offensive stool that the clinician calls melena. Blood from below the junction usually arrives as bright red blood through the rectum, though a brisk upper source can look the same when the bowel moves too quickly for the blood to darken. A volume of perhaps 50 to 100 milliliters is often quoted as the smallest amount that will blacken stool, but treat the figure as an illustration and confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the amount depends on how quickly the blood travels and on how long it rests inside the bowel.

How much blood has been lost governs everything that follows, and it must be answered from the circulation rather than from the laboratory. In the first hours of an acute hemorrhage the concentration of hemoglobin may still look normal, because red cells and plasma are lost together and the blood that remains is not yet diluted. The count falls later, as fluid moves from the tissues into the vessels and as any fluid given to the patient dilutes what is left, so a normal early result is a trap rather than a reassurance. The bedside therefore reads the pulse, the blood pressure, the rate and depth of breathing, the warmth of the hands and feet, the state of alertness, and the volume of urine passed. A pulse above 100 beats per minute and a systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury are traditional markers of significant loss, and each of those figures must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since age, pregnancy, physical fitness and long-standing high blood pressure all move the value that matters. A rise in the pulse when the patient sits or stands is often the earliest sign that the circulation is short of volume.

The history in a patient who is bleeding is short and pointed, because time is being spent while blood is being lost. The clinician asks when the bleeding began, whether it is continuing, how much the patient believes has come away, and whether there has been vomiting of blood, black stool or bright red blood. Previous episodes, a known ulcer, an earlier operation on the stomach or the aorta, and any known disease of the liver are asked for by name, because each moves the differential diagnosis sharply. Medicines matter enormously, and the clinician asks about anti-inflammatory painkillers, about drugs that thin the blood and about alcohol, since some of these injure the lining of the stomach and others make a bleed that has started harder to stop. The clinician also asks about weight loss, a change in the habit of the bowel, and a family history of cancer of the stomach or bowel, because a first bleed in an older adult may be the presenting sign of a tumor.

The examination begins at the door, with the clinician noting whether the patient is pale, sweating, restless, drowsy or confused, because these are the outward signs of a failing circulation. The pulse and the pressure are recorded with the patient lying, sitting and standing where that is safe, and the respiratory rate is counted rather than estimated. The abdomen is inspected for distension, for prominent veins on the wall, for a scar from earlier surgery and for the rounded fullness of free fluid, and it is palpated for an enlarged liver or spleen and for tenderness. The rectal examination is not optional in a gut bleed, since it confirms whether blood is present, describes its color, and can reveal a mass that the rest of the examination has not reached. The skin and the eyes are examined for yellowing, for small spider-like vessels on the upper trunk, for redness of the palms and for bruising, since each of these points towards the liver as the origin of the problem.

A variceal hemorrhage is the bleed that kills most quickly, and it deserves its own reasoning. Long-standing liver disease raises the pressure in the vein that drains the gut, and that pressure is carried backward into the veins of the esophagus and the upper stomach, which swell and become thin-walled. When one of them bursts, the patient vomits a large volume of blood, the pressure falls, and the liver that caused the problem is often no longer able to make the factors that clot the blood. The findings that reveal it are the marks of chronic liver disease, an enlarged spleen, free fluid in the abdomen, a history of heavy alcohol use or long-standing viral hepatitis, and a previous episode of bleeding. The clinician who sees fresh blood in the vomit of a patient with any of those features should treat the source as variceal until it is shown otherwise, and where endoscopy is not available the decision is to begin the journey to a place that has it immediately.

Peptic ulcer disease remains the most common cause of a major upper bleed in many settings, and it has two faces. The first is the chronic ulcer that erodes into a vessel and bleeds, sometimes painlessly, sometimes after a period of indigestion or treatment with anti-inflammatory painkillers. The second is the perforated ulcer, in which the wall of the stomach or the duodenum gives way and its contents spill into the abdomen, producing sudden severe generalized pain, a rigid abdomen that moves little with breathing, and a patient who lies very still because any movement hurts. The finding that reveals the perforation best is the rigid abdomen together with a loss of the normal dullness over the liver, since gas escaping under the diaphragm can press against that organ and change its note. Either face of the ulcer can coexist with the other, and a patient who has bled and then develops severe pain has almost certainly perforated as well.

A ruptured aortic graft is the diagnosis that is missed because the clinician does not ask about surgery. In a patient who has had a graft placed on the aorta, an abnormal connection can form between the graft and the bowel, and it typically produces a small warning bleed that stops on its own before a massive and usually fatal one follows. The presentation is therefore bleeding from the gut, most often from above or from a site that endoscopy cannot identify, in a patient with a history of aortic surgery and often with pain in the back or the abdomen. The finding that reveals it is the combination of that surgical history with a bleed that has no obvious cause, and the clinician should ask directly about any previous operation on the aorta in every patient who bleeds from the gut. A pulsatile, expansile mass in the upper abdomen may also be present, and its presence makes the situation more urgent still.

Bleeding from below the duodenum has a different list of causes, and the age of the patient reorders it. In a young person, bleeding that comes and goes, particularly painless bright red blood on the paper, is often from a crack at the anal margin or from swollen veins in the anal canal, but that assumption must be made carefully. In an older person the common causes shift towards outpouchings of the wall of the colon, towards abnormally fragile vessels in the lining of the bowel, towards inflammation of the bowel and towards a tumor. Infection and inflammation produce bleeding with diarrhea, urgency and cramping, and the bleed is usually only part of a picture that also includes fever. A tumor of the colon may bleed slowly and invisibly, producing anemia and fatigue rather than a visible loss, which is why the clinician never dismisses a first episode of rectal bleeding in an older adult as hemorrhoids.

Once a bleed is recognized, the next decision is how urgently it must be managed, and that decision rests on a few features rather than on the appearance of the blood alone. Continuing bleeding, unstable vital signs, a pressure that falls when the patient sits up, a very low count on arrival, an age in the later decades, serious disease of the heart, lung or kidney, and treatment that thins the blood all push the patient towards urgent action. Formal scores exist that combine such features, among them the score named for Glasgow and Blatchford, and they formalize the reasoning that some patients with a normal pulse and pressure still need close observation and early endoscopy. This book does not restate the contents of any such score, because each was derived in a particular population and is revised from time to time, so read the current description and check it against the local protocol before using it to decide anything. What matters at the bedside is that normal first observations in a patient who has bled a large volume are a moment to keep watching, not one to relax.

Jaundice is the yellowing of the skin, the whites of the eyes and the deep tissues that appears when bilirubin, the yellow pigment made from worn-out red cells, accumulates faster than the liver can process and clear it. The reasoning divides it into three broad places where the process can fail, which are before the liver, inside the liver and after it. Before the liver means that the pigment is produced in excessive amounts, usually because red cells are destroyed too quickly, so the liver is overwhelmed. Inside the liver means that the organ itself is injured and cannot take up, process or release the pigment, which happens in infection, in damage from alcohol or medicines and in long-standing scarring. After the liver means that bile is made but cannot drain, because a stone or a tumor is blocking a duct, and the pigment is pushed back into the blood. The distinction matters because the treatment, the urgency and the danger are entirely different in each case.

The color of the urine and the stool together form the most useful piece of information the patient can give, and they are asked for explicitly rather than inferred. Dark urine that stains the water like tea means that processed bilirubin is reaching the urine, which points to the liver or to an obstruction after it. Stools that have become pale, clay-colored or putty-colored mean that bile is not reaching the gut, which points to obstruction or to severe injury of the liver, while normally colored stools make complete obstruction unlikely. In jaundice that begins before the liver, the urine usually stays clear of bilirubin, the stools keep their normal color, and the patient is anemic and may have an enlarged spleen. The clinician also asks about itching, which accompanies cholestasis, about pain, which is more typical of stones and of infection than of tumor, and about fever with chills, which suggests infection behind an obstruction.

The speed and the shape of the jaundice carry as much meaning as its presence, and so does the rest of the history. Jaundice that appears within days of an illness like influenza, deepens rapidly and then begins to fade suggests acute hepatitis, particularly in a young person with dark urine and a tender liver. Jaundice that comes in waves with severe pain suggests a stone passing through the duct, while jaundice that deepens steadily over weeks without pain suggests a growing obstruction, most often a tumor. A patient who has had jaundice before, or who has known gallstones or surgery on the biliary tree, brings a different set of probabilities to the same yellow skin. The clinician also asks about weight loss, a new diagnosis of diabetes, treatment with a medicine that can injure the liver, the use of alcohol, recent travel and sexual history, since each of these can redirect the reasoning.

The examination of the jaundiced patient is a search for the organ that has failed and for the marks of long-standing disease. The liver is assessed by its span from the upper border percussed in the chest to the lower edge, by the character of that edge, by whether the surface is smooth or irregular, by whether it is tender and by whether it moves with breathing. A tender, smooth, enlarged liver suggests acute inflammation, a hard, irregular, non-tender liver suggests scarring or a tumor, and a small shrunken liver suggests advanced disease. The spleen is sought below the left rib margin and described by its size, since an enlarged spleen accompanies the destruction of red cells, infection and the raised pressure of liver disease. The clinician also looks for the marks of chronic liver disease, among them small spider-like vessels on the upper trunk, redness of the palms, enlargement of the breasts in a man, clubbing of the fingers and a coarse tremor of the outstretched hands.

One physical finding deserves its own paragraph, because it points towards a cancer rather than a stone. When jaundice is deep but painless and the gallbladder can be felt as a smooth, rounded, non-tender swelling below the right rib margin, the obstruction is more likely to be a slowly growing tumor of the head of the pancreas or of the bile ducts than a stone. The reasoning is that a stone usually scars the gallbladder and prevents it from distending, while a tumor obstructs gradually and allows the organ to fill. This is a tendency and not a law, so it should raise the probability of a tumor rather than settle the diagnosis. The findings to seek with it are weight loss, a mass in the upper abdomen or a recent diagnosis of diabetes, and where imaging exists such a patient needs it promptly.

Cholangitis is the infection that develops when the biliary tree is obstructed and bacteria multiply behind the block, and it can progress to a life-threatening illness within hours. The classical pattern is fever with chills, jaundice and pain in the right upper abdomen, and a later description adds a falling blood pressure and confusion. No single part of that pattern is required for the diagnosis, and a patient who presents with fever and jaundice alone may already be seriously ill. The clinician should therefore treat any patient with jaundice and a temperature as potentially infected until proven otherwise, and should look deliberately for the signs of shock, which include a rapid pulse, cool hands and feet and a reduced volume of urine. A delay in relieving the obstruction is the delay that kills these patients, and the decision to move them is a clinical one made at the bedside.

Obstructive jaundice deserves a separate caution because its benign and its malignant causes look alike at first. A stone in the common duct causes pain and often infection. A tumor of the head of the pancreas, of the bile ducts or of the ampulla where the ducts enter the bowel causes jaundice that is usually painless, progressive and unrelenting, and it is the reason that obstructive jaundice in an older adult must be treated as a malignancy until it is excluded. The patient may also describe itching, pale stools, dark urine, weight loss and a new and unexplained diabetes, and the gallbladder may be palpable below the rib margin. The clinician who assumes a stone because stones are common will occasionally be wrong in the way that matters most, so keep both possibilities visible until the evidence separates them.

Jaundice that begins before the liver is the least common of the three groups, and it is recognized by the combination of anemia, an enlarged spleen and a liver that is normal or only mildly abnormal. The pigment is produced faster than the liver can handle, and the patient may be pale, tired and short of breath rather than deeply yellow. The causes include inherited diseases of the red cell, destruction of red cells by antibodies, a reaction to a medicine, and infection with a parasite such as malaria. The urine stays clear of bilirubin because the pigment has not yet been processed by the liver, and the stools keep their normal color for the same reason.

Several patients deserve special caution because the usual signs mislead in them. The older patient may be taking a medicine that prevents the heart rate from rising, so the tachycardia that would have warned the clinician never appears. The trained athlete may have a resting pulse far lower than the average, so a rate that would alarm most adults looks normal in him, and the direction of change matters more than the absolute number. The patient with dark skin may show jaundice first in the sclera and under the tongue rather than in the skin, and pallor may be difficult to see, so the clinician looks at the conjunctivae, the palms and the lining of the mouth. The patient whose kidneys are failing may not produce the changes in urine output that would otherwise signal a failing circulation, and the pregnant patient, the patient with a disorder of bleeding and the patient whose immune system is suppressed by illness or treatment all change the pace of the decision rather than the principles of it.

In a hospital with a laboratory, imaging and an endoscopy service, the assessment becomes a set of questions asked in a deliberate order. Blood is taken for the count, for the clotting of the blood, for the function of the kidney and the liver and for the group and cross-match that allows blood to be replaced, while the patient is examined and monitored rather than sent away to wait. A tube passed into the stomach can show whether fresh blood is present, and where it is, endoscopy can find the source and treat it during the same procedure. Computed tomography, or CT, is used when the source is not found by endoscopy or when bleeding continues, and it can show a tumor, an abnormal tangle of vessels or blood within the wall of the bowel. The intensive care unit, or ICU, is the place for the patient whose circulation or breathing needs continuous support, and the decision to move such a patient there rests on the whole clinical picture.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch and a thermometer, the same reasoning is compressed into fewer decisions. The clinician counts the pulse and the breathing rate, measures the temperature, records the pressure if a cuff is available, looks at the eyes and the skin in good light, feels the abdomen for a liver, a spleen and free fluid, and performs the rectal examination when a bleed is suspected. The color of the urine can be seen in a clear container, and the color of the stool can be described by the patient and confirmed on the glove. If the patient is bleeding, is pale or sweating, has a rapid pulse or a falling pressure, or is jaundiced with a fever, the task is no longer diagnosis but safe and rapid transfer, with the airway protected, the patient kept warm and lying flat, and nothing given by mouth if an operation may be needed. If the patient is stable and the bleeding has stopped, the task is to record what was found, to arrange the earliest possible assessment and to tell the patient exactly what should bring him back sooner.

A constructed illustration may help to fix the reasoning, and it describes no real person. Imagine an older man with known cirrhosis who arrives with vomiting of fresh blood, a pulse of 120 beats per minute and a pressure of 80 millimeters of mercury, and whose abdomen is distended with fluid and whose spleen is felt below the left rib margin; the working diagnosis is a variceal hemorrhage until it is proven otherwise. Both of those figures are illustrations, and the values that should trigger action must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because they differ with age, with physical fitness and with the definition being used. Now imagine a woman of middle age whose skin has turned yellow over several weeks, whose stools have become pale, whose urine is dark and who has lost weight without pain; the reasoning points towards obstruction and towards a tumor rather than towards a stone. In each of these, the point is not the answer but the way one further question moves the order of the possibilities.

The record of a patient who has bled or turned yellow should show what was found, what was considered and what the patient was told to watch for. It should state the color and the amount of any blood, the observations and their timing, the findings of the abdominal and rectal examinations and the reasoning that led to the plan. Where a diagnosis was not established, the note should say so plainly and should name the possibilities that remain, so that the next clinician does not begin from nothing. Safety-netting is part of the diagnosis rather than a courtesy after it, and the patient should be told which symptoms mean return immediately, among them fresh bleeding, vomiting of blood, black stool, fever with jaundice, confusion and pain that becomes severe. The patient should also be told where to go and how quickly, in words that assume no medical knowledge, and the advice should be written down wherever literacy allows.

A small number of errors in reasoning account for most of the harm in these two presentations. The first is to attribute rectal bleeding to hemorrhoids in a patient whose age makes a tumor more likely, and the second is to accept a normal early blood count as proof that a hemorrhage has been small. The third is to attribute painless jaundice to a mild viral illness in a patient whose jaundice is deep, progressive and accompanied by weight loss. The fourth is to treat a patient with a temperature and jaundice as a routine case rather than as a possible infection of the biliary tree. The fifth is to forget that a patient who has had surgery on the aorta can bleed from the graft, and the sixth is to let a single normal examination close the question in a patient who is clearly unwell.

To summarize, bleeding from the gut and jaundice are each an invitation to find the source, to judge the loss, and to name the dangerous possibility before the comfortable one. In bleeding, the appearance of the blood separates an upper from a lower source only roughly, the circulation tells the truth about volume before the blood count does, and a variceal hemorrhage, a perforated ulcer and a bleeding aortic graft must be excluded early. In jaundice, the color of the urine and the stool and the character of the liver and spleen place the patient before, within or after the liver, and an obstruction that is painless and progressive is a malignancy until it is shown not to be. Cholangitis is the diagnosis that turns jaundice into an emergency, and it must be recognized from the combination of fever, yellowing and pain rather than awaited with certainty. Every number in this chapter, whether a pulse, a pressure, a volume, a temperature or an interval, is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such figures differ between countries, between editions and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision or clinical judgment. In the hospital with endoscopy and in the clinic with a stethoscope and a torch, the question is the same, and the answer that matters most is how fast this patient must travel and to what destination.

# Chapter 28 — Palpitations, Syncope and Collapse

Palpitations and syncope lead the clinician down the same path, because both ask what the heart was doing when the patient felt or looked wrong, and whether the circulation failed briefly or is failing now. A palpitation is an unexpected awareness of the heartbeat, described by its rate, its regularity, and its duration. Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness from a fall in blood flow to the whole brain, with complete recovery, and a collapse is that same event seen by a witness, who may describe it differently from the patient. The lethal causes hide inside these ordinary words, and they are named as the symptom is presented rather than deferred. They are a tachyarrhythmia that has compromised the circulation, complete heart block, narrowing of the aortic valve, a clot in the pulmonary arteries, a ruptured aortic aneurysm, a pregnancy implanted outside the uterus, bleeding around the brain, and a hemorrhage from the gut. Each has a finding that would reveal it at the bedside, and that finding is given with the cause. This is educational material and cannot replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

The description the patient gives is the most powerful instrument for a palpitation, and it is available everywhere. The clinician asks what the heartbeat felt like, when it began, whether the start and the end were sudden or gradual, how long it lasted, and how often it has happened. A heartbeat that starts and stops in an instant usually points to a short circuit in the electrical system, while a rhythm that accelerates and fades over some seconds usually points to an irritable focus firing on its own. Regularity carries as much information as rate, and a single extra beat followed by a pause is usually benign in a healthy heart. The same sensation in a scarred heart may mark a dangerous tendency, so the clinician reads every description with the state of the heart in mind.

A fast and perfectly regular rhythm suggests a reentrant circuit, and its common forms differ by how narrow or wide the electrical wave looks. A fast and irregularly irregular rhythm, in which no two intervals are alike, suggests that the upper chambers are firing chaotically and the lower chambers are following at random. A rhythm that is slow when it should be fast, during exertion or fever, is a warning in itself. The clinician matches the description to a mechanism and then asks whether that mechanism is dangerous in this particular heart, because the same rhythm can be trivial in one patient and lethal in another.

Duration and circumstance change the meaning of the complaint and the plan that follows. A palpitation that ends quickly may need only an explanation and advice to return if it changes, while a rhythm that persists for a long stretch can exhaust the heart and lower the pressure even while the patient is still walking. The clinician asks what the patient was doing when it began, whether it starts on standing, on effort, on bending, after alcohol, after fever, or at rest, and whether anything reliably stops it. Palpitations that begin on standing and resolve on lying flat suggest a rhythm sensitive to posture or a fall in pressure when upright.

The features that accompany the palpitation show how much the circulation is suffering. Chest pain, breathlessness, sweating, impending faintness, confusion, or an actual loss of consciousness turn a nuisance into an emergency. The finding that reveals a tachyarrhythmia with hemodynamic compromise is not the rate alone but a fast rhythm with a falling pressure, cool clammy skin, an altered mental state, or fluid in the lungs, and its presence converts the next step from investigation into resuscitation. A pulse of 150 beats per minute may be tolerated by a young person with a healthy heart and may be enough to decompensate an older person with a weak ventricle, so the number cannot be read without the patient attached to it. Treat that rate as an illustration of the reasoning and confirm the figure your service treats as dangerous against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold is changed by age, by pregnancy, and by the health of the heart muscle.

The state of the heart underneath changes the probability that a palpitation or a faint is lethal. A previous heart attack, heart failure, valve disease, or surgery on the heart raises the risk that a rhythm disturbance will be poorly tolerated and that it signals a structural problem. The murmur of a narrowed aortic valve is the classic example, because a valve that cannot open fully limits the output of the heart during exertion and can cause a faint at the moment the patient most needs flow. The finding that reveals it is a harsh ejection murmur best heard at the upper right of the chest and conducted to the neck, with a pulse that rises slowly and weakly and a narrow pulse pressure. Aortic stenosis is one of the lethal causes named at the start, so it must be sought in every patient who faints on exertion, because that faint is the warning before a cardiac arrest.

Complete heart block is the other electrical emergency hidden in this symptom. Conduction between the upper and lower chambers fails, the lower chambers escape at their own slow rate, and the brain may be starved of flow without warning. The patient often describes a fall without a prodrome, sometimes with a brief convulsion as the brain is deprived, which is why the event is easily mislabeled as a seizure. The finding that reveals it is a pulse that is slow and does not rise when the patient is asked to exert, with a tracing that shows the upper and lower chambers beating independently. A rate below 40 beats per minute at rest is the kind of number that should draw attention, but confirm that cut-off against the current guideline and the local protocol, because a slow rate means different things in a trained athlete, an older person, and a patient taking a drug that slows conduction. When the block is symptomatic and persistent, the decision to implant a permanent pacing device is the right answer, while when it is transient and caused by a reversible trigger such as a drug or an electrolyte disturbance, that same decision is the wrong one until the trigger is corrected.

Syncope is approached as a question of mechanism, and the mechanisms are three. In cardiac syncope the heart fails to deliver enough blood, because the rhythm is too fast, too slow, or because a structural obstruction prevents the output. In reflex syncope a normal reflex fires at the wrong moment, as in the faint after pain, heat, emotion, prolonged standing, or coughing. In orthostatic syncope the pressure falls because the patient has risen and the circulation cannot compensate, whether from loss of fluid, from a drug, or from nerve damage. Placing the event in one of these groups narrows the investigations and the urgency, because the cardiac group carries the greatest danger. A fourth possibility is never forgotten, which is that the event was not syncope at all but a seizure, a low blood sugar, an intoxication, or a psychological attack.

Cardiac syncope has a signature that should stop the clinician's hand. It often arrives without warning, at exertion or while the patient is lying down, and recovery may be quick or may leave the patient pale and breathless. A family history of sudden death in a young relative, a known heart condition, or a previous heart attack makes this explanation far more likely. The finding that reveals it may be a murmur, an irregular pulse, a displaced and forceful heartbeat, a raised jugular venous pressure, or an abnormal tracing, and any of these changes the plan at once. Fainting during exertion must not be filed as a simple faint, because it points to a fixed obstruction or a dangerous rhythm that exertion has provoked. The greater the danger in a symptom, the more important it is that the examination be complete before a reassuring label is applied.

Reflex syncope behaves in almost the opposite way, and its complete pattern is the reassurance the clinician is looking for. There is usually a warning of warmth, nausea, a gray or green tinge to the vision, a roar in the ears, and a feeling of detachment before the patient slides down. The event happens while standing, often after a trigger such as the sight of blood, a painful procedure, a hot room, a long queue, or a bout of coughing, and the patient recovers quickly once horizontal. The finding that supports the diagnosis is the whole scene rather than one sign, and the absence of structural heart disease and of an abnormal tracing is what allows the clinician to rest on it. A story that does not fit this pattern neatly should not be given the label of a simple faint merely because the label is comfortable.

Orthostatic syncope is diagnosed at the bedside with a blood pressure cuff, a watch, and a willingness to repeat the measurement. The pressure is taken with the patient lying quietly and then again after standing, and the finding that matters is a fall in the systolic pressure together with the symptoms the patient recognizes. A fall of 20 millimeters of mercury or more in the systolic pressure after standing is often quoted as the threshold, but that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it is adjusted for age, for the baseline pressure, and for whether the patient has high blood pressure at rest. The pulse response is as informative as the pressure, since a rise in pulse suggests that the nerves are working and the problem is volume, while a pulse that fails to rise suggests a failure of the autonomic response. The causes to seek are dehydration, blood loss, prolonged bed rest, a drug that lowers the pressure or relaxes the vessels, and the nerve damage that accompanies diabetes and some other neurological disorders.

The history of the event is taken in three parts. Before the event the clinician wants the position, the activity, the warning, and the circumstances, because a faint on exertion and a faint after a hot bath are different diseases. During the event the clinician wants what the witnesses saw, because the patient has no memory to offer, and the color of the face, the pattern of breathing, the movements, and any injury are the data. After the event the clinician wants how quickly consciousness returned, whether there was confusion, and whether the same thing has happened before. The witness is interviewed deliberately about whether the eyes were open, whether the patient was pale, blue, or flushed, whether the breathing was quiet or absent, and whether the limbs stiffened or stayed limp. A short-lived event with a few jerks at the end may be a faint rather than a seizure, because a brain starved of blood can produce a brief convulsion, and the witness account is what separates the two.

The examination is focused and unhurried, and it begins with the patient lying comfortably at rest. The pulse is counted rather than estimated, and both wrists are felt because a difference between them may point to a problem in the aorta. The heart is listened to in a quiet room, with attention to the murmurs and the added sounds, and the jugular venous pressure is examined in the neck because a raised pressure points to a failing or obstructed heart. The pressure is measured in both arms and then on standing, the lungs are listened to for fluid, and the abdomen is palpated for a pulsatile expansile mass or a tender swelling. The skin is inspected for pallor, bruising, or the small red spots that suggest bleeding, and the legs are examined for swelling or for the tender cord of a clot in the deep veins.

A hemorrhage from the gut can present as a faint before any blood is seen by the patient. The finding that reveals it is a black, tarry stool, which the patient may describe only if asked about the color of the stool rather than the presence of blood, and which may be found only on a rectal examination. The patient may also report vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, and the pulse rises and the pressure falls before the blood count changes, because the body loses whole blood and the remaining fluid has not yet diluted the count. A normal blood count early in a major bleed is therefore no reassurance at all, and the clinician who waits for the laboratory may wait too long. The decision to treat as an emergency rests on the combination of a faint, a fast pulse, a fall in pressure on standing, and the stool, and it does not wait for anemia to appear.

A ruptured aortic aneurysm is another cause of collapse, and its window for treatment is short. The patient is often older, with a history of high blood pressure or smoking, and the pain may be felt in the abdomen, the flank, or the back. The finding that reveals it is a pulsatile and expansile mass in the upper abdomen, felt with both hands placed on either side, with a falling pressure and a rapid pulse. The examiner must palpate the aorta gently and must not delay the decision while trying to be certain, because the examination can be almost normal in the moments before the circulation fails. A patient with a known aneurysm and new back pain has a rupture until imaging or surgery proves otherwise, and the distance to a surgeon decides how fast the journey must begin.

A pregnancy implanted outside the uterus must be considered in every woman of childbearing age who faints with abdominal pain. The finding that reveals it is lower abdominal pain, often one-sided, with a missed or unusual period, a tender mass beside the uterus, pain when the cervix is moved, and the signs of internal bleeding with a rising pulse and a falling pressure. A pregnancy test changes the reasoning more than any other single step, and where no test exists the menstrual history and the signs of early pregnancy must carry the weight. The patient may have slight vaginal bleeding that she attributes to a period, and the clinician who accepts that explanation without asking about its timing may miss the diagnosis. A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is a surgical emergency, and the decision does not wait for imaging to confirm it.

Bleeding around the brain can also present as a collapse, and its warning may be a headache the patient remembers as the worst of his life. The classic story is a sudden severe headache, sometimes with vomiting, neck stiffness, and a brief loss of consciousness at the moment of the bleed. The finding that reveals it is neck stiffness on examination, with a headache of sudden onset and a patient who is drowsy or confused, and the diagnosis is confirmed by imaging or by examination of the fluid around the brain. The clinician must ask specifically about a sudden headache in any patient who collapsed, because the patient may remember only the fall. A normal examination does not exclude a small bleed, so a patient with a warning headache is treated as a possible bleed until the question is settled.

A clot in the pulmonary arteries can announce itself as a faint, particularly when it is large enough to obstruct the output of the heart. The patient may describe breathlessness, chest pain, or a sense of doom, and the examination may show a rapid pulse, a rapid breathing rate, a low oxygen level, and a leg swollen or tender from a clot in the deep veins. The finding that reveals it is the combination of a faint with breathlessness, a fast heart rate, and signs of a clot in the leg, in a patient who has been immobile, pregnant, recently operated on, or has had a previous clot. The pressure may be low and the neck veins raised, which points to a strain on the right side of the heart.

The electrocardiogram, or ECG, is the single most useful test in these symptoms, and it is read as a set of questions rather than as a picture. The clinician asks what the rhythm is, how fast or slow it is, whether conduction between the upper and lower chambers is normal, whether the intervals are prolonged, and whether there is evidence of a previous heart attack, of thickened muscle, or of an unstable blood supply. The tracing may be normal between episodes, and a normal tracing in a patient with a compelling story is not reassurance but a reason to pursue a recording during the symptoms. The finding that changes everything is often a short run of an abnormal rhythm captured while the patient felt the symptom, which is why the timing of the recording matters more than its number of leads. In a hospital the patient can be monitored continuously, and an ambulatory monitor can be worn while the patient goes about ordinary life, with longer recordings used when the episodes are rare.

In a well-resourced hospital the assessment moves quickly because the tools are at hand. The patient is attached to a monitor, a tracing is taken immediately, blood is drawn for the tests that could explain the event, and imaging such as computed tomography, or CT, and magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, is arranged for the brain, the lungs, the aorta, or the pelvis according to the working hypothesis. Monitoring may continue on a ward, and a rhythm nurse or a device clinic may review the recording, while the intensive care unit, or ICU, is involved when the circulation is unstable or the rhythm dangerous. A normal set of tests does not cancel a dangerous story, and the decision about observation and about the pace of further investigation is made on the clinical picture. Every number that returns from the laboratory or the monitor is read against the patient, and the reference ranges used to interpret them must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because those ranges are set differently in different laboratories and editions.

Where there is no monitor and no laboratory, the same reasoning is performed with a stethoscope, a torch, a watch, and a thermometer, and it is not a lesser medicine. The pulse is counted rather than estimated, and the rhythm is described in words, because an irregularity felt at the wrist is a finding even when no tracing exists. The heart is listened to with the patient both lying and standing, any murmur or added sound is noted, and the neck veins are inspected with the patient propped at an angle. The pressure is measured lying and standing, and the patient is watched during the change for the symptoms he described. The eyes are examined with the torch for pallor that might suggest anemia, the stool is checked for evidence of bleeding, and the abdomen is palpated for a mass or a tender swelling. The thermometer may reveal a fever that points to infection, and although a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is treated as a fever in many settings, that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold is defined differently in different ages and populations.

When a single tracing is the only one that will ever be available, the clinician treats it as one frame of a moving picture. A normal tracing taken after the event says that the heart is not permanently in a dangerous rhythm, but it does not say what the rhythm was during the faint. The witness account then carries the weight the monitor would have carried, and the quality of that account depends entirely on the questions asked. The clinician also uses time as a substitute for equipment, repeating the pulse, the pressure, and the examination after the patient has stood, after a meal, and after exertion if it is safe. A patient whose story is dangerous but whose tests are normal is admitted or transferred rather than reassured, because the absence of evidence is not the absence of disease.

The decisions that follow the assessment concern place and pace rather than a particular drug. A patient with a dangerous rhythm and a compromised circulation needs immediate resuscitation, and the decision to treat belongs to the team that can support the airway, the breathing, and the circulation while the rhythm is corrected. A patient with a slow rhythm and symptoms that persist needs a permanent pacing decision, while the same patient with a transient cause needs that cause corrected first. A patient with a reflex faint and a complete, reassuring story needs explanation, advice about triggers, and a plan to return if the pattern changes. A patient with blood loss needs the source found and controlled, and the decision to replace blood depends on how much has been lost and how well the patient is compensating, not on a single number. The clinician names the decision and the finding that would justify it, and leaves the exact treatment to the protocol and the team that will carry it out.

Safety-netting protects the patient when the diagnosis is uncertain, and it matters especially here because the dangerous episodes are often over by the time the patient is seen. The patient is told what to watch for, which findings should bring him back at once, and where to go if the clinic is closed. The record should state whether the patient had a warning, whether the event occurred on exertion, whether there was a witness, and whether the pressure fell on standing, because those four facts decide much of the risk. A normal examination and a normal tracing do not exclude a dangerous rhythm that has not yet been captured, a small bleed around the brain, a clot that has not yet grown, or a leak from an aneurysm that has sealed itself for the moment. A record that says only that the patient felt faint leaves the next clinician with no way to judge the danger.

Two constructed illustrations show how one finding can reverse the order of a differential, and neither describes a real patient. Imagine an older man who faints while carrying shopping, who has no warning, and whose pulse is slow and does not rise when he is asked to walk, so the description alone already points to a cardiac cause and the tracing confirms that conduction has failed. Now imagine a young woman who faints in a warm queue after a long stand, who feels sick and warm beforehand, and whose pulse and pressure recover as soon as she lies down, so the scene fits a reflex faint and the absence of heart disease and of an abnormal tracing supports it. Change one detail in the second story, so that the faint happens while she sits at rest and there is no warning, and the reflex explanation loses its force. They are constructed examples built for teaching, and real patients are more variable and more surprising than any of them.

Distinguishing a faint from a seizure is one of the most consequential judgments in this chapter. A faint usually begins with a warning, is provoked by standing or by a trigger, lasts a short time, and ends with the patient oriented once the brain is perfused again. A seizure may begin without warning, may be followed by a slow return to full awareness, and is often accompanied by tongue biting on the side, incontinence, and a prolonged period of unresponsiveness. The two overlap, because a faint can produce a few jerks when the brain is briefly deprived of blood, and a seizure can be caused by a sudden fall in pressure. The witness account is the decisive evidence in most cases, and the clinician should record the exact sequence rather than the label the family has already applied.

To summarize, palpitations and syncope are read by matching the patient's description and the witness account to a mechanism, and by dividing the faint into a cardiac, a reflex, and an orthostatic cause, with the cardiac group carrying the greatest danger. The lethal possibilities are named as the symptom is described, among them a tachyarrhythmia with hemodynamic compromise, complete heart block, aortic stenosis, a pulmonary embolism, a ruptured aortic aneurysm, an ectopic pregnancy, a subarachnoid hemorrhage, and a gastrointestinal bleed, each with the finding that would reveal it. The examination of the heart, the pressure on standing, the pulse counted by hand, and the search for pallor, melena, and a tender abdomen are the same reasoning in a hospital full of monitors and in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer. Every rate, pressure, temperature, interval, threshold, and reference range in this chapter is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material and cannot replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and no illustration in it describes a real patient. If the patient in front of you is deteriorating, the reasoning pauses and the patient is treated, because no diagnosis is worth the delay of someone who is becoming more ill.

# Chapter 29 — Back and Joint Pain

Back pain is the complaint that fills more clinics than almost any other, and joint pain follows close behind, yet both are discussed badly because they are sorted by how much the patient complains rather than by what is producing the pain. A mild ache in a young person can be the first sign of a serious infection, while a dramatic pain in an older person can be a strain that resolves without any decision at all, and the volume of the complaint separates neither. This chapter therefore sorts back pain by mechanism: the pain that comes from the mechanical behavior of the spine, the pain that comes from infection, the pain that comes from a tumor, the pain that comes from a fracture, and the pain that comes from inflammation of the joints of the spine. It treats the joint in the same way, separating the single hot joint from the many painful joints and from the pain that is felt in a joint but produced somewhere else. Each of these mechanisms is examined in a hospital where urgent imaging is available and again in a clinic where a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer are the whole instrument set. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient.

Five dangers must be named where the pain is described, because each is revealed by a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. Compression of the spinal cord by a tumor, an abscess, or a broken vertebra threatens permanent paralysis, and the finding that reveals it is a level below which sensation or power is altered. The cauda equina syndrome, in which the bundle of nerves below the end of the cord is compressed, threatens permanent loss of bladder and bowel control, and the findings are numbness in the saddle area and a disturbance of bladder function. A spinal epidural abscess and vertebral osteomyelitis are infections of the spine that can destroy it or spread to the fluid around the brain, and the finding that suggests them is focal tenderness over one vertebra in a patient with fever or with a reason to have infection in the blood. A leaking aneurysm of the abdominal aorta presents as sudden severe back or abdominal pain and can kill quickly, and the findings are a pulsatile mass, a falling pressure, and a difference between the pulses in the two legs. A fracture of a vertebra may be the first sign that bone has been weakened by a tumor or by thinning, and the finding is tenderness over the spinous process after minor trauma or even without any trauma remembered.

Mechanical back pain is the most common kind and the easiest to accept too quickly. It is pain that behaves like a strain: it begins with a movement, a lift, or a twist, it is worse when the spine is loaded or moved and better when the patient lies still, it does not wake the patient in the night, and it is not accompanied by fever, weight loss, or any change in the legs or the bladder. It is common in people who do physical work, who sit for long periods, who are deconditioned, or who have carried something awkwardly, and most such episodes settle over days or weeks without any specific diagnosis being reached. The trap is that a mechanical explanation is so common that it arrives before the dangerous alternatives have been considered, and a clinician who accepts it on the first sentence of the story stops looking for the findings that would overturn it. The safe habit is to name the mechanical hypothesis and then deliberately search for the features that do not belong to it.

The duration of the pain is the first feature that changes the ranking, and it is worth asking for precisely rather than approximately. Pain present for a few days is usually acute and mechanical, while pain present for weeks or months invites the infectious, malignant, and inflammatory explanations. A commonly taught boundary places chronic pain beyond about 6 weeks, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning rather than a rule of nature, so check it against the guideline in use where you work, because the interval is drawn differently in different services and editions. What matters is not the label but the trajectory: pain that is improving, pain that is static, and pain that is worsening tell three different stories. Longstanding pain that has changed character in recent days deserves particular attention, because a new behavior in an old problem is often the only signal of a new disease.

Pain that travels from the back into the leg is a different mechanism from pain confined to the back, and the difference is worth listening for. Nerve root pain follows the line of a nerve, it usually passes below the knee, it is often sharp or burning, and it is worsened by coughing, sneezing, or straining because that raises the pressure around the nerve. A straight leg raise reproduces the pain when the nerve is stretched, and the same maneuver performed on the other side may reproduce it in the first leg, which is a stronger finding. The distribution of the pain, the weakness the patient reports, and the reflex that is reduced together point to the level of the root that is compressed. The clinician should still ask what is compressing the root, because a disc is the common answer and a tumor or an abscess is the one that must not be missed.

The cauda equina syndrome is the emergency that every clinician who touches a back must be able to recognize, because the damage it causes can become permanent if the decision is delayed. The nerves below the end of the spinal cord carry sensation from the saddle area and the genitals and control the bladder, the bowel, and the muscles of the feet. The patient may describe numbness when wiping, a loss of feeling during sex, difficulty starting to pass urine or a loss of the ability to hold it, and weakness or altered feeling in both legs. The examiner looks for reduced sensation in the saddle region, a reduced anal tone on the gloved finger, and weakness of the muscles of the foot, and the finding that most often settles the question is a bladder that retains urine when the patient believes it has emptied.
