This is a condition in which the decision to image and to involve a surgeon is made on the clinical findings rather than on the result of a test, and no clinician should wait for a scan before considering it. A patient with back pain and a disturbance of bladder function is a patient who must travel now.

Compression of the spinal cord itself is the second emergency, and it announces itself with a pattern that differs from the cauda equina syndrome. The patient may have a known cancer, or may have lost weight, or may have pain that wakes him from sleep and is worse when lying flat, and the pain may be described as a band around the chest or the abdomen. Weakness that begins in the legs and moves upward, a level on the trunk below which sensation feels different, and difficulty passing urine all point to the cord rather than to a single root. The finding that reveals it is the sensory level together with the pattern of weakness, and the examination must include the power of the legs, the reflexes, and the sensation on both sides of the trunk. Cord compression from a tumor is treated as an emergency because the ability to walk that is lost before treatment is often not regained afterwards.

Infection of the spine is easily missed because it begins quietly and because the patient may have no fever at all. Vertebral osteomyelitis is infection of a vertebral body, and a spinal epidural abscess is a collection of pus between the bone and the covering of the cord; the two frequently occur together, and both are more likely in a patient with diabetes, with infection in the bloodstream, with a history of injecting drugs, with a recent spinal procedure, or with a line or a device in the body. The pain is usually focal, aching, and present at rest, it is tender when one spinous process is pressed, and it may be worse at night. Fever and a raised marker of inflammation support the diagnosis, but their absence does not remove it, and a patient whose pain is severe enough to prevent sleep deserves the question to be asked. The finding that reveals the abscess is a neurological deficit that appears or progresses while the patient is being observed, and that finding converts a diagnostic problem into an emergency.

A leaking aneurysm of the abdominal aorta is the third emergency, and it presents as back pain more often than many clinicians expect. The patient is usually older, often a smoker, and may have known disease of the arteries or high blood pressure, and the pain arrives suddenly and severely, often in the back or the flank rather than the abdomen. The patient may faint or feel the world closing in, and the examination may find a pulsatile mass in the abdomen, a pressure that has fallen, and pulses in the legs that differ from one another or are absent. A systolic pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury in such a patient is treated as a warning of shock, but that figure is an illustration and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the pressure that matters depends on the patient's usual value and on age. The finding that reveals the diagnosis may be nothing more than the combination of sudden back pain, a pulsatile mass, and a patient who looks unwell, and that combination should send the patient to a place where surgery can be done without any delay for other tests.

A fracture of a vertebra is the fourth mechanism, and the question is not whether bone broke but why it broke. In a young person a fracture follows a fall or a crash, and the finding is midline tenderness over the injured bone with pain on any movement. In an older person, and especially in one who has taken steroid medicine for a long time, who has an eating disorder, or whose bone has been weakened by a tumor, a fracture can occur with a trivial movement or with no remembered injury at all, and the patient may only notice a loss of height or a new stoop. The examiner looks for a step in the line of the spinous processes, tenderness in the midline rather than in the muscles, and any neurological deficit below the level. A fracture in a patient whose bone is invaded by tumor is the finding that reveals the cancer, and a fracture in a patient with thin bone is the finding that reveals the disease of bone.

Inflammatory back pain is the fifth mechanism, and its features are almost the mirror image of mechanical pain. It begins in a younger person, often before the age of 45, though that figure is only an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the age boundary is stated differently between services and editions. It comes on gradually over weeks, it is worst in the second half of the night and in the morning, and it improves with movement and exercise rather than with rest. Morning stiffness that lasts longer than about 30 minutes is a commonly taught feature, but treat that interval as an illustration and confirm it against the guideline in use where you work, because the boundary is described differently in different editions. The inflammation may also affect the eye, the skin, the gut, or the tendons where they attach to bone, and the patient may mention a red painful eye, a rash, diarrhea, or heel pain without connecting it to the back. The decision that follows is whether the pattern justifies a trial of treatment for inflammation, and the finding that would make that decision wrong is a clear mechanical or malignant explanation that accounts for the pain.

The features that should stop a clinician from settling on a mechanical explanation can be gathered into a short list, and the list is worth running through deliberately at every visit. They are pain that begins before the age of 20 or after the age of 50, pain that follows a fall or a crash, pain that is worse at night or at rest, a history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, fever, a suppressed immune defense, a recent infection or spinal procedure, and any weakness, numbness, or disturbance of the bladder or bowel. The ages of 20 and 50 are quoted here as illustrations of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the ages at which the ranking changes are given differently in different services. The list is not a diagnosis and its absence is not proof of safety, because a dangerous cause can begin without any of these features. Its value is that it forces the clinician to ask the questions while the patient can still answer them.

The single hot joint is the emergency of joint pain, and it must be treated as infection until the assessment says otherwise. The patient holds the joint still, refuses to bear weight on it, and may have a fever and a rapid pulse; the joint is swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender, and the range of movement is reduced in every direction. A crystal arthritis such as gout can produce a joint that looks identical, and a flare of inflammation in a joint that has been replaced, or in a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, can be even harder to distinguish. The finding that reveals the diagnosis is fluid drawn from the joint, examined for organisms and for crystals, and the decision to draw it should be made before treatment begins wherever that is possible. The finding that would make treatment for infection the wrong answer is a joint that is already draining, or a clear crystal arthritis in a patient who is not systemically unwell, and even then the patient must be reviewed closely.

When many joints are painful, the pattern of which joints are involved carries more information than the number of joints. An inflammatory pattern tends to affect the same joints on both sides, to favor the small joints of the hands and the feet and the wrists, to be worst in the morning, and to be accompanied by swelling that is visible and by a general sense of illness. A degenerative pattern tends to affect the large weight-bearing joints, to be worse after use and better after rest, to involve the joints at the base of the thumb and at the ends of the fingers, and to be unaccompanied by fever or weight loss. The clinician should ask about the skin, the eyes, the mouth, the gut, and the urinary tract, because inflammation in those places belongs to the same diseases as the joint pain and may be the finding that names it. The distinction matters because the decision is different in each case, and the finding that would send the patient urgently to a hospital is a single joint that becomes hot and swollen within many painful joints.

Pain felt in a joint or in the back may be produced somewhere else, and the examiner who does not consider referral will treat the wrong place. Disease of the hip commonly presents as pain in the knee or the thigh, and the finding is a hip whose movement is reduced and painful while the knee itself is normal. Disease of the shoulder may present as pain in the arm, and a problem in the neck may present as pain in the shoulder, which is why the joint above and the joint below are always examined. Pain from the kidney travels from the loin toward the groin, pain from the pancreas is felt as a band across the upper back, and pain from the heart may be felt in the arm or the jaw rather than the chest. The rule that ties these together is that every structure sharing a nerve supply with the painful site can be the source, and the examination must include that structure.

The history is the instrument that decides the ranking before the patient is touched, and the Oldcarts framework keeps the account complete. The clinician asks about the onset, the site, the radiation, the character, what makes it better and worse, the timing, and what the patient believes it means, and then asks what has changed in the legs, the bladder, the bowel, and the general health. The occupational history matters, because heavy lifting, prolonged standing, driving, and vibration all load the spine, and the social history matters, because alcohol, smoking, and the medicines already taken change the list of likely causes. The clinician should ask directly about weight loss, night sweats, fever, a previous cancer, a previous episode of tuberculosis, and any recent infection or procedure, because these are the questions that separate the dangerous mechanisms from the benign one. The account of what the patient has already tried, and whether it helped, is often as informative as the account of the pain itself.

The examination of the back is a sequence of observations, and each has a reason. The clinician watches the patient walk and undress, looks at the posture and the curve of the spine from behind, and looks for a step, a tilt, or a patch of hair or skin that marks a hidden defect in the bone beneath. The spinous processes are pressed one at a time while the patient watches for the exact spot that hurts, because tenderness in the midline points to bone and tenderness beside it points to muscle or joint. Movement is tested in flexion, extension, side bending, and rotation, and the clinician notes the range and whether it reproduces the radiating pain. The sacroiliac joints are examined by pressing and by stressing them, the abdomen is examined because the aorta and the organs in front of the spine can produce the pain, and the pulses in the legs and the skin of the feet are checked. The examination is not complete until the nervous system has been tested and the patient has been asked, directly, about the saddle area and about the bladder.

The neurological examination is what converts the history into a decision, and it is performed in a fixed order so that nothing is skipped. Power is tested in the hip, the knee, the ankle, and the great toe, sensation is tested in the saddle region and down each leg, and the reflexes at the knee and the ankle are compared on the two sides. The finding that reveals compression of the cord is a level on the trunk below which sensation is reduced, and the finding that reveals compression of the cauda equina is reduced sensation in the saddle with a reduced anal tone. The examiner should not rely on a single reflex or a single movement, because the nervous system is examined as a pattern and one weak muscle may mean nothing. The gait should be watched, because a patient may walk badly for a reason that the examination of the legs at rest does not explain. Every patient with back pain and any neurological symptom, however slight, deserves this examination and a decision about it before leaving.

In a hospital the reasoning chooses the image rather than the image choosing the diagnosis. A plain radiograph is quick and shows the shape of the bones, a fracture, or a destructive lesion, but it is often normal in early infection and in early cancer, and a normal radiograph therefore cannot remove the suspicion. A computed tomography, or CT, scan shows bone in fine detail and is useful when a fracture or a tumor of bone is the question, while magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, shows the cord and the nerves and the fluid around them and is the examination that answers the question of compression, of an abscess, or of infection within the disc and the bone. The clinician who has formed a hypothesis already knows which image to ask for, and should say what either result would change before the request is made. The decision to image urgently is driven by the findings on examination rather than by the severity of the pain, and the patient with a neurological deficit is imaged at once and discussed with a surgeon while the imaging is arranged.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is done with fewer inputs, and it is not a lesser form of it. The history is taken with more care rather than less, because it is the instrument that never runs out, and it is repeated at the next visit rather than replaced. The torch makes the skin over the spine visible and allows the throat, the eyes, and the perineum to be inspected; the thermometer turns the impression of fever into a figure that can be recorded and compared; the stethoscope allows the abdomen to be listened to and the pulses to be heard. The examination of power, sensation, reflexes, and the saddle area requires no equipment at all and should be performed in every patient with back pain and any symptom in the legs or the bladder. The decision that follows is rarely a diagnosis but a plan: whether the patient can be watched at home, whether treatment can be started on the clinical picture, and whether the journey to a hospital must begin today.

The decision to refer is itself a diagnostic act, and it rests on the history and the examination rather than on a test that is not available. The patient must travel now when there is any weakness, any numbness in the saddle, any disturbance of the bladder or bowel, a fever with focal spinal tenderness, a known cancer with new back pain, or a sudden severe pain in an older patient that could be an aneurysm. The patient must travel soon when the pain has the features of infection or of inflammation, when weight is being lost, or when the pain has not responded to the measures already tried, although the interval that separates soon from now varies and should be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The patients who can be watched at home are those whose pain behaves mechanically, who have no features that suggest a dangerous mechanism, and who can return without difficulty if something changes. The clinician should say which of these three groups the patient belongs to, and should record the reason, because a decision that cannot be inspected cannot be corrected.

The treatment decision belongs to diagnosis because it is reached from the findings, and this book names the decision rather than the medicine. Treatment for infection is the right answer when the history and the examination point to infection of the spine or of a joint and the patient is unwell, and the finding that makes it wrong is a clear alternative explanation such as a confirmed crystal arthritis or a mechanical pain with no supporting features. Surgery is the right answer when there is compression of the cord or the cauda equina, when an abscess must be drained, or when a vertebra has been destroyed and is unstable, and the finding that makes it wrong is a stable spine with no neurological deficit. Treatment for inflammation is the right answer when the pattern of inflammatory back pain is clear and no infection is present, and the finding that makes it wrong is any evidence of infection, because suppressing inflammation in an infected spine is harmful. Naming the finding rather than the medicine keeps the reasoning portable, and it is the reasoning, not the prescription, that this book is written to teach.

To summarize, back and joint pain are sorted by mechanism rather than by the loudness of the complaint, and the mechanisms to keep apart are the mechanical, the infectious, the malignant, the fractured, and the inflammatory. The dangerous causes are named where the pain is described: compression of the cord, the cauda equina syndrome with its saddle numbness and its bladder disturbance, vertebral osteomyelitis and the spinal epidural abscess, the leaking aneurysm of the abdominal aorta, and the fracture that reveals a weakened or invaded bone. The joint is examined for the single hot joint, which is treated as infection until the fluid is examined, for the polyarticular pattern that separates inflammation from degeneration, and for the pain that is referred from the hip, the kidney, the pancreas, or the heart. Every age, interval, pressure, and reference range in this chapter is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient with back pain and a new neurological finding, or with a joint that is hot and swollen and a fever, is moved to a place where the decision can be made, and the search for the exact cause continues from there.

# Chapter 30 — Weight Loss, Fatigue and Anorexia

Three complaints arrive together so often that they are best treated as one problem rather than three, and the reasoning that organizes them is a deliberate hunt for disease the patient has not yet named. Unintentional weight loss, fatigue, and loss of appetite, which clinicians call anorexia, overlap in their causes and reinforce one another in their effects, and each is vague enough on its own to be dismissed as stress, age, or overwork. The clinician who waits for the patient to volunteer a diagnosis will wait past the moment when the diagnosis could have been made, because the patient usually arrives with a symptom and no explanation, and often with a private fear that has not been spoken. The organizing principle of this chapter is measurement before interpretation: what has actually changed in the body, over what interval, and in which direction. Two dangers must be named here, at the point where the symptoms are described, because each is revealed by a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. The weight loss that has no explanation is a cancer until the assessment says otherwise, and the findings that betray it include a new mass, a lymph node that is hard and fixed, blood in the stool or the urine, a mole that has changed, and bleeding after the menopause. Fatigue is not always a mood, and it may be the voice of a failing heart or a falling blood count, announced by a raised jugular venous pressure, by crackles at the lung bases, or by pallor of the conjunctivae and the palms.

The three symptoms travel together because the same illnesses produce all of them, and because each one can make the others worse. A tumor, a chronic infection, or an inflammatory disease releases substances that suppress appetite and consume energy, so that the patient eats less while the body demands more, and the weight falls from both sides at once. Lost weight then removes the reserve that would have carried the patient through the illness, and muscle that is broken down for energy leaves the patient weaker and more tired, which reduces activity and appetite still further. The loss of appetite has its own consequences, because a patient who eats little takes in too little protein, iron, and vitamins, and a shortage of these produces fatigue and pallor that look like a separate disease. Fatigue also has many causes that have nothing to do with weight, among them anemia, a failing heart, a thyroid that is underactive, depression, poor sleep, and the sedating effect of medicines, which is why the three complaints must be examined separately even when they are considered together. The clinician should resist the temptation to give the whole picture one name too early, because the patient may carry two conditions, and a treatable one may hide behind a dramatic one.

The single most useful act in the assessment of weight loss is to measure it rather than accept it as a report. A patient's recollection of how much has been lost is shaped by the fit of clothing, by the comment of a relative, and by the meaning the loss carries, and it is frequently wrong in both directions. The clinician therefore weighs the patient on a reliable scale, in similar clothing, at the same time of day, and records the value beside the previous one, so that a trend can be seen rather than a moment. Where no previous record exists, the patient's own clothes, a belt that had to be tightened, a ring that has become loose, and photographs from a few years earlier can be used as witnesses, and the clinician should ask who else has noticed the change and when. A loss of more than 5 kilograms over 6 months is often taken as the point at which assessment is warranted, but both the amount and the interval are conventions rather than natural laws, so they must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, where they may be stated differently. The direction of the weight matters as much as the amount, because a patient who is still losing is in a different position from one whose weight has fallen and then settled, and the clinician should record the trajectory at every visit rather than the latest value alone. The scale should also be used in the patient who is not obviously thin, because a person who began with a large body can lose a great deal and still look well nourished.

Weight must be interpreted in relation to the patient's height, which is why the body mass index is useful as a description, though it is a crude one. The body mass index relates weight to height and is used to place a patient in a band, with a value below 18.5 often described as underweight, but that edge is an illustration and shifts with age, population, and edition, so confirm the value your service uses against the current guideline and the local protocol. The measure has obvious limits that the clinician should state aloud: it cannot distinguish fat from muscle, it does not say where fat is stored, and it is distorted by fluid retained as edema, by ascites, by a large tumor, and by pregnancy. A patient with a normal body mass index may have lost a great deal of muscle, and a patient with a low one may be lean rather than ill, which is why serial weights and the appearance of the body carry more information than a single value. The next question is whether the loss was intended, because a patient may have changed diet deliberately or may be taking a medicine that reduces appetite, and the finding of a deliberate program changes the whole interpretation. Alongside the weight, the clinician should ask what the patient eats in an ordinary day, who prepares it, and whether the food is available, because the answer often reveals the cause without a test.

Fatigue is the most easily misunderstood of the three complaints, and the clinician should unpack the word before reasoning from it. Patients use fatigue to describe at least four different experiences: a sense that effort costs more than it should and that rest does not restore the energy, a loss of power in a limb or a group of muscles that can be demonstrated on testing, a discomfort of breathing that appears on exertion, and a tendency to fall asleep during the day. True fatigue is a feeling rather than a measurable loss, and it is defined by its relation to effort and by the recovery that follows; weakness, by contrast, is found when the clinician tests power and finds it reduced, and breathlessness is found when the patient describes it, which clinicians call dyspnea, or when the breathing climbs on walking. The pattern in time is often more informative than the severity, so the clinician asks whether the tiredness is worst in the morning or the evening, whether it comes in waves, how long it lasts after effort, whether sleep refreshes it, and whether it began suddenly or crept in over months. Fatigue that has lasted more than a month deserves a deliberate search rather than reassurance, and the interval that should prompt that search must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the boundary is drawn differently in different services. The clinician should also ask what the patient has stopped doing, because a change in work, in walking, or in housework is a more reliable measure of fatigue than any adjective.

The hunt begins with a history that is broad on purpose, because the causes of this triad range from a curable infection to a hidden cancer, and narrow questions find only what is already suspected. The Vindicate framework is one way of keeping the search open, since it prompts the clinician to consider infection, cancer, disease of the blood vessels, inflammatory disease, degenerative disease, and the effects of medicines and social circumstances in the same patient rather than one after another. The clinician asks directly about fever and night sweats, a cough that has lasted for weeks, blood in the sputum, diarrhea or a change in bowel habit, blood in the stool, urinary symptoms, pain anywhere, and the pattern of menstruation. The history also covers travel and residence, contact with animals, water and food sources, alcohol and other substance use, smoking, whether there is any risk of a sexually transmitted infection, dental health, and difficulty in swallowing, because each of these changes the short list of likely causes. Every medicine should be reviewed by name and by purpose, including supplements and traditional remedies, since some cause loss of appetite, weight change, or fatigue directly. The clinician should ask what the patient believes is happening and what the patient fears, because the answer often names the diagnosis that has been quietly worrying the patient, and it also reveals how the illness is understood at home. A family history of cancer, tuberculosis, thyroid disease, or diabetes belongs in the same conversation, as does the question of who else in the household is unwell.

The examination of a patient with this triad is a systematic search for a cause, and it is performed in a fixed order so that nothing is skipped. The clinician begins with general appearance, hydration, and the distribution of fat and muscle, looking for wasting at the temples, loose rings, a watch that now turns on the wrist, and clothing that is too large. The skin is inspected for pallor, bruising, pigmentation, rashes, and dryness, and the hair and nails for thinning and brittleness, because these reflect long-standing shortage as well as recent illness. The lymph nodes are palpated in every accessible region, including the neck, the armpits, the groin, and above the collarbone, and the thyroid is felt for enlargement or a nodule. The mouth is examined with a torch for ulcers, thrush, a coated tongue, and poor teeth, and the abdomen is examined for an enlarged liver or spleen, a mass, or ascites, with a rectal or pelvic examination when the history suggests a source there. The heart and lungs are examined for the signs that betray failure or infection, and the nervous system is examined for weakness, altered sensation, and a change in the reflexes that might indicate disease of the nerves or the spinal cord. In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same examination is performed as completely as the setting allows, and the clinician should repeat it at the next visit rather than treat one normal examination as proof that nothing is wrong.

The weight loss that has no explanation is treated as a cancer until the assessment says otherwise, and the clinician's task is to look for the site rather than to wait for the patient to point to it. The clues are often small and specific: a cough that has changed or that brings blood, a hoarse voice that persists, difficulty in swallowing, a change in bowel habit, blood in the stool, urinary symptoms in an older man, a lump in the breast or the testicle, bleeding after the menopause, a mole that has altered in color or shape, and pain in a bone that is worse at night. Night sweats that soak the bedding, an itch without a rash, and an enlarged lymph node that is hard, fixed, and painless are findings of particular weight, because they suggest disease of the blood or the lymph nodes. In a hospital the reasoning directs the choice of test rather than following it: a tumor in the chest or the abdomen is sought with computed tomography or with magnetic resonance imaging, an ulcer or a growth in the gut is seen through an endoscope, and the diagnosis is settled by a sample of tissue examined under the microscope. The clinician should decide what each possible result would change before ordering it, because an image that would not alter the plan exposes the patient to cost and risk for nothing. In a clinic with none of these tools, the decision that matters is not the diagnosis but the referral, and it rests on the pattern, the interval, the presence of a mass, and the red flags in the history. The finding that makes cancer treatment the right answer is a confirmed tumor, and the finding that makes it the wrong answer is a benign explanation that fully accounts for the weight loss, the fatigue, and the loss of appetite together.

Tuberculosis is one of the infections that most often hides inside this triad, and it must be considered in every patient with weight loss, night sweats, a prolonged fever, and a cough that does not settle, whatever the first suspicion was. The disease can lie in the lung or outside it, and it is more common and more easily missed in a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, so a normal chest radiograph does not exclude it. The finding that reveals it is the organism identified in the sputum, in fluid, or in a sample of tissue, and where that is not possible the clinical picture, the image, and the response to treatment may have to carry the decision together, with the help of the program that manages the disease. Infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, produces weight loss, a chronic diarrhea, thrush in the mouth, enlarged lymph nodes, and a fatigue that no rest relieves, and it deserves testing in any patient with this picture. Testing is offered with counseling and consent, because the result changes not only the patient's own care but the care of others, and the finding that makes treatment the right answer is a confirmed infection, while the finding that makes it the wrong answer is a different confirmed cause that explains the picture completely. Other chronic infections belong in the same frame, among them an abscess in the abdomen or beside the kidney, infection of the lining of the heart, and infection of a bone, each of which can produce weight loss and fatigue for weeks before it declares itself. These are found by looking deliberately at the places that are easy to forget, including the teeth, the back, the perineum, and every line or wound in the body.

Diabetes is a cause that the clinician can often suspect from the history alone, because the weight loss is accompanied by an appetite that is preserved or even increased, together with thirst, a large volume of urine, blurred vision, and a fatigue that fluctuates with the glucose. A bedside test of the urine or a drop of blood can confirm the suspicion in a clinic with almost no equipment, and a fasting glucose of 7 millimoles per liter is one commonly used line for the diagnosis, though that value must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol because the threshold differs between populations and editions. The danger that follows unrecognized diabetes is severe dehydration and a build-up of acid in the blood, and the finding that reveals it is deep rapid breathing, a fruity odor on the breath, drowsiness, and a passage of large volumes of urine, which together demand urgent help. An overactive thyroid produces weight loss with a good appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, tremor, palpitations, and a fast pulse, and the finding may be a smooth enlarged gland or a single nodule felt in the neck. An underactive thyroid produces the opposite picture of fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, and slowed thought, and in an older patient it may present with weight loss rather than gain, so the laboratory is needed to separate the two. Adrenal insufficiency is a rarer but dangerous cause of fatigue and weight loss, and the findings that suggest it are a fall in blood pressure on standing, a darkening of the skin creases and the gums, and a craving for salt. Each of these conditions changes the plan when it is found, and each is found by a test that is cheap and widely available, which is why the search for them should not wait for the patient to become more ill.

When appetite is preserved and weight still falls, the clinician should think about food that is eaten but not absorbed, and about a body that is burning more than it takes in. Disease of the small bowel, among them celiac disease and tropical sprue, damages the surface that absorbs nutrients and produces diarrhea, bloating, anemia, and a stool that is pale, bulky, and difficult to flush away. Disease of the pancreas reduces the enzymes that digest fat, so the stool becomes greasy and the patient loses weight despite eating well, and disease of the liver or the bile ducts interferes with the absorption of fat and vitamins in a similar way. Chronic infection of the gut and inflammatory bowel disease produce weight loss with diarrhea, blood, and abdominal pain, and they are often accompanied by mouth ulcers, joint pain, and a rash that the patient has learned to ignore. The history should search for difficulty in swallowing, pain on swallowing, a sore mouth, and bad teeth, because these reduce the intake of food directly and are easily overlooked in a patient who is trying to eat. In a hospital the stool can be examined for fat, the blood for antibodies and shortages, and the small bowel for damage through a biopsy, while in a clinic with no laboratory the appearance of the stool and the patient's own account of it are the evidence that directs referral.

Anemia is among the commonest explanations for fatigue, and it deserves a deliberate search because it is usually treatable and because it may point to a source of bleeding that is not benign. The findings are pallor of the conjunctivae, the palms, and the creases of the hand, a fast pulse, breathlessness on effort, and a murmur that is soft and heard across the whole chest rather than in one place. A hemoglobin of 10 grams per deciliter is one value that is often described as mild anemia, but the line that matters depends on age, sex, pregnancy, and altitude, so it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The clinician should then hunt for the site of blood loss rather than stop at the diagnosis of anemia, asking about heavy menstruation, bleeding between periods, blood in the stool, dark stools, and blood in the urine, and testing the stool when that is possible. In an older patient, an anemia caused by a shortage of iron is treated as a possible cancer of the gut until the gut has been examined, because the tumor may bleed slowly for months before the patient notices anything. The heart can also be the cause of the fatigue, and the findings that reveal a failing heart are a raised jugular venous pressure, crackles at the base of the lungs, a third heart sound, swelling of the ankles, and breathlessness on lying flat. In advanced heart failure the patient may also lose appetite and weight, so the cardiac examination belongs in every assessment of this triad, however little else the history suggests.

Depression can produce all three symptoms at once, with a loss of appetite, a weight that falls, a fatigue that is worst in the morning, an inability to take pleasure in anything, and a disturbed sleep that ends too early. It is a real diagnosis and a treatable one, and the clinician should ask about mood directly rather than wait for the patient to raise it, because the question is rarely resented when it is asked with care. But depression is also a diagnosis that can hide another, and the finding that should stop the clinician from resting on it is any red flag in the history or the examination, such as a mass, a blood loss, a fever, or a weight loss that continues after the mood has improved. In a younger patient, especially a young woman, a deliberate restriction of food may explain the weight loss, and the condition is then an eating disorder in which the appetite is denied rather than lost, and the danger there is not the weight itself but the disturbance of body salts that can follow the return to eating, a risk that belongs to the clinician who supervises it. The social history is part of the same assessment, because food may be unavailable, cooking may have become impossible, income may have fallen, or the patient may be living alone after a bereavement, and none of these will be found unless the question is asked plainly. Alcohol and other substances may replace food and damage the liver, the gut, and the nerves, and medicines prescribed for another condition may reduce appetite or cause fatigue, so the list of medicines should be read again with this question in mind. Abuse and neglect, in an older person or in anyone who depends on another for care, are causes that the clinician must be willing to consider, because an unexplained weight loss in a person who is not in control of their own food is a serious finding.

The two settings in which this problem is met call for the same reasoning and offer very different instruments. In a well-resourced hospital the clinician can order a blood count, a glucose, tests of thyroid, liver, kidney, and bowel function, markers of inflammation, a chest radiograph, and cultures, and can reach for computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, endoscopy, and biopsy when the question demands them, but each of these is worth doing only if its result would change what happens next. In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is carried by the history and by repeated examination, and the instruments that remain are more powerful than they look. The scale measures the weight and its direction, the thermometer turns the impression of fever into a number that can be compared with the next one, the torch makes the mouth, the skin, the eyes, and the perineum visible, and a strip of urine test paper can detect glucose, protein, and blood. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is one common line for fever, but the accepted value depends on where it was measured and on the patient, so confirm the threshold your service uses against the current guideline and the local protocol. The decision in either setting is often the same: whether the patient can be watched, whether a treatable cause should be treated before the diagnosis is complete, and whether the journey to a hospital must start now. Follow-up is part of the diagnosis rather than an afterthought, so the clinician should give the patient a card on which the weight is recorded and a date on which to return, and should say plainly which changes should bring the patient back sooner, among them a weight that keeps falling, a new pain, bleeding, a fever that will not settle, or a worsening that the patient can see for himself.

A constructed illustration may make these habits concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a description of any real person. Imagine a middle-aged patient who has lost a large amount of weight over several months without trying, whose appetite is good, and whose only complaint is that clothes no longer fit, and in whom a urine test finds glucose and a blood test confirms diabetes. Now imagine an older patient who reports tiredness rather than weight loss, whose examination finds pale conjunctivae and a soft murmur, and whose stool test is positive for blood, so that the search turns to the gut rather than to the mood. Now imagine a young patient with fatigue, a reduced appetite, and a weight that has fallen, whose examination, weight record, and blood tests are all normal, and in whom the mood is low and the sleep is broken, so that the working diagnosis is depression while the red flags are written down and the patient is asked to return. None of these people is real, and none of these stories should be applied to a real patient without a full assessment. What the three share is the move that matters: the clinician asked what had actually changed, sought the finding that the symptom pointed to, and decided with both the likelihood and the danger in view.

To summarize, weight loss, fatigue, and anorexia are three symptoms that belong to one assessment, because the same diseases produce them and because each can worsen the others. The clinician measures the weight rather than accepting a report of it, distinguishes loss of appetite from appetite preserved, and separates true fatigue from weakness, from breathlessness, and from sleepiness, because each distinction changes the list of causes. The dangerous possibilities are named at the bedside and not deferred: the weight loss that is a cancer until the assessment says otherwise, the fatigue that is a failing heart or a falling blood count, tuberculosis, and infection with the human immunodeficiency virus. The hunt is the same in a hospital with a laboratory and a scanner and in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, and in both it is directed by the history, by repeated examination, and by the decision to refer when the pattern is not explained. Every value in this chapter, whether a weight, an interval, a body mass index, a glucose, a hemoglobin, or a temperature, is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such values differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and the patient who is losing weight without explanation deserves a plan for review and a clear statement of the signs that should bring them back sooner.

# Chapter 31 — Edema, Swelling and Lumps

Swelling is a sign a patient can often see before any clinician looks, and because it is visible it is easy to accept as a fact rather than read as a sign. A swollen leg, a puffy face, and a lump in the neck look alike in a waiting room and mean different things at the bedside, and what separates them is pattern rather than size. The organizing question is not how large the swelling has become but whether it is generalized or local, whether it pits under the finger, whether it is tender, and how it behaves with posture and time. Those four observations, made with the eyes and the hands, divide the problem more usefully than any laboratory result, because each points to a different mechanism and a different list of causes. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient.

Certain swellings can kill, and they deserve to be named before the ordinary reasoning begins. The first is the leg that swells on one side after a long journey, an operation, a cast, or any stretch of immobility, because such a leg may hold a clot in its deep veins. The danger is not the leg but the lung, since a fragment of the clot can travel and block the circulation there, and what reveals that complication is sudden breathlessness, chest pain, a racing pulse, or faintness that arrives without warning. The finding that points to the clot is a calf warmer, more tender, and larger than its partner, often with pitting that stops below the knee. A calf that measures 3 centimeters more in circumference than the other is one commonly taught marker, and that figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such boundaries are drawn differently in different countries and revised between editions. A swollen leg with any chest symptom needs urgent help, because waiting for the leg to declare itself may lose the moment when treatment would have worked.

The lump that beats is the second danger, and it is an artery that has widened and thinned rather than a growth. It may lie behind the knee, in the groin, or deep in the abdomen, and it expands in every direction with each pulse, felt as a push rather than a flick transmitted from elsewhere. That expansile movement, sometimes with a vibration or a sound heard through the stethoscope, betrays an aneurysm, and a clinician who mistakes it for an ordinary node and presses hard on it has risked a rupture. The third danger is the lymph node that is hard, irregular, and fixed, because such a node is a cancer until the assessment says otherwise, and what reveals it is fixation to the skin or the tissues beneath. The fourth is the warm, red, severely tender swelling that spreads through a limb while the patient is feverish, and the greatest warning is pain out of proportion to the appearance, blistering, or a patch of skin that has gone numb.

The movement of fluid explains why edema appears where it does, and it can be understood without a single formula. Fluid is pushed out of the smallest blood vessels by the pressure inside them, drawn back by the proteins held in the blood, and whatever remains is collected by the lymphatic channels. Edema appears when one of those four elements fails, namely when the pressure inside the vessel rises, the protein in the blood falls, the vessel wall becomes leaky, or the drainage is blocked. Each failure produces a different distribution, a different feel under the hand, and a different behavior over the day, so the mechanism is the first branch of the differential diagnosis. A clinician who reasons from the mechanism will examine the heart, the liver, the kidney, and the veins in the same patient instead of choosing among them by habit.

When the pressure inside the vessels is too high, fluid gathers in the parts of the body that lie lowest, because gravity decides where the extra pressure is greatest. That is why the legs swell toward evening in a person with a failing heart or an obstructed vein, and why the ankles are noticed first. The swelling pits easily under a finger, it is usually the same on both sides when the heart is the cause, and it may climb higher as the day goes on. A raised pressure in the veins of the neck points to the heart rather than the kidney, and crackles at the lung bases, a heart murmur, or an impulse displaced to the left belong to the same story. The abdomen may fill with fluid as well, so a swollen belly with swollen legs should suggest one engine rather than two separate diseases.

When the protein in the blood falls, fluid leaves the vessels all over the body rather than only in the dependent parts, and the face is often puffy on waking because the fluid pooled there overnight. The kidney can lose large amounts of protein in the urine, the liver can fail to make it, and chronic poor nutrition can do the same, so a generalized pitting swelling with frothy urine or a wasted appearance sends the clinician to those organs. A leaky vessel wall produces a local and often tender swelling, which is the mechanism of inflammation and severe infection, and it develops quickly and may be warm or red. A blocked lymphatic channel produces a swelling that is firm, heavy, and does not pit, because the fluid is rich in protein and the tissues thicken with time. An arm that swells years after an operation or radiotherapy, or a leg swollen where a parasitic worm blocks the lymphatics, follows the same logic.

Pitting is tested by pressing a finger firmly over the swelling against a bone for several seconds, then watching whether a dent remains and how long it takes to fill. A dent that persists shows that fluid is free to move in the tissues, and its depth and duration are recorded in words so that the next examiner can compare. The behavior of the swelling with posture and time is the most informative observation the patient can supply, because a face puffy on waking and normal by noon describes a different mechanism from a leg thin in the morning and tight by evening. The clinician asks when the swelling is worst, what makes it better, whether raising the limb reduces it, and whether it has changed over weeks or hours, and whether it follows gravity and settles with rest, since a swelling that ignores both is usually not fluid.

A swelling that does not pit is a different problem, and the hand should say so at once, because fat, tumor, and thickened lymphatic tissue resist the finger. The skin over it may be dimpled, shiny, or fixed, and each tells the clinician more than the measurement of the lump. Tenderness changes the list of causes sharply, because an inflamed swelling is usually hot, red, and painful, while a painless one is more often a tumor, a chronic venous change, or a lymphatic problem. A swelling that is severely painful out of proportion to its appearance, that is spreading quickly, and that has lost sensation over part of its surface may be a deep infection destroying tissue, and the finding of numbness or of skin that does not bleed demands an immediate surgical opinion.

The history is taken like any other history, but with particular attention to time and to the organs that govern fluid. The clinician asks when the swelling began, whether it started on one side, whether it has spread, and what the patient was doing, including travel, surgery, immobility, or a long period in bed. Questions about breathlessness on lying flat, waking at night short of breath, chest pain, and the passage of urine belong in the first minutes, because they name the heart and the kidney without any test. The patient is asked about weight change, alcohol, the medicines already taken, and any previous clot, cancer, or operation, since each moves a diagnosis up or down the list.

Edema is a final common pathway, so the examination is organized to find which organ is failing rather than to confirm a single guess. The clinician begins with the general look, noting the distribution of the swelling, the pitting, the color of the skin, and the state of the veins, and then turns to the heart. The jugular venous pressure, which is the height of the pulse seen in the veins of the neck, is the most useful single sign, because it separates a heart that cannot cope from a kidney or a liver that has failed. A pressure raised to about 10 millimeters of mercury above the level of the right atrium is one commonly taught boundary, and it is offered here only to show the shape of the reasoning, so confirm what your own service accepts against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the reference differs between editions and between one ward and another. The finding of a raised jugular venous pressure with swollen legs and crackles in the lungs makes the heart the engine of the problem, while the same finding in a patient whose legs are thin suggests that the veins themselves are obstructed.

The kidney announces itself through the urine, the blood pressure, and the face, and all three can be assessed almost anywhere. The clinician asks whether the patient passes less urine than usual, whether it is frothy, whether it has changed color, and whether blood has been visible, and then looks at the face and the eyelids in the morning light. The blood pressure is measured with the patient seated and the arm supported, and a systolic pressure of 140 millimeters of mercury with a diastolic pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury is a widely quoted limit that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the boundary depends on age, pregnancy, and the setting in which it is applied. In a clinic without a laboratory the urine can be inspected in a clear container and the patient asked to collect it over a full day, which turns a vague complaint into a quantity that can be recorded. The finding of blood in the urine together with a generalized swelling makes the kidney the leading organ, and that patient needs assessment for a disease of the filtering units that may be treatable.

The liver produces the proteins that hold fluid in the vessels and also governs the pressure in the veins that drain the gut, so it can produce swelling in two separate ways. The clinician looks for yellow color in the eyes, for small branching red marks on the upper body, and for redness of the palms, and feels for a liver that is enlarged, hard, or irregular. The abdomen is examined for fluid, because a patient with a failing liver often has a swollen belly and thin limbs rather than swollen legs alone. The history of alcohol, of previous jaundice, of injections or blood products, and of a family illness belongs here, and because a patient may be reluctant to give it, the questions are asked plainly and without reproach. Poor nutrition must also be considered, because a poor diet can lower the proteins without any organ being inflamed, and the finding that points there is a wasted appearance with a generalized and painless swelling.

The veins of the legs are examined by looking at both limbs from the groin to the ankle, with the patient standing if possible, because a vein that is invisible lying down may be obvious when the blood has to rise against gravity. The clinician looks for dilated twisting veins, for brown staining of the skin above the ankle, for eczema, for hardening of the fat beneath the skin, and for an ulcer at the inner ankle. The swelling of chronic venous disease is usually present on both sides, worse after standing, better after a night in bed, and it pits at first and becomes firm with time. The finding that separates it from an acute clot is that it has been present for months or years and is neither warm nor tender. A clinician should still ask about a recent clot, because the two conditions can coexist and old venous disease does not protect a patient from a new one.

A leg that has swollen suddenly and on one side must be treated as a clot until that is excluded, and the examination is designed to answer that question carefully. The clinician inspects both legs in good light, notes the color and warmth, feels the calf gently rather than deeply, and measures the same point on each limb with a tape. The finding that supports the diagnosis is a swollen, tender, warm calf with pitting on the affected side, sometimes with discomfort when the foot is bent upward, although none of these signs is reliable enough to settle the matter alone. The interval that matters most is the recent one, because the risk is greatest in the first 3 months after an operation, a long journey, or a period of immobility, and that interval is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since different services draw the window differently. In a hospital the veins can be examined with ultrasound, and a blood test that measures the breakdown products of a clot can help to set the diagnosis aside in a patient whose probability is low, while a clinic with none of these should not attempt to exclude the diagnosis by examination alone and should refer instead.

A lump is described before it is interpreted, and the description follows a fixed order so that nothing is left out. The clinician records the site, the size, the shape, the consistency, the mobility, whether it is attached to the skin or to the tissues beneath, whether it is tender, whether it pulses, and what the skin over it looks like. The neighboring lymph nodes and the rest of the drainage region are examined in the same session, because the lump may be the visible part of a disease that has already spread. The clinician then decides from which layer the lump arises, whether the skin, the fat beneath it, the fibrous sheet that covers the muscle, the muscle itself, the bone, a gland, a lymph node, or a blood vessel. Each layer has its own list of causes, and naming the layer usually removes more of the uncertainty than any other single step.

The site of a lump carries information because the drainage of each region of the body is known. A node in the neck drains the skin, the mouth, the throat, and the ear, a node in the armpit drains the arm, the breast, and the chest wall, and a node in the groin drains the leg, the perineum, and the skin below the waist. The node that sits just above the collarbone deserves particular respect, because disease in the chest or the abdomen can announce itself there while the patient feels entirely well. In the neck the clinician also watches the thyroid gland, because a swelling in the front of the neck that rises when the patient swallows arises from that gland, and a single hard nodule, a fixed gland, or a hoarse voice raises the question of cancer. A node enlarged in a region where the skin is broken or inflamed is usually reacting to that local problem, and the finding that would make reaction the right answer is a node that shrinks as the infection settles.

Consistency and mobility do most of the work when a lump is examined. A soft, tender, freely mobile lump that has appeared over a few days is usually an inflamed node or a small collection of pus, while a firm, rubbery, mobile lump is more often a tumor of the lymph glands and a hard, irregular, fixed lump most strongly suggests a cancer. The clinician tests mobility by moving the lump over the tissues beneath it with the flat of the fingers, and tests attachment to the skin by trying to lift the skin away from it. The finding of skin that dimples or retracts when the lump is lifted, or of a lump that will not move at all, should stop the examiner and trigger a referral. A node that stays enlarged for more than 3 weeks after the infection that seemed to explain it deserves its own assessment, and that interval is a teaching figure that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because follow-up periods differ between services and editions.

The lump that pulsates is examined with great care because the hand can do harm. The clinician places the fingers on either side of the swelling and asks whether it widens in every direction with each beat, which is the behavior of an artery that has dilated, or whether the movement is merely transmitted from a vessel lying beneath an ordinary mass. The finding of an expansile pulsation, sometimes with a vibration or a sound heard through the stethoscope, identifies the swelling as an aneurysm, and the examiner should then stop pressing and look for signs that it is leaking or about to rupture. Pain that is new and severe in the back or the abdomen, a falling blood pressure, a racing pulse, and a pulsatile mass together describe a vascular emergency that needs help immediately. In the abdomen the mass may be felt only when the patient relaxes the wall and the clinician uses both hands at the level of the navel, and behind the knee the same swelling may be mistaken for a joint or a cyst until the pulse is felt.

Lumps in the groin and the scrotum are common and are separated by a few simple observations. The clinician asks the patient to cough and watches whether the swelling expands with the cough, because a hernia does and a lymph node does not, and then asks whether the swelling can be pushed back. A swelling in the scrotum that can be made to disappear by gentle pressure and that returns on standing is likely a hernia, while one that surrounds the testis and transmits light from a torch held against it is likely a collection of fluid. The finding that must never be missed is a firm lump within the testis itself, because a lump of that kind is a cancer until the assessment says otherwise. A swollen abdomen is a related problem, decided by whether the swelling is fluid, gas, fat, an enlarged organ, or a mass. The finding of an irregular, hard abdominal mass together with weight loss and a poor appetite, or of dullness in the flanks that moves when the patient turns onto one side, is the one that demands urgent assessment.

In a well-resourced hospital the assessment is extended by imaging and by the laboratory, but the reasoning that directs them is unchanged. Ultrasound can show whether a vein is blocked, whether the liver is smooth or irregular, whether the kidney is swollen, whether a node is solid or fluid, and whether the abdomen contains free fluid, and it does all of this at the bedside. Computed tomography, or CT, and magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answer questions about deep structures the hand cannot reach, and a clinician who has formed a hypothesis already knows which image to ask for. The laboratory adds a blood count, an assessment of the proteins in the blood, a test of kidney function, and the examination of the urine, each of which answers a specific question in the reasoning. A test is worth ordering only when its result would change what is done next, and a fever of 38 degrees Celsius in a patient with a tender swelling is one widely used marker of infection, though that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold for fever shifts with the site of measurement and the age of the patient.

Where there is no imaging, the same assessment is made with a stethoscope, a torch, a thermometer, and a tape, and it is not a lesser form of reasoning. The tape measures the two limbs at the same point so that a difference can be recorded and compared at the next visit, and the torch makes a scrotal swelling transmit light and a lesion visible in the mouth or the throat. The clinician examines the drainage region of every lump, looks at the urine in a clear container, and measures the blood pressure, and then decides whether the patient can be watched or must travel. A period of about 24 hours of elevation and observation is sometimes enough to separate a venous swelling from an inflammatory one, and that interval is offered as an illustration, so check the current guideline and the local protocol, because the acceptable period of watching depends on the patient and the setting. The finding that makes watching the wrong answer is any chest symptom, a spreading redness, a rapidly growing lump, or a patient who looks unwell, and in those cases the journey begins now.

Treatment is part of diagnosis, and in swelling it is usually a decision about the mechanism rather than about a medicine. Treatment is the right answer when a clot is confirmed or strongly suspected and the risk of bleeding does not outweigh the risk of the clot, and it is the wrong answer when the leg swelling is clearly venous and long-standing, because treating that patient as though a clot were present exposes them to harm for no benefit. A medicine that removes fluid is the right answer when the swelling comes from a heart that is overloaded, and the wrong answer when the swelling comes from a blocked lymphatic channel, which does not respond to it at all. A support stocking is the right answer for a swollen leg whose cause is venous and whose arterial supply is sound, and the wrong answer when the pulses in the foot are poor, because compression can then damage the limb. An antibiotic is the right answer when the swelling is infected and the patient is systemically unwell, and the wrong answer when the appearance is inflammation from another cause and the patient is stable.

A clinician who sends a patient with a swelling home must say clearly what should bring that patient back sooner. The patient or the family should be told to return for breathlessness, chest pain, a swelling that grows quickly, a redness that spreads, a fever, a lump that becomes fixed, or any change in the color of a limb. A review arranged in advance is worth more than a promise to return if things worsen, because many patients cannot judge that for themselves. The record should show the distribution of the swelling, whether it pitted, whether it was tender, the measurements of both limbs, the nodes examined, and the reasoning that was considered and set aside, and a record that lists findings without the thinking forces the next reader to begin again.

A constructed illustration may fix these habits, and it is a teaching device rather than a portrait of any real person. Imagine a patient who arrives with a left leg that has swollen over two days after a long journey, with a calf that is warm and tender and larger than its partner, and no chest symptoms at all. The immediate reasoning names the clot and asks about the lung, and the examination records the measurements, looks for a raised jugular venous pressure, and listens to the chest. Now imagine another patient whose face is puffy in the morning and whose ankles swell by evening, with frothy urine and a blood pressure higher than expected, in whom the kidney is the leading organ from the first minutes. What the two share is the move that matters, which is that the clinician asked the organizing question first and let the pattern choose the next examination.

To summarize, a swelling is interpreted by its distribution, by whether it pits, by whether it is tender, and by how it behaves with posture and time, and those four observations organize everything that follows. The mechanisms are the movement of fluid described in words, namely pressure that pushes it out, protein that holds it in, a wall that lets it through, and drainage that fails, and each mechanism predicts a different picture. The dangers are named at the bedside and not deferred: the unilateral swollen leg with a clot and the lung behind it, the pulsatile mass that is an aneurysm, the hard fixed node that is a cancer until proven otherwise, and the rapidly spreading painful swelling that is a surgical emergency. The same patient is examined through the heart, the liver, the kidney, and the veins, and a lump is described by site, size, consistency, mobility, attachment, and the state of the surrounding skin, with the drainage region examined in the same session. In a hospital the assessment is extended by ultrasound, by computed tomography, and by the laboratory, and in a clinic it is made with a stethoscope, a torch, a thermometer, and a tape, and the reasoning is the same in both rooms. Every score, cut-off, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, or interval mentioned in this chapter is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient whose swelling is spreading, whose breathing is changing, or whose lump is hard and fixed is helped first, and the exact cause is settled afterwards.

# Chapter 32 — Urinary Symptoms and Hematuria

Urinary symptoms describe a tract rather than a disease, and the reasoning they invite is a question of place and of mechanism. A patient who burns when passing urine, a patient who cannot pass urine at all, and a patient whose urine has turned the color of tea may share nothing except the organ that produced the complaint. The first task is therefore to locate the problem along a line that runs from the two kidneys, down the ureters, into the bladder, through the prostate in the man, and out along the urethra. The second task is to decide whether the blood, if blood is present, has come from the filtering tissue of the kidney or from the plumbing below it, because those two answers send the patient in different directions. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient.

Three dangers deserve to be named before the ordinary reasoning begins, because each is revealed by a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. An infection that sits behind an obstruction can destroy the kidney and spill into the bloodstream, and the finding that betrays it is a feverish patient with a rigor, a tender loin, a palpable mass, or a history of stones. A patient in acute retention may be in severe pain with a distended bladder, and the danger is not the discomfort but the pressure that climbs back to the kidneys, revealed by a palpable bladder with a falling passage of urine and a blood test that is no longer normal. Visible blood in the urine is a malignancy until it has been investigated and set aside, and the finding that reveals it is a tumor seen when the inside of the bladder is inspected or when the kidneys are imaged.

The urinary tract is best pictured as a tree of tubes with a reservoir at the base, and the symptoms name the level at which the trouble lies. Pain that begins in the loin and travels around the flank toward the groin belongs above the bladder, in the kidney or the ureter, and it is felt as a deep ache or as waves of colic. Frequency, urgency, and pain in the lower abdomen belong to the bladder, and burning at the moment of passing urine belongs to the bladder or to the urethra. In the man, hesitancy, a stream that starts slowly and stops weakly, terminal dribbling, and a sense of incomplete emptying belong to the prostate and the bladder outlet. Incontinence describes a failure of storage or of control and must be classified before it is explained, because the same wet patient may have a full bladder, an irritable bladder, a weak sphincter, or a body that cannot reach a toilet in time.

The history of a urinary complaint is taken with the Oldcarts framework, which keeps the account complete without turning it into an interrogation. The clinician asks when the symptom began, how it has behaved since, what makes it better or worse, and what the patient has already tried. The color of the urine is asked about explicitly and in the patient's own words, because red, pink, smoky, tea-colored, and the dark brown of cola describe different mechanisms, and because a patient may not volunteer a change that seems embarrassing or unimportant. The timing of the blood within the stream matters, since blood at the very start points to the urethra, blood throughout the stream points higher, and blood only at the end points to the bladder neck or the prostate. Fever, rigors, weight loss, night sweats, a change in bowel habit, a previous stone, a previous catheter, and every medicine the patient takes belong in the same account, because each of them changes the list of likely causes.

Frequency means the bladder empties too often, and it means little until the volume passed each time is known. A patient who passes small amounts many times has an irritable or a reduced bladder, while a patient who passes large amounts often has a problem of volume rather than of storage, and the two suggest entirely different causes, among them diabetes and a kidney that cannot concentrate the urine. Dysuria, the pain or burning on passing urine, is most often caused by infection, but it also accompanies stones, tumors, and the inflammation of the bladder that follows pelvic treatment. Urgency is the sudden and compelling need to pass urine, and when it comes with frequency and pain it makes infection likely, while when it stands alone in an older person it may be the only sign of a bladder that has become unstable. Nocturia, the need to wake and pass urine at night, is a symptom of the aging bladder, of heart failure, of diabetes, and of a prostate that does not empty, and it deserves the same careful questioning as any pain.

A urinary infection is the most common explanation for frequency, urgency, and dysuria in an otherwise healthy young woman, and the reasoning changes when the infection moves above the bladder or meets a blocked system. Infection of the bladder produces pain, frequency, and a cloudy or offensive urine, and it rarely produces fever. Infection of the kidney produces fever, a rigor, pain in the loin, vomiting, and tenderness when the kidney is pressed or struck, and this is a different illness with a different tempo. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is often taught as the line above which fever is present, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold shifts with the route of measurement, the age of the patient, and the edition being consulted. The features that move infection up the list are pregnancy, a stone, a catheter, diabetes, a suppressed immune defense, a congenital abnormality of the tract, because each makes the infection more likely to spread or to recur.

A stone in the ureter produces one of the most distinctive pains in medicine, and it also produces one of the most dangerous mimics. The pain of colic begins in the loin and moves downward and forward toward the groin, comes in waves that make the patient restless, and is often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and blood in the urine that may be visible only under the microscope. A stone larger than 5 millimeters is less likely to pass on its own, but that size is offered only as an illustration and should be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the measurement that matters depends on where the stone sits and on the patient. An aneurysm of the abdominal aorta that begins to leak can produce pain in the flank or the loin that is mistaken for colic, and the findings that betray it are a pulsatile mass, a falling pressure, and a pain that does not match the urinary story. The clinician who assumes a stone in an older patient with a first episode of this pain has made a lethal assumption.

Voiding symptoms in the man describe the outflow, and the examination that answers them is the rectal examination. A prostate that is enlarged, smooth, and firm is the ordinary enlargement of age, and it explains hesitancy, a weak stream, terminal dribbling, and a bladder that does not empty. A prostate that is hard, irregular, or fixed, with a nodule that feels like a pebble within the gland, raises the possibility of cancer, and the finding that confirms it is a sample of tissue taken from the gland. The blood test that measures a prostate protein is a common source of confusion, because it is raised by enlargement, by infection, by recent catheterization, and by cancer alike, so a single raised value does not diagnose the disease. The clinician must therefore treat the test as one piece of evidence, set its interpretation beside the current guideline and the local protocol, and place it beside the rectal findings and the symptom story before drawing a conclusion.

Acute retention is a patient who wants to pass urine and cannot, and it is a urological emergency recognized by the symptom and the examination rather than by any test. The lower abdomen is uncomfortable and full, the bladder is palpable and dull when tapped, and the patient may be agitated, sweating, and in obvious distress. Chronic retention has a quieter face, and it may present with overflow, in which the patient dribbles constantly and the bladder is never empty, or with a gradual failure of the kidneys discovered only when the blood is tested. A pulse of 110 beats per minute in a blocked and infected system is a warning rather than a diagnosis, and that rate must be read against the current guideline and the local protocol, because what is fast for one patient is ordinary for another. The finding that changes the urgency of either picture is a kidney swollen by back pressure, a blood test that is no longer normal, a high potassium, or signs of infection behind the obstruction, because these mean the system is both blocked and threatened.

Incontinence is not one condition but several, and the history separates them with a few simple observations. Stress incontinence is the leakage of a small amount of urine on coughing, laughing, lifting, or sneezing, and it points to a sphincter or a pelvic floor that has lost its support. Urge incontinence is the loss of urine that follows a sudden and overwhelming desire to pass it, and it points to a bladder that contracts without warning. Overflow incontinence is the constant dribbling of a bladder that is always full, and it points to obstruction or to a bladder that has lost its nerve supply. A clinician who assumes that an older person wets the bed because of age, and who does not examine the abdomen, the perineum, and the nervous system, will miss the retained bladder, the pelvic mass, and the spinal cord problem that would have changed the management completely.

The most dangerous cause of a change in bladder control is compression of the spinal cord or of the nerves that leave its lower end, and it must be sought in any patient who suddenly cannot pass urine or becomes incontinent. The findings that reveal it are pain in the back, weakness or numbness in both legs, and a loss of sensation around the saddle area between the legs, together with a bladder that is painless and full. The loss of the ability to pass urine may come before the weakness, which is why it is never dismissed as a urinary problem alone. This is a surgical emergency because the damage becomes permanent with time, and the patient examined early is the one who may recover. A clinician who treats such a patient for a urinary infection while the legs are growing weak has misread the whole problem.

Blood in the urine is the finding that most changes the reasoning, and it must first be confirmed and then classified. Visible blood is blood the patient or the clinician can see, and non-visible blood is blood found only when the sample is tested. Before any of this is accepted, the clinician should establish that the color really is blood, because beets, blackberries, and certain medicines can color the urine red or brown without any bleeding at all. In women, blood may come from the menstrual flow, and a sample collected during a period can mislead the whole assessment. A dipstick that reports blood is not a diagnosis of bleeding, and a positive result must be confirmed by looking at the urine under the microscope before a patient is sent down a long and anxious path.
