Once blood is confirmed, the next question is whether it came through the filter or from the plumbing, and several clues separate the two. Glomerular bleeding tends to make the urine brown, smoky, or the color of tea rather than bright red, and it usually does not produce clots. It is commonly accompanied by protein in the urine, by red cells that are deformed under the microscope, and by casts, which are small plugs of material that form in the tubules of the kidney. The patient may also have swelling around the eyes in the morning, a raised pressure, a rash, joint pains, or a recent sore throat or skin infection, and any of these points to the kidney. Urological bleeding is more often bright red, may contain clots, and may come with colic, obstruction, or the symptoms of a bladder infection. Inflammation of the filtering tissue is a serious diagnosis, and one form of it can destroy kidney function quickly, so a patient with these features needs a specialist and often a hospital.

Malignancy of the kidney, the bladder, or the prostate can all present with blood in the urine, and the cruel feature of that presentation is how well the patient often looks. A tumor of the bladder typically causes visible blood that comes and goes and is not painful, and the bleeding may stop for a time and seem to have resolved. A tumor of the kidney may cause blood, pain in the loin, and a mass that can be felt, but any one of the three may be the only sign. Cancer of the prostate may announce itself through a hard gland on rectal examination rather than through blood, and blood may never appear at all. The findings that reveal these tumors are the direct inspection of the bladder through a thin telescope, the imaging of the kidneys, and the sample of tissue, and none of them can be replaced by a normal dipstick result. The rule that must be spoken plainly is that visible blood in the urine is treated as a malignancy until the appropriate investigation has shown that it is not.

Blood that is found only on testing is a different problem, and its meaning depends heavily on the patient. In a young person after vigorous exercise, during an infection, or at the time of a period, it may mean nothing, and a repeat test once the provoking factor has passed is the sensible first step. In an older person, in a smoker, in someone who has worked with certain industrial chemicals, and in a patient with a history of stones or of pelvic treatment, the same finding may be the first evidence of a tumor. The decision is not whether blood is present but who should be investigated and how, and that decision turns on age, on risk factors, and on whether the blood persists when the test is repeated. The share of such patients who turn out to have a serious cause varies widely between populations, so any figure quoted for it belongs to the current guideline and the local protocol, because the clinics being compared are never quite the same.

Pain in the loin is not always the kidney, and the structures that share the neighborhood must be remembered. A stone produces waves of pain and blood, an infection produces fever and tenderness, and a tumor produces a dull ache with weight loss and sometimes blood. A clot that blocks the artery of the kidney produces sudden severe pain in the loin with blood in the urine, and it is easily mistaken for a stone; the patient often has a rhythm disturbance of the heart or disease of its vessels, and the diagnosis is made by imaging the artery. The leaking aneurysm, a problem in the spine, in the muscle wall of the back, or in the lower ribs can all be felt in the same place. The clinician who examines the back, the abdomen, the pulses in the groin, and the urine before settling on a kidney stone will avoid the mistakes that these shared territories create.

Obstruction of the urinary tract is a problem of pressure, and it can exist without pain or infection. In the man it is usually the prostate; in the woman it may be a pelvic mass, a prolapse, or a bladder that has lost its nerve supply; in the child it may be a congenital narrowing present since birth. The kidney under pressure loses its ability to filter, and the loss is silent until the blood is tested or until the patient becomes unwell with an infection. The finding that identifies it is an empty bladder after the patient has tried to pass urine, or a kidney that is swollen when it is imaged, together with a blood chemistry that shows what has accumulated. The clinician who treats the infection and never asks whether the system is draining will meet the same patient again with the same problem, or with a worse one.

Any patient with a catheter in the bladder has a foreign body in the tract, and the tube changes the meaning of every symptom and every test. A catheter is a common source of infection in hospital, and the longer it stays the more likely it is to produce one; the finding that suggests it is fever with tenderness over the kidney or a cloudy urine in a patient who was previously stable. A catheter can also obstruct, leak around its side, or produce bleeding from the lining of the bladder, and the clinician must check that it is draining rather than assume that it is. In a patient with a catheter who becomes confused or unwell, the tube belongs in the assessment of the source, and the decision about whether to change it is a clinical one. The clinician should also ask whether the catheter is still needed, because the best prevention is removal of a tube no longer doing useful work.

Several groups deserve a higher level of caution because the ordinary signs are altered in them. A child with a urinary infection may have fever alone, or vomiting, or simply a failure to thrive, and a young child needs a urine sample obtained properly rather than a diagnosis made on the smell of a diaper. A pregnant woman may carry bacteria in the urine without symptoms, and the risk to her and to the pregnancy is high enough that the finding is sought deliberately and treated, and the exact criteria belong to the local guideline and the obstetric protocol. An older person may present with confusion, a fall, or a refusal to eat rather than with pain or frequency, and the bladder may be full without complaint. A patient whose immune defenses are suppressed may have a severe infection with almost no fever, so a low threshold for investigation is the right posture rather than a reassuring wait.

Urethral discharge, discomfort on passing urine, and a new sexual partner belong to a different list, and the sexually transmitted infections must be named rather than avoided. Infection with gonorrhea, with chlamydia, with trichomonas, and with the viruses that cause genital herpes produce burning on passing urine and a discharge, and they may be mistaken for an ordinary bladder infection. The finding that reveals them is the organism identified in a sample from the urethra or the cervix, or in the first part of the urine, and a patient whose symptoms persist after a bladder infection has been treated deserves that search. The examination of the genitals, the skin, and the lymph nodes in the groin belongs in the assessment, and the patient should be offered testing for HIV and for other infections at the same visit. The clinician who treats the symptom and does not name the infection leaves the patient and the partner exposed to the same problem again.

In a clinic that has a stethoscope, a torch, a thermometer, and a dipstick, the urinary patient can still be sorted with skill. The history and the examination carry most of the information, and the dipstick adds a few crucial facts: whether blood is present, whether protein is present, whether the urine is concentrated, and whether infection is likely. The clinician examines the abdomen for a palpable bladder or a mass, the loin for tenderness, the genitalia for discharge or ulceration, and the nervous system for the weakness and the saddle numbness that would mean compression of the cord. A urine sample should be collected cleanly and inspected by eye for color and clarity, and the dipstick should be read within the time its maker specifies, since a result read too late is worthless. Where no laboratory exists, the decision is not a diagnosis but a direction, and the finding that forces the journey to a hospital is a retained bladder, a fever with loin pain, or visible blood in the urine.

In a hospital the same reasoning is extended with tools that answer specific questions rather than with more guesswork. A urine sample is examined under the microscope and sent for culture, so that the organism is named and its sensitivity is known, and the culture is the finding that turns a guess into a decision. Ultrasound shows whether the kidneys are swollen, whether a stone is blocking the flow, and whether the bladder empties, and it is available at the bedside in many services. Computed tomography, or CT, answers questions about stones and tumors that ultrasound cannot, and magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, is used when the soft tissues of the tract and their surroundings must be seen in detail. A cystoscopy lets the clinician look directly at the lining of the bladder, which is the only way to exclude the small tumor that a scan may not show, and the urology team on call is the ally who turns a suspicion into a plan.

The decision about treatment is part of the diagnostic process, and in the urinary tract it is often delicate. Treatment for an infection is the right answer when the picture fits, when the patient is stable, and when the sample that will identify the organism has been taken first, because a culture taken after treatment has begun may never name the cause. Treatment is the wrong answer when the system is obstructed, because medicine alone cannot reach an infected kidney that is under pressure, and the finding that should change the plan is a swollen kidney, a full bladder, or a patient who is not improving. Treating blood in the urine without a diagnosis is also the wrong answer, because stopping the bleeding does not remove the tumor that caused it, and the finding that makes treatment appropriate is a cause that has been identified and named. Drainage and the relief of an obstruction are diagnostic acts as well as therapeutic ones, because the patient who improves once the pressure is relieved has confirmed the mechanism.

Two constructed illustrations may make the pattern concrete, and both are teaching devices rather than portraits of real people. The first is a young woman with burning on passing urine, frequency, and a cloudy sample, who has no fever and no pain in the loin, and in whom the decision is to treat a bladder infection on the clinical picture and to explain which features would move the problem higher. The second is an older man with a single episode of painless visible blood in the urine, no fever, and an unremarkable examination, in whom the correct next step is referral for direct inspection of the bladder rather than a repeat test and a reassuring word. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment. What the two share is that the visible symptom, burning in one and blood in the other, was placed beside the danger it might represent before the plan was made.

A clinician who sends a urinary patient home must say what should bring that patient back, and must write down what was found and what was considered. The patient should be told to return if the pain in the loin worsens, if a fever or a rigor appears, if the urine becomes visibly bloody, if the passage of urine stops or slows, or if vomiting prevents fluids from staying down. A repeat test arranged for a patient with blood found only on testing is worth more than a promise to return if things change, because the finding may clear and then mean nothing, or persist and then mean everything. The record should show the color of the urine as the patient described it, the timing of the blood within the stream, the state of the bladder after voiding, and the reasons why a more serious cause was or was not pursued. The most useful sentence in the note is often the one that names what remains uncertain and what has been arranged to settle it.

To summarize, urinary symptoms are organized first by where they arise along the tract and second by whether the blood comes from the filter or from the plumbing, and those two questions decide most of what follows. The dangers are named at the bedside and not deferred: the infected system that is obstructed, the retention that is quietly damaging the kidneys, the compression of the cord that presents as a bladder problem, and the visible blood that is a malignancy until it has been investigated. The history, taken with the Oldcarts framework, and the examination, which includes the abdomen, the loin, the genitalia, the back, and the nervous system, carry more of the answer than any single test. Every figure in this chapter, whether a temperature, a rate, a size, or an interval, is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who cannot pass urine, who is feverish with a tender loin, or who is losing blood visibly is helped first and investigated at the same time, because the diagnosis can wait and the patient cannot.

# Chapter 33 — Altered Consciousness, Confusion and Seizures

A patient who is not thinking clearly presents the most time-critical problem in medicine, because the brain tolerates the loss of oxygen, glucose, and blood flow only briefly. A disturbance of consciousness is therefore an emergency, and the differential that explains it must be run in minutes rather than days. The reasoning turns on two questions asked at once: has the brain itself been injured, or is it reacting to something outside it, such as a poison, an infection, or a failing organ. The states range from the patient who cannot be roused, through the patient who is awake but inattentive, to the patient who has had a seizure and now looks well. This chapter is educational material, it is not a protocol, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the guideline of your own service.

The lethal possibilities must be named at once, each with the finding that reveals it. Hypoglycemia is revealed by a bedside glucose below the accepted threshold, and it is the cause that most often reverses completely once corrected. Hypoxia is revealed by the work of breathing, by blue lips and tongue, or by a chest that barely moves air. A stroke is revealed by a sudden focal deficit, such as weakness of one side, a gaze turned to one side, or a drifting arm. Meningitis and encephalitis are revealed by fever with a stiff neck, a dislike of light, a rash that does not fade under pressure, or a change in behavior with a seizure. Status epilepticus is revealed by a seizure that will not stop, or by attacks from which the patient does not wake, while raised pressure inside the head, head injury, poisoning, sepsis, and metabolic derangement complete the list.

The first question is not the diagnosis but whether the patient can be woken and whether the airway is safe, because that answer decides everything that follows. A patient who responds to voice and protects the airway can be examined in an orderly way. One who does not respond, whose breathing is noisy, or whose chest barely moves needs attention before any diagnostic reasoning begins. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, starts at once in the patient with no pulse, and the search resumes when a circulation is restored. In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer this moment decides whether the patient can be watched, carried, or must travel now.

Consciousness has two components, and separating them makes the assessment precise. Arousal is the level of wakefulness, the degree to which the patient is alert and responsive. Content is what the mind does with that wakefulness, including attention, orientation, memory, language, and the hold on a train of thought. A patient can be fully awake with profoundly disordered content, which is delirium and psychosis, or drowsy with content that stays intact once roused. The record should carry both the ease of rousing and the quality of what the patient says, because a note that says only that the patient was drowsy has lost half the information.

The Glasgow coma scale is the standard way of recording the level of consciousness, and it separates eye opening, verbal response, and motor response. The three components should be written down separately, because they carry different information and the motor response is the most informative. A single figure means far less than the trend, so the score belongs in the record with the time it was taken. The figure at which a service becomes alarmed is not universal, so confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol, where the threshold and the version of the scale may be stated differently. Where a formal scale is impractical, a short ladder of alert, responsive to voice, responsive to pain, and unresponsive detects a change when it is recorded honestly.

Delirium is the most common disturbance of consciousness in hospital practice, and it is a syndrome rather than a disease, so its presence demands a search for the cause. It develops over hours to days, fluctuates through the day, and its cardinal feature is inattention, so that the patient loses the thread of a question. Orientation is usually disturbed, often to time before place and to place before person, which is why a patient who knows his own name may still be severely delirious. Some patients are restless and hallucinating, which is the hyperactive form everyone notices, while others are quiet and slow, which is the hypoactive form mistaken for depression, fatigue, or good behavior, and the interval over which delirium develops is an illustration, so confirm the definition against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Dementia is a different problem, a chronic and progressive decline in cognition that begins slowly and leaves arousal intact until late. The patient is usually alert and may be fully oriented early, and the family can often date the change in memory or word finding to months. The dangerous error is to attribute a new confusion to a known dementia, because delirium is far more likely to explain a change that arrived over a short interval. Delirium is superimposed on dementia more often than it occurs in a normal brain, so the change from baseline rather than the baseline itself is the message.

Psychosis is the third state to separate, defined by a disturbance of content while consciousness, attention, and orientation remain largely intact. Such a patient may hear voices, hold a fixed false belief, or behave strangely, but can usually say where he is and can attend to a conversation. The distinction matters because a psychotic patient can be examined and can agree to simple steps, while a delirious patient cannot reliably do either. It matters also because a first episode of psychosis in an adult may be the surface of an organic cause, including encephalitis, a drug effect, a metabolic disturbance, or a lesion in the brain, and a clinician who labels such a patient psychiatric without examining the temperature, the pupils, the neck, and the glucose has made a diagnosis by assumption.

The reversible causes are sought systematically, and a framework such as Vindicate forces the clinician to walk through the systems rather than stop at the first plausible answer. The search covers infection of the brain, its coverings, and elsewhere; metabolic and endocrine derangement, including glucose, sodium, calcium, and disorders of the thyroid and adrenal glands; drugs and poisons, including prescribed medicines, alcohol, and traditional remedies; structural disease, including stroke, bleeding, tumor, and raised pressure inside the head; and trauma the patient cannot report. Seizures, failure of the liver or kidney, deficiency of thiamine and vitamin B twelve, and withdrawal from alcohol or sedatives belong in the same sweep. The framework does not rank the causes and cannot say which one is present, because it only guarantees that none has been forgotten by accident, and the ranking comes from the story, the examination, and the few available tests.

The history in a patient who cannot give it must be taken from someone else, and the family, the friend, and the ambulance crew are primary sources rather than interruptions. The useful questions are what the patient was like at baseline, when the change began, whether it came suddenly or crept in, and whether it has fluctuated. A witness to a collapse can describe what the patient did before falling, what the limbs did, how long it lasted, and what the patient was like afterwards, and that account is often worth more than any test. The medicine list and the pill bottles in the bag are part of the examination, because a new, doubled, or stopped medicine explains a great deal of confusion, and where no history is available the clinician must record that fact rather than assume it was normal.

The examination follows a fixed order so that the urgent parts are never postponed by the interesting parts. The clinician confirms the airway, counts the breathing, feels the pulse, measures the blood pressure, takes the temperature, and checks the oxygen saturation if a device is available. The glucose is measured at the bedside, because it is the one reversible cause that changes management at once. The pupils are examined with a torch, and their size, equality, and response to light are recorded, since a difference between the two sides suggests pressure inside the head while pinpoint pupils suggest an opioid effect. The neck is tested for stiffness, the skin is searched for a rash, a wound, a bite, a needle mark, or jaundice, and a patient who cannot give a history should be undressed and examined completely on the assumption that injury is present.

Hypoglycemia must be excluded first and by measurement rather than impression, because it can produce every picture in this chapter, from confusion to deep coma and seizures. It is most likely in the patient who takes insulin or another medicine that lowers glucose, in the patient who has not eaten after activity or illness, and in the patient with advanced liver or kidney disease or severe infection. The finding that reveals it is a bedside glucose below the accepted threshold, and that threshold should be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it differs between services and patient groups. Where no meter is available the decision becomes clinical, and the balance of risk favors treating a patient who might be hypoglycemic rather than waiting for a test that may never arrive.

Hypoxia and a failure to clear carbon dioxide are the next causes, and they are found with the eyes and the hands before any machine is needed. A hypoxic patient may be restless, confused, or drowsy, with blue lips, tongue, and nail beds, although the change is easier to see in some skin tones than others. A patient retaining carbon dioxide is often drowsy, warm, and flushed, with a headache and a bounding pulse, and may be a person with known lung disease. A falling breathing rate, a chest that moves very little, or a noisy airway demands action before diagnosis, and a normal oxygen reading does not exclude the retention of carbon dioxide.

A stroke is a lethal and time-dependent cause of altered consciousness, and the finding that reveals it is a sudden focal deficit rather than a symmetrical drowsiness. The patient may have weakness of one side, a drifting arm, slurred or absent speech, a gaze turned to one side, or a neglect of one half of the world. A stroke in the back of the brain may present without weakness, with unsteadiness, double vision, difficulty swallowing, or a drowsiness easily attributed to tiredness. The time at which the patient was last known to be well is among the most important facts, because it decides which treatments are possible, and that interval differs between services and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, while a low glucose must always be excluded because hypoglycemia imitates stroke perfectly.

Infection of the coverings of the brain and infection of the brain itself are the next dangers, and both can kill within hours. The patient with meningitis has fever, severe headache, a stiff neck, and a dislike of bright light, and may vomit, while a rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed against it is a finding of great importance. The patient with encephalitis is more likely to present with a change in behavior, a seizure, or a fever with confusion, and the neck may be supple. The diagnosis is revealed by examination of the fluid that surrounds the brain, after the safety questions about pressure inside the head have been answered, and where the picture is convincing and that examination cannot be done at once, treating on the clinical suspicion is usually right. Everyone who examines such a patient must use personal protective equipment, or PPE, according to the local protocol, and must remember that in the older patient, in the patient with infection by the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, and in the patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, the neck may be supple and the fever absent.

Raised pressure inside the head is a mechanism rather than a diagnosis, produced by bleeding, swelling, a tumor, an obstruction to the flow of fluid, or infection. The patient becomes progressively drowsy, complains of a headache that is worse on lying flat or on waking, vomits without nausea, and may have a rising blood pressure with a slowing pulse. The pupils may become unequal and then fixed, and the level of consciousness may fall in steps rather than smoothly. The finding at the bedside is a falling level of consciousness with a new pupil change, and the level of pressure or pulse that should cause alarm is not the same in every service, so confirm any such threshold against the current guideline and the local protocol. A lumbar puncture in such a patient can be fatal, which is why the patient with these signs needs senior help and a place where that help exists, without waiting for tests that can be done on arrival.

A head injury is easily missed in the patient who cannot say what happened, in the patient who smells of alcohol, and in the older patient who takes a medicine that prevents clotting. The bleeding may be slow, so the patient can be awake and talking at the first assessment and deteriorate over the following hours, and this interval of apparent recovery is the trap. The finding that reveals the expanding collection is a falling level of consciousness, a new weakness on one side, a worsening headache, vomiting, or a pupil that dilates. A patient whose injury was significant and whose examination is not perfectly normal should be sent where imaging and observation are possible, and a patient sent home must be given a clear account of what should bring him back, given to a person who will stay with him.

A seizure is a symptom rather than a diagnosis, and the question that organizes the assessment is not whether the event was a seizure but what caused it. A first seizure in an adult is a structural or metabolic question until it has been answered, and the causes include stroke, bleeding, tumor, infection, a scar from an old injury, a metabolic derangement, a poison, and withdrawal from alcohol or sedatives. A seizure in a patient with a known diagnosis of epilepsy is still a question about why it happened now, whether a missed medicine, an infection, a lack of sleep, or a new structural problem lies behind it. The clinician should resist the comfort of the familiar label, because the distinction between a provoked seizure and one arising from a permanent tendency changes the decision about long-term management, which belongs to a specialist and to the current guideline.

The witness account is the most valuable evidence in a suspected seizure, and it should be obtained before it fades from memory. The clinician asks what the patient was doing before the event, whether there was a warning, whether the eyes turned or the head deviated, and what the limbs did on each side. The color of the face, frothing at the mouth, a bite to the side of the tongue, and loss of control of the bladder are all useful details. A collapse with brief jerking and a rapid recovery is more typical of a faint, while a slow recovery with confusion and headache is more typical of a seizure. A patient who remains weak on one side may simply have weakness that follows a seizure, but a deficit that persists beyond the expected recovery points to a structural cause, and that expected interval is an illustration, so confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Status epilepticus is a medical emergency in which a seizure does not stop by itself, or in which seizures recur without the patient recovering consciousness in between. It is lethal through the strain it puts on breathing, the heart, and the brain, and it is one of the few situations in which diagnosis and treatment must begin at the same moment. The finding that reveals it is simply that the event is continuing, or that the patient is not waking between events, and it requires no laboratory. The duration that separates a prolonged seizure from status epilepticus is stated differently in different guidelines and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because acting on a remembered figure can waste the time that matters. Treatment is right when the event is continuing or recurring, when the airway or the breathing is compromised, and when the glucose is low, while it is wrong when the events have stopped and the priority is to find the cause.

Poisoning and the effects of drugs are among the most reversible causes of altered consciousness, and the clues are often on the body rather than in the blood. The patient with an opioid effect has pinpoint pupils, a slow breathing rate, and a deepening drowsiness, while the patient with a sedative effect is drowsy but rousable, and the patient with alcohol intoxication has the smell on the breath and a coarse tremor. Carbon monoxide poisoning produces headache, confusion, and a cherry-red color in some patients, but that color is not reliable, and the diagnosis is suspected from the setting, such as a fire, a faulty heater, or a shared illness in a household. Withdrawal from alcohol or sedatives produces tremor, sweating, a rising pulse, hallucinations, and seizures, so the medicine list and the empty bottles are the best test available and should be read rather than remembered.

Sepsis is a cause of confusion that must be named, because it is common and because the confusion may be its first and only sign, particularly in the older patient and the patient whose immune defenses are suppressed. The finding that reveals it is not the fever, which may be absent, but the combination of a rapid pulse, a climbing breathing rate, a falling blood pressure, cool or mottled skin, and a shrinking passage of urine. A systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the point at which shock must be assumed, but that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the pressure that matters depends on the patient's usual value and on age and pregnancy. A patient with HIV infection, or a patient taking a medicine that suppresses the immune response, may show none of the classical signs, so the threshold for suspicion must be lower rather than higher, and the examination must look at the chest, the abdomen, the urine, the skin, the joints, and every line and tube in the body.

Metabolic derangement is the group of causes the examination cannot see, and it is found by measuring what can be measured and by reasoning from the pattern of the illness. A low or high sodium, a high calcium, a rising urea and creatinine, a failing liver, and a disturbance of the thyroid or adrenal gland all produce drowsiness, confusion, or coma. The patient with liver failure has a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands, a jaundiced skin, and a musty breath, while the patient with kidney failure may have a dry mouth and deep sighing breathing, and the patient with a high calcium may be drowsy and passing large volumes of urine. Deficiency of thiamine and of vitamin B twelve can produce confusion and unsteadiness, and is common in patients who are malnourished, who drink heavily, or who have had surgery on the gut, so where no laboratory exists the clinician must treat what is plausible and transfer the patient.

In a well-resourced hospital the patient passes through a sequence designed to miss nothing, though it must still be driven by a person who is thinking. The glucose is measured immediately, the oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood are checked, and the electrolytes, kidney and liver function, calcium, blood count, and markers of infection are sent. Computed tomography of the head is performed early in any patient with a focal deficit, a head injury, a suspected rise in pressure, or an unexplained coma, and magnetic resonance imaging answers questions the earlier scan cannot. Electroencephalography is used when the question is whether the brain is having seizures that cannot be seen from the outside, and cultures and a screen for poisons each answer a question the clinician should be able to state in advance. The intensive care unit, or ICU, is where a patient who cannot protect the airway or who is having continuous seizures is cared for, and the decision to move there rests on the clinical picture rather than on a completed diagnosis.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is compressed into fewer steps and sharper decisions. The first question remains whether the patient can be woken and whether the airway is safe, and that answer decides the journey rather than the diagnosis. The clinician counts the breathing, feels the pulse, takes the temperature, and examines the pupils with the torch, because these require nothing but attention. Where the patient cannot be woken, where the breathing is inadequate, where fever with a stiff neck is present, where a focal deficit has appeared, or where a seizure is continuing, the journey starts now and treatment begins on the way. Where the patient is awake, oriented, and improving and a clear reversible cause has been corrected, observation with a defined plan may be right, and the record and the safety plan are the only things that travel with the patient.

Because the level of consciousness is a moving quantity, repeated observation is worth more than any single assessment, and the interval between observations is itself a clinical decision. A patient unchanged at the next review is a different patient from one who has drifted from alert to responsive to voice over the same period. The clinician should record the time of each assessment and what changed since the last, and where the setting cannot provide reliable observation, that inability is itself a reason to transfer. Several habits of thought cause harm here more often than ignorance does, and the first is anchoring on the most visible explanation, such as alcohol on the breath, then failing to look for the head injury, the low glucose, or the infection beside it. Others are treating a normal scan as a completed diagnosis, assuming that a psychiatric label explains the confusion of the present, and failing to ask a witness, and each is corrected by naming the leading explanation, stating what would prove it wrong, and going to look.

A constructed illustration may make the reasoning concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine an older man brought to a clinic by his daughter because he has been confused since morning, and imagine that the clinician records that he is awake but inattentive, with a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius and a breathing rate of 28 breaths per minute. That temperature is an illustration of the threshold that defines fever and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and the same is true of the breathing rate. The clinician finds a red, warm area over the hip and a chest that is dull at one base, and decides that the confusion is delirium with two possible sources rather than a dementia that was never there before. The patient is transferred with a note recording the level of consciousness, the temperature, the breathing rate, the glucose, and the findings on the skin and chest, and no part of this story describes a real patient or should be applied to one.

To summarize, altered consciousness and seizure are emergencies in which the first questions are whether the patient can be woken and whether the airway is safe. The lethal causes are named at the outset with the finding that reveals each, including hypoglycemia, hypoxia, stroke, meningitis, encephalitis, status epilepticus, raised pressure inside the head, head injury, poisoning, sepsis, and metabolic derangement. Delirium, dementia, and psychosis are separated by the speed of onset, the fluctuation, the attention, and the preservation of orientation, and a new confusion in a patient with a known dementia is treated as delirium until its cause is found. A seizure is examined for what caused it and not only for what it looked like, and the witness account and the trajectory over repeated observations carry more weight than any single test. Every score, cut-off, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, and duration in this chapter is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and when the patient is deteriorating the reasoning pauses and the patient is helped first.

# Chapter 34 — Rash and Skin Complaints

A rash is a sign the patient can see and the clinician can also see, yet it is one of the hardest problems to reason about, because the eye recognizes a pattern long before it can say what the pattern means. The skin reflects what is happening within it and beneath it, so the same red eruption may be a local irritation, a reaction to a medicine, or the first sign of an infection in the bloodstream. The reasoning here is a sequence of questions rather than a list of diseases: what shape is the lesion, how are the lesions arranged, and is the patient systemically well or ill. That last question overrides the others, because a comfortable patient with an itchy rash sits in a different position from one with the same rash who has a fever, a rapid pulse, and the look of serious illness. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient.

Before the ordinary patterns are described, the eruptions that kill must be named where the rash is first seen, since each is revealed by a finding that can be sought at once. A rash of small spots that do not fade when a clear glass is pressed against it is bleeding into the skin, and it may be the purpura of meningococcal disease, a bloodstream infection, or a failure of the clotting system, so it is treated as an emergency until explained. Red skin that then peels in sheets, especially after a new medicine and with involvement of the mouth, the eyes, or the genitals, raises toxic epidermal necrolysis, in which the skin detaches and the barrier against infection is gone. Pain far worse than the skin suggests, with spreading dusky redness, a hard feel to the tissue, or crackling under the fingers, points to necrotizing fasciitis, which is a surgical emergency. Fever with a widespread rash, a swollen face, enlarged lymph nodes, and a rising eosinophil count after a new medicine raises the drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, in which organs as well as skin are attacked.

The first skill is description, performed in words that another clinician can picture without seeing the patient. A macule is a flat change in color, a papule is a small raised solid lesion, and a plaque is a larger raised area with a flat top, while a vesicle is a small fluid-filled blister, a bulla is a larger one, and a pustule is filled with pus. A wheal is a raised, pale, itchy swelling that comes and goes, a nodule is a solid lesion deeper in the skin, and a scale is a flake of dead surface, while a crust is dried fluid and an erosion is a shallow break in the surface. A clinician who says only that a patient has a red rash has said almost nothing, while one who describes raised, scaly plaques with sharply defined edges on both elbows has begun to make a diagnosis. Description also slows the mind, since finding the right word forces the eye to look a second time, and the second look is where the useful findings live.

Morphology is only half of the description, and distribution is the other half. The examiner notes whether the lesions are scattered or grouped, whether they follow a line, a band, or a circle, whether they cluster around hair follicles, and whether they are symmetric between the two sides of the body. Distribution may follow the territory of a single nerve, as it does when the chickenpox virus wakes in one band of skin, it may favor surfaces that face the sun, it may collect in the creases of the elbows and the knees, or it may begin on the trunk and spread toward the limbs. The palms, the soles, the scalp, the nails, and the mouth are part of the distribution and are examined every time, because a rash that involves them belongs to a different list of causes from one that spares them. Two patients described in the same words can have entirely different diseases, and the distribution is often what separates them.

The single most useful maneuver in this chapter is a press on the skin, and it takes nothing beyond a clear glass, a lens, or a finger. Firm pressure on a red lesion that fades and then refills means the redness comes from dilated blood vessels, which is the ordinary behavior of inflammation, while pressure that changes nothing means blood has left the vessels and lies in the tissue. The smallest bleeding spots are called petechiae and larger ones purpura, and the measurement commonly taught to separate them is a diameter of 2 millimeters, but that figure illustrates the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because texts and departments draw the boundary differently. The distinction matters far less than the non-blanching itself, which raises the possibilities of infection in the bloodstream, a disorder of the platelets, a failure of the clotting system, or an inflammation of the blood vessels. The examiner should also look for the same change in the mouth, the conjunctivae, and the nail beds, since bleeding in several places is more alarming than bleeding confined to one.

Fever with a rash changes the whole approach, because a systemic infection can be present before any other sign is visible. The clinician asks which came first, the fever or the rash, how long separates them, and whether the patient has been where a particular infection is common, and these questions narrow the field before the skin is examined. A rash that follows fever, cough, and red eyes, beginning on the face and spreading downward, suggests a viral exanthem. Fever also raises the possibility that the rash is a reaction to a medicine given for the fever, which is why everything the patient has taken, including anything bought without a prescription, belongs in the history. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is treated as significant in some services and ignored in others, so the threshold used where you work must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it varies with the site of measurement, the age of the patient, and the edition of the reference. Mucosal involvement is the finding that turns a skin problem into a systemic one, and it is the most commonly missed part of the examination. The examiner looks inside the mouth, at the eyes, and at the genitals and the anal area, since eroded mucous membranes with peeling skin need urgent assessment.

The examination of the skin is systematic, unhurried, and performed in the best light available. The patient should be undressed enough for the whole surface to be seen, with a gown or a sheet for warmth and dignity, and the examination moves from the scalp to the soles rather than jumping to the most obvious lesion. Daylight is the best illuminant, because it shows subtle differences in color that an electric bulb flattens, and the examiner should look from the side as well as from above, since a raised edge and a fine scale are easier to see when light grazes the surface. Gloves, a clean surface, and hand hygiene before and after contact belong to the examination of every patient with a rash, because some eruptions are infectious and some skin is broken. The appearance of a rash depends on the color of the skin beneath it, so erythema is harder to see against brown or black skin, and the examiner relies there on warmth, swelling, tenderness, and a change in texture rather than redness alone, comparing the two sides and asking whether a patch feels different.

The symptoms that accompany a rash are as informative as its appearance, and they are obtained before the skin is touched. The clinician asks whether it itches, hurts, burns, or is numb, and whether the feeling is constant or comes and goes, because an itchy rash and a painful rash belong to different lists of causes; an itch that is worst at night suggests scabies or eczema, while burning or stinging may be a reaction to a medicine or a sign that nerves are involved. Some parts of the body hide a rash unless deliberately examined. The scalp must be parted and looked at directly, the area behind the ears inspected, and the spaces between the toes, the soles, the palms, and the nails examined, since these are frequent sites of fungal infection and psoriasis. A patient who is immobile should be turned and the pressure areas over the sacrum, the heels, and the hips examined, because a change there may be the first sign of an injury that will deepen unless relieved.

Eczema, also called atopic dermatitis, is the most common itchy rash of childhood, and it continues into adult life in many people. It favors the creases of the elbows and the knees in children and the hands, the neck, and the eyelids in adults, and it usually begins as small itchy blisters on red skin. The itch dominates the symptom and is often worse at night, and long continued scratching thickens the skin into a leathery texture while the scratches break the surface and allow bacteria to enter, which is why a sudden increase in redness, weeping, and pain may mean infection rather than a flare. The diagnosis is made from the pattern, the itch, the age at onset, and the personal or family history of asthma, hay fever, or eczema, and no test is needed in the ordinary case. A finding that would make the diagnosis wrong is a rash respecting a boundary the disease does not, such as an edge as sharp as a line or an area limited to one part of the body.

Psoriasis is the other great scaly eruption, and it is separated from eczema by the sharpness of its edges and the thickness of its scale. The typical lesion is a raised, red plaque covered by silvery flakes, with a clearly defined border, and it prefers the outer surfaces of the elbows and the knees, the lower back, the scalp, and the nails. The scales are dry rather than weeping, and the nails may show small pits, a separation of the nail from its bed, or a yellow-brown discoloration, while the joints may be painful and swollen in a patient whose skin disease has been long-standing. New lesions can appear where the skin has been injured, which is one reason the patient's account of a scratch, a burn, or a surgical scar matters. Psoriasis affects the whole body rather than the skin alone, so the joints, the mood, and the general health of a patient who has carried it a long time deserve attention.

Fungal infection of the skin is recognized by its edge, because the fungus is most active at the boundary of a lesion and has usually cleared the middle. The result is a ring with a raised, scaly, sometimes red border and a paler center, which is why the old name for it describes a worm even though no worm is involved. The infection may affect the feet and the spaces between the toes, the groin, the trunk, the scalp, or the nails, and each site has its own appearance and its own list of alternatives. On the scalp the hair may break and fall, and in a child with patches of hair loss and scaling the possibility of fungal infection must be considered before it is attributed to habit or stress. A scale scraped from the active edge and examined under the microscope after preparation with potassium hydroxide, or grown in a culture, settles the question where such a service exists, while a rash already treated with a steroid cream can deceive because the steroid flattens the active edge.

Scabies is a small mite that burrows into the surface of the skin, and it produces an itch famous for being worse at night and for affecting several members of the same household. The burrow is a thin, gray, slightly raised line a few millimeters long, found most often in the webs of the fingers, the wrists, the waist, the genital area, and the breasts, while the face and the neck are usually spared in adults. The diagnosis is clinical in most settings, and the finding that supports it is the itch in a family member or a sexual partner together with the distribution of the rash. Any figure used to describe the burrow is only an illustration, so the length that matters in your own practice should be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since teaching texts state such measurements differently. The decision to treat the whole household at the same time is a diagnostic act as much as a therapeutic one, and the finding that would make that decision wrong is a rash sparing the typical sites and having another explanation.

Urticaria is the rash of raised, pale, intensely itchy wheals that appear quickly and move from place to place, and the individual lesion is said to fade without leaving a mark. The speed and the transience are the diagnostic features, and the interval usually quoted for a single lesion illustrates rather than fixes the rule, so confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol, since textbooks draw that boundary differently. A rash whose individual spots stay fixed in one place is probably not ordinary urticaria, so the question the clinician asks is not what the rash looks like now but what it looked like earlier. Angiedema is the same process deeper in the tissue, and it swells the eyelids, the lips, the tongue, and sometimes the throat, and that swelling is the dangerous part because it can obstruct the airway. The finding that would make urgent treatment unnecessary is a rash that is mild, stable, and free of swelling of the mouth or throat, though a patient whose voice is changing is treated without waiting for certainty.

A drug eruption is one of the most common reasons for a rash to appear in a patient who is already unwell, and its timing is the clue that points to it. The usual pattern is a red, blotchy rash that begins on the trunk and spreads, sometimes with fever and itch, and it can be difficult to separate from a viral exanthem. The history must include everything the patient has taken, including medicines bought without a prescription, traditional remedies, and anything given by injection, together with the date each started, and it should also ask about work, hobbies, new products, and plants. The decision to stop a suspected medicine is a diagnostic act as well as a treatment, and the finding that would make a drug the wrong answer is a rash that began before the medicine was started or one with a pattern the drug does not explain.

A rash is sometimes the most accessible evidence of a disease happening elsewhere, and the examiner who thinks only about the skin will miss it. A rash with painful joints, mouth ulcers, hair loss, and a change in the color of the fingers in the cold suggests an inflammatory disease of the connective tissue, and the same conditions may inflame the kidney, the lung, and the nerves. A rash with fever, a murmur, and a history of valve disease or of injecting drugs suggests an infection of the lining of the heart, and the skin signs may be small and easy to overlook. A rash with a rise in the eosinophil count, a swollen face, and an enlarged liver or spleen suggests a systemic drug reaction rather than a simple eruption. In each of these situations the skin is the door and not the room, and the decision is how much of the body to investigate before the picture declares itself.

The patient whose skin is blistering and peeling is among the most urgent in this chapter, because loss of the skin barrier threatens life. The clinician looks for skin that slides away when pressed or rubbed, for large blisters that join together, for raw surfaces where the top layer has separated, and for involvement of the mouth, the eyes, and the genitals. The cause may be a severe drug reaction, an infection, a burn, or an immune disease that splits the skin, and the treatment and the isolation required differ with the cause, so the history of medicines and the speed of the spread are essential. The extent of peeling matters, but it must be judged by someone who can see the whole patient, and any figure quoted for the proportion of skin involved is only an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since grading systems differ between services. The finding that would make this presentation less urgent is a small, stable blister in a patient who is otherwise well, which is a different problem with a different pace.

Necrotizing fasciitis is the infection that destroys tissue beneath the skin, and it is named again here because the skin at the beginning can look almost innocent. The earliest complaint is pain out of proportion to what is visible, because the process follows the layers of tissue rather than the surface, and as it advances the skin becomes dusky, then purple, then gray, while blisters, a crackling sensation under the fingers, and numbness may appear as nerves are destroyed. Fever, a rapid pulse, and the look of serious illness are common, but their absence does not exclude the diagnosis, and the patient with diabetes, liver disease, or a suppressed immune defense is at particular risk. The decision that matters is whether to take the patient to surgery, and the finding that supports it is a spread that is visibly advancing or a wound that does not behave as a simple infection should. Where imaging exists it may show the depth of the process, but it must not delay the call to the surgeon, because this diagnosis is made by the eye and confirmed in the operating room.

Any rash in a patient who is becoming ill is assessed for the signs of organ failure, because the skin may be the visible part of an infection that is already systemic. The clinician looks at the color and warmth of the hands and feet, the time for color to return after pressure, the rate of breathing, the pulse, the level of alertness, and the passage of urine. A patient who is confused, breathing quickly, and whose hands are cold despite a warm trunk needs treatment and senior help immediately, and the rash is the least important finding in that assessment. The decision about treatment is made on the whole picture rather than the appearance of the skin, because a patient with a non-blanching rash and a fever may need treatment before any result returns. The finding that would make treatment the wrong answer is a clear, benign explanation for every abnormal sign together with a patient who looks well, and even then the patient should be watched rather than sent away without a plan.

In the dermatology clinic the description is made with better light, more time, and tools the field clinic does not have. A magnifying instrument with its own light reveals the fine structure of a lesion, a camera records it so that change over time becomes visible, and a biopsy takes a small piece of skin for examination under the microscope, which is decisive for many tumors and several inflammatory diseases. Scrapings and swabs can identify a fungus, a bacterium, or a virus, blood tests can detect the antibodies and organ involvement that point to a connective tissue disease, and patch testing can identify a contact allergy. The reasoning behind each test is the same as everywhere else, because the clinician should know what a positive result and a negative result would each change before the test is ordered. None of these tools replaces the history and the examination, and many experienced clinicians reach the correct diagnosis before the first test is requested.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is applied with fewer instruments and more care. The torch is held to the side rather than straight on, because a side light reveals the raise and the scale that a direct light hides, and the examiner uses the brightest natural light available. The whole skin is still examined, and the patient is asked to point to every place that itches, hurts, or looks different, while a mirror or the help of a family member allows parts the patient cannot see to be examined. Where the light is poor and the lesions are subtle, the honest answer may be that the diagnosis cannot be made today, and the right decision is to ask the patient to return in daylight rather than to guess. A return visit, with the reason explained and the journey made worthwhile, is a diagnostic instrument in its own right, and it should be arranged deliberately rather than promised vaguely.

The treatment of a skin problem is part of the diagnostic reasoning, and the decision is often made at the same visit. Treatment is the right answer when the picture fits a condition that responds to it and the patient is not systemically ill, and it is also right when a serious infection is suspected and waiting for confirmation would put the patient at risk. Treatment is the wrong answer when the rash signals a systemic disease that has not been assessed, when a medicine is the likely cause and stopping it is the safer test, and when the diagnosis is uncertain enough that treating now would hide the very finding that would settle it. A clinician who applies a cream to a rash that is part of a drug reaction, or who treats a spreading infection as a local problem, may delay the decision that matters most. Naming the finding that would justify treatment, and the finding that would forbid it, is more useful than naming a product.

A rash should be written down in words that allow another clinician to picture it without seeing the patient. The record should describe the individual lesion, the arrangement, the distribution, the extent, the color, the texture, and the state of the mucous membranes, together with what the patient says about the itch, the pain, and the timing, while the general condition, the temperature, the pulse, the breathing, and the medicines taken belong in the same note. When the diagnosis is uncertain, the clinician should say so plainly and record what was considered and what was set aside, so that the next reader can continue the reasoning rather than begin it again. The patient should leave with clear instructions about what should bring them back, including a rash that spreads quickly, a fever, a sore mouth or eyes, a blister, a growing area of pain, or any difficulty breathing. A return visit arranged in advance is worth more than a warning to come back if things get worse, because a frightened or unwell patient may not judge that for themselves.

A constructed illustration may make the method concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than a portrait of any real person. Imagine a traveler with a fever, a headache, and a rash of small spots that do not fade when a clear glass is pressed against them, in whom the non-blanching rash is noticed at once and changes the whole plan because the clinician was taught to press before deciding. Now imagine a child with an itchy rash in the creases of the elbows whose family also itches at night, in whom the household history turns a vague eczema into a clear diagnosis that can be made locally. Now imagine a patient who started a new medicine recently and who now has a fever, a swollen face, and a widespread rash, in whom the combination is recognized as a systemic drug reaction rather than a simple eruption.

It is worth saying plainly that a pattern is not a patient. The pictures and the names in this chapter were assembled from groups of people, usually in a particular climate, age group, and setting, so a description that fits most of them will mislead in the patient who does not fit. A teaching framework tells the clinician which questions to ask and which dangers to exclude, not what the answer must be. The same eruption on a fair arm and on a dark arm, or in a newborn and in an older person, may belong to a different list of causes.

To summarize, a rash is a visible sign whose meaning depends on the shape of the lesion, its distribution, the speed of its appearance, and above all on whether the patient is systemically well or ill. The non-blanching rash, the peeling skin with mucosal involvement, the spreading area of pain worse than it looks, and the fever with a widespread eruption after a new medicine are named at the bedside and not deferred, and each demands senior help. Eczema, psoriasis, fungal infection, scabies, urticaria, viral exanthem, and drug eruption are separated by pattern, distribution, itch, timing, and the general state of the patient rather than by any single sign. Every figure in this chapter, whether a temperature, a size, an interval, or a proportion, is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and a patient with a rash who looks unwell is assessed and helped first, with the exact name of the eruption settled afterward.

# Chapter 35 — Bleeding, Bruising and Anemia

Bleeding that will not stop, bruises that appear without a cause, and the tiredness of a falling hemoglobin lead a clinician to the same small set of questions, because each describes a failure in the blood, in the vessel, or in the marrow. The clinician asks whether the problem lies in the platelets, in the clotting factors that turn blood from liquid to gel, or in the vessels themselves, and whether an anemia comes from blood that is lost, made too slowly, or destroyed too fast. This chapter is educational material, and it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the rules of your own service. The reasoning that organizes the subject is mechanism, because a pattern read correctly points toward the right part of the system long before any laboratory speaks, while a single number alone points nowhere.

Five dangerous possibilities must be named before the ordinary reasoning begins, and each is revealed by a finding that can be sought within minutes. The slow bleed from the gastrointestinal tract may produce no visible blood and announce itself only as a falling hemoglobin in a tired patient whose stool has turned black and tarry. Marrow failure presents as bruising and tiny red spots with pallor, fever, and a mouth that will not heal, and is revealed by that combination rather than by any single mark. A hemolytic crisis destroys red cells suddenly, so the patient turns yellow in the eyes, passes dark urine, and feels pain in the back or the abdomen while the hemoglobin falls fast. Advanced liver disease has stopped making clotting proteins and has opened vessels under high pressure that can bleed heavily into the gut. Bleeding into a closed space, above all into the skull, may follow a trivial injury and is revealed by a headache, vomiting, drowsiness, or a change in behavior rather than by any external mark.

The pattern of bleeding separates these mechanisms more reliably than the volume of blood lost. A platelet problem bleeds from surfaces, so the patient reports bleeding gums, nosebleeds that are hard to stop, and small flat red spots that do not fade when pressed, with small scattered bruises. Bleeding begins at once after a cut, stops with pressure, and then restarts, because the first plug that seals the vessel is the part the platelets were meant to build. A count below 20 thousand per microliter is often quoted as the level at which spontaneous bleeding becomes likely, but that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since laboratories draw the line differently. A normal count does not exclude a platelet that works badly, as happens with some medicines, in kidney failure, and in certain inherited conditions.

A clotting factor problem bleeds into tissues rather than from surfaces, and its signature is the deep bleed. The patient describes a joint that swells and becomes hot and painful without injury, or a muscle that grows tight and hard after a knock that seemed minor, and bleeding after surgery or a dental extraction may begin hours later. Large bruises that spread under the skin, bleed into the gut wall, or track along a limb are more typical of a factor problem than of a platelet one. A family history of bleeding after circumcision, after a first tooth was pulled, or of a woman who has always had heavy periods points toward an inherited disorder of clotting. The clotting times are the tests that address this mechanism, and any cut-off used to interpret them must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol before it is trusted.

The third mechanism is the vessel itself, and here the tests are often normal, which is exactly why the clinician must think of it. A vessel made fragile by age, by a deficiency of vitamin C, by a connective tissue disease, or by a medicine that weakens the wall produces bruises that appear with little or no trauma, often on the forearms and the backs of the hands of an older person. Inflammatory disease of the vessels produces raised, tender, red or purple spots that may itch or burn and tend to appear in crops on the lower legs. The distinction matters because these conditions are treated by addressing the underlying process rather than replacing something the blood lacks, so the finding that would make a platelet or factor treatment wrong is a normal count, normal clotting times, and a rash that is raised to the touch.

Bruising deserves its own questions because a bruise is a mark in time as well as in space. The clinician asks where the bruise is, what the patient was doing when it appeared, whether the story matches the site, and how the color has changed since it was noticed. Bruises over the shins and knees of a mobile toddler and over the bony points of an older person are ordinary, while bruises on the ears, the neck, the trunk, the buttocks, the genitals, and the soft parts of the arms and thighs are not. Marks carrying the shape of a hand, a belt, or a cord, marks in a child who cannot yet move independently, and marks clustered at different stages of healing require the clinician to consider deliberate injury and to follow the local process for protecting children. The finding that raises this concern is never a single bruise but a pattern, an explanation that does not fit, or a delay in seeking care.

The medicines a patient takes are part of the examination, and in bleeding they are often the whole answer. The clinician asks about every drug by name and purpose, including those bought without a prescription and those taken as herbs or traditional preparations, because many common substances change the platelets, the clotting, or the vessel wall. Drugs that thin the blood deliberately, drugs that reduce inflammation, some antibiotics, some drugs used for seizures, and heavy alcohol all belong on this list. The decision that follows concerns whether the medicine explains the bleeding well enough to leave the diagnosis there, or whether the picture holds features the medicine cannot explain, such as bruising in a patient who takes nothing at all.

The family history is asked in a way that turns a complaint into a pattern. The clinician does not ask only whether relatives bleed, because many people do not know, but asks specifically about bleeding after operations, childbirth, dental work, and injuries that would not normally bleed. Heavy periods across several generations, a brother or an uncle who needed treatment after a small cut, and a family in which boys died young in a pattern never explained are clues of the first importance. A family from a region where an inherited blood disorder is common, and an anemia in childhood that was never investigated, belong in the same conversation, and the answers may need a second visit.

The examination of a patient who bleeds is performed from the outside inward, with the skin read as carefully as any laboratory report. The clinician looks at the whole skin, including the scalp, the back, the buttocks, and the inside of the mouth, and notes the size, shape, color, and distribution of every mark. The gums, the nose, the conjunctivae, and the fingertips are inspected for bleeding spots that may be the only sign of a low platelet count. The joints are felt for warmth and swelling, the muscles for tenderness and tightness, and the abdomen for an enlarged spleen or liver. The eyes are examined for a hemorrhage in the retina, and throughout the clinician asks whether the pattern is one of surfaces, of deep tissues, or of fragile vessels.

Bleeding into the head is the lethal possibility that must be considered whenever a patient who bruises easily develops a headache, vomits, becomes drowsy, or behaves differently. It is especially likely after a fall in an older person, in a patient who takes a medicine that thins the blood, and in a patient whose platelets are low or whose clotting is impaired by liver disease. The finding that reveals it may be nothing more than a headache that will not settle, a change in the level of consciousness, a new weakness, or a pupil larger on one side, and in an older patient the injury may have been forgotten. The clinician should not wait for these signs to become obvious, because the window in which bleeding around the brain can be treated is short, and the decision to seek imaging is made on suspicion rather than certainty. In a hospital the answer comes from computed tomography, or CT, of the head, and in a clinic without it the answer is an immediate referral.

Anemia is not a diagnosis and not a number, it is a state that must be explained, and the explanation is always one of three mechanisms. Red cells are lost, made too slowly, or destroyed before their time, and each mechanism has its own history, its own examination, and its own reasoning. A single hemoglobin value tells the clinician how far the blood has fallen but nothing about why, and the same value may mean a slow bleed that has gone on for months, a marrow that failed within weeks, or a destruction that began yesterday. This is why the history and the examination come before the count, and why the count is then read as confirmation or as surprise.

Blood loss is the most common mechanism, and its pattern tells the clinician whether it is acute or chronic. Acute loss pours out quickly and the patient may be pale, sweaty, breathless, and faint, with a rapid pulse and a falling pressure, while the hemoglobin may still read normal in the first hours because the blood has not yet been diluted. That lag is a trap, and the findings that save the patient are the pulse, the pressure, and the appearance rather than the first count. Chronic loss leaks slowly and the patient adapts, so the hemoglobin falls gradually and the patient reports tiredness, breathlessness on effort, a sore tongue, and a craving to chew ice or earth. The slow bleed from the gastrointestinal tract may come from a stomach ulcer, from inflammation of the gut, from a polyp, or from a tumor, and the finding that reveals it may be a black stool or simply an anemia that will not correct. Any hemoglobin figure used to define anemia, such as 7 grams per deciliter, is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the reference range depends on age, sex, pregnancy, and the laboratory that issued it.

The history of blood loss is taken in a systematic way, because the patient rarely volunteers the whole story. The clinician asks about the color and frequency of the stool, about blood on the paper or in the bowl, about painkillers that irritate the gut, and about any change in bowel habit that has lasted for weeks. In a woman the menstrual history is taken in detail, including the number of days, the number of pads or cloths used, the presence of clots, and bleeding between periods, because heavy periods are a common and easily missed cause of iron deficiency. A duration such as 3 weeks is often used to separate a recent change from a longstanding one, and that interval must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol because the boundary is drawn differently in different settings. The best question is often the simplest, which is whether the patient has noticed anything that seemed like blood.

Underproduction is the mechanism the clinician thinks of when there is no bleeding to find and the patient does not look as though red cells are being destroyed. Iron, folate, and cobalamin are the raw materials of red cells, and a lack of any of them produces cells that are smaller or larger than normal and a marrow that cannot keep up. The tongue is the first instrument here, because it may be smooth, sore, shiny, or stripped of its papillae, and these changes may precede the fall in the count. The nails carry the same message, since a severe deficiency may hollow them into a spoon shape, crack them, or leave them ridged and brittle. Chronic disease, infection, inflammation, kidney failure, and cancer suppress the marrow in a different way, and their anemia is usually mild and does not respond to iron. A marrow that fails completely produces the picture named earlier, with bruising, tiny red spots, fever, and infection alongside the anemia.

Destruction of red cells produces the most dramatic and the most easily missed picture. The patient may become yellow in the eyes, pass urine that is dark like tea, feel pain in the back, the abdomen, or the limbs, and become breathless and tired within a day or two. The spleen may enlarge and become tender, and the patient may describe earlier episodes called jaundice in childhood or after an infection, a food, or a medicine. A crisis can be triggered by an infection, by a medicine, by a transfusion of incompatible blood, by a defect inherited in the red cell itself, or by an immune attack, and the findings that reveal it are a falling hemoglobin with a rising count of young red cells and a rise in the substance that makes the skin yellow. The danger is that the fall can be very fast, so the clinician must consider it before the patient is profoundly unwell, and must not dismiss yellow eyes as a liver problem alone. The decision to give blood turns on how fast the hemoglobin is falling and how the patient looks rather than on one number, and the finding that would make that decision unnecessary is a stable patient with a mild fall and a clear, treatable trigger.

Marrow failure and cancer of the blood deserve their own paragraph because they present as bruising and are easily attributed to clumsiness. The patient, often a child or a young adult, reports bruises that appeared without a cause, tiny red spots on the legs, bleeding gums, a fever that will not settle, and a tiredness that has grown over a few weeks. The examination may show pallor, enlarged lymph nodes, an enlarged spleen or liver, tenderness over the breastbone, and a gum that is swollen or bleeding, and any of these in a patient with unexplained bruising changes the pace of the encounter. A complete blood count and a peripheral blood smear point toward the marrow, and where the diagnosis is suspected the patient must be referred urgently for the specialist test that samples the marrow itself. The finding that would make a benign explanation safe is a clear injury that matches the bruise, a normal count, and a patient who is otherwise entirely well, and even then the clinician arranges a review.

Advanced liver disease combines bleeding and anemia at the same time, and it is common enough to be named in every clinic. The liver makes the proteins that clot the blood, and when it fails those proteins are scarce, so a patient with cirrhosis bruises easily, bleeds from the gums and the nose, and may bleed heavily from enlarged veins in the esophagus that are opened by high pressure in the portal circulation. The same patient may be anemic from that bleeding, from an enlarged spleen that traps red cells, from poor nutrition, and from the direct effect of alcohol on the marrow. The examination looks for yellow eyes, ascites, an enlarged spleen, spider angiomas on the skin, redness of the palms, and a flapping tremor of the hands, and each of these findings changes the interpretation of a bruise. The finding that makes the bleeding a liver problem rather than a platelet one is the whole picture of chronic liver disease with a prolonged clotting time and a low platelet count. Any threshold used to grade the severity of liver disease must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because those tools were derived in particular populations.

Pregnancy is a state in which anemia is expected and in which it is therefore missed. The volume of plasma rises more than the mass of red cells, so the concentration of hemoglobin falls as a matter of course, and a value that would alarm a clinician in a man may be ordinary in a woman who is expecting. The growing fetus and the placenta consume iron and folate, and vomiting early in pregnancy may reduce what the mother can take in, so a true deficiency can hide inside a normal-looking dilution.
