The danger is a bleed that is not noticed, from the gut or from the genital tract, and the clinician must ask directly about bleeding in pregnancy rather than wait for the patient to mention it. The examination includes the conjunctivae, the tongue, the nails, and the size of the spleen, and any figure quoted for hemoglobin in pregnancy must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol used by the maternity service.

Anemia in childhood has its own causes and its own dangers, and the same reasoning is performed on a smaller patient. A child grows quickly and needs iron in proportion, so a diet of milk alone after the first year, a diet poor in meat and vegetables, and a period of rapid growth all produce a deficiency that shows as pallor, tiredness, poor appetite, and a child who is slower than usual. Intestinal worms take blood or nutrients from the gut, and malaria destroys red cells, so a child in a region where these are common must have them considered before the anemia is attributed to diet. An inherited disorder of the red cell, such as sickle cell disease, may present as episodes of pain, yellow eyes, an enlarged spleen, and a sudden severe anemia during an infection. Bruising in a child who is not yet walking, or in a pattern that does not match the story, must raise the question of deliberate injury alongside the question of a bleeding disorder, and exposure to lead and chronic infection must also be weighed.

Pallor is the sign every clinician learns first and trusts too much, so it deserves an account of its own limits. The color of a person's skin is the product of the blood, the pigment in the skin, and the light in the room, so pallor is easier to see in one patient than another and is more convincing when the clinician knows the patient's usual appearance. The conjunctivae of the lower lid are examined by drawing the lid down and looking at the inside surface in good light, and the palms, the creases of the hand, the nail beds, and the inside of the mouth are examined in the same way. The finding is most useful when it is marked, when it is new, and when it comes with a rapid pulse or breathlessness on effort, because a mild pallor is a poor test on its own. In a clinic with nothing but a torch and a thermometer, the conjunctivae, the tongue, the nails, the pulse, and the history of bleeding and diet are the whole assessment, and they are enough to decide whether the patient must travel for a count.

The tongue and the nails are examined because they show a deficiency before the count does, and because they are available in every clinic. A tongue that is smooth, shiny, sore, and without its normal rough surface suggests a lack of iron, of folate, or of cobalamin, and it may be accompanied by cracks at the corners of the mouth and by a burning sensation. The nails may become thin and brittle, develop ridges, split, or curve upward at the edges into a spoon shape, and a patient who reports that the nails break easily is describing the same deficiency in the language of daily life. Fingernails can also show small dark lines under them, which may be tiny bleeds from a problem with clots or the heart valves, and pale bands across the nail bed, which may follow an illness or a poisoning. These findings are suggestive rather than decisive, so the clinician uses them to build a hypothesis and then confirms it with the count and the smear where those are available.

The spleen is examined in every patient with anemia or bleeding because its size changes the list of causes. It sits under the left ribs and is normally not felt, so a spleen that can be touched below the rib margin is enlarged. The examiner stands on the patient's right side, places the left hand behind the lower left ribs, and asks the patient to breathe in while the right hand is brought up under the rib margin, feeling for the tip of the organ as it descends. An enlarged spleen is distinguished from an enlarged kidney or a mass by its notch, by its movement with breathing, and by the fact that the examiner cannot get above it, but the confident answer usually requires an ultrasound in a hospital. Enlargement suggests a destructive process, an infection, a disease of the blood, or a raised pressure in the portal circulation, and tenderness over it may signal an infection or an impending rupture, so that patient should not be sent home to wait.

The history for anemia is taken with the same discipline as the examination, and it is built from a short list of questions asked in every patient. The clinician asks about diet, including meat, green vegetables, and how often each is eaten, about the craving to chew ice, earth, or starch, which is a curious clue to iron deficiency, and about the amount of alcohol taken. The medicinal history is taken again here, because painkillers, drugs that reduce stomach acid, drugs used after a transplant, some antibiotics, and some drugs used for seizures all change the marrow or the gut. The clinician asks about chronic illness of the kidney, the joints, or the bowel, about previous surgery on the stomach or the bowel, about pregnancy and childbirth, and about any family history of anemia, yellow eyes, or an enlarged spleen. The travel history matters because parasites, malaria, and tuberculosis all change the picture, and the occupation matters because exposure to lead produces an anemia that will not correct with iron.

In a well-resourced hospital the reasoning is unchanged and the evidence is wider. The complete blood count gives the hemoglobin, the number and size of the red cells, the white cells, and the platelets, and the peripheral blood smear lets a trained eye see the shape of the cells and often the diagnosis itself. The count of young red cells answers whether the marrow is responding, the iron and vitamin studies name the missing raw material, and tests of the clotting times describe the coagulation system. Where bleeding from the gut is suspected, an endoscopy looks directly at the esophagus, the stomach, and the first part of the bowel, and a colonoscopy examines the rest, chosen by the site the history has suggested. Imaging by ultrasound, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging finds an enlarged spleen, a mass, or blood inside a closed space, and a sample of the marrow may be needed when the count suggests a failure of production. Every reference range in this paragraph is a property of the laboratory that issued it, so the clinician must confirm the values against the current guideline and the local protocol before acting on them.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is performed with fewer instruments. The torch makes the conjunctivae, the tongue, the gums, the nails, and the skin visible, and the clinician counts the pulse and the breathing rather than estimating them, records the temperature, and feels the abdomen for the spleen and the liver. The diet, the menstrual history, the stool color, the medicines, and the family history carry the diagnosis in most cases, and the clinician who takes them carefully can often name the likely mechanism without any test. The decision that follows is a direction rather than a diagnosis, which is whether the patient needs a blood count urgently, whether a course of iron is justified while the cause is sought, and what the patient should watch for in the meantime. Treatment with iron is the right decision when the picture clearly fits a deficiency and there is no suggestion of a bleed that needs investigation, and it is the wrong decision when the patient has an unexplained anemia with a positive stool test, because replacing the iron can conceal a cancer while it corrects the count.

To summarize, bleeding, bruising, and anemia are read by mechanism and pattern rather than by quantity, and the pattern separates a platelet problem from a clotting problem from a fragile vessel. The slow bleed from the gut, the marrow that fails and presents as bruising, the hemolytic crisis, the bleeding of advanced liver disease, and the anemias of pregnancy and of childhood are named early because each is revealed by a finding that can be sought at the bedside. The conjunctivae, the tongue, the nails, and the spleen carry the assessment as far in a clinic as the count and the smear carry it in a hospital, and the two worlds ask the same questions. Every score, cut-off, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, and duration in this chapter is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who is bleeding now, or who has a headache and is drowsy after a trivial injury, is helped first and explained afterward.

# Chapter 36 — Pain Assessment Across Ages and Cultures

Pain is the symptom that brings more people to a clinician than any other, and it is the one the clinician can never see directly. It is a private experience generated in a nervous system, reported in a language, and shaped by a lifetime of previous pain, so that two patients with the same injury may describe different sensations and behave in different ways. Pain must nevertheless be measured, and measured with the same care as a pulse or a temperature, because measurement is what turns a complaint into a finding that can be compared, recorded, and acted on. The reasoning in this chapter is organized around four axes that correct one another: the patient's own account, the behavior an observer can see, the effect of the pain on what the patient can do, and the response to whatever has already been tried. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient.

The dangerous possibilities are named before the ordinary assessment begins, because each announces itself through a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. The pain that is being treated rather than explained is the hazard running through this chapter, and the analgesia that conceals a surgical abdomen is its clearest form. A patient whose abdomen becomes rigid and board-like, who guards involuntarily and flinches when the examiner's hand withdraws, or whose pain is far greater than the tenderness suggests, may have a perforated organ or a strangulated bowel, and nothing given for relief should be allowed to postpone the decision about surgery. Pain that is sudden and tearing and travels to the back may signal a tear in the aorta, while severe lower abdominal pain in a woman of childbearing age with bleeding and a positive pregnancy test must be treated as a pregnancy outside the uterus until it is proved otherwise.

Pain resists measurement because there is no independent reference standard for it. A temperature can be repeated with a thermometer and a pulse can be counted against a watch, but nothing outside the patient can confirm that the pain is what the patient says it is. The patient's report is therefore not one piece of evidence among several; it is the measurement itself, and a clinician who treats it as an impression to be corrected has already begun to reason badly. That report is also not a raw signal, because it is filtered through expectation, fear, previous experience, cultural meaning, the words available in the patient's language, and what the patient believes will happen if the pain is admitted. A patient who has been disbelieved before may understate the pain, and a patient who hopes for treatment may overstate it, and both are telling the truth about their situation.

The first axis is the account, and it is taken in the patient's own words rather than in the clinician's categories. For an acute pain the Socrates framework keeps the account complete: the site and whether it moves, the onset and what the patient was doing, the character of the sensation, whether it radiates and where, the associated symptoms, the timing, and the factors that make it better or worse. The Oldcarts framework extends the same discipline to the whole history and is useful when the complaint is a pattern of illness rather than a single pain. Both frameworks are nets with holes, and the clinician should know what each one leaves out, because the Socrates questions were designed for pain in the chest of an articulate adult and can miss the pain of a small child, of a person with dementia, or of a patient who describes the sensation through a metaphor the clinician does not recognize.

The character of the pain is a clue to its mechanism, and the mechanism tells the clinician what to examine and what to fear. Visceral pain is dull, deep, poorly localized, and often accompanied by nausea and sweating, because the organs are supplied by nerves that do not report position precisely. Somatic pain is sharp and well localized, and it worsens when the affected part is moved, which is why a patient with inflammation of the peritoneum lies still while a patient with colic of the bowel or the kidney cannot. Neuropathic pain is burning, shooting, electric, or numb, and it follows the territory of a nerve rather than the shape of an organ, so the examination must test sensation, power, and reflexes along that territory.

Referred pain is felt far from its source because the nerves of the organ and the nerves of the distant site enter the spinal cord at the same level. Irritation of the diaphragm by blood, pus, or a pregnancy outside the uterus can produce pain at the tip of the shoulder, so a patient with shoulder pain and a soft abdomen may still have a catastrophe inside. Pain from the heart is often felt in the jaw, the throat, or the inner arm rather than in the chest, and pain from the pancreas or the aorta is often felt in the back. Disease of the hip is frequently reported as pain in the knee, and disease of the spine as pain around the trunk, so the clinician examines the joint above and below the place the patient points to. The place the patient points to is a starting point, not the answer.

The second axis is the effect of the pain on what the patient can actually do, and it is the axis that travels best between languages and cultures. A patient who cannot bear weight, cannot sleep, cannot eat, cannot dress, or cannot hold a child has conveyed something that no number can substitute for. The clinician therefore asks what the pain has stopped, what it has changed, and how the day is now arranged around it, and those answers can be compared between one visit and the next. A pain that confines a previously active person to a chair carries a different weight from the same pain in someone whose life is already limited, and the change from the patient's own baseline is often more informative than the absolute severity. This is also the measurement that a family member or a nurse can report when the patient cannot.

The third axis is the response to whatever has already been tried, which is a natural experiment the patient has usually performed. The clinician asks what was taken, whether it was prescribed or bought, how much was taken, whether it helped at all, how long the relief lasted, and when the pain returned. None of that is a dose to be repeated or adjusted, because this book gives no doses, and the account is evidence about the character of the pain and about the direction the diagnosis should take. The finding that would make stronger treatment the right answer is severe pain with a diagnosis already established and a plan in motion; the finding that would make it the wrong answer is a patient who is deteriorating, in whom relief could hide the change that should call the surgeon.

Formal scales are the fourth kind of measurement, and they are useful only when their limits are understood. The verbal descriptor scale asks the patient to choose a word such as none, mild, moderate, or severe, while the numeric rating scale asks for a number between 0 and 10, and the arithmetic of that range is an illustration of the reasoning that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the wording and the anchors differ between services and editions. A number is reliable within one patient over time and unreliable between patients, because the same number may mean a mild inconvenience to one person and an unbearable state to another. The faces scales ask a child to point to the face that matches the feeling, which turns the question into a comparison rather than an act of arithmetic, and they are used only in children old enough to understand the sequence, an age that varies with the child and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol.

When the patient cannot report, the clinician measures behavior instead, and in patients who are confused or who have dementia that is a structured task rather than a general impression. A behavioral scale records what can be seen: the face, the posture and restlessness of the body, the tensing of muscles, the sounds the patient makes, the response to comfort, and the pattern of breathing. Such observations are weaker than a report and should never replace one when a report is possible, but they are far better than the assumption that a patient who does not complain is free of pain. The vital signs belong in the same supporting role and no more, because a pulse of 110 beats per minute, a raised pressure, sweating, pallor, and wide pupils may accompany severe pain, yet each reading must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the heart rate that alarms one service is ordinary in another and the response is blunted by age, by training, by diabetes, and by medicines that slow the heart.

Pain is also missed because it is never reported, and the reasons are usually practical rather than mysterious. A patient may believe that suffering should be borne, may fear that admission will lead to an operation, may be unable to pay, may have been dismissed at an earlier visit, or may not have the words in the language of the consultation. The clinician carries assumptions about who suffers more and who complains more, and those assumptions are a common source of unequal treatment. Culture shapes how pain is expressed, what it means, who is permitted to speak about it, and what is expected of a sick person, but it does not change the capacity to feel, and treating a group as though its members feel less is a mistake that harms patients. The correct posture is to ask, to accept the first account, and to let the patient's own description set the standard.

Language is where the assessment most often fails, and the failure is quiet. When the clinician and the patient do not share a fluent language, the interview should be conducted with a trained interpreter rather than with a child or a relative, because a child may be frightened or ashamed and a relative may soften the message to protect the patient or the family. Many languages have no single word for the sensations the clinician is asking about, and a pain described as heavy, hot, pulling, or like a tight band may be pointing to exactly the mechanism the clinician needs. The clinician should use the patient's own word back in the next question and should ask about the worst pain the patient has ever experienced, because that comparison is more informative than any absolute number. When no trained interpreter is available, the clinician slows down, uses simple sentences, avoids metaphor, and accepts that some of the account will be lost rather than pretending it was heard.

Older adults require a different calibration, and the first correction is the belief that pain is a normal part of growing old. The older patient may understate the pain, may attribute it to arthritis or to age, and may present instead with a change in function, a fall, or a new confusion. The dangerous processes also present differently, because a heart attack may produce only breathlessness, sweating, or a feeling of indigestion, and an inflamed or perforated abdomen may be surprisingly soft rather than rigid. The finding that should prompt a full search is therefore not the severity the patient reports but the change from what that patient could do last week.

In infants and young children the assessment is almost entirely behavioral, and the parent is the most useful instrument. The clinician asks how the child feeds, sleeps, plays, and is consoled, and compares today with what the parent describes as normal, because a change in feeding or in temperament may be the first sign of a serious cause. An infant in pain may draw up the legs, screw up the face, and cry in a high pitch, but a child who is quiet, floppy, and unwilling to move may be more ill than one who screams. The dangerous findings at this age are a limb that is not used, a joint that is swollen or hot, an abdomen that is tender and distended with bilious vomiting, a fever with irritability that cannot be consoled, and a headache with a change in consciousness. The tools designed for children, including the faces scales, depend on the age and the development of the child, and the age at which each may be used must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than assumed.

Adolescents present a special problem because their pain is often dismissed as emotional before it has been examined, and because they may not disclose what they fear. Recurrent headache, abdominal pain, and limb pain are common at this age and are usually benign, but the same complaints can be the face of a tumor, an infection, or an inflammatory disease, and the clinician who attributes them to stress without examining the patient will miss that second group. Function is the most useful measure here, because an adolescent who has stopped attending school or has withdrawn from sport is telling the clinician something a number on a scale will not. A normal examination in a distressed adolescent is a reason to look again with a plan, not a reason to conclude that the pain is not real.

Pain in pregnancy is an emergency until it is explained, because the list of causes contains several that threaten two lives. A woman of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain, bleeding, or fainting may have a pregnancy implanted outside the uterus, and the finding that reveals it is a positive pregnancy test with an empty uterus on ultrasound, sometimes with free fluid in the abdomen and pain at the shoulder tip. The clinician must assess the fetus as well, because the well-being of the baby is part of the mother's assessment, and the decision to refer is made on the mother's signs and the fetal signs together. No decision about pain relief should delay that referral.

Acute pain and chronic pain are different problems, and the difference changes the question the clinician is asking. Acute pain is a warning of tissue injury and it has a purpose, so the search is directed at the injury and its cause, while chronic pain has lost that warning function and has become a condition shaped by the nervous system, by sleep, by mood, and by the patient's circumstances. A duration of 3 months is often used to separate the two, though that boundary is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because different services draw it at different points. The clinician should beware the label of the frequent attender, since familiarity with a patient's chronic pain is exactly what makes a new and dangerous pain easy to overlook.

The safest habit in chronic pain is to treat a change in character as a new pain. A pain that has moved, changed quality, begun to wake the patient at night, or appeared in a new place deserves the same search as a pain that has never been assessed before. Certain companions narrow that search at once: fever suggests infection, weight loss and night sweats suggest a tumor or tuberculosis, a new weakness or numbness suggests compression of a nerve or the spinal cord, bleeding suggests an ulcer or a tumor, and fainting with pain suggests hemorrhage or a sudden fall in the output of the heart. Compression of the spinal cord is one of the few pain emergencies in which hours matter, and the findings that reveal it are progressive weakness, a band of numbness around the trunk, difficulty passing urine, and a loss of sensation in the saddle area. Any of those findings in a patient with back pain turns a clinic visit into an immediate referral.

Some of the most lethal causes produce pain out of proportion to what the examination shows, and the clinician must learn to distrust the calm abdomen as much as the rigid one. When the blood supply to the bowel is interrupted, the pain is severe and continuous and often far greater than the tenderness, and the patient may be older or may have a rhythm disturbance of the heart that has thrown a clot; the finding that reveals it is an abdomen that becomes tender only late, alongside a rising lactate and a patient who is more unwell than the examination suggests. A limb that is tense, swollen, and painful on passive stretching of the muscles may be losing its blood supply or developing a compartment syndrome, and a rapidly spreading, exquisitely tender area of skin with a dusky center may be a necrotizing infection of the soft tissue. Each of these is a reason to call for help and to move the patient now rather than to wait for the next review.

Acute pain in the scrotum must be resolved in minutes rather than days, because a testis that twists on its cord can be saved if it is untwisted in time. A young man or adolescent with sudden severe pain in the testis, a high-riding and tender testis, and no urinary symptoms should be treated as having a twisted testis until a surgeon says otherwise, because an infection of the genital tract is a much less likely explanation at this age and is the error that costs the organ. The examination is performed gently and with a chaperone, and the finding that supports torsion is a testis that is tender, high, and horizontal, sometimes with loss of the normal reflex on the same side. The interval within which the testis can be saved is often quoted as 6 hours, but that interval is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it depends on how completely the blood supply is interrupted. A patient who is embarrassed, or a teenager who will not mention the pain, must be asked directly, because the question is the only way the diagnosis will be made.

The decision about treating pain sits inside the diagnostic process and can either support it or conceal it. Relief must not be withheld from a suffering patient merely to preserve the purity of an examination, because pain itself causes harm, and in most cases the examination and the conversation remain interpretable after relief has been given. The finding that would make treatment the right answer is a patient whose diagnosis is established or whose plan is already moving and whose suffering is significant; the finding that would make it the wrong answer is an unstable abdomen, or a patient with signs of bleeding or shock in whom relief could remove the last visible evidence of deterioration. This book gives no doses and no regimens, and the choice of medicine and its amount belongs to the clinician who knows the patient and to the local protocol.

The record of pain is part of the diagnosis, and it should be written so that the next clinician can see what changed. The note should carry the patient's own words, the scale used and the number chosen, the functional effect at the time of the visit, what the patient had already taken, and what the clinician found on examination. Soap notes give a familiar shape to this record, but the shape matters less than the content, and a note that contains a number and nothing else cannot be interpreted by anyone who was not present. Reassessment is the act most often omitted and the one that converts a single measurement into a trajectory, and the interval between the first and the second assessment should be chosen for the condition and confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because a patient with acute pain needs to be seen again far sooner than one whose pain is stable and chronic.

In a well-resourced hospital the assessment is extended by instruments, but the reasoning that directs them is unchanged. The electrocardiogram, or ECG, is the first test in pain of the chest, the upper abdomen, the jaw, or the arm, because a heart attack can imitate many other complaints, while blood tests can reveal anemia, infection, inflammation, or damage to the heart muscle and ultrasound at the bedside can show free fluid, an enlarged organ, or a pregnancy outside the uterus. Computed tomography, or CT, and magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answer questions that the hands cannot reach, and their role is to confirm or exclude a hypothesis the clinician has already formed rather than to generate one at random. None of these instruments removes the need for repeated examination, because a scan taken early in an illness can be normal while the process that will declare itself is still developing.

Where there is no laboratory, no imaging, and no colleague, the same assessment is conducted with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, and it is not a lesser form of reasoning. The torch makes the skin, the mouth, the throat, the ears, and the eyes visible, the thermometer turns a suspicion of infection into a measurement, and a watch allows the pulse and the breathing to be counted rather than guessed. The examination is repeated at intervals, and the position of comfort, the ability to walk, the tenderness on gentle pressing, and the change over hours become the substitute for the scanner. The decision that follows is usually one of three: to watch with a clear plan and a time to return, to treat on the clinical picture while continuing the search, or to begin the journey to a hospital now.

The decision to refer is itself a diagnostic act, and it should be based on findings rather than on the clinician's discomfort alone. Pain with a rigid abdomen, pain with signs of shock, pain with bleeding, pain in pregnancy, pain in the scrotum, pain after trauma, pain with a new weakness or numbness, and pain in a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed or whose blood is thinned by medicine all belong in a place where surgery and imaging exist. The patient and the family should be told exactly which signs must bring them back and when, in concrete terms rather than a general instruction to return if things get worse. The record should show what was excluded, what remains uncertain, and what the plan is if the pain does not follow the expected course.

Two constructed illustrations may make the method concrete, and neither describes a real person. Imagine an older woman brought to a clinic because she has stopped walking; she says the hip merely aches, and the clinician, following the axis of function rather than the axis of severity, examines her and finds that the leg is shortened and rotated, with a fracture the mild report had hidden. Now imagine a teenager who arrives with abdominal pain and is about to be sent home with a diagnosis of a stomach upset, until the clinician asks directly about the scrotum and finds a tender, high-riding testis that needs a surgeon at once. Both stories are teaching devices built to show a single habit, and neither should be applied to a real patient without a full assessment. The shared habit is the refusal to let a comfortable explanation close the search before the dangerous one has been considered.

The patient who cannot speak at all requires the most disciplined assessment, because none of the four axes can be taken for granted. A patient who is unconscious, sedated, paralyzed, or unable to produce language after a stroke may still be in severe pain, and the clinician must then rely on behavior, on the observations of those who know the patient, and on the nature of the illness itself. In such patients the threshold both for treating pain and for investigating its cause is lowered rather than raised, because the usual warning of a complaint has been removed. At the end of life the assessment widens to include what has been called total pain, in which physical discomfort is bound together with fear, grief, loneliness, and the meaning the patient gives to the illness, so that treating only the body may leave the suffering untouched.

To summarize, pain is a subjective experience that must still be measured with the discipline given to a pulse, through the patient's account, the behavior that can be observed, the effect on what the patient can do, and the response to what has already been tried. The dangerous causes are named at the outset and not deferred: the analgesia that conceals a surgical abdomen, the tearing pain of a damaged aorta, the pain of a pregnancy outside the uterus, the pain out of proportion to the examination, and the twisted testis that must reach a surgeon. The tools for those who cannot speak, the faces scales for children and the behavioral scales for the confused and those with dementia, are aids to judgment and never replacements for a report when a report is possible. Culture shapes how pain is expressed and what it means, but never how much a person can feel, and the clinician's own assumptions about who suffers more are among the most common sources of error. Every score, cut-off, pressure, rate, interval, and duration in this chapter is an illustration of the reasoning and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material; it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient in severe pain who is deteriorating is helped first, and the explanation is completed afterwards.

# Chapter 37 — The First Minute

Every chapter in this book has asked the clinician to reason toward a diagnosis, but this one inverts the order, because the first act is not to name the disease but to recognize that the patient is dangerously ill at all. The airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure sequence organizes that recognition, and its logic is simple: some threats kill quickly and must be answered before any history is taken. A patient who cannot move air, whose breathing has stopped or become agonal, whose pulse cannot be felt, whose seizure is still running, or whose blood glucose is dangerously low is a patient in whom the diagnosis can wait and the treatment cannot. The phrase the first minute is a figure of speech, and any clock time in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the intervals that define urgency differ between services. This chapter is educational material and it cannot replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

The recognition itself is the hardest skill here, because it is a judgment about the whole person rather than a measurement of one part. The clinician looks for the patient who is gray or mottled, who sweats without exertion, who sits bolt upright because lying flat is unbearable, who cannot finish a sentence, or who is restless in a way that does not fit the story. Any of these may mean nothing alone, but several together, or one of them in a patient whose family says he is not himself, is a reason to act before the explanation is complete. The clinician's own alarm is a piece of data, because the sense that something is badly wrong is the accumulated pattern recognition of every sick patient seen before. Recognition and the sequence happen together, and a patient who looks seriously unwell is treated as seriously unwell until a reason is found.

The lethal causes of a collapsed or deteriorating patient deserve to be named at the start, because each announces itself through a finding that can be sought in the first minute. Hemorrhage hides in the abdomen, the chest, the gut, the pelvis, and the tissues around a broken bone, and it is revealed by a climbing pulse, cool clammy skin, a pressure that falls on sitting, and a belly or limb that is swelling. Hypoxia is revealed by agitation or drowsiness with a risen breathing rate, a chest that moves unevenly, and lips or tongue that have lost their color, though no single sign is reliable. Sepsis is revealed by fever or an abnormally low temperature with a fast pulse, a raised breathing rate, confusion, and a falling pressure, and the quick sequential organ failure assessment is one way of formalizing that combination. Cardiac arrest is revealed by a patient who does not respond, does not breathe normally, and has no pulse that can be felt. Stroke is revealed by a face that droops, an arm that drifts downward when both are held out, and speech that has become slurred or lost, and any figure quoted here must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such values vary between countries and editions.

The sequence has an order because each step depends on the one before it. Air must move before oxygen can reach the blood, the blood must circulate before it can carry that oxygen to the brain, and the brain must respond before the clinician can judge how much of it is working. Exposure comes last because undressing a patient costs warmth and dignity, and it is worth that cost only when a hidden injury or rash cannot be found any other way. When the clinician works alone the steps blur into one continuous act, and the only rule that survives is that treatment precedes diagnosis.

The airway is assessed first because a complete obstruction kills quickly, and the assessment takes only seconds. The clinician looks at the chest and abdomen for movement, listens at the mouth for air, and feels for the movement of air against the cheek, and silence with a chest that is not rising demands action at once. A partial obstruction makes its own sounds, among them a harsh noise on breathing in, a gurgle, a snore in a deeply unconscious patient, or a voice that has changed. The patient who drools, whose neck is swelling, whose throat is burned, or who makes a harsh noise after a sting may be losing the airway even while talking. In the hospital the call for help goes out before the airway closes, while in the clinic the clinician tilts the head, lifts the chin, removes what can be seen, and supports the airway with a bag and a mask.

Breathing is assessed by counting rather than glancing, and the count is the cheapest and most sensitive measurement in the first minute. The clinician watches the rise of the chest, the use of the muscles between the ribs and above the collarbones, the flaring of the nostrils, and the position the patient has chosen, then counts the breaths over a full interval with a watch. Absent or agonal breathing, in which gasps come at long and irregular intervals, means cardiac arrest and compressions until help arrives, and it is easily mistaken for normal breathing. Any figure quoted for the rate at which breathing should cause alarm is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because normal ranges differ with age, pregnancy, altitude, and the reference in use.

Circulation is assessed by feeling for a pulse, looking at the skin, and asking what the pressure is doing. The clinician feels the wrist and, when no pulse is found there, the neck or the groin, and no central pulse in an unresponsive patient who is not breathing defines cardiac arrest for the purpose of action. The quality of the pulse matters too, since a thin, fast pulse suggests a circulation that is emptying while a bounding pulse suggests one that is dilated and losing its tone. The skin is the window the clinician already has, and cool, clammy, mottled skin with a slow refill after pressure tells of blood being sent to the center and away from the limbs. The figure of 90 millimeters of mercury often quoted for the systolic pressure is an illustration and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the value that should prompt action varies with the patient's usual pressure, with age, and with pregnancy.

Disability means the brain, and it is assessed by the level of response, the pupils, the movement of the limbs on each side, and the blood glucose. The Glasgow coma scale records the response to voice, to pain, and to command, and the reasoning it formalizes is a graded search for how much of the brain is still answering; its contents and the score at which alarm is raised must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the version in use varies between services. A patient who was alert and is now drowsy, or drowsy and now unrousable, has declared a deterioration that no laboratory result is needed to confirm. The pupils are compared for size and for the speed with which they narrow to light, and a difference between the two sides demands urgent explanation. The blood glucose is measured whenever the equipment exists, because a low glucose can imitate a stroke, a seizure, a drunken state, and a psychiatric emergency, and it is the most reversible of the lethal causes.

Exposure closes the sequence because the answer is often under the clothing, and a clinician who does not look will not find the wound, the rash, the distended abdomen, or the swollen limb. The patient is undressed enough to be examined, kept covered where possible, and warmed actively, because cold impairs clotting and worsens the shock the clinician is trying to treat. The examination is quick and deliberate, so the back is rolled to be seen, the perineum is inspected when bleeding or trauma is possible, the limbs are compared for swelling, and every line and dressing is looked at directly. The skin is searched for a rash that does not fade when pressed, for puncture marks, and for the pale, cold, mottled pattern that speaks of a circulation in retreat. The dignity of the patient is part of the task, and in a clinic with only a torch the light turns an impression into a finding.

In a hospital the first minute is a performance by several people at once, and the reasoning lies in directing them. One person calls for the resuscitation team, one opens the airway and supports breathing, one attaches the monitor and the pressure cuff, one finds a vein and takes the samples that will answer later questions, and one writes the times and findings. The monitor is an instrument of the first minute and not a substitute for the examination, because a tracing can be believed while the patient in front of it is deteriorating. The trolley is prepared before it is needed, and the rule that treatment precedes diagnosis means the team acts on the findings it has while the cause is pursued once the immediate threats are answered.

Alone in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is compressed into what two hands can do. The clinician puts a hand on the chest to feel whether it rises, bends an ear to the mouth to hear whether air moves, feels the neck for a pulse, and holds a finger on the wrist to count. A bag and a mask allow breathing to be supported, a watch allows the rate to be counted rather than guessed, and the torch makes the pupils, the throat, and the skin visible. The clinician alone must also decide when to call for help, and that call is part of the treatment, because the patient who must travel should begin that journey early. What the clinic lacks in equipment it partly replaces with continuity, since the same clinician who looks again shortly may see the change a monitor would have shown.

Hemorrhage is the lethal cause most easily hidden, because blood can be lost into spaces the clinician cannot see. Trauma conceals blood in the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis, and around a fractured thigh, and the signs are a climbing pulse, cool clammy skin, a pressure that falls on sitting, and a swelling or belly that grows between examinations. A gastrointestinal bleed may present first as weakness, sweating, and a black stool rather than as visible blood, and a patient who has taken a medicine that reduces stomach acid may bleed without pain. A ruptured ectopic pregnancy in a woman of childbearing age can kill quickly, and the findings that reveal it are lower abdominal pain, a missed or unusual period, shoulder tip pain from blood under the diaphragm, and the signs of internal bleeding. The decision is whether the loss is continuing and whether the patient must go where it can be stopped, and a pulse and a pressure moving in the wrong direction make observation the wrong answer.

Hypoxia is the quiet death, and the patient who is not obviously struggling may be the closest to it. Its causes in the first minute include a blocked airway, a chest that cannot expand, fluid in the lungs, a clot in the lung, a collapsed lung under pressure, a severe asthma attack, and a depression of breathing by a medicine or a poison. The findings are a risen breathing rate, restlessness or drowsiness, a chest that moves uneasily on one side, a windpipe that has shifted, and lips or tongue that have changed color, but skin color is a poor guide in dark skin, in anemia, and in a failing circulation. A pulse oximeter is useful when it exists, and it can be wrong when the circulation to the finger is poor, the skin is cold, or the pigment in the blood is abnormal. Any figure given for an oxygen saturation below which action is required is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted value differs with age, altitude, pregnancy, and the purpose for which it is used.

Sepsis is named early because it kills through the response to infection rather than through the infection alone, and it can present looking like almost anything. The findings that should raise it are fever or an abnormally low temperature, a fast pulse, a raised breathing rate, confusion or drowsiness, cool or mottled skin, and a pressure that has fallen or falls on sitting. The quick sequential organ failure assessment formalizes that combination at the bedside, and the reasoning it captures is a search for the failing organ rather than for the organism; its contents and its trigger must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the thresholds vary between services. The patient who is compensating well deserves particular care, because a normal pressure with a fast pulse, a raised breathing rate, and cold extremities is a patient spending the last of the reserve. A patient with a suspected infection and any sign of organ failure needs help and treatment now, and a clinic without a laboratory reaches the same decision from the pulse, the breathing rate, the temperature, the skin, and the passage of urine.

Cardiac arrest is recognized rather than predicted, and recognition depends on two questions asked in the right order, which are whether the patient responds and whether the breathing is normal. A patient who does not respond and is not breathing normally, with occasional irregular gasps, is treated as being in cardiac arrest, and the pulse check must be brief because a long search delays the compressions that matter. A patient with agonal breathing and no pulse that can be found has already answered the question, and the answer is to begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, and to call for the team and the equipment. In the clinic the clinician begins compressions, calls for help, and continues until the patient recovers or help arrives, because compressions need no equipment at all. Any figure quoted for how long the pulse check may take, or for the rate at which compressions are delivered, is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such figures are revised and differ between training bodies.

Stroke is the emergency in which time is brain, and the first minute is when it is usually made or missed. The findings are a face that has fallen on one side, an arm that drifts downward when both are held out with the eyes closed, and speech that has become slurred, jumbled, or absent, and any of these appearing suddenly with a normal blood glucose is a reason to move quickly. The blood glucose is measured because low and very high values can each imitate a stroke, and a seizure that has just ended can leave a weakness that fades over the following minutes, so the examination is repeated. A stroke in the back of the brain may present without weakness, with a sudden loss of balance, double vision, difficulty swallowing, or confusion mistaken for drunkenness, so a strong arm does not exclude it. The decision is where the patient should be taken, and any figure quoted for the interval in which clot-directed treatment is still possible is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it differs between services and editions.

A low blood glucose deserves its own place because it is the treatable imitation of every other emergency. It can present as confusion, agitation, drowsiness, a seizure, a weakness on one side, strange behavior, or a patient who appears drunk, and in a patient who takes a medicine for diabetes the history alone should raise it. The measurement is made with a meter when one exists, and a low reading in a patient without symptoms may need confirmation by a laboratory method, because meters vary. A figure such as 3 millimoles per liter is often spoken of as the level below which the brain begins to suffer, but that value is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted threshold differs with age, pregnancy, and the reference in use. The decision is whether to correct the glucose at once, and the finding that makes it right is a low reading with a patient who is not fully awake, while the finding that makes it wrong is a normal reading with another explanation for the behavior.

A seizure that is still running when the patient arrives demands action in the first minute, because a brain that seizes without pause suffers injury that continues after the movement stops. The clinician notes the time the seizure began, protects the patient from injury without restraining the limbs or putting anything in the mouth, and looks at once for the treatable causes, among them a low blood glucose, a low sodium, an infection, a poison, and a cause related to pregnancy. A seizure that has stopped still leaves the patient at risk, because the breathing may be poor, the airway soiled, and a second seizure may follow. The distinction between a continuing seizure and a patient who is shaking from another cause is made by watching the pattern, the eyes, and the response, and by asking a witness what happened before the movement began. Any figure given for the duration at which a seizure becomes an emergency is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the definition is drawn differently between services.

Anaphylaxis is named here because it can kill within the first minute through the airway, the breathing, or the circulation, and the first decision is made on the clinical picture rather than on a test. The findings are a sudden illness after a sting, a food, or a medicine, with swelling of the lips or tongue, a hoarse voice, a harsh noise on breathing in, a wheeze, raised itching welts, vomiting, and a pressure that is falling. The patient may describe a sense of doom or a tightness in the throat, and a clinician who waits for the rash may lose the airway while waiting, since the skin may be spared. The decision is whether to treat at once on the picture, and the finding that makes treatment right is any of those features appearing suddenly in a patient who was well, while the finding that makes it wrong is a different explanation that accounts for all of them.

The clinician is also part of the scene, and the first minute includes the judgment of whether the patient can be approached safely. A patient who has collapsed in a confined space, beside a fire, after a chemical exposure, or with a history suggesting an infectious hazard may put the clinician at risk, and a rescuer who becomes the second casualty has failed the patient. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, is put on before contact when the history allows, and the hands are cleaned before and after every patient, because the same hands carry infection from the patient who is bleeding to the patient who is not. Where a needlestick or a splash has occurred, the local protocol for reporting and assessment begins immediately, and the decision about treatment for the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, or for another infection carried in blood belongs to the service that manages such exposures.

The sequence is harder to read in the patients whose signs are muted, and those are exactly the patients most likely to be missed. A frail older patient may present with confusion, a fall, or a refusal to eat, with no fever and no pain, and the first minute may reveal only that the patient is not the person the family knows. A child may compensate for a long time and then deteriorate suddenly, and poor perfusion in a child is best read from behavior, color, feeding, and alertness rather than from a single pressure. A pregnant woman has a raised pulse and a lower pressure as part of her normal state, so a value that would reassure in another patient may already represent a loss of reserve. A patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, whether by HIV infection, a cancer treatment, or a long course of steroids, may carry a severe infection with almost no signs, so the threshold for acting must be lower.

The first minute is also where the reasoning can go wrong, and the commonest error is to fall in love with a label before the findings have earned it. A patient labeled as drunk, as anxious, as having had a seizure, or as having had a simple faint may then be examined in a way that confirms the label and misses the stroke, the low glucose, the sepsis, or the bleed beneath it. The clinician must hold several possibilities at once and name what would change the mind, because that discipline is the protection against anchoring. Soap notes, which organize the record into subjective, objective, assessment and plan, offer a structure for this, and the record should say what the next observer is to look for rather than only what has been concluded, so that the next reader can continue the thought.

The patient and the family are part of the first minute even when the patient cannot speak, because the person who knows the patient best is often in the room. The clinician asks what happened, what the patient's usual state is, what medicines are taken, and what allergies exist, since those answers direct the reasoning while the examination continues. Consent for examination and treatment in an emergency is presumed where the patient cannot give it and delay would cause harm, and the local protocol governs how that presumption is recorded. The family should be told what is being done and why, in words they can follow, and where a language or cultural difference stands between them and the clinician, an interpreter is found early rather than late.

The rule that treatment precedes diagnosis is the heart of this chapter, and it is a statement about the order of decisions rather than about the value of diagnosis. Treatment is the right answer in the first minute when the airway is obstructed, when breathing has stopped or become agonal, when no pulse can be felt, when a seizure continues, when the blood glucose is low, or when the signs of shock or severe hypoxia are present, because waiting for certainty then carries a cost that cannot be recovered. Treatment is the wrong answer when the patient is stable, when the picture is explained by a cause that needs no emergency treatment, and when treating would destroy the evidence the diagnosis depends on, as when samples must be taken before an antibiotic is given. The clinician should say which finding would justify acting and which would forbid it, because that habit transfers between settings even when the available treatments do not. Naming the decision rather than a specific medicine is deliberate in a book about diagnosis, and the choice of what to give belongs with the team, the guideline, and the patient in front of you.

Two constructed illustrations may fix the habit, and neither is a portrait of a real person. Imagine a man brought to a clinic after a collapse, cool and clammy, with no pulse felt at the wrist, fast breathing, and an abdomen that is beginning to distend, and the clinician does not wait to learn which organ is bleeding but begins the journey to surgical help while supporting the airway and the circulation. Now imagine a woman who is drowsy and has been labeled as having had too much to drink, in whom a glucose measurement is low and whose alertness returns once the glucose is corrected, so the label dissolves in the first minute. The findings in these stories are illustrations and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the values that trigger action differ between services. The sequence is not the whole of resuscitation, and it has succeeded when the patient is alive to receive a proper history and examination.

To summarize, the first minute is not a diagnosis but a recognition, and the airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure sequence exists to find the threats that kill before any cause is named. The findings that demand action are the obstructed airway, the absent or agonal breathing, the pulse that cannot be felt, the seizure that is continuing, and the blood glucose that is low, and each is met with treatment rather than a further question. The lethal causes named at the bedside are hemorrhage, hypoxia, sepsis, cardiac arrest, and stroke, and each carries a revealing finding, among them a climbing pulse with a swelling belly, a risen breathing rate with drowsiness, a fever with confusion and cold skin, absent response with abnormal breathing, and a face that droops with an arm that drifts. The same reasoning is used by a team with a monitor and a trolley and by a clinician alone with a bag and a mask, a torch, a watch, and a hand on the chest. Every number in this chapter, whether a rate, a pressure, a temperature, an oxygen saturation, a score, or a duration, is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who looks critically ill is treated as critically ill first, and the diagnosis is settled afterwards.

# Chapter 38 — Shock

Shock is the state in which the circulation no longer delivers enough oxygen and fuel to the tissues, and it is diagnosed at the bedside rather than in the laboratory. It is not the same as a low blood pressure, although the two often travel together, and a patient may be in shock while the cuff still shows an acceptable figure. The reasoning is mechanical, because every cause belongs to one of four mechanisms: the container has lost its contents, the vessels have opened too wide, the pump has failed, or the outflow is blocked. Those mechanisms produce different findings, and the findings are what separate them in the first minutes. The urgency is identical in all of them, because tissue that is not perfused begins to die, and the patient who is compensating well may be closest to stopping. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

The lethal causes deserve to be named before the ordinary reasoning, each with the finding that would reveal it. Hemorrhage is the most common, and the finding that betrays it is a rising pulse with a falling pressure in a patient who has a source of bleeding, or a source concealed in the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis, the thigh, or the gut. Tension pneumothorax gives a sudden breathlessness, absent breath sounds on one side, a hollow note when that side is tapped, a windpipe pushed away, and visibly distended neck veins. Cardiac tamponade gives a falling pressure, distended neck veins, and heart sounds that are muffled, which is why a penetrating wound near the heart is never watched quietly. Pulmonary embolism may present as a sudden collapse with a clear chest, a fast pulse, poor oxygen levels, and a pressure that will not hold. Anaphylaxis arrives within minutes of an exposure, with swollen lips, a hoarse voice, a rash, a wheeze, and a pressure that falls while the skin may first feel warm.

Perfusion is not the same as pressure, and confusing the two is the central error this chapter exists to prevent. Blood pressure is the product of how much blood the heart pushes out and how much resistance the vessels offer, so a patient can defend a normal figure by narrowing every vessel while the tissues beyond are starved. When cells are deprived of oxygen they switch to a wasteful form of metabolism, producing lactate and acid. This is why confusion, a rising breathing rate, and a shrinking urine output may appear before the pressure changes at all. The skin, the brain, and the kidney complain first, because the body sacrifices them in that order to protect the heart and the brainstem. What the examiner is really looking for is the direction of travel, whether the patient is holding the circulation together or beginning to lose it.

Blood pressure is still worth measuring carefully, because its errors are more often errors of technique than of interpretation. The cuff must fit the arm, the arm must rest at the level of the heart, and the patient should be still before the reading. A systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury is widely taught as the point at which shock must be assumed, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the value that should trigger action differs with age, pregnancy, and usual baseline. The more useful comparison is with the patient's own normal pressure, which is why asking about previous readings belongs to the examination rather than to a history that may be skipped. A pressure that has fallen by 40 millimeters of mercury from a known usual value matters even when the new figure still looks respectable, and that comparison must also be checked against the local standard, since the threshold for concern varies between services. Both arms should be measured when the first reading is unexpected, and the reading should be repeated before any decision rests on it.

The pulse pressure is the difference between the systolic and the diastolic figure, and it carries information that neither figure carries alone. A narrow pulse pressure suggests that the heart is ejecting a small volume into a tightly constricted circulation, which is the pattern of hemorrhage, dehydration, and tamponade. A wide pulse pressure suggests that the vessels are open too wide, which is the pattern of the early septic patient and of some forms of anaphylaxis. The character of the pulse matters as much as its rate, because a thready pulse barely felt under the fingers is different from a full bounding one, and both may be fast. The normal resting pulse for an adult is often quoted as between 60 and 100 beats per minute, but that range is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it shifts with age, fitness, medicines, and pregnancy. The clinician should record the rate, the rhythm, the volume, and the patient's own baseline together, because a rate that is normal for one person may alarm another.

Capillary refill is the cheapest perfusion test in medicine, and it is performed by pressing the skin over the sternum, or a fingertip, until the color blanches, then releasing and counting how long the color takes to return. A return within about 2 seconds is usually taken as reassuring, while a delay beyond 3 seconds suggests that the periphery is being starved, but those figures are illustrations of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the timing depends on the room, the age of the patient, and the method used. The central sites, the sternum and the forehead, are more reliable than the fingers, which are affected by cold and by narrowing of the arteries. The sign becomes far stronger when it is joined to the temperature of the skin and the mental state, because no single bedside finding is sufficient by itself. The examiner should also look for mottling over the knees and the shins, which is a patchy blue and white discoloration that appears when blood is redirected away from the surface.

The temperature and moisture of the skin divide the causes of shock into two broad families. A cold, clammy patient with pale or mottled skin and cool knees has a circulation that is tightly shut down, and that pattern belongs to hemorrhage, dehydration, a failing heart, and the obstructive causes. A warm patient with flushed skin, wide vessels, and a bounding pulse has a circulation that has opened too wide, and that pattern belongs to the septic, the anaphylactic, and the neurogenic causes. The distinction is a starting point rather than a verdict, because sepsis often begins warm and turns cold as the patient deteriorates. A patient with a failing heart may have cool limbs and a high jugular venous pressure, while a patient who is bleeding has cool limbs and a low one, so the neck veins separate the two. The clinician who feels the hands and the knees and compares them with the trunk is gathering this information with no instrument at all.

The patient who is compensating well is the patient most easily lost, because the numbers remain acceptable while the reserve is spent. The first response to a falling circulating volume is a rising pulse and a tightening of the peripheral vessels, and the pressure is defended until that compensation fails. A young, fit adult can lose a large proportion of the blood volume, often quoted as around 30 per cent, before the systolic pressure falls, but that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The findings that announce the approaching failure are the ones the numbers hide: anxiety or drowsiness, a climbing breathing rate, a falling urine output, cool mottled skin, and a narrowing pulse pressure. The clinician who records these observations at intervals and compares them will see the change before the pressure admits it. A normal pressure in a patient who looks unwell is a reason to examine again, not a reason to relax.

The history is taken quickly and often from someone other than the patient, because confusion is one of the earliest effects of poor perfusion. A family member or the person who brought the patient may know what happened, what medicines are taken, and what the patient was doing in the hours before. The speed of the onset is the first question, because a collapse in seconds suggests an embolism, a rhythm disturbance, a tamponade, or an allergic reaction, while a decline over hours suggests bleeding, infection, or dehydration. The next questions concern loss: blood from any site, vomiting, diarrhea, heavy menstrual bleeding, a pregnancy that may lie outside the uterus, or a recent procedure. Then come the questions about the chest, the breathing, the abdomen, and the urine, and finally those about medicines, allergies, and previous illness. The clinician should ask directly about a possible pregnancy in any woman of childbearing age, because that answer changes the differential within seconds, and the account should be written down with the time it was given.

The examination follows a fixed order so that nothing important is skipped and nothing important is delayed. The clinician begins at the end of the bed with the general appearance, the work of breathing, the level of alertness, and the color of the skin. The pulse, the pressure, the breathing rate, and the temperature are then measured and written down with the time, followed by the temperature gradient from trunk to knee. The neck is examined for the jugular venous pressure, which is the single most useful bedside sign for separating a pump problem from a volume problem. A collapsed venous pressure points toward lost filling, or toward vessels that have opened too wide, while a raised one points toward a pump that cannot move what it receives, or toward a physical obstruction to filling. The chest is examined for breath sounds and dullness, the heart for murmurs and muffled tones, and the abdomen for distension, tenderness, and a pulsatile mass, and every wound and line is inspected directly.

The examiner should also look for the pulsus paradoxus, an exaggerated fall in the systolic pressure during inspiration, which is sought by watching the gauge or feeling the pulse while the patient breathes quietly. Two bedside maneuvers then ask whether the heart can use more filling, and both are interpreted as tests rather than treatments. In the passive leg raise the legs are lifted while the trunk stays flat, which briefly returns blood to the heart and produces a measurable change in the pulse or the pressure. A rise in the pressure, or a fall in the pulse, suggests a circulation that is short of volume and can respond to it, while no change suggests that the pump or the obstruction is the problem. The same question can be asked with a small fluid challenge, and the finding that makes filling the right answer is a clear improvement in the pressure and in the signs of perfusion. The findings that make it the wrong answer are a rise in the jugular venous pressure, new crackles, or worsening breathlessness, and no quantity or rate of fluid belongs in this chapter.

Hypovolemic shock is the mechanism in which the container has lost its contents, and it is divided by what has been lost. Blood loss is the most urgent form, and it may be visible or concealed, with the concealed sites being the chest, the abdominal cavity, the space behind the peritoneum, the pelvis, the thigh, and the gut. Water and salt loss occurs with prolonged vomiting, diarrhea, heavy sweating, and the passage of large volumes of dilute urine, and the findings are a fast thready pulse, cool pale skin, delayed refill, a narrow pulse pressure, thirst, and a falling urine output. A patient who has bled into the abdomen may show nothing more than a rising pulse, a falling pressure, and a distended tender abdomen, with no wound anywhere on the skin. Bleeding into the chest gives breathlessness and dullness at the lung base, a fracture of the thigh bone can hold a large volume inside the limb, and a patient taking a medicine that prevents clotting may bleed severely from a source that would otherwise stop. The finding that reveals concealed bleeding is a patient with the signs of shock and no visible reason for them, and a normal blood count early after acute bleeding proves nothing.

Tension pneumothorax is an obstructive cause in which air collects in the chest under pressure and prevents the heart from filling. It occurs after trauma, after a procedure on the chest, in a patient with lung disease, and sometimes in a patient being ventilated by machine. The findings are a sudden worsening of breathing, absent breath sounds on one side, a hollow note when that side is tapped, neck veins that are visibly distended, and a windpipe pushed toward the opposite side. The pressure falls, the pulse rises, and the patient becomes agitated and then drowsy as the heart is compressed. The finding that makes the diagnosis is the combination of a distressed patient, one silent side of the chest, and a rising venous pressure, and the decision is to release the trapped air before any image is taken, because waiting for a chest radiograph here risks the patient's life. The finding that would make that decision wrong is a chest that is dull and quiet because of fluid rather than air, and in a clinic far from imaging the same signs and the same decision apply.

Cardiac tamponade occurs when fluid or blood collects in the sac around the heart and prevents it from filling. It follows penetrating wounds of the chest, heart surgery, inflammation of the pericardium, cancer, and kidney failure. The classical findings are a falling pressure, distended neck veins, and heart sounds that are muffled or difficult to hear. The pulse may fall noticeably during inspiration, the heart may look large on an image, and the tracing on an electrocardiogram, or ECG, may suggest that the heart is being compressed. The finding that confirms it at the bedside is fluid or blood seen around the heart on an ultrasound examination, and the decision is to drain that collection urgently, which belongs to a clinician trained and equipped to do it. The finding that would make drainage the wrong answer is a different cause of the same signs, such as a tension pneumothorax, and every figure associated with these signs must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Pulmonary embolism occurs when a clot travels from a vein, usually in the leg or the pelvis, and lodges in the arteries of the lung. It may present as a sudden breathlessness, a sharp chest pain, a cough with blood, a fainting episode, or a cardiac arrest, and the examination may find a clear chest despite severe breathlessness. The findings that point to it are a fast pulse, poor oxygen levels in the blood, a raised jugular venous pressure, and signs of strain on the right side of the heart. The risk factors belong in the history: recent surgery, immobility, a long journey, cancer, pregnancy, the period after childbirth, a previous clot, and a medicine that prevents clotting which has recently been stopped. The finding that reveals it in a well-resourced setting is an image of the lung arteries, and at the bedside it is an ultrasound showing a struggling right ventricle or a clot in a large vein. The decision to break up the clot with treatment belongs to the clinician who can weigh the confirmation against the risk of bleeding, and the finding that would make that treatment wrong is active bleeding or a recent operation that cannot tolerate it.

Anaphylaxis is a distributive cause that unfolds within minutes of an exposure, and it is unique among these emergencies because it is treated on the clinical picture and not on a test. It follows a sting, a food, a medicine, a vaccine, or contact with latex, and it may follow an exposure the patient has tolerated many times before. The findings are a sudden rash or flushing, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, a hoarse voice, a wheeze, vomiting and abdominal cramps, and a pressure that falls while the skin is still warm. The clinician should look for swelling in the airway before anything else, because a patient whose voice has changed or who is struggling to swallow is losing the airway while the pressure is still being measured. The finding that makes treatment the right answer is a sudden illness with skin, airway, breathing, or circulatory signs after a plausible exposure, and the decision is made at once, because waiting to see whether the reaction is severe enough can be fatal. The finding that would make treatment the wrong answer is a clear alternative explanation, such as a fainting episode with no skin or airway signs, although anaphylaxis can occur without any rash at all.

Septic shock is the most common distributive cause, and it is the subject of the next chapter, so only its place in this reasoning is described here. It occurs when the response to an infection damages the circulation and the organs, and the earliest sign is often a warm periphery, a wide pulse pressure, and a fast pulse while the pressure is still held. As the process advances the periphery turns cold and mottled, the pressure falls, the breathing rate climbs, and the urine output shrinks. The source may be anywhere, and the hunt for it includes the lungs, the urine, the abdomen, the skin, the joints, the lines and tubes in the body, and the heart valves. A patient who is older, who is receiving treatment that suppresses the immune response, or who has recently had surgery may show none of the classical signs, and a new confusion may be the only clue. The finding that makes the diagnosis likely is infection together with evidence that an organ is failing, and the decision to treat before the organism is known is made on that picture rather than on a single laboratory value.

Cardiogenic shock is the mechanism in which the pump has failed, and its most common cause is a heart attack that has damaged a large part of the muscle. The findings are a cold clammy patient with a raised jugular venous pressure, crackles at the bases of the lungs, a fast pulse, and a low pressure that does not improve when the patient is filled. The pattern may be confused with hypovolemic shock, and the venous pressure and the lung sounds are the findings that separate them, because a patient who is bleeding has a flat neck and a clear chest. A new murmur in this setting suggests that a valve, or the wall between the chambers, has ruptured, and it changes the urgency of the surgical decision. Other causes include a rhythm disturbance that is too fast or too slow, inflammation of the heart muscle, a failing valve, and the final stage of long-standing heart disease. The finding that makes support of the pump the right answer is a heart that fails to empty despite adequate filling, while the finding that makes it the wrong answer is a circulation that is empty and simply needs volume.

The remaining mechanisms are less common but must be held in mind, because each has a specific answer. Neurogenic shock follows an injury to the spinal cord, and it produces a low pressure with a slow pulse and warm dry skin, which is the opposite of the fast pulse of hemorrhage, so the pulse is the finding that separates them. Adrenal crisis occurs in a patient whose adrenal glands cannot respond to stress, often after long treatment with steroids is stopped, and it produces a pressure that refuses to rise despite filling, with nausea, weakness, low sugar, and disturbed salt balance. A child, a pregnant woman, and an older patient each change the usual signs, because the child defends the pressure until collapse, the pregnant woman has more blood to lose before the pressure speaks, and the older patient may take medicines that blunt the response. In all of them the trend, the skin, the mental state, and the urine output carry more weight than a single measurement.

In a well-resourced hospital the same reasoning is supported by instruments, and they change the confidence of the answer rather than its logic.
