A catheter placed in an artery gives a continuous pressure reading and allows the examiner to see the pulse pressure breath by breath, which is useful when the cuff reading is unreliable. An ultrasound examination of the heart at the bedside is the most informative single test in this chapter, because it shows whether the chambers are full or empty, whether the muscle is contracting, whether a valve has failed, whether fluid surrounds the heart, and whether the right side is strained. Repeated measures of lactate and blood gases, a catheter in the bladder, and tests of kidney function, liver function, blood sugar, and salt balance show which organs have suffered, while cultures show what organism is responsible when infection is the cause. Every reference range and every figure from the laboratory must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the values differ between laboratories and the units differ between countries.

In a clinic whose equipment is a stethoscope, a torch, a thermometer, and a watch, the same differentiation is made with the same reasoning and fewer numbers. The watch allows the pulse and the breathing rate to be counted rather than estimated, and the count is repeated so that the trend becomes visible. The thermometer turns an impression of fever or of cold into a figure that can be compared over time, and the torch makes the mouth, the throat, the skin, the eyes, and the nails visible. The blood pressure cuff remains one of the most powerful tools in the room, provided the cuff fits and the technique is repeated, and the skin of the knees, the temperature of the hands, the refill over the sternum, and the alertness of the patient supply the rest of the picture. A patient with cold mottled skin, a rising breathing rate, a falling pressure, a change in alertness, or a suspected concealed loss of blood must travel, and the journey should begin before the picture becomes unmistakable. A patient with warm skin, a steady pulse, and a stable mental state may be watched while the cause is pursued, provided that the review is arranged and the patient can return, and the transfer should carry a clear description of the findings and the time they were recorded.

A constructed illustration may fix these habits, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a young man brought in after a motorcycle crash, who is awake and talking, whose pressure measures close to his usual figure, and whose pulse is 120 beats per minute. The examiner notices that his hands and knees are cool, that the color over his kneecaps is mottled, that his capillary refill is delayed, and that his abdomen is becoming distended and tender. The pressure may still look acceptable, but the direction of the pulse and the skin says that the compensation is nearly spent, and the concealed source is in the abdomen. That figure and that rate are illustrations of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the threshold for alarm varies with age and with the definition in use. The lesson is not the number but the move, because the clinician who examined the skin and the abdomen found what the pressure had not yet admitted.

The whole process in shock is a loop that turns faster than in any other chapter. The clinician forms a mechanism from the history and the first look, predicts the findings it should produce, and examines deliberately to test the prediction. The result either supports the mechanism or forces a revision, and the revision is repeated as often as the patient's condition requires. The findings that matter most are the ones that change, because a pressure that is stable while the skin cools and the breathing climbs is not stability at all. A patient who improves and then worsens is a familiar pattern, and the second decline usually means that the original cause continued quietly while the first problem was being managed. The speed of the loop is set by the patient and not by the ward round, and a patient who is deteriorating earns a shorter interval between examinations.

To summarize, shock is a failure of tissue perfusion rather than a number on a gauge, and it is organized by four mechanisms: a container that has lost its contents, vessels that have opened too wide, a pump that has failed, and an obstruction that prevents filling. The lethal causes are named at once, among them hemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism, and anaphylaxis, and each carries a finding that can be sought with the hands and the eyes. The blood pressure is valuable but late, the pulse pressure and the capillary refill add meaning to it, and the temperature of the skin separates the shut-down circulation from the wide-open one. The patient who compensates well is the patient to watch most closely, because the pressure is the last sign to change, especially in the young, the pregnant, the athletic, and the child. Every figure in this chapter, whether a pressure, a rate, a proportion, or a duration, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such values differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and the treatment of shock belongs to the clinician who is with the patient and to the system that supports that clinician.

# Chapter 39 — Sepsis Recognition

Sepsis is the name clinicians give to the moment when the body's response to an infection stops protecting the patient and begins to injure the organs instead. It is not a single value that can be read from a thermometer or a laboratory report, and no one sign proves it, because the same findings that announce it in one patient are that patient's ordinary state in another. Sepsis is recognized by its trajectory, by the direction in which the patient is moving over hours rather than by the position of any one measurement. A patient whose breathing rate has climbed at two successive reviews, whose pressure has fallen since the last observation, and whose family says he is not himself is a different patient from one whose single reading happens to sit at the same number. The reasoning is built on comparison, against the patient's own baseline, against the previous set of observations, and against the story of how the illness began. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

The lethal possibility must be named before the comfortable one, and here it is the patient who is dying of infection while the examination still looks unremarkable. Septic shock kills in hours, and the finding that reveals it is not a dramatic fever but a pressure that will not hold, a mind that has wandered, and skin that looks mottled and cool at the edges. The patient whose immune defenses have been stripped by disease or treatment may carry a bloodstream infection with no fever and no localizing sign at all, so that a change in behavior is the only evidence available before the pressure falls. The patient with a new murmur and a fever may be developing an infection on a heart valve, and that murmur heard for the first time turns a vague febrile illness into a specific hunt with a specific deadline. The patient with a rigid, board-like abdomen has a perforated organ until proven otherwise, and no amount of fever reasoning substitutes for the surgical decision this finding demands. The patient whose skin is already mottled has moved past the earliest stage, and the mottling signals that blood is being directed away from the periphery toward the vital centers, a compensation that cannot continue.

Infection and sepsis are not the same thing, and the difference is the whole point of the distinction. Infection describes organisms in the body, in a wound, in the urine, in the lung, or in the blood, while sepsis describes a response to that infection which has become dysregulated and which is damaging organs the organisms themselves have not reached. The lungs stiffen and the patient breathes faster, the vessels dilate and the pressure falls, the kidneys slow, the brain clouds, and the clotting system becomes unstable, and these features make sepsis a different problem from the pneumonia or the urinary infection that started it. A patient can therefore have a serious infection without sepsis, and sepsis can be declared before any organism has been found, because the recognition rests on the response and on evidence of organ injury rather than on a positive culture. The definition has been redrawn more than once, and each revision has moved the boundary, so the current definition must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it is used to classify a real patient. What has not changed is the clinical task, which is to notice the patient whose response to infection has become dangerous, and to notice it early enough that the organs can still recover.

The systemic inflammatory response syndrome was an attempt to make the impression that a patient looks infected into something countable. It formalizes a small set of observations made at the bedside anyway, the temperature, the pulse, the breathing rate, and the white cell count, and it proposes that when enough of them are abnormal the patient is mounting a systemic response. Its limitation matters more than its virtue, because the syndrome does not require an infection and is met by burns, trauma, pancreatitis, autoimmune disease, a recent operation, and the inflammation that follows childbirth, so it labels many people as infected who are not. It is equally poor at the reverse, since a patient can be dying of infection without meeting its criteria, particularly an older patient, a patient taking steroids, or a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed. A temperature above 38 degrees Celsius is the figure most often taught as the line at which fever is said to be present, and that number is offered as an illustration of the reasoning rather than as a rule; it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because accepted values differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. The lesson it leaves behind is that a group of ordinary observations taken together can raise a suspicion, but the suspicion still has to be tested against the patient in front of you.

The quick sequential organ failure assessment is a newer attempt to solve a different problem, which is how to recognize the patient with a suspected infection who is at risk of dying before any blood test has returned. It formalizes three things any clinician anywhere can observe, namely how fast the patient is breathing, whether the mind has changed from its usual state, and how low the systolic pressure has fallen. Its chief limitation is that it is not sensitive, so a patient who does not meet its criteria may still be severely ill, and a clinician who lets a low count close the question will miss the patient it was meant to catch. It was derived in a particular population and not for children, pregnant women, or patients whose immune defenses are suppressed, so its meaning shifts in those groups. Many services have adapted it by adding the oxygen saturation, the urine output, or a laboratory measure, and a breathing rate above 22 breaths per minute and a systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury are the figures most often quoted within it; because the items and the values differ between services and editions, the version in use and its figures must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The signs that precede the obvious fever are the ones that save patients, and they are found by watching the patient rather than by reading a result. A new confusion is often the earliest, and it is the one most easily attributed to age, to the hour, or to the strange surroundings of a hospital. The person who knows the patient best, the spouse, the son, the daughter, or the carer, can say whether this is new, and that question is worth more than any screening test. A breathing rate that has risen is the second sign, and it is the vital sign most often guessed rather than counted, which is why a ward that counts it discovers deterioration and a ward that estimates it does not. A pressure that has fallen, whether or not it has crossed any line, is the third, and the direction of the fall matters more than the absolute figure. A passage of urine that has dwindled to a trickle is the fourth, noticed only when the urine is measured and written down, because a patient who is not passing urine does not complain of it.

Because sepsis is recognized by its trajectory, the repeated set of observations is the most important investigation in this chapter and the one that costs nothing. The same pressure that looks reassuring at the first reading can look ominous beside the reading taken earlier, and the same breathing rate can look ordinary until it is compared with what the patient was doing at home. This is the reasoning that the early warning scores formalize, by combining routine observations into a single number that rises as the patient deteriorates and by prompting a response when it does. The Glasgow coma scale is the way the level of consciousness is recorded, and the reasoning it formalizes is the response to voice, to command, and to pain. A change of a few points in a patient whose baseline is known carries more information than the absolute number, and the version in use and the value at which it should cause alarm must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. An early warning score is only a summary of what has been recorded, so a chart with a blank column cannot warn anyone, and a patient whose score is unchanged but whose family says something is wrong deserves a second look, because the clinician's unease is itself an observation that no score contains.

The fever that everyone expects may be absent, and a clinician who waits for it will arrive late. An older patient whose infection is severe may have a temperature that is barely raised, or a temperature that has fallen below the usual range, and that low temperature is a warning rather than a comfort. The same is true of the patient whose immune defenses are suppressed by illness or treatment, and of the patient with poorly controlled diabetes, in whom the response to infection is blunted and the ordinary signs are muted. In these patients the presentation may be a fall, a refusal to eat, a new drowsiness, a loss of continence, or a conversation that no longer makes sense, so the infection announces itself through function rather than through temperature. A temperature of 36 degrees Celsius in a frail older patient who was at 37 degrees Celsius the day before may carry more information than a fever in a healthy young adult, and both figures are illustrative and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the usual range is drawn differently between laboratories and age groups. The absence of fever therefore never excludes a serious infection, and the threshold for asking for help in these patients is lower rather than higher.

The hunt for the source begins with the history, before the patient is touched, because the answer is often in what the patient or the family says rather than in what the examination finds. The clinician uses the Oldcarts framework to keep the account of the present illness complete, then broadens the questions to the exposures that change the list of likely organisms. Where has the patient traveled, what animals are kept at home, what water is drunk, what food has been eaten away from home, and has there been an injection, a dental procedure, an operation, or a device placed in the body. Whether there is a risk of a sexually transmitted infection, whether the patient takes steroids or treatment that suppresses the immune system, whether there has been a recent course of antibiotics, and whether the patient is pregnant all belong in the same conversation. The clinician should also ask what the patient is normally like, how much they normally eat, drink, and pass urine, because a change from the baseline is the earliest evidence available.

The examination of a patient with suspected sepsis is a deliberate search for a focus, performed in a fixed order so that nothing is forgotten while the patient is deteriorating. It begins with the general appearance, the work of breathing, the color of the skin, and the level of consciousness, then moves to the skin from the scalp to the soles in search of a rash, a puncture mark, an ulcer, a bite, or a red and warm area. The throat, the ears, the nose, the mouth, and the teeth are inspected with a torch, because an abscess in a tooth or a hidden infection in a sinus can sustain a bloodstream infection for a long time. The chest is examined for crackles and dullness, the heart for a new murmur, the abdomen for tenderness, rigidity, an enlarged organ, or a mass, and the joints for swelling and warmth. The examiner then looks at the places that are easy to forget, namely the back, the spine, the groins, the perineum, the pressure areas over the heels and the sacrum, and every wound, line, tube, and device in the body, since an infection hidden in a line or a drain is invisible to a clinician who does not look at it directly.

The patient whose immune defenses are suppressed is the one in whom the usual reasoning fails most completely, and the patient with a low neutrophil count is its clearest example. A low neutrophil count, produced by a cancer of the blood, by treatment that suppresses the marrow, or by a transplant, removes the cells that make pus and inflammation, so an infection can spread without producing a single localizing sign. In such a patient a fever may be the only abnormal finding, and sometimes even the fever is absent, so the clinician is left with a patient who simply looks unwell and a history of treatment that suppressed the marrow. Advanced infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, long courses of steroids, and some treatments for autoimmune disease produce a similar blurring of the picture, though usually to a lesser degree. The decision that follows is that a new fever, or a new deterioration, is treated as an emergency rather than watched, and the threshold for seeking senior help is lowered rather than raised. The finding that would make treatment the wrong answer is a clear non-infectious explanation, such as a reaction to a medicine, a clot, or the underlying disease itself, and even then the patient must be reviewed closely.

A fever with a murmur that is new, or a murmur that has changed, is a specific problem with a specific deadline, and it is the infection of the lining of the heart. The patients most at risk are those with a damaged or prosthetic valve, a pacemaker or another device inside the heart, a history of injecting drugs, or a recent procedure on the teeth or the gut, and in these people the fever may be low and persistent rather than dramatic. The finding that reveals the diagnosis is the murmur itself, heard for the first time or heard to be different from the last description, and an examiner who listens carefully in every febrile patient is the one who finds it. The other clues are small and easily missed, being tiny bleeding spots under the nails or in the eye, tender red nodules on the fingers or toes, an enlarged spleen, and a patient who is anemic or whose urine contains blood. The decision that follows is whether to take blood cultures before any treatment begins, because cultures drawn after the first treatment are far less likely to name the organism. The finding that would make the diagnosis the wrong answer is another focus that fully explains the fever, though a patient with a prosthetic valve and a fever should be discussed with a senior colleague before that alternative is accepted.

A rigid, board-like abdomen in a patient with fever is a surgical emergency and not a problem for the treatment decision alone. Rigidity is the abdominal wall held tight in a way the patient cannot relax on request, and it usually means that the peritoneum has been irritated by a perforated organ, by pus, or by blood. The supporting signs are pain on the slightest movement or cough, rebound tenderness, quiet bowel sounds, a rising pulse, and a pressure that is falling. The abdomen can lie, because an older patient, a patient taking steroids, and a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed may have a perforated organ with only mild tenderness and a vague story of not feeling well. The decision it forces is about surgery and senior help rather than about which treatment to choose, and it should be made at the bedside without waiting for an image that may delay the operating room. The finding that would make the catastrophe less likely is a soft abdomen that stays soft on repeated examination, while a patient who is getting worse with each review confirms it.

The skin is the organ that can be examined most quickly at the bedside, and what it shows in sepsis is the redistribution of blood away from the surface. The findings are cool hands and feet, a capillary refill that is visibly delayed when the clinician presses the fingertip and counts, mottling over the knees and the thighs, and a dusky or gray color that the family notices before the clinician does. A rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed against it is a different and even more urgent finding, because it may mean that organisms are in the bloodstream and that the clotting system has begun to fail. One presentation on the skin deserves to be named separately because it kills quickly and is easily dismissed as a bruise, and that is a necrotizing infection of the soft tissue. The findings that reveal it are pain far worse than the appearance suggests, an area that is swollen and discolored, a numbness or loss of sensation over that area, blisters or fluid seeping from the skin, and sometimes a crackling sensation when the skin is pressed. The decision in that situation is surgical and immediate, because the treatment is the removal of the dead tissue, and the finding that would make it wrong is a superficial infection clearly confined to the surface in a patient who is stable and improving.

In a hospital with a laboratory, the recognition of sepsis is supported by tests that sharpen the picture but do not replace the examination. A blood count, a measure of inflammation such as C-reactive protein, a measure of kidney function, a measure of the acidity of the blood, and a measure of lactate are the ordinary set, and each answers a particular question about which organs are already involved. A lactate above 2 millimoles per liter is often quoted as evidence that the tissues are not receiving enough oxygen, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the value depends on the method and on the laboratory. Blood cultures should be taken before treatment whenever that is possible without delay, because the organism is the one piece of information that treatment cannot recover once it has begun. Imaging by chest radiograph, by ultrasound, by computed tomography, or CT, and by magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, is chosen by the question it has to answer, and an electrocardiogram, or ECG, belongs in the assessment of a patient whose picture could also be explained by a heart attack. A lumbar puncture belongs in the patient with signs of meningitis once the questions of safety have been answered, and the transfer of a patient to an intensive care unit, or ICU, rests on the trajectory rather than on a single number.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, a thermometer, and a watch, the recognition of sepsis is made with the same reasoning and a smaller set of instruments. The breathing rate is counted rather than guessed, the pulse is counted in the same way, and the temperature is taken with the same thermometer each time so that the readings can be compared. The torch makes the throat, the ears, the skin, the eyes, and the perineum visible, and the watch allows the observations to be placed in time, so a set of observations with times beside them is the closest thing to a laboratory that a clinic possesses. The urine is measured where that can be done, the abdomen is pressed gently and then pressed again later, and the patient is asked to return, or to be brought back, at a stated interval rather than whenever it is convenient. The decision the clinic faces is not usually a diagnosis but a plan, which is whether the patient can be watched here, whether treatment should begin on the clinical picture, and whether the journey must begin now. A patient who is deteriorating in the clinic must travel, and the clinician who sends that patient with a written summary of what has been observed gives the receiving team information that cannot be reconstructed later.

The decision about treatment is part of diagnosis and not a separate step, and in sepsis it is often made before any organism has been named. Treatment is the right answer when the signs of organ failure are already present, when the pressure is low and does not improve when the patient is laid flat, when the mind has changed from its baseline or the breathing rate is climbing, and when a focus is strongly suspected that would respond. Treatment is the wrong answer when the picture is explained by something that is not infection, such as a clot in the lung, bleeding inside the body, a heart that is failing, or a reaction to a medicine, and when treating before the samples are taken would destroy the evidence on which diagnosis depends. This book gives no doses, regimens, rates, or durations for any drug, because it is a book about diagnosis and because those decisions belong to the current guideline, the local protocol, the patient, and the organism. Fluid given into a vein is often part of the immediate response, and whether it is given, and how much, turns on whether the pressure and the perfusion improve, while the most useful thing a diagnosing clinician can say is what finding would make treatment right and what finding would make it wrong, because that reasoning transfers between settings even when the medicines do not.

A constructed illustration may make the reasoning concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine an older woman brought to a clinic because her family says she is confused and not herself, with a temperature only slightly raised, a breathing rate of 24 breaths per minute, and a blood pressure of 100 millimeters of mercury. Those figures are illustrations of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the values that should prompt action differ with age and with the usual blood pressure. The clinician counts the breathing rate again, looks at the skin with the torch, finds a red and warm area over the hip, and arranges the journey to hospital on the basis of the whole picture rather than the temperature alone. Now imagine a young man receiving treatment for a cancer of the blood, who feels shivery and unwell but looks entirely ordinary, and whose only abnormal finding is a fever that has appeared since the last review. His immune defenses have been suppressed by the treatment, so the ordinary signs are not available, and the decision to treat him as an emergency is made from the history and the trajectory rather than from a focus that can be found. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment.

The record of a patient with suspected sepsis should show the thinking and not only the numbers, including the time of each set of observations, the breathing rate as counted, the direction of the pressure, and what the family said about the baseline. The clinician should write down what was considered and what was set aside, so that the next reader can pick up the thread rather than start again. Safety netting is part of the decision, because a patient who is sent home or watched must be told which signs should bring him back, how quickly to return, and where to go. The patient and the family should be told that a new confusion, a difficulty in breathing, a passage of urine that stops, a rash that does not fade when pressed, or a shivering attack are reasons to return at once. A follow-up visit arranged in advance is worth more than a promise to return if things worsen, because a patient who is becoming septic may not be able to judge that for himself. The clinician who is uncertain should say so, and should convert that uncertainty into a plan for review rather than into a confident answer that the evidence does not support.

To summarize, sepsis is a dysregulated response to infection that is recognized by its trajectory and by the evidence of organ injury rather than by any single value, and the signs that precede the obvious fever are a new confusion, a raised breathing rate, a falling pressure, and a shrinking passage of urine. The systemic inflammatory response syndrome and the quick sequential organ failure assessment are best understood as attempts to formalize the observations a clinician makes anyway, each with real limitations and each adapted locally, so the version in use must always be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The dangerous presentations are named at the bedside and not deferred, among them the patient whose immune defenses are suppressed and whose signs are silent, the patient with a new murmur, the patient with a rigid abdomen, and the patient whose skin is already mottled or whose soft tissue is dying. Treatment is a decision about the patient rather than about a drug, and this chapter gives no doses, regimens, rates, or durations, because those belong to the protocol of your own service. Every figure in this chapter is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and a patient who looks unwell is treated and helped first while the exact cause is settled afterwards.

# Chapter 40 — Respiratory Failure and Airway Compromise

Breathing can fail in two different ways, and telling them apart organizes this chapter. In one, the lungs receive air but cannot move its oxygen into the blood. In the other, air never arrives in sufficient quantity, or the pump that drives it is losing strength, so carbon dioxide accumulates while oxygen falls. The first is a failure of oxygenation, the second a failure of ventilation, and they behave differently at the bedside even when the distress looks the same. The clinician who can decide which failure is present knows where to look and how quickly to move. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, not a protocol, and not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient.

The lethal causes must be named while the subject is described, each with the finding that would reveal it. Epiglottitis, an infection that swells the flap above the voice box, gives a sudden fever, drooling, a muffled voice, and a patient who refuses to lie down. A foreign body gives a sudden onset during eating or play, a cough that will not settle, and breath sounds that differ between the two sides of the chest. Anaphylaxis gives swelling of the lips, tongue, and throat with wheeze and a falling pressure. A hematoma in the neck, after surgery, injury, or a procedure on the large vessels, closes the airway from outside as it expands. An abscess beside the tonsil gives fever, a muffled voice, drooling, and a tender swollen neck. An exhausted patient who is about to stop breathing is the last of these dangers, and the finding is a fading effort, a falling breathing rate, and a drowsiness that can look almost like calm.

Oxygenation fails when blood travels through regions of lung that are perfused but not ventilated, so it returns to the heart without picking up oxygen. Pneumonia fills the air spaces with fluid and cells, pulmonary edema floods them from the capillaries, and acute respiratory distress syndrome makes both lungs stiff and wet after injury or severe infection. A collapsed segment leaves blood flowing past an airway that no longer opens, and a large clot in the pulmonary arteries wastes ventilation on regions that receive no blood. Because carbon dioxide crosses the lung far more easily than oxygen, a patient whose only problem is oxygenation can keep the carbon dioxide normal or low by breathing harder. The price of that effort is work, and when the work cannot be sustained the same patient retains carbon dioxide and becomes a ventilatory failure as well. A normal carbon dioxide in a struggling patient is therefore evidence of effort rather than reassurance.

Ventilation fails when the pump that moves air is weakened or when the airway resists the flow. The pump begins in the brain, travels down the spinal cord, crosses the junction between nerve and muscle, and ends in the diaphragm and the chest wall muscles. A sedative medicine, a stroke, a head injury, a disease of the spinal cord, a disorder of the peripheral nerves, and a disease of the muscles all reduce the air moved with each breath. Obstruction of the airway adds a second load, because the muscles must pull against a narrowed tube. Carbon dioxide then accumulates, producing a warm flushed face, a bounding pulse, a headache, a fine tremor of the hands, and a drowsiness that deepens as the level rises. A patient in this state may breathe quietly and look deceptively peaceful, and that quiet is the danger rather than the comfort.

The work of breathing and the mental state are the two bedside discriminators, and both are visible before any instrument is applied. The clinician looks for neck muscles that stand out with each breath, for skin drawn in between the ribs and above the breastbone, and for nostrils that flare in a child. The patient may sit forward with the arms braced on the knees, using the shoulders as an extra pump, and may purse the lips to hold the airway open during a slow expiration. Sweating, a look of alarm, and an inability to finish a sentence in one breath show that the demand has outgrown the reserve, while quiet drowsiness may mean the drive to breathe is fading. A respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute is often quoted as a point of alarm, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the rate that should worry a clinician depends on age, pregnancy, and the usual state of the patient. The Glasgow coma scale is the usual way of recording consciousness, and its exact contents and the figure that should cause alarm must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the version in use varies between services and editions.

The movement of the chest wall tells the clinician where the resistance lies. A chest that rises fully on both sides but admits little air suggests obstruction above the lungs, because the pump is working and the air is not arriving. A chest that barely moves, with the abdomen drawn inward as the diaphragm descends, suggests weak muscles, and that inward movement against the expected outward movement is called paradoxical breathing. A long wheezing expiration with a barrel-shaped chest suggests obstruction in the smaller airways, while a chest that moves less on one side suggests air or fluid that has separated the lung from the wall. Where the problem lies decides the urgency more than the size of the disturbance does, because a little swelling above the voice box can close a narrow tube. Sorting the patient by the site of the problem is the first diagnostic act, and it is done with the eyes and the ears before any test.

The signs of an airway that is narrowing rather than already closed must be recognized from a distance. Stridor is the harsh musical sound of turbulent air through a narrowed segment, and its timing carries the message. Inspiratory stridor points above the chest, expiratory stridor points to the smaller airways below, and stridor in both phases points to the windpipe or the voice box. The sound is a late sign, because a tube must already be narrowed before flow becomes turbulent, and a tired patient may lose the stridor as the effort fails. The disappearance of a loud stridor is therefore warning rather than improvement, just as a silent chest in severe asthma signals danger. A changed voice is often earlier: hoarseness means swollen, inflamed, or paralyzed cords, and a muffled voice means the space above the cords is filling.

Drooling and an inability to lie flat mean the airway has narrowed enough to change behavior, and they should stop the examination rather than prompt more of it. A patient who cannot swallow his own saliva, or who speaks as if the mouth is full, is protecting an airway that is partly closed. The same meaning belongs to a patient who will not lie back, who sits bolt upright, or who becomes distressed when the head is lowered, because the tongue and swollen tissue fall backward. The clinician should not force such a patient to lie down, and should not pass an instrument into the throat in the hope of seeing the swelling. The character of the cough adds information: a barking cough in a young child belongs to swelling below the cords, a muffled cough to swelling above them, a weak cough to failing muscles or nerves, and a wet cough with fever and crackles to infection of the lung tissue. The neck should be examined for swelling, bruising, or a scar, and felt for crackling under the skin, which means air has escaped into the tissues.

Epiglottitis is the prototype of the narrowed upper airway, and it is diagnosed from the story and the posture rather than from inspection. It begins quickly, with a high fever, a severe sore throat, and a rapid decline, and it is most feared in the young child who has not been immunized, though adults are affected as well. The patient drools, speaks with a muffled voice, sits forward with the chin extended, and resists lying down, and there may be no cough because the swollen structures do not move. Attempting to examine the throat with a spatula can provoke a spasm and close the airway completely, so the instrument is left alone. The patient is kept calm, upright, and accompanied, and the combination of drooling, a muffled voice, and a refusal to lie flat should trigger a call for help at once. What the clinician must not do is observe such a patient in the hope that the picture becomes clearer.

A foreign body in the airway presents as narrowing rather than closure. In a young child it follows a moment of eating, playing, or crying with something in the mouth, and the story may be missing because no adult saw it. In an adult it follows a meal in a patient with difficulty swallowing, a reduced level of consciousness, or a disorder of the nerves and muscles of the throat. The finding that reveals it is a difference between the two sides of the chest, with a wheeze or reduced breath sounds on one side and no fever, while a complete obstruction produces no air movement at all. A foreign body lodged for some time can produce fever, cough, and a shadow on the radiograph, and it is then mistaken for infection. A one-sided wheeze in a patient who has never wheezed before should raise the question of a foreign body before asthma.

Anaphylaxis is the danger most easily missed when the skin is spared. It follows a food, a medicine, a sting, or a contact within a short interval, and it produces swelling of the lips, tongue, and throat with wheeze, a falling pressure, and a sense of impending doom. The skin signs of hives and flushing are common but not universal, and their absence must not exclude the diagnosis when breathing and pressure are changing. The finding that reveals it is the rapid involvement of more than one system, such as swelling of the face with wheeze, or a rash with a falling pressure, in a patient who was well moments before. A patient with a known allergy, a previous reaction, or a self-injecting device at home is at higher risk, and that history belongs in the first questions. The decision to treat is made on the clinical picture, because waiting for confirmation here costs the airway itself.

A hematoma in the neck is a mechanical emergency that is easily overlooked, because the patient may look well at first. It follows surgery on the thyroid or the neck, a procedure on the large vessels, an injury, or a line placed into a large vein, and it is more likely in a patient who takes a medicine that prevents clotting. The swelling expands inside a compartment that cannot stretch, and it pushes the windpipe aside, compresses the veins, and finally closes the airway. The early findings are a tense tender neck, a new hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, and a feeling of pressure, while the late findings are stridor, a displaced windpipe, and a patient who can no longer lie flat. Because the change can occur very quickly, a patient who has just had such a procedure is watched closely and the neck is examined at every review. A quiet period can precede a sudden deterioration, and that pattern is the reason for vigilance rather than a reason to relax it.

An abscess beside the tonsil, or one that has spread into the deep spaces of the neck, begins as a severe sore throat with fever and develops a muffled voice, drooling, difficulty opening the mouth, and offensive breath. The finding that reveals it is a swelling that pushes the soft palate and the uvula to one side, while a patient who cannot open the mouth widely is showing a protective spasm. The exhausted patient is the next danger, and it most often surprises the clinician who was reassured by the first examination. Exhaustion develops when the muscles of breathing have worked against a load too long, and it is recognized by a fall in the breathing rate after a period of rapid breathing, a weaker cough, and drowsiness that replaces agitation. A rising carbon dioxide level produces its own drowsiness, so the patient may appear calm while the blood is becoming more acid, and that calm is the most deceptive sign in this chapter.

A tension pneumothorax is the lethal cause that must be recognized from bedside findings alone, because waiting for an image can cost the patient's life. Air enters the space around the lung and cannot escape, and the pressure rises until it pushes the heart and great veins aside, so the return of blood to the heart falls. The signs are sudden severe breathlessness, absent breath sounds on one side, a chest that is hyperresonant to percussion, distended neck veins, and a falling pressure with a rapid pulse. The windpipe may be shifted away from the affected side, though that is a late sign, and the patient may be restless, sweaty, and confused. The clinician who finds this combination must treat it as a mechanical emergency and call for the help and equipment to relieve the pressure, rather than wait for a radiograph. In a clinic with no imaging, the same combination is the reason to begin the journey at once.

A large clot in the pulmonary arteries is the second lethal cause of sudden breathlessness, and its examination is often deceptively quiet. The patient becomes suddenly short of breath, often with pleuritic pain, a rapid pulse, and a low oxygen, while the chest sounds clear and the radiograph may be normal. The risk factors include recent surgery, a period of immobility, a long journey, active cancer, pregnancy, a previous clot, and a medicine that prevents clotting having been stopped. In the massive form the pressure falls, the neck veins are distended, and the patient may lose consciousness. The finding that most changes the decision is the combination of sudden breathlessness with a clear chest and a risk factor, and the test that answers the question must be chosen according to what is available. Where there is no test, the decision is whether the patient can travel to a place where one exists, and the answer is usually that he must.

Disease within the lung tissue produces a different pattern, and the common causes are told apart by the story, the examination, and the radiograph. Pneumonia gives fever, a productive cough, crackles over one region, and dullness to percussion, and the oxygen falls in proportion to the lung involved. Pulmonary edema from a failing heart gives breathlessness that is worse when lying flat, crackles at the bases, distended neck veins, and swollen ankles. Acute respiratory distress syndrome follows severe infection, injury, an operation, or inflammation of the pancreas, and it makes both lungs stiff and wet so that oxygen falls severely while the chest sounds quiet. Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are failures of airflow that can progress to a failure of ventilation when the effort cannot be sustained, and their dangerous signs are a silent chest, a patient who can no longer speak, and a drowsiness that suggests retained carbon dioxide. In a patient with long-standing disease who tends to retain carbon dioxide, oxygen given without attention to the target can worsen the retention, so the target and the monitoring must be set by the current guideline and the local protocol.

The assessment begins with a rapid ordered look that takes only a few moments. The clinician asks a simple question and listens to whether the answer comes in a full sentence, a few words, or not at all, because that observation measures the reserve better than any instrument. He watches the position, the work of breathing, the color of the lips and tongue, the movement of the chest, and the level of awareness, and he listens for stridor, wheeze, or a muffled voice. If the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally, the response is cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, with a call for help, and no further diagnosis is attempted at that moment. If the patient is breathing but the effort is exhausting or the airway is narrowing, the response is to keep him upright, stay with him, and summon the people and equipment that can secure the airway. This first look decides whether the rest of the assessment happens here or somewhere else.

The oximeter changed the bedside assessment of oxygenation, and its limits matter as much as its reading. It measures the proportion of hemoglobin carrying oxygen in the small vessels under the probe, and it says nothing about ventilation, so a patient with an acceptable reading may still be retaining carbon dioxide. The reading is unreliable when the circulation to the finger is poor, when the patient is cold or moving, when the probe is badly placed, and when the skin is deeply pigmented, in which case the device may read higher than the truth. It is also misled by carbon monoxide, which binds to hemoglobin and makes the reading look falsely reassuring. A saturation of 90 per cent is widely quoted as a level below which concern is justified, but that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the boundary depends on the patient's usual state, on altitude, and on the condition being treated. The trend over time and the clinical picture are what the reading is used for, never the single figure alone.

An arterial blood gas separates the two failures directly, because it measures oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acidity at the same moment. A low partial pressure of oxygen with a normal or low partial pressure of carbon dioxide belongs to a failure of oxygenation, while a high carbon dioxide with a low oxygen and an acid blood belongs to a failure of ventilation. A partial pressure of oxygen of 60 millimeters of mercury and a partial pressure of carbon dioxide of 50 millimeters of mercury are figures often quoted as points of concern, but both are illustrations of the reasoning and each must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the acceptable values vary with age, altitude, and the laboratory that reports them. The acidity and the bicarbonate tell the clinician how long the problem has been present, because a kidney with time to compensate will show a higher bicarbonate. A blood gas is a picture of one moment, and it is read beside the work of breathing and the mental state rather than in place of them.

Imaging answers questions that the hands and ears cannot, and each image is chosen to answer a particular question. A chest radiograph shows air around the lung, pneumonia, collapse, fluid in the pleural space, and the size of the heart, and it is the first image in most hospitals. A bedside ultrasound can show fluid around the lung, a failing heart, a clot in the leg, and the movement of the diaphragm while the patient is still being examined. Computed tomography, or CT, gives the most complete picture of lung tissue and vessels, while magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answers particular questions the other methods cannot. Other tests add detail: a peak expiratory flow below half of the predicted value is often treated as a sign of severe asthma, though that boundary is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because predicted values depend on age, sex, height, and the reference population used. None of these tests may delay the treatment of a tension pneumothorax or the support of a patient who is tiring.

In a clinic that has a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same assessment is performed with different instruments and the same reasoning. The watch takes the place of the oximeter, because the breathing rate counted over a full interval is one of the most reliable signs of a failing respiratory system, and it is repeated to show its direction. The eyes take the place of the blood gas, because the work of breathing, the ability to speak, the position, the color, and the mental state together tell the clinician whether ventilation is adequate. The decision there is not a diagnosis but a direction: a patient with stridor at rest, drooling, a muffled voice, or a refusal to lie flat must not be watched, because the airway may close before help can be arranged. A patient who is exhausted, drowsy, unable to speak, or whose breathing rate is falling after a period of rapid breathing must be moved at once, and a patient with absent breath sounds on one side or a falling pressure may have a tension pneumothorax or a massive clot, so the journey is part of the treatment. A patient who is comfortable, speaking in full sentences, and symmetrical on examination may be watched, provided the plan for review is explicit and the patient can return.

Simple maneuvers can be diagnostic as well as helpful, and the clinician should notice what changes them. Lifting the chin and jaw forward opens the airway when the tongue is the obstruction, and improvement with that movement points to position rather than to swelling in the tissues. The treatment decision in this chapter is not about which medicine to give but about which failure is present and how soon it must be answered. Treatment is the right answer when the airway is narrowing with drooling, stridor, a changed voice, or an inability to lie flat, and also when the patient is tiring or the carbon dioxide is rising with an acid blood. It is the wrong first answer when the patient is alert, speaking comfortably, and moving air well, and when an intervention on the airway would add risk without changing the course.

Children and older adults sit at opposite ends of the same problem, and both need their own warning. A young child increases the breathing rate and effort long before the oxygen falls, so an acceptable reading can coexist with a serious problem, and the fall, when it comes, is sudden. Croup produces a barking cough, a hoarse voice, and an inspiratory stridor worse at night, while epiglottitis produces drooling, a muffled voice, and a child who will not lie down, and a foreign body produces a sudden onset and a one-sided wheeze in a child who was well a moment before. Stridor at rest is a different finding from stridor that appears only with crying, and sedating a struggling child can remove the drive to breathe. In the older adult the signs are quieter: fever may be absent or low, the breathing rate may rise only a little, and the first change may be confusion, a fall, or a refusal to eat. A patient with long-standing lung disease may live with a low oxygen and a high carbon dioxide at baseline, so the useful comparison is with his own previous values and usual activity rather than with a rule from a different population.

A constructed illustration may fix these habits, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of a real person. Imagine a young child who was well in the morning, who now sits forward with a muffled voice, drools into a bowl, and refuses to lie back, with a fever that the thermometer confirms. The clinician who recognizes the posture, keeps the child upright, and calls for help is doing the diagnostic work, while the clinician who reaches for a spatula is taking a risk the story has already warned against. Now imagine an adult a few hours after an operation on the neck, whose dressing is tight, whose voice has become hoarse, and whose neck is swelling and tender, observed closely because the finding is a change rather than a dramatic sign. Neither patient is real, and neither should be used as a pattern for a real person without a full assessment. The record and the conversation are part of the diagnosis: the clinician writes what was found, what was decided, and what should bring the patient back, such as a muffled voice, difficulty swallowing saliva, breathlessness at rest, or a new drowsiness.

To summarize, breathing fails either at the exchange of oxygen or at the movement of air, and the bedside separates the two by the work of breathing, the mental state, the movement of the chest wall, and the place where the problem lies. The narrowing airway is recognized before it closes, through stridor, a changed voice, drooling, a muffled cough, and the refusal to lie flat, and the lethal causes are named at once, among them epiglottitis, a foreign body, anaphylaxis, a hematoma in the neck, an expanding abscess beside the tonsil, a tension pneumothorax, a large clot in the lungs, and the exhausted patient whose effort is fading. The same reasoning is performed in a hospital where an oximeter, a blood gas, and a ventilator are within reach and in a clinic that has a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, where the question is whether help must be called now. Every figure in this chapter, whether a temperature, a rate, a pressure, a partial pressure, a saturation, or a score, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such values differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who is tiring, drooling, or unable to lie flat is a patient to help now, and the diagnosis is completed afterwards.

# Chapter 41 — Acute Neurological Emergencies

Acute neurological emergencies are the presentations in which a mistake is measured in minutes rather than in days, and they are organized here by the decision each one forces rather than by the anatomy each one damages. A stroke forces a decision about time, because brain tissue that is not perfused is lost and the chance to restore flow closes as the clock runs. Meningitis forces a decision about treatment before proof, because the organism is not yet known and the patient may worsen while the laboratory works. A seizure that will not stop forces a decision about the failure of the mechanism that normally terminates it. Raised pressure inside the skull forces a decision about the threat of herniation, in which the brain is pushed through the openings that confine it and the patient dies of compression rather than of the original disease. Each of these forces a different set of findings, yet all are assessed by the same short examination performed in the same order. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it cannot replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your service.

Danger is named before the ordinary reasoning begins, because each of these killers announces itself through a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. A sudden severe headache that reached its worst in an instant may mean bleeding around the brain, and the finding that supports it is a neck that resists flexion with a dislike of light in a patient whose consciousness is otherwise preserved. Fever, headache, and a rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed on it may mean infection of the membranes around the brain and of the bloodstream at once, and that rash is the finding that ends the debate about whether to act. A seizure that continues without recovery between attacks means the brain's own stopping mechanism has failed. A consciousness that is falling, pupils that have become unequal, and breathing that has become irregular mean raised pressure inside the skull that is threatening herniation, and the pupil that dilates and no longer reacts is the finding that turns a headache into an emergency.

The first minute is spent on the things that kill before the diagnosis is made, in the same order in every setting. The airway is looked at and listened to, because a patient who cannot protect it or who breathes noisily needs help before any imaging is discussed. Breathing is assessed by counting the respiratory rate and watching the chest, and the oxygen saturation is measured where an oximeter exists. The circulation is assessed by the pulse, the pressure, and the color and warmth of the skin, since a brain that is not perfused cannot be assessed properly whatever its disease. The blood glucose is measured at once, because a low blood sugar imitates every emergency in this chapter and is reversed far more easily than any of them. The temperature is recorded, because fever points toward infection and a very high temperature can itself drive a seizure.

The level of consciousness is the most useful observation in a neurological emergency, because it is the first thing to change and the easiest to record. The Glasgow coma scale is the way this book records it, and the reasoning it formalizes is simple: how the eyes open, what the voice produces, and what the limbs do in response to a command or to pain. Its value is not the exact figure but the fact that the same observer, or a different one, can compare one hour with the next and see a direction, and it is the direction rather than the single reading that should change the plan. The contents of the scale, the way the parts are added, and the figure at which a service becomes alarmed must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the version in use differs between hospitals and editions. A patient who is drowsy but rousable is a different problem from one who responds only to pain, and a patient who has become less responsive since the last observation is deteriorating whatever the figure says. Where the scale is not used, the clinician should still describe the behavior in words, because a clear sentence about what the patient did is worth more than a figure no one can interpret.

Lateralizing signs are the findings that suggest a lesion on one side of the brain, and they are sought deliberately rather than noticed by accident. The face is examined for a droop of the mouth and a failure to close one eye, and the patient is asked to show the teeth and to squeeze the examiner's fingers with each hand. The arms are compared by asking the patient to hold both out with the eyes closed, because an arm that drifts downward and inward reveals a weakness the patient may not report. The legs are compared in the same way, and where the patient cannot cooperate the response to pain on each side is observed. Speech is tested by asking the patient to name ordinary objects and to repeat a sentence, since difficulty in finding or producing words points to the language areas of the dominant side. The visual fields are checked by asking the patient to look at the examiner's nose and to say when a moving finger appears in each part of the view, because a field missing on one side is easily missed.

The neck and the back of the eye are examined next, because they answer two different dangers at once. The examiner asks the patient to touch the chin to the chest and watches for resistance, then lifts the head gently to see whether the hips and knees flex, another sign of irritation of the membranes. Resistance in a patient with fever and headache supports infection of the membranes, while resistance in a patient with a sudden severe headache supports bleeding around the brain. The fundus is examined with an ophthalmoscope where one exists, and the finding sought is a swollen optic disc with blurred margins, which suggests that pressure inside the skull has been raised for some time. The pupils are compared for size and reaction to light, and eye movements are tested in all directions to look for a palsy of the nerves that serve them. The corneal reflex, the gag reflex, and the strength of the cough are noted in the patient who is not fully conscious, because they describe how the brainstem is working and whether the airway is at risk. Papilledema takes time to develop, so its absence in a patient who became ill very recently does not exclude raised pressure, and a normal fundus must never be used to dismiss it.

The pattern of the seizure carries as much information as the event itself, and the account must come from someone who watched it, not only from the patient. The clinician asks where the movement began, whether it stayed on one side, whether the eyes turned, whether the patient was aware, and how long the event lasted. A seizure that begins in one hand and spreads up the arm, or that begins with a smell, a flash of light, or an unpleasant feeling in the stomach, is focal in onset and points to a lesion in a particular region. A seizure that involves both sides from the first moment is more often generalized, though a focal onset can be missed when no one saw the beginning. The state afterwards matters, because weakness of one arm or one side that clears over the following hours, known as a Todd paresis, is strong evidence that the event was a seizure rather than a stroke. A return to full consciousness between events is reassuring, while a patient who does not wake between seizures has entered the dangerous state in which the brain cannot stop. A first seizure in an adult, a seizure with fever, and a seizure after a head injury each raise different possibilities and each needs its own assessment.

Stroke is the emergency in which time is the substance of the decision, because brain tissue deprived of blood is lost at a rate that can be measured, and the chance to restore flow closes with every minute. The clinician must establish when the patient was last known to be well, which is not the same as when the symptoms were noticed, and must write that time down where everyone can see it. The decision that follows is whether the patient is a candidate for treatment that dissolves a clot, and that decision belongs to a team with imaging and a protocol rather than to a single pair of hands. The interval within which such treatment can be considered is often quoted as a number of hours from the onset, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it has been revised repeatedly and differs between services and countries. Treatment is the right answer when the patient arrives inside the accepted interval, when the symptoms are disabling, and when imaging has excluded bleeding. Treatment is the wrong answer when the scan shows hemorrhage, when the patient is already improving steadily, or when the time of onset cannot be established and the risk cannot be judged. The clinician who cannot obtain imaging must still decide whether to move the patient, and that decision rests on the same time of onset.

No examination can separate a clot from a bleed with certainty, and the clinician who pretends otherwise will eventually harm a patient. The findings that raise the probability of bleeding are a sudden onset with a headache that peaked at once, vomiting, a falling level of consciousness, and a pressure that climbs while the pulse slows. The findings that raise the probability of a clot are a stepwise or gradual onset, a clear time of onset, and a deficit that matches the territory of one artery without early loss of consciousness. The most important step, however, is to look for the conditions that imitate a stroke and are treated differently, because several are common and reversible. A low blood sugar is the first, and its threshold is defined by the laboratory that measures it, so that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the level at which symptoms appear varies with the patient. A seizure that has left a weakness behind, an infection of the brain, a migraine with a prolonged deficit, and a metabolic disturbance can each present exactly as a stroke. The clinician who treats the first computed tomography, or CT, as the end of the assessment rather than the beginning of it will miss the mimic that was never vascular.

Meningitis is the emergency in which treatment begins before the diagnosis is confirmed, because the organism is not yet known and the delay spent waiting for proof can cost the patient his life. The classical findings are fever, a severe headache, a dislike of light, vomiting, and a neck that resists flexion, and later the level of consciousness falls. A temperature above 38 degrees Celsius is often taught as the line at which fever is present, but that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold shifts with the site of measurement, the age of the patient, and the edition of the reference. A rash that does not fade when pressed is the finding that should end all hesitation, because it points to infection in the bloodstream as well as in the membranes, and that combination can progress within hours. The clinician must also weigh the age and the immune state of the patient, since an older person, a person taking treatment that suppresses the immune response, and a person living with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, may show few of these signs and may present only with confusion. The decision to treat before confirmation is right when the picture is convincing, when the patient is deteriorating, or when a lumbar puncture cannot be performed safely at once. The decision is wrong when a clear alternative explains the picture completely and the patient is stable enough for the diagnosis to be completed first.

A seizure that does not stop is a failure of the mechanism that normally ends it, and that failure is the emergency rather than the seizure itself. The definition rests on a duration, and the duration usually quoted is about 5 minutes of continuous seizure activity or of repeated seizures without recovery, a figure offered here as an illustration of the reasoning and to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services draw the line at different points. The finding that reveals the danger is a patient who is not waking between events, whose movements may become subtle or hidden while the brain continues to discharge. A patient who has stopped moving but remains unconscious and unresponsive is not necessarily improving, and the clinician who assumes recovery at that moment may miss activity that is still going on. The cause must be sought at the same time as the seizure is brought under control, because a low blood sugar, a low sodium level, an infection of the brain, a medicine that was missed or withdrawn, and a new structural lesion each demand a different response. The pattern of the movements should be described in words, including which side moved first and whether the eyes turned, because those details decide what happens after the event. Treatment is the right answer when the seizure is continuing or recurring, and the wrong answer when the movement has a cause that is not epileptic, such as a faint or a shaking attack from which the patient can be distracted.

Raised pressure inside the skull is dangerous not because of the pressure itself but because of what it does to the brain, which is pushed through the rigid openings at the base of the skull in a process called herniation. The findings that suggest it are a headache worse on waking or on lying flat, vomiting without nausea, a level of consciousness that is falling, and a pressure that is high while the pulse is slow and the breathing irregular. The pupil that becomes fixed and dilated on one side is the classic sign of part of the temporal lobe being pushed downward, and it may appear before the consciousness changes. The clinician should look for a recent head injury, a fever that suggests a collection of pus, a history of cancer that suggests a secondary deposit, and the use of treatment that thins the blood, because each changes the speed of the deterioration. The patient should be positioned with the head of the bed raised where that is tolerated, the neck should not be obstructed, and the blood pressure should not be allowed to fall, since the brain depends on that pressure. A lumbar puncture in this patient can remove the pressure that is holding the herniation back, and it is the wrong decision when any of these findings is present until imaging and advice have been obtained.

Bleeding around the brain from a ruptured aneurysm announces itself through the history rather than through the examination. The patient describes a headache that reached its worst within an instant, often with vomiting, neck stiffness, and a dislike of light, and some patients report a smaller warning headache in the days before. The examination may be entirely normal, which is why the description of the onset carries the whole diagnosis, and a patient sent home with a diagnosis of migraine after such a description is a patient at risk. Clotting in the veins that drain the brain is a less familiar danger that produces headache, seizures, weakness on one side, and a level of consciousness that fluctuates, and it is more common in pregnancy, after childbirth, in dehydration, and in conditions that make the blood clot more easily. An infection confined to a collection of pus inside the skull, an inflammation of the brain itself, and a rise in blood pressure severe enough to damage the brain each imitate the emergencies already described. A tumor that bleeds, a disorder that makes the blood too thick, and a poison such as carbon monoxide can also present this way, and the history is the only place where they are found.

The most important group after the structural emergencies is the group of systemic causes that present as neurological emergencies and are corrected by treating the body rather than the brain. A low blood sugar, a low sodium level, a high calcium level, a failing kidney, a failing liver, an infection, and the withdrawal of alcohol or of sedative medicine can each produce confusion, seizures, or coma that looks exactly like a primary disease of the brain. The clinician must therefore measure what can be measured, and where nothing can be measured must ask what the patient has been drinking, eating, and taking, and what has changed in the days before the illness. An infection of the brain can follow an infection elsewhere, and in a patient living with HIV the list of causes is wider and the usual signs are less reliable. Tuberculosis of the membranes around the brain, a fungal infection, and a parasitic infection of the brain each occur in particular places and in particular patients, and the travel history and the immune history decide whether they belong on the list. These causes are named because they are treatable, and because a clinician who searches only for stroke and meningitis will send away the patient whose confusion was metabolic. The finding that changes the plan is a measurement that was not expected to be abnormal, so the tests that would reveal these causes belong early.

In a hospital the assessment is the same, but the questions can be answered within minutes and the order in which they are answered changes. Computed tomography, or CT, of the head is performed first in most patients with a suspected stroke, because it separates bleeding from a clot, and that separation decides whether clot-dissolving treatment is possible. Computed tomography of the blood vessels, magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, and a study of the vessels in the neck answer further questions when the first image is not enough, and the clinician should know which question each test is meant to settle before it is ordered. An electrocardiogram, or ECG, is recorded in every patient with a new neurological deficit, because a clot formed in the heart is a common cause of stroke and the rhythm of the heart may be the source. Blood is sent for sugar, sodium, calcium, and the tests of kidney, liver, and clotting function, since each changes the ranking of the differential. A lumbar puncture is performed when infection or bleeding around the brain is suspected and the safety questions have been answered, and the fluid is examined for cells, protein, sugar, and organisms.

In a clinic that has a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the task is not the same diagnosis but the same reasoning pushed to a single decision. That decision is whether the patient can be watched where he is or must begin a journey, and the journey itself may take hours and may worsen the patient on the way. Some diagnoses can be made without any image at all: a fever with a rash that does not fade, a seizure that will not stop, a pupil that has changed, and a limb that has become weak are each recognizable at the bedside, and each demands action rather than investigation. The torch makes the pupils visible and the thermometer turns fever into a number. The clinician should record the time of onset, the level of consciousness, the weakness, the neck, and the pupils, and should repeat the observation at short intervals, because a patient who is worse on the second look must travel. A patient with a seizure that has stopped, who has woken fully, and whose examination is normal can sometimes be watched, provided that someone can observe him and a plan for review exists. A patient with fever and a rash that does not fade, with a falling level of consciousness, with a new weakness, or with a pupil that has changed must be moved, and the decision should be made early rather than after a second examination confirms what the first suggested. A normal examination in a patient who worries the clinician is a reason to look again and to discuss, never a reason to relax, and the honesty of that uncertainty is part of the reasoning.

Treatment enters this chapter only as a decision, because the doses and the regimens belong to the protocol of the service and not to a book about diagnosis. Treatment is the right answer when a treatable cause is strongly suspected and the patient is deteriorating, when the findings point to infection of the membranes and waiting for confirmation would cost more than acting, or when a seizure has not stopped and the brain is being damaged with every minute. Treatment is the wrong answer when the scan has shown bleeding and the treatment designed for a clot would make it worse, when a metabolic cause such as a low blood sugar explains the whole picture and is corrected directly, or when an attack that is not epileptic is mistaken for a seizure and the patient is quietened for it. The finding that usually decides is not the dramatic one but the one that appeared on the second examination, the pupil that changed, the arm that drifted further, the fever that climbed, or the glucose that was never measured. The clinician should ask what finding would make the treatment right and what finding would make it wrong, and should write both down before the treatment is given, because that habit protects the patient from the momentum of the clinician. Naming the decision rather than the medicine is what transfers between settings.

A constructed illustration may fix these habits, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a description of any real person. Imagine a man of about 60 who was last seen well at breakfast, who now cannot lift his right arm and cannot find words for ordinary objects, and whose blood sugar is normal when it is measured at once. The time of onset is written down, the weakness is recorded, and the scan shows no bleeding, so the decision about clot-dissolving treatment can be made by the team that owns that protocol. Now imagine a young woman brought to a clinic with fever, a severe headache, and a rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed on it, whose neck resists flexion and who is becoming drowsy. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment. What the two share is the move that matters: the clinician looked for the finding that would change the decision rather than waiting for the diagnosis to become obvious.

The record of a neurological emergency should show the reasoning and not only the findings, because the next reader must see what was considered and what was set aside. The time of onset belongs at the top, together with the level of consciousness at each observation, the weakness on each side, the pupils, the neck, the temperature, and the blood sugar. The patient or the family should be told which signs must bring him back or must bring him to a hospital, and that advice must be specific enough to be followed, including a new weakness, a headache that reached its worst in an instant, a seizure that will not stop, a fever with a rash that does not fade, and a fall in the level of consciousness. A follow-up visit arranged in advance is worth more than a promise to return if things worsen, because many patients cannot judge that for themselves. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. No patient in this chapter is real, and any resemblance to a person you have met is a coincidence of the disease rather than a portrait.
