To summarize, the acute neurological emergencies are grouped by the decision each one forces, so that stroke is read against the clock, meningitis is treated before it is confirmed, a seizure that will not stop is recognized as a failure of the usual termination, and raised pressure inside the skull is feared for the herniation it threatens. The examination is short and always the same, moving from the level of consciousness to the lateralizing signs, the neck, the fundi, the pupils, and the pattern of the event, and the findings that separate bleeding from a clot from an infection from a metabolic cause are found in the history and in a few measurements rather than in a single image. Every score, interval, pressure, temperature, and rate named in this chapter is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. The hospital answers the same questions with imaging, laboratory tests, and a team, while the clinic answers them with a torch, a thermometer, and the decision about whether the patient can be moved at all. The dangers are named at the bedside and not deferred: a headache that reached its worst in an instant, a rash that does not fade when pressed, a pupil that has changed, and a patient who does not wake between seizures. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who is deteriorating is helped and moved first, and the exact cause is settled afterwards.

# Chapter 42 — Acute Abdomen, Trauma and Hemorrhage

The abdomen that has been injured and the abdomen that has not share a single emergency, and the first question in both is the same: is this patient bleeding inside, and if so, where. A spleen that has ruptured, a liver that has torn, a hemorrhage behind the peritoneum, a bowel that has perforated, a pelvis that has broken, a pregnancy that has burst outside the uterus, and an aneurysm that is leaking all announce themselves through that question before they announce themselves through any name. The reasoning of this chapter is therefore organized by the search for hidden blood and for peritoneal irritation rather than by a catalog of diagnoses, because the patient who is bleeding is treated before the cause of the bleeding is settled. The history and the examination are the instruments, and in this subject they are more powerful than any single test, because a reassuring result obtained early can be falsely reassuring while the patient is still losing volume. This chapter is educational material; it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. Nothing in it should be applied to a real person without a full assessment by the clinician who is actually with that person.

A short list of lethal possibilities deserves to be named at once, each with the finding that would betray it. A ruptured spleen produces pain and tenderness in the left upper abdomen, and often a pain felt at the tip of the left shoulder when blood irritates the diaphragm beneath it. A laceration of the liver tells the same story on the right side, with right upper abdominal tenderness and pain referred to the tip of the right shoulder. A hemorrhage into the space behind the peritoneum may produce almost no abdominal signs at all, and the clue is a patient who looks far worse than the soft abdomen suggests, sometimes with a faint discoloration of the flank. A perforated bowel produces a sudden severe pain and a board-like rigidity of the abdominal wall, with bowel sounds that have fallen quiet. A fractured pelvis can bleed heavily into that same hidden space, and the findings are instability when the pelvis is gently compressed, blood at the urinary opening, and swelling or bruising in the perineum. A pregnancy that has ruptured outside the uterus produces lower abdominal pain, a missed or unusual period, and the signs of internal bleeding in a woman of childbearing age. A leaking aneurysm of the abdominal aorta produces pain that reaches the back together with a pulsatile, expansile mass in the upper abdomen.

The mechanism of injury sets the probability before the patient is touched, and it is worth as much as any single sign. A collision at speed, a fall from a height, a pedestrian struck by a vehicle, a rollover, and an ejection from the vehicle all raise the likelihood of injury to solid organs and to the great vessels. The damage to the vehicle is part of the mechanism, because a deformed steering wheel or a cracked dashboard tells the clinician where the body met the machine. Whether a restraint was used changes what is likely, and a bruise running across the abdomen from a seat belt is a finding that should be looked for and recorded rather than dismissed as an incidental mark. The mechanism also has limits, because an older patient whose blood is thinned by medicine, or a patient whose spleen is enlarged by infection, can hemorrhage after an injury that would leave a healthy young person almost untouched. The mechanism raises or lowers suspicion, and it never makes or excludes a diagnosis on its own. A clinician who records the mechanism carefully, and then examines the patient rather than the story, has used it correctly.

The assessment of the injured patient follows a fixed order that exists to find the threats to life in the sequence in which they kill. The clinician first checks whether the airway is open and protected, then whether breathing is adequate on both sides of the chest, then whether the circulation is failing, then the level of consciousness, and finally exposes the whole body to look for the injuries that clothing conceals. The abdomen is examined during the circulatory step and then again at the end, because it is one of the places where bleeding hides without any external wound. The same sequence is used at the roadside, in a district clinic, and in a hospital, and only the tools that accompany each step change. A finding at any step is addressed before the next step is completed, because a patient who cannot breathe will not benefit from a perfect abdominal examination. The person who follows the order under pressure is the one who finds the quiet injuries.

Internal bleeding announces itself through the circulation before it announces itself through the abdomen, and the earliest signs are easy to miss. The pulse rises, the skin becomes cool and clammy, the extremities grow pale or mottled, and the passage of urine shrinks before the pressure does. A young and fit patient can hold the pressure at a deceptively normal level while losing a large volume, and then collapse suddenly when that compensation is exhausted, so a single normal pressure is never reassurance. A pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the point at which shock must be assumed, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the value that matters depends on the patient's usual pressure and on age and pregnancy. A pulse of 110 beats per minute deserves the same caution, and the accepted rate at which a patient is said to be tachycardic varies with age, fitness, and the reference in use, so verify it against the guideline and the protocol that govern your own service. The clinician should compare the patient with the patient an hour earlier rather than with a number written on a chart. A patient who is quietly deteriorating is the patient who is bleeding.

The abdomen that has not been injured presents the same emergency under a different story, and the first question is unchanged. Peritonitis, which is inflammation of the lining of the abdominal cavity, produces pain on the slightest movement, a tightening of the abdominal wall that the patient cannot relax on request, and pain when the examining hand is lifted away. Internal bleeding without trauma is less obvious, and its causes are few enough to be held in mind as a short list: a pregnancy outside the uterus, an aneurysm that is leaking, an ovary that has bled, a spleen enlarged by infection and then ruptured, and a tumor that has eroded a vessel. Each of these can produce a patient who looks pale and anxious, whose pulse has climbed, and whose abdomen is only vaguely tender at the first examination. The clinician who asks about the last period, about previous aneurysms, and about any recent illness has already begun the diagnosis before touching the abdomen. A soft abdomen in a patient who looks unwell is a reason to examine again rather than a reason to relax.

A pregnancy that has implanted outside the uterus is the diagnosis most often missed in a woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain, and it can kill within hours of rupture. The classical story is a missed or unusual period, pain in the lower abdomen that may begin on one side, a small amount of vaginal bleeding, and a fainting episode or a sense of dizziness on standing. The pain at the tip of the shoulder appears when blood has reached the diaphragm, and it is a sign that the bleeding has become significant rather than trivial. On examination the lower abdomen is tender, and moving the cervix produces pain that the patient feels deep inside, so the pelvic examination is performed with consent and a chaperone. The test that settles the question is a pregnancy test, and in any woman of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain it should be performed before any other explanation is accepted. A woman whose pressure is falling, or who has fainted, must travel immediately to a place where surgery is possible. The decision to operate is made on the clinical picture rather than on an imaging result that would take longer than the patient has.

A leaking aneurysm of the abdominal aorta is the second hidden hemorrhage that must be recognized at the bedside. It occurs most often in older people, particularly in men who have smoked, and the pain is typically felt in the abdomen, the back, or the flank, and may be described as boring or tearing. The finding that reveals it is a mass in the upper abdomen that expands with each pulse, and the examiner should feel for it gently and deliberately in any older patient with new abdominal or back pain. The patient may also have a falling pressure, a rapid pulse, and a fainting episode, and the combination of back pain, a pulsatile mass, and circulatory collapse is the picture that demands an immediate call for surgical help. The clinician should not delay that call in order to obtain a scan in a patient who is unstable, because the examination has already answered the question that matters most. Where the patient is stable, imaging may be used to define the extent of the disease, but it is arranged alongside the surgical decision and never in place of it.

A perforated bowel is the third emergency that presents without any external injury, and its signature is the sudden onset of severe pain together with a rigid abdominal wall. The patient often describes a moment when something gave way, and thereafter the pain is constant and made worse by the slightest movement, by coughing, or by the vibration of a footstep. The abdomen is board-like and quiet, and the normal dullness over the liver may be lost when free gas has escaped beneath the diaphragm. A chest radiograph taken with the patient upright may show that gas, but the film can be normal early in the illness, so a normal image does not exclude the diagnosis. The clinician must also keep in mind the conditions that imitate it, among them inflammation of the pancreas, which produces severe pain but a less rigid abdomen, and a stone in the kidney, which produces waves of pain without peritoneal irritation. The decision in perforation is surgical and it is urgent, because the longer the contamination continues the more dangerous the operation becomes.

A fractured pelvis is both an injury and a source of hidden hemorrhage, and the two facts must be held together. The pelvis is a ring, and a break in one part is usually accompanied by a break or a ligament injury in another, so instability is the finding that matters more than any single crack. The clinician compresses the pelvis gently and once, watching the patient's face, because repeated or forceful compression can dislodge a clot and restart the bleeding. Other findings that point to a pelvic injury are blood at the urinary opening, an inability to pass urine, bruising in the perineum or the scrotum, and a difference in the height of the legs. A rectal or vaginal examination may reveal a bone fragment, and it is performed when the mechanism or the findings suggest that the rectum or the vagina has been injured. Bleeding from a fractured pelvis collects behind the peritoneum, where it cannot be seen or felt by the hand, so the abdomen may remain soft while the patient loses a large volume. The finding that would make the diagnosis wrong is a second source of bleeding that fully explains the picture, and the search for that source continues even when the pelvis is clearly broken.

The abdominal examination in the injured patient is performed in the same fixed order as in any other patient, but the gentleness matters more because the abdominal wall is often guarding in defense. Inspection looks for distension, for bruising, for a seat belt mark, and for any wound, and the clinician should look at the back, the flanks, and the perineum as well as the front. Auscultation is performed before palpation, and the finding of quiet or absent bowel sounds supports the suspicion of peritoneal irritation, although normal sounds do not exclude it. Percussion is used gently to detect tenderness and to look for the loss of liver dullness that suggests free gas. Palpation begins away from the region that hurts and ends at the place the patient identifies as the worst, so that the patient does not tense the whole abdomen before the examination has begun. Involuntary guarding is a tightening that the patient cannot control, and rigidity is that guarding taken to a board-like extreme, so both are signs of peritoneal irritation rather than of a particular organ.

When consciousness is impaired, the patient's account of pain cannot be used, and the clinician must rely on physical findings that do not depend on speech. Distension that appears or increases, tenderness produced by the gentlest palpation, guarding that persists as the hand is lifted, and rigidity all remain interpretable. A change in the pattern of breathing, a falling pressure, a rising pulse, cool and clammy skin, and a shrinking passage of urine are signs that the body offers without words. The level of consciousness is itself a measured observation, and the Glasgow coma scale is the common way of recording it; a score of 8 or less is widely used as a point of concern, but that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the scale, its contents, and the figure that should prompt action are stated differently in different services and editions. A patient who cannot report pain must be examined more often rather than less, because the absence of a complaint is not the absence of injury. The clinician should record the findings and the time of each examination, so that a change becomes visible even when the patient cannot describe it.

In a hospital the examination is used to direct the tools, and each tool answers a question that the clinician has already formed. A bedside ultrasound examination that looks for free fluid in the abdomen and around the heart can be performed while the patient is still being examined, and it changes the pace of everything that follows when fluid is found. Computed tomography, or CT, defines injury to the spleen, the liver, the kidneys, and the pancreas, and it shows bleeding behind the peritoneum that the hand cannot reach, but it is used only when the patient is stable enough to tolerate the journey and the time. A chest radiograph is taken to look for free gas under the diaphragm, for fractured ribs, and for an injury to the diaphragm itself, and a radiograph of the pelvis is taken when the mechanism suggests a break. A pregnancy test is performed in every woman of childbearing age, because the answer changes the entire plan. The clinician who says what each test is expected to show before it is ordered will recognize a surprise for what it is, and will know when a normal result contradicts the examination rather than confirming it.

Where there is no scanner and no operating room, the same reasoning is compressed into three decisions: whether the patient can be kept safely here, how the patient should be moved, and how the bleeding that can be seen should be controlled. The clinic's equipment of a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer is enough to count the pulse and the breathing, to look at the skin and the eyes, and to measure a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or more if fever is present, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the meaning of a temperature differs with the site of measurement and the edition of the reference being used. The torch makes the mouth, the ears, the skin, the perineum, and the urinary opening visible, and those are the places where a hidden injury is found. A watch allows the pulse and the breathing to be counted rather than estimated, and the count repeated after an interval such as 1 hour, which is offered as an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the safe interval between observations differs with the patient and the setting. A patient who is pale, restless, and becoming drowsy after an injury must begin the journey at once, even when the abdomen still feels soft and the story sounds reassuring.

Control of external bleeding is the one intervention that the clinic can perform well, and it is done with the hands before anything else. Direct pressure on the wound, applied firmly and held long enough for the clot to form, stops most bleeding, and the pressure is maintained rather than lifted repeatedly to look underneath. A wound that continues to bleed despite pressure can be packed firmly with clean material, and the packing is left in place while the patient is moved rather than removed for inspection. A limb wound that cannot be controlled by these measures may require a constriction band placed above the wound, and when one is used the time of its application is recorded and the limb is not left unwatched, because the tissue beyond the band is at risk. The pelvis, which can bleed into the hidden space behind the peritoneum, is steadied with a binder or with a sheet tied firmly around it, and the legs are kept together rather than splayed. Bleeding into the abdomen itself cannot be controlled from outside, and the only treatment for it is surgery, which is why the patient must travel rather than wait.

The way a patient is positioned and handled during transfer is part of the treatment and part of the diagnosis. The injured patient is laid flat and kept warm, because cold worsens bleeding and interferes with the body's ability to compensate for it. Nothing is given by mouth, because the patient may need an operation and because vomiting can block the airway in a person who is drowsy. A fractured limb is splinted before the journey, and the splint is checked so that it does not press on the skin or restrict the circulation. A patient with a suspected pelvic injury is moved as a single unit, with the pelvis supported from below, and a patient with an abdominal injury is moved gently, because jolting can restart bleeding and worsen pain. The receiving hospital should be told what is known before the patient arrives, including the mechanism, the findings, the trend of the pulse and the pressure, and what has already been done.

Not every injury is accidental, and the pattern of injury sometimes contains the diagnosis that the mechanism does not explain. An injury that does not fit the story, a delay in seeking help that is difficult to account for, and bruises or fractures of clearly different ages should raise the possibility of an assault or of abuse, whether the patient is a child, an older person, or a dependent adult. The clinician's duty in that situation is to protect the patient, to examine and document carefully, and to involve the person or the service responsible for safeguarding, rather than to confront the family in a way that may place the patient at further risk. The same care applies to a patient whose injuries suggest self-harm, because the physical emergency and the mental emergency are treated together. Documentation matters especially here, because a precise record of what was seen, in the patient's own words where possible, may later protect the patient as much as any treatment. These are uncomfortable thoughts, and they belong in the first assessment rather than after the third visit.

Certain patients deserve a lower threshold for concern because their bodies hide bleeding or compensate badly. A child has a smaller volume of blood and can maintain a normal pressure until the loss is severe, then deteriorate very quickly, so a pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury has a different meaning in a child, and the figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol and against the reference range for that child's age. An older patient may be taking a medicine that thins the blood or a medicine that blunts the heart's response, so a serious injury can produce few signs and a soft abdomen. A patient who is pregnant has organs displaced and an abdominal wall stretched, so pain and tenderness are shifted and muted, and the safety of both the woman and the unborn child must be weighed in every decision. A patient whose spleen is enlarged by a blood disorder or by an infection such as infectious mononucleosis can rupture it with very little force. In all of these people the decision rests on the repeated examination and on the trend rather than on any single set of findings.

The single most useful diagnostic instrument in this chapter is the repetition of the examination, performed by the same clinician and recorded in a form that allows comparison. An abdomen that is soft and only vaguely tender at the first look may become rigid and silent an hour later, and that change is the diagnosis arriving. The findings worth recording at each review are the level of consciousness, the pulse, the breathing, the pressure, the color and warmth of the skin, the passage of urine, and the abdominal signs themselves. Where the patient is observed rather than operated upon, the plan should state the interval between observations and what would end the period of watching, so that a deterioration is not met with a decision to wait again. The clinician should also record what was considered and what was set aside, because the next reader must be able to see the reasoning and not only the conclusion. Observation is not the absence of a decision; it is a decision with conditions attached, and those conditions must be written down where the next clinician can find them.

A constructed illustration may make the reasoning concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a man of middle age who was the driver in a collision and who now complains of pain in the left upper abdomen and at the tip of the left shoulder, whose pulse has risen and whose skin is cool, and in whom the abdomen is only mildly tender; the shoulder tip pain sends the clinician back to the spleen, and the journey to the operating room begins. Now imagine a young woman with lower abdominal pain, a period that is late, and a fainting episode, in whom a pregnancy test is performed before any other explanation is considered, and whose lower abdomen is tender with pain on moving the cervix. None of these people is real, and none should be read as a portrait. Each is constructed only to show how one examination finding can reorder the whole differential and change the plan within a minute.

A patient who is sent home after an injury must be given a plan that is specific enough to follow, and the clinician must be able to justify the decision to send that patient at all. The patient and the family should be told which signs should bring them back, among them increasing pain, a swollen or hardening abdomen, vomiting, a fever, dizziness on standing, and any new confusion, and they should be told how quickly to return and where to go. The record should show the examination findings, the trend of the observations, the mechanism, the reasoning that led to the plan, and the advice that was given, because a note that contains only a conclusion cannot be reviewed by anyone else. Where the patient is a child or an older person, the person who will watch them at home should hear the same advice directly rather than receive it secondhand. Follow-up should be arranged rather than promised, because many patients cannot judge their own condition and may not seek help until the illness is advanced. This chapter is educational material, and it cannot take the place of training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

To summarize, the abdomen after injury and the abdomen without injury ask the same first question, which is whether the patient is bleeding inside and where that blood is collecting. The lethal causes are named at the bedside together with the finding that reveals each one: a ruptured spleen with pain at the tip of the left shoulder, a torn liver with right upper abdominal tenderness, a hemorrhage behind the peritoneum with a patient who looks worse than the abdomen suggests, a perforated bowel with a rigid and silent abdomen, a fractured pelvis with instability and blood at the urinary opening, a pregnancy ruptured outside the uterus with a late period and fainting, and a leaking aneurysm with a pulsatile expansile mass. When consciousness is impaired the clinician relies on distension, guarding, rigidity, the color of the skin, and the trend of the pulse and the pressure, and the examination is repeated because the change is the diagnosis. The same reasoning serves in a hospital with a scanner and an operating room and in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, where the decisions are whether to transport, how to position, and how to control the bleeding that can be seen. Every score, pressure, temperature, rate, volume, and interval named in this chapter is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This is educational material, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

# Chapter 43 — Metabolic Emergencies

The metabolic emergency is a disturbance of the body's chemistry severe enough to threaten the brain, the heart, or the breathing, and it is dangerous because it is both easily missed and often reversible. What organizes this chapter is one habit, which is that the bedside question of whether the chemistry has gone wrong is asked before the comfortable explanations are accepted, because drowsiness, weakness, and confusion can come from a stroke, an infection, or a number nobody measured. The reasoning runs from the history to a few bedside observations and only then to the laboratory, which confirms rather than replaces the clinical idea. This chapter is educational material only, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

Four dangers deserve naming before the ordinary reasoning begins, each with the finding that betrays it. Hypoglycemia comes first, because it is common, it mimics every neurological presentation, and it can leave lasting damage if it is not found quickly; the revealing finding is a glucose measured at the bedside rather than assumed. A potassium far outside its ordinary range comes second, because it can stop the heart without warning, and the finding is a change in the electrical tracing of the heart or a weakness no other cause explains. The hyperglycemic crises come third, announced by deep sighing breathing, profound thirst and urination, dehydration, and a breath smelling of ketones. Poisoning comes fourth, and it may be the only diagnosis in a patient who was well a few hours earlier; the revealing finding is often a companion who is also unwell, and carbon monoxide is betrayed by more than one person in the same room sharing the same headache and confusion.

The history that carries a metabolic diagnosis is short and specific, and it is asked even when the patient cannot answer. The clinician asks what was last eaten and drunk, whether there has been vomiting or diarrhea, how much urine has been passed, and whether there is unusual thirst. The questions turn to what the patient takes, including medicines for diabetes, water tablets, steroids, and anything bought without a prescription, and whether any of it was missed, doubled, or changed. The account of what was swallowed, when, how much, and with what is the center of every suspected poisoning, and it is asked without accusation or surprise.

The examination is brief and directed, and its purpose is to find the system that is compensating and the one that is failing. The clinician records consciousness, the rate and depth of breathing, the pulse, the pressure, the temperature, and the hydration of skin and mouth. The breath is smelled, the skin is examined for color, moisture, and coolness, the pupils are inspected with the torch, and the muscles are tested for tone and power. The single most useful instrument is a glucose meter, because it answers in a minute a question the rest of the examination can only suggest, and a clinic that has one holds a decisive advantage.

Hypoglycemia must be considered in every patient whose consciousness is altered, whatever the story suggests. The brain depends on a continuous supply of glucose and has almost no store, so a low glucose first changes behavior or awareness, and that change can look like drunkenness, a stroke, a seizure, or exhaustion. Sweating, trembling, hunger, and a racing heart may warn the patient, but those signs can be absent, especially after many years of diabetes when the warning responses fade. A patient can converse normally and become unresponsive shortly afterwards, so one lucid moment proves nothing about the glucose now. A glucose of about 3.5 millimoles per liter is often named as the boundary, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since meters, laboratories, and services draw the line differently.

Hypoglycemia is most likely in those who take medicines that lower the glucose, and the risk rises when the amount changes, a meal is missed, alcohol is taken, or an infection or kidney injury appears. Advanced kidney disease, a day of vomiting, fasting before a procedure, and the small stores of a newborn create vulnerability without any diabetes at all. In a clinic with a glucose meter and no laboratory, this is the first thing excluded in any patient who is drowsy, sweating, fitting, or behaving strangely, because it is the one cause that can be corrected on the spot. If the syndrome disappears when the glucose is restored, the clinician has found the explanation rather than guessed it.

Diabetic ketoacidosis develops when there is not enough insulin for the body to use glucose, so the cells behave as though starving while the blood is full of sugar. The body breaks down fat, and the acids produced accumulate faster than they can be removed, which makes the condition a metabolic acidosis with ketones in the blood and the urine. The history is usually a story of days rather than hours, with increasing thirst, large volumes of urine, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain that can suggest a surgical emergency. The patient may know the sugar is high, may have run out of treatment, or may have an infection such as pneumonia or a urinary infection that pushed control out of balance.

On examination the patient is usually dehydrated, with a dry mouth and reduced skin turgor, and the eyes may be sunken in a child or an older person. The breathing is deep and sighing rather than rapid and shallow, the body's attempt to blow off acid, so it is a sign of severity rather than comfort. A breathing rate of 30 breaths per minute in an adult is often used as a marker of that severity, yet the figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the rate that should alarm depends on age, setting, and the definition in use. The breath may smell sweet and fruity of ketones, though its absence proves nothing, and a fever should always be sought, because infection is the usual trigger even when no fever appears in a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed.

The most dangerous part of ketoacidosis is not the sugar but the potassium, because the total amount in the body falls even while the measured level may be high or normal. A potassium of 6 millimoles per liter in this setting is often treated as an emergency, but that figure is an illustration rather than a universal law and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services and editions set the point of alarm at different levels. The potassium has moved out of the cells as the acid rose, so a normal or raised reading hides a serious deficit that will declare itself as treatment moves it back. Abdominal pain in ketoacidosis is a great mimic, because it can be severe, provoke vomiting, and settle as the acidosis is corrected, yet it can also be a genuine surgical emergency; pain that worsens as the chemistry improves belongs to a surgeon rather than to the glucose meter.

Several conditions produce the same acidotic picture, and each has a distinguishing feature. Starvation ketosis follows a long period without food, particularly in a child or a pregnant woman, and usually produces milder acidosis with a low or normal sugar. Alcoholic ketoacidosis follows a stretch of heavy drinking with poor eating, suggested by vomiting, abdominal pain, and a sugar that is not markedly raised. Lactic acidosis arises when tissues receive too little oxygen, as in shock, sepsis, or a failing heart, so the pressure, the color of the skin, and the urine carry more information than the sugar. Kidney failure accumulates its own acid, suggested by a long kidney history, a reduced urine output, and a swollen rather than dehydrated patient.

Two poisonings belong in this list because they are easily mistaken for a metabolic disease. Methanol and ethylene glycol are alcohols that are not the ordinary drinking alcohol, and both produce a severe acidosis with a raised gap between the measured ions; methanol suggests itself through visual disturbance, and ethylene glycol through flank pain and later kidney injury. Salicylate poisoning can produce fast deep breathing with an acid base balance that moves in either direction, and the patient may sweat, vomit, and hear ringing in the ears. A raised gap also appears in kidney failure, lactic acidosis, and ketoacidosis, so it raises a question rather than answering one, and the interval after which it is safe to discharge such a patient must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol for that substance.

Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state is the other great hyperglycemic emergency and behaves differently in ways that matter at the bedside. It tends to appear in an older patient with type 2 diabetes, often with an infection or a stretch of poor drinking, and it develops more slowly, so the patient may be profoundly dehydrated and drowsy when help is sought. The sugar is usually higher than in ketoacidosis while ketones are absent or minimal, because there is enough insulin to prevent fat breakdown but not enough to control glucose. A glucose above 30 millimoles per liter is commonly quoted alongside this state, and that figure is only an illustration, so verify it against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the boundary differs between editions and laboratories. The danger is the extreme loss of water from the circulation, which can lead to clots, kidney injury, and a falling level of consciousness, and the signs of stroke or infection must be sought at the same time.

Electrolytes are the charged particles on which nerves, muscles, and the heart depend, and their disturbances cause symptoms because the electrical behavior of cells depends on the difference between the inside and the outside of the membrane. A small change in potassium, calcium, magnesium, or sodium can therefore produce weakness, cramp, an irregular heartbeat, or a seizure, and the same change can cause no symptoms until the moment it becomes dangerous. The blood level is only a partial guide, because it does not show what is stored in the cells, so a serious total deficit can sit behind a normal reading. The clinician should ask what the patient has lost, what the patient has taken, and what the kidneys are doing, because those three questions explain most electrolyte emergencies before any result returns.

Potassium is the electrolyte whose disturbance most often kills quickly, because the rhythm of the heart depends on it and the first symptom can be a cardiac arrest. A high potassium is suggested by weakness climbing from the legs, a slow or irregular pulse, numbness and tingling, and a change in the electrical tracing; kidney failure, medicines that hold potassium in the body, and severe muscle injury are the usual settings. A low potassium is suggested by cramp, fatigue, constipation, a fast pulse, and, in the worst cases, weakness of the muscles of breathing, and it usually follows vomiting, diarrhea, or water tablets. The electrical tracing may be the first place a dangerous potassium is seen and in some patients the only clue, so an electrocardiogram should be recorded when the possibility is serious. The tracing can also look deceptively ordinary, so a normal tracing does not settle the question, and the figure that demands urgent action is stated differently by different services and must be measured against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Calcium and magnesium come next, because they govern the excitability of nerve and muscle and a disturbance of one often accompanies the other. A low calcium produces tingling around the mouth and in the hands and feet, cramp, a spasm of the hand when a pressure cuff is inflated, a twitch of the face when the facial nerve is tapped, and in severe cases a seizure or a spasm of the airway. It appears in disease of the parathyroid glands, severe inflammation of the pancreas, long-standing kidney failure, and after major illness, and a low magnesium will keep the calcium low until it is corrected. A high calcium produces thirst, frequent urination, constipation, drowsiness, and confusion, and is a cause of an altered mental state easily attributed to age. The clinician should test for these signs with the pressure cuff and the tapping finger, because they cost nothing, and should confirm the levels that define danger against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Sodium disturbance is the electrolyte problem that most often presents as a change in the mind, and the speed of the change matters more than the number itself. A sodium that has fallen slowly may produce headache, nausea, confusion, unsteadiness, and a fall, while the same level reached quickly can cause a seizure, a coma, and swelling of the brain. A risen sodium produces thirst, weakness, and confusion, and in the extreme a shrinkage of brain cells that pulls on the vessels within the skull. The causes come from the history and the examination, since vomiting and diarrhea lose salt and water while heart, liver, and kidney failure retain water, and some medicines shift the balance silently. The clinician must ask about weight change, dryness of mouth and skin, fullness of the neck veins, and swelling of the legs, because those findings divide the causes, and the rate at which a sodium may safely be corrected must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Poisoning is a diagnostic subject in its own right, approached with the discipline of any other emergency rather than as a separate specialty. The clinician asks what was taken, when, how much, and what else was taken with it, because the combination often matters more than any single substance. The questions turn to how it entered the body, whether swallowed, breathed, injected, or absorbed through the skin, and whether the exposure was single or repeated. The reason should be asked about with care, because a deliberate overdose carries a risk of a further attempt and different needs from an accidental one. The clinician also asks what the patient ate and drank, whether a container can be read, and whether anyone else is affected, since a shared exposure points to a hazard in the home or the workplace, and a reported amount is often only an estimate made under stress.

The examination of the poisoned patient is a survey of what the substance has done rather than a hunt for its name. The clinician records the rate and depth of breathing, the pulse, the pressure, and the temperature, because the pattern of those signs often points to the class of poison. The pupils are examined with the torch, the skin is inspected for moisture, color, rash, and needle marks, and the mouth is examined for burns, smell, and fragments of a tablet. A temperature above 39 degrees Celsius, or a fall far below the ordinary range, is a reason to seek urgent help, and the figure that should alarm must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted boundary shifts with age and with the condition measured.

Toxidromes are patterns of observable signs that suggest a class of substance, and they are described here by what the clinician can see rather than by a list of antidotes. The patient who is drowsy or unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, and a normal or slow pulse fits the pattern of opioid excess, and the finding that confirms it is the reversal of the picture when the effect is blocked. The patient who is drowsy but easily roused, slurs words, and has normal pupils fits the pattern of a sedative, where the danger is loss of the airway and aspiration of stomach contents. The patient who smells of alcohol may also have a head injury, a low glucose, or a metabolic disturbance, so intoxication is a reason to look further and never a reason to stop. A recognized pattern narrows the search but is not a diagnosis and does not exclude a second poison or a coexisting illness.

Three further patterns are worth fixing in memory because each has a characteristic appearance at the bedside. The agitated, sweaty, hot patient with a fast pulse and wide pupils fits the pattern of a stimulant, and the danger is a rising temperature, a seizure, and an irregular heart rhythm. The flushed, dry patient with wide pupils, a full bladder, and a confused or hallucinating mind fits the pattern of an anticholinergic substance, and the dry skin separates it from the sweating patient. The patient who is drooling and tearing, with small pupils, a slow pulse, a wheeze, vomiting, diarrhea, and incontinence of urine and stool, fits the pattern of a cholinergic poison such as an agricultural insecticide, one of the few true emergencies of poisoning because the breathing can fail quickly.

Carbon monoxide deserves its own place because it kills without warning and because ordinary instruments mislead. It is produced by any fire burning without enough air, such as a stove, a heater, or a charcoal fire in a closed room, and it binds to the oxygen carrier of the blood far more tightly than oxygen, so tissues are starved while the blood looks normal. The patient complains of headache, nausea, dizziness, and difficulty thinking, and may be found drowsy or unresponsive, and the revealing finding is often another person or a pet in the same space with the same symptoms. The cherry red skin color sometimes described is unreliable and often absent, and a pulse oximeter can read a normal saturation in a patient who is seriously poisoned, because the device cannot tell the poisoned carrier from the healthy one. When this poisoning is suspected, the patient must be removed from the source and given oxygen while help is summoned, and the decision about further treatment belongs to a service with the right facilities.

Some poisons do their harm long after the first effects have passed, and these are the exposures most easily sent home too early. A common pain medicine taken in a large amount can injure the liver after a delay of a day or more while the patient feels only mildly unwell, and the finding that identifies the injury is a rise in the liver tests rather than the patient's appearance. Certain mushrooms produce vomiting and diarrhea that settle before the liver fails, and that apparent improvement is the most dangerous moment. Methanol and ethylene glycol act after the substance has been converted into a toxic product, so a patient who looks well in the first hours may be in the calm before a severe acidosis. Iron and some other substances injure the stomach and the liver in stages, and the interval after which a patient is safe to discharge depends on the substance and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The treatment decision in a metabolic or toxic emergency follows the same reasoning as any other, and this book names the decision rather than the medicine. Treatment is the right answer when a dangerous level of a reversible substance is present or rising, when there is organ injury, or when the patient is deteriorating and the diagnosis is secure enough to act on. Treatment is the wrong answer when the exposure was trivial and the patient is well, when another cause explains the picture entirely, and when acting before the relevant samples are taken would destroy the evidence the diagnosis depends on. In poisoning the clinician must ask whether reversing the effect will conceal the signs that show the poison is still acting, because a patient who looks better after an antidote may still be absorbing what was swallowed. The finding that settles the question is the direction of the patient over the next hour rather than a single reading.

In a hospital the laboratory turns the clinical idea into measurements, and each measurement should answer a question the clinician has already asked. Glucose is measured first and confirmed by the laboratory when the meter reading is inconsistent with the patient, and the salts allow the gap between the measured ions to be calculated, which points toward the class of acidosis. Kidney function, liver tests, and the blood count identify the injured organ and the infection that may have started the whole disturbance. The acidity of the blood and the gases within it show whether the breathing is compensating and how well the lungs work, and the ketones confirm the ketoacidotic process. The blood gas deserves to be read as a story, asking whether the blood is acid or alkaline, whether the change comes from breathing or metabolism, and whether the body is compensating as expected, while remembering that a patient can carry two disturbances at once and that the figures defining a normal gas must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The patient who seems to improve can be the patient in the most danger, and this pattern appears in almost every metabolic emergency. A corrected glucose may leave a brain injury that the sugar cannot undo, and a ketoacidosis that is improving may be followed by a fall in potassium or by swelling of the brain, particularly in a child. A poisoned patient may pass through an apparent calm between the first effects and the delayed injury to the liver, the kidney, or the brain, and the clinician reassured by that calm may send the patient away too soon. A patient whose breathing slows because the acidosis is corrected is improving, while one whose breathing slows because the effort of compensating is exhausted is deteriorating, and only repeated observations with their direction can separate the two.

In a clinic whose equipment is a stethoscope, a torch, a thermometer, and a glucose meter, the same reasoning is carried by the history and a few bedside observations. Glucose is measured in every patient who is drowsy, confused, fitting, sweating, or unwell, and it is measured again after any correction, because one reading can mislead and the direction of change is what matters. The urine can be tested for ketones where a strip is available, and the torch makes the pupils, mouth, skin, and needle marks visible. The clinic's decisions are made earlier than the hospital's, because a low glucose that corrects fully with a clear cause may be observed and fed with an explicit plan for review. Deep sighing breathing with ketones, a suspected poisoning with drowsiness or slow breathing, or a weakness suggesting a dangerous electrolyte disturbance means the journey must begin now, and hypoglycemia must be excluded before any other explanation is accepted.

The record should show the reasoning and not only the results. It should contain the time of each glucose measurement, what the patient was doing then, what was given and why, and what changed afterwards, so that the next clinician sees a direction rather than a point. It should name the poisons considered and those set aside, with the reason, because a recorded suspicion can be revisited and a forgotten one is lost. The patient sent home must be told exactly what should bring him back, including drowsiness, confusion, vomiting that will not stop, a return of thirst and urination, or worsening weakness, and a follow-up visit arranged in advance is worth more than a promise to return if things worsen.

A constructed illustration may fix these habits, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine an older man brought to a clinic because he has become drowsy and stopped eating for a few days, with a dry mouth, a fast pulse, and a glucose meter reading far above the ordinary range while his urine tests free of ketones. Those figures are illustrations of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the values that define a hyperglycemic emergency differ between editions and laboratories. The absence of ketones does not make him safe, because his danger lies in the water he has lost and the infection that may have started the decline, so the decision is transport. Now imagine a young woman found unresponsive at home with a slow pulse, pinpoint pupils, shallow breathing, and a low glucose, in whom both explanations must be addressed at once; neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment.

To summarize, the metabolic emergency is a disturbance of the body's chemistry that threatens the brain, the heart, or the breathing, and it is dangerous because it is both easily missed and often reversible. The causes that must be named early are hypoglycemia in every patient with altered consciousness, a potassium far outside its ordinary range, the hyperglycemic crises, and poisoning. The reasoning begins with the history of food, fluid, urine, medicines, alcohol, and what was swallowed, continues with a brief examination and a glucose at the bedside, and only then turns to the laboratory, which in the hospital and the clinic alike confirms rather than replaces the clinical idea. Diabetic ketoacidosis and its mimics, the hyperosmolar state, and the electrolyte disturbances that cause weakness, arrhythmia, or seizure are separated by the story and by repeated observation rather than by a single result. Poisoning is a diagnostic subject in its own right, approached through the questions of what, when, how much, and with what, and its toxidromes are read as observable patterns rather than a list of antidotes. Every figure in this chapter, whether a level, a rate, a pressure, a temperature, a gap, or an interval, is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and the patient who is deteriorating is helped first while the exact cause is settled afterwards.

# Chapter 44 — Deterioration and Early Warning

Deterioration is rarely a single dramatic event; it is a slope, and the task is to notice the tilt before the patient reaches the bottom. The reasoning here is temporal rather than anatomical, because the question is not what disease the patient has but which way the patient is traveling and how fast. A patient who looks stable may be compensating for a process that is already winning, and the signs that announce the loss of that compensation are quiet and easy to explain away. They are almost always present for hours before the crisis, so the clinician usually has time, provided the time is used. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, not a protocol, and not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the local protocol of your own service.

Several lethal causes of deterioration must be named before the ordinary discussion begins, each with the finding that reveals it. Sepsis, organ failure caused by the response to infection, announces itself through a rising breathing rate, a falling pressure, new confusion, and skin that has turned mottled or cool, and the earliest clue is often the breathing rather than the temperature. Major hemorrhage after trauma or surgery declares itself through a pulse that climbs while the pressure holds, then pallor, restlessness, thirst, and a shrinking passage of urine. Bleeding inside the skull after a head injury reveals itself through a falling level of consciousness, a worsening headache, vomiting, and one pupil larger than the other. Severe pancreatitis and the postoperative patient both deteriorate quietly, and in each the first warning is often a change in breathing, mental state, or color rather than pain.

The body defends its vital functions through compensation, and compensation is why deterioration is so easy to miss. As the circulation fails, the heart rate rises, the vessels of the skin and gut narrow to preserve flow to the brain and kidney, and the breathing rate climbs to correct the acid that accumulates. The patient may therefore hold an acceptable pressure, keep a warm skin, and continue to walk and talk while the reserve behind that appearance is spent. Compensation is a loan, and deterioration is the moment the loan is called in; the skill is to recognize the borrowing before the default. A clinician who waits for the pressure to fall is waiting for the last stage of a process that began hours earlier.

The respiratory rate is the earliest and most neglected warning sign, neglected because it is boring to count. Pain, anxiety, and fever all raise the rate, so a rapid rate is easily attributed to something benign; the error is to do so without asking whether the rise is new. A rate that has climbed from the patient's own baseline over successive observations carries far more than a single figure. A rate above 20 breaths per minute is often used as the point at which concern begins, but that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted boundary shifts with age, pregnancy, and the edition of the reference in use. Counting for a full minute, with the patient unaware, remains the cheapest and most sensitive test in medicine.

A change in mental state is the second quiet herald, and it is most often blamed on age, exhaustion, or the hour of the night. New confusion, drowsiness, agitation, or a sudden inability to follow a conversation may be the first evidence that the brain is short of oxygen, blood, or the right chemical environment. In an older patient, an infection, a low blood sugar, a stroke, or a reaction to a medicine may present as confusion alone, with no fever and no pain. The clinician must establish the patient's usual mental state from the patient, the family, or the record, because a change can only be recognized against a baseline. A patient who was lucid this morning and is vague this evening has deteriorated, whatever the cause proves to be.

Urine output is the window through which the clinician watches the kidney, and the kidney often complains first when the circulation is inadequate. Output that shrinks over successive hours suggests that blood flow to the kidney has fallen, whether from fluid loss, a failing heart, or the widened vessels of infection. A patient who has passed no urine for several hours, or whose output has halved, is telling the clinician something no pressure reading can. A commonly quoted figure is a urine output below half a milliliter for each kilogram of body weight in each hour, but that threshold is an illustration and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since it varies with age, body size, and the definition used by the service. In a clinic without a catheter the question is simpler and just as useful: when did the patient last pass urine, how much, and has that changed?

The color of the patient can be read from the end of the bed and changes before the numbers do. Pallor, a gray or dusky tinge, mottling of the knees and elbows, and coolness of the hands and feet all speak of blood diverted from the skin. The examiner presses a fingertip on the sternum or knee for a few seconds and watches the color return; a delay beyond about 3 seconds is often taught as poor perfusion, but that figure is illustrative and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because both the method and the boundary differ between services. The lips, tongue, and conjunctivae should be examined with a torch, because cyanosis, jaundice, and severe anemia each carry a different meaning. A patient whose color has changed since the last observation has deteriorated, even when the temperature, pulse, and pressure are unchanged.

The oxygen saturation is another number that can mislead, whether displayed on a monitor or inferred from color. A reading that looks acceptable does not prove that the patient is ventilating well, because it describes the oxygen carried in the blood and says nothing about the removal of carbon dioxide. The reading is also unreliable when the hands are cold, when the patient is moving, when the nail is painted, and in patients with darker skin, in whom the device may overestimate the true value. The clinician should treat saturation as one clue among several and return to the breathing rate and the work of breathing, which need no device. Where a value is used as a trigger for action, that trigger must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because practice differs between services and devices.

The person who knows the patient best often detects deterioration first, and that observation deserves to be treated as data. A relative who says the patient is not himself, that the color is wrong, or that something feels different is reporting a comparison the clinician, meeting the patient, cannot make. That intuition is not a diagnosis, but it is a sensitive alarm, and the response is to re-examine rather than reassure. The clinician should ask what exactly has changed, when, and what the patient was like yesterday, then look again with those answers in mind. A family's concern dismissed as anxiety is a missed observation, and the record should show it was heard.

A single normal value is the most seductive reassurance in medicine, and it is why warning systems exist. An acceptable pressure, a settling temperature, a falling pulse, or a laboratory result that looks unremarkable can each quiet the clinician while the patient continues to worsen. The pressure is the clearest example, because it is the last vital sign to change and may stay normal until the reserve is nearly gone. The temperature is another, because a serious infection can produce a normal or low temperature, especially in the very old, the very young, and the patient whose immune defenses are suppressed. The remedy is not to distrust every number but to read each as part of a sequence, asking what it was an hour ago and which way it is moving.

Early warning scores were designed to formalize this reasoning, and the reasoning, not the arithmetic, is what the listener should carry. The insight is that several mildly abnormal signs, taken together, predict deterioration far better than any one alone. A score assembles the breathing rate, the saturation, the temperature, the pressure, the pulse, and the level of consciousness, gives each a weight, and produces a number that rises as the patient drifts. The value lies less in the figure than in the obligation it creates: a rising score demands that a named person attend, assess, and decide. A score does not diagnose and does not replace the examination, and it can falsely reassure when the signs are abnormal in a direction it does not capture.

The score is a rule derived from a population, and like every rule it carries assumptions the clinician must know. It was built and validated in particular patients, often on hospital wards, and it may behave differently in pregnancy, in a child, and in the patient whose usual pressure or saturation is already abnormal. The quick sequential organ failure assessment, which asks about the breathing rate, the mental state, and the pressure, formalizes a similar logic and carries the same limits. A patient with long-standing lung disease may live at values that would alarm a healthy person, so deterioration means a change from the personal baseline rather than a return to the textbook. Those usual values should be recorded, and wherever fixed figures define the acceptable range, they must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the range differs with age, pregnancy, and chronic disease.

The patient who is compensating is the patient in greatest danger, and the compensation is invisible unless deliberately sought. The young, the fit, and the patient with good reserve can hold the pressure, keep the mind clear, and continue to walk and talk while the circulation fails underneath. The signs are subtle: a resting pulse faster than the patient admits to noticing, a breathing rate that is up, a cool periphery with a warm trunk, and an anxiety out of proportion to the situation. The clinician should compare the patient with the patient's own earlier state rather than with a general impression of how ill a person ought to look. When the reserve runs out, the change can be abrupt and irreversible within minutes, and the pressure that finally falls is the last event rather than the first.

Improvement and exhaustion can look alike, and telling them apart is among the hardest judgments in acute care. A patient whose pulse has fallen and who seems calmer may be recovering, or may be tiring toward failure, and the distinguishing question is what the other signs are doing. If the breathing rate is still high, the skin still cool, and the urine still scanty while the pulse has come down, the fall may reflect exhaustion rather than recovery. A patient who was restless and is now quiet, or who fought the oxygen mask and now accepts it without protest, may be losing the struggle rather than winning it. The clinician should read the work of breathing and the level of consciousness beside the pulse, because improvement should appear in the whole picture and not in one number.

Certain situations carry a known risk of deterioration, and sepsis is the first among them. Sepsis is organ failure caused by the response to infection, and a patient can move from looking unwell to critically ill within hours. The findings that demand action are a breathing rate that has climbed, a changed mental state, a pressure below the accepted threshold for that patient, mottled or cold skin, and a falling urine output. A normal temperature does not exclude it, and the older patient, the patient receiving treatment that suppresses the immune response, and the patient with diabetes may show little fever at all. A suspected infection should be assessed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the thresholds and definitions differ between services and editions, and the decision to treat rests on the clinical picture rather than a single result.

Hemorrhage is the second expected cause, and its danger is that the visible loss understates the hidden one. Bleeding into the chest, abdomen, pelvis, or gut may leave little external evidence, and the patient may look surprisingly well until compensation fails. The early findings are a rising pulse, a narrowing pulse pressure, restlessness, thirst, and pallor, with the pressure falling only late. Bleeding into the gut is often announced by vomiting blood or passing black stool, but a slow loss may show only as weakness, breathlessness on effort, and a falling hemoglobin. In a patient after trauma or surgery, or in a woman with abdominal pain and a missed period, bleeding should be assumed until excluded, because the revealing sign is often the pulse rather than any single test. Any figure defining the rate of rise that demands action must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since those boundaries are drawn differently in different settings.

A head injury is the third expected situation, and it is dangerous because the patient may be lucid for a period before worsening. Bleeding inside the skull raises the pressure within it, producing a brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, and then a worsening headache, vomiting, and drowsiness. The finding that reveals it is a pupil larger than the other and sluggish to react, with a rising pressure and a slowing pulse, and that combination needs immediate senior help and imaging. The Glasgow coma scale is the standard way of recording consciousness, and the reasoning it formalizes is the response to voice, to pain, and to command; its exact contents and the figure that should cause alarm must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the version in use varies between services and editions. Older age, alcohol, and a medicine that thins the blood each lower the threshold for observation and imaging.

Severe pancreatitis is the fourth situation, and its early appearance can badly understate its course. The pain is often severe and boring, reaching to the back and easing when the patient leans forward, with vomiting that does not relieve it. The danger lies not only in the pancreas but in the fluid lost into the tissues, the falling circulating volume, and the distant organ failure that follows, so a patient who seems stable may deteriorate over the next day. The findings that matter are a rising pulse, a climbing breathing rate, a falling urine output, and a pressure drifting down, with bruising around the umbilicus or flanks in the most severe cases. Scoring systems exist to predict severity, and their thresholds must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since they were derived in particular populations and their boundaries differ between editions.

The postoperative patient is the fifth situation, and surgery itself supplies a plausible explanation for almost every warning sign. Pain, nausea, a raised pulse, and a rapid breathing rate are all expected after an operation, and that expectation is what makes deterioration easy to excuse. The clinician must ask which findings are proportionate to the procedure and the time since it was performed, and which have appeared or worsened in a way the operation does not explain. The treatable causes include bleeding, infection, a clot in the lung, an airway problem, a collection of pus, and the effects of the anesthetic and the medicines given for pain, and each shows itself through a different part of the assessment. A patient whose breathing rate climbs, whose mental state changes, or whose wound or drain changes character should be reassessed at once, and the figures defining the acceptable range after surgery must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because they vary with the operation and the service.

Pain can be a herald of deterioration as well as a symptom to be relieved, and a new pain deserves an explanation rather than only an analgesic. Sudden severe pain in the chest, back, abdomen, or head may mark a clot in the lung, a dissection of the aorta, a perforated organ, or bleeding inside the skull, and each can be present while the vital signs still look acceptable. Pain that is severe beyond the appearance of the patient is a warning in its own right and should prompt a fuller assessment. The patient who cannot report pain, because of sedation, dementia, a language barrier, or critical illness, must be watched through behavior, posture, and the signs the body shows without words.

The setting changes the tools but not the reasoning, and the contrast is sharpest in how observations are gathered. On a monitored ward the pulse, pressure, saturation, and heart rhythm are displayed continuously, and alarms announce a change at once. That abundance has its own hazard, because a clinician can become a reader of screens rather than an examiner of patients, and no monitor shows the color of the skin, the work of breathing, or the confusion the family noticed. Where observations are written by hand every 4 hours, the record between those times is a blank, and the patient may deteriorate unseen. The interval of 4 hours is a convention rather than a law and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the appropriate frequency differs with the patient's condition, the service, and the resources available. The clinician who increases the frequency when worried is using time itself as a diagnostic instrument.

In a well-resourced hospital, deterioration is anticipated through a system rather than the memory of one clinician. The observations are charted and scored, a rising score triggers a call to a designated responder, and the laboratory and imaging service answer questions within minutes or hours. The arterial blood gas, the lactate, the blood count, and the chest radiograph each add a piece to the picture, while ultrasound and CT can find the collection of blood or pus the examination suspected. The senior clinician who attends should ask not only what is wrong but what is changing, and should set an explicit plan for the next observation and the trigger for calling again. The machinery never replaces standing at the bedside, and the clinician who does both catches the deterioration the monitor shows only as a number.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is carried by the hands and the watch. The breathing rate is counted for a full minute, the pulse is felt and counted, and the temperature is written down with the time beside it. The torch shows the color of the lips and tongue, the size of the pupils, the moisture of the skin, and the rash that would otherwise be missed, while the stethoscope reveals the breathing and heart sounds a monitor would have displayed. The urine is collected and measured where possible, and the patient is asked when urine was last passed. The clinic's disadvantage is the absence of tests; its advantage is continuity, because the same clinician may see the patient again in an hour and compare rather than guess.

Deterioration is often missed at the joints of care rather than at the bedside, and those joints are the handover and the escalation. At night the observations are less frequent, the laboratory slower, and the senior help further away, so a change noticed at noon may be recorded only as a note that the patient slept badly. The clinician on duty should visit the patients flagged during the day, read the trend rather than the last set of numbers, and ask the nursing staff which patient worries them most. A request for help with no named recipient and no expected time of arrival is not an escalation but a hope. The behavior of the team is part of the system, and a hierarchy that discourages the junior voice disables it; a nurse who has watched the patient all shift often notices the change first.

Trajectory is the central concept of this chapter, and it is measured rather than remembered. Each set of observations should be documented with its time, so that the direction of travel is visible to the next reader. A patient whose breathing rate has risen twice, whose urine has fallen, and whose mental state has shifted is deteriorating, even when the latest pressure is normal and the temperature has settled. Two observations separated by an interval are worth more than one perfect examination, and the interval should be chosen according to risk rather than routine. Where the patient is stable a longer interval is reasonable, and where the patient worries the clinician it should shorten; the frequency chosen must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the recommended interval differs with the condition, the setting, and the staffing available.

The treatment decision in deterioration turns on the same logic as the diagnosis, and it belongs to the clinician who knows the patient. Treatment is the right answer when the patient looks seriously ill, when the signs of organ failure are present, when the trajectory is clearly downward despite initial measures, or when a treatable cause such as infection or bleeding is strongly suspected and waiting would cost more than acting. Treatment is the wrong answer when a clear alternative explanation accounts for the findings, when the patient is stable and the diagnosis can be completed safely first, and when treating before the samples are taken would destroy the evidence the diagnosis depends on. Naming the finding that would justify or forbid treatment is more useful than naming a medicine, because the reasoning travels between settings even when the drugs do not. No drug, no dose, and no regimen appear anywhere in this chapter, and that omission is deliberate: the decision, not the prescription, is what this book teaches.

A constructed illustration may fix these habits, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than a portrait of any real person. Imagine an older man a few days after an operation, described as comfortable, whose temperature is normal and whose pressure is unchanged from the morning. The nurse mentions that he seems vague, that his breathing is faster than yesterday, and that he has passed very little urine, and the clinician who listens counts the rate, looks at the color of the skin, and finds it mottled at the knees. The picture is one of a patient who is compensating and losing, and the response is not a new medicine but a full reassessment, samples, help, and a shorter interval before the next observation. Now imagine the same findings in a young woman with a fever and a cough, where the breathing rate is explained by pain and the confusion by a sleepless night, and where the safe answer is still to look again in an hour. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment.

When a patient is not admitted, the early warning reasoning follows the patient home as specific advice. The patient and family should be told which changes must bring them back, how quickly, and where to go at that hour, in words they can repeat rather than a general instruction to return if worse. The signs worth naming are a breathing rate the patient can feel is too fast, a new confusion or drowsiness, a color that has changed, a passage of urine that has stopped or nearly stopped, a fever that will not settle, and a pain that is worsening. A follow-up visit arranged in advance is worth more than a promise, because many patients cannot judge their own deterioration and will wait for permission. The record should show what was said, because safety netting that is not documented cannot be reviewed.

Every figure in this chapter, whether a breathing rate, a pressure, a temperature, a urine volume, an interval between observations, or a score, is an illustration of reasoning rather than a rule to apply unchanged. Such numbers are drawn from particular populations, editions, and laboratories, and they differ between countries and services, so each must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it influences care. The clinician who understands why the breathing rate rises, why the urine falls, and why the confusion appears can work without any score at all, and can use a score well when one is available. That understanding is what this book is for, and it is what remains when the chart, the monitor, and the laboratory are taken away.

To summarize, deterioration is a slope rather than an event, and it is recognized by the direction of travel rather than by a single reading. The quiet heralds are a rising breathing rate, a new confusion, a shrinking passage of urine, a change in color, and the relative who says that something is wrong. The lethal causes, among them sepsis, major hemorrhage, bleeding inside the skull, severe pancreatitis, and the complications of surgery, are named at the bedside with the finding that reveals each. A single normal value reassures too easily, the compensating patient is in the most danger, and improvement must be distinguished from exhaustion by looking at the whole picture. Early warning scores formalize several mildly abnormal signs, and their trigger points must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because they differ between countries, editions, and services. The same vigilance is possible on a monitored ward and in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, because the reasoning, not the machinery, detects the patient who is slipping. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who worries the clinician is one to be reassessed, discussed with a senior colleague, and watched more closely, never one to be reassured and left.

# Chapter 45 — Cardiovascular Disease

Cardiovascular disease is a single phrase for two different kinds of failure, and the clinician who keeps them apart reasons better. One is a failure of the pump, in which the heart cannot move blood forward without demanding more pressure or more filling than the body can provide.
