The other is a failure of the pipes, in which the vessels that carry blood are narrowed, blocked, stretched, or torn. The two overlap, since a blocked pipe starves the pump and a failing pump congests the vessels, but the questions they ask are distinct. This chapter follows the diseases as a patient brings them: a pressure found by chance, a chest discomfort on effort, a breathlessness that grows, a heartbeat that has lost its rhythm, a murmur heard through a stethoscope, and a swollen leg or a sudden shortness of breath. The material is educational and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Several lethal possibilities should be named before any comfortable explanation is entertained, because each announces itself with a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. The patient with crushing central chest pain, cold sweat, nausea, and pain running into the jaw or the arm may be having an acute myocardial infarction, and a normal examination does not exclude it, so the electrocardiogram, or ECG, and the history together carry the decision. The patient with a sudden tearing pain that moves between the chest and the back, together with a difference in the pulses or the pressures between the two arms, may have a dissection of the aorta, which is a diagnosis made on suspicion rather than on any single sign. The patient who becomes suddenly breathless may have a clot in the lung, and the finding that supports it is a swollen, tender calf on one side, although the leg may look entirely normal. The patient whose heart races or stops and who faints, sweats, or cannot be roused may have a rhythm that has made the circulation fail, and that patient is treated before the rhythm is named. The patient with a fever and a new murmur may have an infection on a valve, and a murmur that was not there before turns a vague illness into a specific search. These are the presentations in which the next few minutes matter more than the next few tests, and they are kept in view throughout.

Understanding what the patient feels begins with the cycle of the heart, which fills while it relaxes and empties while it contracts. When the pump weakens, the pressure inside the chambers rises and is transmitted backward to the lungs and to the veins, and it is that backward pressure, rather than the weakness itself, that produces most of the symptoms. Breathlessness on effort appears first, because the lungs are the first place to feel congestion when the patient moves. Breathlessness on lying flat, which the patient describes as needing extra pillows, and breathlessness that wakes the patient at night are later and more specific signs of the same mechanism. Swelling of the ankles follows, because the pressure in the veins of the leg rises and fluid leaves the vessels, and fatigue is the quietest symptom and the easiest to attribute to age or to a lack of fitness. The clinician who understands this backward march of pressure knows what to ask, and knows in what order the findings tend to appear.

The examination of the heart follows a fixed order so that nothing is skipped and each finding is understood before the next is sought. The pulse is felt for its rate, its rhythm, its volume, and the character of its rise, and a pulse that is slow to rise or that collapses quickly says as much as any murmur. The pressure is taken in both arms when a dissection is possible and with the patient standing when fainting is part of the story. The jugular venous pressure is the window on the right side of the heart, and it is judged by watching the column of blood in the neck as the patient lies at an angle. The heart is examined by looking for the position of the apex beat and by listening through the stethoscope over the valve areas with the patient turned, sitting, and holding the breath as each position requires, and the lungs, the liver, and the legs are examined in the same sitting. Each step is a question whose answer changes the next, so the order is part of the reasoning rather than a ritual.

High blood pressure is the most common cardiovascular disease and the one most often discovered without the patient feeling anything at all. It damages the arteries quietly for years and declares itself through what it has already done: a stroke, a heart attack, a weakened pump, a damaged kidney, or a change in the vessels at the back of the eye. A cut-off such as 140 over 90 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the line above which the diagnosis is made, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line differs between countries, between editions, and between the ways a measurement is taken. The measurement itself is a skill, so the cuff must be the right size for the arm, the patient must be seated and rested, and the arm must be supported at the level of the heart. A single high reading is not a diagnosis, and the clinician who repeats the measurement, and who arranges readings at home or across a day where that is possible, will separate the patient whose pressure is always high from the patient whose pressure rises only in the consulting room. The examination then looks for damage, among which are an enlarged heart, an abnormal sound in the arteries of the neck, changes in the vessels of the retina, protein in the urine, and a raised substance in the blood that speaks of the kidney. The patient with a very high reading together with chest pain, breathlessness, a severe headache, visual disturbance, or a change in consciousness may be in a hypertensive emergency and needs treatment and senior help at once.

The decision to treat high pressure is a decision about risk rather than about a single number. The finding that makes treatment the right answer is damage already present, another risk factor such as diabetes, or a pressure that stays high when measured properly and repeatedly. The finding that makes treatment the wrong answer for now is a pressure raised only in the clinic, because treating that patient may do harm without benefit. In a clinic with no laboratory, the reasoning still works, because the eye, the heart, and the urine give real evidence of damage, and the one limit that remains is the fine judgment about kidney function, which should be stated to the patient rather than hidden.

Ischemic heart disease appears in two forms that must be separated at the bedside, the stable and the acute. Stable angina is a predictable discomfort in the chest that comes with effort and settles with rest, and its predictability is its most reassuring feature. The patient typically feels it behind the breastbone, sometimes as a pressure or a heaviness rather than a pain, and it may travel to the left arm, the jaw, the throat, or the upper abdomen. The clinician asks how far the patient can walk before it begins, what makes it come and go, and whether the pattern has changed in recent weeks, using the Socrates framework to keep the questions in order. A typical episode lasts a few minutes and eases within a short rest, and that window is offered only as a teaching illustration, because the duration that should raise concern is stated differently in different sources and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol. The differential diagnosis includes reflux from the esophagus, pain from the muscles and ribs of the chest wall, and anxiety, and the clinician who considers all three is less likely to be misled by a story that seems clear.

The acute form of ischemic heart disease is the one that kills, and it is recognized by a change in the pattern rather than by the severity of the pain. A discomfort that is new, that comes at rest, that lasts longer than the patient's usual angina, or that wakes the patient from sleep is acute until proved otherwise, and it belongs to the same family as the classic crushing pain with sweating and nausea. The examination may be entirely normal, and that normality is a trap, because a normal examination never excludes an acute myocardial infarction. Where an ECG exists it is performed early and repeated, since a single tracing taken at the wrong moment may look innocent, and where a laboratory exists the substances released by damaged heart muscle are measured and repeated. In the clinic with no ECG, the decision is not the diagnosis but the journey, and a patient with new or changing chest discomfort who looks unwell, who is sweating, or whose pulse or pressure is abnormal must travel to a place where the tracing can be done. The finding that would make immediate treatment the wrong answer is a confirmed alternative cause that fully explains the picture, and even then the patient must be observed while confidence grows.

Heart failure is a syndrome rather than a disease, and it is the final common path of many causes, so the first task is to identify what sort of failure it is and what produced it. The failing pump has a weak muscle that dilates and cannot empty, and this patient usually has an apex beat displaced outward and downward, a third heart sound, and congestion of the lungs and the veins. The stiff heart has a thick muscle that cannot relax, and it is often seen in older patients with a long history of high pressure, in people with diabetes, and in those whose rhythm has become irregular; the heart is not weak in this pattern, but it is unable to fill. The two differ in what helps and in what harms, so the distinction is not academic. The findings that separate them are the size and position of the apex beat, the sounds heard at the apex and the base, the appearance of the ECG, and the estimate of how much blood leaves the heart with each beat, which in a well-equipped hospital comes from an ultrasound of the heart. The patient whose symptoms come with a normal-sized heart and preserved emptying may have a lung problem, an anemia, a thyroid disorder, or a failure of the heart to fill, and each of those changes the plan. Confirming which pattern is present matters even more than naming the syndrome, because the pattern decides whether the treatment given is likely to help or to harm.

Acute pulmonary edema is the lethal face of heart failure, and it announces itself with a patient who cannot lie flat, who is fighting to breathe, and who may cough up frothy, blood-stained sputum. That patient needs treatment and senior help immediately, and the finding that would make a different diagnosis more likely, such as a widespread infection of the lungs, changes only the treatment and not the urgency. Between emergencies, the examination seeks the signs of congestion one by one: a raised jugular venous pressure, judged by the height of the column in the neck relative to the angle of the sternum, with a figure such as 3 centimeters above that angle offered as a teaching illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because the reference point and the technique vary between services. Crackles at the lung bases, dullness where fluid has collected around a lung, an enlarged and tender liver, swelling of the ankles that pits when pressed, and a weight that has climbed by several kilograms over a few days all point the same way. The weight is worth a word of its own, because a gain of 2 kilograms over 3 days is often described as a sign of retained fluid, and both the figure and the interval are illustrations to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the meaningful change depends on the patient's usual weight and on the scale in use. A blood test for a natriuretic peptide can support the diagnosis, but its reference range is set by the laboratory that performs it and must be confirmed locally rather than taken from a textbook. The clinician who weighs the patient at every visit and records the trend has a measure that costs almost nothing and reflects the whole circulation.

An arrhythmia is a disorder of the rate, the rhythm, or the order in which the heart's chambers contract, and its importance lies less in its name than in what it does to the circulation. The patient may describe a racing heart, an irregular flutter, a pause, dizziness, breathlessness, or a faint, and the examination may find a pulse that is too fast, too slow, or irregular in a way the hand can feel. An irregularly irregular pulse, in which the beats come without any pattern, suggests atrial fibrillation, and the finding that often accompanies it is a difference between the rate felt at the wrist and the rate heard at the heart, because not every beat moves enough blood to reach the arm. Atrial fibrillation matters for two reasons that are easy to state and easy to forget: it allows clots to form in the heart and travel to the brain, and it takes away the contribution of the atria to filling, which can tip a borderline heart into failure. A rate above 150 beats per minute or a rate below 40 beats per minute may be poorly tolerated, but the figure at which a particular patient becomes unstable depends on the heart itself, so any such number must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol and never applied as a rule. The patient whose rhythm is fast or slow and who has a falling pressure, a change in consciousness, chest pain, or breathlessness is unstable, and the rhythm is treated before it has been fully identified. The patient who is pulseless and unresponsive needs cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, at once, and the tracing that names the rhythm comes after the hands have started.

Valvular disease is heard before it is understood, and the murmur is the beginning of the reasoning rather than the end of it. A narrowed aortic valve produces a harsh murmur in systole that travels to the neck, and the pulse is slow to rise and small in volume; the patient may have chest pain on effort, breathlessness, or a faint on exertion, and the faint on effort is a warning that cannot be ignored. A leaking mitral valve produces a murmur that runs through systole and travels toward the armpit, and its consequences are an enlarging heart, an irregular rhythm, and a slow decline in the ability to exercise. A narrowed mitral valve produces a low rumble in diastole that is heard best with the bell of the stethoscope and with the patient lying on the left side, and because it raises the pressure in the lungs it may produce breathlessness, coughing of blood, and a raised pressure on the right side of the heart. A leaking aortic valve produces an early diastolic murmur and a pulse that is large and collapsing, and the patient may notice the head nodding with each beat. A murmur is not automatically a disease, and the clinician should judge it by its timing in the cycle, its site, where it travels, what it does when the patient stands or holds the breath, and what else the examination shows. A murmur described by its loudness on a scale of 6 is an illustration of a convention that differs between examiners and between editions, so any such grade must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol and never carried in a note without the description that produced it.

The consequences of a valve lesion are what decide when it must be addressed, and those consequences include a heart that enlarges, a rhythm that becomes irregular, a pressure in the lungs that rises, and symptoms that limit the patient's life. A damaged or replaced valve is also a place where infection can settle, and a fever with a new or changed murmur in such a patient is an emergency of its own; the finding that makes treatment the right answer is a positive culture from blood drawn before any medicine is given, and the finding that makes it the wrong answer is a clear alternative source of the fever that fully explains the illness. Rheumatic heart disease remains a common cause of valve damage in many parts of the world, and it begins with a throat infection in childhood and returns years later as a murmur, an arrhythmia, or breathlessness. A previous sore throat that was not treated is worth asking about in any young patient with a murmur, because the question costs nothing and the answer changes the whole story. The patient with a new murmur and breathlessness or fever should be referred for an ultrasound of the heart where one can be reached, and where it cannot, the decision is whether to begin treatment and travel.

Venous thromboembolism is the clot that forms in a deep vein and the clot that breaks away to the lung, and it must be considered in any unexplained breathlessness or swelling of a leg. The reason is that the second half of the disease kills, sometimes within minutes, and the examination of a patient who dies a few hours later was often described as normal beforehand. The findings of a clot in the leg are swelling of one calf, warmth, tenderness, and a difference in circumference between the two sides, but the leg may look and feel entirely ordinary, and the absence of those signs proves nothing. The findings of a clot in the lung are a sudden breathlessness, a rapid pulse, pain in the chest that worsens with a breath, a cough that may bring blood, and sometimes a faint, and the patient may have no chest signs at all. The risk factors belong in the history: a recent operation, a long period of immobility whether in bed or on a journey, a cancer, a pregnancy or the weeks after birth, the use of hormones, a previous clot, a close relative with one, and an inherited tendency of the blood to clot. The clinician who asks those questions before examining the leg is doing the reasoning in the right order, and a patient with a sudden breathlessness and a normal examination is a patient to be taken seriously, because that combination is the one that most often delays the diagnosis.

Where tests exist, they are chosen to answer a question that the clinical assessment has already framed. A blood test for the product of clot breakdown, known as D-dimer, is useful when the probability is low, because a normal result in that setting makes the diagnosis very unlikely, while a raised result is common in many other conditions and settles nothing on its own. The Wells score formalizes the reasoning about the probability of a clot in the leg or the lung, and any cut-off attached to it is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the version in the original paper and the versions in use today do not set the same line. An ultrasound of the leg veins and a computed tomography, or CT, of the lung arteries are the decisive images where they are available, and each carries its own limits, including the clot that is too small or too peripheral to see. In a clinic with no laboratory and no imaging, the reasoning has to carry the whole weight, and it is still strong: a patient with a plausible story and a high probability is treated while traveling, because the harm of a missed clot is greater than the harm of treatment given on a good clinical case. The finding that would make that decision the wrong answer is a likely bleeding tendency or an alternative explanation that accounts for every symptom, and the clinician who writes down the probability, the reasoning behind it, and the plan for review makes the uncertainty visible rather than hiding it.

In a hospital, the cardiovascular examination is followed by a set of tests that are chosen to answer specific questions. The ECG answers the question of rhythm and of the pattern of injury or strain, and it is repeated because a single tracing is a snapshot of a moment that has passed. An ultrasound of the heart answers the question of how the chambers are sized, how the valves move, and how much blood leaves with each beat, and it is the most informative single test in most cases. A stress test answers whether the demand of exercise provokes the evidence of a narrowed artery, and angiography answers directly which vessels are narrowed and how badly. An ultrasound of the leg veins and a CT of the lung arteries answer the questions of venous thromboembolism, while a CT or a magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, of the aorta answers the questions raised by a tearing pain. Blood tests for the substances released by heart muscle, for the salts, for the kidney, and for the blood count answer questions about damage and about cause, and each should be ordered because its result would change something. The clinician who knows what each test would mean before it is performed is using the hospital well, and the clinician who treats a test as an answer rather than as a question will be misled by a normal result in a patient who is clearly unwell.

The clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer is not a lesser place to reason, and much of cardiovascular diagnosis is made there. The history carries more weight than ever, because there is no test to correct it: how far the patient can walk, how many pillows are needed to sleep, what has changed in the last week, and what the patient can no longer do. The pulse and the pressure can be counted and recorded properly, and a resting rate above 100 beats per minute or a breathing rate above 20 breaths per minute is a finding to record and to follow rather than a diagnosis; the line at which such a rate becomes abnormal shifts with age, fitness, and medication, so confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol. The jugular venous pressure can be seen in good light, the heart can be listened to in the positions that bring each murmur out, and the legs can be pressed for swelling. The torch makes the vessels of the eye and the color of the skin visible, the thermometer turns the impression of fever into something repeatable, and a watch makes the rate a measurement rather than a guess. A walk along the corridor, with the patient observed while walking and asked what the patient feels, is one of the most useful tests in medicine and requires no equipment at all. The decision that follows is usually not a diagnosis but a plan, which is to watch and review, to begin treatment on the clinical findings, or to send the patient onward now, and a normal examination in a patient whose story is alarming is a reason to look again.

To summarize, cardiovascular disease is approached as a failure of the pump and a failure of the pipes, and the reasoning follows the patient's presentation rather than a list of diagnoses. High pressure is sought because it damages quietly; chest discomfort is separated into the predictable and the acute; breathlessness and swelling are read as the backward march of pressure from a heart that cannot keep up; an irregular or extreme rate is judged by what it does to the circulation rather than by its name; a murmur is interpreted by its timing, its site, and its consequences; and venous thromboembolism is considered in every unexplained breathlessness or swollen leg because it can kill within minutes. The lethal possibilities are named where they appear, together with the finding that reveals them, and the patient who is unstable is treated before the diagnosis is complete. Every figure in this chapter, whether a pressure, a cut-off, a rate, a temperature, a duration, or a reference range, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient whose story worries the clinician deserves another look, another set of observations, and a clear plan, and the reasoning in this chapter is the tool for that, not a substitute for being with the patient.

# Chapter 46 — Respiratory Disease

Respiratory disease is organized by the pattern each illness produces rather than by a list of names. The clinician listens first for the tempo, because an illness that has developed over an hour asks a different question from one that has developed over a year, and then for the dominant disturbance, whether that lies in the airways, in the air sacs, in the pleural space, or in the vessels that carry blood through the lung. A cough, a fever, a wheeze, a chest pain, and a breathlessness that is worse on effort are the raw material, and the way they combine points more reliably to a mechanism than any single symptom can. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

The causes that kill must be named before the comfortable ones, each with the finding that would reveal it. A patient with asthma who becomes too breathless to speak and whose chest falls silent has a silent chest, a sign of failing air movement rather than of improvement. A patient with sudden breathlessness, pain on one side, absent breath sounds, and a falling pressure may have a tension pneumothorax, recognized and acted on at the bedside before any image is taken. A large pleural effusion gives stony dullness over half the chest, reduced breath sounds, and a windpipe pushed away from the affected side, and the danger is respiratory failure as the good lung is compressed. A clot in the lung may leave the chest sounding entirely normal, and that mismatch between severe breathlessness and a quiet examination should raise the possibility rather than dismiss it. A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who is drowsy during an exacerbation may be retaining carbon dioxide, and a patient with pneumonia who is cold, hypotensive, and passing little urine has moved into septic shock.

Breathlessness appears whenever the work of breathing rises or the oxygen in the blood falls, and disease of the chest disturbs one of four structures. The airways can narrow, as in asthma and in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, so that air leaves the chest slowly and each breath costs more effort. The air sacs can fill with fluid, pus, or blood, as in pneumonia and in pulmonary edema, so that a region of lung is supplied with blood but not with air. The pleural space can fill with air, fluid, or pus, so that the lung is compressed and cannot expand, and the pulmonary vessels can be blocked, as in pulmonary embolism, so that part of the circulation is wasted. The clinician who places the story into one of these four disturbances already knows which signs to seek, and the same reasoning must serve in two different rooms, because a clinician who reasons well without imaging will use it better when it exists.

The assessment begins with the patient's appearance and the simple observations that cost nothing. The respiratory rate is the most sensitive vital sign in chest disease and the one most often estimated rather than counted, so it should be counted and recorded. A rate of 30 breaths per minute in an adult is often quoted as a sign of serious illness, and that number is an illustration of the reasoning which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold that should prompt action varies between services and editions. The ability to speak in full sentences and to walk without stopping are practical measures of reserve, and a patient who can no longer complete a sentence is more concerning than any single number. The work of breathing shows in the neck muscles, in the drawing in of the spaces between the ribs, in sweating, and in a posture that fixes the shoulders.

The history is taken in a disciplined way, and the first thing to establish is the tempo. Breathlessness that arrives over minutes suggests a clot, a pneumothorax, or an attack of asthma, while breathlessness that has grown over weeks suggests pneumonia that is not resolving, a large effusion, anemia, or a failing heart. A cough present for days is a different problem from one present for months, and the clinician should ask when it began and what has changed. A dry cough suggests an interstitial process, an early viral illness, or a reaction to a medicine, while a productive cough suggests infection. Any blood in the sputum must be asked for, because patients often do not volunteer it, and hemoptysis can come from an infection, a tumor, a clot, a damaged vessel, or tuberculosis. Fever, shivering, night sweats, weight loss, and a change in voice belong in the same account.

The context in which the illness appears changes what it probably means. Smoking, present and past, is the strongest single piece of history in chronic airway disease and in lung cancer, and the number of years and the amount should be recorded. Occupation matters, because exposure to dust, asbestos, silica, and fumes produces disease years after the exposure has ended. The clinician asks about travel, contact with someone who has tuberculosis, crowded living, and contact with birds, animals, or molds. A history of allergy, eczema, or hay fever raises the probability of asthma, while a previous clot, a recent operation, immobility, pregnancy, a cancer, or treatment with estrogen raises the probability of pulmonary embolism.

The examination is performed in a fixed order so that no region is skipped, and it begins before the stethoscope is used. The clinician inspects the shape and movement of the chest, the use of the accessory muscles, and the position the patient has chosen, then examines the hands for clubbing, the lips for central cyanosis, and the ankles for swelling. Percussion from side to side and from top to bottom distinguishes the resonant note from the dull note of fluid or consolidation and the hyper-resonant note of trapped air. Auscultation follows, listening for breath sounds that are reduced, bronchial, or absent, for crackles, wheeze, and a pleural rub, and comparing one side with the other. Auscultation is powerful and also limited, because a normal chest does not exclude a clot in the lung, an early infection, or a small effusion, and a quiet chest may mean either that disease is absent or that so little air is moving that nothing can be heard. The clinician should therefore look for signs outside the chest, among them clubbing, cyanosis, a raised jugular venous pressure, a tender swollen leg, and enlarged nodes above the collarbone, and should repeat the examination in a patient who is deteriorating.

Pneumonia is infection of the lung tissue, and it produces a recognizable pattern when the history and examination are put together. The patient is usually feverish, with a cough, sputum, breathlessness, and a pain in the side that catches on breathing. The examination may show dullness over the affected region, crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and an increased transmission of the spoken voice, and these together point to solid lung rather than air. The finding that separates pneumonia from other causes of febrile breathlessness is a focal abnormality that corresponds to the symptoms, because a pneumothorax gives hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds, a large effusion gives stony dullness with reduced breath sounds, and a clot typically gives a normal chest. The older patient may have none of the classical signs and may present with confusion or a fall. A pneumonia that does not resolve as expected deserves a second look, because a tumor obstructing a bronchus can produce an infection that clears partially and then returns in the same place.

The severity of pneumonia is judged by how the patient is behaving rather than by the radiograph alone. Confusion, a climbing breathing rate, a falling pressure, and advanced age all raise the risk, and a formal severity score such as the Curb sixty-five score organizes exactly those features into a decision about where the patient should be treated. Its contents and the figure at which it should change the plan must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the components and thresholds differ between editions and services. The score supports the examination and never replaces it, since a patient who looks unwell is treated as unwell whatever the arithmetic says. Treatment is the right answer when the picture is compatible and the patient is unwell, and the wrong answer when a clear non-infectious cause explains the findings, while samples that name the organism are most useful taken before treatment begins.

Asthma is a disease of variable airway narrowing, and its signature is that it changes. The patient describes attacks of breathlessness, wheeze, and cough that come and go, often worse at night and provoked by cold air, exercise, dust, or infection. Between attacks the examination may be completely normal, which is why the history carries more weight than the examination. Severity is assessed by the ability to speak and by the work of breathing, and the peak flow measurement is a supporting number rather than the arbiter. A peak flow that has fallen to less than half of the patient's usual best is often used to mark a severe attack, and that proportion is an illustration of the reasoning which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the fraction that should trigger alarm differs between age groups, services, and editions. The most dangerous finding is the disappearance of the wheeze, because a silent chest means that so little air is moving that no sound is made.

Drowsiness, exhaustion, and a slowing of the breathing rate are signs that the patient is losing the fight and need help at once, and a patient who can speak only in single words is in a severe attack. A normal peak flow in a struggling patient does not make a severe attack mild. Treatment is the right answer when the patient cannot speak comfortably, when the work of breathing is visible, or when repeated relief has not lasted, and it is the wrong answer to rely on a single measure of airflow while the patient is tiring. The finding that would make a clinician reconsider the diagnosis is a focal chest abnormality, a fever with a productive cough, or a sudden onset with one-sided pain, each pointing away from asthma and toward infection, a pneumothorax, or a clot. The interval over which improvement should be expected is a local matter, and the expected timing must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it differs with the treatment given and the setting.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a persistent narrowing of the airways that develops over years, usually in a person who has smoked. The patient describes a cough with sputum for years, breathlessness that has crept up on effort, and a chest that may be barrel-shaped with a prolonged expiration. An exacerbation is recognized by a change from the patient's usual state, most often breathlessness that is worse, more sputum, sputum that has changed in color, and a sense of being unwell. Fever may be absent and the chest may sound unchanged, so a clinician who relies on auscultation alone will miss the deterioration. The patient who is tiring must be recognized early, because drowsiness, confusion, a headache, and a bounding pulse may mean that carbon dioxide is accumulating. A patient who was fighting to breathe and now seems settled may be deteriorating rather than improving. Treatment is right when the patient is failing to clear carbon dioxide or cannot maintain the work of breathing, and the finding that would give pause is a clear alternative cause.

Tuberculosis is an infection that develops slowly, and its leading symptom is a cough that persists. A cough lasting more than 2 or 3 weeks, particularly with night sweats, fever, weight loss, and a loss of appetite, should raise the possibility, and that interval is an illustration of the reasoning which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the duration that should trigger investigation is stated differently in different countries and editions. Blood in the sputum is a warning sign at any time and may be the only symptom the patient mentions. The disease may affect the pleura, the lymph nodes, the spine, the kidney, or the lining of the brain, so a respiratory complaint may be absent altogether. The clinician should ask about contact with a person who has tuberculosis, about crowded living, about previous treatment, and about infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV.

The examination in tuberculosis is often normal, and that is one of its most important limitations. The classical findings of wasting, fever, enlarged neck nodes, and changes at the top of one lung are often absent, and a chest radiograph may be normal in early disease, in a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, and in disease outside the lung. Because examination and image are both unreliable, the diagnosis rests on identifying the organism, and sputum is the sample that usually provides it. Where the patient cannot produce sputum, the absence of a sample is not the end of the investigation, and other ways of obtaining material must be considered. Tuberculosis is transmitted through the air, so a patient with a prolonged cough who is unwell should be separated from others, and the clinician should use the protective clothing and mask that the local protocol requires. The combination of HIV infection and tuberculosis is common and dangerous, because each worsens the other.

Inflammation of the pleura without fluid produces a sharp pain that catches on breathing and on coughing, and the finding is a pleural rub, a coarse grating sound heard on both inspiration and expiration. When fluid accumulates in the pleural space, a small effusion may produce nothing at all, while a larger one gives stony dullness to percussion, reduced breath sounds, and a reduced transmission of the spoken voice over the fluid. As the effusion grows, the lung is compressed and the windpipe may be pushed toward the opposite side, and the patient becomes breathless on less and less effort. The danger of a large effusion is respiratory failure, and the danger of an infected effusion is sepsis, so a large or infected collection needs drainage and help without delay. The character of the fluid matters, because clear fluid, cloudy fluid, blood, and pus each point to a different cause, and the sample taken by a needle is what distinguishes them. A patient whose fever persists after an effusion is drained may have an empyema that has not been fully evacuated.

A pneumothorax is air in the pleural space, and its presentation depends on how much air has entered and how quickly. A spontaneous pneumothorax in a tall young person or in a patient with chronic lung disease produces a sudden pain on one side and breathlessness, with absent breath sounds and a hyper-resonant note over the affected side. A tension pneumothorax is the lethal form, in which air enters with each breath and cannot escape, so that the pressure rises, the lung collapses, the windpipe is pushed to the opposite side, the neck veins become distended, and the pressure falls. That diagnosis is made at the bedside and must be acted on before any image is obtained, because waiting for a radiograph in that situation can cost the patient's life. The clinician should suspect it in any patient who becomes suddenly breathless and shocked after an injury, after a procedure on the chest, or without any apparent cause. The finding that argues against it is breath sounds that are present and equal on both sides.

Pulmonary embolism is a clot that has traveled to the lung, and it is the diagnosis most often missed because the chest sounds normal. The patient may present with sudden breathlessness, a sharp pain on breathing, a cough, blood in the sputum, a racing pulse, or a fainting episode, any of which may occur alone. The risk factors should be sought deliberately, among them a previous clot, a recent operation, immobility, a long journey, a swollen tender leg, a cancer, pregnancy, and treatment with estrogen. The clinician should examine the legs for a difference in size and for tenderness along the deep veins, because that finding supports the diagnosis when the chest is unhelpful. A clinical prediction rule such as the Wells score organizes these features into a probability, and its exact contents and thresholds must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the rule has been revised. The mismatch between severe breathlessness and a calm chest is the central clue, and it should make the clinician ask about risk factors rather than move on.

A massive embolism is the form that kills within minutes, and it announces itself through the heart rather than the lung. The patient may collapse, become pale and sweaty, have a very rapid pulse, and show a raised jugular venous pressure, while the chest remains quiet and the blood pressure falls. The patient may be confused or lose consciousness because the circulation is failing rather than because the lungs have stopped working, and help must be summoned at once without waiting for a confirmatory test. The finding that supports the diagnosis is a sudden collapse with a normal chest and a strain on the right side of the heart, while the finding that points elsewhere is a chest full of crackles with a raised jugular venous pressure in a patient known to have a failing heart. A normal chest examination in a patient who has collapsed is a reason for urgency, not reassurance.

Assembling the differential means sorting the findings by the mechanism they suggest and ranking the possibilities by both likelihood and danger. Breathlessness with a focal chest sign, fever, and sputum places infection high; a silent chest with a history of attacks places asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease high; stony dullness places fluid in the pleural space high; a normal chest with a risk factor places a clot high; and sudden breathlessness with absent breath sounds places a pneumothorax high. The clinician should then add the causes that do not live in the lung, several of which imitate respiratory disease closely enough to mislead. Heart failure gives breathlessness that is worse lying flat, a raised jugular venous pressure, crackles at both bases, and ankle swelling, while anemia gives breathlessness on effort with a normal chest and a low concentration of hemoglobin in the blood. A metabolic disturbance that makes the blood acidic produces deep, sighing breathing without primary lung disease, and a large abdomen, a weak diaphragm, a muscle disease, or a poisoning can each reduce breathing without any abnormality inside the lung.

In a hospital the examination becomes the set of questions that tests are asked to answer. A chest radiograph shows consolidation, a large effusion, a pneumothorax, and the size of the heart, and it should be requested with a specific question rather than as a routine. A blood count, a measure of inflammation, and a measurement of oxygen and carbon dioxide answer different questions about infection, severity, and ventilation, while a sample of sputum can identify the organism in pneumonia and in tuberculosis. An ultrasound of the chest can detect a small effusion that a radiograph misses, computed tomography gives a detailed view of the lung tissue and its vessels, and spirometry separates the obstructive pattern from the restrictive one when the patient is well enough. The value of a test lies in the decision it changes, so a clinician who cannot say what either result would mean should not order it. A normal result in a patient with a high probability of disease is more often a reason to doubt the test than a reason to relax.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is conducted with fewer instruments and no less care. The respiratory rate is counted with a watch, the temperature is measured and recorded with its route, and the oxygen saturation is estimated from the patient's color and effort where no instrument exists. The stethoscope allows the clinician to compare the two sides of the chest, to hear crackles, wheeze, a rub, and a difference in breath sounds, and to detect dullness a hand cannot feel. The torch makes the throat, mouth, nose, and ear visible, and the sputum can be examined for color and volume or sent to a laboratory if the result would change the plan. What the clinic lacks in imaging it can partly replace with systematic examination, repeated observation, and a clear note of what was found. The central decision is whether the patient can be watched here or must travel, and a patient who is drowsy, whose breathing is visibly labored, whose chest is silent, or whose breathlessness appeared suddenly must go.

Treatment is part of diagnosis, and in respiratory disease the decision is often made before the cause is certain. In pleural disease the decision is whether the collection must be drained, and the finding that supports drainage is a large collection compressing the lung or an infected one causing fever and sepsis. In pneumothorax the decision is whether the air must be released at once, and the finding that supports immediate action is the tension pattern with a falling pressure and a shifted windpipe, while a small collection in a stable patient may be watched. In pulmonary embolism the decision is whether to treat for a clot, and the finding that supports it is a compatible picture with a high probability and no alternative explanation, while a clear alternative cause turns the decision the other way. In tuberculosis the treatment decision belongs to the program that manages the disease, and the finding that supports it is a compatible illness with the organism identified or strongly suspected. The specific medicines, their amounts, and the timing of their use belong to the current guideline and the local protocol, and this book names only the decisions they serve.

A patient with respiratory disease who is sent home must be given clear instructions about when to return. The signs that matter include a breathlessness that worsens, a chest that becomes painful, blood in the sputum, a fever that will not settle, a new drowsiness or confusion, a blue tinge to the lips, and a reduced ability to speak or eat. A follow-up visit arranged in advance is worth more than a promise to return if things worsen, because many patients cannot judge that for themselves. The record should show the reasoning and not only the numbers, including the respiratory rate and how it has changed, the work of breathing, the findings on each side of the chest, the appearance of the sputum, the risk factors for a clot, and what was considered and set aside. Infants and young children may deteriorate quickly, and older adults may present with confusion rather than a cough, so in these groups the trajectory over hours matters more than the first examination.

A constructed illustration may fix these habits, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a young patient with known asthma who arrives unable to speak in full sentences, sitting forward and sweating, with a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute and an almost silent chest. That rate is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the figure that should trigger alarm varies with age and with the service. The clinician recognizes the silent chest as a sign of failing air movement rather than of improvement, and the plan changes within minutes. Now imagine an older patient who has been in bed after an operation and becomes suddenly breathless with a pulse of 120 beats per minute, a painful calf, and a chest that sounds entirely normal, in whom the mismatch between severe breathlessness and a calm chest prompts the search for a clot. The exact pulse at which a clinician should act is not fixed, and that figure too must be checked against the current guidance and the local protocol, because it changes with age, fitness, and the definition being used. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment.

To summarize, respiratory disease is read from the tempo of the complaint and from the mechanism it disturbs, whether that is the airway, the air sac, the pleural space, or the vessels within the lung, and the examination follows a fixed order so that no region is missed. The dangers are named where each disease appears: the silent chest of a tiring patient with asthma, the large effusion that compresses the good lung, the tension pneumothorax recognized at the bedside, the drowsy patient who is retaining carbon dioxide, and the patient with a clot in the lung whose chest sounds entirely normal. Pneumonia is separated from other causes of febrile breathlessness by a focal abnormality that matches the symptoms. Tuberculosis is considered in every cough that persists, because the examination and the radiograph are both unreliable and the organism must be found. Pleural disease and pulmonary embolism each carry a specific finding that turns a vague breathlessness into a decision, and the same reasoning serves in a hospital and in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer. Every figure in this chapter, whether a rate, a pressure, a temperature, a proportion, a score, or an interval, is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or local protocol, and a patient who looks unwell is helped first while the cause is settled afterwards.

# Chapter 47 — Gastrointestinal and Hepatic Disease

The gut and the liver announce themselves through patterns rather than single symptoms, and this chapter follows those patterns: the obstruction of a tube, the inflammation of a wall, the loss of continuity, the failure of a factory, and the rise in pressure when blood cannot pass freely through the liver. The same ache beneath the breastbone may belong to the stomach, the pancreas, the gallbladder, or the heart, and the same yellowing of the eyes may be the fading trace of a mild infection or the first sign of a liver losing its function. The clinician's work is to decide which pattern the story fits, and then to ask which dangerous member of that pattern could produce the same picture. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is no substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient.

A short list of lethal possibilities belongs at the front, each paired with the finding that would reveal it. A perforated peptic ulcer declares itself through sudden severe pain with a rigid, motionless abdomen, and the loss of the normal dullness over the liver is the clue that gas has escaped beneath the diaphragm. A variceal hemorrhage appears in a patient who already carries the marks of chronic liver disease, who vomits a large volume of fresh blood and then turns pale, sweaty, and faint. Ascending cholangitis, which is infection behind a blocked bile duct, shows itself as fever with shivering, yellowing of the skin and eyes, and pain in the right upper abdomen. Pancreatic necrosis is betrayed not by the first hours of pain but by a patient who fails to improve, in whom organ failure persists and fever develops, and fulminant hepatic failure is revealed by a drowsy or confused patient, a liver that can no longer be felt as it shrinks, and blood that will not clot.

Disease of the gut and the liver is often advanced before it is noticed, partly because of its nerve supply and partly because of the reserve of the liver. The organs of the abdomen are supplied by nerves that sense stretching and contraction rather than precise location, so an early tumor, an early ulcer, or an early scar produces a discomfort the patient cannot place. The liver continues to work while much of it is being replaced by scar, which is why a patient may feel entirely well while the disease is already established. The first sign is therefore often not pain but a change in what the body can do, whether the failure to clear a yellow pigment, the failure to clot blood, or the accumulation of fluid in the abdomen.

Peptic disease begins where the lining of the stomach or the duodenum is injured faster than it can repair itself, and the two injuries that matter most are infection by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori and the repeated use of medicines that reduce the protection of the stomach. The injury is usually painless until it is deep, so a patient may carry an ulcer for a long time and remember only a period of indigestion, and the pain characteristically comes when the stomach is empty and eases with food. The same disease can produce no pain at all and declare itself by bleeding, which is why an unexplained anemia in an older patient is a reason to think of the stomach. The clinician should ask about painkillers taken for joints or headaches, because many patients do not consider these to be medicines. The finding that would make ulcer disease unlikely is a pain clearly provoked by food and relieved by fasting, or a picture the history explains better as something else.

The two complications that convert peptic disease into an emergency are bleeding and perforation, and each has its own bedside signature. Bleeding may be small and chronic and show itself only as a falling blood count, or it may be sudden and large, with vomited blood or black, tarry stool and the signs of a circulation short of volume. Perforation produces the moment the patient remembers exactly, a severe pain that starts in the upper abdomen and spreads, and an abdomen that is rigid and still. The finding that reveals perforation most clearly is the rigid abdomen together with the loss of the normal dullness over the liver, since gas beneath the diaphragm changes the note obtained when that area is tapped. The decision that follows is surgical rather than medical, and the finding that would make that decision wrong is another cause such as pancreatitis or a clot in the mesenteric vessels.

Acute hepatitis is inflammation of the liver that develops over days, and its cause is usually one of the viruses named by letters, most often hepatitis A, hepatitis B, or hepatitis E. The illness begins like an ordinary infection, with fever, aching, nausea, and poor appetite, and the yellowing of the skin and eyes appears afterwards, often as the patient begins to feel better. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is often used as the line above which fever is recorded, but that figure is only an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted value changes with the route of measurement and the edition of the reference. Hepatitis A and hepatitis E are usually spread by contaminated water and food and usually resolve, while hepatitis B can pass through blood, sexual contact, and from a mother to her child, and it may become persistent.

The danger hidden inside acute hepatitis is fulminant hepatic failure, in which the liver loses its function faster than it can be repaired. The earliest sign is often a change in behavior or sleep rather than pain, and a patient who becomes drowsy, irritable, or difficult to rouse during a bout of hepatitis must be treated as an emergency. The breath may take on a sweet odor, the liver that was enlarged may become impossible to feel as it shrinks, and the blood stops clotting, so the patient bleeds from the gums, the nose, or the gut. A coarse flapping tremor may appear when the hands are held out, and the Glasgow coma scale records the level of consciousness through the response to voice, to pain, and to command; its contents and the figure that should cause alarm must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the version in use varies between services. The decision then is transfer to a unit that can support the failing organs, unless another cause such as low sugar or an infection of the brain explains the drowsiness.

Chronic hepatitis is the form that matters most for the clinician in a clinic, because it is quiet and because it ends in cirrhosis and in cancer of the liver. The boundary between acute and chronic is usually drawn at 6 months, and that interval is an illustration of the reasoning which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the definition shifts between services and editions. Hepatitis B becomes persistent most often in those infected very young, and it can be passed from a mother to her newborn, which is why the test belongs in the care of every pregnant woman wherever it can be offered. The patient usually has no symptoms at all, and testing is offered to anyone from a region where the virus is common, to a person who has injected drugs, and to a person with infection by the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV.

Cirrhosis is the end of a long process in which working liver tissue is replaced by scar, and its signs on examination follow directly from what the liver can no longer do. The liver stops clearing a pigment, so the eyes and skin may yellow, and it cannot make the proteins that hold fluid inside the vessels, so the legs swell and the abdomen fills. The pressure in the vein that drains the gut rises, and blood finds other routes back to the heart, which produces swollen veins at the lower end of the esophagus, dilated veins around the navel, and an enlarged spleen. The skin of the upper trunk may carry small red vessels with fine legs, the palms may be red, and the patient may bruise easily because the clotting factors are no longer made. Hormonal changes appear as loss of body hair, enlargement of the breast tissue in men, and shrinkage of the testicles, and the clinician who finds these signs knows that a jaundiced patient has chronic disease rather than a passing infection.

Decompensation is the moment when a compensated cirrhosis tips into failure, and it is recognized by four events that may arrive in any order. Fluid collects in the abdomen, and the examination finds a rounded, tense belly, shifting dullness when the patient turns, and a fluid thrill that confirms the fluid is free rather than contained. The brain is affected by substances the liver no longer clears, and the patient becomes forgetful, drowsy, or confused, sometimes with the flapping tremor described earlier. The swollen veins in the esophagus may burst, and the patient bleeds from the mouth or passes black stool. The fluid in the abdomen may itself become infected, which produces fever, pain, and a worsening of the general state, and this is easily missed because the signs are mild, so each of these events demands a decision rather than a period of waiting.

A variceal hemorrhage is the bleed that kills most quickly, and it deserves its own reasoning. Long-standing liver disease raises the pressure in the vein that drains the gut, and that pressure is carried backward into the veins of the esophagus and the upper stomach, which swell and become thin-walled. When one of them bursts, the patient vomits a large volume of blood, the pressure falls, and the liver that caused the problem is often no longer able to make the factors that clot the blood. The findings that reveal it are the marks of chronic liver disease, an enlarged spleen, free fluid in the abdomen, a history of heavy alcohol use or long-standing viral hepatitis, and a previous episode of bleeding. Where endoscopy is available the airway and the circulation are secured first and the esophagus is examined as soon as the patient is stable, and where it is not, the whole decision is to begin the journey to a place that has endoscopy and blood, immediately rather than after a second look.

Ascending cholangitis is an infection that climbs the bile ducts behind an obstruction, and it is dangerous because it can move from a fever to a failure of the circulation within hours. The classical picture is fever with shivering, yellowing of the skin and eyes, and pain in the right upper abdomen, and the patient may become confused or drowsy while the pressure falls. The finding that reveals the obstruction most reliably is a dilated duct system on ultrasound, and where that is available it should be sought at once. The decision is to relieve the obstruction and to treat the infection, and the finding that would make treatment alone the wrong answer is a duct that is completely blocked, because the pressure must be released for the treatment to work.

Acute pancreatitis is inflammation of a gland that lies behind the stomach, and it is usually caused by a stone passing through the bile duct or by alcohol, though many cases have no identified cause. The pain is steady, severe, and boring, it sits in the upper abdomen, and it often travels to the back and eases when the patient leans forward, while vomiting does not relieve it. The abdomen may be only mildly tender at first, which is one of the traps of the disease, because the pain is far greater than the examination suggests. The finding that would make pancreatitis unlikely is a pain that is clearly colicky and comes in waves, or an examination that finds another explanation such as a perforated ulcer or a blocked mesenteric vessel.

The severity of pancreatitis is judged at the bedside by what the disease is doing to the rest of the body rather than by the level of the enzymes. Mild disease settles within days, while severe disease is marked by organ failure that does not correct, and the clinician watches the pressure, the breathing, the urine output, and the level of consciousness to detect it. A systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the point at which the circulation must be considered compromised, and that figure is an illustration which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the pressure that matters depends on the patient's usual value, on age, and on any medicine being taken. A failure that persists beyond the first 2 days is a different illness from one that corrects when the circulation is supported, and that interval must also be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the definitions used by different services do not agree. The appearance of fever, a rising pulse, or a fall in the oxygen level of the blood suggests that part of the gland has died, which is pancreatic necrosis, and imaging confirms it, but a patient who seems to improve and then worsens is the one most likely to be developing infected dead tissue.

Appendicitis is the commonest surgical emergency of the abdomen, and its diagnostic value lies in the movement of the pain. The earliest pain is a vague ache around the navel, caused by the appendix stretching before it is inflamed enough to touch the wall, and it is often accompanied by loss of appetite, nausea, and a mild fever. Over some hours the pain moves to the right lower abdomen, becomes sharp and well localized, and is made worse by movement, by coughing, and by the jarring of a heel drop. The examination then finds tenderness at a point in the right lower quadrant, guarding of the wall, and pain in that place when the left side of the abdomen is pressed, which is the sign that the inflammation has reached the peritoneum.

Several dangerous conditions imitate appendicitis, and they must be considered before the diagnosis is settled. In any woman of childbearing age, a pregnancy outside the uterus produces pain, fainting, and the signs of internal bleeding, and a pregnancy test is the single step that changes the reasoning more than any other. Torsion of an ovary, an infection of the kidney, a stone in the ureter, and a twisted piece of bowel each produce pain in the same region, and the clinician who examines the urine, the flank, and the hernial openings will not be caught by surprise. In children the lymph nodes inside the abdomen can inflame after a viral illness and produce an almost identical picture, which is why repeated examination over hours is the safest course when the child is stable. In older adults the appendix may lie behind the colon or low in the pelvis, so the pain and the tenderness appear elsewhere, and in pregnancy the growing uterus pushes the appendix upward and the diagnosis is easier to miss.

Inflammatory bowel disease is a group of conditions in which the immune system attacks the lining of the gut, and the two main forms are ulcerative colitis, which affects the colon continuously from the rectum, and Crohn disease, which can affect any part of the gut in patches and can burrow through the wall. Ulcerative colitis produces bloody diarrhea, urgency, cramping pain before the stool, and a feeling of incomplete emptying, and the attacks come and go over months and years. Crohn disease produces pain, diarrhea that may not contain blood, weight loss, fever, and a tender mass in the right lower abdomen, and because the disease reaches through the wall it can form tunnels to other organs, narrow the bowel, or open onto the skin. The clinician should ask about blood in the stool, weight, night symptoms, and family history, and should not settle on irritable bowel when any of these are present.

What makes inflammatory bowel disease worth its own reasoning is that it speaks through organs far from the gut. The joints may swell and hurt, especially the large joints of the legs and arms, and pain in the lower back that is worse at rest and improves with movement suggests inflammation of the spine rather than a mechanical strain. The skin may show tender red nodules on the shins or painful ulcers that do not heal, and the eyes may become red, painful, and sensitive to light, which is a reason to ask about vision directly because the patient may not connect it with the bowel. The mouth may carry ulcers, and the liver and bile ducts may develop a chronic inflammation that appears as an abnormal liver test long before any symptom. A blood count may fall because of ongoing loss of blood and of inflammation, so the patient may be anemic without any visible bleeding, and the joint, skin, and eye problems often follow the activity of the bowel while the liver and spine problems run their own course.

The complications of inflammatory bowel disease are the reason the diagnosis matters, and the most feared is a sudden widening of the colon with loss of its muscle tone, which produces a distended, tender abdomen, fever, a fast pulse, and a patient who looks toxic. A narrowing of the bowel produces colicky pain, distension, and vomiting, and a tunnel between the bowel and the bladder, the vagina, or the skin produces a discharge that the patient may find hard to describe. Bleeding can be heavy, and long-standing disease of the colon raises the risk of cancer, which is why the duration and the extent of the disease are recorded with care. The decision to treat the inflammation is the right answer when there is clear evidence of active disease in the bowel, when the complications are absent, and when infection has been excluded. It is the wrong answer when the patient has a fever and bloody diarrhea that may be an infection rather than a flare, because suppressing the immune response in that situation can be dangerous, and the stool test together with the story of travel and recent treatment is what decides between the two.

The history of a digestive complaint is taken with a discipline that leaves nothing to memory, and the Oldcarts framework is a useful way to keep the account complete. The clinician asks about the site, the way the symptom began, its character, what makes it better or worse, and what accompanies it, and then asks the patient to compare this episode with any earlier one. The bowel habit belongs in the same conversation, including the frequency, the consistency, the color, any blood, any mucus, and any change in what the patient considers normal. Medicines are asked for by name and by purpose, with particular attention to painkillers, and alcohol and tobacco are recorded in the patient's own units rather than dismissed. Travel, water, food, sexual history, injections, and family history of cancer or of bowel disease complete a picture that no examination can replace.

The examination begins before the hand touches the abdomen, with the general appearance, the color of the skin and eyes, the state of hydration, and the alertness of the patient. The hands are examined for redness of the palms, the nails for clubbing or a change in shape, and the eyes for yellowing, because each is a visible sign of disease that has been present for some time. The abdomen is then inspected, listened to, percussed, and finally palpated, with the most painful area left until the end, and the hernial openings, the groins, and the umbilicus are sought in every patient. The liver is measured by its span, the spleen is sought as a dullness that moves with breathing, and free fluid is detected by shifting dullness and by a thrill. A rectal examination is performed when there is bleeding or an unexplained picture, and the testicles are examined in every man or boy with abdominal pain, because torsion can present as abdominal pain alone.

In a hospital the laboratory and the imaging are asked specific questions, and the reasoning that directs them is the reasoning used at the bedside. The pattern of the liver tests is more informative than any single value, because a rise dominated by the enzymes released from liver cells points toward hepatitis, while a rise dominated by the enzymes of the bile ducts points toward obstruction. Ultrasound answers whether the bile ducts are dilated, whether the liver is irregular, whether the spleen is enlarged, and whether fluid is present, and it is the first image to obtain in most patients with jaundice. Computed tomography, or CT, and magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answer particular questions about the pancreas, the ducts, and masses that ultrasound cannot reach, while endoscopy looks directly at the lining of the esophagus, the stomach, and the colon and can take a sample.

Where no laboratory and no imaging exist, the diagnostic task narrows to one decision: can this patient be watched here, or must this patient travel. The clinic has three instruments that never fail, which are the history, the repeated examination, and the observation of the patient over time, and they are used more thoroughly rather than less. A patient with a soft abdomen, stable vital signs, a pain that is settling, and a plan for review within hours may be watched, provided the patient can return and the clinician writes down what should prompt a return sooner. A patient with a rigid abdomen, a falling pressure, a rising pulse, vomiting of blood, a pain severe beyond the appearance of the abdomen, or a fever with yellowing and confusion must travel, and that decision should be made early rather than after a second examination confirms what the first already suggested. The clinician should not be reassured by a normal temperature in an older or immune-suppressed patient, because the response may be blunted while the disease advances, and pain relief may make the abdomen look calmer without changing the disease behind it.

A constructed illustration may fix these habits, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a man of about 50 who has drunk heavily for many years, who arrives with vomiting of fresh blood and black stool, and whose palms are red and whose abdomen is distended with fluid. Those details are the marks of chronic liver disease, and the source of the blood must be treated as variceal until endoscopy shows otherwise. Now imagine a woman of about 25 with pain that began around the navel and has moved to the right lower abdomen, whose pulse is 110 beats per minute and whose temperature is 38 degrees Celsius, and each of those figures must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the values that should trigger action differ with age, fitness, pregnancy, and the definitions in use. The first patient needs a unit with endoscopy, blood, and a surgeon, and the second needs a surgeon's opinion before the picture becomes obvious, and neither story should be applied to a living person without a full assessment.

The record of a digestive illness should show the thinking and not only the findings, including what was considered, what was excluded, and what would change the plan at the next review. The clinician should write down the time of each examination and what changed since the last, because the trajectory of an abdominal illness is often the most important single piece of evidence. Safety netting belongs in the record and in the conversation, since the patient must be told which symptoms should bring him back, how quickly, and where to go if the clinic is closed. The signs worth naming are a pain that becomes severe or generalized, vomiting of blood or black stool, a fever with yellowing, a swelling of the abdomen, a new confusion, and the inability to pass stool or gas.

To summarize, gastrointestinal and hepatic disease is read by pattern: the obstruction of a tube, the inflammation of a wall, the loss of continuity, the failure of the liver as a factory, and the rise in pressure that follows when blood cannot pass through it. The dangerous possibilities are named where the disease is described, among them a perforated ulcer, a variceal hemorrhage, ascending cholangitis, pancreatic necrosis, and fulminant hepatic failure, and each is paired with the finding that reveals it. Peptic disease, acute and chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis with its stigmata, pancreatitis, appendicitis, and inflammatory bowel disease with its manifestations far from the gut are all approached in the same way, from the history and the examination toward a ranked list that weighs both likelihood and danger. The same reasoning serves in a hospital where endoscopy, imaging, and surgery are at hand and in a clinic where the recognition of the abdomen that must travel is the whole diagnostic task. Every number in this chapter, whether a temperature, a pressure, an interval, a score, or a laboratory value, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. The clinician who examines again, records the change, and asks for help early will serve the patient better than the one who waits for the picture to become unmistakable.

# Chapter 48 — Endocrine and Metabolic Disease

The endocrine and metabolic diseases arrive dressed as ordinary complaints. The patient who is tired, thirsty, passing urine at night, losing or gaining weight, feeling the cold, or feeling too warm rarely says the word hormone, and a clinician who waits for an endocrine vocabulary will wait a long time. The reasoning that organizes this chapter is one idea: a hormone is a messenger, so a disorder of a gland is a disorder of a signal, and the findings are the predictable consequences of too much or too little of one messenger acting on organs built to respond to it. Once the clinician knows what the messenger normally does, excess and deficiency can be reasoned out rather than memorized, and the examination becomes a set of confirmations instead of a search. That is why the history and the hands still carry most of the diagnosis, and why a laboratory that measures hormones within hours confirms a hypothesis rather than replacing it. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

Two of the lethal presentations are metabolic, and either can be present before any disease of a gland has been named. Hypoglycemia, a glucose too low for the brain to work with, produces sweating, trembling, hunger, a racing heart, confusion, peculiar behavior, and finally a decline in consciousness, and the finding that reveals it is a low glucose measured during the episode or a recovery that follows its correction. The patient who takes insulin or another medicine that lowers glucose is the one in whom it must be suspected first, and a drowsy patient without an obvious cause is the one in whom it must not be missed. Diabetic ketoacidosis announces itself with deep sighing breathing, a breath that smells of acetone, vomiting, abdominal pain, thirst, heavy urination, and a drowsiness that can be mistaken for a surgical abdomen. The finding that identifies it is a raised glucose with ketones in the blood or the urine and a shift in the body's acid balance. Neither emergency can be settled by the shape of the illness alone, which is why both are named before the ordinary reasoning begins.

The other fatal presentations belong to the thyroid, the adrenal gland, and calcium, and each is revealed by a pattern rather than by a single number. Thyroid storm is severe overactivity of the thyroid gland, usually in a patient with known disease who is then stressed by infection, surgery, or childbirth, and it produces fever, a pulse far faster than the temperature would explain, agitation, sweating, and sometimes heart failure or a decline in consciousness. The patient with warm moist skin, a fine tremor, and a staring look is the one in whom it must be considered. Myxedema coma is the opposite extreme in long-standing untreated thyroid failure, and it produces a low temperature, a slow pulse, shallow breathing, dry skin, a hoarse voice, and a stupor that deepens. Adrenal crisis is the failure of the adrenal gland to make the hormone that maintains pressure and salt balance, and it presents as shock that the obvious cause does not explain, with a fall in pressure on standing, abdominal pain, vomiting, and sometimes darkened skin. Hypercalcemia produces confusion, constipation, abdominal pain, thirst, heavy urination, weakness, and stones in the kidney, and the finding that reveals it is a raised calcium on the laboratory result, sometimes with a shortened interval on the electrocardiogram, or ECG.

None of that list needs to be memorized once the underlying loop is understood, because each gland corrects itself through a signal that travels back to the brain. The hypothalamus senses what the body needs and instructs the pituitary, which instructs the thyroid, the adrenal cortex, and the gonads, and each target gland sends a signal back that quietens the instruction when enough hormone is present. This is why a hormone result must be read as a pair rather than as a single value: a low target hormone with a high instructing hormone means the gland itself has failed, while a low target hormone with a low instructing hormone means the problem lies above it. A clinician who holds this loop in mind can predict that a failing thyroid will slow the pulse and cool the body, while an overactive one will speed the pulse and warm it, and can then look for exactly that.
