Diabetes is the endocrine disease that most often walks in through the ordinary door, and it appears in two main forms. In type 1 diabetes the cells that make insulin are destroyed, usually by an immune attack, so the hormone that moves glucose into the tissues disappears and glucose accumulates in the blood while the cells starve; this form tends to appear in the young and to declare itself quickly. In type 2 diabetes the hormone is still made but the tissues answer it poorly, so the gland works harder until it cannot keep the glucose down; this form appears later, is often silent, and is frequently found beside raised pressure and a large waist. The classic symptoms of both are thirst, passing large volumes of urine, particularly at night, weight loss, blurred vision, tiredness, and repeated infections of the skin or the genital tract. The weight loss of type 1 diabetes is the loss of muscle and fat because the body cannot use the glucose it has, which is why a young person who loses weight while eating well is a diagnostic signal rather than a good sign. Nothing here is a matter of discipline; it is a failure of a signal, and the clinician who hears it early can prevent the emergencies that follow.

The diagnosis rests on measuring glucose rather than on the story alone, and the figures used to draw the line are illustrations that must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because thresholds differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. A fasting glucose at or above 7 millimoles per liter is commonly used as one such line, and the listener should treat that figure as reasoning made visible rather than as a rule that can be applied without the local standard. The glycated hemoglobin, which reflects the average glucose over the preceding weeks, is used in many services, and its own threshold must be confirmed in the same way, since assays and populations differ. What matters diagnostically is that a single raised value is not a diagnosis; it is a reason to repeat the measurement, to ask whether the patient was fasting, and to ask whether illness or a steroid was raising the glucose. In a clinic without a laboratory, the same reasoning is carried by the history of thirst and heavy urination, by the smell of acetone on the breath, by a wound that will not heal, and by the weight measured at successive visits.

Diabetic ketoacidosis occurs when insulin is so deficient that the body breaks down fat for fuel and makes acids called ketones faster than it can clear them, and it is most common in type 1 diabetes, though it can appear in type 2 diabetes under severe stress. The patient is thirsty, passes large volumes of urine, vomits, complains of abdominal pain, breathes deeply and rapidly, and may have a fruity smell on the breath, while the skin is dry and consciousness can fall. The findings that identify it are a raised glucose, ketones in the blood or the urine, and a shift in the acid balance, and the clinician must look for the infection, the missed medicine, the heart attack, or the pregnancy that provoked it. The hyperosmolar state belongs to type 2 diabetes, where enough insulin remains to prevent ketones but not enough to hold glucose down; the glucose climbs very high over days, the patient passes enormous volumes of urine and becomes profoundly dry, and drowsiness deepens. Because ketones are absent, that picture can be mistaken for a stroke or an infection.

Hypoglycemia is the mirror emergency and the more immediately dangerous of the two, because the brain has no store of glucose and begins to fail within minutes. The early signs come from the body's own alarm, with sweating, trembling, a racing heart, pallor, hunger, and a feeling of dread, and they may be absent in a patient who has had diabetes for many years or who takes a medicine that blocks them. The later signs are the signs of a brain without fuel: confusion, strange behavior that may be mistaken for drunkenness, difficulty speaking, blurred vision, a seizure, and a decline in consciousness. The finding that confirms it is a low glucose measured during the episode, and the finding that proves it afterwards is a recovery that follows the correction of glucose, which is one of the few diagnostic acts in medicine that is also the treatment. The clinician should ask who is at risk: the patient who has taken too much glucose lowering medicine, eaten too little, exercised unusually, or drunk alcohol, and the patient whose kidneys or liver are failing. The finding that would make the correction of glucose the wrong answer is another cause of the same picture, such as a stroke or a seizure disorder, but when the glucose is low the correction is never wrong to try.

The complications of diabetes are where ordinary complaints return, and each is the predictable consequence of glucose damaging small and large vessels and the nerves. Damage to the vessels of the eye causes bleeding and swelling in the retina, which is why the back of the eye is examined in every patient with diabetes, and why failing vision in such a patient is not automatically a matter of new glasses. Damage to the vessels of the kidney causes protein to leak into the urine and the filtering power to fall, and it declares itself first through a urine test rather than through symptoms. Damage to the nerves causes numbness in a glove and stocking pattern, burning pain at night, and the loss of the warning sensation that protects the foot, so a patient can walk on a blister until it becomes an ulcer and then a deep infection. Damage to the large vessels causes heart attacks, strokes, and poor circulation in the legs, and the patient with diabetes may not feel the chest pain that would bring another patient to the door. The clinician who examines the feet, the eyes, and the urine at every opportunity is doing the highest yield examination in this chapter, and it costs almost nothing.

An overactive thyroid gland floods the body with a messenger that sets the metabolic rate higher, and every sign can be predicted from that single effect. The patient loses weight while eating well, feels hot, sweats, has a racing and sometimes irregular pulse, feels anxious and restless, has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands, and passes frequent stools. The skin is warm and moist, the hair thins, the eyes may bulge or stare, the neck may show an enlarged gland, and a woman may notice that her periods have become light or have stopped. In an older patient the same excess may appear only as an irregular pulse, breathlessness, or weight loss, and the diagnosis is easily missed. Thyroid storm is this state pushed to an extreme by stress, and it is why a patient with a racing pulse, a fever, and agitation must have the thyroid considered even when an infection seems to explain everything. Where a laboratory exists, the finding that reveals the excess is a raised thyroid hormone level with a suppressed instructing hormone, and where it does not, the combination of warm moist skin, a tremor, a goiter, and weight loss has to carry the diagnosis.

An underactive thyroid gland produces the mirror image, and again every sign follows from a metabolic rate that has fallen. The patient gains weight, feels cold when others are comfortable, moves and speaks slowly, sleeps more, has constipation, dry skin, coarse hair, and a low mood that can be mistaken for depression. The pulse is slow, the tendon reflexes relax slowly when they are tapped, the voice may become hoarse, the face puffy, and the ankles may swell without heart or kidney disease. In an older patient the picture can be mistaken for dementia, and in a pregnant patient it matters for the developing child. Myxedema coma is the extreme form, arriving when long-standing thyroid failure is stressed by cold, infection, or a sedative medicine, and the temperature falls, the pulse slows, breathing becomes shallow, and consciousness declines. The finding that reveals the underlying state is a low thyroid hormone level with a raised instructing hormone, but in the clinic the diagnosis is made from the appearance, the slow pulse, the cool skin, and the history, and the medicine, when it is given, is judged by the response.

The adrenal cortex makes two kinds of hormone that matter here: cortisol, which defends the body against stress, and aldosterone, which holds salt and water and keeps the pressure up. When the gland itself fails, both are lost, and the patient complains of tiredness, weakness, weight loss, dizziness on standing, a craving for salt, nausea, and abdominal pain, while the skin may darken in the creases, the scars, and the gums. The finding that suggests it is a fall in pressure when the patient stands, and the laboratory may show a low sodium with a raised potassium, a pattern few other conditions produce. Adrenal crisis is the decompensation, presenting as shock, dehydration, vomiting, abdominal pain, and confusion, often after an infection or a surgical procedure in a patient whose glands cannot answer the demand. The finding that reveals it is a low cortisol measured at the moment of stress together with the clinical picture, and the response to the correction of the missing hormone is itself strong evidence. This is the diagnosis behind a patient who does not improve with the treatment that should have worked, and it is why the history of steroid medicines is asked in every collapse.

Too much cortisol produces a different and equally predictable set of signs, whether the excess comes from a tumor of the pituitary, a tumor of the adrenal gland, or, most commonly, a steroid medicine taken for another disease. The patient gains weight around the trunk while the arms and legs stay thin, the face becomes round and red, the skin thins and bruises easily, purple stretch marks appear on the abdomen, the thigh muscles weaken, and the pressure rises. The finding that reveals the cause is the level of cortisol and its behavior over the day, but the first step is always to ask what medicines the patient takes, because a steroid is the commonest explanation and the one the clinician can see. It is also the reason a steroid must never be stopped suddenly after a long course, since the suppressed adrenal glands may not wake up in time and the withdrawal can produce a crisis. When the problem lies above the adrenal glands, the signs of cortisol excess are joined by headache, visual disturbance, and a loss of other hormones, and the finding that points upward is a visual field missing its outer half.

Calcium is the metabolic subject that connects the bones, the kidneys, the gut, and the nerves, and its disorders show how a single ion can produce a whole patient. When calcium is too high, the patient may have stones in the kidney, bone pain, abdominal pain with constipation, confusion, drowsiness, thirst, and heavy urination, and the causes to consider are an overactive parathyroid gland and a cancer that releases a substance mimicking it. The finding that reveals it is a raised calcium on the laboratory result, and the electrocardiogram, or ECG, may show a shortened interval, but a single raised value must be repeated and read with the level of the protein that carries calcium in the blood. When calcium is too low, the nerves become excitable, and the patient has tingling around the mouth and in the fingers, cramps, muscle twitching, and sometimes a seizure or a spasm of the hand when the arm is compressed; the finding at the bedside is a twitch of the face when the nerve in front of the ear is tapped. Both extremes must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because reference ranges are set by the laboratory and the level at which treatment begins depends on the symptoms and the speed of the change.

Obesity belongs in this chapter as a diagnostic subject and not as a moral one, and the first task is to measure it rather than to judge it. The body mass index is a weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters, a rough tool that says nothing about where the fat lies, while a waist circumference adds the information that matters most, because fat around the abdominal organs is the fat that is metabolically active. The figures often quoted for these measures are illustrations of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the boundaries differ with ancestry, age, and the purpose for which the measure is used. A body mass index of 30 kilograms per square meter and a waist above 94 centimeters in a man or 80 centimeters in a woman are commonly used as such boundaries, and they are reasoning made visible rather than universal rules. The diagnostic value of the examination is to separate the common picture, in which weight gain comes from food and inactivity, from the uncommon pictures with another cause: an underactive thyroid, an excess of cortisol, a tumor of the pituitary, a medicine such as a steroid, and a disorder of the ovary.

The history in endocrine disease is asked in the same disciplined way as anywhere else, and the Oldcarts framework keeps the account complete while the mind runs ahead. The clinician asks about change in weight, appetite, thirst, urine volume, bowel habit, heat and cold tolerance, sweating, mood, energy, sleep, sexual function, and menstrual history, and about every medicine the patient takes, including every steroid, every supplement, and every product bought without a prescription. The family history matters more here than in most chapters, because many endocrine diseases cluster in families, and the past history matters for surgery, radiation to the neck, head injury, childbirth, and autoimmune disease. The pregnancy history and the medicines taken in pregnancy belong in the same conversation, since thyroid disease and diabetes both change the care of a mother and a child.

The examination begins before the patient is undressed, with the weight, the height, the waist, the pulse, the pressure, and the temperature, and with the general impression of the face, the skin, and the way the patient moves. The clinician looks for a fine tremor of the outstretched hands, warm or cool skin, dry or moist palms, thinned hair, a puffy face, a hoarse voice, and a slow or quick way of talking and moving. The neck is inspected and palpated while the patient swallows, because the thyroid gland rises with the swallow and a nodule or a goiter is often found only this way, and the eyes are examined for a stare, a bulge, and a lid that lags behind the movement of the eyeball. The eyes are also examined for the pale inner lining that suggests anemia, and the mouth for darkening of the gums, which belongs to adrenal failure. The abdomen is examined for the distribution of fat and for purple stretch marks, the legs for swelling, and the feet for numbness, ulcers, and the pulses that should be felt. The pressure is measured with the patient lying and then standing, and the proximal muscles are tested by asking the patient to rise from a chair, because weakness there is a sign the clinician can see while the patient moves.

In a hospital the laboratory turns a hypothesis into a result within hours, and the reasoning that directs it is the same reasoning used at the bedside. A glucose measurement at the bedside answers the first question in any patient who is confused, drowsy, or unwell, and it is the single most useful test in these emergencies because it is immediate and because its correction treats what it finds. The thyroid hormones with the instructing hormone answer the thyroid question, cortisol measured at the moment of stress answers the adrenal question, and calcium, sodium, potassium, and the acid balance answer the metabolic questions, and each must be read against the reference range of the laboratory that produced it. Imaging by ultrasound, computed tomography, or CT, and by magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, finds tumors of the pituitary and the adrenal glands, while a sample of a thyroid nodule examined under the microscope names the cells. The clinician should say what he expects each test to show before it is sent, so that a result at the edge of the reference range is recognized as an uncertainty rather than absorbed as an answer.

In a clinic whose equipment is a stethoscope, a torch, a thermometer, and perhaps a urine test, the endocrine diagnosis rests on the appearance, the history, and the response to a single correction, and it is a serious form of reasoning rather than a lesser one. The clinician weighs the patient at every visit and records the change, counts the pulse, measures the pressure lying and standing, and examines the skin, the hair, the face, the eyes, the neck, and the feet in a fixed order so that nothing is skipped. A urine test that shows glucose and ketones changes the plan within minutes, and an inexpensive measurement of glucose in a drop of blood, where it exists, does the same. The response to a correction is the clinic's laboratory: a drowsy patient who wakes when glucose is given has hypoglycemia, a patient whose pressure returns when the missing hormone is replaced has adrenal failure, and a patient whose confusion clears when calcium is corrected has hypercalcemia. That logic has limits, because a response can be produced by more than one cause, so the clinician should record what was given, what changed, and what did not. The decision that matters most here is not which diagnosis to name but whether the patient can be watched in this clinic or must begin a journey to a hospital now.

The treatment decision follows the same rule as everywhere in this book: name the finding that would make treatment right and the finding that would make it wrong, and leave the dose, the route, and the duration to the protocol that governs the place where the patient lies. Treatment is the right answer when an emergency threatens the brain, the circulation, or the acid balance, when a deficiency is producing symptoms that limit life, or when an excess is damaging an organ that cannot wait. It is the wrong answer when the abnormality is mild and found by chance, when it is likely to be the effect of another illness or medicine, when it is measured at a time of acute stress, and when the patient is stable enough to allow the diagnosis to be completed first. The record of an endocrine problem should show the reasoning and not only the numbers, and a patient sent home must be told which changes should bring him back: vomiting, fever, a drowsy or confused state, a wound that will not heal, a pulse that feels too fast or too slow, or a weight that continues to fall.

A constructed illustration may make these habits concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine an older man brought in drowsy after several days of thirst, heavy urination, and a chest infection, whose bedside glucose is markedly raised, whose skin is dry, and whose breathing is deep; the clinician who measures the glucose first finds the thread that explains the confusion and then looks for the infection that provoked it. Now imagine a patient who collapses after an illness and whose pressure does not respond to the treatment that should have worked, in whom a fall in pressure on standing and darkening of the gums are the clues that lead to the adrenal gland. None of these patients is real, and none of the stories should be applied to a real person without a full assessment, but each shows a different road into the same reasoning.

To summarize, the endocrine and metabolic diseases are disorders of messengers, and the signs of each are the predictable consequences of too much or too little of a signal acting on organs built to answer it. The lethal presentations are named at the bedside and each carries its revealing finding: hypoglycemia, a low glucose with a confused or drowsy patient; diabetic ketoacidosis, deep sighing breathing with ketones and an acid shift; thyroid storm, fever with a pulse out of proportion to it; myxedema coma, hypothermia with a slow pulse and declining consciousness; adrenal crisis, shock that the obvious cause does not explain; and hypercalcemia, a new confusion with constipation, thirst, and a raised calcium. The reasoning is the same where a laboratory measures hormones within hours and where a clinic has only a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, because in both places the history and the examination form the hypothesis and the test confirms it. Every score, threshold, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, and duration named in this chapter is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who is drowsy, thirsty, or collapsing without an explanation deserves a glucose measurement and a second look before any other answer is accepted.

# Chapter 49 — Renal and Urological Disease

The kidney is the organ that keeps the internal environment stable while it removes what the body cannot use, and when it fails, the failure is read not from the organ itself but from what the blood and the urine reveal about it. Renal and urological disease is therefore organized around one question that decides almost everything that follows: where in the stream the problem has occurred. The stream begins before the kidney, in the circulation that must deliver enough blood at enough pressure; it continues inside the kidney, in the filters and the tubules; and it ends after the kidney, in the tubes that carry urine to the bladder and then out of the body. A problem in any of those three places can produce the same symptoms and the same blood results, yet each demands a different action, and separating them early is the work of this chapter. This is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the local protocol of your own service.

Three dangers deserve to be named before the ordinary reasoning begins, because each is exposed by a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. An infected kidney that is also obstructed can destroy the organ and seed the bloodstream within hours, and the finding that betrays it is a fever with a tender, swollen flank on one side, often with a bladder that cannot empty and a collecting system that is dilated behind the blockage. Advanced kidney failure kills through what the kidney can no longer remove, and the findings that announce it are a potassium that has climbed with the changes it makes on an electrocardiogram, or ECG, deep sighing breathing from acid that cannot be excreted, confusion with a flapping tremor, or a rubbing sound heard over the heart when the pericardium is inflamed. The patient whose urine output has quietly stopped is the third danger, because a complete absence of urine is easy to overlook in someone who looks settled and complains of nothing. Each is treated as a question to be answered rather than a diagnosis assumed, and the answer is found by looking, measuring, and testing in a fixed order.

Once the dangers are in mind, the ordinary assessment is built on the division of kidney injury into the prerenal, the renal, and the postrenal. The prerenal problem is a kidney that is not being perfused well enough to work, the renal problem is injury to the kidney's own tissue, and the postrenal problem is an obstruction that prevents the urine from leaving. The division matters because it decides the action rather than the label, since a prerenal kidney usually recovers when the circulation is restored, a renal kidney may need time and specific treatment, and a postrenal kidney may recover as soon as the blockage is relieved. The clinician who asks which of the three is dominant at this moment is already closer to the right decision than one who recites a list of kidney diseases.

The first part of the stream is the circulation, and a kidney that is not perfused cannot make urine whatever its own structure may be. The causes are those that reduce the effective volume of blood, among them bleeding, vomiting, diarrhea, burns, a fever with poor intake, and the movement of fluid into the tissues or the abdominal cavity where it does no good. Heart failure and advanced liver disease reduce the flow forward even when the body is swollen with fluid, which is why a patient can be edematous and still be short of the volume that the kidney needs. Medicines that narrow the vessels or interfere with the kidney's own regulation of its blood flow are a common and often reversible cause, so the history of what was started and when belongs in every renal assessment. The findings that point here are a low jugular venous pressure, a pulse that rises on standing, dry mucous membranes, a falling weight, and a small volume of dark, concentrated urine, and the decisive test is the response to restoring the circulation.

When the problem lies inside the kidney, the picture changes, because restoring the circulation no longer repairs it. The filters may be inflamed by the body's own defenses in the glomerular diseases, injured by a prolonged lack of blood or by a poison, or damaged by an allergic reaction to a medicine that produces inflammation between the tubules. The findings that point to the glomerulus are blood and protein in the urine together, swelling around the eyes in the morning, a rising blood pressure, and sometimes a rash, joint pain, or a recent sore throat or skin infection that preceded the illness. A kidney injured by a medicine or by a period of low blood flow usually produces a milder sediment in the urine, and the history of the preceding days and weeks is what separates the two. A sample of kidney tissue may be needed to name the process, and the decision to ask for it belongs to the clinician who can act on the answer.

The end of the stream is the part that can be relieved, which makes it the most important to exclude in any patient who is unwell. Urine leaves the kidney through a narrow tube that can be blocked by a stone, a blood clot, a tumor, a narrowed segment, or a mass pressing from outside, and below the bladder the prostate, a stricture, a loaded bowel, or a bladder muscle that has failed can obstruct the flow. The finding that reveals obstruction above the bladder is a flank that is tender on one side, sometimes with an enlarged kidney felt by the examining hand, while obstruction at the bladder is revealed by a rounded, dull swelling above the pubic bone that the patient cannot empty. An obstructed kidney that becomes infected is the emergency that must never be missed, because treatment alone cannot clear an infection that sits behind a blockage, and the finding that secures it is a dilated collecting system in a patient who is clearly septic. Relief of the obstruction is a diagnostic act as well as a treatment, since the urine that follows confirms the cause and the change in the blood results confirms the effect.

The examination of the renal patient is first an examination of volume, and it begins with the general appearance. The clinician looks at the mucous membranes, the skin turgor, the eyes, and the weight compared with the last recorded weight, because a change in weight is the most reliable available measure of fluid gained or lost. The jugular venous pressure is estimated with the patient reclined, the pulse is felt for rate and volume and felt again after standing, and the blood pressure is measured lying and standing, since a fall on standing is a sign of a circulation that is short of volume. The skin is examined for pallor, bruising, scratching marks, a rash, and the small bleeding spots of a vasculitis, and the legs and the lower back are pressed for edema. Every one of these findings is combined with the others rather than trusted alone, because dryness, swelling, and a low pressure each mean different things in different patients.

The abdomen is then examined with the kidney in mind, since the kidney lies behind the peritoneum where its signs are easy to miss. The clinician inspects the flanks for swelling, asymmetry, and the scar of an earlier operation, and percusses the renal angle at the back with the flat of the hand before pressing more firmly, because tenderness there is a useful localizing sign. The kidneys are sought by bimanual palpation, with one hand lifting from behind and the other pressing forward, and a palpable kidney is described by its size, its surface, and whether it moves with breathing. The bladder is examined above the pubic bone for a rounded, dull swelling that the patient cannot empty, and the groin and the genitalia are inspected in any man with urinary symptoms. A bruit heard over the flank or the upper abdomen suggests that the blood supply to the kidney is narrowed, and it is worth seeking in a patient with difficult blood pressure or deteriorating function.

Urine is the kidney's report, and its volume, color, and contents carry more information than any single blood value. The volume is measured rather than estimated, over a fixed interval and against the fluid the patient has taken, and in a hospital this is done every hour or every few hours while in a clinic a jug and a watch may be all that is needed. An output of 400 milliliters in a day is often quoted as the point at which urine is said to be reduced, and a passage of almost nothing over 2 days is called anuria, but both figures are conventions that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the boundaries are written differently for children and adults and for different services. The passage of a small volume of concentrated urine suggests that the kidney is working while the circulation is short, whereas a normal volume of dilute urine in a patient who is clearly unwell suggests that the kidney has lost its ability to concentrate. A complete absence of urine is a different problem again, and the first question is whether the bladder is full or empty, because retention and failure look alike to the patient and entirely different to the examiner.

Chronic kidney disease is recognized from its consequences and its duration rather than from a single reading, because one abnormal value may be a passing injury. A kidney that has been damaged for months loses its ability to make red blood cells, so anemia appears; it loses its ability to activate vitamin D and to clear phosphate, so the bones soften and the calcium falls; it cannot excrete acid, so the blood becomes acidic; and it cannot rid the body of potassium, so the potassium creeps upward. The estimated glomerular filtration rate, calculated from the blood creatinine together with age and sex, is the figure used to describe the stage of the loss, and the boundaries between the stages must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since laboratories and editions report the value differently. A previous measurement of kidney function, an old record of the urine, or a note of an earlier blood result is worth more than any calculation made today, because it establishes the baseline against which the present value must be read. In chronic disease the kidneys are usually small and the patient anemic, while in an acute injury the kidneys are often of normal size and the illness is short with a clear trigger.

Infection of the urinary tract is the commonest renal problem in ordinary practice, and it is a spectrum rather than a single illness. At one end is the uncomplicated infection of the bladder, which produces burning on passing urine, a need to go often and urgently, pain above the pubic bone, and urine that is cloudy or offensive, with no fever and no flank pain. At the other end is infection that has climbed to the kidney and from there into the blood, which produces fever, shivering, pain in one flank, vomiting, and sometimes confusion or a fall in blood pressure. Between those ends lie the infections that are complicated by an underlying problem, among them a stone, a catheter, a pregnancy, diabetes, a kidney that is malformed, a prostate that does not drain, or defenses suppressed by illness or treatment. The place of a patient on that spectrum is decided by the whole picture rather than by a urine test alone, because a positive test can be a harmless finding in someone with no symptoms.

The dangerous forms of urinary infection are named as they arise, together with the finding that reveals each. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or above with pain in one flank suggests that the kidney is involved, though that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A patient with a known stone, a recent instrument passed into the urinary tract, or a known obstruction who becomes feverish may have an infected obstructed kidney, and the finding that reveals it is a dilated collecting system behind the blockage. An older patient may show no urinary symptoms at all and present instead with confusion, a fall, or a general decline, so the urine is examined in any unexplained illness in that group. A pregnant woman with a urinary infection and fever is treated as a more serious problem than the same infection outside pregnancy, because the risks to her and to the fetus are greater, and the decision to involve obstetric care is made early rather than late.

The diagnosis of urinary infection rests on the combination of symptoms, signs, and a test of the urine, and it is easily overcalled. A dipstick that reacts to nitrite or to leukocyte products supports the diagnosis, but neither finding is decisive, and a sample from a bag, a catheter, or a container that has stood too long may grow organisms that were never causing disease. Where a laboratory exists, a sample sent before treatment begins names the organism and its resistance, which matters most in a patient who is seriously ill, in a man, and in pregnancy. Where no laboratory exists, the clinician reasons from the symptoms, the temperature, the flank, and the bladder, and treats when the picture is convincing while watching for the findings that would demand referral. A patient who fails to improve, whose fever climbs, or who develops flank pain or vomiting needs reassessment rather than another course by habit.

Stones are common, they hurt intensely, and their importance lies less in the stone itself than in what it obstructs. The pain of a stone in the ureter begins in the flank and travels downward toward the groin, comes in waves, and is so severe that the patient cannot lie still, which is a useful contrast with the patient who has peritonitis and holds himself motionless. Blood in the urine is often present, though its absence means nothing, and the patient may be nauseated, may pass small gravel, and may have a frequency that mimics infection. The finding that turns a stone into an emergency is obstruction with infection, or obstruction of a single working kidney, and the anuria that follows complete blockage is a quiet catastrophe. A stone of 5 millimeters is often expected to pass on its own, but whether a particular stone will pass depends on its size, its position, and the anatomy of the patient, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the guidance differs between services and editions.

Pain in the flank is not always renal, and the clinician who assumes a stone may miss a lethal alternative. A leaking or ruptured aneurysm of the aorta produces pain that bores into the back or the flank, sometimes with a pulsatile mass and a falling blood pressure, and it must be considered in any older patient with sudden severe flank or back pain. A systolic reading below 90 millimeters of mercury is a late and dangerous sign in that situation and must never be awaited, though it is a common teaching illustration that needs checking against the current guideline and the local protocol. Infection of the kidney, inflammation of the pancreas, an inflamed gallbladder, a twisted ovary, an ectopic pregnancy, a spinal problem, and a torn muscle can each present in the same region, and the urine, the temperature, and the abdominal examination separate them. A patient with flank pain who is passing no urine, who has only one kidney, or who is feverish needs a decision rather than reassurance, and the findings that would make a stone the wrong answer are a pulsatile abdominal mass, a positive pregnancy test, or a fever with a tender flank that does not fit the colicky pattern.

Blood in the urine is a finding that must always be explained, and the explanation depends on where in the tract it came from. Blood that is mixed evenly through the urine, brownish or smoky, with protein and no clots, usually comes from the kidney itself, while bright blood with clots, or blood at the start or the end of the stream, points to the bladder or the lower tract. The finding that should most concern the clinician is painless visible blood in an older patient, in a smoker, or in someone with a history of exposure to dyes or rubber, because a tumor of the urinary tract can bleed without hurting and can be present for a long time before anything else appears. A young patient with visible blood after a sore throat or a skin infection may have inflammation of the glomerulus, and the findings that point there are blood and protein together with a rising blood pressure and swelling. A patient with visible blood needs the cause identified rather than the symptom treated, and where resources allow the urine is examined under the microscope, sent for culture, and the upper tract imaged.

The glomerular diseases deserve separate mention because they present through the whole body rather than through the urinary tract alone. The filters leak protein when they are inflamed, so the urine becomes frothy, the face and the ankles swell, and the weight rises; they leak blood, so the urine darkens; and they lose the ability to regulate salt and pressure, so the blood pressure climbs. The patient may report a recent infection, a rash, joint pains, mouth ulcers, hair loss, or a change in the color of the fingers in the cold, and any of these turns the urinary findings into a systemic question. A large loss of protein in the urine is dangerous, because it reduces the protein in the blood and increases the tendency to form clots. The findings that demand urgent help are breathlessness from fluid in the lungs, a blood pressure that is dangerously high, a rapidly rising creatinine, or a patient who is passing almost no urine.

Retention of urine is the urological emergency that is often mistaken for kidney failure, and the distinction is made with the hands. The patient cannot pass urine, has pain and a swelling above the pubic bone, and may leak small amounts constantly, which is overflow rather than control; the bladder is felt as a rounded, dull, tender mass that rises out of the pelvis as it fills, and catheterization releases a large volume and gives immediate relief. The causes include an enlarged prostate, a stricture, a stone, constipation, a nerve injury, and medicines that weaken the bladder, and in a catheterized patient the catheter itself may be blocked. Long-standing retention can damage the kidneys silently, so a patient with a chronically full bladder, a poor stream, and a rising creatinine needs assessment even when he is not in pain. A patient whose bladder control has changed suddenly, especially with back pain, weakness or numbness in the legs, or numbness around the saddle area, may have compression of the spinal cord or the nerves below it, and that patient needs urgent help rather than a wait.

Treatment in renal disease is a decision about which problem is reversible, and the finding that makes treatment right is the reversible one. A patient whose circulation is short needs volume restored, and the finding that supports that decision is a low jugular venous pressure with a concentrated urine that improves as the circulation is filled. A patient with obstruction and infection needs the kidney drained, while a patient with obstruction alone may be watched briefly if the kidney is working and the patient is comfortable. A patient whose kidney function has fallen for a long time may need preparation for replacement treatment rather than a search for a cure, and the findings that indicate this are small kidneys, anemia, bone change, and a history of abnormal results over months. The decision to start, to withhold, or to stop any of these treatments belongs to the clinician who is with the patient and knows the protocol, and the reasoning is set out here only so that the listener can follow it. A rapidly worsening picture, an uncertain cause, or a failure to respond makes the next step help rather than another observation.

In a hospital the renal patient is assessed with the laboratory and the imaging service, but the questions remain the same. The blood is examined for creatinine, potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, and the count of red cells, while the urine is examined for protein, blood, cells, casts, and organisms, and each test is worth sending only if its result would change what is done next. An ultrasound at the bedside can show whether the collecting systems are dilated, whether the bladder is full, and whether the kidneys are small, which answers the first three questions of this chapter within minutes. A computed tomography scan with contrast may be needed to find a stone or a mass, though the contrast itself must be weighed against the risk of further injury in a kidney that is already failing. A kidney biopsy names a glomerular disease that no other test can identify, and a culture with its sensitivities directs treatment when the infection is severe or has not responded. The clinician should say what each test is expected to show before it is ordered, so that a contradictory result is recognized as a surprise.

Where the equipment is a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is conducted with fewer answers available. The clinician measures the temperature and counts the pulse and the breathing, looks at the patient's color and hydration, examines the flanks with both hands, and percusses the bladder above the pubic bone. A jug and a watch turn the urine into a figure that can be followed, and the torch makes the meatus, the perineum, and the skin visible. The urine itself is inspected for color, cloudiness, blood, and clots, and a dipstick, if one is available, extends the examination rather than replacing it. The decision that follows is usually not a diagnosis but a disposition, which is whether the patient can be treated here, whether the obstruction can be relieved, and whether the journey must begin now. A patient with fever and a tender flank, a patient who is passing no urine with a full bladder, and a patient who is breathless with swelling and a rising blood pressure are all patients for whom the journey should start before the picture is complete, and the clinic's strength is that it can see the patient again, so that strength should be used deliberately.

A patient sent home with a renal or urinary problem must be told what would bring him back, and the instructions should name the findings rather than the disease. The patient should return if the pain worsens, if a fever appears or climbs, if he cannot pass urine at all, if he passes blood or clots, if he vomits and cannot keep fluid down, if he becomes breathless or swollen, or if he becomes confused or unusually sleepy. An arranged review is worth more than an open invitation, and the clinician should say where to go if the patient cannot wait. The record should show the urine volume with the time, the weight, the blood pressure lying and standing, the medicines recently started or stopped, and the reasoning that led to the plan. A note that records only a diagnosis leaves the next clinician unable to see what was considered, and in kidney disease the trajectory over hours matters most.

Two constructed illustrations may fix the habits of this chapter, and neither describes a real person. Imagine a woman of about 60 who arrives with fever, shivering, and pain in the right flank, whose urine is cloudy and whose blood pressure is falling; the clinician's first thought is not the urine test but the possibility of an infected obstructed kidney, and an ultrasound showing a dilated system changes the plan within the hour. Now imagine a young man in a clinic who has taken a painkiller for a sore back, has passed almost no urine for a day, and whose weight has risen; the questions about the medicine and the fluid intake are asked before any assumption is made. Neither story is real and neither should be applied to a patient, for they exist only to show how one finding can reverse the order of a differential.

To summarize, renal and urological disease is organized by asking where in the stream the problem lies, whether before the kidney in the circulation, inside it in the filters and tubules, or after it in the tubes and the bladder. The dangers are named at the bedside and not deferred, among them the infected obstructed kidney with a tender flank and a dilated collecting system, the advanced kidney failure whose consequences show on an electrocardiogram and in the breathing, the confusion, and the heart sounds, and the patient whose urine output has quietly stopped. The examination is an examination of volume as much as of organs, and the urine volume measured over time against the intake and the weight carries more than any single blood value. The same reasoning serves in a hospital with a laboratory and an imaging service and in a clinic where a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer must carry the decision. Every figure here, whether a temperature, a pressure, a volume, a concentration, or a duration, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient whose urine has stopped, whose flank is tender with fever, or whose kidney function is failing without explanation needs help and re-examination, never reassurance.

# Chapter 50 — Hematology and Oncology

Hematology and oncology meet at the bedside wherever a patient arrives with a tiredness that will not lift, a lump that was not there before, a fever with no source, or a bruise that appeared without a fall. The reasoning that organizes both subjects begins with what the patient noticed rather than with what the laboratory will later report. The blood is a tissue that can be sampled directly, which is its great advantage, and it is also a tissue that fails quietly, which is its great danger, because a marrow that produces too few cells gives no pain until the shortage becomes severe. A missed cancer is among the most serious diagnostic failures of ordinary practice, and it is usually missed not because the signs were absent but because they were never assembled. The clinician's task is to decide which product of the marrow is missing, why it is missing, and whether the cause must be answered today or can be investigated calmly over the following weeks. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

Several dangers must be named before the ordinary reasoning begins, each with the finding that would reveal it. The patient whose marrow is suppressed and who develops a fever may have an infection in the bloodstream that the ordinary defenses cannot contain, and the finding is a raised temperature in someone known to have too few infection-fighting white cells. The patient with an extreme number of abnormal white cells may have sludging of the blood in the small vessels of the lung and the brain, revealed by breathlessness, confusion, a headache, or a change in vision. A patient with a known or suspected cancer who develops a band of pain around the chest or the abdomen, weakness in the legs, and difficulty passing urine may have compression of the spinal cord, and that combination demands immediate help rather than an appointment next week. The patient whose face and neck swell, whose veins stand out on the chest wall, and who becomes breathless when lying flat may have obstruction of the large vein that returns blood to the heart. Each of these is a reason to act at once and to confirm afterwards, and none of them should wait for a scheduled review.

The marrow produces three things, and the reasoning from a low count follows the product that is missing. Red cells carry oxygen, and their shortage produces pallor, tiredness, breathlessness on effort, a racing pulse, and sometimes a rushing sound in the ears. White cells defend against infection, and their shortage produces fever, mouth ulcers, a sore throat, and infections that behave unusually or last longer than expected. Platelets seal small breaks in the vessels, and their shortage produces bleeding into the skin, bleeding from the gums and the nose, and bleeding that will not stop after a small cut. A count that shows one line low asks one question, a count that shows two asks another, and a count that shows all three low asks whether the whole marrow is being suppressed, replaced, or destroyed. This division turns a set of numbers into questions that the history and the examination can begin to answer.

Anemia is a finding and never a diagnosis, and the clinician who stops at the word has stopped before the work begins. The history asks how long the tiredness has been present, whether it came on slowly or suddenly, whether there has been bleeding from any site, whether the diet contains enough iron, and whether a long-standing illness, an infection, a pregnancy, or a medicine could explain it. The examination looks for pallor in the conjunctiva and the palms, for a smooth and sore tongue, for brittle nails, for an enlarged spleen, and for any sign of blood loss from the bowel or the womb. The pace matters more than the depth, because an anemia that develops over months allows the body to adapt, while one that develops in hours may present as collapse. A heart that races and a pressure that falls in an anemic patient are signs that the compensation is failing rather than that the anemia is mild.

The most important single step in anemia is the discovery of iron deficiency in an adult, because in a man or in a woman past the change of life it usually means that blood is being lost from somewhere, and the loss may be from a cancer of the bowel. The finding that reveals it is a low amount of iron in the blood together with a low store of iron, sometimes with small and pale red cells on the film, in a patient who has noticed nothing else. The stool may look normal and the bleeding may be invisible, so a normal appearance of the stool is not reassurance. The clinician must ask about a change in bowel habit, a sense of incomplete emptying, pain on passing stool, and any family history of cancer of the bowel. Iron deficiency in a young woman with heavy periods has an obvious explanation, but even then a second cause should be sought rather than assumed away. The figure that defines a low iron store is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since laboratories report it in different units and with different boundaries.

Marrow failure is recognized by the failure of more than one product at once. A patient may present with an infection that will not settle, bleeding from the gums, and a tiredness that has been growing for weeks, and that combination should raise the possibility that the marrow itself is the problem. The causes range from a shortage of a vitamin, through a medicine or a poison that suppresses the marrow, to a cancer of the blood that fills the marrow with abnormal cells, and to a marrow that has simply stopped working. The finding that begins to separate them is the film, where the appearance of the cells and the presence of immature forms change the direction of the search. The dangerous presentation is the patient with too few infection-fighting cells who develops a fever, because infection can advance within hours while the usual signs of inflammation are blunted or absent. In that patient, treatment is the right answer before the cause is confirmed, and the finding that would make treatment wrong is a clear alternative explanation for the fever, such as a reaction to a medicine.

Bleeding and bruising are read by their pattern, and the pattern points to the part of the clotting system that has failed. Small round spots that do not fade when pressed, called petechiae, together with bleeding from the gums, the nose, or the bowel, suggest that the platelets are too few or are not working, and they appear in a patient whose clotting proteins may be entirely normal. Large bruises in unusual places, bleeding into a joint, and bleeding that restarts hours after a cut has stopped suggest a problem with the clotting proteins, whether inherited or acquired. The history should ask about a tendency present since childhood, about medicines that thin the blood, about liver disease, and about a recent infection or pregnancy. The dangerous event is bleeding into the brain, and the finding that should raise it is a sudden severe headache with drowsiness, vomiting, or weakness in a patient known to have a bleeding tendency.

An enlarged lymph node is a common finding and a rare cancer, and the reasoning lies in the features of the node together with the story around it. A node that is small, tender, mobile, and accompanied by a sore throat or a skin infection is usually reactive, and it settles as the infection settles. A node that is hard, painless, fixed to the tissues beneath it, and growing over weeks deserves a different answer, especially when it sits above the collarbone, because that site drains the chest and the abdomen. The examination should describe the size, consistency, mobility, and exact site of every enlarged node, and it should look in the armpit, the groin, and the bend of the elbow as well as the neck. It should also look for an enlarged spleen, an enlarged liver, a rash, a wound, and a source of infection in the mouth, the throat, or the skin. The finding that would make a cancer the wrong answer is a clear local infection that fully explains the node together with a node that shrinks as that infection resolves, though the shrinkage must then be confirmed rather than assumed.

Any mass that a patient can feel, or that a clinician finds, must be explained rather than watched indefinitely, and the explanation follows the region in which it lies. A lump in the breast that is hard, irregular, fixed, or accompanied by a change in the skin or the nipple requires assessment, and what matters is not the texture alone but the whole pattern including the armpit. A lump in the testicle that is painless but firm, or a testicle that has become heavy, must never be treated as an infection without review, because delay changes the outcome. A lump in the neck, the mouth, or the throat that persists beyond the ordinary course of a sore throat, especially with hoarseness or difficulty swallowing, requires examination of the whole upper airway. A change in a mole, an ulcer that will not heal, and a new lump in the abdomen all belong to the same rule, which is that a persistent unexplained mass earns a diagnosis rather than a wait. The size at which a node or a lump becomes concerning is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted figure varies with the site and with the age of the patient.

Some cancers announce themselves through general symptoms that have no localizing sign, and these are the symptoms most easily attributed to stress, age, or a passing illness. Weight loss that was not intended, night sweats that soak the bedding, an itching that has no rash, a fever that comes and goes, and a loss of appetite or an early fullness after eating all belong in a short list that deserves investigation. The clinician should ask about the time course, whether the weight loss was deliberate, what the patient has stopped eating, and whether there is pain anywhere that has not yet been mentioned. The examination then looks for an enlarged liver or spleen, for enlarged nodes, for a mass, for pallor, and for a change in the skin or the nails. Fatigue is the most common of these symptoms and the least specific, and it acquires meaning only from its duration and from what accompanies it. The finding that reassures is a benign explanation that accounts for all the symptoms and that responds as expected, while a normal result in a patient whose story remains unexplained is a reason to continue rather than to stop.

Leukemia is better understood at the bedside by the speed at which it presents than by its classification, because the classification belongs to the specialist and the presentation belongs to the clinician who meets the patient first. The acute form arrives over days or a few weeks with the signs of marrow failure, so the patient may have an infection, bleeding, and profound tiredness together, and the film shows immature cells. The chronic form is often found by accident when a blood count is done for another reason, and the patient may have an enlarged spleen, a mild tiredness, or no symptoms at all, so the finding is the count rather than the complaint. The dangerous presentation of the acute form is the sludging of abnormal cells in the small vessels, revealed by breathlessness, confusion, a headache, and blurred vision in a patient whose count is extremely high. Whenever that combination is present, the patient needs urgent specialist help, and the clinician should not wait for a confirmatory test before asking for it. The exact figure that defines a dangerously high count is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold that triggers action differs between services and editions.

Lymphoma presents in much the same way whether it is given one name or another, and the reasoning follows the node and the general symptoms rather than the microscopic label. The patient may notice a painless lump in the neck, the armpit, or the groin, or may come with weight loss, night sweats, and itching, and sometimes with a fever that comes and goes. The examination looks for nodes in every accessible region, for an enlarged spleen and liver, and for a mass in the abdomen, and it records whether the nodes lie on both sides of the diaphragm, because that distribution guides the referral. The general symptoms matter because they change how quickly the patient should be seen, and the clinician should ask about them directly rather than wait for the patient to volunteer them. The dangerous complications are compression of the spinal cord, obstruction of the large vein returning blood to the heart, and blockage of the airway by a mass in the chest, and each has a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. A patient who is breathless when lying flat, whose face is swollen, or whose voice has changed must be treated as an emergency rather than as an outpatient.

The blood film is the most valuable single test in this chapter, and it is worth understanding what it can and cannot say. It can show the size and color of the red cells, which points toward iron deficiency or a shortage of a vitamin, and it can show immature white cells, which points toward leukemia. It can show whether the platelets are few, large, or clumped, and it can reveal parasites and abnormal shapes that change the whole direction of the assessment. The clinician who requests a film should say what question it is meant to answer, because a film reported without a question is often a film reported without an answer. When the film is abnormal or the picture does not fit, the next step is a sample of the marrow, and that decision belongs to the specialist who will interpret it. A normal film does not exclude serious disease, and it should not be used to dismiss a patient whose story continues to worry the clinician.

The warning signs of cancer are best remembered by walking through the systems rather than by memorizing a list, and the clinician who asks about them routinely will find the cases otherwise missed. In the chest, a cough that has changed or lasted for weeks, blood in the sputum, a hoarse voice, and breathlessness that is new all require a chest radiograph and an assessment of the upper airway. In the gut, difficulty swallowing, persistent indigestion, vomiting of blood, black stool, blood on the stool, and a lasting change in bowel habit are the signs that deserve a look inside. In the urinary tract, blood in the urine that is visible or found on testing, a poor stream, and a new need to pass urine at night require examination and imaging of the urinary tract. In a woman, bleeding after the change of life, bleeding between periods, and a discharge that is bloodstained or foul all require pelvic assessment. Each of these findings is ordinary in itself and becomes important through its persistence and through the age of the patient.

Other systems carry their own signs, and the same rule of persistence applies to every one of them. A lump in the breast or the armpit, a change in the nipple, and a discharge from the nipple in a woman who is not feeding require assessment, and in a man a lump in the breast is uncommon and should be treated with the same care. A change in the size, shape, color, or edge of a mole, an ulcer that will not heal, and a sore that bleeds require inspection of the whole skin rather than of the lesion alone. A new headache different from the patient's usual headache, a change in personality, a weakness on one side, and a seizure in an adult all require imaging of the brain. A lump in the testicle, a change in the voice, and a new and persistent pain in the back that is worse at night belong in the same set, and each should lead to a decision rather than to an explanation that the patient accepts politely. The clinician who names these signs aloud while examining the patient is far less likely to miss them.

Many patients who come with a fear of cancer do not have cancer, and the reasoning that helps them is the same reasoning that helps everyone else, conducted with an explicit acknowledgment of the fear. The clinician should ask what the patient has noticed, what the patient believes it means, and whether someone close has been ill, because the fear itself changes how the story is told and how the examination is received. The finding that reassures is a specific benign explanation that fits all the symptoms, together with a plan that says what will be done, what will be watched, and what should bring the patient back. A normal test on its own is a weak reassurance when the symptom remains, and a clinician who offers only a normal result may leave the fear untouched. Where a genuine risk factor is present, such as age, smoking, a family history, or a previous cancer, the reassurance must come from an appropriate assessment rather than from a kind manner alone. The patient dismissed with an explanation that does not fit the symptoms is the patient who returns later, and sometimes with a disease that has advanced in the interval.

In a hospital the blood count, the film, the clotting tests, and the chemistry of the blood are available together, and the reasoning decides the order in which they are used. The count answers how many of each cell are present, the film answers what they look like, and the clotting tests answer whether the proteins that form a clot are working, so each answers a different question. A sample of the marrow and a biopsy of a node or a mass give the tissue diagnosis, and they are requested when the less invasive tests have pointed to the marrow or to a particular organ. Imaging by computed tomography, or CT, and by magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, shows the extent of a mass, the involvement of nodes, and the state of the organs, and it answers a specific question rather than surveying the whole body. The substances called tumor markers are easily misused, because they can be raised in benign conditions and normal in cancer, and they are best used to follow a disease that is already known rather than to find one that is not. A test is worth ordering when its result would change what is done next, and the clinician who cannot say what either result would mean should not send it.

Where the clinic has a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, and perhaps the ability to send a blood film, the same reasoning is compressed into fewer steps. The history is taken with more care rather than less, because it is the one instrument that never runs out, and the examination is repeated rather than performed only once. The torch makes the mouth, the throat, the eyes, the skin, and the perineum visible, and it allows the conjunctiva and the palms to be inspected for the pallor of anemia. The decision that follows is usually not a diagnosis but a destination, and the clinician must decide whether to treat, to review, or to refer, and must say which finding would change that decision. A blood film, where it can be obtained, is worth more than a general count, because it can show cells that the count alone would hide. A referral made early with a clear question is a better gift to the patient than a diagnosis made late with a confidence the evidence did not support.

The decision about treatment is part of diagnosis even in a chapter about recognition, and it is best expressed as the finding that would make treatment right and the finding that would make it wrong. Treatment is the right answer when a patient with too few infection-fighting cells develops a fever, when abnormal cells are sludging in the small vessels, when the spinal cord is being compressed, and when bleeding continues from a site that cannot be controlled locally. In each of these situations the patient is at immediate risk, and waiting for confirmation would cost more than acting. Treatment is the wrong answer when a clear benign cause explains the findings, when the abnormality is a laboratory artifact that a repeat sample corrects, and when the diagnosis is not yet secure enough to justify a treatment that carries its own harms. The decision to begin or to withhold belongs to the clinician who knows the patient and the local protocol, and it is never made from a single number. The figures that define danger in each of these situations are illustrations of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because they differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories.

A constructed illustration may fix the reasoning, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a man of about 60 who has had back pain for some weeks and now cannot lift his feet properly, who has a band of numbness around the lower chest, and who has had difficulty starting his urine; the combination means compression of the spinal cord until it is proved otherwise, and it is an emergency. Imagine a woman who has lost weight without trying, who sweats at night, and who has a hard node above her left collarbone that does not hurt; that node drains the abdomen, and it earns an urgent assessment rather than a course of antibiotics. Imagine a young man with a painless swelling of one testicle that he mentions almost in passing, and the clinician who examines it and refers immediately rather than treating it as an infection. None of these people is real, and none of these stories should be applied to a real patient without a full assessment. Every age and interval used here is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. What the three stories share is that the decisive finding was available to the hand and the eye before any test was ordered.

Blood diseases and cancers also present through the consequences of a weakened defense against infection, and that route deserves its own place in the reasoning. A patient with a cancer of the blood, a patient receiving treatment that suppresses the marrow, and a patient with advanced infection by the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, may all develop infections that behave unusually or that are caused by organisms which rarely trouble a healthy person. The finding may be a fever with no localizing sign, a mouth ulcer that will not heal, a cough that persists, or a weight loss with diarrhea, and the clinician must ask about the treatments the patient is receiving and about the risk factors for HIV. The examination looks at the mouth, the skin, the nodes, the chest, and the perineum, because these are the places where such infections declare themselves. Tuberculosis belongs in this list, and it can present with a prolonged fever and weight loss in a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, even when the chest radiograph looks unremarkable. The finding that would make an infection the wrong answer is a clear non-infectious cause, but the threshold for treating a suppressed patient on the clinical picture is lower rather than higher.

To summarize, the blood diseases and the cancers are approached through the reasons a patient presents, which are anemia, infection and bleeding from a failing marrow, a node or a mass that must be explained, and the general symptoms of malignancy that have no localizing sign. The dangers are named early and each carries its revealing finding: a fever in a patient whose marrow is suppressed, sludging of abnormal cells in the small vessels, compression of the spinal cord, and obstruction of the large vein returning blood to the heart. Leukemia and lymphoma are read by their speed of onset and by the pattern of nodes and general symptoms rather than by their classification, and iron deficiency in an adult is treated as a possible cancer of the bowel until that possibility is set aside. The warning signs of cancer are sought by walking through the systems, and the patient who fears cancer is answered with a specific benign explanation and a plan rather than with a normal result alone. Every figure in this chapter, whether a count, a size, a reference range, or an interval, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. The same reasoning serves the hospital with a full laboratory and the clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, and in both the decisive step is often the finding that the hand can reach.

# Chapter 51 — Neurology

Neurology is the part of medicine in which the history and the examination decide more than any image, because the nervous system can be localized by reasoning alone and the hand and the eye often name the site first. Two questions are asked of every patient in this chapter: where in the nervous system is the trouble, and how fast is it moving. The first is answered by anatomy, by deciding whether the problem lies in the brain, the brainstem, the spinal cord, the nerve root, the peripheral nerve, the muscle, or the junction between nerve and muscle, since each level gives its own pattern of weakness, reflex change, and sensory loss. The second is answered by time, because the same weakness that has crept over a year means something entirely different from weakness that appeared in an hour. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

The dangerous presentations are named before the ordinary ones, because each carries a finding that can be sought at the bedside and each punishes delay. A stroke that is still within the window in which it might be reversed comes first, and the finding that reveals it is the sudden onset of a focal deficit, such as a face that droops on one side, an arm that drifts when both are held out, or speech that has become slurred or absent. A subarachnoid hemorrhage is so often misread as an ordinary headache that it deserves special suspicion, and the finding is a headache that reached full severity in an instant, sometimes followed by a stiff neck and a dislike of light. Compression of the spinal cord gives a band of pain around the trunk, weakness of both legs, numbness in the saddle region, and difficulty passing urine. A weakness that progresses over hours or days is the fourth, and the pattern that matters climbs from the feet upward while the reflexes disappear, since the danger is failure of the muscles of breathing.

The same reasoning must hold in two very different rooms, though the consequences of the answers differ. In a hospital with computed tomography, or CT, magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, a laboratory, and a specialist within call, the history and examination decide which image to obtain and how urgently. In a clinic whose equipment is a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same history and examination decide whether the patient can be observed here or whether the journey must begin now. A clinician who can localize a lesion by hand and eye uses the scanner better when it exists, because the request already contains the question. What travels between the two settings is the method, not the machinery.

The examination is a process of localization rather than a checklist, and each maneuver is chosen because it separates one level of the nervous system from another. Power is graded by comparing the two sides and by testing the limb against resistance and against gravity, and the distribution of the weakness, whether it is confined to one limb, one side, both legs, or the face and arm together, is more informative than its severity. Reflexes are sought because a brisk reflex points above the level of the reflex arc while a lost reflex points to the arc itself, and weakness with a lost reflex and wasting describes a lower motor neuron problem. Sensation is tested for light touch, pinprick, vibration, and position, and the pattern of loss, whether in a glove, in a stocking, in a band, or below a level, tells the clinician where to look. Coordination, gait, and the ability to stand with the feet together and the eyes closed complete a first survey, and a deficit that was maximal from the first moment points to a vascular event while one that spread over minutes points elsewhere.

Stroke is the sudden loss of function caused by an interruption of the blood supply to part of the brain, whether by a blocked vessel or by a hemorrhage, and its signature is a focal deficit of abrupt onset. The differentiation that matters most is from a seizure, a migraine, and a low blood glucose, because each can imitate a stroke and each is managed differently. A seizure may leave a temporary weakness behind, but the weakness follows the event rather than beginning it, and the account usually includes shaking, a loss of awareness, or a bitten tongue. A migraine may produce weakness or numbness that spreads slowly over many minutes and then resolves, and that march of symptoms separates it from the abrupt arrival of a stroke. A low blood glucose can produce confusion, sweating, a focal deficit, and even coma, and the finding that reveals it is a glucose measurement that is low; the value that defines hypoglycemia must be read against the current guideline and the local protocol, since it differs between laboratories and between patient groups.

A stroke still within the window in which treatment might reverse it is a medical emergency, and everything else pauses while that possibility is settled. The window is measured in hours from the moment the patient was last known to be well, and a figure such as 4 and a half hours is commonly quoted, but that boundary must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it has changed with successive trials and differs between services. The clinician must also establish whether the stroke is caused by a blocked vessel or by bleeding, because the treatments are opposites, and the tool that separates them at speed is the CT scan. A hemorrhage may declare itself by a sudden severe headache, vomiting, or a falling level of consciousness, while a blocked vessel often spares consciousness at the outset. The level of consciousness is recorded with the Glasgow coma scale, whose contents and alarming figure must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since its versions differ.

A subarachnoid hemorrhage is the diagnosis most often lost inside a headache, and it is named early here for that reason. It occurs when a vessel bleeds into the space around the brain, and its classic presentation is a headache of instantaneous onset, the worst the patient has ever felt, sometimes with vomiting, a stiff neck, a brief loss of consciousness, or a dislike of light. It is easily mistaken for migraine or tension, especially when it eases and the patient feels better, and that improvement is a trap because the bleeding may recur. The finding that reveals it in the first hours is a CT scan, and where the scan is negative and the suspicion remains high, the next step is examination of the cerebrospinal fluid obtained by lumbar puncture. A sudden, severe headache unlike any previous headache should not be sent home as a common headache, and the clinician who is unsure should seek advice rather than reassurance.

A transient ischemic attack is a focal neurological deficit that resolves completely, and it matters because it is a warning rather than a harmless event. The symptoms are the same as those of a stroke, including weakness on one side, difficulty speaking, or loss of vision in one eye, but they pass, often within minutes and usually within 24 hours; that outer boundary is a convention rather than a biological truth and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it has been redefined and differs between services. The absence of a deficit at examination proves nothing about the risk that follows, and the patient who has had one deserves the same urgent assessment as the patient who still has symptoms. The clinician should record exactly what the patient experienced and how long it lasted, because the account often reveals a narrowing vessel. The decision that follows is how quickly to investigate, and it is made on the pattern of the episodes rather than on the reassurance of a normal examination.
