A seizure is a sudden, excessive discharge of the brain's electrical activity, and the diagnosis rests on the history rather than on the examination, because the patient is usually recovered by the time the clinician arrives. A witness is therefore more valuable than any instrument, and the questions should establish what happened before the event, how it began, whether it involved one side or both, how long it lasted, whether the tongue was bitten, and how the patient behaved afterwards. The cause must be sought actively, because a first seizure may be provoked by a low blood glucose, an infection of the brain or its coverings, a disturbance of sodium or calcium, alcohol withdrawal, a head injury, a stroke, or a tumor. In a woman in the later stages of pregnancy or shortly after delivery, a seizure may signal a hypertensive emergency of pregnancy, and that possibility must be raised at once. The finding that most often changes the immediate course is a measurement of the blood glucose, because it is quick, widely available, and reversible.

Epilepsy is the tendency to have recurrent seizures that are not provoked by a temporary cause, and it is classified by where the seizure begins and whether awareness is preserved. A focal seizure starts in one part of the brain and may remain confined there, producing a twitching limb, a strange sensation, a smell that is not there, or a period of altered awareness that a witness describes as the patient going blank, and it may then spread to become a generalized convulsion. A generalized seizure begins across the whole brain at once, and the commonest form produces stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking and a period of confusion afterwards. The seizure type matters because it hints at the site and the cause, and because it guides the choice of investigation and the advice given to the patient. The clinician should ask how often seizures occur, what seems to bring them on, whether sleep is being lost, and whether alcohol or missed treatment lies behind a change.

A seizure that does not stop, or that repeats without recovery of consciousness between attacks, is a life-threatening emergency, and so is a seizure that compromises breathing. The patient is protected from injury, turned on the side, given oxygen where it exists, and observed continuously while help is summoned, and nothing is placed in the mouth. The clinician looks for the cause while treating the emergency, because a reversible trigger such as a low blood glucose or an infection may be the whole explanation, and in a pregnant patient a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy must be considered alongside epilepsy. Here the decision is named rather than the drug: treatment is the right answer when seizures continue and the airway cannot be protected, and it is the wrong answer when a single provoked seizure has already stopped and its trigger is being corrected.

Migraine is the commonest imitator of serious neurological disease, and recognizing it is a safety skill rather than a convenience. It produces a headache that is often throbbing, often on one side, often with nausea, vomiting, and a dislike of light or sound, and it may be preceded by an aura of flashing lights, zigzag lines, or a spreading numbness. The aura frightens both patient and clinician, because a tingling that marches from the fingers to the face over several minutes resembles a stroke, and that slow spread distinguishes it, since a vascular deficit arrives at once. A migraine with aura can also be accompanied by weakness, and that combination must be assessed as a possible stroke until the picture is clear, particularly in an older patient or one with risk factors. The diagnosis is made from the pattern over time, not from a single attack, so the clinician asks how many similar episodes there have been and what made them better.

Dementia is a decline in more than one area of mental function that is severe enough to interfere with ordinary life, and it is diagnosed by its pattern of loss and its course. The pattern tells the clinician where the degeneration is concentrated: a failing memory for recent events with preserved social manner suggests disease of the hippocampus and the cortex, difficulty with language points elsewhere, and a change in personality suggests damage to the front of the brain. The course matters as much as the pattern, and a figure such as 6 months of progressive decline describes the tempo rather than a rule, so it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, where the intervals used differ. The causes that must not be missed are the reversible ones, among them a low thyroid hormone level, a deficiency of vitamin B twelve, a chronic infection, a tumor pressing on the brain, a blood collection over the brain, and the effect of medicines. Imaging by CT or MRI is chosen to answer those questions rather than to confirm a suspicion of dementia for its own sake.

Delirium is the great confuser of dementia, and the two must be separated because one is often reversible and the other is not. Delirium develops over hours or days, and its hallmark is a fluctuation of attention and awareness, so a patient who is drowsy and inattentive in the morning may be lucid in the afternoon, and an alert patient may be unable to sustain a conversation or count backwards. Dementia develops over months or years, and attention is usually preserved until late, although a person with dementia is far more vulnerable to delirium when illness, pain, constipation, dehydration, or a new medicine arrives. The two can coexist, and a patient with known dementia who suddenly becomes worse should be assumed to have a delirium until proven otherwise, because the treatable cause is usually the new change. The search examines the temperature, the pulse, the pressure, the breathing, the glucose, the urine, the bowel, and every medicine, and a patient whose confusion comes with a new focal deficit, a headache, a fever with neck stiffness, or a recent fall needs urgent help.

Parkinson disease is recognized by a combination of signs rather than by any one of them, and the reasoning is the same whether or not the patient already carries the label. The cardinal features are a tremor most obvious when the limb is at rest and easing when it is used, a stiffness felt as resistance through the whole range of movement, a slowness in starting and sustaining movement, and a loss of balance that appears later. The face loses its expressiveness, the voice becomes quiet, the handwriting shrinks, the gait becomes shuffling with small steps, and the arms swing less on one side, and these signs are often visible before the patient complains. The tremor must be distinguished from an essential tremor, which is more obvious when the arms are held out and often runs in families, and from a tremor produced by a medicine or an overactive thyroid. The finding that would make the diagnosis wrong is a different explanation for the stiffness and slowing, such as a medicine that blocks dopamine, a stroke in the same pathways, or a thyroid disorder.

Neuropathy is disease of the peripheral nerves, and its distribution is the first thing to establish because the distribution names the likely cause. A polyneuropathy affects many nerves, usually beginning in the feet and climbing toward the knees in a length-dependent pattern that produces numbness, burning, and a loss of vibration and position sense, and the ankle reflexes are lost early. A mononeuropathy affects a single nerve, and a common example is compression of the median nerve at the wrist, which causes tingling in the thumb and the first fingers at night. A mononeuritis multiplex affects several separate nerves at once or in sequence, and a multiple mononeuropathy of this kind suggests disease of the blood vessels, poorly controlled diabetes, or an infection. The pattern of sensory loss, whether in a glove, in a stocking, in a patch, or in a band, and the pattern of weakness, whether it climbs, is symmetrical, or follows one nerve, are the findings that direct the search.

The conditions behind a neuropathy are read from the distribution, the time course, and the rest of the patient's story. Diabetes is the commonest cause of a symmetrical, length-dependent polyneuropathy in many parts of the world, and it often begins before the patient knows that the blood glucose is abnormal. Alcohol use, a deficiency of vitamin B twelve or of other vitamins, a low thyroid hormone level, kidney failure, and a cancer not yet known can each produce the same picture, so the clinician asks about diet, alcohol, medicines, and weight loss. In regions where it occurs, leprosy produces a neuropathy with patches of altered sensation and thickened nerves, and infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, may cause a neuropathy directly or through the medicines used for it. A neuropathy that appears suddenly and spreads quickly, or that comes with weakness of the face or difficulty swallowing, is an emergency rather than a chronic problem.

A rapidly progressive weakness is one of the most important presentations in neurology, because the danger is failure of breathing rather than failure of the limbs. When it begins in the feet and climbs over days, with diminishing reflexes and little or no sensory loss, it suggests an acute inflammatory polyneuropathy, sometimes called Guillain-Barré syndrome, in which the immune system attacks the nerves. The breathing must be watched closely, because the weakness can reach the muscles of respiration, and the ability to speak in full sentences, the strength of the cough, and the movement of the chest are repeated observations rather than single measurements. A figure such as 3 days of progression is a reason for urgent assessment rather than a fixed rule, and any interval used to define rapid progression must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Other causes include a disorder of the junction between nerve and muscle, in which weakness worsens with use, along with poisons, infections, metabolic disturbances, and disease of the spinal cord.

Compression of the spinal cord is a true emergency, because the cord tolerates pressure badly and lost function may become permanent within hours. The usual cause is a cancer that has spread to the spine, but an infection, an abscess, a prolapsed disc, and an injury can do the same, and the patient is often already known to have one of these conditions. The findings that reveal it are back pain worse at night or on coughing, a band of pain or tightness around the trunk, weakness of both legs, numbness in the saddle area between the legs, and difficulty starting the passage of urine or loss of control of the bladder and bowel. The examination should include tone, power, reflexes, and sensation in both legs, and a search for the level below which sensation is altered, since that level points to the site of the compression. Every patient with a known cancer and new back pain or new weakness of the legs must be treated as though the cord is threatened until the question is answered, and the answer usually requires urgent MRI.

Where the resources exist, the neurological emergency is investigated along a fixed path. The CT scan without contrast is the first image in most acute situations because it is fast and separates bleeding from a blocked vessel, and it also shows a fracture, a collection of blood, and a shift of the brain. The MRI gives more detail of the brainstem, the spinal cord, and the nerves, and it is the investigation of choice when the cord is threatened, though it takes longer and demands a patient who can lie still. The lumbar puncture is used when infection of the coverings of the brain is suspected, or when a subarachnoid hemorrhage remains possible after a negative scan, and it is performed only after the safety questions have been answered. An electroencephalogram records the electrical activity of the brain and helps to classify seizures, though it cannot exclude a seizure that did not occur during the recording.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is carried as far as the instruments allow and no further. The stethoscope is used for the heart and the lungs, the torch examines the pupil, the movement of the eyes, the throat, and the skin, and a pupil that is larger than the other and does not react to light, or unequal pupils in a patient whose consciousness is falling, points to pressure inside the head and demands urgency. The thermometer turns the impression of fever into a figure that can be compared with the next reading, and the pulse and the breathing are counted with a watch rather than estimated. The clinician examines the blood pressure, the glucose where a meter exists, and the power, reflexes, and sensation of the limbs, and repeats those observations at intervals the patient's condition allows. The decision that follows is not a diagnosis but a plan: whether to observe, to begin treatment on the clinical picture, or to send the patient now.

The decision about treatment belongs to diagnosis, and in neurology it is often made before the cause is certain. Treatment is the right answer when a stroke is within the window in which the clot might be dissolved or removed and the scan has excluded bleeding, when infection of the coverings of the brain is strongly suspected and delay would cost function, when the cord is compressed and the pressure must be relieved, or when a seizure continues and the airway is at risk. It is the wrong answer when a bleed has not been excluded in a patient who might receive a treatment for a clot, when a single provoked seizure has already stopped and its cause is being corrected, and when the picture fits a condition for which the available treatment would do harm. Naming the finding that would justify or forbid the decision is more useful than naming a drug, because the reasoning travels between settings even when the medicines do not.

A constructed illustration may fix these habits, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a man of about 60 whose wife noticed his speech had become slurred and his right arm weak while they were eating, and the weakness was maximal from the first moment, so the clinician treats it as a possible stroke and arranges imaging at once. Imagine a woman of about 45 who describes a headache that came on like a thunderclap while she lifted a box, and who feels better an hour later and asks to go home, and the clinician who remembers the instantaneous onset keeps her for assessment despite the improvement. Imagine an older man with a known cancer who has new back pain, weakness of both legs, and difficulty passing urine, in whom the saddle numbness is sought deliberately and the spine is imaged urgently. None of these people is real, and each shows how one question changes the order of the plan.

What a patient is told on leaving is part of the diagnosis, and in neurology the advice must be specific because the danger is often a second event. The patient with a transient attack or a minor stroke should be told what to do if the symptoms return, how quickly to seek help, and where to go, and that advice should name the signs in ordinary words, such as a face that droops, an arm that will not lift, or speech that has changed. The patient with a new seizure should be told about the risks of driving, swimming, and working at height, and about the importance of sleep and of avoiding identified triggers. The patient with a headache unlike any previous headache should be told which features would bring her back, and the patient with progressive weakness should have a plan for review rather than a promise to return if things worsen. The record should show what was found, what was considered, what was excluded, and what was arranged.

To summarize, neurology is organized by two questions asked of every patient, where the lesion lies and how quickly it is moving, and the answers are assembled from the history, the examination, and the course over time. The dangerous presentations are named at the bedside and each carries its own revealing finding: a stroke of abrupt onset that may still be within the window for reversal, a subarachnoid hemorrhage disguised as a headache of instantaneous onset, a cord compressed by cancer or infection with a band of pain and a numb saddle, and a weakness that climbs over hours or days while the reflexes disappear. The common imitators, the seizure, the migraine, the low blood glucose, and the delirium, are separated by their timing and their associated features, while epilepsy is read by seizure type, dementia by the pattern of loss, the neuropathies by their distribution, and Parkinson disease by the combination of tremor, rigidity, slowness, and loss of balance. Every figure in this chapter, whether a pressure, a temperature, a rate, a duration, a score, or a laboratory value, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. The same reasoning serves the hospital and the clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, where the task is to recognize the patient who must be referred now. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and a patient whose story is alarming deserves to be examined again and discussed rather than reassured and sent away.

# Chapter 52 — Musculoskeletal and Rheumatology

The musculoskeletal and rheumatic diseases arrive as pain, swelling, or stiffness, and they are organized less by the name of a disease than by the pattern in which the joints and their surrounding tissues are involved. The first questions are therefore structural: how many joints are affected, whether the problem came over hours or over months, and whether it behaves as inflammation or as wear. Those three answers, read together with what the rest of the body shows, reduce a vast list to a few possibilities that can be tested at the bedside. A joint complaint is never only a joint complaint, because the diseases that inflame the synovium can also inflame the skin, the eye, the kidney, the lung, the gut, and the blood vessels. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

The causes that kill or cripple must be named before the comfortable ones, and each carries a finding that betrays it. A single hot, swollen joint is an infection until the fluid proves otherwise, and the finding is a joint the patient refuses to move, with pain at the slightest attempt. Infection of the spine, in the disc, the vertebral body, or the space around the cord, gives pain that wakes the patient at night and is not relieved by rest, often with fever and tenderness over the bone, and the emergency is revealed by new weakness, numbness in the saddle area, or difficulty passing urine or stool. A vasculitic emergency declares itself through the organ it attacks, whether a new headache with jaw pain and disturbed vision in an older patient, a rash of spots that do not fade when pressed, a foot that has suddenly dropped, blood in the urine, or breathlessness with bleeding into the lungs. A fracture dismissed as a strain is another disabling miss, because an older patient who cannot bear weight after a minor fall, or whose back pain followed a stumble, may have a break that the first radiograph does not show. Bone pain at rest and worse at night, in a patient with weight loss or a known cancer, belongs in the same list. These possibilities are named first so that the search begins with them rather than arriving at them last.

The number of joints involved is the first filter, because diseases of one joint are few and urgent while diseases of many joints are numerous and mostly chronic. Arthritis in a single joint has a short list: infection, a crystal, trauma, and a tumor, with infection and crystal first because both can destroy a joint quickly if missed. Arthritis in a few joints adds the infections spread through the blood, the crystal diseases, and the forms of spondyloarthritis. Arthritis in many joints opens the broad territory of the inflammatory diseases, among them rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, together with the viral illnesses that imitate them for a few weeks and then leave. The count is not a diagnosis, but it tells the clinician how much danger to assume before any test is ordered. A patient whose joint count is rising over successive examinations is a different patient from one whose single joint has been unchanged for a year.

The speed with which the problem arrived carries almost as much information as the count. A joint that becomes hot and swollen over hours is an emergency, because infection and crystals both behave that way and there is no time to be wrong. A joint that becomes painful over days or a couple of weeks suggests an inflammatory arthritis or an infection declaring itself slowly, while a problem present for months suggests either a chronic inflammatory disease or a degenerative one. The tempo must be confirmed with the patient rather than assumed, because patients often date the beginning to the moment the pain became unbearable. A useful question is what the patient could do a month ago that is now impossible, since function changes earlier and more honestly than pain. The boundary between acute and chronic is a convention rather than a fact, and the interval used in any guideline must be checked against the current edition and the local protocol, because services draw it differently.

Whether the process behaves as inflammation or as wear is the distinction that organizes the whole chapter, and it is made from the history as much as from the examination. Inflammatory arthritis produces stiffness that is worst after rest, especially in the early morning, and that eases as the joint is used, so the patient describes a slow start to the day and feels better by the afternoon. Degenerative disease behaves in the opposite way: the joint is stiff for a few minutes after rest, hurts more as activity accumulates, and is often easier after a night of sleep. Inflammatory disease brings swelling that feels boggy rather than bony, warmth, and a general sense of illness, while degenerative disease produces bony enlargement, grating, and no systemic features. Morning stiffness lasting longer than about an hour is the figure most often taught as favoring inflammation, but that interval is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted duration varies between services and editions.

Infection of a joint is the diagnosis that must be excluded in every patient with a single hot joint, and it is more easily missed than it should be. The classical picture is fever with a joint that is red, hot, and swollen, held still because movement is unbearable, but the fever may be absent, and in the very young, the very old, the patient with a prosthetic joint, the patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, and the patient who injects drugs the picture may be muted. The knee and the hip are affected most often, and an infection of the hip in a child or an older patient may present only as a refusal to walk or as pain referred to the thigh or the knee. An organism usually reaches a joint through the bloodstream, so the clinician looks for a source in the skin, the teeth, the urine, the gut, or a recent procedure, and takes blood cultures before treatment begins, because cultures drawn afterwards are far less useful. Infection with gonorrhea and other sexually transmitted infections can also settle in a joint, and that possibility changes the questions asked and the examinations performed. The decision that follows is made on the clinical picture and cannot wait for certainty, so a hot joint with a fever is treated as an infection until the fluid says otherwise.

Gout and septic arthritis can look identical at the bedside, and separating them is the central exercise of this chapter. Gout usually arrives at night in a patient who was well the day before, reaches its worst within hours, and is so tender that even the weight of a sheet is intolerable, and the first attack often involves the joint at the base of the big toe. The patient may report earlier attacks that settled on their own, heavy alcohol use, a diet rich in meat and seafood, medicines that raise the uric acid level, or a recent illness or operation that provoked the attack. Examination may show tophi, which are firm deposits under the skin near the joint or on the ear. The two conditions overlap in every direction: gout can produce fever and a raised inflammatory response, an infected joint can contain crystals that were already there, and both can occur together in the same patient. Calcium pyrophosphate crystals produce a very similar attack, often in an older patient and often in the knee or the wrist, and only the crystal seen in the fluid separates them. The level of uric acid in the blood is often normal during an acute attack of gout, so a normal value does not exclude it, and a raised value between attacks does not prove that the current joint is the cause. Because the treatments point in opposite directions, the bedside judgment is a probability and not a proof; only the fluid examined under a polarizing microscope gives the answer, and a hot joint with a fever is safer treated as an infection.

Among the many-jointed inflammatory diseases, rheumatoid arthritis is the one the listener should recognize from the hands alone. It is symmetric, it favors the small joints of the hands and feet, and it spares the joints nearest the fingertips while damaging the knuckles and the wrists, which is the opposite of the pattern in degenerative disease. The patient describes morning stiffness that lasts a long time, swelling that comes and goes, and a tiredness out of proportion to the joint pain, and over months the joints may drift into deformity. Examination looks for boggy swelling of the knuckles, tenderness along the joints of the feet, firm nodules under the skin near the elbow, and the signs of a more aggressive disease elsewhere. The antibodies measured in the blood support the diagnosis but do not make it, and the reference range and the meaning of a positive result must be confirmed against the current guideline and the laboratory's own protocol, because the assays differ between centers. The dangers in a patient who looks like this are an infection in one of the affected joints, an infection elsewhere imitating a flare, and a disease of the blood or the bone marrow producing joint pain as an early sign.

A different pattern of inflammatory disease targets the spine and the places where tendon meets bone, and it appears in younger patients as back pain that behaves in a way ordinary back pain does not. The pain is worse at rest and in the second half of the night, it improves with exercise and not with rest, and it usually begins gradually in a young adult. The examination looks for tenderness where tendons insert at the heel, for loss of the normal curve and movement of the lower spine, and for the extra-articular clues that travel with this group, among them a scaly skin condition, an eye that is red and painful, and inflammation of the bowel. A particular inherited tissue type is more common in these patients, but it is not a test for the disease, because many people carry it without ever becoming ill. Chronic back pain of this kind must also be distinguished from infection and from a tumor, because both can produce night pain and stiffness in the same region. Where the pattern is inflammatory and the patient is young, the decision is to pursue the diagnosis rather than to treat the pain as mechanical.

Back pain becomes a different problem when it is caused by infection or by a tumor, and the features that point that way must be sought deliberately. Infection of the spine is more likely in a patient with diabetes, a patient who injects drugs, a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, a patient on dialysis, and a patient who has had a recent bloodstream infection or a procedure on the spine. The pain is usually constant, worse at night, not relieved by rest, and often accompanied by tenderness when the clinician presses or taps over the affected vertebra, and the patient may look unwell without any obvious fever. Tuberculosis of the spine develops slowly, produces weight loss and night sweats, and can leave a knuckle-shaped deformity of the backbone when several vertebrae are destroyed. A cancer that has spread to the bone, and the cancer of the bone marrow that produces anemia and bone pain, behave in a similar way, and a patient with a known tumor who develops new back pain must be assumed to have disease in the spine until that is excluded. The finding that turns any of these into an emergency is new weakness in the legs, a band of numbness around the trunk, difficulty passing urine or stool, or a loss of bladder or bowel control, because these mean the cord is being compressed. That patient needs magnetic resonance imaging and an urgent decision about decompression, and the interval within which the pressure must be relieved is a local protocol matter to be confirmed in the service where the patient is cared for.

Osteoporosis produces no symptoms at all until it produces a fracture, which is why it is described as presenting with its consequence rather than before it. The bone loses mass and its internal architecture becomes fragile over years, and the patient notices nothing until a fall that would have been harmless breaks a wrist, a hip, or a vertebra. The history that should raise the suspicion includes a fracture after a fall from standing height or less, a loss of height, a stoop, a previous fragility fracture in the patient or a parent, early menopause, a low body weight, long treatment with steroids, smoking, heavy alcohol use, and a diet poor in calcium and vitamin D. Examination looks for the stoop of the upper spine, for tenderness over a compressed vertebra, and for the diseases and medicines that cause bone loss, and it also looks for the reasons the patient fell, because a fracture is usually a fall plus a fragile bone. Measurement of bone density by a special form of radiograph gives a figure compared with a reference population, and that figure and the reference range must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local laboratory protocol, because the equipment, the population, and the reporting convention differ between centers. A fracture can be invisible on the first radiograph, especially in the hip and in some small bones of the wrist and foot, so the injury dismissed as a strain is often this very one, and a patient who cannot bear weight after a fall needs a second image rather than reassurance. The rule that serves is that a patient who cannot use the limb, or whose pain is not settling as a strain should, needs imaging and review arranged rather than assumed.

The vasculitides are diseases in which the blood vessels themselves are inflamed, and they present through whatever organ the inflamed vessels supply rather than through the joints. A large-vessel disease of older patients produces a new headache, tenderness of the scalp, pain in the jaw when chewing, and disturbed vision, and the finding that must never be missed is a sudden loss of vision, which can become permanent within hours and may be preceded by brief episodes of blindness. A disease of the medium and small vessels produces a rash of spots that do not fade when a clear glass is pressed on them, ulcers of the skin, pain and weakness in a limb from inflamed nerves, blood in the urine, and bleeding into the lungs, and any one of these findings in a patient who also has joint pain changes the whole assessment. The kidney is involved more often than any other organ in this group, and the finding is blood and protein in the urine together with a rising waste product in the blood, so a urine test belongs in the assessment of every patient with a suspected rheumatic disease. The inflammatory markers in the blood are often raised, but a normal value does not exclude these diseases, and the definitive answer usually comes from a sample of inflamed tissue examined under the microscope. The decision to treat before that answer is confirmed is made on the danger of the presentation, and the finding that would make it wrong is a confirmed alternative diagnosis that fully explains the picture in a patient whose organs are not threatened.

Lupus is recognized through the way it involves many systems at once rather than through a single criterion, and a clinician who waits for one test to settle the question will miss it. The patient is usually a young woman, though the disease occurs in men and at every age, and the symptoms accumulate over months, among them joint pain and swelling, extreme tiredness, and episodes of fever without an obvious cause. The skin findings include a rash over the cheeks and the bridge of the nose that spares the folds beside it, a rash in the sunlight, sores in the mouth, and hair loss, and the joints are painful and swollen without the destruction seen in rheumatoid arthritis. The serious manifestations involve the kidneys, the nervous system, the blood, the lining of the lungs and heart, and the clotting system, and each is sought rather than waited for, because the disease can be quiet in the joints while it is damaging an organ. The antibodies used in the diagnosis support the impression, but the criteria that list them were built to classify patients for research rather than to diagnose an individual, so their contents must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local laboratory protocol. Because infection is common in these patients and can imitate a flare, and because treating a flare can worsen an infection, the clinician must look deliberately for an infection in every patient who appears to be deteriorating. The finding that changes the decision is a clear source of infection, and the finding that demands action is a new fall in the blood count, a rise in the waste products of the kidney, or a new neurological sign.

The examination of a joint follows the same order as the examination of any other part of the body, and it is performed on both sides for comparison. Inspection looks at the posture of the limb, swelling, redness, wasting of the muscle above and below the joint, and the way the patient stands and walks, because a joint that cannot take weight matters more than a joint that merely aches. Palpation uses the back of the hand to compare warmth, then the fingers to feel for fluid, boggy swelling, bony enlargement, nodules, and tenderness along the joint line, and the squeeze test across the joint detects inflammation of the whole joint rather than of one spot. Movement is tested actively and then passively, and the difference between the two is important: pain only at the end of the range suggests a mechanical block or a strained structure, while pain throughout the movement suggests inflammation of the joint itself. The knee is examined for fluid by pressing it from one side to the other and watching for a bulge, and the hip is examined by rotating the whole leg and measuring how far the limb moves in each direction. The single most useful sign in separating inflammation from wear is warmth felt over the joint compared with the other side, provided the examiner uses the back of the hand rather than the palm.

When fluid can be obtained from a joint, the examination moves from inference to evidence, and the way the sample is handled decides how much it is worth. The fluid should be drawn before treatment begins wherever that is possible, and it should be examined for its cells, for crystals under a polarizing microscope, and for organisms grown in culture, because each question is answered differently and none replaces the others. In a well-resourced hospital the laboratory can also measure the inflammatory markers in the blood, the antibodies associated with the rheumatic diseases, and the level of uric acid, and each result must be read against the reference range of the laboratory that produced it, and such ranges differ between centers and editions, so they must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The clinician should decide what each test would change before sending it, because a test that cannot alter the decision wastes time and may mislead. A radiograph shows the structure of the bone and the degree of damage, an ultrasound performed at the bedside can show fluid and inflammation and can guide the needle, and magnetic resonance imaging or computed tomography answers specific questions about bone, joint, and soft tissue. A test ordered without a question is a result waiting to be misread.

In a clinic whose equipment is a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is carried out with the hands and the eyes, and the standard of thought is not lower because the tools are few. The torch makes the skin, the eyes, the mouth, the scalp, and the nails visible, and those are exactly the places where the extra-articular clues of a rheumatic disease are found. The thermometer turns the impression of fever into a figure that can be recorded and compared over time, though a normal temperature does not exclude an infection of a joint or of the spine, and the finding of a warm joint remains available to any examiner with a hand. A watch allows the pulse to be counted, and counting it rather than estimating it separates the careful clinician from the hurried one, since a rising pulse may be the earliest evidence that a joint infection is spreading. Urine can be inspected and tested where a dipstick is available, and blood or protein in the urine changes the assessment of a patient with joint pain more than any joint sign. What the clinic cannot do is examine the fluid, so the decision becomes whether to treat on suspicion and refer, or whether the patient can be watched, and the reason must be recorded together with a plan for review.

The decision about treatment belongs to the diagnosis even when it is made before the diagnosis is certain, and the reasoning can be stated without naming a medicine. Treatment is the right answer when a joint may be infected and the patient is systemically unwell, when the spine is threatened by compression, when a vasculitis is attacking the eye, the kidney, or the lung, and when an inflammatory arthritis is damaging joints that will not recover. Treatment is the wrong answer when the picture is fully explained by a mechanical or degenerative cause, when infection has not been excluded in a joint that is hot, and when treatment would remove the evidence the diagnosis depends on before the samples are taken. The finding that makes treatment wrong in a hot joint is fluid showing crystals with no organism in a patient who is stable, and the finding that makes it right is fluid showing organisms or a patient who is deteriorating while the result is awaited. In a patient with a possible infection of the spine, the finding that makes immediate action right is a new neurological deficit, and the finding that allows a few hours of investigation is pain without any neurological sign in a stable patient. Naming the finding rather than the drug transfers between settings, because the reasoning does not depend on which medicines happen to be available. Every threshold used in these decisions is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the figures that define danger differ between countries, editions, and services.

A constructed illustration may make these habits concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine an older woman who arrives with a knee that became hot and swollen overnight, a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius, and no history of gout, and whose joint is aspirated before anything is given. That temperature is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the figure that counts as fever varies with the site of measurement and with the patient. Now imagine an older man who stumbled on a step two days earlier, whose back pain is attributed to a strain, and in whom a tap over one vertebra reproduces the pain exactly; that tenderness is the finding which turns a strain into a suspected infection or fracture. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a person without a full assessment. What the two share is the move that matters, which is that the clinician asked the question the label did not.

To summarize, the musculoskeletal and rheumatic diseases are read by the pattern in which they involve the body: how many joints are affected, how quickly the problem arrived, and whether it behaves as inflammation or as wear, with the skin, the eyes, the urine, and the nerves examined for the clues that explain the patient. The dangerous causes are named at the bedside and not deferred, among them septic arthritis, an infection of the spine, a vasculitic emergency, a fracture dismissed as a strain, and a cancer in the bone, and each carries a finding that reveals it. Gout and septic arthritis are separated by the history and the signs rather than by certainty, and the definitive answer requires the fluid, examined for cells, crystals, and organisms. Lupus is recognized through its multisystem manifestations rather than a single criterion, and osteoporosis presents with its consequence rather than before it, so the fracture is the diagnosis. The same reasoning is carried into a hospital where immunology and imaging are available and into a clinic where a hand on the joint, a torch, a thermometer, and a watch must do the work. Every score, cut-off, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, or duration in this chapter is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and a patient whose joint is hot, whose spine is threatened, or whose vision has changed is a patient to be helped and referred rather than reassured.

# Chapter 53 — Infectious Diseases

Infectious disease is the part of medicine where the diagnosis changes while the clinician is still thinking about it, because the organism is multiplying and the patient's defenses are answering at the same time. The reasoning that organizes this chapter is therefore not a list of organisms but a set of questions that each infection answers differently: how quickly the illness arrived, what the patient was exposed to before it began, what state the patient's defenses were in, and which part of the body the infection has chosen to occupy. An illness that reaches its full force within hours tells a different story from one that has crept up across a week, and a patient who was well last month tells a different story from one whose defenses are suppressed by disease or by treatment. Because the same organism can produce a mild illness in one person and a lethal one in another, the clinician reasons about the host as carefully as about the microbe. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient. The same logic is followed in a hospital where a laboratory can name an organism within hours and in a clinic where a stethoscope, a torch and a thermometer are the whole of the technology, and the difference between the two lies in the tools rather than in the reasoning.

Before any comfortable explanation is accepted, the lethal possibilities must be named, each together with the finding that would reveal it. A patient with fever who becomes drowsy or confused, who has a severe headache and a neck that resists being bent forward, and who develops a rash of small dark spots that do not fade when a clear glass is pressed against them may have meningococcal disease, and that rash is the finding that turns a vague febrile illness into an emergency. A patient who has been in a region where malaria is transmitted and who now has fever with drowsiness, a convulsion, deep and labored breathing, or very little urine may have severe malaria, and the finding that reveals it is the parasite seen in a stained film of blood or detected by a rapid test. A patient with fever and bleeding from the gums, the nose or the bowel, or blood under the skin, especially after travel to an area where viral hemorrhagic fever occurs, must be isolated and cared for with personal protective equipment, known as PPE, while expert advice is sought, because that patient may be infectious to everyone who comes near. A patient with a wound, however minor it seemed at the time, who then cannot open the mouth fully, whose face takes on a fixed smile, and whose muscles go into spasm at a sudden noise or a bright light has tetanus, and the spasm provoked by stimulation is the finding that names it. A patient, often a child, who at first appears to have an ordinary viral illness and who then becomes floppy, mottled, cold or difficult to rouse is showing the pattern of a viral illness that is in truth an early bacterial sepsis, and the change in the patient between two observations is the finding that matters most.

The first of the organizing questions is tempo, because how fast an illness has moved narrows the field before any test is ordered. The second question is exposure, and the clinician asks it in a fixed order so that nothing is missed: where the patient has lived and traveled in recent weeks and months, what insects bite in those places, what water is drunk and used for washing, what animals are kept or encountered, what food has been eaten away from home, and whether there has been a bite, a wound, a procedure, an injection, or a device placed inside the body. The third question is the state of the patient's defenses, because the same organism behaves differently in a person whose immunity is intact and in one whose immunity has been weakened by illness, by treatment, by age, or by the loss of a spleen. The fourth is the syndrome, which is the part of the body the infection has occupied, and it directs the examination from the first minute, so the clinician keeps the Oldcarts framework in mind while taking the history and then moves deliberately from the general appearance to the skin, the mouth, the chest, the abdomen and the hidden sites. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is often taught as the line above which fever is present, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be checked against the guideline in force where the clinician works and against the local protocol, because the accepted line differs between countries, has been redrawn between editions, and depends on where the measurement was taken.

Infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, is the diagnosis that changes the meaning of every other infection, and it is considered in any patient whose illnesses are unusual in kind, frequency or severity. The conditions that signal it are a weight loss the patient cannot explain, night sweats, a diarrhea that persists, a white coating on the tongue or the inside of the cheeks, shingles appearing at a young age, repeated infections of the lung or the sinuses, lymph nodes that stay enlarged, and certain tumors of the lymph system. None of those findings proves the diagnosis, and the finding that does prove it is a test performed on the blood or on a sample taken from the mouth, offered with consent and with a conversation about what the result will mean for the patient and for others. The clinician must remember that an early test can be negative while the virus is present, and the interval during which that can happen is described differently by different tests, so the period to be trusted must come from the current guideline and the laboratory's own protocol rather than from memory. A diagnosis of HIV is not the end of the reasoning but the beginning of a new set of questions, because the state of the patient's defenses, the organs already affected and the other infections present all change what must be sought next.

Sexually transmitted infections are approached without judgment, because shame is the reason patients delay and the reason histories remain incomplete. The clinician asks directly about genital sores or ulcers, discharge, pain on passing urine, bleeding between periods, pain during intercourse, and about the number and health of partners, and then asks about the same matters for the partner where that is possible. Some of these infections announce themselves with a single painless ulcer, which may be syphilis and which will heal without treatment while the organism spreads, later producing a rash on the palms and the soles, hair loss, and damage to the heart or the nervous system that appears years afterward. Others produce a discharge and a burning on passing urine, and these may be gonorrhea or infection with chlamydia, which can scar the tubes in a woman and lead later to infertility or to a pregnancy that implants outside the womb. Herpes produces painful blisters that break and crust and may return in episodes, and infection with the human papillomavirus may cause no symptoms at all until a wart or a change on the neck of the womb is found. The examination requires privacy, a good light and a chaperone, and the clinic with a torch can inspect the genitals, the anus and the mouth, although the cervix and the deeper organs need a speculum and, where possible, a laboratory. The most important decision is often not diagnostic but preventive, because an infection in a pregnant woman can pass to the baby and cause infection of the eye, pneumonia, or a serious generalized illness, and the finding that would make treatment during pregnancy the right answer is a positive test or a partner known to be infected.

Malaria is the tropical fever that kills most quickly, and it is placed first among them because a patient who looks comfortable at midday can be dying by night. The exposure history is the key that opens the diagnosis, since a patient who lives in or has traveled to a region where the parasite is transmitted, who has not used the preventive measures available or has used them incompletely, and who has been bitten by mosquitoes during the hours of darkness is a patient in whom malaria must be actively excluded rather than assumed away. The fever may come in waves with a shaking chill, a rise in temperature and heavy sweating as the episode passes, and the patient may be anemic, jaundiced, or have a spleen that can be felt below the ribs. The finding that reveals malaria is the parasite seen under a microscope in a stained film of blood, or its product detected by a rapid test, and neither the pattern nor the height of the fever can replace those tests, because other infections imitate them closely. The signs that mark the change from simple to severe disease are drowsiness or confusion, a convulsion, breathing that is deep and labored, a low passage of urine, dark urine, bleeding, and a falling pressure; a breathing rate above 30 breaths per minute in an adult belongs in that same group, and the level at which each sign becomes alarming is stated differently in different services and editions, so it should be taken from the current guideline and the local protocol rather than recalled from a book. Where a test cannot be performed, the travel history together with the clinical picture must carry the decision, and a patient who cannot be tested and cannot be watched is a patient who must travel to a place where both are possible.

Other tropical fevers are separated by the same exposure history and by the tempo of the illness rather than by geography alone. Dengue arrives suddenly with a severe pain behind the eyes, pain in the muscles and the bones, a rash and a falling platelet count, and the patient who seems to improve as the fever falls is often the one in whom fluid leaks from the circulation and the pressure drops, so the pressure, the pulse and the urine are watched more closely than the temperature. Typhoid climbs in steps across the first days with a headache, a poor appetite, abdominal discomfort and a pulse that is slower than the temperature would suggest, and the organism is grown from blood taken early in the illness, before treatment can remove it from the sample. Leptospirosis follows contact with water or soil contaminated by the urine of animals, and it produces severe pain in the calves, red eyes, headache and sometimes jaundice and injury to the kidney. The rickettsial infections are spread by ticks, fleas and mites, and they may leave a dark scab at the site of the bite with a rash that spreads from the trunk or the limbs, and they are easily mistaken for a viral illness unless the history of bites and of rural or camp exposure is asked.

Viral hemorrhagic fever is the diagnosis that changes how the patient is handled before it is confirmed, and the clinician must act on the possibility rather than on the answer. The pattern that should raise it is a fever with bleeding from the gums, the nose or the bowel, or blood in the skin, in a patient who has recently been in an area where the disease occurs, especially where there has been contact with another person who was ill in the same way. Because the disease spreads through contact with blood and body fluids, the patient is isolated at once, gloves, gown, mask and eye protection are worn, and the number of staff who enter the room is kept to the minimum needed. The clinician does not wait for the laboratory before taking those steps, because the risk is not only to the patient but to everyone who touches the patient and to those who handle the samples afterward. Advice is sought from the service responsible for such infections, and the samples are taken, labeled and transported according to the local protocol rather than by improvisation. The finding that would set the possibility aside is a clear alternative diagnosis that fully explains the bleeding, such as a known disorder of the clotting system or a complication of a medicine, and even then the isolation is lifted only when the responsible clinician is satisfied.

Tetanus is a diagnosis made entirely at the bedside, because no laboratory confirms it and no laboratory is needed. The organism enters through a wound, which may be so small that the patient does not mention it, and it produces a toxin that reaches the nervous system after an interval that varies from days to weeks. The earliest signs are a stiffness in the jaw that makes it hard to open the mouth, difficulty in swallowing, and a stiffness of the neck and the back that differs from the resistance of meningitis, because the patient is fully awake and the muscles are rigid rather than tender. The finding that names the disease is a spasm of the muscles provoked by a sudden noise, a bright light or an attempt to move the patient, and the spasm may be strong enough to arch the back or to stop the breathing, so the patient must be handled gently and treated in a place where the airway can be supported. Prevention is the part of this disease that matters most, and the decision about vaccination and about cleaning a wound belongs to the clinician who sees the injury, guided by the patient's history of immunization and by the current guideline and the local protocol rather than by a remembered schedule. The finding that would make tetanus the wrong diagnosis is a clear alternative cause of the muscle stiffness, such as a reaction to a medicine or an infection of the jaw or the neck.

Meningococcal disease deserves its own paragraph, because the distance between the first symptom and death can be measured in hours and because the patient may look deceptively well at the first examination. It begins as a fever with a headache, an aching body and a dislike of light, and the child may be irritable in a way the parent has not seen before, while a neck that resists being bent forward is the classic sign but may be absent in a young infant, in an older person and in anyone whose defenses are suppressed. The finding that should stop the clinician cold is a rash of small red or purple spots that do not disappear when a clear glass is pressed firmly against the skin, and that finding, together with cold hands, a rapid pulse and a falling pressure, means the patient must be treated immediately and moved to a place where the airway, the breathing and the circulation can be supported. A systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the point at which shock must be assumed, but the figure is offered here as an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the pressure that matters depends on the patient's usual reading, on age and on pregnancy. In a hospital the diagnosis is pursued with blood cultures drawn before treatment and with a sample of the fluid around the spine once the safety of that procedure has been considered, and the organism can sometimes be identified within hours. In a clinic with a torch and a thermometer the decision is made on the rash, the level of consciousness and the pressure, and treatment begins on the clinical picture while the journey to hospital is arranged, because waiting for a result the clinic cannot obtain is not a plan.

Most infections that walk into a clinic are viral and self-limiting, and the work of diagnosis is to recognize the few that are bacterial without treating the many as though they were. A viral illness of the upper airway usually begins with a sore throat, a runny nose, sneezing, a cough and a fever that settles over a few days, and the patient or the parent can often describe a similar illness in the household during the same weeks. A fever that has lasted more than 3 days without localizing signs is a reason to look again, although the interval that should prompt concern is not the same everywhere and must be verified against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the usual course of these illnesses is described differently in different populations and in successive editions. The findings that turn the balance toward a bacterial cause are a fever that persists beyond the expected course, a localized pain or swelling, a discharge of pus, difficulty breathing, a breathing rate that is high for the age, a stiff neck, or a level of alertness that has fallen, and each of these is an answer to the question of where the infection has settled. A sore throat with a high fever, swollen tonsils bearing white patches, tender nodes in the neck, and a cough that is absent is more likely to be bacterial than a sore throat with a cough and a runny nose. In the young child the integrated management of childhood illness approach offers a syndromic method, asking first about the general danger signs and then about the symptoms that name the common infections, and it is deliberately designed for the clinic where no laboratory exists. The clinician who uses such a framework must still say what it excludes and what it assumes, because a rule tested in one population can mislead in another.

The patient whose defenses are not ordinary is the patient in whom the usual signs are least reliable, and a short list of such patients should run through the clinician's mind with every fever. A newborn with a fever, or even with a low temperature and poor feeding, is an emergency, because the signs of serious infection are subtle and the illness can progress within hours. An older patient may have no fever at all and may present instead with a fall, a confusion, a refusal to eat or a loss of continence, and the finding that matters is a change from the patient's usual state rather than any single measurement. A patient without a spleen, a patient receiving treatment that suppresses the immune response, a patient with a cancer of the blood or the lymph system, a patient with a line or a device in a vein, and a patient with a replaced joint or heart valve are all at risk of infections that behave differently and may need treatment before the organism is named. In each of these patients the threshold for seeking help and for starting treatment is lower rather than higher, and the finding that would make treatment the wrong answer is a clear non-infectious explanation that accounts for the whole picture.

In a hospital the reasoning is the same, but the laboratory shortens each loop of it by naming the organism sooner. Blood cultures taken before the first treatment are the single most valuable samples in a patient with suspected infection of the bloodstream, and the timing of the draw matters more than the number of bottles, because the organism leaves the blood in waves and a sample taken at the right moment may be the only one that grows. A sample of urine, a sample of sputum, a swab from a wound or a throat, and a sample of fluid from a collection each answer a particular question, and the clinician should be able to say what a positive or a negative result would change before the sample is sent. Staining the sample and looking at it under the microscope can give a first answer quickly, and methods that detect the organism's own material, such as the polymerase chain reaction, can identify it faster still, but each method has a limit, and a negative result never cancels a clinical picture that is clear. The patient who is drowsy, breathing fast, cold at the extremities or passing very little urine belongs in the intensive care unit, known as ICU, and the decision to move that patient is made on the clinical findings rather than on the result of a test, while the decisions about supporting the airway, giving extra oxygen or giving fluids follow the measured level and the clinical picture rather than any figure carried in a book. The laboratory is an extension of the reasoning and not a replacement for it, and a clinician who treats every positive result as a disease and every negative result as reassurance will be wrong in both directions.

Where no laboratory exists, the decision is made on the syndrome and then reviewed as the patient declares himself, and this is a discipline rather than a compromise. The clinician asks the four organizing questions of tempo, exposure, defenses and syndrome, performs a complete examination of the skin, the mouth, the throat, the chest, the abdomen, the joints and the hidden sites, and then states plainly what is believed and what remains uncertain. The plan that follows takes one of three shapes: the patient can be watched with a defined time set for review, the patient should begin treatment now on the clinical findings, or the patient must travel to a hospital without delay. Whichever is chosen, the patient or the family is told exactly which signs should bring them back or send them onward, among them a fever that will not settle, a new drowsiness or confusion, difficulty breathing, a rash that does not fade when pressed, a stiff neck, a reduced passage of urine, or a deterioration the family can see for itself. Treatment begun on a clinical case is reviewed when the patient returns, because the diagnosis at the first visit is a hypothesis and the second visit is where it is tested, and a patient who is not improving as expected is a patient whose diagnosis should be reconsidered rather than treated harder. The clinician who records the reasoning, the uncertainty and the plan for review has done the most valuable thing that can be done without a laboratory.

The decision about treatment is part of diagnosis, and in infection it is often made before the organism is known. Treatment is likely to be the right answer when the patient looks seriously ill, when there are signs that an organ is failing, when the defenses are suppressed, when a life-threatening cause such as malaria or meningitis is plausible, or when the patient cannot be observed and the chance to treat may not come again. Treatment is likely to be the wrong answer when the picture is clearly a mild viral illness with no localizing sign and no danger sign, when a non-infectious cause explains everything, or when giving treatment before the samples are taken would destroy the evidence on which the diagnosis depends. The clinician should also weigh the cost of treating everyone, because unnecessary treatment exposes the patient to harm, hides the real diagnosis, and breeds resistance that will make the next patient harder to help. Prevention belongs in the same reasoning, since the decision to offer a vaccine, to clean and cover a wound, to provide a bed net, or to advise on safe water and food is a diagnostic act when it rests on the exposure history the clinician has just taken. The details of every preventive decision, including who should receive a vaccine and when, are set by the current guideline and the local protocol and are not carried in this chapter, because the schedules differ between countries and are revised between editions. What this chapter carries is the finding that would make a decision right, the finding that would make it wrong, and the honesty to say when the answer is not yet known.

To summarize, infectious disease is organized by four questions that every infection answers differently, which are how fast the illness moved, what the patient was exposed to, what state the patient's defenses were in, and which part of the body the infection has occupied. The lethal possibilities are named where the presentation appears and not deferred, among them meningococcal disease with its rash that does not fade, severe malaria with its drowsiness and labored breathing, a viral hemorrhagic fever with its fever and bleeding, tetanus with its spasm provoked by stimulation, and the ordinary-looking viral illness that is in truth an early bacterial sepsis. Infection with the human immunodeficiency virus is sought through the conditions that signal it; sexually transmitted infections are taken without judgment and with attention to the partner and to pregnancy; the tropical fevers are separated by exposure and tempo; and the common viral illnesses are distinguished from the bacterial ones that imitate them by the focal signs, the duration and the trajectory. Every figure in this chapter, whether a temperature, a pressure, a rate, a duration, an interval or a reference range, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. The same logic runs in the hospital where an organism can be named within hours and in the clinic where the decision is made on the syndrome and reviewed as the patient declares himself, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who is deteriorating is treated and helped first, and the organism is named afterward.

# Chapter 54 — Dermatology

The skin is the one organ a patient can show and a clinician can see without an instrument, and it is also the organ whose diseases are most often misread, because a rash is a pattern rather than a sentence. Dermatology rewards a method: describe what is there before naming it, compare one part of the body with another, consider the whole patient, and ask what has already been applied. That method, rather than a memory for esoteric names, separates the clinician who recognizes the common diseases from the one who does not. This chapter follows the common skin diseases by their distribution and their evolution, returns to the eruptions that kill, and ends with the same reasoning in a hospital and in a clinic where the only record is a careful description in the notes. The material is educational and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Several dangerous eruptions must be named before any comfortable diagnosis is entertained, because each is revealed by a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. A rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed against it may mean bleeding into the skin, and a feverish, unwell patient with such a rash may have an infection in the bloodstream that kills within hours. A rash involving the lips, the mouth, the eyes, or the genitals, especially with fever and skin that burns, may be a blistering reaction to a medicine that can strip the skin from large areas of the body. Skin that is dusky, intensely painful, and spreading fast, with pain far greater than the appearance suggests, may be a necrotizing infection of the deep tissues rather than a simple cellulitis. A lesion that grows, changes, bleeds, or refuses to heal may be a skin cancer, and pale skin and years of sun exposure are not the only risks. A patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, whether by infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, by a transplant, or by cancer treatment, may show any of these dangers in a muted form that is easy to dismiss.

The method works because the skin shows its mechanism on the surface. Disease in the outer layer scales, blisters, or breaks; disease in the deeper layer swells, reddens, or lumps; disease in the vessels bleeds or blocks; and disease in the fat beneath produces nodules and dimpling. Distribution adds meaning, because a rash in the creases speaks of an internal tendency, a rash on exposed surfaces speaks of something outside the body, and a rash following a nerve speaks of a structure beneath the skin. Evolution adds more, since the same disease looks different on the first day, at its height, and as it fades. A clinician who records what the rash is doing today, and what it did last week, has narrowed the field more than any single name can.

Describing a rash needs a small, precise vocabulary, and using it well is worth more than knowing many diagnoses. A macule is a flat change in color, a papule is a small raised lesion, and a plaque is a larger raised area with a flat top. A vesicle is a small blister, a bulla is a larger one, and a pustule is filled with pus. A wheal is a transient raised swelling, a nodule is a deeper solid lump, and a scale is a flake of detached surface skin. Crust is dried fluid, an erosion is a break that does not pass through the full thickness of the skin, and an ulcer is a break that does. Purpura is bleeding into the skin that does not fade when pressed, and it is the most important of these words because of what it can mean; alongside the lesion the clinician records color, warmth, tenderness, border, surface, arrangement, and the exact parts of the body involved.

The examination begins in good daylight, because skin color is almost impossible to judge under the yellow light of a ward at night, and a torch is a poor substitute when it is all there is. The patient must be undressed far enough to show the whole eruption, which often means examining the back, the buttocks, the groins, the armpits, the feet, and the spaces between the toes, since patients show the part that itches and hide the part that shames them. The scalp, the nails, and the moist linings of the mouth, the eyes, and the genitals are part of the skin examination and are often where the diagnosis is made. The clinician compares one side with the other and the lesions with each other, because a rash in which every lesion looks the same suggests one mechanism while a rash of mixed stages suggests another. The fingers feel for warmth, hardening, and tenderness, and the hand can detect a deep swelling the eye cannot see. What is built is not a snapshot but a map, and every later decision is read against that map.

The skin is not a separate organ, and the patient must be considered as a whole before the rash is named. Fever, weight loss, night sweats, joint pain and swelling, mouth ulcers, eye redness, and a general feeling of illness change the meaning of a skin finding, because they move the reasoning from a local problem to a systemic one. The medicines the patient takes, including those bought without a prescription, are among the commonest causes of a new rash, and the timing of each against the timing of the eruption is the clue. The history should also ask about travel, animals, work with chemicals or plants, new cosmetics or detergents, sexual history where infection of the skin or the genitals is possible, and whether anyone else at home or at work has the same complaint. The question most often omitted is what has already been applied, because a market cream, a traditional preparation, a bleaching agent, or a steroid obtained without a prescription can change the eruption before the clinician sees it, hiding the scale of psoriasis or making a fungal infection look like eczema. Where an applied substance is suspected, the finding that supports the diagnosis is a rash that settles when it is withdrawn.

Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is the commonest inflammatory rash of childhood, recognized by its itch, its distribution, and its course rather than by any single lesion. The itch comes before the rash, and the family describes scratching that disturbs sleep and skin that feels dry and rough. In infancy the eruption favors the cheeks, the scalp, and the outer surfaces of the arms and legs, while in older children and adults it settles into the creases of the elbows and knees, the neck, and the backs of the hands, a shift that reflects how the child moves and what the child touches. The lesions begin as red, poorly defined patches with small papules and progress to dryness, scaling, thickening, and darkened skin lines where scratching has gone on for a long time. The course is one of flares and remissions, and the clinician should ask what precedes a flare, since heat, wool, soap, dust, stress, and infection all appear in different patients. A sudden worsening with crusting, weeping, and tenderness suggests that bacteria have entered damaged skin, and a widespread eruption with fever and blisters in a child with eczema may be a serious viral infection of the skin that needs urgent help.

Psoriasis is a disease of accelerated turnover of the skin, and it declares itself through well-defined plaques with a silvery scale on the outer surfaces of the elbows and knees, the scalp, the lower back, and the buttocks. The plaques are raised, sharply bordered, and often symmetrical, and the scale is thick and dry, so that scraping it away reveals small bleeding points beneath. The nails are part of the diagnosis, and pitting, thickening, separation of the nail from its bed, and yellow-brown discoloration are found in patients whose joints or scalp are involved. New lesions appear along a scratch or a surgical scar, the tendency of the disease to follow injury, and the center of an old plaque may clear and leave a ring easily mistaken for a fungal infection. Psoriasis is not only a skin disease, since a proportion of patients develop a painful, swollen joint disease that can damage the joints permanently if it goes unrecognized. The clinician should ask every patient with psoriasis about joint pain, morning stiffness, and swelling of the fingers and toes, and should examine the joints rather than accept a denial of symptoms.

Fungal infections of the skin are common everywhere, and they are recognized by their shape, their site, and their slow spread rather than by an itch alone. A ring-shaped lesion with a raised, scaly, active edge and a paler center is the classic appearance, and the diagnosis is supported when scale examined under the microscope shows the organism. On the feet the infection sits between the toes, where skin is moist and cracked, and on the soles, where it may look like dry, thickened skin easily mistaken for eczema. On the scalp it causes patches of hair loss with broken hairs and scaling, most often in children, in whom it must be treated properly because it can spread and leave permanent hair loss. In the groin and under the breasts it produces a red, itchy rash with a border more active at the edge, while the same areas may instead be infected by yeast, which tends to give a uniform red rash with satellite spots. The nails become thick, discolored, and crumbly, and nail disease is often the reason a skin infection keeps returning on the hands and feet; a topical steroid given without an antifungal can make the whole picture worse.

Bacterial infection of the skin ranges from a minor nuisance to a threat to life, and the boundary is crossed faster than most clinicians expect. Impetigo begins as small blisters or pustules that break and leave a thick, golden crust, most often around the nose and mouth of a child, and the fingers carry it to other parts of the body. Ecthyma is a deeper form that leaves a punched-out ulcer, and folliculitis is an infection of the hair follicles that appears as tender red papules and pustules in the beard, on the scalp, or on the limbs. Cellulitis is an infection of the deeper skin and fat that produces a warm, red, tender, swollen area with an indistinct border, often with fever and enlarged lymph nodes, and erysipelas is a more superficial form with a raised, sharply defined edge. The clinician should mark the edge of a spreading cellulitis and record the time, because the direction of change over hours is more reliable than the appearance at one visit; a red, swollen leg in a patient with diabetes or poor circulation is not automatically cellulitis, and pain out of proportion to the appearance with rapid worsening should shift the diagnosis.

The necrotizing infection of the deep tissues must be named early, because it destroys muscle and fat within hours while the surface may look deceptively mild. The pain is severe and continuous, far greater than the visible redness suggests, and it often begins before the skin changes at all. The skin then becomes dusky, gray, or blue, blisters of dark fluid appear, the area becomes numb, and a crackling sensation may be felt where gas has formed in the tissues. A falling blood pressure, confusion, or rapid breathing points to the whole-body response that follows. The finding that most strongly supports the diagnosis is the combination of disproportionate pain, rapid spread, and dusky skin, while a stable, well-demarcated, tender red area that improves over the next few hours argues against it. This is a surgical emergency as much as a medical one, and a delay spent on naming the organism is a delay in the only treatment that works.

Infestations are common, curable, and constantly missed, and each has a pattern that gives it away.
