Scabies produces an intense itch that is worse at night, a rash in the web spaces of the fingers, the wrists, the armpits, the waist, and the genitals, and small burrows that can often be seen with a magnifier and a good light. The itch is caused by an immune reaction rather than by the mite itself, so it may take weeks to appear after a first infestation and only days after a later one, and the whole household must be considered because the infestation spreads by close contact. Head lice produce itching of the scalp and visible eggs glued to the hair shafts, and body lice live in the seams of clothing and mark crowded living conditions. Insect bites produce crops of itchy papules in groups or in lines, and the distribution is often the clue, since bites on the ankles suggest fleas and bites under a waistband suggest a bed. A creeping, red, raised line that moves slowly across the foot is the track of a larva migrating through the skin, and the clinician who treats one patient without treating the household is likely to see the same eruption again.

A medicine can produce almost any rash, and a new eruption in a patient who has started a drug within the previous weeks should be treated as drug-related until proved otherwise. The commonest pattern is a red, widespread, blotchy rash that begins on the trunk and spreads outward, often with itching, and it appears some days after the drug was started rather than at once. Hives are raised, itchy, transient swellings that move from place to place within hours, and they may be part of a reaction that also involves the lips, the tongue, or the throat, which is the form that can obstruct the airway and must be treated as an emergency. A fixed drug eruption is a round, dusky patch that appears in the same place each time the drug is taken, and a reaction to light appears only on skin exposed to the sun. Some reactions come with fever, swollen lymph nodes, an enlarged liver or spleen, and a rise in a particular white cell in the blood, and that combination is serious, requiring the drug to be stopped and the patient managed in hospital. The clinician should ask about every substance, including herbal preparations and medicines prescribed elsewhere, and should record the drug, the day it was started, and the day the rash appeared.

The blistering drug reaction is the eruption that most often kills, and it begins with fever, burning or painful skin, and a feeling of illness before any rash is visible. The skin then develops dusky patches and flaccid blisters, and it may shear away with gentle pressure, leaving raw, weeping surfaces. The moist linings of the mouth, the eyes, and the genitals are involved in the severe forms, and the patient may be unable to eat or to open the eyes because of the pain. The extent of skin loss is used to judge severity, and a figure such as one tenth of the body surface offered as a teaching illustration must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the way the area is estimated and the line that defines the severe form vary between services and editions. The finding that makes stopping the suspected drug the right answer is a temporal link between the drug and the eruption together with the characteristic skin and mucosal changes, and any patient with fever, skin pain, and mucosal involvement needs immediate senior help and a transfer decided before the diagnosis is certain.

A rash that does not disappear when a clear glass is pressed firmly against it is a finding that changes the whole assessment, because it means blood has escaped into the skin. The commonest important cause is infection in the bloodstream, and a feverish, drowsy, cold, or painful patient with such a rash may deteriorate within hours. The rash may begin as a few small spots and spread quickly, and it is often found first on the legs, the buttocks, or the pressure areas, so a patient who is unwell must be examined completely rather than at the site of complaint. Not every non-blanching rash is infection, since a low platelet count, a disease of the blood vessels, a reaction to a medicine, and a bleeding disorder can all produce the same appearance, and the clinician should look for bleeding gums, nosebleeds, bruises without injury, and an enlarged spleen. The finding that most strongly supports infection is a patient who looks seriously ill with fever and a spreading rash, while a rash in a patient who looks well and has other evidence of a bleeding tendency supports another cause. When infection is possible the patient must be treated and helped at once, without waiting for the rash to declare itself further.

Skin cancer is the diagnosis that must not be missed among the many harmless lumps and spots that patients bring, and the single most useful clue is change. A lesion that is growing, that has become darker or more varied in color, that has an irregular border, that bleeds or itches without cause, or that has failed to heal over weeks deserves close examination and, where possible, a sample. The dark tumors are the most dangerous because they spread early, and they occur on the palms, the soles, and under the nails as well as on sun-exposed areas, so a dark lesion in a place never sunburned must not be dismissed. A figure such as 6 millimeters has often been taught as the size above which a dark lesion raises concern, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the size that matters depends on the site, the patient, and the edition of the advice being followed. The pale, pearly lump with tiny visible vessels, the scaly patch that will not heal, and the ulcer with a rolled edge are the other common skin cancers, and each is cured by removal when found early. A patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, a patient with albinism, and a patient with many moles or a family history of skin cancer are at higher risk and deserve particular care. The finding that confirms the diagnosis is tissue examined under the microscope, and until that is done the clinician should record the size, the site, the color, and the change that prompted the visit.

The skin often speaks for an organ the clinician cannot see. A persistent purple-red rash on the face across the cheeks and the bridge of the nose, especially with joint pain, hair loss, mouth ulcers, and fever, may be part of a disease of the connective tissue, and the clinician should examine the joints, the urine, and the blood. Painful red nodules on the shins, often with fever and joint pain, point to inflammation beneath the skin that may follow an infection, a bowel disease, or a medicine. A velvety, darkened thickening of the skin of the neck and the armpits is associated with insulin resistance and with some cancers, and a sudden appearance of many such areas should prompt a search for a hidden tumor. Yellow deposits around the eyes, a purple discoloration of the eyelids, and firm lumps in the skin may each signal a systemic disorder, and so may a rash that appears in the same place as a joint that is inflamed. The clinician who examines the skin with the rest of the body in mind, and who asks what else has changed, will find diagnoses that a skin-only approach would miss.

Certain patients require a different reading of the same skin. In a newborn, a rash may be a common and harmless adjustment of the skin or the first sign of a serious infection, and a baby who is unwell, feeding poorly, or has a rash that does not blanch should be assessed urgently. In an older patient the skin is thin and fragile, so a pressure injury can begin as a red area that does not fade, and the clinician must look at the heels, the sacrum, the hips, and the ears of every patient who cannot move independently. In a patient with darker skin the redness of inflammation is often seen as a purple, brown, or gray change rather than as red, so an eruption can be missed by an examiner who looks only for the familiar color, and the same is true of cyanosis, jaundice, and pallor. In pregnancy, an itchy eruption with blisters, or one with fever and systemic symptoms, must be assessed without delay because some rashes endanger the mother or the baby. In a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, a common infection can look unusual, spread widely, and fail to respond as expected, so the clinician should lower the threshold for seeking help; the same lesion means different things in a newborn, an older adult, and a patient with darker skin.

In a well-resourced hospital the same clinical method is extended with instruments and with help. A dermatoscope, which is a magnifier with a light, reveals the fine structures of a pigmented lesion and helps the clinician decide whether it needs to be sampled, and it is a tool for better description rather than a substitute for judgment. A scraping of scale examined with a simple stain confirms a fungal infection within minutes, a swab identifies bacteria, and a sample of skin examined under the microscope settles the diagnosis of a blistering disease or a tumor. A lamp that shines a particular kind of light can show some infections of the hair and the skin, and patch testing can name a contact allergen. A colleague who examines the patient, or a written description compared with the one already in the record, is often the most useful step when the diagnosis is uncertain, because two descriptions of the same rash are worth more than one. Blood tests and imaging may be needed when the skin finding is part of a systemic disease, and each is chosen because its result would change what is done next.

In a clinic with a torch, a magnifier, and no laboratory, the skin can still be assessed well, because the skin is the one organ that can be examined directly. The torch is held to the side so that the surface texture, the scale, and the raised edge cast shadows that make them visible, and the magnifier turns a burrow or a tiny vessel into something the clinician can describe. A wooden stick, a fingernail, and a clean glass are enough to test whether a rash blanches, and a tape measure or a piece of string makes the size and the spread of a lesion recordable from one visit to the next. The thermometer turns the impression of fever into something that can be recorded and compared, and the stethoscope and the hands complete the general examination that a rash with fever always demands. The clinician should write a description that another clinician could recognize, naming the lesion, its color, its border, its surface, its arrangement, and every part of the body involved, together with what has been applied and what else the patient reports. Where the diagnosis cannot be made, the honest record of an uncertain rash and a plan for review is better than a confident wrong name, because the name may travel with the patient and mislead the next clinician. The patient and the family should be told which changes should bring them back: a rash that spreads quickly, a fever, a rash that does not fade when pressed, pain out of proportion, blistering, or a lesion that grows or bleeds. Follow-up should be arranged rather than promised, and the day of review written down, because a patient asked to return only if things worsen may not be able to judge that.

To summarize, dermatology is pattern recognition disciplined by description, and the clinician who describes before naming will recognize more than the clinician who names first. The common diseases are separated by their distribution and their evolution: eczema in the creases with itch, psoriasis on the outer surfaces with silvery scale, fungal infection at the active edge, bacterial infection with warmth and crusting, infestations with itch that follows the household, and drug eruptions with a new medicine in the recent past. Four habits organize the assessment of any unfamiliar rash: describe the lesion precisely, compare one area and one stage with another, consider the whole patient, and ask what has been applied. The dangers are named at the bedside rather than deferred: the rash that does not blanch, the rash with mucosal involvement, the blistering drug reaction, the necrotizing infection whose pain exceeds its appearance, and the lesion that is a skin cancer. Every figure in this chapter, whether a size, an area, an interval, or a reference range, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. The same method works with a dermatoscope and a colleague and with a torch, a magnifier, and a careful note, and the writing down is part of the diagnosis rather than a chore after it. A patient whose rash worries the clinician deserves another look, a clear explanation, and a plan for what should bring them back.

# Chapter 55 — ENT and Ophthalmology

Vision and hearing are the two senses through which a person stays in contact with the world, and the structures that carry them are packed into the front of the head, where an illness in one can imitate an illness in another. A patient comes with a red eye, a blurred view, a lost field of vision, a blocked or ringing ear, a discharge, a blocked nose, or a sore throat, and the first task is not to name the disease but to decide what it threatens. The reasoning that organizes this chapter is therefore a question of urgency and of place: whether the problem threatens sight or hearing within hours, and where along the pathway the fault lies. A patient whose retina has lifted, whose cornea is infected, whose eye has closed its drainage angle, or whose optic nerve is being starved by inflamed arteries may lose the function permanently while waiting for a routine appointment. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

The dangers deserve to be named before any comfortable explanation is entertained, because each announces itself through a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. A painful red eye with a hazy cornea, a partly dilated pupil that does not react, and halos around lights may be acute angle closure glaucoma, in which the drainage angle has shut and the pressure is rising against the optic nerve. A sudden shower of flashes and floating spots followed by a curtain across the vision suggests a detached retina. A painful red eye in a contact lens wearer, with a white spot on the cornea that takes up fluorescein dye, is a corneal ulcer until proved otherwise. An older patient with a new headache, tenderness over the scalp, and pain in the jaw on chewing may have giant cell arteritis, and the finding that supports it is a pale and swollen optic disc with a raised marker of inflammation in the blood. A hearing loss that arrives suddenly in one ear, without pain or discharge, is an emergency of the inner ear, and a sore throat with one-sided swelling, a muffled voice, or drooling may be a collection of pus beside the tonsil or behind the throat. A firm, painless lump in the neck of an adult, hoarseness that does not settle, or an ulcer in the mouth that will not heal belongs on the same list, because a tumor of the head and neck can present in any of those ways.

The eye can be understood as a camera with a lens in front, a film behind, and a fluid-filled space between them whose pressure must stay within a narrow range. The cornea and the lens bend light onto the retina, the retina turns light into a signal, and the optic nerve carries that signal to the brain, so a failure anywhere along the chain produces the same complaint of poor vision while demanding a different answer. The clinician therefore asks where the fault lies: on the surface, in the transparent media, in the retina, in the nerve, or in the brain. The ear follows a similar logic, because sound travels through the canal, strikes the drum, and is carried by three small bones into a fluid-filled inner ear where hair cells turn the vibration into a nerve signal. A problem before the inner ear is a conductive loss, and a problem in the inner ear or the nerve is a sensorineural loss, and the two produce the same report of deafness while pointing to entirely different causes. In both systems the most useful bedside question is the question of place.

A patient who has lost vision is asked to describe it in time, and the shape of that description often names the cause. Loss that arrives in an instant and without pain may be a blockage of an artery feeding the retina, a bleed into the jelly of the eye, or a detachment, while loss that builds over hours or days with pain suggests inflammation of the cornea, the iris, or the optic nerve. Loss that is transient, lasting seconds to minutes and then recovering, may be a warning from a narrowed artery in the neck, and it deserves the same seriousness as a stroke, because the same narrowing can produce a permanent one. Loss that comes with flashes of light, new floating shapes, and a dark curtain drawn from the side is the classic story of a detached retina, and it is a reason to send the patient for expert examination at once rather than to watch. A gradual painless loss in both eyes over years is the ordinary cataract or the ordinary effect of age, and it is the least urgent of these, which is exactly why the urgent ones must be excluded first.

Vision is measured before it is explained, and the measurement can be made without equipment. A patient who can read the smallest line of a chart, or any ordinary printed page held at a fixed distance, has useful central vision, and a patient who cannot read but who can count fingers, see a hand move, or tell light from dark still has an eye that can be assessed. A pinhole made in a card sharpens the vision of an eye whose problem is a refractive error and does nothing for an eye whose problem is in the retina, the nerve, or the media, so the pinhole is a small test with a large answer. The visual fields are examined by confrontation, with the examiner's face level with the patient's and a moving finger brought in from each side, and a defect that stops at the midline points to the eye or its nerve while a defect that crosses it points to the brain. The pupils are examined with a torch for their size, their shape, and their reaction, and the light is swung from one eye to the other to find a pupil that dilates rather than constricts when the light moves to it, which means the retina or the optic nerve of that eye is not working.

The red eye is the commonest eye complaint and the one most often dismissed, so the work is to separate the many benign causes from the few dangerous ones. Infection of the conjunctiva produces a diffuse redness that is worst at the edges, a discharge that may be watery or thick, itching in the allergic form, and vision that stays normal once the discharge is wiped away. A corneal ulcer is different, because the pain is severe, light is unbearable, there is a feeling of something in the eye, the redness is concentrated around the cornea, and vision is blurred. The finding that reveals it is a defect on the cornea that stains with fluorescein and glows under blue light, and a contact lens wearer with a red and painful eye must be assumed to have one, because such an infection can destroy the cornea within a short time. Inflammation inside the eye, in the iris and the tissues around it, gives a deep aching pain, a dislike of light, a small pupil, and a rim of redness around the cornea, and it is often linked to a disease of the joints, the bowel, or the spine.

Acute angle closure glaucoma is the red eye that blinds, and it happens when the drainage angle at the edge of the iris closes and the fluid inside the eye can no longer leave. The pressure then rises quickly, the cornea becomes cloudy, and the optic nerve, which has no defense against pressure, begins to lose fibers. The patient is usually older and often farsighted, and describes severe pain in and around the eye, a headache, nausea and vomiting, and colored halos around lights. The examination finds a partly dilated pupil that does not react, a cornea that looks steamy, and an eye that feels harder than the other one through the closed lid. The finding that would make a calm diagnosis of simple conjunctivitis wrong is any of these together with a red eye that hurts deeply and disturbs vision. A figure such as 21 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the upper limit of normal pressure inside the eye, but it is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the instruments, the technique, and the accepted range differ between services. The decision that follows is urgent referral for treatment that lowers the pressure, and the finding that would change that decision is a clear alternative such as a superficial infection with discharge, itching, and normal vision.

Giant cell arteritis is an inflammation of the large and medium arteries of the head and neck, and it matters because it can close the artery that supplies the eye and leave the patient blind in one eye and then in the other. The patient is usually older than 50 years, and though that age is offered as a guide and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, the reasoning behind it is that the disease becomes common only in later life. The symptoms before the visual loss are a new headache, tenderness of the scalp when the hair is brushed, pain in the jaw or the tongue when the patient chews or talks, pain in the shoulders and hips, and a general sense of illness. The visual loss may be sudden and painless, or it may come in brief spells that recover, and either pattern demands immediate action. The finding that supports the diagnosis is a pale and swollen optic disc when the back of the eye is examined, together with a raised sedimentation rate or another marker of inflammation in the blood, and a sample of the temporal artery examined under the microscope confirms it, though the result may take days. Because the loss can become permanent while those results are awaited, the decision to begin treatment is made on suspicion, and the finding that would make that decision wrong is a different cause that fully explains the picture.

In a well-resourced hospital the eye is examined with a slit lamp, which brings a magnified beam of light onto the surface and allows the cornea, the front chamber, the iris, and the lens to be seen in detail. Fluorescein is used with a blue light to show a defect in the cornea, and the depth of the front chamber is judged to decide whether the angle is narrow and whether the pupil can be safely dilated. The pressure inside the eye is measured with an instrument that rests gently on the cornea, and the back of the eye is examined through a dilated pupil to see the retina, the optic disc, and the vessels. Where a detachment is suspected, an ultrasound of the eye can show the retina when blood or a cataract blocks the view. Each test answers a question that the bedside examination has already raised, and a test ordered without such a question produces a result that no one can use. The rule that protects the patient is simple: the eye that hurts deeply and sees halos is not an eye to dilate until the angle has been shown to be open.

The patient who cannot hear is asked whether the loss came suddenly or slowly, whether one ear or both are affected, and what accompanies it. A slowly progressive loss in both ears, worse in noisy places and in conversation against background sound, suggests the ordinary loss of age or of years of noise. A loss with a discharge, a perforated drum, or a change in pressure suggests disease of the canal, the drum, or the middle ear. Sudden loss in one ear with ringing, and sometimes with dizziness, is a different matter, because it may be an injury of the inner ear and it must be treated as an emergency of hearing, since the chance of recovery falls when the patient is seen late. The finding that reveals it is a loss that goes to the better ear when a vibrating fork is placed on the middle of the forehead, together with a normal canal and a normal drum, because a conductive loss sends the sound to the affected side while a sensorineural loss sends it to the healthy one. A tumor of the nerve that carries hearing and balance can produce a loss that is gradual and one-sided, often with ringing and unsteadiness, and it is a reason to image the pathway where imaging exists.

Sudden sensorineural hearing loss deserves its own place because it is the ear's equivalent of a stroke and because it is so easily attributed to wax. The loss usually appears over hours, and a figure such as 3 days is often quoted as the interval within which the diagnosis is made, but that interval is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the definitions in use differ between services and editions. The patient may wake with the loss, or notice it while using the telephone, and there is often a loud ringing and a sense of fullness rather than pain. The examination of the canal and the drum is normal, and the fork placed on the forehead is heard in the better ear, which places the fault beyond the middle ear. The decision to treat is made on the clinical picture and does not wait for a hearing test where access to one is delayed, and the finding that would make that decision wrong is an obvious cause in the canal or the middle ear that explains the loss completely. An audiometer measures the softest tone the patient can hear at each frequency, and the values it reports are set by the equipment and the reference tables in use and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A discharging ear has a short list of causes and one dangerous direction of spread. Infection of the canal, common after swimming or after scratching with a finger or a stick, gives itching, pain when the ear is pulled, and a scanty discharge, and the drum is usually intact and visible once the debris is cleared. Infection of the middle ear that has burst through the drum gives a discharge that follows pain and fever, and the patient often feels better once the drum has opened, though the infection continues behind it. A discharge that has lasted for weeks or months, with an unpleasant smell and material that looks like skin debris in the canal, may be a cholesteatoma, a growing collection of skin in the middle ear that destroys bone and can reach the brain. The spread of infection to the bone behind the ear produces mastoiditis, and its findings are swelling and redness over the bone, an ear pushed forward, and a fever, and a temperature such as 38 degrees Celsius supports it, though the line at which fever is called present varies with the site and the method of measurement and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A facial weakness, a severe headache, a stiff neck, or a change in consciousness in a patient with an ear infection means that the infection has reached the nerve or the brain, and that patient needs urgent help. A discharging ear in a patient with diabetes or with immune defenses suppressed, especially with severe pain at night and fleshy tissue in the canal, may be a destructive infection of the base of the skull and is a diagnosis not to miss.

The blocked nose is usually a nuisance and occasionally a warning. A blockage that shifts from side to side with the position of the head, with sneezing, itching, and a clear discharge, is the allergic nose, and a blockage with a thick discharge, facial pain, and a poor sense of smell follows a cold or an infection of the sinuses. A blockage that is fixed to one side and does not clear, especially with a blood-stained discharge, a loss of smell, an ache in the face or the ear, and a lump in the neck, may be a tumor of the nose or the space behind it, and that possibility must be named because it is easily treated as a simple cold for months. Bleeding from the nose is anterior in most patients and comes from a visible vessel on the front part of the septum, but bleeding that pours backward into the throat, that comes from an older patient with a high pressure, or that follows an injury or a medicine that thins the blood is a different problem and may need expert packing. A torch and a spoon handle are enough to see the front of the nose and to decide whether the bleeding can be stopped simply or whether the patient must travel.

Sore throat is the commonest reason for a visit and the place where a dangerous cause hides inside a familiar one. Most sore throats are viral, with a cough, a runny nose, a hoarse voice, and a fever that settles, and they need no specific treatment beyond comfort. Infection with the streptococcus bacterium is more likely when there is fever, pus on the tonsils, tender lymph nodes in the neck, and no cough, and the Centor score is one attempt to formalize that reasoning; its contents and any cut-off attached to it are an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the thresholds differ between editions and populations. The finding that changes everything is asymmetry: a swelling on one side of the throat that pushes the uvula to the other side, a voice that sounds muffled, drooling, and difficulty opening the mouth mean a collection of pus beside the tonsil. A collection behind the throat is more common in children, and it produces a stiff neck, a refusal to swallow, a muffled voice, and difficulty breathing, and the neck may look full on one side. Neither collection responds to tablets alone, and both require expert drainage, so the decision is where the patient should be examined next rather than which medicine to use.

The sore throat that threatens the airway is the one that must be recognized without touching the patient. Inflammation of the flap that covers the windpipe, which is rare but lethal, produces a sudden severe sore throat, a muffled voice, drooling, a high fever, and a posture in which the patient sits forward with the chin up and the arms braced, and the breathing is noisy and labored. The patient looks frightened and still, and the throat should not be examined with a tongue depressor in this setting, because the act can close the airway completely. The finding that reveals the danger is stridor, a harsh noise heard on inspiration, together with drooling and a refusal to swallow, and any of these in a patient who is febrile and unwell must bring senior help and equipment to the bedside rather than a walk to another room.

A tumor of the head and neck announces itself in ordinary ways, and the clinician who waits for a dramatic sign will miss it. The risk is concentrated in people who use tobacco and drink alcohol heavily, and it is also seen in people with a long-standing infection of the throat or with a poor diet. The symptoms to take seriously are hoarseness or a change in the voice that has lasted more than a few weeks, a sore throat on one side that does not settle, blood in the saliva, a lump in the neck, an ulcer in the mouth that will not heal, pain in one ear with a normal ear, and a blockage of one side of the nose. The interval that turns an ordinary hoarseness into a concern is commonly given as a few weeks, and that interval is offered as an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the recommended period differs between services and editions. The finding that matters most is a neck lump in an adult that is firm, painless, and fixed, which is a cancer until proved otherwise, and a single enlarged node on one side of the neck deserves examination of the whole upper airway and food passage rather than a course of antibiotics. The decision is referral to a center where the airway can be examined directly and a sample taken, and the finding that would make that decision less urgent is a clear infection that resolves completely with the expected time course.

In the hospital the examination of the ear, nose and throat is extended by instruments that answer precise questions. An audiometer measures hearing thresholds across frequencies and separates a conductive loss from a sensorineural one, and a test of the movement of the drum and the small bones shows whether the middle ear is working. A flexible instrument passed through the nose allows the space behind the nose, the base of the tongue, and the voice box to be seen directly, which is the decisive step in a patient with hoarseness or a neck lump. A computed tomography, or CT, scan of the sinuses, the ear, or the neck shows bone and the spread of infection, and a magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, scan shows the soft tissues, the nerves, and the brain more clearly, and each is chosen only when its result would change the plan. A biopsy of a lump, an ulcer, or the lining of the nose gives the diagnosis that no image can give. The clinician who knows which question is unanswered will use the hospital well, and the clinician who orders everything will be left with findings that no one can interpret.

Where the clinic has only a torch, a spoon, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is carried out with fewer instruments and no less care. The torch examines the pupil and its reaction, and the light swung from one eye to the other will show a pupil that fails to constrict, which points to the retina or the nerve behind it. The back of the eye can be seen only with an instrument, but the red glow reflected from the pupil through the torch shows that the media are clear, and the bowl of a polished spoon held close to the eye and lit from the side can give a crude magnified view of the front of the eye. A torch held at the outer side of the eye and shone across the front of the eye casts a shadow on the inner part of the iris when the angle is narrow, which is a warning not to dilate the pupil. Hearing is tested with a whispered voice at arm's length in a quiet room, with the other ear masked by rubbing a finger against it if a second person is available to help. The spoon handle depresses the tongue to see the throat and the tonsils, but never in the patient who is drooling and struggling to breathe. The thermometer, the pulse, and the breathing rate turn the impression of illness into something recordable, and the decision is again about the journey rather than the label.

The decision that follows any of these assessments is usually not a diagnosis but a plan, and the plan should say what finding would change it. Referral now is the right answer when sight or hearing is threatened, when the airway is in question, when a collection of pus is suspected, when a lump is firm and fixed, or when the patient is febrile and unwell. Watching at home is the right answer when the findings are those of a simple illness that will settle, when the patient understands what to return for, and when a review has been arranged rather than merely promised. The clinician should name the signs that must bring the patient back: a curtain across the vision, a sudden loss of hearing, a red eye that hurts and blurs, a swelling in the neck that grows, difficulty breathing or swallowing, and a fever that will not settle.

To summarize, the eye and the ear, nose and throat are best approached by asking first what the symptom threatens and where the fault lies, since the same complaint of poor vision or poor hearing may come from a surface that will heal or from a nerve that will not. The dangerous causes are named where their symptoms appear: acute angle closure glaucoma with a painful red eye, a hazy cornea, and halos; a detached retina with flashes, floaters, and a curtain; a corneal ulcer in a contact lens wearer; giant cell arteritis in an older patient with headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw pain; sudden sensorineural hearing loss in a normal-looking ear; a collection of pus beside or behind the throat; an airway threatened by inflammation of the flap over the windpipe; and a tumor of the head and neck presenting as hoarseness, an ulcer, or a firm neck lump. The bedside examination, done with a torch, a spoon, and a whispered voice, or with a slit lamp, an audiometer, and a scanner, is chosen to answer the question of place, and the reasoning transfers between the two settings even when the instruments do not. Every figure in this chapter, whether a temperature, an age, an interval, a threshold, or a reference range, is an illustration of that reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient whose sight, hearing, or breathing is at risk is helped first, and the clinician who arranges the next step clearly has done the most important part of the work.

# Chapter 56 — Psychiatry

Psychiatry is the part of medicine in which the organ under examination is the mind, and the clinician who treats it as separate from the body makes two opposite mistakes. The first is to accept a psychiatric label as the whole explanation, so that a patient who is anxious or depressed is never examined for the physical disease that produced the mood. The second is to treat a psychiatric symptom as a failure of character, so that the patient is blamed rather than assessed. The reasoning here is the reasoning of the rest of this book: a problem is described, a differential diagnosis is assembled, the dangerous causes are placed first, and the findings raise or lower each possibility. Psychiatry differs in that the history is the principal instrument and the patient's account of the inner world is the chief evidence. This chapter is educational material, it is not a protocol, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Several lethal possibilities must be named before any comfortable psychiatric explanation is accepted, because each announces itself with a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. The patient who is confused, inattentive, and fluctuating through the day may have delirium, which is a disorder of the body expressing itself through the brain, and the finding is attention that cannot be held with an alertness that changes from hour to hour. The patient who is drowsy, sweating, feverish, rigid, and tremulous after a medicine that alters dopamine or serotonin may have a drug-induced emergency, and the finding is rigidity with fever in a mind that has suddenly changed. The patient whose speech has stopped, whose body holds a posture, and who will not eat or drink may have catatonia, which is an emergency rather than an attitude, and the finding is the stillness with resistance to being moved. The patient who is agitated, hallucinating, and trembling after heavy alcohol use may be in withdrawal, which kills through seizures, an abnormal rhythm of the heart, or infection, and the finding is the tremor with a racing pulse and a rising temperature. The patient who is despondent and has spoken of death is at risk of suicide, and the finding that raises urgency is a plan, a means, and the intention to use them.

The mental state examination is the psychiatric equivalent of the physical examination, and it is structured so that nothing is left to impression. The clinician observes appearance and behavior first, because dress, grooming, posture, eye contact, and movement are visible before a word is spoken. Speech is judged for its rate, volume, and whether it can be interrupted, since pressure of speech and the leap from one idea to the next carry information the content alone does not. Thought is examined for its form, whether it moves in a straight line or jumps, and for its content, which includes preoccupations, delusions, and ideas of harm, while perception is examined for hallucinations, which are perceptions without an object. Attention is tested by reciting the months in reverse or counting backward in sevens, and recent memory by naming 3 objects and asking for them after a delay. Where a formal cognitive score is used, its contents and the figure at which it raises concern vary between versions and populations, so the result must be read against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than against memory.

Delirium is the presentation most often mistaken for a psychiatric disorder, and the mistake is dangerous because delirium is almost always a symptom of something physical. It develops over a short interval, and the interval that defines it is stated differently in different editions, so any figure offered for it is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the boundary between delirium and a chronic decline is drawn differently in different countries and services. The two most useful features are inattention and fluctuation, so the patient cannot hold a task and the alertness rises and falls across the day, often worse at night. Orientation may be disturbed, but a patient can be fully oriented and still be delirious, and the patient may hallucinate, most often visually, and may be frightened by what is seen. Whenever delirium is present, the clinician stops looking for a psychiatric explanation and begins a physical search.

The physical search for the cause of delirium follows a fixed list, because the causes that kill are common and treatable. Infection is the most frequent, and in an older patient the infection may be in the chest, the urine, the skin, or the bloodstream, with a temperature barely raised or absent. A shortage of oxygen from lung disease or from a clot in the lung, a low sodium, a failing liver or kidney, and a disturbance of calcium all alter the mind before they alter anything the clinician can see. A blood glucose below 3 millimoles per liter can produce confusion and sweating, and that figure is a reference range each laboratory sets for itself, so the value that matters must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Medicines are a leading cause, including sedatives, drugs for pain, drugs for the bladder, steroids, and anything recently started, stopped, or increased. Alcohol and sedative withdrawal, a head injury, a seizure, an infection of the brain or its coverings, and a stroke or a bleed inside the skull belong in the same list. The finding that most often reveals the cause is the combination of what changed, a temperature, a blood glucose where it can be measured, and every medicine the patient takes.

Depression is not sadness, and the difference matters because the decision to treat depends on the syndrome rather than the mood. The reasoning rests on features that must be present together for a sustained interval: a low mood, a loss of interest, a change in sleep and appetite, a change in weight, fatigue, poor concentration, guilt, and thoughts of death. How long those features must last is set differently in different manuals, so the interval is only an illustration; verify it in the guideline your service follows and in the local protocol, because the editions in circulation do not draw the line in the same place. Depression commonly presents as a physical complaint, with headache, back pain, insomnia, or a fatigue the patient believes is bodily, and a clinician who looks only for sadness will miss it. A loss of 5 per cent of body weight over a few weeks is often quoted as a sign of physical illness, but the figure and the interval must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold differs between countries, editions, and laboratories. The severity matters more than the label, because a patient with psychotic features, with a refusal to eat, or with a settled intention to die is in a different category from mild symptoms.

A long list of physical illnesses imitates depression, and the search for them is part of the assessment rather than a separate errand. An underactive thyroid produces low mood, fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and slowed thinking, and the finding is a slow pulse, dry skin, and a swelling at the front of the neck. Anemia produces fatigue, breathlessness, and pallor, and the finding is the pale conjunctiva and the rapid pulse. A cancer that has not declared itself, an infection such as tuberculosis or infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, a deficiency of folate or of thiamine, an underactive adrenal gland, and a high calcium can all present this way. Medicines are a frequent cause, including steroids and some drugs for blood pressure, and the history of what was started before the mood changed is the key. The finding that makes a physical cause less likely is a clear psychosocial story with a normal examination and normal tests where those exist, and even then the two can coexist.

Suicide risk is assessed directly, in plain words, and the fear that asking will plant the idea is not supported by evidence; the patient who has been waiting to be asked is often relieved. The clinician asks whether the patient has thought about death, whether the thought has become a wish to die, whether there is a plan, whether the means are available, and whether the patient intends to act. Past attempts, a family history of suicide, a recent loss, a serious physical illness, chronic pain, isolation, and heavy drinking all raise the level, and a patient who is agitated, sleepless, and hopeless is at greater risk than one who is withdrawn and silent. The clinician must ask about access to means, including medicines kept at home, firearms, and other dangerous items, because reducing access is one of the few measures that reliably lowers risk. No score replaces the conversation, and a low figure on any checklist must never be used to send a patient home against the clinician's own unease.

Mania is a sustained elevation or irritability of mood with an increase in activity and energy, and it is dangerous because the patient may not see it as illness. The patient sleeps very little without feeling tired, speaks rapidly, moves from one idea to the next, feels unusually important, spends money or takes risks, and may become grandiose or irritable when opposed. How long the picture must last before it is called mania is set differently in different manuals, so the interval is only an illustration; verify it in the guideline your service follows and in the local protocol, since the editions and countries that use them do not agree. A first episode of mania in an older patient deserves a physical search, since steroids, thyroid disease, stimulant drugs, and delirium can all produce the picture. The risk is harm through reckless behavior, harm to others, and exhaustion, and it is highest when the mood is mixed with despair, because that combination carries suicide risk. The finding that changes the plan is a patient who cannot be kept safe by those around them, because that patient needs a place where observation is possible.

Psychosis is the presence of delusions, hallucinations, or a disorganization of thought so marked that the patient cannot be understood, and the first task is to decide whether it is primary or secondary to something else. A hallucination in clear consciousness suggests a primary psychotic illness, while a visual hallucination in a patient whose alertness fluctuates points toward delirium and a physical cause. A first episode in a young person may begin a lifelong illness, but the same picture can follow cannabis, stimulant drugs, or a steroid, and the finding that would change the diagnosis is a clear link in time to a substance. Red flags that demand a physical search are a fever, a headache, a stiff neck, a seizure, focal weakness, an abnormal level of alertness, and a first presentation at an unusual age. A patient with HIV infection or another cause of immune suppression can develop an infection or a tumor of the brain that presents as psychosis. The finding that most often reveals a secondary cause is a focal neurological sign or an abnormal level of consciousness, and either one moves the patient to a medical pathway at once.

Anxiety is a normal response that becomes a disorder when it is disproportionate, persistent, and disabling, and it is a positive diagnosis rather than a diagnosis of exclusion. The patient describes worry that cannot be controlled, restlessness, a racing heart, breathlessness, sweating, tremor, chest tightness, dizziness, and a fear of losing control or of dying. The mimic list includes a heart attack, an abnormal rhythm of the heart, a clot in the lung, a low blood glucose, an overactive thyroid, an adrenal tumor, asthma, and withdrawal from alcohol or sedatives. Where an electrocardiogram, or ECG, is available it answers one of those questions and not all of them, because a normal tracing does not exclude a clot in the lung. The examination looks for a rapid or irregular pulse, a raised pressure, a tremor, a swelling in the neck, and signs in the chest, and the clinician who finds none has lowered the probability of physical disease without excluding it. Alcohol and sedatives are a common hidden cause, because the patient may be in withdrawal between doses, and the finding is a tremor and a pulse faster than the story would suggest.

Substance use is a medical condition with a physical examination, and the withdrawal states are emergencies that must be recognized before the patient deteriorates. Alcohol withdrawal begins after the last drink, and the interval over which it appears is stated in different sources, so any figure given for it is a teaching illustration that must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services organize their observation periods differently. The early features are tremor, sweating, a racing pulse, anxiety, and insomnia, and they may progress to seizures and then to a confused, hallucinating, feverish state that can kill. A patient with a rapid pulse above 120 beats per minute, a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or more, sweating, and confusion after stopping alcohol is severely ill, and both of those numbers are illustrations to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the values that should cause alarm depend on the patient, the country, and the edition of the reference in use. Opioid withdrawal is extremely uncomfortable but rarely lethal, while opioid intoxication kills through a slow breathing rate and a reduced level of consciousness, and the finding is pinpoint pupils with shallow breathing.

An assessment never becomes grounds for dismissing a physical complaint, and this is the single most important rule in psychiatric practice. A patient with a known mental illness can develop a heart attack, a pneumonia, a broken bone, or a clot in the lung, and the symptoms will be attributed to the mind unless the clinician actively looks for the physical cause. The error is more common in patients who cannot give a clear history, including patients with a communication difficulty, patients who are sedated, and patients who are in pain but do not complain. A new confusion or a change in behavior in such a patient is a physical alarm, not a relapse, until proven otherwise. The clinician who writes down what was considered, what was excluded, and what remains uncertain has protected both the patient and the reasoning.

In a clinic with time and privacy, the psychiatric assessment is done slowly, and the setting itself is part of the treatment. The clinician sits at the same level as the patient, allows silence, and lets the patient set the order of the story before directing it. Privacy allows the questions that are hard to ask elsewhere, about mood, about sex, about violence at home, about drinking, and about suicide, and the clinician should explain why each is asked so that it does not feel like an interrogation. The physical examination is still performed, because the body is where many psychiatric presentations begin, and the clinician looks at the thyroid, the skin, the tongue, the weight, the pulse, the pressure, and the color of the conjunctiva. A thermometer and a torch extend the examination, and a watch turns the pulse and the breathing into measurements rather than impressions. Where the patient cannot speak freely, a family member may be seen separately with permission, and that second account often changes the picture.

In a general hospital the same assessment is compressed and performed at the bedside of a patient who may not want to be seen. The referral question must be read carefully, because the team that asks for help is often asking whether the patient is safe, whether the behavior is a medical symptom, or whether the patient can decide about treatment, and the answer to each is different. The consultant gathers collateral history from the nursing staff and the family, since the patient may be too ill, too drowsy, or too suspicious to give it, and the nurses often hold the most useful observations. Restlessness, aggression, and refusal in a hospital bed are frequently caused by pain, a full bladder, constipation, a shortage of oxygen, sepsis, withdrawal, or a medicine, and each is sought before any psychiatric label is applied. The clinician examines the body as thoroughly as the ward allows, because an uncooperative patient may still have a wound, an ulcer, a swollen joint, or a distended abdomen.

Capacity is a decision-specific judgment and not a global label, so the question is always whether this patient can make this decision at this time. The clinician asks whether the patient can understand the information, retain it long enough to weigh it, use it to reach a choice, and communicate that choice. A patient who disagrees with the team does not lack capacity, and a patient with a psychiatric diagnosis does not automatically lack it either. Capacity can be lost for one decision and preserved for another, and it can change as the illness changes, so the assessment is repeated when the situation changes. A patient who lacks capacity must still be involved as far as possible, and the decision must be made in the patient's best interest with the people who know the patient involved. When there is doubt, the clinician should seek help rather than settle the question alone, because the consequences of a wrong judgment fall on the patient.

The decision to treat a psychiatric illness is a diagnostic decision as much as any other, and it is made on the severity, the risk, and the cause rather than the name alone. Treatment is the right answer when a severe depression has psychotic features, when catatonia threatens nutrition and hydration, when delirium has a treatable physical cause, when a withdrawal state is progressing toward seizures, and when the risk of suicide cannot be managed where the patient is. Treatment is the wrong answer when a physical cause has been missed, when the presentation is a response to a life event that is resolving with support, and when the medicine that would be chosen could harm a patient whose illness is not of that kind. The finding that supports the choice is the response over time and the absence of the harm that was feared, and the finding that would reverse it is a new physical sign or a deterioration in the mental state. Naming the decision and the evidence for it is more useful than naming a dose, because this book teaches reasoning and not prescribing.

A constructed illustration may make the reasoning concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than a portrait of any real person. Imagine a man in his sixties brought to a clinic because his family says he has become quiet and has stopped eating, and in the first minutes the clinician notices that he is slow, cold, constipated, and that his pulse is slow; the mood looks like depression and the examination suggests the thyroid. Now imagine a young woman brought to an emergency department because she has not slept and believes the neighbors are watching her, and the clinician finds a fever, a stiff neck, and a fluctuating alertness that move her care in a different direction within minutes. Neither person is real, and neither story should be applied to a real patient without a full assessment.

A patient who is sent home after a psychiatric assessment must leave with a plan that is clear and written down, because the risk of suicide is highest in the period after discharge. The plan names the warning signs the patient and the family should watch for, the person to call, and the place to go at any hour. The clinician should reduce access to the means of self-harm in the home, involve the family where the patient agrees, and make sure the next appointment is real rather than promised. A follow-up interval is a figure like any other, so the time between visits must be set against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the appropriate interval depends on the severity of the illness and the support available. The patient should be told that returning sooner is not a failure, and that a new physical symptom deserves the same attention as a new mental one.

Psychiatry across the lifespan changes the weighting of causes rather than the method, and some periods of life carry a much higher risk of severe illness. In an older patient, delirium, depression, dementia, and the effects of medicines overlap, and the same presentation may contain all four, so the physical search and the cognitive assessment are done together. The weeks after childbirth are the most important window of risk, because a woman who becomes sleepless, confused, suspicious, or preoccupied with the baby may have postpartum psychosis, an emergency for the mother and the infant. The finding that should change the plan is a mother who is not sleeping at all, whose speech is disorganized, or who believes the baby is damaged or that she must harm herself, and that woman needs help and observation now rather than an appointment later. Other windows include the period after a bereavement, after a serious illness or an operation, and after a discharge from hospital, and a previous severe episode or violence at home lowers the threshold for help.

The differential diagnosis in psychiatry is assembled as anywhere else, by running through the great classes of disease before settling on a favored explanation. The Vindicate framework asks the clinician to consider in turn the vascular, the infectious, the neoplastic, the degenerative, the iatrogenic, the congenital, the autoimmune, the traumatic, and the endocrine or metabolic causes of the picture. In a patient with a change in mood or behavior, the vascular cause may be a stroke or a bleed inside the skull, the infectious cause may be an infection of the brain or the body, and the metabolic cause may be a disturbance of the thyroid, the glucose, or the sodium. The iatrogenic group deserves particular attention, because a medicine recently started, increased, or stopped is one of the most common causes of a new psychiatric symptom. Each possibility is then raised or lowered by the history, the examination, and the tests that exist, and the ranking is decided by both likelihood and danger.

The interview is the principal instrument of psychiatric assessment, and how it is conducted decides how much the patient will reveal. The clinician begins with open questions, allows the patient to finish, and uses silence rather than filling it, because the most important sentence often follows a pause. Distress is expressed differently in different cultures and families, and a symptom that seems disproportionate in one setting may be an ordinary language of suffering in another, so the clinician asks what it means to this patient. Where the patient and the clinician do not share a language, an interpreter who is not a family member is preferable, because a relative may soften, omit, or add to what is said. The clinician should be honest about the limits of confidentiality, especially when the risk of harm to the patient or another person is present.

The physical examination of a patient with a psychiatric presentation is not a formality, and several findings are visible only if the clinician looks for them. Scars on the forearms, the thighs, or the abdomen may be the record of earlier self-harm, and puncture marks in the veins of the arms, the legs, or the neck suggest injecting drug use. The weight, the hydration, the state of the teeth, and the color of the conjunctiva tell the clinician how long the illness has lasted and how much the body has suffered. A tremor, a rapid pulse, sweating, and a swollen neck point toward thyroid disease or withdrawal, while a slow pulse, dry skin, and slowed movement point toward an underactive thyroid. The skin is examined for a rash, a bruise, an ulcer, and a wound, and the abdomen for a full bladder and a loaded bowel, since both can produce agitation in a patient who cannot explain the discomfort.

To summarize, psychiatric presentations are assessed with the same method as every other problem in this book: the history first, the dangerous causes named early, the body examined as carefully as the mind, and the findings used to rank the differential diagnosis. Delirium is treated as a physical illness until proved otherwise; suicide risk is asked about directly and without euphemism, and no checklist takes the place of the conversation; depression, anxiety, mania, and psychosis are each examined for the physical illnesses that imitate them, including thyroid disease, anemia, infection, a deficiency of a vitamin, medicines, and the withdrawal states. The mental state examination supplies the structure, and it is carried into a clinic with time and privacy and into a hospital bedside where the patient does not wish to be seen. Assessment never becomes a reason to dismiss a physical complaint, and a new confusion or a new behavior in a patient with a psychiatric diagnosis is a medical alarm until it is explained. Every figure in this chapter, whether a score, a cut-off, a temperature, a rate, a reference range, or an interval, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

# Chapter 57 — Pregnancy and Obstetrics

A pregnant woman is two patients at once, and most decisions in obstetrics follow from that fact. The clinician asks whether the pregnancy is normal for its stage and whether the symptom belongs to pregnancy or to a disease that pregnancy has made more likely. Pregnancy changes the baseline, so a pulse, a pressure, or a swelling may carry a different meaning here than in another patient. It also changes the consequences, because a delay for the mother is usually a delay for the baby, and a minor condition can become lethal. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the local protocol of the service in which the woman is seen.

Several lethal possibilities must be named before any comfortable explanation is accepted, because each is betrayed by a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. The woman of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain, a missed period, and faintness may have an ectopic pregnancy, and the finding is one-sided tenderness with shoulder tip pain. The woman bleeding in late pregnancy may have a placenta previa or a placental abruption, separated by whether the uterus is soft and painless or tense and tender. Sudden tearing pain in labor with loss of the baby's heartbeat may mean a uterine rupture, a surgical emergency recognized on suspicion. Fever, a rapid pulse, and an offensive discharge after birth mean puerperal sepsis until another cause is found, and breathlessness with a swollen calf may mean a clot in the lung. Pre-eclampsia runs behind all of these, because it can turn a mild headache into a seizure or a stroke.

The first step is to establish whether the woman is pregnant and how far the pregnancy has advanced, because every finding is read against that stage. A missed period, breast tenderness, nausea, urinary frequency, and fatigue are the usual early symptoms, and a test for the hormone human chorionic gonadotropin confirms the diagnosis where one exists. Where no test exists, the clinician relies on the history and on a softened, bluish cervix with an enlarged uterus. The date is usually estimated from the first day of the last menstrual period, and that estimate is approximate and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the method differs between services. Menstrual dates can mislead after a recent pregnancy or with an irregular cycle, and an early ultrasound measurement is more reliable where it can be obtained.

The history in pregnancy is an obstetric history as well as a medical one. The clinician asks how many pregnancies the woman has had, how many ended in birth, how many ended early, and how each one ended. A previous cesarean birth, a previous stillbirth, a previous pre-eclampsia, or a previous heavy bleeding after birth all raise the chance of the same problem returning. The medical past belongs in the same conversation, among it high blood pressure, diabetes, kidney disease, epilepsy, asthma, sickle cell disease, tuberculosis, and any previous clot. The medicines she takes, including treatment for infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, must be asked about without judgment. Social questions decide whether any plan is possible, so the clinician asks who is at home, how she would reach a hospital, and whether she is safe from violence.

Pregnancy alters the vital signs and produces symptoms that would be alarming in a patient who is not pregnant. The blood pressure usually falls a little in the middle months because the vessels relax, so a reading that would be ordinary elsewhere may be an early rise for this woman. The pulse rate climbs, and a rate of 100 beats per minute at rest may be normal near the end of pregnancy, though that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted range varies with the stage of pregnancy. Nausea, heartburn, constipation, and swelling of the feet and ankles are common, but swelling of the face and hands belongs to the assessment of pre-eclampsia. Faintness, palpitations, and fatigue are frequent, and they should still prompt a search for anemia, an arrhythmia, a clot in the lung, and a thyroid disorder. The temperature should not be raised by pregnancy itself, so a fever must be explained.

The laboratory and the examination also change in pregnancy, and a finding read without that knowledge can mislead. The blood count usually falls a little because the plasma increases more than the red cells, so a mild anemia of dilution is normal, while a genuinely low count with a low measure of stored iron points to a deficiency that must be corrected. The white cell count rises slightly and climbs further during labor, so it cannot be used alone to confirm infection. The blood clots more readily, which protects the woman at birth and endangers her afterwards. Substances that measure thyroid function shift at the start of pregnancy, so the reference range is set by the laboratory and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The legs should be examined for a difference in size, warmth, and tenderness, because a clot in a deep vein is common in pregnancy and may show nothing.

The abdominal examination in pregnancy has its own language, and each part answers a question about the baby. The uterus is measured from the pubic bone to the top of the fundus, and the height in centimeters usually follows the weeks of pregnancy after the middle of the second trimester, a guide that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the expected values differ with the woman's size and the number of babies. The clinician decides how the baby lies, whether head down, bottom down, or across, and feels which part is presenting at the brim of the pelvis. Listening for the baby's heartbeat with a stethoscope designed for the purpose, or with a hand held still, confirms that the baby is alive. The baby's movements are the cheapest and most sensitive report of wellbeing that exists, and a change in the pattern the woman knows is a reason to act rather than to wait.

Every antenatal contact, however brief, is an opportunity to look for the small number of signs that change everything. The clinician asks about bleeding from the vagina, pain in the abdomen, headache that will not settle, flashing lights or blurred vision, pain under the ribs on the right, sudden swelling of the face or hands, fever, and an offensive discharge. The woman is asked about the baby's movements, leakage of fluid, breathlessness, chest pain, a painful swollen leg, and any convulsion or loss of consciousness. The pressure is measured, the urine is tested for protein, the temperature is taken, and the abdomen is examined. The purpose of this fixed set of questions is recognition of the woman who must leave immediately, while she is still able to leave.

Pre-eclampsia is the disease that most often turns a normal pregnancy into an emergency, and it begins as a disorder of the placenta. It appears after the twentieth week of pregnancy, and the period over which it may start and progress must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted boundaries are stated differently in different services. The placenta releases substances that injure the lining of the blood vessels, so the pressure rises, protein leaks into the urine, fluid moves into the tissues, and the platelets fall. The woman may feel entirely well at the beginning, which is why the pressure and the urine are measured at every visit rather than only when she complains. The risk is higher in a first or multiple pregnancy, in a woman who has had pre-eclampsia before, and in a woman with high blood pressure, diabetes, kidney disease, or a high body mass index. The condition can also appear for the first time during labor or in the days after birth.

The assessment of pre-eclampsia rests on two measurements and a set of questions. The pressure is measured with the woman seated and rested, with a cuff of the right size, and a figure such as 140 over 90 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the line at which the diagnosis is considered; that figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line differs between countries, editions, and ways of measuring. Protein in the urine supports the diagnosis, but a woman with a raised pressure and no protein may still have the disease, so its absence never excludes it. The clinician asks about headache, visual disturbance, pain under the ribs on the right, vomiting, and sudden swelling, because these move the assessment to a severe form of the disease. The examination looks for brisk reflexes, clonus at the ankle, fluid in the lungs, and tenderness in the upper abdomen.

Severe pre-eclampsia is recognized by the company it keeps rather than by the pressure alone. A severe unrelenting headache, flashing lights or loss of vision, pain in the upper abdomen, vomiting, breathlessness from fluid in the lungs, and a falling passage of urine all point to organs that are being injured. A seizure in a woman with a raised pressure is eclampsia, a life-threatening event treated as an emergency while the cause is confirmed. A pattern of breaking down of red cells, raised liver enzymes, and a low platelet count is another severe form that may appear with little or no raised pressure. The decision to deliver is made by the team, guided by the condition of the woman and of the baby rather than by a single figure.

The treatment decisions in pre-eclampsia are decisions about delivery and protection of the mother, not prescriptions that can be carried away from a book. Treatment is the right answer when the pressure is high and repeated, when there is protein in the urine with symptoms, when the blood tests show organ injury, or when the baby is not growing or moving as it should. The finding that makes delivery the wrong answer for now is a mild picture in a baby too immature to be born safely, in which case the woman is watched closely where the team can act at once. Where the team decides to prevent or treat a seizure, the medicine is chosen and given under the local protocol, and the listener should understand the reasoning rather than the amount. The clinician in a small clinic who recognizes the disease and starts the journey is doing more for the woman than one who waits for certainty.

Bleeding in early pregnancy is common, and the task is to separate the small bleeds that settle from the few that kill. The clinician asks how much blood has been lost, whether it is bright or dark, whether there is pain and where it is, and whether tissue has passed. The examination looks for a rising pulse, a falling pressure, tenderness in the abdomen, and a uterus that is tender or the wrong size for the dates. An ectopic pregnancy must be excluded in every woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain and a missed period, because it can bleed inside the abdomen and kill within hours. The findings that betray a leak are tenderness on one side, shoulder tip pain, a rising pulse, a falling pressure, and fullness in the lower abdomen, and an ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a mass beside it or fluid in the abdomen.

Miscarriage is far more common than ectopic pregnancy, and the danger is bleeding rather than rupture. A threatened miscarriage is bleeding with a closed cervix and a living pregnancy, and it often settles, though the woman must be told what would bring her back. An inevitable miscarriage is bleeding with an open cervix, an incomplete miscarriage leaves tissue behind with continuing bleeding and cramping, and a complete miscarriage has emptied the uterus. A missed miscarriage is a pregnancy that has stopped developing without bleeding, and it is found when the uterus is smaller than the dates or when the baby's heartbeat cannot be found. The clinician judges the amount of blood lost, the pulse, the pressure, and the tenderness, because the woman who is bleeding heavily needs help now rather than a diagnosis.

Bleeding in the second half of pregnancy is a different problem, and its causes are distinguished by pain and by the state of the uterus. The clinician asks whether the bleeding is painless or painful, whether it began suddenly, whether there was a fall or a blow to the abdomen, and whether the baby is moving as usual. The pressure and the pulse are measured at once, the abdomen is examined for tenderness and for the tone of the uterus, and the baby's heartbeat is listened for, because a mother who is stable may be carrying a baby who is not. The most important rule is that a digital examination of the vagina and the cervix is withheld until a placenta lying low has been excluded, because a finger in the cervix can provoke bleeding that cannot be stopped. Any woman with bleeding in late pregnancy belongs where an operating room and blood are available, because the blood that is visible may understate the blood that has been lost.

A placenta previa is a placenta that lies over the opening of the cervix, and it announces itself with painless, bright red bleeding that often begins without warning. The uterus is relaxed and not tender, the baby's presenting part may be high or lying across rather than head down, and the bleeding may stop and then return heavier, which is why a first small bleed is never dismissed. The danger is sudden heavy hemorrhage as the lower part of the uterus stretches or as labor begins, and it can kill the mother and the baby. The finding that reveals it is the placenta seen covering the cervical opening on ultrasound, and where no ultrasound exists the combination of painless bleeding, a soft uterus, and a baby that is not head down should carry the diagnosis. The woman is kept at rest where blood and an operating room are ready, and the way the baby will be born is usually by cesarean birth.

A placental abruption is the early separation of a normally placed placenta from the wall of the uterus, and it is the painful counterpart of placenta previa. The bleeding may be visible or concealed behind the placenta, and this is why the amount of blood seen can badly mislead the clinician. The uterus is tense and tender, often hard to the touch and painful to press, and the woman may have constant pain with a uterus that does not relax between contractions. The findings that reveal the danger are a rising pulse, a falling pressure, a baby that is not moving or whose heartbeat is abnormal, and a uterus larger than the dates because of blood trapped inside. The woman needs to be moved at once to a place where the baby can be monitored and where a birth can be carried out quickly, because abruption is a race against bleeding that continues behind the scenes.

A uterine rupture is a tear in the wall of the uterus, and it is one of the few diagnoses made almost entirely on the story and the feel of the abdomen. It happens most often in a woman who has had a previous cesarean birth or previous surgery on the uterus, and it may happen during a long or obstructed labor. The woman describes a sudden severe pain that may be tearing in character, the contractions may stop, and the shape of the abdomen may change as the baby and the placenta move into the abdominal cavity. The clinician may feel the baby's parts unusually easily through the abdominal wall, the baby's heartbeat may be lost, and the mother may become shocked from bleeding that is largely hidden. Any woman with a previous uterine scar and sudden pain, bleeding, or loss of the baby's heartbeat must be treated as having a rupture until the operating room says otherwise.

Bleeding after birth is the other great obstetric hemorrhage, and its commonest cause is a uterus that does not contract once the placenta is delivered. The clinician assesses the amount of blood lost, the pulse, the pressure, the color of the skin, and the level of consciousness, and looks for a uterus that is soft and enlarged rather than firm and low. Other causes belong in the same assessment, among them retained pieces of placenta, a tear in the cervix or the vagina, and a disorder of clotting. The finding that makes the decision to act right is continuing bleeding with a rising pulse and a falling pressure, and bleeding that has clearly stopped with a firm uterus is what would make a wait reasonable.
