The woman must be where blood can be replaced and the cause treated, and the clinician who cannot control the bleeding must arrange transfer rather than watch.

The woman with puerperal sepsis has a fever, a rapid pulse, chills, and pain in the lower abdomen, and she may have an offensive discharge and a uterus that is tender and larger than it should be. The infection may also begin in a tear, a surgical cut, a breast, the urine, the lungs, or a wound from a cesarean birth, so every site must be examined rather than assumed to be the womb. The warning findings are a rapid pulse that does not settle, rapid breathing, confusion, a falling pressure, and a reduced passage of urine. The patient whose infection has become severe needs treatment and senior help at once, and the decision to give an antibiotic before the organism is known is right when the picture is severe and wrong when a clear non-infectious cause explains everything.

A clot in a deep vein and a clot that travels to the lung are more common in pregnancy and after birth than at any other time in a young woman's life, and the second half of the disease kills quickly. The risk is highest after a cesarean birth, after a long labor, with immobility, with a high body mass index, with a previous clot, and with pre-eclampsia. The finding in the leg is swelling of one calf, warmth, tenderness, and a difference in size between the two sides, but the leg may look and feel entirely normal, so a normal examination proves nothing. The finding in the lung is a sudden breathlessness, chest pain that worsens with a breath, a rapid pulse, and a cough that may bring blood, and the chest may sound clear. Where tests exist they help, and where they do not, a woman with a plausible story is treated while she travels, because the harm of a missed clot is greater than the harm of treatment given on a good clinical case.

Heart disease is among the leading causes of death in pregnancy, and it is dangerous because the extra work of pregnancy unmasks a heart that was coping before. The woman may have been told years earlier that she had a murmur or a damaged valve, and the findings that reveal the problem are breathlessness worse than expected, a loud or new murmur, an abnormal pressure or pulse, and a faint on effort. The woman is offered testing for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis, and a positive result is what makes treatment the right answer, while a sexually transmitted infection may cause no symptoms, so questions about discharge, pain, and a partner with symptoms belong in the history. A fever in a region where malaria is transmitted is a malaria test and a journey, not a wait, because the disease can cause severe anemia and death of the baby.

In a hospital with an ultrasound, a laboratory, and an operating room, the assessment moves from suspicion to precision with tests chosen to answer specific questions. An ultrasound answers whether the pregnancy is inside the uterus, whether it is alive, how far it has advanced, where the placenta lies, and how the baby is growing, and it is the single most useful image in obstetrics. A blood count, a measure of stored iron, a clotting test, a blood group, and tests of liver and kidney function answer questions about the mother that the bedside cannot answer. An ECG and an ultrasound of the heart answer the questions raised by breathlessness or a murmur, and a CT or an MRI is used sparingly in pregnancy and only when the answer would change what is done. The operating room and the intensive care unit, or ICU, are the destinations for the woman whose bleeding, pressure, or infection cannot be controlled.

The clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer has no ultrasound and no laboratory, and yet most of the important decisions can still be made there. The history carries the greatest weight, because it never runs out: the date of the last period, the number of previous births, what happened in each, what the woman is feeling now, and how the baby is moving. The pressure is measured with a cuff, the temperature is taken, and the urine is examined for protein with a dipstick where one is available and by eye where one is not. The torch makes the gums and the conjunctiva visible for pallor, the skin visible for jaundice and rash, and the cervix visible when it is safe to look. The abdomen is palpated for the size of the uterus, the lie of the baby, and the presenting part, and a tape measure turns the fundal height into a figure that can be compared at the next visit.

The most important skill of all is recognition of the woman who must leave immediately, and the list is short enough to be remembered under pressure. She is the woman who is bleeding at any stage, especially with pain, fainting, or a uterus that is hard and tender. She is the woman in late pregnancy or after birth who has a severe headache, flashing lights, blurred vision, pain under the ribs on the right, or a fit. She is the woman with a fever and a rapid pulse who looks seriously ill, and the woman who is breathless with a swollen leg or chest pain. She is the woman whose baby has stopped moving, whose waters have broken with a green or offensive fluid, or whose baby is lying across at the time of birth. Any one of these findings is enough to start the journey, and the clinician who cannot test must rely on honest judgment rather than on false reassurance.

The weeks after birth are part of obstetrics, and they carry their own emergencies as well as their own quiet dangers. The uterus should shrink steadily and the bleeding should lessen over the first days, and a uterus that stays large or a bleeding that increases must be explained. The clinician examines the perineum or the abdominal wound, the breasts, the legs, the chest, and the temperature, because infection and clots may begin in any of those places, and pre-eclampsia can appear for the first time after birth. Communication decides whether any plan is possible, so the clinician asks who can bring the woman to a hospital, how long the journey takes, what it costs, and whether anyone at home would oppose it. A written referral should carry the dates, the findings, the pressure, the urine result, what has been done, and what is feared.

A constructed illustration may make these habits concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a woman early in pregnancy with a dull pain on one side, a small amount of bleeding, and faintness when she stands, in whom the clinician finds tenderness on that side and a rising pulse, and who is sent onward at once because the combination means an ectopic pregnancy until proved otherwise. Imagine also a woman near the end of pregnancy with a headache that will not settle and swelling of her hands, whose pressure is high and whose urine shows protein, and who is kept where the baby can be monitored. Neither woman is real, and each shows the same move, which is that the clinician asked the question the ordinary routine would have skipped.

To summarize, pregnancy changes the normal examination and creates its own diagnoses, so every finding is read against the stage of the pregnancy and against the woman's own baseline. The dangerous conditions are named where they appear, among them an ectopic pregnancy, a placental abruption, a placenta previa, a uterine rupture, puerperal sepsis, pre-eclampsia with its seizures and its organ injury, and thromboembolism, and each is recognized by a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. Bleeding in early pregnancy is separated by whether the pregnancy is inside the uterus and whether the woman is stable, and bleeding in late pregnancy by whether the uterus is painless or painful and tense, with the digital examination withheld until a low placenta has been excluded. A woman who is bleeding, fitting, feverish, breathless, or whose baby has stopped moving must travel now, and the clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer can recognize her. Every figure here must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

# Chapter 58 — Newborns and Infants

The newborn brings no account of himself, so the whole history must come from the mother, the birth, and the body in front of the clinician. He cannot say where it hurts, cannot describe a change over days, and cannot cooperate with an examination that depends on answers. The reasoning rests instead on observation, on what happened before and around the birth, and on a few signs that mean serious illness. This chapter treats the newborn and the young infant as one patient with a language of his own. That language is spoken through the cry, the tone, the feeding, the temperature, the breathing, the color, the weight, and the jaundice. The first task is not to name a disease but to decide whether the baby is well, unwell in a way that can be watched, or unwell in a way that will kill him before morning. The material is educational and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the baby is seen.

Several lethal possibilities must be named before any comfortable explanation is entertained, because each is revealed by a finding sought in the first minutes. A baby who feeds poorly, feels cold, breathes with effort, and has become floppy may have an infection of the bloodstream. The alarm is a baby who is not behaving as he did yesterday, not any single number on the thermometer. A baby who collapses after feeding, pale and mottled, with pulses that cannot be felt in the groin, may have a congenital heart lesion. The weak groin pulse is the finding, and the lesion declares itself as the vessel that kept the circulation open begins to close. A baby who vomits green fluid and has a swollen abdomen may have a bowel obstruction, and a twist of the gut on its own blood supply is lethal. A baby who was well and then refuses feeds and becomes drowsy may have a metabolic disease, and a jaundice that is early or persistent must not wait for the next visit.

The history of a newborn is the history of his mother and of the pregnancy, and it is taken as carefully as any adult history. The clinician asks about infections during pregnancy, among them syphilis, HIV, hepatitis, and infection with group B streptococcus. Diabetes, high blood pressure, medicines, traditional remedies, smoking, alcohol, and drugs belong in the same conversation. The birth supplies its own account: how labor began, how long the membranes were ruptured, whether the fluid was stained with meconium, whether the mother had a fever, and whether instruments were used. The baby's story since birth follows: how he fed in the first hours, whether he has passed urine and meconium, how often he feeds now, and whether his color has changed. The family history matters more here than in adult medicine, since inherited diseases of the blood, of metabolism, and of the heart may declare themselves in the first days.

The Apgar score formalizes the baby's condition in the first minutes after birth, and it is a starting point for observation rather than a diagnosis. It records five things the examiner can see and feel: the color, the heart rate, the response to a mild stimulus, the muscle tone, and the effort of breathing. The reasoning it organizes is simply whether the baby is making the transition to life outside the womb. The score is usually recorded at 1 minute and again at 5 minutes, and those intervals are illustrations that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since practice differs between units and editions. A low score directs the clinician to help the baby breathe and to keep him warm, and it says nothing by itself about the cause or the future. The score must never be used to diagnose asphyxia or to predict how a child will develop, because it was designed for neither purpose.

The signs that must be recognized without any history are few, and they are learned by looking at the baby rather than at a monitor. A baby who is unusually quiet, who does not wake for feeds, who lies with his limbs extended rather than drawn up, or who feels limp when lifted is not merely sleepy. The work of breathing is the most visible signal: a rising rate, a grunt at the end of each breath, flaring of the nostrils, and drawing in of the ribs all mean the baby is using accessory muscles. Color is read in good light on the lips and tongue rather than on the hands and feet, because the extremities of a newborn are often blue while the center is well. The mother's own impression that something is wrong is a clinical finding, and it should be recorded and taken seriously rather than set aside.

The newborn loses heat quickly and defends his temperature poorly, so the thermometer measures two dangers at once. An ordinary temperature lies somewhere between 36.5 and 37.5 degrees Celsius when measured by an appropriate method. That range is a teaching illustration which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted values differ with the site of measurement and the age of the baby. A low temperature is often the first sign of serious infection, and it is missed more easily than a fever because the baby simply feels cool and is assumed to be cold. A raised temperature may mean infection, but it may also mean the baby is overwrapped or the room is hot, so the measurement is repeated after a layer is removed. Every temperature is read with the behavior, the feeding, and the breathing, since a number alone decides nothing.

The breathing of a newborn is counted over a full minute while the baby is calm, because the rate changes with crying and feeding. A rate of 40 to 60 breaths per minute is often quoted as the ordinary range. That figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the range shifts with age, sleep, and the protocol in use. A rate above the accepted line, sustained over repeated counts, is a sign of respiratory difficulty or of metabolic compensation. Grunting, flaring, and drawing in of the chest wall show that the baby is working to keep the lungs open, and any of them in a baby who feeds poorly is serious. Pauses in breathing, especially pauses long enough to change the color or the tone, are a danger sign rather than the irregular breathing of a healthy newborn.

Infection of the bloodstream, called sepsis in this age group, is the great imitator of the newborn period. It must be considered in every baby who is not behaving normally, because the immature defenses produce vague and general signs rather than a local focus. The classic picture is a baby who feeds less, sleeps more, feels cold, breathes faster, and has a temperature that is unstable in either direction. Early infection, acquired around birth, is suggested by maternal fever, prolonged rupture of the membranes, prematurity, and organisms carried in the birth canal. Infection appearing after the first days is suggested by a line or device in the body, by poor hygiene around the umbilicus, or by an outbreak in the unit. The finding that reveals it is not one sign but the combination, together with a blood culture drawn before treatment begins, and the decision to treat on the clinical picture is usually right when the baby looks unwell and the history carries risk.

Some congenital heart lesions are silent until a vessel called the ductus arteriosus begins to close, and then the baby collapses. This vessel keeps blood flowing between the great arteries before birth, and it normally narrows in the first days and weeks of life. The interval over which it closes is offered as an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the timing differs between babies and descriptions. A baby whose circulation depends on that vessel may feed and appear well at first, then become pale, mottled, sweaty, and difficult to rouse, with a racing heart and a pressure that cannot be maintained. The finding that reveals a narrowing of the aorta is weak or absent pulses in the groin while the pulses in the arms are strong. A murmur may be present, but its absence proves nothing, and a screening measurement of oxygen saturation before discharge looks for exactly this possibility.

Color is examined in good light at the center of the body, because the hands and feet of a healthy newborn are often blue and this peripheral blue is not central cyanosis. Central cyanosis, seen on the lips, the tongue, and the inside of the mouth, means that the blood leaving the heart carries too little oxygen, and it demands immediate attention. Its causes include a heart lesion that lets deoxygenated blood into the circulation, a lung problem that prevents oxygen from entering the blood, and an infection that has made the baby very ill. Pallor points toward anemia, blood loss, or shock, while a mottled, grayish skin with cool limbs points toward a failing circulation. A baby who is blue at the center, or gray and cold, travels to a hospital now, whatever the rest of the examination shows.

Vomiting in a newborn is common and usually innocent, but the color of the vomit changes its meaning. A baby who vomits green or bile-stained fluid may have an obstruction of the bowel, and that finding alone sends the baby for assessment rather than prompting a change of feed. The lethal form is a twist of the gut on its own blood supply, in which the baby becomes unwell quickly and the abdomen becomes tense and tender. A baby who has not passed meconium within the first 24 to 48 hours of life also raises the possibility of obstruction or of a disease of the nerve cells of the bowel. That interval must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and where an ultrasound or a contrast study exists it answers the question of where the blockage lies.

Feeding difficulty is the most sensitive single sign of illness in this age group, and it is assessed by watching a feed rather than by asking about it. The clinician observes how the baby takes the breast or the bottle, whether he latches, sucks in bursts, pauses to breathe, and tires before taking enough. A healthy newborn feeds often, in the ordinary case every 2 to 3 hours, and that interval is a teaching illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol. The baby who fed well and now refuses, who takes a little and vomits, or who feeds greedily and then breathes rapidly has a symptom rather than a habit. Poor feeding is read together with the weight, the urine, and the stool, because a baby taking too little will show the effect in all three. The finding that makes a feed the wrong answer is a baby who turns blue, chokes, or becomes exhausted while feeding.

Weight turns the mother's impression into a figure, and in a clinic with a cloth sling and a spring scale it is the most useful instrument available. A birth weight is recorded for every baby, and the ordinary range is generally described as somewhere between 2.5 and 4 kilograms. That range is offered only as an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the distribution differs with the population and the length of the pregnancy. Almost every baby loses some weight in the first days, in the region of 7 to 10 per cent of the birth weight, and that figure too is an illustration to be verified locally rather than carried as a rule. The trend then matters more than any single reading, and failure to regain the birth weight by the accepted age, often described as around 10 to 14 days, should be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol. A scale that is not calibrated and a sling weighed with the baby's clothes will produce a misleading trend, so the same method is used at every visit.

The cry and the tone are the newborn's vocabulary, and both change before any laboratory value does. A high-pitched, shrill cry with irritability, arching of the back, and a refusal to be consoled may mean irritation of the brain or its coverings, or severe discomfort from the gut, and either way it must be explained. A weak, hoarse, or absent cry raises the possibility of a neuromuscular problem or of a baby too ill to protest. The mother's statement that the cry is different from usual is more valuable than any description of its pitch, and it should be recorded in her own words. Tone is examined by observing the posture at rest and by handling the limbs, since a healthy newborn keeps his arms and legs flexed and resists being extended. Tone is judged against the baby's age in the womb, because a baby born early is expected to be floppier than one born at term.

Jaundice is the most common problem of the newborn period, and it becomes a diagnostic question the moment its timing is known. A yellow color appearing within the first 24 hours of life is never treated as ordinary, because it suggests that blood is being broken down faster than the liver can handle, and that boundary must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since services differ. Jaundice that appears after the first day and settles over the following days is usually the ordinary kind that follows immature handling of bilirubin. Its peak is often placed around days 3 to 5 and its resolution by about 14 days, and both figures are illustrations that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the timing shifts with feeding, prematurity, and local practice. Extent carries information too, so the baby is examined undressed in good daylight and the clinician notes how far down the body the yellow color reaches. Jaundice that has reached the palms and soles is deeper than jaundice confined to the face, and pale, chalky stools with dark urine point away from the ordinary explanation.

Jaundice that is hemolytic arises because red blood cells are destroyed too quickly, and it declares itself early and often deeply. Its causes include incompatibility between the blood group of the mother and that of the baby, an inherited abnormality of the red cell, and an infection acquired before birth. The finding that reveals it is a falling blood count with a rapidly rising level of bilirubin, and the rate of the rise matters more than a single measurement. The danger is injury to the brain from bilirubin that is not bound in the blood, and that injury can appear in a baby who looks alert. The level is therefore followed and treated according to the local protocol rather than according to how the baby appears.

Jaundice that is obstructive is caused by bile that cannot leave the liver, and it must never drift past the ordinary review. The classic causes are a blocked bile duct present from birth, a swelling of the liver from infection, and a metabolic disease that damages the liver. The findings that reveal it are jaundice persisting well beyond the usual settling, stools that are pale or the color of putty, dark urine, and an enlarged, firm liver. A jaundice that has not settled by the accepted age, often taken as around 14 days, must be reassessed, and that boundary is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because services differ in how long they wait. Surgical correction of a blocked bile duct succeeds far more often early in life than late, so the diagnosis is a matter of days and not of watchful waiting. Any baby with pale stools and dark urine needs assessment where the bile pigment can be measured and the liver can be imaged.

A metabolic disease punishes the clinician who becomes comfortable with a well-looking baby, because the first days are often entirely normal. The inborn errors of metabolism appear when the baby is exposed to feeds he cannot process, so the story is one of apparent health followed by poor feeding, vomiting, and drowsiness. Some babies also have seizures or an unusual smell, and the examination may show nothing specific. The findings that support the diagnosis include a low level of glucose in the blood, an acid load in the blood, a raised level of ammonia, and a baby who worsens when fed and improves when not. A newborn screening test taken from a heel prick can identify several of these diseases before they declare themselves, so the clinician asks whether the test was done and what it showed. In a clinic with no laboratory, a baby who was well and is now not, with vomiting and drowsiness, is reason enough to travel.

Two derangements deserve separate mention because they are common, dangerous, and detectable with little equipment. A low level of glucose in the blood is a particular risk in the baby who is small, born early, cold, or not feeding, and it may present only as drowsiness, jitteriness, sweating, or refusal to feed. The measurement must be interpreted against the reference range used by the local laboratory, because the line that defines a low value differs between methods and services. Dehydration develops quickly in a newborn, because there is little reserve, and the signs are a sunken soft spot, a dry mouth, fewer wet diapers, weight loss beyond the expected, and lethargy. The decision to give fluid into a vein is made on those findings rather than on a single measurement, and the finding that would make that decision wrong is a baby who is feeding well and passing urine normally. In a clinic without a laboratory, the weight trend, the number of wet diapers, and the soft spot are the whole of the assessment.

The complete examination of the newborn is performed in a warm, quiet place, with the mother present, because it is also an opportunity to teach her what is normal. The clinician begins at the head, feeling the soft spots and the sutures, looking at the face for symmetry, examining the eyes for the red reflex that reveals a clouding of the lens or a tumor behind it, and inspecting the palate for a cleft. The neck, clavicles, and arms are examined for a fracture or weakness, and the heart is listened to while the pulses in the groin are felt and compared with those in the arms. The abdomen is examined gently for enlarged organs and for a mass, and the umbilical cord is inspected for redness, discharge, or bleeding. The genitalia and the anus are always looked at directly, and the hips are examined with the maneuvers that look for a dislocation, since a hip found early can be treated without surgery. The examination is not finished until the baby has been weighed, measured, and watched feeding.

The skin is a diagnostic surface, and many findings on it are normal variations that must be distinguished from disease. A pale, mottled, or dusky color, small bleeding spots, pustules, or a rash that does not fade when pressed all change the assessment. Redness around the base of the cord, a foul discharge, or bleeding from the stump are reasons to look further and to act. The neurological assessment is conducted largely by watching, and it asks whether the brain and nerves work as expected for the age in the womb. The clinician observes posture, spontaneous movements, the symmetry of the face when the baby cries, and the reflexes every newborn should have, among them the startle reflex, the grasp, the rooting, and the suck. Seizures in the newborn are easily missed, because they may look like a flicker of the eye, a chewing movement, or a pause in breathing rather than the shaking of an older child.

In a neonatal unit, the examination is followed by tests chosen to answer questions the clinical assessment has already framed. A blood count answers the question of anemia and infection, a culture of blood answers the question of which organism is present, and a measurement of glucose, salts, and acid answers the question of metabolic derangement. A chest radiograph answers the question of lung disease and of the position of lines and tubes. An ultrasound of the head answers the question of bleeding or fluid in the brain in a baby born early, an ultrasound of the heart answers the question of structure and flow, and an abdominal radiograph answers the question of obstruction when bilious vomiting is present. Where a CT or an MRI is needed, it is chosen for a specific question, and the smallest exposure and the safest transport are part of the decision. Every reference range must be the one issued for newborns by the local laboratory and confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer is not a lesser place to reason, and most decisions that save newborn lives are made in such a room. The baby is undressed in a warm place, weighed in a cloth sling on a spring scale, and examined from head to foot with the torch for the mouth, the red reflex, the skin, the cord, and the anus. The breathing is counted with a watch over a full minute, the heart is listened to, the pulses in the groin are felt, and the temperature is repeated if it is unusual. The integrated management of childhood illness provides a systematic way of assessing the sick young infant, and the reasoning it formalizes is the same one described here. Feeding, activity, breathing, temperature, and signs of local infection are combined into a decision about what to do next. The mother is asked directly about feeding, urine, stool, vomiting, and the color of the skin, because in this age group she is the monitoring system, and a baby judged well still needs a clear plan for review.

The decision that ends most newborn consultations is not a diagnosis but a question about the journey, and it should be made explicitly. The findings that mean the journey cannot wait until morning are bilious vomiting, blue or gray color at the center, floppiness or difficulty rousing, breathing with effort or pausing, an unstable temperature, and a baby who has stopped feeding and is passing no urine. The findings that allow a baby to be watched at home are equally specific: feeding well, passing urine, a normal temperature, a normal breathing pattern, and a mother able and willing to return. Every plan of watchful waiting must include what the mother should look for, when she should return, and how she will get there. A follow-up visit arranged in advance is worth more than an instruction to return if things worsen, because many families cannot judge that for themselves. The finding that makes a decision to watch the wrong one is any doubt about the mother's ability to observe and to return, and in that case the baby travels.

A constructed illustration may make these habits concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than a portrait of any real baby. Imagine a baby of a few days who has fed poorly since the previous evening, feels cool, breathes rapidly with a grunt, and lies floppy, whose mother says the membranes were ruptured for a long time before the birth; the combination is treated as infection until proved otherwise. Now imagine a baby of the same age who has vomited green fluid twice, whose abdomen is swollen, and who has passed no stool since birth; the finding of bile in the vomit changes everything, so the baby is kept from feeding and sent for assessment. A third baby turns yellow on the second day, feeds well, passes urine and normal stool, and fades by the end of the week, so the ordinary explanation is reasonable and the baby is reviewed rather than admitted. None of these babies is real, and none of these stories should be applied to a real baby without a full assessment. What all three share is the move that matters, which is to look for the finding that would change the plan rather than to wait for a test to provide one.

To summarize, the newborn is a patient whose history is told by his mother and whose signs must be read from his behavior. The assessment is organized around feeding, tone, cry, temperature, breathing, color, weight, and jaundice. The lethal possibilities are named at the bedside rather than deferred: sepsis in the baby who is not behaving normally, a congenital heart lesion that declares itself as a collapse when the ductus arteriosus closes, a bowel obstruction revealed by green vomit and a distended abdomen, a metabolic disease that follows apparent health, and a jaundice that is hemolytic or obstructive. Every score, cut-off, reference range, temperature, rate, weight, and interval in this chapter is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. The Apgar score describes the condition at birth and diagnoses nothing, and it must not be used to predict a child's future. The same reasoning runs in a neonatal unit and in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, where the weight in a cloth sling, the count of the breaths, the pulses in the groin, and the mother's account carry the decision. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A baby who worries the clinician is examined again, observed for a defined interval, and moved to a place of safety when the findings or the doubt require it.

# Chapter 59 — Children

The child is not a small adult, and the reasoning that works in the grown patient fails in him for reasons that are easy to state. Growth and development change the normal itself, so the same pulse, the same breathing rate, the same pressure, and the same behavior mean different things at different ages, and the clinician who carries an adult reference into the pediatric room will misjudge the child in front of him. The second difference is that the child rarely gives the history, so the account comes from a caregiver who is frightened, and the task is to hear what the caregiver knows while watching what the child shows. The third difference is that a small number of illnesses account for most of the deaths in childhood, and each of them announces itself through signs that can be sought in the first minutes. This chapter organizes the assessment first by the developmental expectations for each age, because the normal is what makes the abnormal visible, and then by the complaints that bring the child: fever, difficulty breathing, diarrhea with dehydration, and failure to grow. The integrated management of childhood illness is used throughout as a systematic approach to those complaints, a way of asking the same questions in the same order so that nothing is left out when the room is busy and the queue is long. This chapter is educational material; it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

Before any comfortable explanation is entertained, the lethal possibilities should be named, each with the finding that betrays it. A child who is breathing fast, drawing in the lower ribs, grunting, or unable to feed may have a severe pneumonia, and the finding that confirms the severity is the visible effort of breathing together with a fall in the oxygen level measured by a device, where such a device exists. A child with fever, a bulging soft spot on the top of the head, a stiff neck, a dislike of light, a seizure, or a level of alertness that is not right may have meningitis, and the sign that must never be missed is a rash that does not fade when pressed. A child with diarrhea who has sunken eyes, a skin fold that returns slowly, and a drowsiness may be severely dehydrated, and the finding that reveals the depth of the loss is the combination of those signs rather than any single one of them. A child who is wasted, whose feet hold a pitting swelling, or whose hair and skin have changed may have severe malnutrition, and the danger is that such a child can die from an infection that produces almost no fever and from a fall in the sugar of the blood. The child who has become quiet when he should be crying, who lies still, who does not resist examination, or whom the caregiver cannot wake is the child who worries the clinician most, and that quietness is a sign in its own right rather than a gap in the examination.

The developmental expectations are the reference range of childhood, and they belong in the assessment as surely as the chest or the abdomen. A newborn fixes briefly on a face and startles at a sudden noise. By about 6 to 8 weeks he smiles in response to a face, and by 4 to 6 months he holds his head steady and reaches for objects, and those ages are offered as an illustration of the sequence rather than as a rule, because the local schedule and the current guideline state the boundaries differently and must be consulted. He sits without support near the middle of the first year, pulls himself to stand and walks in the second year, and speaks single words before joining two of them, and each step is a question about the brain rather than a competition about timing, so the exact month printed in any chart should be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol. What matters more than the date of any single step is the direction of travel, because a child who is gaining skills is usually on a different path from a child who has lost them. Loss of a milestone already gained, a stiffness or a floppiness that has newly appeared, a hand preference that arrives too early, or a failure to use one side of the body are findings that demand an explanation, and the possibilities they raise include an infection of the nervous system, a bleed or a clot inside the head, a tumor, a long-standing shortage of oxygen or of thyroid hormone, and the effects of a heavy metal or of an injury that was not accidental.

The history in a child is taken from the caregiver, and it is taken with the child present, because the child's behavior during the conversation is itself evidence. The clinician asks who the child lives with, who prepares the food, and who noticed the illness first, and then asks what the child eats and drinks in a day, how many wet cloths or diapers there have been, how feeding compares with a week ago, and whether there has been vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or a rash. The birth history belongs in the same conversation, including the weight at birth, the events of the delivery, the age at which the child first fed, and whether any illness, medicine, or injury touched the mother during the pregnancy. The immunization record should be looked at rather than asked about, because a card answers in a way that memory cannot, and a missing dose changes the list of diseases that must be considered. The family history asks about a similar illness in a brother or sister, a death of a young child in the family, a long illness in a parent, a known shortage of blood, and any inherited disease the family has been told about. The social history asks where the household gets its water, how it disposes of waste, whether animals share the house, whether the sleeping place is shared and how it is covered, and whether the family can reach a clinic and by what means. Each of those answers does not produce a diagnosis on its own, but together they decide which of the dangerous possibilities deserves the next question.

The examination begins with the child observed at a distance, before any instrument is used and often before the child is undressed. The clinician notes whether the child is alert and looking around, whether he is playful or listless, whether he lies still or moves restlessly, how he responds to the caregiver, and whether the cry is strong, weak, high-pitched, or absent. The color of the lips and the tongue, the work of the muscles between the ribs and above the breastbone, the position the child chooses, and the way he holds his head are all read at this stage, and the reading costs nothing. The quiet child who does not cry when a stranger approaches, or whose cry has become a whimper, is a child to be taken seriously, and the same is true of the child who feels floppy when lifted or who arches stiffly backward. A child who can be consoled and who reaches for a toy is usually reassuring, while a child who cannot be consoled, or who alternates between irritability and drowsiness, is a child whose brain or circulation may be in trouble. The hands and feet are touched for warmth, the skin is pressed for a rash that fails to fade, and the whole surface is inspected for marks, because a pattern of injury that does not match the story told belongs in the differential diagnosis from the beginning.

Fever in a child must be taken more seriously the younger the child is, because the ability to localize an infection and to mount the usual signs is least in the first months of life. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is often used as the line above which fever is said to be present, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line depends on the site of measurement and on the age of the child. The measurement itself is a skill, since the same thermometer used in the armpit, in the ear, on the skin, or in the mouth gives figures that are not interchangeable, so the record should name the route as well as the number. The fever is only the beginning of the question, and the rest of the assessment looks for a source and for the child behind the fever, because a child who is drinking, playing, and passing urine is more reassuring than any single reading would suggest. A rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed against it, a stiff neck, a headache the child can describe only by holding his head, a complaint of pain in the ear, a refusal to move an arm or a leg, and a passage of urine that has become painful or frequent each narrow the search in a different direction. In a region where malaria is transmitted, the fever of any child must be tested for the parasite at once, and where no test exists the residence and travel history carries the decision, because a child who appears well in the morning can deteriorate within hours. A fever that lasts for several days without settling, or that comes with a loss of weight, a cough that lingers, or a swelling of the neck, needs a longer look rather than another medicine, and the interval that counts as prolonged is stated differently in different services and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A child with a cough is assessed by counting the breaths and by looking at what breathing costs him, and both are done before the stethoscope is taken out. The breathing must be counted while the child is calm and the count taken again whenever the first attempt is interrupted, because crying, feeding, and fever all raise the rate, and the observer should count more than once when the first count is borderline. The drawing in of the lower ribs on inspiration, called chest indrawing, is the sign that separates a child who needs close attention from one who may be watched at home, and a child who grunts with each breath, whose nostrils flare, or whose head nods with the effort is working too hard. A breathing rate of 50 breaths per minute is often quoted as the line above which a young child deserves treatment for pneumonia, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold changes with age and the published guides do not draw it in the same place. Where a device for measuring the oxygen level in the blood exists it should be used, and the finding that decides the need for oxygen is a saturation below the local threshold, which the protocol of the service sets rather than this book. The examiner then listens for the sounds that distinguish the patterns, since a widespread wheeze with a prolonged outward breath suggests a narrowing of the small airways, fine crackles in one place suggest fluid or pus in the lung, and a harsh sound on inspiration with difficulty swallowing suggests an obstruction above the vocal cords that must be handled as an emergency. The child who cannot drink, who vomits everything, who is drowsy, or who has a blue tinge to the lips has a severe illness whatever the breath count was, and treatment and the journey to a hospital should begin together.

Dehydration is graded by signs that any clinician can observe with the hands and the eyes, and the ladder runs from no dehydration through some to severe. The clinician asks whether the child is thirsty and drinks eagerly, whether the eyes are sunken, whether a fold of skin on the abdomen returns slowly, whether the mouth is dry, whether tears appear when the child cries, and how much urine has been passed. Severe dehydration is present when the child is lethargic or unconscious, when the eyes are very sunken, when the skin fold returns very slowly, and when the child cannot drink or drinks poorly, and that combination is the one that demands fluid into a vein rather than by mouth. The decision about how much fluid and by which route is a decision about the findings and not a number to be taken from a page, and the same is true of fluid given by mouth, because the amount changes with weight, with the degree of loss, and with the plan in force where the child is treated. The finding that would make fluid into a vein the wrong answer is a child who is alert, drinking well, and passing urine, in whom the mouth route is safer and simpler, while the finding that would make it the right answer is a child who cannot swallow or who deteriorates while being rehydrated by mouth. A child given fluid too quickly can develop swelling of the brain or of the lungs, so the speed must be set by the protocol in use and watched against the child's breathing, alertness, and urine rather than given from memory. The caregiver should be shown how to prepare the home solution and told what should bring the child back, and that instruction is part of the treatment rather than an extra.

Malnutrition is diagnosed by measurement and by looking, and the two must be done together, because a child with swelling of both feet may weigh more than his true tissue would suggest. Weight is plotted against the growth chart for the child's age, the length or height is measured and plotted in the same way, and the circumference of the middle of the upper arm is taken with a tape, since a measurement of 115 millimeters is often used as a line that identifies severe wasting, though that number is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the tape, the chart, and the line differ between services. Both feet are pressed for a pitting edema that is symmetrical, and the hair is inspected for thinning and loss of color, the skin for peeling and dark patches, and the eyes for the dry, dull change that speaks of a shortage of vitamin A. The dangerous complications of severe malnutrition are infections that produce no fever, a fall in the sugar of the blood, a fall in body temperature, and a shortage of the salts in the blood, and each of these can kill a child who looks calm. The decision to treat begins with warmth, feeding, and a search for infection, and the amount and the speed of feeding are set by the protocol of the service that knows the child, because a starved child fed too fast can develop a dangerous shift of salts and fluid. The finding that would make a simple feeding plan the wrong answer is a child who is not gaining at the review, who has diarrhea, or whose edema is increasing, and that child needs a review of the whole plan rather than more of the same.

Infection of the membranes around the brain is the diagnosis that must be considered in every child with fever and a change in behavior, and the classic signs are often absent in the youngest. The soft spot on the top of the head may be bulging in an infant, the neck may resist flexion, the child may cry when handled or dislike the light, and a seizure or a drowsiness may be the only sign. The rash that does not fade with pressure is the finding that must be sought over the whole body, because it may mark an infection of the bloodstream that progresses within hours. Where a lumbar puncture can be done it answers the question directly, but it is deferred when the child is unstable, when there are signs of raised pressure inside the head, or when the skin over the site is infected, and treatment then begins on the clinical picture while the test waits. Where a computed tomography, or CT, scanner exists it is used to answer the question of raised pressure before the needle is placed, and where it does not, the decision is made on the examination and on the judgment of the senior clinician who has been called. The level of consciousness is recorded with the Glasgow coma scale, which formalizes the response to voice, to pain, and to command, and the exact contents of that scale and the figure at which it should cause alarm must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the version in use varies between services and between editions. A child who has a seizure for the first time, whose seizure lasts a long time, or who does not return to his usual self afterward needs treatment and senior help at once.

Vomiting and diarrhea are the complaints that most often bring a child to a clinic, and most of the time they settle by themselves, but a small number of patterns demand immediate action. Green, bile-stained vomiting in a young infant is a warning of an obstruction of the bowel and not of a simple feeding problem, and it must be treated as an emergency until it is explained. A child who draws his legs up and screams in waves, who passes a stool mixed with blood and mucus, or in whom a sausage-shaped mass can be felt in the abdomen may have an intussusception, in which one part of the bowel has slid into the next, and that diagnosis is made on suspicion and confirmed by an ultrasound where one is available. Pain that begins around the navel and settles in the right lower abdomen, with tenderness there, a refusal to walk, and a rising pulse, suggests appendicitis, and the examination is repeated rather than trusted once, because the signs often take hours to declare themselves. Distension of the abdomen, absent bowel sounds, and a tender lump in the groin or at the umbilicus each ask a different question, and the whole abdomen is examined gently, with the child's face watched rather than the examiner's hands. A rectal examination is performed only when it will change the decision, and the genitalia are inspected in every child with abdominal pain, because a torsion of the testis is a surgical emergency that can present as abdominal pain alone.

Some children are brought with nothing that a first look can explain, and the value of the assessment is largely in deciding who may go home and who may not. A child who looks well, drinks, plays, and has no danger sign may still carry an infection of the urine, the ear, the throat, or the lung, so the ear is examined with the torch, the throat is looked at, the chest is listened to, and a sample of urine is obtained before a course of treatment is considered. A sample of urine collected in a bag is useful when it is normal, because a clean result makes an infection of the urine unlikely, while a contaminated one settles nothing, and a sample taken directly from the bladder or after careful cleansing answers the question better. The child who is failing to grow, who tires during feeding, who sweats on the head while feeding, or who breathes fast at rest may have a heart lesion rather than an infection, and the cluster of findings is a murmur together with an enlarged liver, a fast pulse, and a difference between the pulses felt in the arm and in the leg. The child with a limp, a warm swollen joint, or a refusal to bear weight on a leg must be examined for an infection in the joint or the bone, because that is a surgical emergency, and a tumor of the bone belongs in the same list. The child who has been well and then has a long fever with a falling weight, a swelling of the neck, or a dark patch on the skin needs a test for tuberculosis and for a cancer of the blood, because both imitate ordinary illness and both are easier to treat when they are found early.

In a pediatric ward the assessment is the same, but it is written in a chart, repeated at set hours, and supported by tests that answer specific questions. The nurse counts the breaths and the pulse and records the trend, the laboratory measures the blood count, the salts, and the sugar, the laboratory grows the organism from the blood, the urine, or the fluid around the brain, and a chest radiograph shows the lung beneath the place where the sound was dull. An ultrasound answers the question of a collection of pus or of an obstruction, and a CT or a magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answers the question of the brain when the signs point there. In a village with a mid-level provider and a single register, none of those tools may exist, and the reasoning must carry more weight rather than less. The register is not a lesser instrument, since it holds the weight of every child seen, the immunization given, the treatment started, and the date of the next visit, and a line of weights falling across the page makes malnutrition visible before a single measurement looks alarming. The provider counts the breaths with a watch, looks in the ear and the throat with the torch, presses the skin for a fold and the feet for edema, and then decides among the plans available, which are to treat and review, to refer now, or to send home with clear instructions about what should bring the child back. The decision to refer is a diagnosis in its own right when the tools are absent, and the provider who names the danger sign, writes it in the register, and arranges the journey has done the most important part of the work.

A constructed illustration may make these habits concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real child. Imagine a child of a few months brought to a village clinic with a cough, a fever, and a refusal to feed, whose breathing is counted twice at 60 breaths per minute, whose lower ribs are drawn in with every breath, and in whom the provider sees the effort and arranges the journey to a hospital at once, even though the clinic has no oxygen and no radiograph. That count and the indrawing are the findings that make the referral right, and the figure itself, like every other figure in this chapter, must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line that separates fast from too fast is drawn differently in different guides. Now imagine a child in a pediatric ward whose weight has fallen on the chart over 3 weeks, a trend whose meaning depends on the chart in use and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, whose feet hold a pitting swelling, and whose temperature is low rather than high, and in whom the search for infection finds nothing until the whole body is examined again. Neither child is real, and neither story should be applied to a real patient without a full assessment, yet the two share the move that matters, which is that the clinician looked for the danger sign first, and the finding rather than the diagnosis decided the next step.

To summarize, the child is assessed against the developmental expectations of his age, because the normal is what makes the abnormal visible, and then against the small number of illnesses that kill. The dangerous possibilities are named where the child is seen and not deferred, and they are severe pneumonia with fast breathing and chest indrawing, meningitis with a change in behavior and the rash that does not fade, severe dehydration with sunken eyes and a slow skin fold, severe malnutrition with edema and an infection that shows no fever, and the child who has gone quiet when he should be crying. The integrated management of childhood illness gives the order of the questions, and the same order holds in a pediatric ward with a laboratory and in a village with a mid-level provider and a single register, where the register itself becomes a diagnostic tool as the line of weights falls. Every figure in this chapter, whether a temperature, a breathing rate, a measurement, a score, an age, or a duration, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between the charts and the laboratories in use. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A child who is quiet, who cannot feed, or whose caregiver is frightened deserves another look, and the finding that changes the plan is usually the one that was sought in the first minute.

# Chapter 60 — Adolescents

The adolescent is neither a large child nor a small adult, and a method built for either will fail him in a particular way. A child is examined through the parent who answers for him, an adult speaks for himself, and the adolescent sits between the two, able to give a full account and often unwilling to give it in front of the person who brought him. His body changes fast enough that every measurement is a moving target, so the normal for his age is a range rather than a line. The illnesses that begin now often announce themselves through behavior rather than through a single complaint. The organizing idea of this chapter is developmental: ask first what is normal for this stage, then ask what has departed from it, and remember that this is educational material which does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

Several possibilities at this age can kill, and each is named here with the finding that reveals it, because deferring them is how they are missed. A young person who has harmed himself, who wishes to be dead, or who has begun to give away what he owns may be at risk of suicide, and the finding that matters is not the wound but the intent, learned only by asking directly. One who has lost weight, fears food, purges, or exercises past exhaustion may have an eating disorder, and its severity shows in a slow pulse, a fallen temperature, and a pressure that drops on standing. One brought in drowsy or unrousable may be intoxicated, and the pupils, the speed of breathing, the smell of the breath, and marks of injection narrow the cause. A young woman with lower abdominal pain and fever may have a pelvic infection, and the emergency behind it is a pregnancy outside the uterus, revealed by a positive pregnancy test and pain on one side. One with bone pain that wakes him at night, bruising, night sweats, or a lump that will not go away may have a malignancy of the young, revealed by a blood count or an imaging study.

Growth and puberty are the first instruments of diagnosis here, because the normal is what makes the abnormal visible. The clinician establishes where the young person stands on the curve of height and weight for age and sex, whether growth has been steady, and whether the pubertal changes have begun in the expected order and time, and judges puberty as a sequence of stages rather than a moment. A healthy young person may still be earlier or later than his classmates, so the comparison that matters is with his own earlier measurements, and a height that has crossed downward through several channels, a growth spurt that never came, or a stalled puberty changes reassurance into investigation. The organic causes must not be missed: a long-standing illness of the gut, kidney, heart, or lung, a disorder of the thyroid or growth hormone, a tumor near the pituitary, and, in a young woman who has never menstruated, a chromosomal or anatomical cause. The findings that point away from simple delay are a falling growth rate, a headache or changed vision, a lost sense of smell, a swollen thyroid, a chronic bowel complaint, and a pubertal stage that has not advanced over a long interval, while a growth rate below 4 centimeters a year is offered as an illustration of when to investigate and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because charts and editions state it differently.

The consultation is arranged in two parts, and the order is itself part of the care. The clinician begins with the young person and the parent together, which respects the worried parent and lets the family account be heard, and then asks to speak with the young person alone, which is where most of the important history is given. Before the parent leaves, the clinician states plainly what will be kept private and what will not, so the young person is not asked to trust a promise that cannot be kept. A confidence may be broken when someone is in danger, whether the young person, another person, or a child in the household, and when the law requires a report of abuse or of an age of consent that has been crossed. The adolescent is told who else will be spoken to, what will be said, and why, and the age at which he may be seen alone or consent to his own care is set by law rather than medicine, so it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol of the jurisdiction.

Once the two are alone, the history is taken in the ordinary structure, using the Oldcarts framework so that nothing about the complaint is left out, but the questions are asked in a register an adolescent will answer. The clinician avoids the interrogative tone, gives the young person the first word on every subject, and asks about the complaint in his own terms before offering the medical vocabulary. The domains to cover are the home and who lives in it, the school or work and how it is going, the friendships and activities, the use of alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, and other substances, the sexual history, and the mood, sleep, and appetite. The clinician also asks what the young person believes is wrong, because that belief shapes whether he accepts the plan and whether he returns. A history taken this way takes longer than one taken from a parent, and it is the single measure that most often changes the diagnosis at this age.

A set of subjects is almost never raised with a parent in the room, and each changes the diagnosis if it becomes known. He may not say in front of a parent that he is sexually active, that a contact was unwanted, that his attraction is to the same sex, that he does not feel at home in the body he was born in, that he has been drinking or using a substance, that he has been hurt at home, or that he has thought about ending his life. The clinician therefore returns to these subjects in the private part of the visit and asks in plain language, without a preamble that signals alarm. The young person who is asked about his safety at home, about who shares his bed, and about the gender he understands himself to be is being told that these things are speakable. Gender and sexual identity are not diseases, but the distress around them is real and carries a greater risk of self-harm, so the assessment must include them rather than avoid them.

The menstrual history is a vital sign here and is too often left to the parent to describe. The clinician asks when the periods began, how far apart they are, how long they last, how heavy the flow is, whether they are painful, and whether they have stopped, and records the answers in the young person's own words. A period that has never begun by the expected age, one that has stopped after starting, and one that has become very heavy or painful each open a different line of reasoning: pregnancy, a hormonal disorder, a bleeding tendency, an infection, or an anatomical problem. Pregnancy must be considered in any adolescent with abdominal pain, vomiting, fainting, or a missed period, and it is considered privately and without judgment, because the fear of the reaction is exactly what delays the diagnosis. The finding that settles it is a pregnancy test, and where the test exists it should be offered to every young woman of this age with abdominal pain, whatever the story suggests, while where no test exists the clinician reasons from the history, the examination, and the passage of time and is explicit about the uncertainty that remains.

Mental illness is the epidemic of this age, and much of it is invisible unless it is sought. Depression may present as irritability rather than sadness, as a fall in school performance, as a withdrawal from friends, or as a headache or stomach ache with no explanation, while anxiety may present as a refusal to attend school, as a panic described as a physical illness, as a preoccupation with the body, or as a sleep that will not come. Attention deficit and hyperactivity are usually recognized earlier, but may first be noticed when the demands of secondary school rise above the young person's ability to compensate, and psychosis announces itself through withdrawal, decline, suspicion, or speech that has become hard to follow. The clinician asks about mood, sleep, appetite, energy, guilt, concentration, and the wish to be dead, and asks specifically about self-harm, because the question does not plant the idea and the silence does not remove it. The risk of harm to the self and to others is assessed in every young person with a mental complaint, and the assessment includes intent, plan, means, and protective factors, because the protective factors are what the plan will lean on, while a physical cause such as infection, a thyroid disorder, a low sugar, a drug, or a disease of the brain is excluded first, and any figure on a score or questionnaire must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since instruments differ between services and editions.

Self-harm and suicidal intent are related but not identical, and separating them is the most important judgment in this part of the chapter. Self-harm without the wish to die is often a way of managing unbearable feeling, of punishing the self, or of communicating a distress that has no words, and it marks great suffering even when the wound is superficial. Suicidal intent is present when the young person wishes to be dead, has a plan, has the means within reach, has made an attempt, or has become suddenly calm after agitation, because that calm may be the resolution before the act. The findings that raise risk are a previous attempt, a family history of suicide, a recent loss or humiliation, an alcohol or drug problem, an isolating illness, and access to a lethal method at home. The clinician asks directly whether he has thought about ending his life, whether he has a plan, and whether he has acted, then asks what has kept him alive, and the decision that follows is about safety rather than diagnosis, including what he will do before the next contact, who will be with him, and what will be removed from the home, while any number on a risk scale aids the reasoning and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol.

An eating disorder is a diagnosis of behavior and physiology at once, and the examination is as important as the history. The young person may restrict food, purge by vomiting or laxatives, exercise to exhaustion, or eat in secret and compensate, and the account may be denied completely and still be visible in the body. The findings are a fall in weight or a failure to gain what growth requires, a slow pulse, a low pressure that drops further on standing, a low temperature, cold hands and feet, fine downy hair on the face and arms, swollen salivary glands, eroded tooth enamel, calluses on the knuckles, and a dry skin. In a young woman the periods may stop and in a young man sexual development may stall, while the laboratory, where it exists, shows disturbed salts, a low blood sugar, and poor liver or kidney function. The young person who has lost a great deal of weight is at risk during the early part of any refeeding, so that decision belongs where the salts and the heart rhythm can be watched, and a pulse below 50 beats per minute or a temperature below 36 degrees Celsius is offered as an illustration of severity that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line at which the body is failing is recorded differently in different services.

Substance use is common at this age, and the diagnostic task is to separate ordinary experiment from intoxication, dependence, and complication. The clinician asks, without shock and without euphemism, what the young person has used, how often, by what route, in what company, and what it has cost him in money, school, relationships, and sleep. Alcohol is the substance most often involved and the one most easily underestimated, because its effects on judgment, mood, and risk are absorbed into the story of a difficult week. Cannabis may present as a loss of drive, a fall in performance, a persistent cough, or a psychosis in a vulnerable young person, while synthetic stimulants may present as agitation, a racing heart, a high temperature, and paranoia. Opioids and sedatives present with slow breathing, pinpoint pupils, and reduced consciousness, and the finding that makes reversal of the intoxication right is inadequate breathing together with a consciousness that cannot be roused, while injection brings infection of the blood, skin, and heart valves, and a fall, a fight, or an assault may hide behind the drug.

Sexual health is asked about as directly as any other system, and the questions are the same for a young man as for a young woman. The clinician asks whether the young person is sexually active, whether the activity is wanted, whether a barrier or another method is used, whether a partner has had an infection, and whether any contact was coerced or with someone older or in a position of power. A sexually transmitted infection may be silent, and the finding that reveals it may be a discharge, a sore, a rash, a growth, a burning on passing urine, or nothing at all, which is why testing is offered rather than withheld until symptoms appear. Pelvic inflammatory disease is the infection that ascends from the cervix to the uterus and the tubes, and it presents with lower abdominal pain, discharge, fever, pain during intercourse, and tenderness on moving the cervix, while its consequence is scarring of the tubes, which brings infertility and a pregnancy outside the uterus. The finding that reveals the surgical emergency behind such a presentation is a positive pregnancy test with one-sided pain and a falling blood count, and that combination is treated as an emergency before any test confirms it, while the decision to test for the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, is offered with counseling and consent, and the interval after which a negative result becomes reliable must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A malignancy in an adolescent is uncommon, and its danger lies in the ease with which its early symptoms are attributed to sport, growth, or mood. A cancer of the blood may present with pallor, tiredness, fever, bruising without injury, bleeding from the gums or nose, and bone or joint pain that wakes the young person at night. A lymphoma may present as a lump in the neck, armpit, or groin that does not settle, with night sweats, weight loss, and itching of the skin. A tumor of bone usually presents as pain near the knee or shoulder that is worse at night and out of proportion to activity, and a swelling over it turns the story serious. A tumor of the brain may present with morning headache, vomiting, changed vision, weakness, or a decline in school performance, and the finding that reveals it may be a swollen optic disc seen through the torch or ophthalmoscope, while a germ cell tumor of the testis presents as a lump the young man may notice in the shower but not mention, which is why examining the testes is part of examining every adolescent boy who will allow it.

Many adolescents live with a chronic illness that began in childhood, and the reasoning here is shaped by the transfer from pediatric to adult care. The conditions that matter most are diabetes, asthma, epilepsy, sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, inflammatory bowel disease, heart disease present from birth, and the late effects of a cancer treated in childhood. The questions change with the transfer: who holds the knowledge of the illness, who decides about treatment, whether the young person can describe his own condition and its warning signs, and whether he understands what happens if he stops. A decline in control that appears as a new symptom may be the first sign of a depression, a substance, a difficulty at home, or a simple failure to fill a prescription, and each is a diagnosis in its own right. The transfer should be planned rather than allowed to happen, because a gap in care is a diagnosis of omission that shows up later as an emergency, and the age at which a service hands the young person over is a local convention to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Sport is the setting in which the most dangerous cardiac condition of this age is found, and the finding is easy to miss because it appears only under effort. A young athlete who faints during exercise, rather than after it, may have a structural disease of the heart, a disorder of the heart muscle, or an abnormal pathway of conduction, and a faint during exertion is never attributed to heat until the heart has been considered. The history that matters is a previous faint, chest pain on effort, breathlessness out of proportion to the exercise, palpitation, and a family history of sudden death in a young relative. The examination may find a murmur that changes with standing or with the strain of a held breath, a displaced impulse, or a pressure that differs between the arms. An electrocardiogram, or ECG, should be obtained where it exists, and an ultrasound of the heart names most of these conditions, so the young person with a positive finding is referred before the next competition rather than after it, while in a clinic without either instrument the decision is the referral, and the finding that makes it urgent is the faint during effort.

The risk-taking that shapes this age is asked about in the same breath as the symptoms, because the injury of today and the diagnosis of tomorrow both come from it. The clinician asks about the use of a seatbelt and helmet, about driving and riding with a driver who has been drinking, about carrying a weapon, about physical fights, and about any contact that was not wanted. A head injury is common here, and its warning findings are a loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, a worsening headache, deepening drowsiness, weakness on one side, a seizure, and fluid or blood from the nose or ear. A young person who is repeatedly injured is telling the clinician something about his circumstances, and the pattern may point to violence at home, bullying at school, or a risk he has not named. The clinician asks without moralizing, because a young person who feels judged will end the conversation, and the answers change the plan, whether it is a discussion about safety, a referral, or a report the law requires.

Some adolescents arrive acutely, and a few of the emergencies of this age present through the abdomen or through a faint. The young woman with sudden severe pain in one side of the lower abdomen, a missed period, and a fainting may have a pregnancy outside the uterus, which can bleed into the abdomen and kill quickly, and the findings that reveal it are tenderness on that side, a falling blood count, and a positive pregnancy test. The young person with pain that begins around the navel and settles in the right lower abdomen, with fever, loss of appetite, and tenderness worst when the hand is released, may have appendicitis, and the finding that decides the operation is the examination repeated rather than a single opinion. A twisted ovary presents with sudden severe pain and vomiting, and is a surgical emergency that an ultrasound names if the young person reaches a place where one exists. A faint on standing is common and often benign, but a faint during exercise, with chest pain, or with a family history of sudden death is a cardiac presentation until proved otherwise. In a clinic with no tests, the decision is not the diagnosis but the journey, and the finding that makes the journey immediate is severe pain, a racing pulse, a falling pressure, or a young person who looks unwell.

In a hospital the assessment of an adolescent can answer in hours questions that would otherwise take weeks, and the choice of tests follows the reasoning rather than replacing it. A pregnancy test is among the first tests in any young woman with abdominal pain, a missed period, a faint, or vomiting, and it is offered privately with the result handled according to the young person's wishes within the limits of the law. A blood count answers the question of anemia, infection, and a malignancy of the blood, a test of the salts and sugar answers the question raised by purging, starvation, or diabetes, and a test of liver and kidney function answers the question of overdose or long-standing illness. An ultrasound is the study of choice in the pelvis, because it names the pregnancy outside the uterus, the ovarian cyst, the twisted ovary, and the collection of pus without radiation, while computed tomography, or CT, and magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answer questions about the head, chest, and bone. A screen for substances is useful when it will change management and is ordered with the young person's knowledge, because a covert test destroys the trust on which the next disclosure depends, and the laboratory sets its own reference ranges, so every figure returned must be read against the interval of that laboratory and confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer is not a poorer place to reason, and at this age the instruments that cost nothing matter most. A chart on the wall and a pen allow height, weight, and body mass index to be plotted at every visit, and the trend across months is worth more than any single measurement, while the body mass index is a ratio read against the age and sex of the young person and against the chart in use, so its reference interval must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The torch makes the throat, ears, eyes, pupils, skin, and scars visible, and a bright light on the arms and thighs finds the marks a sleeve was hiding. The thermometer and a watch turn the impression of illness into a temperature, a pulse, and a breathing rate that can be repeated and compared, and the pressure can be taken with a cuff that fits the arm.
