A urine dipstick, where it exists, answers the question of infection, sugar, and protein, and a pregnancy test kit answers the question that must not be left to guesswork, while the examination is completed by watching the young person walk, by listening to how he speaks about his own life, and by asking the question the clinician has been avoiding.

Explaining the plan to the young person and to the parent is a skill of its own, and it is where the boundary set at the beginning is kept or broken. The clinician tells the young person first what has been found and what it means, in words that belong to him, and asks what he wants the parent to know. The parent is then given what is necessary for safety and care, and is helped to understand what the young person needs rather than what the parent fears. Where the two disagree, the clinician holds both in the room without pretending the disagreement has gone, because a plan imposed on either will fail. The clinician says plainly what happens next, who to contact, what would make the situation urgent, and what the young person is responsible for, and checks that both have understood by asking them to repeat it back. Follow-up is part of the treatment here, so the clinician arranges a review soon enough to matter, names the findings that should bring the young person back earlier, and contacts rather than discharges one who misses an appointment, because the absence may itself be the symptom.

To summarize, the adolescent is reasoned about through development, through confidentiality, and through the things said only when the parent has left the room, and every judgment begins with what is normal for that young person's stage. The dangers are named early and with the finding that reveals them: self-harm and suicide, an eating disorder, a substance intoxication, a pelvic infection with a pregnancy outside the uterus behind it, and a malignancy of the young. Growth and puberty are plotted rather than estimated, the mood, sleep, appetite, self-harm, substance, and sexual history are asked about directly, and the chronic illness of childhood is handed over with the young person's own knowledge rather than without it. The same consultation is conducted with the parent in the room and with the young person alone, and both are told plainly what will and will not be shared. Every figure in this chapter, whether an age, a temperature, a rate, a pressure, a growth rate, or a reference interval, is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories, and between the charts used for growth. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A young person who is listened to alone, asked the direct question, and given a clear plan is safer than one who is investigated thoroughly and heard not at all.

# Chapter 61 — Older Adults

The older patient is the one in whom the textbook picture is most often missing, and this chapter is arranged around that fact. The familiar presentation of an illness belongs to a younger body with reserve to spare, while the same disease in an older body may announce itself only as a fall, a confusion, a refusal to eat, or a quiet loss of the ability to dress and walk. A clinician who waits for the expected symptom will wait past the moment when the diagnosis was still simple, and a clinician who treats the change in function as the presenting complaint will usually find the disease behind it. Age by itself is not a diagnosis, and the years a patient carries say less than the state of that patient's reserve, muscle, memory, and medicines. This chapter follows the older patient through the four changes that most often bring the illness into view, which are a fall, a confusion, a loss of appetite, and a decline in what the patient could formerly do. It is educational material, not medical advice, not a protocol, and not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the rules of the service in which the patient is seen.

The dangers that hide inside these quiet presentations should be named before a comfortable explanation is accepted, because each is revealed by a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. An older patient with a new confusion and an ordinary temperature may have an infection in the bloodstream, and the finding that betrays it is often a climb in the breathing rate or a sudden loss of the ability to walk rather than any fever at all. The patient who has fallen and cannot put weight on a leg may have a fracture of the hip, and the finding is a limb that lies shortened and turned outward, even though the patient may deny pain. The patient whose confusion comes and goes, who has a headache, or who has grown weak on one side may have blood collecting over the surface of the brain, and the finding that confirms it is seen on a computed tomography, or CT, scan of the head after an injury so slight that nobody remembers it. The patient who becomes breathless, clammy, or faint without chest pain may be having a myocardial infarction, and the finding is the tracing on an electrocardiogram, or ECG, together with the substances released by damaged heart muscle. A new symptom that began after a medicine was added or increased may be caused by that medicine, and dehydration, the easiest danger to overlook, is revealed by a dry mouth, a rising pulse, and urine that has become scanty and dark.

Why older patients present this way lies in reserve rather than in any single organ. With age the reserve of every system shrinks, so the heart, the kidney, the lung, and the brain have less room to absorb a new demand before they fail visibly. The immune response also changes, so fever may be blunted or absent even in severe infection, and pain is perceived and reported differently, so a patient with long-standing arthritis may not separate a new injury from the pain that is always there. The senses fade as well, so a hearing loss or a failing eye changes the history that can be taken and the examination that can be trusted. The age at which a person is counted old is conventionally placed at 65 years, and that line is an administrative convenience rather than a biological fact, so any such figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services and studies draw it in different places. What matters at the bedside is not the birth date but how much reserve this particular patient has left.

Because the usual symptoms are unreliable, the clinician measures the older patient against the patient's own recent self, and function becomes the most informative vital sign. The questions that matter are practical: whether the patient could walk to the toilet unaided last month, cook a meal, manage the tablets, and climb the stairs, and whether any of that was lost, and over what period. A decline over days points to a new acute illness, while a decline that has crept over months points toward something chronic, progressive, or social. Dressing, washing, feeding, walking, and using the toilet are the ordinary acts that reveal reserve, and the clinician who records them has a baseline against which every later change can be judged. A patient whose function is stable is reassuring even when one number is abnormal, and a patient whose function has dropped is worrying even when every number looks acceptable.

Taking the history from an older patient is a skill that must be adapted rather than abandoned. The clinician sits at eye level, faces the patient in good light, speaks slowly and in a lower voice, and checks that the hearing aid is in place and working before deciding that an answer was confused. A relative or a neighbor who sees the patient daily is a legitimate witness, and the account should be gathered from both without setting one against the other. The Oldcarts framework still organizes the present illness, but the questions are asked in simpler language and repeated without impatience, because fatigue and deafness shorten attention. The review of systems must ask directly about falls, dizziness, incontinence, constipation, sleep, appetite, weight, mood, and memory, since each is often accepted as a normal part of age instead of a symptom.

Frailty is the clinical state that explains much of this, and it changes both the diagnosis and the decision. It is not the same as age and not the same as disability, but a state of reduced reserve in which a small insult produces a large collapse, so that a mild infection becomes a fall, a fall becomes a fracture, and a fracture becomes a permanent loss of independence. The frail patient tolerates illness badly, recovers slowly, and is at greater risk from the investigations and treatments offered than a robust patient of the same age, so recognizing frailty changes the threshold for admission, the intensity of treatment, and the honesty of the conversation about what is likely to happen. A walking speed, a grip, a weight that has fallen, a report of exhaustion, and a low level of activity are the observations from which the state is judged, and several scores have been built from them. No score replaces the clinician's eyes, and any figure attached to such a score is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the versions in use do not set the same line and were derived in populations that may not resemble the patient before you.

A fall is a symptom and never a diagnosis, and the reasoning that follows it asks what made this patient fall today. The clinician looks for a cardiac rhythm disturbance, a stroke, an injury or a painful joint, an infection or a low blood sugar, and a sedative or a medicine that lowers the pressure. The circumstances are more useful than the injury: what the patient was doing, whether there was warning, whether consciousness was lost, how long the patient lay on the floor, and whether anyone saw it. A fall with no warning and no memory of falling suggests a rhythm disturbance, while a trip over a rug suggests something about the environment, and the pressure is measured lying and then standing. A fall of 20 millimeters of mercury on standing is often taught as a meaningful drop, though that figure and the way it is measured must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the technique and the accepted line vary between services. A fracture may hide here without the pain and deformity a younger patient would show, and an unexplained inability to walk must be treated as a fracture until an image proves otherwise.

Confusion is the second great atypical presentation, and the first task is to separate a delirium from a dementia. A delirium is a disturbance of attention and awareness that develops over a short period, fluctuates through the day, and is caused by something else, whether an infection, a medicine, a metabolic upset, pain, or a change in surroundings. A dementia is a chronic and progressive decline in several areas of thinking that leaves attention relatively intact until late and does not fluctuate in the same way. The two are not alternatives, because a patient with dementia is the patient most likely to become delirious, and the delirium settles on top of the dementia like an acute illness on a chronic one. The most useful bedside test of delirium is attention, examined by asking the patient to repeat a short list of words, to count backward, or to name the days of the week in reverse. A confusion assumed to be dementia and left unexamined is one of the commonest ways a treatable illness in an older patient is missed, and a sudden worsening of a known dementia is a delirium until proved otherwise.

The search for the cause of a delirium is a systematic hunt and not a guess. Infection is the commonest trigger, and it may be in the chest, the urine, the skin, the abdomen, or a line in the vein, and it may produce no fever at all. Medicines come next, especially sedatives, medicines for the bladder, strong painkillers, steroids, and anything recently added or increased. Metabolic causes include a low blood sugar, a disturbed salt balance, a failing kidney or liver, a low oxygen level, and a thyroid disorder, and each leaves a trace that can be sought. The clinician should also consider alcohol or sedative withdrawal, a stroke, and an infection of the brain or its covering, and should look for a focal weakness, a headache, a stiff neck, or a seizure. The finding that must not be missed is a treatable cause, so an older patient with a new confusion deserves a full examination, a set of observations, and a review of the medicine list before any label is written.

Medicines are the third great theme of the older patient, because they produce symptoms that imitate disease and because the patient is usually taking several at once. The list a patient reports from memory is rarely complete, so the clinician asks to see every container, including those from another doctor, those bought without a prescription, and those stopped but never discarded. A single new symptom that appears within days or weeks of a new medicine is that medicine until proved otherwise, and the reasoning rests on the timing rather than on the shape of the symptom. Dizziness, drowsiness, confusion, a dry mouth, constipation, a fall, an irregular heartbeat, and a loss of bladder control are all common effects of ordinary medicines, and each is easily mistaken for a new disease. The clinician who reads the labels, counts the containers, and asks what each one is for will often find the answer in the bag.

When several medicines act together, the effects may be greater than any one of them alone, and the combination rather than the single drug becomes the cause. The clinician looks for two medicines that do the same thing, two that interact, and a medicine prescribed to treat the side effect of another, which is the pattern sometimes called a prescribing cascade. The decision to stop a medicine is itself a diagnostic test, and it is made by the clinician who knows the patient and the indication, because some medicines must never be stopped suddenly and withdrawal can produce its own illness. The finding that makes withdrawal of a suspected medicine right is a symptom that began with the drug and settles when it is removed, while the finding that makes it wrong is a strong indication that the medicine is protecting the patient from something worse. The reason for every change should be written down and explained to the patient and the family, because a list adjusted in silence will be restored at the next visit.

Dehydration and poor nutrition arrive quietly and produce a picture that is mistaken for disease. The sensation of thirst fades with age, so a patient who does not feel thirsty may still be short of water, especially during an illness, in hot weather, or when a diuretic or a laxative is being taken. The finding that suggests it is a dry mouth and tongue, a pulse that has risen, a pressure that falls on standing, a scanty and dark passage of urine, and a weight that has dropped without intent, though skin and eyes are less reliable in an old body than the textbook suggests. Poor intake has many causes, among them a painful mouth, bad teeth, difficulty swallowing, nausea, constipation, depression, a medicine, and a loss of smell and taste, and each must be looked for rather than assumed. Swallowing is examined directly, because a patient who coughs or changes voice after drinking is at risk of inhaling, which can lead to an infection of the lung. The decision about fluid is clinical rather than numerical, and the finding that makes it right is a dry patient who cannot take enough by mouth, while the finding that makes it wrong is a circulation already overloaded.

Sepsis in the older patient is the lethal cause that most often presents without its classic signs, and it deserves its own warning. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is traditionally taught as the line above which fever is present, and a temperature below 36 degrees Celsius is sometimes just as important here, but both figures are illustrations that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted thresholds differ between countries, editions, and the sites at which temperature is measured. A breathing rate above 20 breaths per minute or a systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury may be the only abnormality, and those numbers likewise belong to the local guideline rather than to this book and should be checked against the current protocol where the patient is seen. The change that matters most is often a new confusion or a new inability to stand, and the family may describe the patient as simply not himself. The clinician must move quickly, because an older patient with an infection can pass from vague illness to organ failure in a short time, and that is exactly why early treatment on suspicion is often the right decision. The finding that would make treatment the wrong answer is a clear and different cause that fully explains the picture, and even then the patient must be watched.

A myocardial infarction in an older patient may occur with no chest pain at all, so the possibility must stay in view in any sudden change of condition. The presentation may be a new breathlessness, a faint, a confusion, a weakness that came on suddenly, a feeling of indigestion, or a decline that nobody can explain, and the danger is that these are attributed to age or to a chest infection. The finding that reveals it is the ECG, taken early and repeated, together with the substances released by damaged heart muscle, whose reference ranges are set by the laboratory that measures them and must be read from the local report and the current guideline rather than from a textbook. Where there is no ECG, a sudden deterioration with sweating, a fall in the pressure, or a new irregularity of the pulse is a reason to arrange urgent transfer rather than to wait, because waiting for confirmation can cost the heart muscle that is still salvageable.

A subdural hematoma, which is blood collecting over the surface of the brain, is a danger of the older patient because the brain shrinks with age and the veins that cross the space become stretched and fragile, so a trivial injury can tear one. The patient may not recall any injury, and the bleeding may declare itself days or weeks later, so a clear history of trauma is not required to consider it. The presentation is typically a fluctuating confusion, a headache that is worse in the morning or on lying down, a slowing of the pulse, a weakness on one side, a difficulty with speech, or a drowsiness that deepens. The finding that confirms it is a CT of the head, and where that is not available the clinician should treat a fluctuating confusion after any fall as a possible bleed and arrange transfer. The patient must be asked about any blood-thinning medicine, including one bought without a prescription, because that changes both the probability and the urgency. A confusion that no cause explains should always return the clinician to the question of a head injury, however slight or distant it seemed.

Other lethal causes belong in the same early list, because each can present as a general decline rather than as a localized complaint. A clot in the lung may appear as sudden breathlessness, fainting, or a decline in exercise tolerance rather than as chest pain, and the finding that supports it is a swollen or tender calf on one side, although the leg may look normal. A tear in the aorta may present as pain that moves between the chest and the back, or as a sudden collapse, and the finding that suggests it is a difference in the pulses or the pressures between the two arms. An inability to pass urine may produce agitation and confusion rather than a complaint about the bladder, and the finding is a tender, distended lower abdomen. A stroke may present as a confusion, a fall, or a sudden neglect of one side of the body, and the finding is a weakness or a change in speech that was not there before.

The examination of an older patient must be adapted, because the standard sequence assumes a body that can cooperate and a room that is warm. The clinician ensures privacy, warmth, good light, and enough time, and asks the patient to undress only as far as the examination requires, because cold provokes shivering, raises the pressure, and makes the pulse harder to count. Hearing and vision are assessed early, since a patient who cannot see or hear will appear confused, uncooperative, or demented when the true problem is sensory. The pulse is counted for a full interval rather than guessed, the pressure is taken in both arms and then with the patient standing, and the breathing rate is counted while the patient is unaware of being watched. The older patient tires quickly, so the examination is performed in stages with rest between, and a gentle technique matters more here than elsewhere, because the skin tears, the bones break, and the joints hurt under a hand that has not adjusted. Certain regions must be examined in every older patient, among them the pressure areas over the heels, hips, spine, and shoulders, the feet for a wound that a patient with diabetes may not feel, the mouth for a dry tongue or an ill-fitting denture, and the abdomen for a full bladder or a loaded bowel.

In a hospital with imaging and a specialist team, the older patient still needs the reasoning before the tests, because the tests are chosen to answer the questions the examination has raised. A CT of the head answers the question of bleeding or stroke after a fall or a new confusion, an image of the hip or the spine answers the question of a fracture, and a chest radiograph answers the question of infection or fluid in the lung. An ECG answers the question of rhythm and injury, and blood tests answer the questions of infection, salts, kidney function, blood count, and thyroid, each of which may explain a decline. The specialist team in the care of older people adds an assessment of mobility, thinking, mood, continence, nutrition, and the home, and its members are often the ones who notice that the patient cannot return to the place he came from without help. The ward environment itself can produce a delirium, so sleep, light, noise, orientation, hydration, and the presence of a familiar person are part of the treatment as much as any medicine.

At home, or in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the reasoning is the same, and the house becomes part of the examination. The carpet that slides, the loose stair rod, the low chair that the patient cannot rise from, the poor light on the way to the toilet, the distance to the bathroom at night, and the pill organizer filled by several different hands are clinical findings rather than domestic details. The temperature is taken with a thermometer and recorded together with the route used, the pulse and breathing are counted with a watch, and the torch makes the throat, the ears, the mouth, the feet, and the skin visible. Where a cuff is available, the pressure is measured sitting and standing, and a walking test along the corridor or the yard, with the patient observed and asked how it feels, is one of the most informative examinations in medicine. The decision that follows is often not a diagnosis but a plan about whether the patient can be safely watched at home, and the finding that makes that decision wrong is an inability to eat, drink, walk, or be safe alone.

The capacity of the older patient to make decisions deserves an explicit assessment rather than an assumption drawn from age or from a diagnosis of dementia. Capacity is specific to the decision at hand, so a patient may be able to choose what to eat and not to consent to an operation, and it is judged by whether the patient understands the information, retains it, weighs it, and can communicate a choice. Communication must be made as easy as possible before capacity is judged, with the hearing aid, the glasses, an interpreter, a quiet room, and enough time, because a failure to communicate is not the same as an inability to decide. The clinician should ask what matters to the patient, what the patient expects from treatment, and what the patient would not want, and should record those answers for the next clinician. The family may speak for a patient who cannot, but the clinician must check that the family is expressing the patient's wishes rather than its own. These conversations are part of diagnosis, because the goals they reveal change which investigations and treatments are worth pursuing.

A constructed illustration may make these habits concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine an older woman brought to a clinic because she has stopped eating and has become vague over a few days, and whose family says she was walking and cooking a week ago. She is not hot to the touch, her breathing is a little quick, and she cannot say where she is though she knows her name. The clinician does not settle for the word confusion, and finds instead a small wound on the shin that the family had not noticed and a passage of urine that has become small and dark. The wound is the likely source, the dehydration is a treatable burden on top of it, and the record now names the baseline function against which the next visit can be judged. Nothing here is real, and the story should not be applied to any living patient without a full assessment.

The older patient who is sent home must leave with a plan written in ordinary language and understood by the patient and the family. The clinician should say what has been found, what remains uncertain, what has been changed in the medicines and why, and which signs should bring the patient back sooner, among them a new confusion, a fall, a fever, a refusal to drink, a breathlessness, or a return of something the patient had recovered from. A visit arranged in advance is worth more than a promise to return if things worsen, because the patient and the family may not judge a slow decline as a reason to call. The record should show the baseline function, the medicine list as actually taken, and the plan for review, so that the next clinician inherits a story rather than a set of numbers. Where the patient's goals are comfort rather than cure, that decision belongs in the same record and should be honored.

To summarize, the older patient most often presents through a change in function rather than a classic symptom, so a fall, a confusion, a loss of appetite, and a decline in what the patient could formerly do are treated as the beginning of the reasoning and not the whole of it. The lethal causes are named at the bedside and matched to the finding that reveals them: sepsis without fever, a hip fracture that does not hurt, a bleed over the brain after an injury nobody remembers, a myocardial infarction without chest pain, a medicine that has become the disease, and dehydration that has gone unnoticed. Frailty changes both the diagnosis and the decision, delirium must be separated from the dementia it so often accompanies, and every medicine the patient actually takes is part of the assessment. Every score, cut-off, pressure, temperature, rate, and reference range in this chapter is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. The same reasoning works in the hospital with its imaging and its specialist team and in the home where the carpet, the stairs, and the pill organizer are examined alongside the patient.

# Chapter 62 — Immunocompromised Patients

The patient whose immune defenses have failed is the patient in whom the diagnostic method itself breaks down, because nearly every sign the clinician relies upon is produced by the immune response. Redness, warmth, swelling, pus, fever, a raised white cell count, and the shadow on a chest radiograph are all the work of a system that is reacting. When that reaction is blunted, the disease advances while the signs it would have made do not appear, so a chest that sounds clear and a temperature that is normal may accompany a severe infection. Two errors follow, and both are dangerous: accepting a reassuring examination and waiting, and attributing every complaint to the underlying condition while a treatable infection is missed. This chapter holds both errors in view, and it is educational material that does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Certain possibilities must be named before any comfortable explanation is accepted, because each can kill quickly and each announces itself through a finding that can be sought deliberately. The patient whose neutrophil count has fallen may have a neutropenic sepsis, and the finding that betrays it is often nothing more than a fever, with no source anywhere in the body. The patient with a dry cough, breathlessness on exertion, and a falling oxygen level may have pneumocystis pneumonia, and the finding that reveals it is the desaturation that appears when the patient walks, while the chest sounds nearly normal. The patient with a fever that persists despite treatment may have a disseminated fungal infection, and the clue is often a small skin lesion, an eye finding, or a fever that nothing else explains. The patient who met tuberculosis in the past may reactivate it when immunity falls, and the finding is the organism identified in sputum or in another sample, because the radiograph and the symptoms may be unremarkable. The patient with a headache, a change in behavior, or a seizure may have an infection of the central nervous system, and the finding is the abnormal spinal fluid or the lesion on imaging, since the neck may be supple and the classic signs absent.

Immunity is not one thing but a series of layers, and the infection that appears tells the clinician which layer has failed. The first is the barrier of skin and mucous membranes, and when a line, a catheter, or a course of treatment breaks it, organisms that live on the surface enter directly. The second is the neutrophil, the cell that rushes to a site of invasion and consumes bacteria, and when it is reduced, the infections are bacterial and fungal and they arrive quickly. The third is the lymphocyte that coordinates the response and the lymphocyte that produces antibody, and when these are weakened, the infections are the ones that live inside cells, among them viruses, mycobacteria, and certain fungi. The spleen filters the blood and removes organisms that carry a capsule, and a patient without a working spleen is vulnerable to exactly those. The reasons a patient reaches this state therefore predict the risk: infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV; treatment of cancer with medicines that suppress the marrow; transplantation, which requires suppression to prevent rejection or graft-versus-host disease; the biologic medicines; treatment with steroids; a cancer of the blood; malnutrition; poorly controlled diabetes; and advanced age. The task is not to memorize the list but to ask which of these applies to this patient, because the answer predicts what is likely to go wrong.

Fever must be read differently in such a patient, because the response that produces it is itself part of what has failed. The temperature may be the only abnormal finding, and sometimes even the temperature is absent, since the same blunted response that hides redness and pus can hide the rise in temperature as well. A fever of 38 degrees Celsius is commonly taught as the line above which fever is considered present, but in this group the figure is an illustration of the reasoning rather than a threshold to rely on, and it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted value varies with the site of measurement, the age of the patient, and the edition of the reference being followed. The corollary is uncomfortable and important, since a normal temperature does not exclude a serious infection, and a change in behavior, a new confusion, a fall, or a refusal to eat may be the whole of the presentation. The clinician should record the temperature by the same route each time and treat the trend as carrying more weight than any single reading, because the absence of localizing signs is not reassurance here but the reason to look harder.

The history is the most productive instrument in these patients, and it is taken with the specific aim of naming the immune defect. The clinician asks which medicines the patient takes, including those prescribed for another condition, because steroids and the biologic medicines are often not described as treatment for the immune system at all. It is worth asking directly about treatment for cancer, about a transplant and when it took place, about the spleen, and about any illness of the blood, because a patient may not connect an operation years ago with the present fever. Exposure matters as much here as anywhere, so the questions should cover soil, building work, birds and their droppings, farm animals, unpasteurized milk and cheese, untreated water, and anyone with a cough or a rash, while travel and residence determine which infections are even possible. Every line, catheter, drain, and prosthetic device belongs in the same account, together with how long each has been there, and the patient's own account of previous infections is often more specific than any test that follows.

Two dimensions of the defect change the whole probability list, and they are the depth of the suppression and the time since it began. A neutrophil count that has fallen below 500 cells in each microliter is often quoted as the level at which the risk of an overwhelming bacterial infection rises sharply, and that figure is offered as a picture of the reasoning rather than a universal rule, so it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, where the line and the units of reporting may be stated differently. A helper lymphocyte count below 200 cells in each microliter is likewise taught as the point at which certain opportunistic infections become common, and that number is an illustration whose exact value belongs to the current guideline and to the laboratory in use, so it must be checked locally before it is applied. The length of time matters as much as the depth, because a count that has been low only briefly carries a different meaning from one that has been low for a long time, and the period in which the marrow begins to recover is a time when infections can still appear. The clinician who places the patient on this timeline reasons far better than one who counts cells alone.

The examination is performed in a fixed order and must go to the places that are usually left until last. The clinician begins with the general appearance, the level of alertness, the work of breathing, and the state of the circulation, because these decide how much time remains for the rest. The mouth is examined with a torch for thrush, ulcers, and the dry, cracked lining that follows chemotherapy, and the teeth and gums are pressed, since a dental abscess can seed the blood when immunity is low. Every line and catheter is inspected from the skin outward, because the insertion site is a common source and the signs there may be faint, while the perineum and the skin folds are examined directly and gently. A rectal examination is undertaken only when it is clearly needed, because in a patient with a low neutrophil count the examination itself can injure the lining, and the eyes, sinuses, and ears are checked for the changes of a deep infection. The examiner who looks at all of these places without being prompted by a symptom is the one who finds the source.

Neutropenic sepsis is the presentation that must be assumed before it is proved, because it can kill within a short time and because its signs are so few. The patient may have a fever and nothing else, or may look merely tired, and the ordinary signs of infection are missing because the cells that would produce them are absent. The findings that support the diagnosis are a temperature that is raised or has fallen, a pulse and a breathing rate that have climbed, a pressure that is falling, cool or mottled skin, and a reduced passage of urine. A systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the point at which shock is assumed, but that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the pressure that matters depends on the patient's usual value and on age. The decision to treat is made on suspicion, and it is the right decision when the patient is known to be neutropenic or is likely to become so; it would be the wrong decision only if a clear non-infectious cause explained the whole picture, and even then the patient must be watched closely. Blood cultures should be drawn before treatment begins where that can be done without delaying it, because cultures taken afterwards are far less likely to name the organism.

Pneumocystis pneumonia is the infection that best illustrates how misleading a quiet examination can be. It appears in patients whose cellular immunity is deeply suppressed, and it begins with a dry cough, a breathlessness noticed first on exertion, and a tiredness that the patient attributes to the underlying illness. The chest may sound clear and the chest radiograph may look nearly normal early in the disease, which is exactly why the clinician who relies on either alone will be caught out. The finding that reveals it is a fall in oxygen saturation when the patient is asked to walk or to climb a step, because the lungs fail under the demand of exercise before they fail at rest. An oxygen saturation below 92 per cent is often quoted as the level at which the patient needs assessment in a place with oxygen and monitoring, but that figure is a teaching illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the accepted level shifts with the patient, the altitude, and the instrument in use. Treatment is the right answer when the picture fits and the patient is short of oxygen, and the decision to add or to withhold a steroid as part of that treatment belongs to the clinician and to the local protocol rather than to this book.

Reactivation of tuberculosis is the danger that hides in the patient whose immunity has been suppressed by a medicine rather than by a disease. It is most often seen after the biologic medicines that block a single messenger of the immune response, and after treatment with steroids, and it may appear long after the medicine was begun, which is why the connection is easily missed. The presentation is often not the classic one, because the cough may be dry, the fever low, the weight loss attributed to the underlying illness, and the radiograph may show changes in places other than the top of the lung. The finding that reveals it is the organism identified in sputum, in fluid, in a lymph node, or in a sample of tissue, and where that is not possible the clinical picture and the response to treatment may have to carry the decision together, with the current guideline and the local protocol as the authority. A decision to look for latent infection before starting such a medicine is one of the most valuable moves in this field, and the clinician who treats such a fever with an antibacterial medicine alone may watch the patient improve briefly and then relapse.

Disseminated fungal infection is the quietest of the lethal possibilities and the one most often discovered late. It appears in patients whose neutrophil count is very low or whose cellular immunity is deeply impaired, and it may announce itself through nothing more than a fever that will not settle on treatment. The skin may show small, painless lesions that the patient has not noticed, and the eyes may show a change that only an examination of the fundus reveals, and these are the findings that turn a vague fever into a specific hunt. The sinuses, the lungs, and the brain are the places where these infections settle, and the finding that confirms one is the organism grown from blood or tissue, or seen under the microscope in a sample from the affected site, although the blood culture may be negative even in advanced disease. The clinician who waits for a positive culture before acting may wait too long, and the decision to begin treatment on the strength of the clinical picture belongs to the specialist and to the local protocol rather than to this book.

Infection of the central nervous system is the presentation in which the classic signs are least reliable and the consequences of delay are greatest. The patient may have a headache, a fever, a change in behavior, a confusion, or a seizure, and the neck may be perfectly supple, because the inflammation that stiffens it in an ordinary patient may not occur. The causes in this group include a fungus that produces a slowly worsening meningitis, a parasite that forms abscesses in the brain, a virus that damages the white matter, and a cancer of the lymph tissue that grows within the nervous system, and each of these looks different and each demands a different response. The clinician should record the level of consciousness with a formal scale, and the Glasgow coma scale is the one most widely used; it formalizes the response to voice, to pain, and to command, and the figure at which it should cause alarm must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the version in use varies between services and editions. The decisive step is the examination of the spinal fluid, taken after the questions of safety have been answered, together with imaging of the brain where it is available. A change in behavior in an immunosuppressed patient is never merely a mood, and it should be investigated with the same urgency as a fever.

Infection with HIV deserves attention of its own, because it produces a predictable sequence of immune failure and therefore a predictable sequence of infections. The virus destroys the helper lymphocytes over time, and the illnesses that appear change as the count falls, so that the earlier phase is marked by infections of the surface and by tuberculosis, while the later phase opens the door to the opportunistic infections of the lung, the gut, the eye, and the brain. The acute phase may itself cause a fever, a rash, a sore throat, and enlarged lymph nodes, and it is easily mistaken for a common viral illness, which is why the offer of a test after a possible exposure matters so much. The finding that reveals the state of the immune system is the count of helper lymphocytes, and the finding that confirms the infection is the test for the virus itself, and neither should be guessed from the appearance of the patient. The decision to test must be made with consent and with confidentiality, and the conversation around it deserves the same care as the examination. Treatment of the infection is highly effective and belongs to the service that manages it, and this book names the decision rather than the medicine, because a patient with HIV and a fever should never be treated as though the fever were explained by the virus alone.

The transplant recipient presents a different pattern at each stage after the operation, and the stage is as important as the symptoms. In the earliest period the risks are those of any operation, including infection at the wound, in the chest, in the urine, and on the lines, and the organisms are the ones that live in the hospital. In the period that follows, the risks shift to the infections that a suppressed cellular immunity permits, among them a virus of the herpes family, the fungus that causes pneumocystis pneumonia, and tuberculosis. In the later period, as suppression is reduced, the patient becomes vulnerable once more to the infections of ordinary community life, and a pneumonia that would be mild in another person can be severe in this one. In the recipient of marrow or of stem cells there is the added problem of graft-versus-host disease, in which the donated cells attack the patient's own tissues, producing a rash, diarrhea, and liver injury that may be mistaken for infection while it also increases the risk of it. The clinician who asks when the transplant took place, what suppression is being given, and whether there is graft-versus-host disease has already narrowed the list of likely causes.

The biologic medicines and the steroids deserve particular attention because their risk is concentrated and specific. A medicine that blocks a single messenger of inflammation, which is the principle of the biologic treatments, removes one part of the defense while leaving the rest intact, and the infections that follow are the ones that messenger was holding back, of which tuberculosis is the best known and fungal infection another. Both may appear long after the medicine was started, when the connection to the treatment has been forgotten by everyone including the patient, and steroids suppress immunity in a way that depends on the patient and on the medicine. The clinician should therefore ask directly about steroids, about medicines bought without a prescription, about traditional remedies, and about treatments given in another country, because the immune effect of these is often unknown and sometimes substantial. The finding that would justify delaying or stopping such a medicine is an active infection, and that decision belongs to the clinician who prescribed it, together with the specialist and the local protocol, while the most useful act is often a question asked before the medicine is given about exposure to tuberculosis and previous infection.

A patient without a spleen, or with a spleen that no longer works, has a specific and lifelong vulnerability that is easy to overlook. The spleen filters the blood and removes organisms that carry a capsule, and when it is absent those organisms can multiply in the bloodstream with astonishing speed, which is why a fever in such a patient is an emergency rather than a complaint. The history should include removal of the spleen after injury, a spleen damaged by sickle cell disease or by another disorder of the blood, and a spleen shrunk by disease, because the patient may not know that the organ matters. Cancer of the blood and of the marrow produces immune failure by more than one route, since the disease may crowd the marrow so that neutrophils are produced in inadequate numbers, and it may disturb the lymphocytes that coordinate the response and produce antibody. The examination looks for the signs of the underlying disease, among them pallor, bleeding into the skin, enlarged lymph nodes, an enlarged liver or spleen, and bone tenderness, and it looks at the same time for the focus of the present infection. A fever in a patient with a cancer of the blood is often the first sign that the disease has advanced, and it should never be attributed to the cancer alone.

In a hospital the same reasoning is carried out with instruments that can name the organism, but the sequence of the reasoning does not change. The blood count tells the clinician the depth of the suppression, and a count that can be returned while the clinician waits changes the speed of the decision, while a count that will arrive later must not be allowed to delay treatment in a patient who looks unwell. Cultures of the blood, the urine, the sputum, and any fluid collection should be taken before treatment where that can be done without postponing it, because a culture taken afterwards is a weaker witness. Imaging of the chest and of the abdomen, the computed tomography, or CT, scan, the ultrasound, and the magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, each answers a specific question, and the clinician who has formed a hypothesis knows which one to ask for. The polymerase chain reaction, which detects the genetic material of an organism, is useful for the viruses and for some of the difficult bacteria, and a sample of tissue may be the only way to identify a fungus or a mycobacterium. Every test should be ordered because its result would change what is done, and a test whose result would change nothing is a delay rather than a help.

The clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer cannot name the organism, but it can still do the reasoning that decides the next move. The history carries almost the entire weight, so it should be taken with more care rather than less: which medicines, which treatment, which operation, which device, which exposure, which travel, and which infection in the past. The temperature, the pulse, and the breathing counted properly turn an impression into a record that can be compared at the next visit, and the trend of those numbers is often the most sensitive sign available. The torch makes the mouth, the throat, the skin, the perineum, and the fundus of the eye visible, and thrush in the mouth of a patient not known to be immunosuppressed is itself a finding that changes the list of diagnoses. Asking the patient to walk across the room while the breathing and the pulse are observed is a test of the whole circulation and of the lungs, and it costs nothing. The decision that follows is rarely a diagnosis but a plan, and a normal examination in a patient whose history is alarming is a reason to look again rather than a reason to relax.

The decision about treatment is part of diagnosis, and in this group it is often made before the cause is known. Treatment is the right answer when the patient is known or likely to be neutropenic, when the signs of organ failure are present, when the patient looks seriously ill, or when a treatable infection is strongly suspected and waiting would cost more than acting. Treatment is the wrong answer when a clear non-infectious cause explains the whole picture, such as a reaction to a medicine or a clot, and even then the patient must be watched because a second problem may be present. The clinician should name the finding that would justify or forbid the decision rather than the medicine, because the reasoning transfers between settings even when the available medicines do not, and because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from this book. Protection of the patient follows the same reasoning, because a patient with a suppressed immune system should not be placed beside a patient with an infectious illness.

A constructed illustration may make these habits concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a patient receiving chemotherapy who arrives with a fever but no other complaint, whose chest sounds clear and whose only abnormal finding is a pulse that has climbed and a pressure that has begun to fall; the clinician treats on suspicion, takes cultures where that can be done without delay, and searches the perineum and every line for the source. Now imagine a patient whose immunity is suppressed by steroids, who has a dry cough and a breathlessness that the examination at rest does not explain, and in whom the finding that settles the question is a fall in oxygen saturation when asked to walk; the clinician treats the pneumonia on the picture and sends the samples afterwards. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment; what both show is the move that matters, since the examination was not trusted to be reassuring.

To summarize, the immunosuppressed patient is the patient in whom the signs of infection may be absent, so the clinician reasons from the immune defect rather than from the examination alone. The reasons for the state, among them infection with HIV, treatment of cancer, transplantation, the biologic medicines, steroids, and disease of the blood, each predict a different pattern of infection and a different speed of danger. The lethal possibilities are named at the front of the assessment, among them a neutropenic sepsis, a pneumocystis pneumonia, a disseminated fungal infection, a reactivation of tuberculosis, and an infection of the central nervous system. The same reasoning is carried out where a laboratory can return a count while the clinician waits and where the clinician must treat on suspicion because the answer will come after the decision. Every figure in this chapter, whether a count, a cut-off, a temperature, a pressure, an oxygen level, or a duration, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A fever in this group is never dismissed, and the patient whose immunity has failed is met with a lower threshold for action rather than a higher one.

# Chapter 63 — Palliative and End-of-Life Assessment

Palliative and end-of-life assessment begins when the question that organizes care changes. The clinician is no longer asking only what disease is present, but what is happening now, what is likely next, and what would make the remaining time better. Some patients have a cancer that has spread, some have a heart, a kidney, or a lung that is failing beyond repair, and some are very old and frail with many things wrong at once. What they share is that the burden of investigation and of treatment must now be weighed against the comfort it buys. This is educational material, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Causes that can kill or disable within hours should be named before any comfortable assumption is made, because here they are common and each has a finding that can still be sought. A patient with a known cancer who develops a band of pain around the trunk, weakness of the legs, or difficulty passing urine may have compression of the spinal cord, and the finding is a level below which sensation and power are altered. A patient who becomes drowsy, confused, thirsty, and constipated may have a raised calcium level in the blood, and correcting it can restore alertness. A patient who becomes pale, sweaty, and faint, or who vomits blood, may be bleeding, and the finding is a falling pressure with a rising pulse. A patient who is difficult to rouse after a medicine for pain has been increased may be suffering the sedative effect of that medicine, and the finding is a falling breathing rate with small pupils. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius in a previously stable patient should be explained rather than blamed on dying, though the figure that defines fever varies with the route of measurement, so confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Comfort and diagnosis are not opposing duties, and a clinician who treats them as opposites will fail the patient in one direction or the other. Many symptoms at this stage are reversible or partly reversible, and the search for their cause is the same disciplined search taught elsewhere, now directed at what can be relieved. A confusion caused by constipation, by retention of urine, by a medicine, by an infection, or by a dry mouth differs from the confusion of the final hours, and examination tells them apart. A test that would not change comfort may be set aside, while a test that would reveal a treatable cause of suffering is worth doing even in a patient who is clearly dying.

The history uses the same framework as any other, but the questions of most weight are different. The clinician asks what the patient understands, what the patient has been told, and what the patient believes is happening, because those beliefs shape every decision. The patient is asked what matters most now, whether freedom from pain, a particular conversation, being at home, or being spared a particular indignity. Symptoms are recorded with the Oldcarts framework, noting what makes each better or worse and what the family has already tried. The family's understanding, fears, and capacity to give care belong in the same conversation.

Prognosis is a judgment revised as the patient changes, used to decide how much should be done rather than to close a door. One useful discipline is to ask whether the clinician would be surprised if this patient died within a defined period, a question that formalizes an impression experienced clinicians already form. Any interval attached to it is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because published periods differ between services, populations, and editions. Function is the most useful single guide to how much strength remains, and scales that record walking, self-care, and time spent in bed formalize the observation that a decline in these abilities mirrors decline in the whole body.

Pain is the symptom families fear most, and its assessment begins with the recognition that it is usually more than a physical sensation. The clinician asks about site, quality, what brings it on, what relieves it, and what it prevents the patient from doing, and then asks what the pain means to the patient. A new pain, a pain that has changed in character, or a pain in a place where the disease is not known to be should prompt a search for a cause rather than an increase in medicine, because a fracture, a clot, an infection, or a developing compression of the spinal cord can present this way. The finding that makes a medicine for pain right is a pain whose pattern fits the known disease and which the patient reports as eased once treatment begins; the finding that makes it wrong is an unexplained new or worsening pain, or a deepening drowsiness while the pain is chased.

The character of the pain points to the kind of cause and therefore to the kind of relief. A constant, aching pain that is worse with movement usually comes from injury to tissue, while a burning, shooting, or electric pain, sometimes with numbness, usually comes from injury to a nerve, and it often responds poorly to the medicines used for the first. Not every pain needs a medicine, because a full bladder, a constipated bowel, a pressure sore, a tight dressing, a cold room, and an uncomfortable position can all be removed. Some patients cannot report pain at all, and assessment then rests on behavior, including a frown or grimace, a clenched jaw, guarding, restlessness, withdrawal, a cry, or a change in the usual pattern of sleep. A change in behavior should be treated as possible pain until another cause, such as a full bladder, a loaded bowel, a fracture, or an infection, has been sought.

Breathlessness is frightening in a way that pain is not, because it is felt as the threat of suffocation, and its assessment follows the same logic as anywhere else. The clinician looks for causes that can still be relieved, among them fluid around the lung, a pneumonia, a clot in the lung, a failing heart, a narrowed airway, a severe anemia, and weakness of the muscles of breathing. Each announces itself differently: fluid dulls the lung base and reduces breath sounds, infection brings fever and crackles, a clot may bring sudden onset with a normal chest examination, anemia shows pallor and a rapid pulse, and a narrowed airway brings a wheeze or a stridor. The clinician who asks what has changed, and who examines the chest, the neck, the legs, and the color of the patient, finds a treatable cause more often than expected.

The relief of breathlessness is a decision about what will help, made with the patient awake and the family informed. Where fluid around the lung is found, the decision is whether removing it would improve breathing enough to justify the procedure, and the answer depends on how quickly it reaccumulated and how the patient tolerated the last attempt. Where an infection is found in a patient who still wants to live for a defined goal, treatment may be right, while in a patient clearly in the last days comfort measures without antibiotics may be kinder. Oxygen is a treatment like any other, justified when the level of oxygen in the blood is low or when the patient reports relief, not merely because the patient is breathless, and the amount given belongs to the local protocol rather than to a book. A breathing rate above 30 breaths per minute is worth recording and following, but the line at which it alarms shifts with age, illness, and medicines, so confirm any such figure against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Nausea and vomiting are distressing and often reversible, and the search for their cause is one of the most rewarding tasks at this stage. The clinician considers a bowel that is not moving, a stomach that is not emptying, raised pressure inside the head, a raised calcium level, an infection, a disease of the kidney, and the medicines the patient already takes. Timing carries information: vomiting soon after eating suggests a problem of the stomach or its outlet, while vomiting unrelated to meals and worse in the morning may suggest raised pressure inside the head. The finding that makes treatment right is a cause that can be named and corrected; the finding that makes it wrong is a symptom blamed on the illness while a simple cause such as constipation or a medicine is present.

Constipation causes the most preventable suffering in this group, because it is common, easily missed, and produces confusion, pain, nausea, and restlessness that are then blamed on the disease. The abdomen is inspected, felt, and listened to, and a rectal examination may reveal hard stool, an empty rectum with a loaded bowel above it, or a mass. The dangerous possibility is an obstructed or perforated bowel, whose findings are a distended abdomen, vomiting, absent or high-pitched bowel sounds, and severe pain, and that patient needs urgent help rather than another laxative. A patient with a known cancer and new constipation with back pain must also be considered for compression of the spinal cord.

Confusion is the most important diagnosis to make in this population, because it is common, frightening to the patient and the family, and often reversible. The patient may be restless and hallucinating, or quiet, withdrawn, and drowsy, and the quiet form is most often missed because it looks like peaceful acceptance. The clinician asks whether the change came suddenly, whether it fluctuates, whether attention wanders, and whether it is worse in the evening, and then looks for the cause. The causes to seek are an infection, a full bladder, a loaded bowel, a medicine, alcohol withdrawal, a low level of oxygen, a low level of sugar, a raised calcium level, a disease of the kidney or the liver, a new stroke, and untreated pain.

The management of confusion begins with correcting what can be corrected and shaping an environment a confused person can understand. The room is kept quiet and lit, familiar people are present, the patient is told where he or she is, hearing aids and glasses are used, and the day is given a shape with light and activity. A medicine that quiets agitation may sometimes be needed, and the decision belongs to the clinician who knows the patient, because the medicine that calms one patient may deepen the confusion of another. The finding that would make such a medicine wrong is a cause not yet sought, a patient who can be settled otherwise, or a sedation that threatens swallowing and breathing.

The family is often the second patient, and its distress deserves assessment in its own right. The clinician asks who is doing the caring, how much sleep that person is getting, what the family believes is happening, what they fear most, and whether they are arguing about what should be done. Exhaustion, guilt, anger, and the feeling of being unprepared are findings that change the plan, not signs of weakness. A family that cannot lift the patient, cannot give the medicines, or cannot reach help at night is a family whose patient will suffer, whatever the clinical decisions, and where the caregiver is also old or ill the plan must assume that support is needed.

The recognition that a patient is dying is made from a pattern of findings rather than a single sign, and it should be described honestly and without euphemism. In the last days and hours the patient becomes drowsy and then difficult to rouse, takes less food and then less fluid, and may be unable to swallow safely. The hands and feet become cool and may take on a mottled, bluish color, the urine becomes scanty and dark, and the mouth becomes dry. Breathing becomes irregular with pauses and may sound moist or rattly because the patient can no longer clear the throat, which distresses the family but usually not the patient. The pulse becomes rapid and weak, and the patient may become restless or speak of seeing people who have died, which is common and not necessarily a sign of fear.

These signs are not a clock, and the clinician should resist giving an exact time. A patient may live for hours or for days after the breathing changes, and a patient who seems to be dying may rally before declining again, and both are ordinary. Any interval a guideline attaches to these findings is an illustration and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because published durations vary with the cause of death, the setting, and the population studied. What matters more than the prediction is the preparation: whether the family knows what to expect, whether symptoms are controlled, and whether the plan for the final hours is written and understood.

The hardest judgment is to separate a patient who is dying from one who has a treatable cause of looking as though he or she is dying, and the distinction is made by examination rather than mood. A drowsy patient with a rapid pulse and a fever may have an infection that would respond to treatment, and the decision depends on the patient's goals and the likely burden. A drowsy patient with a low level of sugar or a high calcium level may recover alertness if the cause is corrected, and that is worth seeking even near the end. The finding that makes the diagnosis of dying right is a pattern progressive over days, with the signs of the last days present together and no reversible cause found; the finding that makes it wrong is any treatable cause not yet sought.

Some events at this stage are lethal within minutes and must be anticipated rather than discovered, and the team should plan for them with the patient and the family. A patient with a cancer of the head, the neck, or the chest who develops a swollen face and neck, distended veins over the chest, and breathlessness when lying flat may have obstruction of the large vein returning blood to the heart. A patient with a severe headache, vomiting, and a falling level of consciousness may have raised pressure inside the head, and the finding is a new drowsiness with a change in the pupils or in the use of an arm or a leg. A patient who bleeds heavily from the mouth, the nose, or the bowel may be having a final hemorrhage, and the plan for that possibility, including dark towels, a quiet room, and a medicine chosen in advance, is made while the patient can still discuss it.

Not every patient who needs this assessment has a cancer, and the reasoning is adjusted for other trajectories. A patient with a failing heart, a failing kidney, a failing liver, or failing lungs may decline in steps, each severe episode followed by a partial recovery that leaves the patient weaker than before. A patient with advanced dementia may decline over years while the family carries the burden, and the assessment must consider what the patient can still enjoy, what the patient can still recognize, and what the family can sustain. A very old and frail patient may die without a single dominant diagnosis, and the sum of many small failures is then the diagnosis.

In a well-resourced hospital the assessment is carried out with a palliative team available, and what that team adds is time, expertise, and continuity a rotating ward team cannot provide. The triggers for calling them are a patient whose symptoms are not controlled, a patient whose goals of care are unclear or disputed, a family in crisis, and a patient who is dying without a written plan. The palliative team works alongside the treating team rather than replacing it, and the reason to involve it early is that its problems are easier to solve before a crisis than during one. The intensive care unit, or ICU, is not the opposite of palliative care, and the two meet in the patient who needs support for breathing or for the circulation while the goals of care are clarified. Where no such team exists, the same work is done by the clinician who is there, and the telephone is a legitimate instrument of the assessment.

Investigations at this stage are chosen for what they would change, the same test used everywhere in this book. A computed tomography, or CT, scan, or a magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, study, may be the only way to confirm compression of the spinal cord, and then the imaging is urgent because the ability to walk may depend on how soon treatment begins. A chest radiograph may reveal fluid that can be drained, a pneumonia that can be treated, or a fractured rib that explains a pain. A blood count and a measure of the calcium and the salts may reveal an anemia or a raised calcium level that explains drowsiness.

At home, where the family is the nursing staff, the assessment changes shape, and the clinician's most important instrument becomes teaching. The family must be told what to watch for, what to do when they see it, and whom to call, in words they can repeat back. The plan should be written down, because memory fails under strain, and it should name the signs of the last days, the signs that mean a call is needed now, and the person to call at any hour. Where the home has no electricity, no running water, and no transport, the plan must account for that, because a decision that assumes a car and a telephone is not a plan.

Much of the care at home is delivered by telephone, and the quality of that call depends on what was prepared before it. The clinician who knows the patient, the diagnosis, the current symptoms, and the family's capacity can make a safe decision without seeing the patient, and the call should end with a clear instruction about what to do and when to call again. A small supply of medicines kept at home for a crisis, chosen in advance for expected symptoms, is one way to prevent a night of suffering, and the choice and the amount belong to the local protocol and the prescriber rather than to this book. The finding that makes such a plan right is a family that understands when to use it and when to call first; the finding that makes it wrong is a family left alone with medicines and no instruction.

The conversation with the patient and the family is itself a diagnostic act, because it reveals what they understand and what they most need. The clinician asks what the patient has been told, what the patient wants to know, and how much detail the patient wants, since not everyone wants the same information. Plain words should be used for the diagnosis and the prognosis, because a euphemism the family does not share leaves everyone more frightened than before. In some families and cultures the request that the diagnosis be kept from the patient is made with the intent to protect, and the clinician should respond by asking what the patient already understands rather than by refusing outright. The ethical duty is to the patient, and the family is served by being included rather than by being obeyed.

Spiritual and cultural needs are part of the assessment and not an optional addition. The clinician should ask what gives the patient strength, whether the patient wishes to see a religious leader, whether there are rituals or foods or times of prayer that must be respected, and whether the patient fears anything after death. A patient afraid of being abandoned, of being in pain, or of being a burden may suffer more than the physical disease alone would produce, and that suffering will not appear on any examination. The beliefs of the family about death and about who should be present belong in the plan, because a plan that ignores them will fail at the moment it matters.

The assessment of the patient's ability to decide is a clinical skill, not a formality. A patient who can understand the information, retain it long enough to weigh it, and express a choice has the capacity to make that choice, and a patient who cannot needs a decision made in his or her best interest. Capacity is specific to the decision, so a patient may be able to decide about food and not about a major operation, and it may change from hour to hour in a confusion. Where a surrogate decides, that person should be asked what the patient would have wanted, and the answer is often a clear one.

Decisions about treatment are made by weighing the benefit the patient will feel against the burden imposed, and both sides are clinical findings. Fluids into a vein may relieve a dry mouth and a failing circulation, or may worsen the swelling and the breathlessness of a failing heart, and the deciding finding is whether the patient is thirsty and whether the extra fluid is accumulating. An antibiotic may cure a pneumonia and give more time, or add nothing but discomfort when the infection is part of the dying process, and the deciding finding is the patient's own goal and the severity of the illness. Food and fluid by mouth should be offered as long as the patient wants them and can swallow safely, and should not be forced, because forcing adds choking and distress without benefit. Nutrition by tube or into a vein is a treatment with its own burdens, and the finding that makes it right is a patient who may recover enough to enjoy something, while the finding that makes it wrong is a patient who is dying and for whom it prolongs the dying.

Much of the comfort of a dying patient comes from care that is not a medicine at all, and the clinician should assess it as carefully as any symptom. The mouth becomes dry and painful when the patient stops drinking, and cleaning it, moistening it, and treating a fungal infection when present can change the whole experience of the day. The skin over the heels, the hips, and the base of the spine should be inspected at every visit, and a red or broken area treated and the position changed, because a pressure sore can cause more suffering than the disease itself. The Soap notes framework works here as anywhere, provided the assessment section states the reasoning and not only the diagnosis, and the record should name the patient's goals, the family's understanding, and the decisions made and why.

A patient kept at home needs a clear safety plan as much as any other patient in this book. The family should be told which signs mean help is needed at once: a new confusion, a pain that cannot be settled, a difficulty in breathing not eased by the usual measures, a complete inability to pass urine, vomiting that will not stop, a new weakness in the legs, or bleeding that will not stop. The family's needs do not end with the death of the patient, and the clinician should ask how the family is sleeping, whether anyone is alone, and whether there are other dependents. A family present at the death, that understood what was happening, and that was given permission to grieve usually fares better than one kept away.

A constructed illustration may make the reasoning concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than a portrait of any real person. Imagine an older woman with a cancer that has spread, who becomes drowsy and confused over two days while her family assumes the end has come; the clinician who examines her finds a distended bladder, a loaded bowel, and a dry mouth, and the confusion lifts once those are relieved. Now imagine a man in the last week of a long illness who becomes restless and breathless at night, with breaths that become irregular and pause; the clinician recognizes the pattern of the last days, explains it to the family, and stays with them rather than ordering a test that would change nothing. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment. What the two share is the discipline of looking at the patient, naming the cause if there is one, and deciding what will actually help.

To summarize, palliative and end-of-life assessment changes the question from what can be cured to what is happening now and what will happen next, and it does so without abandoning diagnosis. The lethal and reversible causes are named early and sought deliberately, among them compression of the spinal cord, a raised calcium level in the blood, a hemorrhage, an infection, and the sedative effect of a medicine for pain, each with the finding that reveals it. Pain, breathlessness, nausea, constipation, confusion, and the distress of the family are assessed by their cause, because a large share of them can be relieved, and the search is the same disciplined search taught in every other chapter. In a hospital with a palliative team the work is shared and the problems are caught earlier, while at home the family is the nursing staff and the clinician's instrument is teaching that is written down and repeated. Every score, cut-off, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, or duration named in this chapter is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. Comfort and diagnosis are not opposing duties, and the clinician who looks for the treatable cause of suffering is doing the most useful work in the room. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

# Chapter 64 — Laboratory Tests

The laboratory answers questions, but it cannot ask them, and a result that arrives without a question attached is only a number looking for a meaning. A test is worth sending when the clinician has already decided what each possible answer would change, because a result that changes nothing has spent money, time, and the patient's confidence for no return. The reasoning of laboratory medicine is therefore the reasoning of the bedside carried one step further: a probability is formed from the history and the examination, a test is chosen that can move that probability, and the new result is read against the patient rather than against the sheet of paper it is printed on. This chapter treats the laboratory as an extension of clinical reasoning and never as a substitute for it, and it is educational material that does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.
