Four dangerous results deserve to be named before any comfortable reading of a panel begins, because each announces itself through a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. A low glucose is the one laboratory value that can imitate a stroke, a seizure, or drunkenness and can be put right at once, and the finding that betrays it is a patient whose consciousness is altered, who is sweating and shaky and hungry, and whose confusion lifts when the sugar is restored. A rising creatinine speaks of a kidney that is failing, often before the patient feels anything at all, and the finding that reveals it is a shrinking passage of urine together with swelling, breathlessness, or a pressure that has begun to climb. A critical potassium, whether high or low, can stop the heart without warning, and the finding that reveals it is muscle weakness, an irregular pulse, or the tall peaked waves and the widening of the tracing on the electrocardiogram, or ECG. A positive culture in a patient who looks entirely well is the fourth, and it is dangerous not because the patient is ill but because the result invites treatment that may be unnecessary and harmful when the growth is contamination or quiet colonization rather than infection.

A test never creates a diagnosis by itself; it moves a probability from where the history and the examination left it to somewhere new, and the size of that move is what makes the test worth doing. An abnormal value may appear in a person who has no disease at all, because reference ranges are built from a chosen population and a share of healthy people will always fall outside them by chance alone. A normal value may appear in a person who is gravely ill, because a test taken too early, a disease confined to one place, or a result that fluctuates from hour to hour can all leave the paper innocent while the patient is not. The clinician who holds both possibilities in mind reads every result as a change in belief rather than as a verdict.

Every test with a continuous value, such as a glucose, a potassium, or a count of cells, must have a line drawn somewhere to separate the ordinary from the alarming, and wherever that line is drawn something is gained and something is lost. Move the line toward the healthy and the test catches more of the sick, but it also labels more healthy people as abnormal and sends them for further tests that may harm them. This is why a test used to confirm a suspicion that is already strong should be chosen differently from a test used to set aside a suspicion that is faint, and why the same result means different things in a young athlete and in a frail older patient. The exact position of such a line is a local decision, and any figure quoted in this chapter is an illustration of the reasoning rather than a rule to be carried between hospitals.

The complete blood count is the most frequently ordered test in medicine, and it repays being read part by part rather than as a single verdict. The hemoglobin concentration and the hematocrit describe how much oxygen-carrying capacity the blood holds, while the red cell count, the mean corpuscular volume, and the mean corpuscular hemoglobin describe the size and the color of the cells themselves. A low hemoglobin with small pale cells points toward iron deficiency, a loss of blood that has gone on quietly, or a diet that lacks the mineral, while a low hemoglobin with large cells points toward a lack of vitamin B twelve or folate, or toward alcohol, thyroid disease, or a marrow that is being crowded by something else. A hemoglobin of 7 grams per deciliter is often quoted as a level at which transfusion is considered, but that figure is offered here only to show the shape of the reasoning, and it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line depends on the speed of the fall, the symptoms, the heart, and the blood supply of the service.

The white cell count and its differential are read for the direction and the kind of change rather than for the total alone. A count that rises with a majority of neutrophils usually accompanies a bacterial infection, a tissue injury, a burn, or the use of steroids, while a count that rises with lymphocytes accompanies many viral illnesses and some bacterial ones. A fall in all the cell lines together is a finding that must be explained rather than watched, and a very high white cell count with immature forms, especially when the patient has bone pain, bruising, recurring infections, or an enlarged spleen, raises the possibility of leukemia, which is a cancer of the blood-forming tissue. A low white cell count may mean a marrow that is suppressed by disease, by infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, or by a medicine, and such a patient may carry a serious infection with few signs at all.

The platelet count is the part of the count that most directly changes what the clinician is willing to do next, because platelets are the first patch on a torn vessel. A falling count produces bruising without injury, small bleeding spots in the skin, bleeding from the gums or the nose, and, when the count is very low, bleeding into the gut or the brain. A platelet count below 50,000 per microliter is often described as the point at which bleeding becomes a real concern, but the number is a teaching illustration rather than a universal line and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the risk depends on why the count fell, whether there is infection or fever, and whether the patient is already bleeding. A low count may come from a marrow that is not making platelets, from a spleen that is holding them, from an immune attack on them, from sepsis, or from a medicine, and the decision about whether to treat or to watch belongs to the clinician who can see the whole picture. A raised count is more often a reaction to inflammation, bleeding, or iron deficiency than a disease in its own right, and it is followed rather than treated.

The chemistry panel is a set of questions about water, salts, sugar, and the work of the kidneys, and each of its parts is read against the patient rather than against the printed range. The sodium describes the balance of water in the body more than it describes salt itself, so a low sodium may reflect a heart that is failing, a liver that is scarred, a kidney that is leaking, a hormone disturbance, or a medicine that holds water back. A sodium below 125 millimoles per liter is often named as a level at which confusion and seizures become likely, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the danger lies in how quickly the value fell and in the patient's own brain, not in the number alone. The potassium is the electrolyte that most often kills quietly, since both a high and a low value can disturb the rhythm of the heart, and the causes range from kidney failure and medicines to vomiting, diarrhea, and the breakdown of tissue after an injury.

Calcium and magnesium are measured less often and are missed more often, and both can produce dramatic symptoms at the bedside. A low calcium causes tingling around the mouth and in the hands, cramps, spasm of the muscles, and sometimes a seizure, and the examiner may bring it out by tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear or by inflating a pressure cuff on the arm and watching the hand curl. Magnesium is the quiet partner of calcium and of potassium, and a low magnesium will keep a low potassium and a low calcium from correcting until it is found, which is why the clinician who cannot explain a stubborn electrolyte problem should measure it. None of these values carries a fixed meaning apart from the patient, and the reference range issued by the laboratory must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the method of measurement changes the number that is reported.

The tests of kidney function, the urea and the creatinine, are among the most misunderstood results on any panel, because they describe a relationship between the blood and the kidney rather than a fixed property of either. The creatinine depends on how much muscle the patient carries, so a small elderly woman and a large young man can have the same value while their kidneys are working very differently. The urea is influenced by the diet, by bleeding into the gut, by steroids, and by the state of hydration, so it is read alongside the creatinine rather than on its own. An estimate of the filtering work of the kidney, usually called the estimated glomerular filtration rate, is calculated from the creatinine with age and sex, and it too is an estimate rather than a measurement, so it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local laboratory before it is used to make a decision. A creatinine that has risen sharply from the patient's own previous value, or a passage of urine that has fallen away, is a finding to act on today, because a kidney that is injured can often be saved if the cause is found early and lost if it is watched.

The liver tests are a group of measurements that answer different questions, and reading them as one result called liver function is the most common mistake made with them. The bilirubin describes the pigment that accumulates when red cells are broken down faster than the liver can process, when the liver cells are injured, or when the flow of bile is blocked, and the color of the urine helps to separate these possibilities at the bedside. The enzymes, among them alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transferase, are released when cells are damaged or when the bile passages are irritated, and they also come from muscle and from bone, so a raised value is not automatically a liver problem. The albumin and the prothrombin time, reported as the international normalized ratio, describe what the liver is still making, and they are the tests that speak of function rather than of injury. A patient whose bilirubin is climbing while the albumin falls and the clotting time lengthens, especially with drowsiness, bleeding, or a swollen abdomen, may be in liver failure, and that patient needs urgent help rather than an outpatient appointment.

The glucose is the value that can change a patient's condition fastest in either direction, and it is measured in every patient whose consciousness is altered. A low glucose is treated at once on the clinical picture when a reliable measurement supports it, because waiting for a laboratory result while a patient's brain is starved can leave damage that no later result can undo. The finding that would make that decision wrong is a reading from a meter that has not been checked against the patient, or a value that does not fit the picture, so the measurement is repeated and the clinical state is watched while it is repeated. A high glucose with a dry mouth, a great passage of urine, deep rapid breathing, and a fruity odor on the breath suggests ketoacidosis, and the finding of ketones in the urine or in the blood supports it. Both extremes are read with the potassium, because the treatment of a very high glucose moves potassium into the cells and can uncover a dangerous fall.

The inflammatory markers, among them the C-reactive protein, the erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and procalcitonin, are often treated as if they named a disease, and they do not. Each of them rises with inflammation from any cause, including infection, injury, surgery, cancer, and diseases of the connective tissue, and each can be normal in a patient who is seriously ill, particularly early in an infection or when the infection is walled off in one place. A normal marker therefore never sets aside a diagnosis that the history and the examination support, and a raised marker never makes a diagnosis on its own. What these tests do well is follow a trajectory: a value that falls over days in a patient who is improving says something useful, and a value that climbs in a patient who is not tells the clinician to look again. The number must always be read with the patient in front of the clinician, and its reference range must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local laboratory, because the assays and the units differ between services.

The urinalysis is the cheapest window on the inside of the body, and in a clinic with no laboratory it is often the only one. The strip is dipped in a fresh sample of urine and read at the time stated by its maker, because a strip read late will show colors that were never there, and the sample should be collected in the middle of the stream after the opening has been cleaned where that is possible. The strip reports protein, blood, glucose, ketones, nitrite, and the enzyme released by white cells, and each of these asks a different question. Blood in the urine may come from an infection, a stone, an injury, a tumor, or a glomerulus that is inflamed, and a patient with visible blood in the urine needs that bleeding explained rather than covered with an antibiotic and a follow-up that never comes.

The microscopy of the urine adds what the strip cannot see, and it is worth the few minutes it takes wherever a microscope exists. White cells and bacteria together point to infection, red cells of an odd shape point to bleeding from the glomerulus, and casts, which are little molds of the kidney tubes, may show that the disease lies inside the kidney itself. Contamination is the most common explanation for an unexpected result, especially in women, in the elderly, and in any sample that was not collected with care, so a positive result in a patient without symptoms is confirmed before it is treated. A positive nitrite together with fever, pain in the flank, vomiting, and tenderness over the kidney is a different matter, because it suggests infection of the kidney itself, which can lead to infection of the bloodstream and must be treated promptly rather than watched.

Culture is the test that names the organism, and its value depends on when and how the sample was taken far more than on the laboratory that grows it. A sample taken before any treatment gives the best chance of naming the cause, while a sample taken afterwards may grow nothing and leave the clinician guessing. Blood cultures deserve particular care: the skin must be prepared properly, the bottles must be filled with enough blood, and more than one set should be taken from different sites, because a single set that grows an organism living on the skin may be telling the clinician about the skin rather than about the blood. The interval between sets is chosen to catch a release of organisms into the bloodstream rather than to suit the ward routine, and a patient who is seriously ill is treated first while the samples are drawn rather than after.

A positive culture in a patient who looks well is the result that most often leads to unnecessary treatment, and it deserves a deliberate pause. An organism grown from the urine of a patient with no urinary symptoms, from the sputum of a patient with a long-standing cough, or from a wound that is healing quietly may be colonizing rather than invading, and treating it does not help the patient while it selects resistant organisms and exposes the patient to the harm of the medicine. The decision that makes treatment right is a growth of a likely pathogen together with signs that fit it, such as fever, local pain, pus, or a rise in the inflammatory markers, and the decision that makes treatment wrong is a growth in a patient whose story and examination point elsewhere. Where the result is doubtful, the sample is repeated and the patient is examined again rather than treated on the strength of a single report.

Some diagnoses require a test that looks for the organism itself rather than for the body's response to it, and tuberculosis is the classic example. The organism can be seen under the microscope in stained sputum, grown in culture over weeks, or detected by a method that copies its genetic material, known as the polymerase chain reaction, and each approach has its own strength and its own delay. A negative smear does not exclude the disease, particularly in a patient with HIV infection or in disease outside the lung, so the decision to treat is often made on the clinical picture, the chest radiograph, and the judgment of the clinician rather than on a single laboratory report. Antibody tests describe the body's response and can be positive from an old infection or negative in an early one, so they are read with the timing of the illness and with the local prevalence of the disease. Every one of these results is interpreted against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the tests available and the ways they are used differ between countries and between editions.

In a well-resourced hospital the danger is not too few tests but too many, and the reasoning that keeps them useful is the same reasoning used in the clinic. A panel ordered by habit produces numbers that no one has decided how to use, and an unexpected result then generates another test, and then another, while the patient waits and the original question is forgotten. The clinician who asks what would be done differently for each possible answer will send fewer tests and learn more from them, and will know which sample needs to be taken before treatment begins. Repeated measurement is part of the reasoning rather than a failure of the first test, because a value that is changing tells a story that a single value cannot, and the direction of change is often more useful than the value itself. Where the laboratory reports a value that is dangerous, the report should reach a clinician who can act on it, and every service should have a way of making that happen.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the laboratory may be a single strip, a small meter, or nothing at all, and the skill is to choose the one test that changes what happens next. A glucose measurement on a patient with altered consciousness changes everything, because a low value is corrected at once and a normal value sends the reasoning elsewhere. A urine strip in a patient with urinary symptoms or with fever and flank pain may confirm an infection that must be treated or may show blood that must be explained. A test for malaria in a febrile patient who has been in a region where it is transmitted is worth more than any other single test in that setting, and a test for HIV in a patient with weight loss, recurrent infection, or a rash that fits no other pattern opens the door to care. A pregnancy test in a woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain or bleeding changes the list of dangerous causes immediately, and it costs almost nothing.

Where no test exists at all, the reasoning does not become weaker; it becomes the only tool, and it is used with more care rather than less. The history is taken again and more slowly, the examination is repeated at intervals, and the observations are written down so that a trend can be seen. The torch makes the throat, the ears, the eyes, the skin, and the perineum visible, the thermometer turns the impression of fever into something that can be compared, and a watch turns the pulse and the breathing into measurements rather than guesses. The clinician who records these observations honestly, and who says aloud what is uncertain, has done the most important part of what a laboratory would have done.

A laboratory result is only as good as the sample that reached the laboratory, and many wrong results begin long before the machine is switched on. A sample taken from the wrong patient, labeled with the wrong name, left in the sun, delayed for hours, or drawn from an arm that was squeezed for too long can produce a value that sends the reasoning in the wrong direction. Hemolysis, which is the breaking of red cells during collection, releases potassium and other substances into the fluid and can create a critical value that the patient does not have. A result that does not fit the patient should be questioned before it is acted on, and the first step is to repeat it rather than to treat it. The clinician who writes the time of collection and the treatment already given beside the request helps the laboratory and helps the next person who reads the chart.

A constructed illustration may make the place of the laboratory concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a man brought in drowsy and sweating, whose speech is slurred and whose wife says he has been drinking, and whose glucose is found to be low; the reasoning that mattered was not the label but the measurement, and it was made in the first minutes. Now imagine a woman with a long-standing cough whose sputum grows an organism, and who has no fever, no weight loss, and no change in her cough; the finding that makes treatment the right answer would be a change in her symptoms together with the growth, and the finding that makes it wrong is a growth that repeats unchanged while she remains well. Neither story is real, and neither should be applied to a real patient without a full assessment. What the two share is the habit that makes laboratory medicine safe: the result is placed beside the patient, and the reasoning decides.

To summarize, the laboratory extends the reasoning of the bedside and never replaces it, and a test earns its place only when the clinician has decided in advance what each possible answer would change. The count is read part by part; the chemistry is read against the patient rather than against the printed range; the inflammatory markers are used to follow a trajectory and never to name a disease; the liver and kidney tests are interpreted with the age, the muscle, the diet, and the medicines of the patient in mind; the urinalysis is the cheapest window on the body and the one most easily misread; and cultures are taken before treatment and interpreted with the possibility of contamination firmly in view. The dangerous results are named where they appear, among them a low glucose, a rising creatinine, a critical potassium, and a positive culture in a patient who looks well, and each is met with the finding that would confirm or set aside its meaning. Every score, cut-off, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, and duration mentioned in this chapter is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A result is a question asked of the patient, and the clinician who keeps the patient in view will read it correctly more often than the one who reads only the number.

# Chapter 65 — ECG Interpretation

The electrocardiogram, or ECG, records the small electrical currents that spread through the heart with each beat, and it is the most widely available picture of the heart in the world. It does not show the muscle but the order and speed of the electrical wave, so a tracing can be normal in a failing heart and grossly abnormal in one that is coping. Its value lies in the questions it answers at once: Is the rhythm too fast, too slow, or disordered? Is a coronary artery blocked? Has a salt disturbance changed conduction? Because those answers change what is done next, the tracing must be read by a fixed sequence, so that the second abnormality is not lost behind the first. The sequence is rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, the chambers, the segments, and the comparison with any earlier tracing. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the local rules of your own service.

Six patterns must be named before any comfortable explanation is accepted, because each changes what is done at once. Acute coronary occlusion appears as elevation of the segment joining the sharp ventricular complex to the T wave, sometimes with the T wave turned upside down in the views facing the injured wall. A wide complex tachycardia, a fast rhythm whose ventricular complexes are broad, must be treated as ventricular in origin until the tracing and the patient prove otherwise. Complete heart block shows P waves marching at their own rate while the ventricles beat slowly and independently. A high level of potassium first gives tall, narrow, peaked T waves, then a widening ventricular complex and a fading P wave. A clot in the lungs usually gives nothing more than a fast sinus rhythm with strain on the right side of the heart, which is why it is so easily dismissed. The sixth is an abnormally long interval from the start of the ventricular complex to the end of the T wave, the door through which a chaotic rhythm can enter.

The reading begins with the rate, because everything else is judged against it. The rate is counted from the distance between two ventricular complexes, and counting matters because the eye fails when the rhythm is irregular. A fast rate may be compensation for anemia, fever, pain, or a failing heart, and it may also be the disease itself. A slow rate may be normal in a fit young person and lethal in an older one, so the number alone decides nothing. A rate below 60 beats per minute is often called slow and a rate above 100 beats per minute is often called fast, but those lines are illustrations of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted range shifts with age, fitness, pregnancy, and edition. What matters more is whether the rate is keeping the pressure up.

The rhythm is read next, because the rate means little without knowing where the beats come from. A normal rhythm starts in the sinus node, the natural pacemaker in the upper right atrium, travels through the atria, pauses at the junction, and spreads through the ventricles. On the paper this gives a small P wave before every sharp ventricular complex at a constant distance. If each ventricular complex follows a P wave at the same distance, the rhythm is likely sinus. If the P waves are absent or appear at their own rate, the rhythm is generated elsewhere, and the clinician must ask whether that place lies above or below the ventricles, because that is what makes a rhythm dangerous. An irregularly irregular rhythm, with beats falling without pattern, is the signature of atrial fibrillation, and the hand on the pulse feels it too. A fast regular rhythm may instead be an abnormal circuit in the atria, and the P waves often separate the two.

The axis describes the average direction in which the electrical wave travels through the ventricles, read by noticing which recorded views show an upward deflection and which show a downward one. The wave normally travels downward and toward the patient's left. When it turns away from the left, the axis is deviated to the left, often the footprint of damaged conduction, a thick left ventricle, or an unusual route. When it turns toward the right, the axis is deviated to the right, which may mean a thick right ventricle, a clot in the lungs, a damaged left side, or simply a tall, thin, young person. The axis is rarely a diagnosis, but it is a direction sign that tells the clinician where to look next. A change compared with an earlier tracing means far more than any single measurement, and because the normal range depends on age and build, its boundary should be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The intervals are the pauses within the beat, and they are where conduction disease announces itself. The interval from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the ventricular complex measures how long the impulse takes to travel from atria to ventricles; it is normally shorter than about 0.2 seconds, and a longer one means delay at the junction. That figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the upper limit is stated differently in different texts and changes with age. A delay that lengthens with every beat until a ventricular complex is dropped warns that complete block may be coming. The width of the ventricular complex is normally narrower than about 0.12 seconds, and a broader complex means the wave is traveling by a slow route, which is the most useful clue to whether a fast rhythm is dangerous; check that limit against the current guideline and the local protocol, since it moves with age and with the machine. The interval from the ventricular complex to the end of the T wave, when long, allows a second wave to arrive while the ventricles recover, and its limit depends on rate and sex, so confirm it locally.

The chambers are examined next, because a heart that has worked against a load for years leaves its mark. A thickened ventricle produces taller deflections on the side where it lies, telling the clinician that the heart has faced a resistance from high pressure, a narrowed valve, or lung disease that has raised right-sided pressure. An enlarged atrium produces a broader or taller P wave in the views that face it, a clue that the atrium has been stretched by a valve lesion or a long irregular rhythm. These signs do not diagnose the cause; they send the clinician to look for one. They are also easy to overread, since youth, thinness, and athletic training produce tall deflections in a healthy heart. A tracing suggesting a thickened ventricle in a breathless patient is a reason to examine again, not a diagnosis in itself.

The segments are the flat stretches between the waves, and they are where ischemia, injury, and inflammation are written. The segment joining the sharp ventricular complex to the T wave is studied first, because a sudden coronary blockage usually changes it before anything else. Elevation of that segment, especially when limited to the views facing one region and accompanied by the opposite change on the far side, says that a coronary artery is occluded now. Depression of the same segment, or an upside-down T wave, speaks of muscle starved of blood but not yet dying. The T wave also changes with salt disturbance, inflammation of the sac around the heart, stroke, and many innocent variations, so it must be read with the patient present. The dangerous error is to dismiss an elevation as a variant in a patient with chest pain who looks unwell, and the safe habit is to compare with any earlier tracing and repeat the recording while symptoms are present.

The last step is the comparison with a previous tracing, and it most often turns an uncertain reading into a clear one. A deflection that looks abnormal alone may have been there for years, and a genuinely new abnormality may be subtle without anything to compare it with. The clinician should ask for the old tracing before concluding anything and place the two side by side in the same light and at the same calibration. Has the axis changed, has a segment moved, has the complex become wider, has a new rhythm appeared? A small change is more important than a large fixed abnormality that the patient has carried harmlessly for a decade. Where no earlier tracing exists, that absence is a real limitation on the reading and should be recorded as one.

Before any of this, the tracing must be trusted, and the first questions concern the paper and the patient rather than the heart. The name and the time must be checked, because a tracing belonging to another patient is not a rare error. The calibration matters, since the height given to a known voltage and the width given to a known time determine how every measurement is read. In many services that means 10 millimeters for each millivolt and 25 millimeters per second, but these are conventions rather than laws, so confirm them against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the machine, the paper, and the edition of the manual differ between services. Electrode positions matter, because an electrode placed too high or too low produces a pattern that imitates disease and repeats the error on every later tracing. Movement, shivering, a loose electrode, and nearby electrical equipment produce wandering or jagged lines that hide real abnormality. A tracing that cannot be trusted should be repeated rather than interpreted.

Acute coronary occlusion deserves its own reading, because it most often changes what happens at once. The tracing shows elevation of the segment between the ventricular complex and the T wave in the views facing the blocked vessel, and often the opposite depression on the far side. It can be abnormal before the pain is severe and normal while the pain is severe, so neither symptom nor paper is sufficient alone. Inflammation of the sac around the heart most often imitates it, producing widespread rather than regional elevation, often with fever and a rub heard through the stethoscope. An old scar from a previous infarction can hold a segment up for years, which is why comparison matters so much. Where no earlier tracing exists, repeat the recording and look for movement over time. The decision is whether to restore blood flow urgently, and the finding that makes it right is a new regional pattern supported by the story and the examination; a convincing alternative explanation in a patient who looks well makes urgent treatment wrong.

A fast rhythm with wide ventricular complexes is the second emergency, and its reasoning rests on one principle. A wide complex means the wave is traveling slowly through the ventricles, and the most dangerous explanation is that the rhythm arises inside the ventricles, where it can degenerate into a rhythm that pumps no blood. It can also arise above the ventricles and travel down a damaged pathway, and the two may look identical on one sheet. A dissociation between atria and ventricles, with P waves at their own rate bearing no fixed relationship to the complexes, supports a ventricular origin, as does a fusion beat, though it may appear only briefly. Because the distinction can be impossible to make, the safe rule is to treat a wide complex tachycardia as ventricular until proved otherwise, and to treat the patient rather than the paper. The patient who is unconscious, whose pressure has fallen, or who has chest pain is treated at once, and the exact rhythm is named afterwards.

Complete heart block is the third pattern that must be recognized without delay, and it is found by looking at the relationship between atria and ventricles. The P waves continue at a steady rate of their own while the ventricular complexes continue at a much slower rate of their own, and the two never relate to each other. The patient may feel dizzy, may faint, or may have no symptoms, and the danger is that the slow rhythm can stop without warning. The cause may be age-related disease of the conduction tissue, a heart attack damaging the junction, infection, a medicine, or a salt disturbance, so the tracing opens questions rather than closing them. The clinician must decide about continuous monitoring and urgent help, and a slow rate with a faint, a falling pressure, or altered consciousness makes that decision right. A rhythm dropping every second or third beat behaves similarly, and where no monitoring exists the patient must be moved to where there is some, with the tracing traveling alongside.

A high level of potassium in the blood, called hyperkalemia, is the fourth emergency and the one most easily missed, because its first changes are subtle. The earliest finding is a tall, narrow, peaked T wave like a tent, appearing before the patient feels anything. As the level rises, the P wave shrinks and vanishes, the interval from the P wave to the ventricular complex lengthens, and the ventricular complex widens until it merges with the T wave. The rhythm can then slow, become chaotic, or stop, even in a patient who is talking and feels relatively well. Potassium governs how heart muscle returns to its resting state after each beat, and an excess delays that return until conduction fails. Those at risk include patients with failing kidneys, those taking medicines that raise potassium, those with diabetes, and those with severe tissue injury or infection, and the blood test reveals the cause. Where no test exists, a peaked T wave in a patient with a failing kidney or a long illness is an urgent warning. Whether to act on the tracing before the laboratory confirms it depends on how ill the patient is.

The pattern said to accompany a clot in the lungs, called pulmonary embolism, is the fifth emergency, and it is important to understand what it does and does not mean. The commonest finding is simply a fast sinus rhythm, which is not specific, and a normal tracing does not exclude a clot. In a minority, the right side of the heart shows sudden strain, with a tall P wave, axis turned right, and an upside-down T wave in the right-facing views. That classic pattern is rare, and a clinician who waits for it will miss the diagnosis in most patients. The reasoning therefore runs from the patient to the tracing, not the reverse: sudden breathlessness, a fast pulse, chest pain worse on breathing, and a tender or swollen calf raise the probability, and the tracing is used to look for support and alternatives. The finding that would reveal a large clot is sudden right-sided strain in a patient with none of the ordinary lung findings. Where imaging or a laboratory exists the decision is made with them, and where it does not, clinical probability carries the whole weight.

The sixth emergency is the abnormally long interval from the ventricular complex to the end of the T wave, dangerous because it creates the conditions for a chaotic rhythm that can end in death. When the ventricles take too long to recover, a second electrical wave can arrive while they are refractory in some places and ready in others, producing a twisting rhythm that pumps nothing useful. On the paper the interval is visibly stretched, and the T wave may be flat, notched, or followed by a small extra bump. Causes include low potassium, low calcium, low magnesium, certain heart medicines, some antibiotics, some medicines used for mental illness, vomiting and diarrhea, and starvation, and several may coexist. A blood test for the salts and a review of every medicine, including anything bought without a prescription, reveals the cause. Treatment means correcting the cause and withdrawing the offending medicine, and the finding that makes that right is a long interval together with fainting or a chaotic rhythm in the history.

Beyond the emergencies, the tracing answers ordinary questions and opens windows on other systems. Atrial fibrillation produces an irregularly irregular ventricular rate with no consistent P waves, and it matters for the clots it allows to form and for the strain on a heart that has lost atrial filling. A slow rhythm may come from a failing sinus node, a medicine, an underactive thyroid gland, or raised pressure inside the head, and each has a different answer. Low potassium produces a flat T wave with a small extra wave after it, while low calcium stretches the interval from the ventricular complex to the T wave without widening the complex. A medicine that slows conduction, taken in excess or with a failing kidney, produces a characteristic sagging of the segment between the complex and the T wave and a variety of slow rhythms. A large clot in the lungs, a tumor pressing on the heart, fluid around the heart, and a replaced or assisted heart each leave traces of their own. The tracing is therefore read with the medicine list, the salt results, and the story, never alone, because the ECG is a test and not a diagnosis.

In a patient with chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations, or collapse, the tracing answers a specific question rather than being admired. In chest pain the question is whether a coronary artery is occluded, so the tracing is taken early and repeated, especially during symptoms. In breathlessness the question is whether the strain is right-sided, supporting a clot in the lungs, or left-sided, supporting a failing heart. In palpitations or collapse the question is whether the rhythm is fast, slow, or irregular, and whether its complex width makes it dangerous. In an unconscious patient the tracing comes after the hands have begun cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, because a pulse check and compressions precede any electrode. The clinician who states the question before looking at the paper is far less likely to be captured by an incidental finding.

In a well-resourced hospital the reading is a shared act, and the conditions around it matter as much as the tracing. A previous tracing is found and placed beside the new one, a senior colleague looks at anything uncertain, and the patient is examined while the paper is studied. The machine is checked for calibration and electrode placement, and the recording is repeated while the symptom is present, since a single tracing is a snapshot of a moment already gone. The laboratory provides the salts, the substances released by damaged heart muscle, and the blood count, each read against the question that prompted it. Continuous monitoring is used when the rhythm is unstable, with alarm limits set by the team rather than left at the default. An ultrasound of the heart follows when the tracing raises a question about structure or function. If the patient is unstable, the team treats first and studies the paper afterwards.

The clinician alone with one tracing and no one to ask must reason differently, and the safe default is to treat the patient rather than the paper. Without an earlier tracing there is no way to tell whether a strange deflection is old or new, so the clinician leans on the story, the pulse, the pressure, the breathing, and the general appearance. The features readable by any careful clinician are the rate, the rhythm, the width of the ventricular complex, the presence or absence of P waves, and a clear elevation of the segment between the complex and the T wave. Those five answer most urgent questions without a specialist. The difficult features are subtle T wave changes, the axis, and the distinction between a dangerous pattern and an innocent variant, and these should be described honestly as uncertain. A normal tracing in a patient who looks unwell proves nothing, and sending that patient home on the strength of the paper lets the tracing make the decision. The decision is usually a plan rather than a diagnosis: watch and repeat, treat on the clinical picture, or send the patient onward now.

The clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer but no ECG still has the reasoning that the tracing supports. The pulse is felt for rate, rhythm, and volume, and the hand can detect an irregularity that the paper would confirm. The pulse at the wrist and the beat heard at the heart are counted together, and a difference suggests that some beats are too weak to reach the wrist, which is common in irregular rhythms. The rate is counted at rest and written down with the time, because the trend over visits is worth more than any single figure. The stethoscope gives the heart sounds, a murmur, a rub, and the added sounds of a failing heart, and the lungs are listened to for crackles that would explain the breathlessness. The torch makes the vessels at the back of the eye and the color of the skin visible, and the thermometer turns an impression into something measurable. The decision that follows is whether the patient can be watched, whether to treat on the clinical picture, and whether the journey to a place with a tracing must start now.

The reading of tracings has its own characteristic errors, and what is written down matters as much as the reading. The commonest error is to stop at the first abnormal finding and build a story around it, so that a second and more important abnormality is never seen. Another is to accept a suggestive pattern as diagnostic, which happens most with the strain pattern said to accompany a clot in the lungs and with elevation that mimics an infarction. A third is to read the paper without the patient, so that a fast rate is treated as disease when it is a response to pain, and a slow rate is dismissed when it causes a faint. The record should carry the time, whether the patient had symptoms then, the rate, the rhythm, the width of the complex, and any abnormal interval, together with whether an earlier tracing was available and what changed. A tracing called normal in a patient who is clearly unwell should be accompanied by the observation that the test does not exclude the illness.

A constructed illustration may make the difference between the two settings concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than a portrait of any real person. Imagine a patient brought to a hospital with chest pain, where the tracing is taken within minutes and compared with one from a previous admission; the segment that had been flat for years has now risen in the views facing one region of the heart, and the team moves at once to restore blood flow. Now imagine a patient in a small clinic with a racing heart, where a single tracing shows wide complexes and no clear P waves and the nearest help is hours away; the clinician there does not name the rhythm but treats the patient as unstable and arranges immediate transfer, because the width of the complex is enough to know that the rhythm may be dangerous. Both are good uses of the same test, one changing the diagnosis and the other changing the journey. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment. What they share is that the reader asked a question before looking, trusted the findings that could be trusted, and did not wait for certainty before acting. The reasoning is the same; the resources are not.

A clinician who reads a tracing and sends a patient home must say clearly what should bring the patient back. The patient should be told which symptoms matter: chest pain that is new or changing, breathlessness, a fainting, a racing or very slow heartbeat, and a weakness or faintness that was not there before. A follow-up tracing arranged in advance, particularly for an irregular rhythm or a long interval, is worth more than a promise to return if things worsen. The patient should also be told to report every medicine, including anything bought without a prescription and any herbal remedy, because many change the tracing. Where the reading was uncertain, that uncertainty should be shared in plain words rather than hidden.

To summarize, the ECG is read by a fixed sequence of rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, the chambers, the segments, and the comparison with any previous tracing, and the sequence exists so that the second abnormality is not lost behind the first. The six patterns demanding immediate recognition are acute coronary occlusion, the wide complex tachycardia, complete heart block, a high level of potassium, the strain pattern of a clot in the lungs, and the abnormally long interval from the ventricular complex to the end of the T wave, each named with the finding that reveals it. The tracing is one instrument among several and never replaces the history, the examination, or the judgment made at the bedside. Every figure in this chapter, whether a rate, an interval, a calibration, or a reference range, is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. In a well-resourced hospital the reading is shared and the recording repeated while symptoms persist, while the clinician alone with one tracing and no one to ask treats the patient rather than the paper. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or your own service protocol. A patient who looks unwell is helped first, and the tracing is read again afterwards.

# Chapter 66 — Chest and Abdominal X-Ray

A radiograph is a shadow, and the whole skill of reading one follows from that single fact. The beam passes through the patient, and the structures in its path absorb it in proportion to their density, so what reaches the film is not a picture of the body but a record of how much of the beam was taken away, and every black area and every white area is a statement about what lay in the way. This chapter gives a sequence for the chest radiograph and a sequence for the film of the abdomen, chosen so that the reading does not depend on the finding being obvious, because the finding that kills is often the one nobody expected to see. The material is educational and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Four findings deserve to be named before the sequence begins, because each changes what is done within minutes and each is easily missed by an eye looking for something else. Free air under the diaphragm means that a hollow organ has perforated, and it appears as a crescent of gas between the liver and the right dome that has no business being there. A pneumothorax appears as a lung edge with no vessels beyond it, and it becomes a tension when the mediastinum shifts and the patient can no longer breathe. A widened mediastinum after a fall or with tearing chest pain may mean an injury to the aorta, revealed by a silhouette broader than the patient should have, an abnormal contour, a trachea that has moved, or a cap of density at the apex of the lung. A bowel obstruction shows loops that are distended on one side of a blockage and empty on the other, and its danger is not the blockage itself but the loss of blood supply that may follow. Naming them at the start keeps the eye from settling on the first abnormality it finds.

To predict what a disease will look like, the listener has to hold in mind the four densities that a radiograph can tell apart. Air absorbs almost none of the beam and appears black, fat absorbs a little, soft tissue and water absorb more and appear as shades of gray, and bone or metal absorb most and appear white, so a lung that has filled with pus, blood, or water turns from black toward white where the filling has occurred. The same logic explains why a structure hidden behind the heart cannot be seen, because the beam was already weakened by everything it passed through, and all of those structures are added together on one flat image. A clinician who reasons in densities rather than in named diseases can look at an unfamiliar film and say what must be happening inside the chest.

The film is an object before it is an image, and the first step of the sequence has nothing to do with medicine. The name on the film must be checked against the patient in front of the clinician, the date and the time must be read, and the side marker must be confirmed, because a film of the wrong patient or the wrong side has caused more harm than any subtle sign. The clinician also looks for an earlier film of the same patient, since a comparison with a previous study is often worth more than any single observation on the current one. In a hospital the images are stored and can be brought up beside the new one, while in a clinic the earlier film may be a single sheet in a folder that the patient carries, and it should be asked for every time.

The projection is the next question, because the same chest looks different in each of the standard positions. The film taken with the patient standing and the beam passing from back to front is the most faithful, since the heart lies close to the film and is not magnified, and the shoulder blades are rotated clear of the lungs. The film taken at the bedside with a portable machine passes from front to back, the heart appears larger, and the shoulder blades fall across the upper zones, so a heart that looks enlarged on such a film may be entirely normal. Position matters as much as direction, because a patient who is lying flat cannot show free air under the diaphragm, and fluid around the lung spreads out in a layer rather than collecting at the base. Three technical qualities then decide whether the film can be trusted at all: rotation, judged by the position of the two clavicles relative to the spine, penetration, judged by whether the vertebral bodies can be seen faintly behind the heart, and inspiration, judged by the level of the diaphragm and the number of ribs above it. A film that fails these checks is not a film to be read but a film to be repeated.

The lateral film is the companion of the frontal one, and it answers questions that the frontal view cannot. It shows the space behind the breastbone and the space behind the heart, both of which are hidden from the front, and it displays the posterior angle between the diaphragm and the chest wall, where a small collection of fluid may gather before it is visible from the front. The lateral view also shows the spine through the clear lung, and a spine that becomes whiter as it descends is a sign that something behind it has increased in density. Because the two views are taken at right angles, a finding that appears on both can be placed in three dimensions, while a finding on only one should be treated with suspicion until it is confirmed. A clinician who reads only the frontal film is reading one half of the available evidence.

The chest sequence begins with the airway, which is the easiest structure to see and the easiest to forget. The windpipe should run down the midline and divide into the two main bronchi, and a windpipe that is pushed to one side tells the clinician that something on that side is pushing, while a windpipe pulled to one side tells of something that has collapsed and is pulling. The difference is not academic, because a large collection of air or fluid pushes the airway away and demands immediate attention, while collapse of a whole lung pulls it toward the side of the collapse and follows a different path. The clinician also looks at the caliber of the windpipe and the bronchi, since a narrowing near the great vessels or a mass that has grown into the airway may be the reason for a breathlessness that no other sign explains. Following the airway first means that a shift, which is the loudest finding on many chest films, is never missed.

Breathing comes second, and it means the lungs and the covering around them. The two sides are compared for their overall blackness, and any region that is whiter than the same region on the other side must be explained. A patch of lung that has filled with pus produces a consolidation, and the finding that confirms it is the air bronchogram, which is the outline of an air-filled airway running through the white area because the surrounding air sacs have filled while the airway has stayed open. A nodule or a mass is a rounded opacity, and a cavity is a rounded opacity with a darker center, which tells the clinician that tissue inside has died or that a hole has formed. A diffuse increase in the markings of the lung, with lines and small dots rather than one patch, points to disease of the supporting tissue between the air sacs rather than of the air sacs themselves, and that distinction changes the list of causes entirely.

The silhouette sign is the most useful single idea in the reading of a chest film, and it follows directly from the addition of shadows. When two structures of the same density lie against each other, the border between them disappears, so the loss of a border tells the clinician which structure the disease is touching. A whiteness that has erased the right heart border lies in the middle lobe or the inner part of the right lung, one that has erased the left heart border lies in the lingula, and one that has erased a hemidiaphragm lies at the base. Fluid around the lung behaves differently again, because it settles and forms a curved upper edge at the side of the chest, and a large collection pushes the mediastinum away while a collapsed lung pulls it toward the same side.

Circulation is the next step, and it begins with the heart and the central column of the chest. The heart shadow is judged for its size, its shape, and its position, and a heart wider than one half of the width of the chest is the traditional description of enlargement, offered here as an illustration of the reasoning, so confirm the proportion against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the projection and the phase of breathing both change it. A bulge in the contour points to the chamber beneath it, and a double contour on the right may be the first clue to disease in a valve. The mediastinum is where a widened silhouette becomes an emergency, because it may be an acute problem of the aorta in a patient with tearing pain or after a fall, revealed by the widening itself with an abnormal contour or a cap of density at the apex of the lung. A width of 8 centimeters at the level of the aortic arch is a figure often quoted in teaching, offered here only as a teaching figure, so the measurement that should prompt action must be checked against the guideline in force where you work, since it depends on the projection and on how the film was framed. The pulmonary vessels are followed from the center toward the edge, because their pattern tells the clinician whether the pressure behind them has risen.

The picture of a heart that is failing is a picture of pressure that has moved backward, and the radiograph shows it in the order the pressure travels. The heart may be enlarged, the upper lobe vessels may become more prominent than the lower ones because the blood is being sent upward, and the hila may look congested and indistinct. Fluid may collect around both lungs, more often on the right, and it may hide in the fissures between the lobes as a line or a thickening that is easy to overlook. When the fluid enters the air sacs themselves, the whiteness surrounds the hila in a pattern that fades toward the edge of the lung, and a clinician who has seen the same patient earlier will recognize the change faster than any report.

The diaphragm is the fourth step, and it is where two of the dangerous findings live. The domes should be smooth and curved and the angles between the diaphragm and the chest wall should be sharp, because a small collection of fluid may blunt an angle before it is visible anywhere else. Free air under the diaphragm is the finding that means a perforated hollow organ, and it appears as a crescent of gas between the liver and the right dome that does not belong to the stomach or the bowel. The film must be taken with the patient sitting or standing and must include both domes, because a patient lying flat spreads the gas along the front of the abdomen where a chest film cannot see it. On the left side the stomach bubble is normal, so the clinician must judge whether the gas under the left dome has the shape of a stomach or the shape of a free collection, and a sliver of gas that follows the curve of the dome and crosses the midline belongs to a surgical emergency rather than to a clinic visit.

A pneumothorax is the other dangerous finding at this step, and it is recognized by the absence of something rather than by its presence. The lung edge appears as a thin white line, and beyond that line there are no vessels at all, which tells the clinician that the black space is air outside the lung rather than lung that is simply overinflated. When the pressure in that space rises, the mediastinum is pushed to the opposite side, the diaphragm on that side is flattened, and the patient becomes short of breath and unstable; this is the tension pneumothorax, which is treated on the clinical picture before any film is seen. On a film taken with the patient lying flat, the air rises to the front of the chest and may show only as an unusually clear upper zone or a deep groove at the angle, so a film that looks almost normal does not exclude the diagnosis. In a clinic without a radiograph, the same reasoning is carried by the hands and the ears, since breath sounds reduced on one side and a note like a drum when the chest is tapped are the radiographic signs made audible.

Certain places on a chest film are known to hide findings, and the sequence should pause at each of them. The apices come first, because a small pneumothorax or an early scar may sit above the clavicle shadow and be read as nothing. The area behind the heart is next, because a lesion there is invisible from the front unless the clinician looks at the lateral view or notices that the border has changed. The angles below the lungs are the third, because a small effusion blunts an angle before it produces any other sign. The bones are the fourth hiding place, since a rib fracture or a deposit in the spine is easy to pass over while the eye is occupied with the lungs, and the soft tissues of the neck and the chest wall are read in the same sweep. A clinician who visits each of these areas in turn, every time, will find the finding that a quick glance would have missed.

The abdominal film asks a different set of questions, and its value depends entirely on whether the clinician has a question for it. A plain film of the abdomen is a poor tool for the patient with undifferentiated abdominal pain, because most of the causes produce no finding on it, and a normal film is therefore a false comfort. Its real strength lies in four specific questions, which are the pattern of the gas, the outlines of the organs, the presence of free air, and the presence of calcification. The stomach holds a bubble of air, the colon holds gas divided into segments by the folds of its wall, and the small bowel holds very little gas in a healthy person, so gas that is visible in the small bowel in quantity is itself a finding. The small bowel tends to lie centrally and to show fine lines across its whole width, while the colon runs around the edge and shows thicker, incomplete folds of its own, and a difference between two segments of the same bowel is more informative than the absolute size of either.

A bowel obstruction is the dangerous pattern in the abdomen, and it is produced by a simple mechanism. When the bowel is blocked, the segment above the block fills with swallowed air and with the fluid the bowel itself secretes, and it distends against the blockage while the bowel below it empties. The film therefore shows loops that are wider above the block, less gas below it, and, on a film taken with the patient upright, the horizontal line of an air-fluid level in each loop that holds both gas and liquid. A volvulus is a twist, and it produces a single, enormous, gas-filled loop that has lost its normal shape and looks like a bent inner tube or a coffee bean, a surgical emergency rather than a medical one. A bowel that has stopped moving produces distension of both the small and the large bowel without a point of transition, because the bowel has become quiet rather than blocked, and that distinction is an important judgment the film can support. Small bowel loops beyond 3 centimeters across are commonly called dilated, and that figure is offered as a teaching illustration, so confirm the value against the current guideline and the protocol where you work, because it shifts with the part of the bowel and with the magnification of the film.

One film often cannot settle the question, and the change between two films usually can. A repeat film after an interval of 6 hours is often described in teaching as a way to show a pattern that a single film could not, and both the interval and the reasoning behind it belong to local practice, so verify them against the guideline that governs your service, because the useful timing depends on the patient and on the question being asked. What the clinician looks for across the two films is not a different disease but a direction, since loops that have widened further and fluid that has appeared where there was none are statements about movement. Free air in the abdomen is the same danger as free air under the diaphragm, and the gas rises, so an upright chest film is more sensitive for it than a film taken with the patient lying down, while a film taken with the patient lying on the left side lets the gas collect along the wall of the abdomen. A normal film does not exclude a perforation, and a clinician who relies on the film alone may send home a patient who needed an operation.

The outlines of the organs are the next question, and they are read by looking for the shapes that should be there. The liver fills the right upper abdomen, the spleen sits behind the stomach on the left and is usually not visible unless it has enlarged, and the two kidneys lie beside the spine with their long axes tilted toward each other. The muscles beside the spine make a shadow on each side, and the loss of one of those shadows suggests that something is happening in the space behind the abdomen. Calcification is the fourth question, and it most often rewards a careful eye, because calcium absorbs the beam strongly and appears as a white density against the softer gray of the tissue around it. Stones in the kidney and the urinary tract are often seen, and their position along the tube from the kidney to the bladder helps to identify them, while stones in the gallbladder are usually not visible because most contain too little calcium. Calcification in the pancreas appears as scattered white specks across the upper abdomen, and an old infection can leave calcified lymph nodes, but a calcification is never the whole diagnosis.

A constructed illustration may make the sequence concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a young man brought to a hospital after a fall, who is short of breath and whose chest film is taken lying down at the bedside, and in whom the film is rotated, the heart looks large, and the left lung looks darker than the right. The clinician who checks the projection first knows that the heart is magnified by the position, and the clinician who then compares the two sides for vessels rather than for whiteness finds that the left side has no vessels at its edge, which is the pneumothorax that the rotation almost concealed. Imagine instead an older patient with a swollen abdomen and vomiting, whose film shows loops that are wider in one region than another, with air-fluid levels on the upright film and no gas in the lower bowel. The two films look similar to an untrained eye and speak different sentences to a trained one, and neither patient is real, so neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment.

The radiographic finding is what turns a suspicion into a decision. Free air under the diaphragm, or gas in a place where gas cannot normally be, makes the decision to operate the right one, and it makes it urgent, while the finding that would make that decision wrong is gas explained by a recent operation, a tube, or a normal stomach. A pneumothorax with a shifted mediastinum and a struggling patient makes the decision to relieve the pressure before any further image is taken, and a clinician who waits for a second film has misunderstood the priority. A patch of consolidation in a febrile, breathless patient makes treatment of an infection the right answer when the picture fits, and the same patch in a patient who is not infected makes that answer wrong, which is why the film is read beside the patient rather than at a distance. A widened mediastinum in a patient with sudden severe pain makes the decision to seek immediate surgical help the right one, and a normal film in that same patient does not make it wrong.

In a hospital the film is usually read twice, once by the clinician who ordered it and once by the radiologist, and the two readings serve different purposes. The clinician reads with a question in mind, while the radiologist reads with a fixed sequence and a habit of noticing the incidental finding, and neither reading replaces the other. The report should be read as an answer to a question rather than as a diagnosis, and a report that does not address the question asked should be taken back to the radiologist rather than filed and forgotten. When the report and the clinician disagree, the useful move is to look at the film again with the report in hand and the patient in mind, because each of them holds information the other lacks. In a clinic with a light box and no radiologist, the discipline of the sequence matters more rather than less, because there may be a single film, taken at an earlier visit, and nobody to ask. The reading is done on a proper light source in a darkened room with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer close at hand, and what was seen is written down in the order it was sought.

Several habits spoil the reading of a radiograph, and each of them is easy to fall into. Reading the film before seeing the patient is the first, because a film read without a history becomes a hunt for something, anything, and the eye will find it. Treating the film as the diagnosis rather than as a question is the second, because a normal film in a patient with a convincing story is a reason to look further rather than a reason to stop. Accepting a report as the end of the reasoning is the third, and the failure to compare with what came before is the fourth. Every radiograph also has limits that the clinician should be able to state out loud, because a flat addition of a curved body hides what lies behind the heart, and an abdominal film is even less forgiving, since the bowel overlaps itself and the organs lie in front of and behind one another. A clinician who reads in a fixed order, who writes the findings down, and who can say what a film cannot show will avoid all of these traps.

The decision to order a film is part of the reasoning and not a reflex. A chest film is the right answer when the question is whether there is consolidation, fluid around the lung, a pneumothorax, a widened mediastinum, or the pattern of a failing heart, and when the answer will change what is done. It is the wrong answer when the examination has already answered the question, when the patient is too unstable to leave the bedside for anything except a portable film, and when no result could change the plan. In a program that screens for tuberculosis, the chest radiograph has a defined role, and that role is set by the World Health Organization and by the national program rather than by the individual clinician, so it should be checked there. A film that has been read and acted upon still leaves a patient who must be followed, and the signs that should bring that patient back are the same signs that made the film necessary, which are a worsening breathlessness, a new pain, a fever that will not settle, a failure to improve, or a new weakness.

To summarize, the radiograph is a shadow read by a sequence that does not depend on the finding being obvious, and the sequence is what protects the patient from the eye that settles too early. The film is first checked for its patient, its date, its side, its projection, and its technical quality, then the chest is read through the airway, the breathing, the circulation, the diaphragm, the edges, and the bones, and the abdomen through the gas pattern, the organ outlines, the free air, and the calcifications. The dangerous findings are named as the sequence meets them, which are free air under the diaphragm, a pneumothorax, a widened mediastinum, and a bowel obstruction, each with the finding that reveals it. Every figure in this chapter, whether a width, a proportion, a caliber, or an interval, is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and the way each film is taken. The reasoning is the same with a radiologist beside the clinician and with a single film on a light box in a clinic, and this is educational material that does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

# Chapter 67 — Ultrasound at the Bedside

Ultrasound at the bedside is not a small version of the radiology department, and the clinician who treats it that way will use it badly. It is better understood as a physical sign, an extension of the hand that can be laid against the body and made to report whether a space contains fluid or tissue, whether a structure moves, and whether a chamber empties. The reasoning that organizes it is therefore the reasoning of the examination rather than the reasoning of imaging: the clinician decides on one question that matters for the next decision, chooses the view that answers it, and repeats the view when the patient changes. The whole examination may last only a minute or two, and its value lies in that narrowness rather than in completeness. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

To use the probe well, the clinician has to picture what it produces. The machine sends a pulse of sound into the body and listens for what returns, and it draws a picture from the strength and the delay of those returning echoes. Fluid returns very little and appears dark, while the walls of organs, the fibrous sheets that separate tissues, and bone return a great deal and appear bright, and it is the contrast between the two that carries the information. A dark collection in a place where there should be no collection is the finding that usually changes a decision, and a bright line that should move when it is watched is the finding that usually reassures. Because the picture is built from a narrow slice of the body, the clinician must move the probe to build a mental map of the space rather than trusting a single still frame. Nothing in this chapter should be memorized as a set of measurements, because the machine, the probe, the settings, and the patient all change what is displayed.

Several lethal possibilities have a bedside view that reveals them, and naming them before the ordinary reasoning begins keeps attention where it belongs. The patient whose heart is compressed by fluid in the sac around it may be in cardiac tamponade, and the finding that reveals it is a dark rim of fluid together with a chamber that collapses as it fills, often with a large vein in the abdomen that does not change with breathing. The patient with abdominal pain and a missed period may have a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, and the finding that reveals it is dark fluid in the abdomen together with an empty uterus. The older patient with back pain, a pulsating abdominal mass, or a sudden collapse may have a leaking aneurysm of the aorta, and the finding that reveals it is a dilated aorta with dark fluid collecting around it. The patient who has suffered an injury and whose pressure is falling may be bleeding into the abdomen, the chest, or around the heart, and each of those spaces has a view that can be obtained in the resuscitation room.

The probe does not replace the history, the hands, or the stethoscope, and the clinician who reaches for it first usually asks the wrong question. The ordinary examination tells the clinician where to look: a quiet chest on one side suggests fluid or air in that space, a tender right upper abdomen suggests the gallbladder, a pulsating mass suggests the aorta, and a missed period with pain suggests the pelvis. The probe is then used to test that suspicion rather than to survey the body, and a negative view is interpreted in the light of the suspicion that prompted it. This is why a clinician who is unsure what question to ask should not perform the examination at all, because an image made without a question produces an answer that cannot be used. The skill that has to be learned first is not the handling of the probe but the habit of deciding, before the probe is placed, what finding would change the plan.

Competence with the probe is a specific skill, and it is not conferred by owning the machine. A clinician who performs these examinations should have been taught the standard views, should have practiced them under supervision, and should know the limits of what each view can show. Where a service uses bedside ultrasound, it usually keeps a record of who is credentialed for which examination, and the clinician who works outside that record is practicing beyond what can be defended. The learner should keep a log of examinations and compare the interpretation with a formal study when one is available, because that comparison is what corrects a private vocabulary of images. None of this is a reason to withhold the probe in an emergency; it is a reason to use it deliberately and to state honestly what the clinician could and could not see.

The heart is examined at the bedside through windows that avoid the ribs and the lungs, most often below the breastbone and beside it in the third or fourth space on the left. The clinician looks first at the sac around the heart, then at the size of the chambers, then at how well the walls move, and finally at how much blood leaves with each beat. Fluid in the sac appears as a dark band between the heart and the bright line of the pericardium, and its depth and its distribution matter more than its mere presence, because a small collection that has accumulated quickly can compress the heart while a larger one that has accumulated slowly may not. The view of how the heart empties is judged by watching the walls come together, and a heart whose walls barely move is failing, while a heart whose walls move vigorously may be underfilled or may be obstructed. This is a visual judgment that improves with repetition, and it should be described in words that a colleague can follow rather than in a figure that the clinician cannot justify.

The reasoning about tamponade is worth following step by step, because it is the clearest example of a bedside view changing an immediate decision. Fluid collects in the sac until the pressure inside it equals the pressure that fills the heart, and at that point the chambers can no longer expand, so less blood enters and less blood leaves. The patient may be breathless, may have a rapid pulse, may have a falling pressure, and may have distended neck veins, but each of those signs can have another cause. The findings that make the picture convincing are a dark rim of fluid, a chamber that collapses when it should be filling, and a large vein in the abdomen that stays distended instead of narrowing with the breath. When those appear in a patient whose pressure is falling, the decision to remove the fluid belongs to the clinician who can do it safely, and the probe has done its work by moving that decision earlier. The finding that would make the diagnosis less likely is a heart that fills normally with no collapse and no distended vein, and even then the patient must be watched.

A view of the heart that shows weak contraction tells the clinician that the pump is failing, and a view that shows a normal-sized chamber with vigorous contraction makes failure of the pump less likely, but neither view excludes the other causes of the same symptoms.
