A clot in the lung, a loss of blood, an infection, and a leaky valve can all produce breathlessness with a heart that looks busy on the screen. The view cannot measure the pressure inside the chambers, cannot show the coronary arteries, and cannot reliably show a clot inside the heart. The clinician who uses it must therefore say what was seen and what remains possible, and should not allow a reassuring image to close a question that the history has opened. Where a fuller study is available, the bedside view is a bridge to it rather than a replacement for it.

The chest is examined for fluid around the lung, which appears as a dark region above the bright line of the diaphragm, and for air outside the lung, which changes the way the two layers of the pleura move against each other. A normal examination shows the lung sliding against the chest wall with each breath, a shimmering movement that is easier to recognize than to describe. When air lies between the layers, that movement disappears, and the point at which the sliding reappears marks the edge of the air. The clinician who watches for that movement must be sure the probe is in the right place and the patient is breathing before concluding that it is absent, because a still image from a poor window can mimic the finding. A small collection of fluid or a small rim of air may be invisible at the bedside, so a normal view is not the same as a normal chest. The chest radiograph and the computed tomography, or CT, remain the studies that answer the question fully where they are available.

The patient who becomes suddenly breathless after an injury, a procedure, or a line placed in the chest is the patient in whom the view of the pleura is most valuable, because the decision it informs is immediate. If the sliding is absent on one side and the patient is unstable, the clinician treats for air in the chest before any image confirms it, and the probe has supported a decision that could not wait. The view is less useful in the patient who is stable and whose breathlessness has many possible causes, because it cannot distinguish a small collection of air from a large one by itself. A layer of air may also be missed in the patient who has been ventilated, whose lungs may not move as they should. The clinician should therefore treat a negative view as one piece of information and not as a verdict, and should keep the clinical picture in charge.

The abdomen is examined for free fluid, which collects in the dependent parts and appears as dark streaks between the bright loops of bowel. In the injured patient, the presence of fluid in more than one place changes the decision about surgery, and its absence in a single view does not exclude bleeding, because blood may lie where the probe is not. In the patient with abdominal pain, a small amount of free fluid may accompany inflammation, and a large amount with a tender abdomen is a reason to think of a perforated organ or a collection of pus. The clinician looks for fluid beside the liver, around the spleen, in the flanks, and deep in the pelvis, and repeats the examination if the first view is not conclusive. What the view cannot do is tell the clinician what the fluid contains, because blood, pus, urine, and the fluid of ascites all appear dark. That limit is why the view is always read together with the history, the examination, and, where it exists, the laboratory.

The aorta is examined along its course in the abdomen, and the clinician measures its width at the point where it is widest, looking at it in more than one direction so that an oblique view does not exaggerate the size. An aneurysm is a segment that has stretched, and a leaking aneurysm is one that has begun to release blood into the tissues around it. A width of 3 centimeters is often quoted as the point above which an abdominal aorta is called dilated, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line varies with age, sex, and body size. The finding that matters most is not the figure itself but a dilated segment together with dark fluid in the space around it, which suggests that blood has escaped and makes the patient a surgical emergency. The view also shows the aorta in only part of its length, so a normal appearance in the abdomen says nothing about the portion in the chest.

The gallbladder is examined for stones, for thickening of its wall, and for fluid around it, and the finding that supports inflammation of the gallbladder is a tender organ with a thickened wall and a collection of fluid beside it. Stones appear as bright shapes that cast a dark shadow behind them, and their mere presence is common in people who have no symptoms at all, so a stone alone is not the diagnosis. The view is most useful when the history and the examination already point to the right upper abdomen, and it is easily made difficult by gas in the bowel, by a patient who cannot lie still, or by a gallbladder that is hidden behind the ribs. It cannot show the ducts clearly, and it cannot tell the clinician whether a stone is blocking the flow of bile, which is a question for a formal study or for the laboratory. The clinician should describe what was seen and what could not be seen, and should not let a normal-looking gallbladder overrule a story of recurring pain after fatty meals.

The kidneys are examined for dark fluid in the collecting system, which appears as branching spaces inside the bright tissue of the kidney, and that finding suggests that urine is not draining. Obstruction is the usual cause, and it may come from a stone, a tumor, a clot, an enlarged prostate, or pressure from outside. The view can show that the system is dilated, but it cannot tell whether the obstruction is recent or has been present for years, and it cannot always separate obstruction from a normal variant or from the dilation of pregnancy. A patient with a single working kidney, or with obstruction on both sides, may have little time before the chemistry of the blood becomes dangerous, so the finding of dilation in that patient deserves an urgent conversation. The clinician should also remember that a kidney can be obstructed without dilation early in the process, and that a normal view does not exclude a stone that is causing severe pain.

The pregnant uterus is examined for the position of the pregnancy, the amount of fluid, the presence of a heartbeat, and the movement of the fetus, and each of these answers a different question. The danger that this view is used to address is the ectopic pregnancy, in which the pregnancy lies outside the uterus and may rupture, and the finding that reveals it is an empty uterus together with free fluid in the abdomen in a patient who has a positive pregnancy test and pain. An empty uterus on its own does not prove an ectopic pregnancy, because the pregnancy may simply be earlier than the view can show, and the clinician must combine the view with the result of the pregnancy test, the history, and the trend of the hormone level if it can be measured. The view cannot exclude an ectopic pregnancy with certainty, and a patient with pain and a positive test who has no intrauterine pregnancy must be managed as a possible ectopic until someone with the right skills has settled the question. In a clinic where the probe is the only imaging, this view is often the one that decides whether the patient can be watched or must travel at once.

In the injured patient the bedside examination is performed as a rapid sequence, and the reasoning is that the patient may be bleeding where no external wound can show it. The clinician looks for fluid around the heart, fluid in the chest, fluid in the abdomen, and air outside the lung, and returns to the same views after any change in the patient's condition. The sequence is repeated because a patient who was bleeding slowly at the first look may have a large collection a short time later, and because the decision to operate is often made on a repeated finding rather than a single one. A normal first sequence is reassuring only for the moment in which it was performed, and it never replaces the observation of the patient, the pressure, the pulse, and the urine. Where the patient is stable and the injury is complex, the full study by CT gives more complete information, and the bedside view has served its purpose by identifying who cannot wait for it.

The patient who arrives breathless and undifferentiated is a good example of how views are combined into one question. The clinician examines the heart for fluid and for weak contraction, the chest for fluid and for air, the large vein in the abdomen for its size and its change with breathing, and the legs for a clot in the deep veins. Each view narrows the field, and together they may separate a failing heart, an infection of the lungs, a clot in the lung, and a collection of fluid or air around the lung, which are the causes that most often look alike. The views must be performed in an order that follows the danger, so that the immediately treatable cause is sought first and the patient is not left waiting while a complete survey is assembled. Where the probe cannot answer the question, the clinician says so and arranges the study that can, and a normal set of views in a patient who is working hard to breathe is a reason to keep looking rather than a reason to relax.

A swollen leg is another problem in which the bedside view can change a decision within minutes. The clinician presses the probe along the deep veins of the thigh and the calf and watches whether the walls of the vein come together, because a vein that stays open and does not compress may contain a clot. The finding of a vein that will not compress supports the diagnosis, and its absence in a single view does not exclude it, because a clot may lie below the knee, in the pelvis, or in a segment that the probe did not reach. The view is also used to distinguish swelling caused by fluid in the tissues from swelling caused by a collection of blood or pus, which are managed differently. Where the probability of a clot is low and a reliable blood test is available, that test may settle the question, and where it is high the clinician treats while arranging the confirmatory study. The clinician who records which deep veins were seen and compressed, and which segments were not, has written a note that a colleague can trust.

In a clinic without a laboratory, a patient with abdominal pain can be examined with the same probe, and the questions are chosen from the story rather than from a list. A young patient with a missed period is examined for a pregnancy in the uterus and for fluid in the abdomen, because a ruptured ectopic pregnancy is the danger that must be set aside first. An older patient with back pain and a pulsating sensation is examined for the aorta, because a leaking aneurysm is the danger in that story. A patient with pain after fatty food is examined for the gallbladder, and a patient with pain in the flank and a change in the urine is examined for the kidneys. Each view is followed by the question of what its result would mean, and the answer decides whether the patient is observed at the clinic, treated on the clinical findings, or sent onward now. A probe that cannot answer the question has still been useful, because it tells the clinician that the decision must be made on other grounds.

In a well-resourced hospital the bedside examination sits inside a larger system, and its role is to answer the question that cannot wait for the formal study. It identifies the patient with fluid around the heart, the patient bleeding into the abdomen, and the patient with air outside the lung, and it sends each of them to the right next step without delay. The formal ultrasound performed by a trained sonographer or a radiologist remains the study that measures, characterizes, and documents, and the bedside view is not a substitute for it. Computed tomography, or CT, and magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answer questions that the probe cannot reach, including the detail of the organs, the vessels in the chest, and the brain. The clinician who uses the probe in the hospital must therefore know which questions belong to it and which belong to the department, and must not let the convenience of the bedside view delay a definitive test. Used in that way, the probe shortens the time to the right decision rather than replacing the decision itself.

In a clinic where the probe is the only imaging, the same reasoning is stretched to cover more ground, and the clinician must be honest about how far it can go. Electricity, a charged battery, a supply of gel, and a probe that is kept clean are the practical requirements, and a service that cannot maintain them cannot rely on the examination. The views that repay the effort most are the heart for fluid, the abdomen for free fluid and for the aorta, the kidneys for obstruction, the gallbladder for inflammation, and the uterus in a patient who may be pregnant. The clinician who finds a dangerous picture in such a clinic has gained the most valuable thing available, which is time, because the decision to travel can be made before the patient collapses. The clinician who finds nothing must still decide what the absence means, and in most cases it means that the question remains open and the patient must be watched or referred.

The limits of the bedside examination deserve a paragraph of their own, because most harm comes from what it cannot do. It cannot see through bone or through gas, so the ribs, the bowel, and the lungs hide much of what lies behind them. It cannot show a structure that the operator does not know how to find, and it cannot show what the operator does not think to look for. It rewards confidence, which is a dangerous quality in an operator whose skill is small, and it can produce a normal-looking image that closes a question which should have stayed open. The clinician should therefore treat every view as a question that was asked of one small window, and should say plainly what the window did not include, because a fuller study, a second opinion, or simply more time with the patient may answer what the probe could not.

A constructed illustration may show how the reasoning works, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a young patient who arrives with lower abdominal pain and a missed period, whose pregnancy test is positive, and in whom the probe shows an empty uterus and dark fluid in the abdomen; the clinician recognizes the pattern of a possible ruptured ectopic pregnancy and arranges urgent surgical care while keeping the patient still. Now imagine an older patient in a clinic with sudden back pain and a pulsating feeling in the abdomen, in whom the probe shows a dilated aorta with dark fluid around it; the clinician stops examining, calls for help, and arranges transfer for the leaking aneurysm that the picture suggests. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment.

A clinician who sends a patient home after a bedside examination should say what should bring the patient back. The patient or the family should be told which signs matter, among them a worsening pain, a fever, a faint, a change in consciousness, a failure to pass urine, bleeding, and a breathlessness that grows. A follow-up visit arranged in advance is worth more than a promise to return if things worsen, because many patients cannot judge when their illness has changed. Where the probe was used to set aside a dangerous cause, the clinician should say what would have to happen for that conclusion to be reconsidered. The habit of stating the uncertainty out loud is what makes a limited examination safe rather than merely convenient.

To summarize, ultrasound at the bedside is best understood as a physical sign rather than an imaging study, performed to answer one question that matters for the next decision and repeated as the patient changes. The views that a clinician can learn are few and each carries a clear purpose: the heart for fluid and for a failing ventricle, the chest for fluid and for air outside the lung, the abdomen for free fluid, the aorta, and the gallbladder, the kidneys for obstruction, and the pregnant uterus for the position and the heartbeat. The dangerous findings are named where the view is described, among them a cardiac tamponade, a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, and a leaking aneurysm, and each is revealed by a pattern rather than by a single measurement. What a view can set aside is narrow and what it cannot set aside is wide, so a normal image never closes a question that the history has opened. Every figure in this chapter, whether a width, a depth, a stage of pregnancy, or any other measurement, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. The same reasoning serves the resuscitation room and the clinic where the probe is the only imaging, because the question, the view, and the limit are the same in both. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who looks unwell is treated and helped first, and the probe is used to make that help faster rather than to delay it.

# Chapter 68 — Point-of-Care and Rapid Tests

A point-of-care test is a test performed where the patient is, by the clinician who is already caring for that patient, and answered quickly enough that it can change what happens in the next few minutes. The idea is old, since the urine dipstick and the blood glucose strip have been at the bedside for decades, but the range of tests that now fit in a hand has grown until a clinic without a laboratory can measure things that once required a hospital. The reasoning that organizes this chapter is that a rapid test is a question asked at the bedside rather than an answer delivered from a machine, and it must be judged by three things: what it actually measures, how often it is wrong, and what the clinician will do differently once the result is known. A result that cannot alter a decision is not a test but an expense, and a result that is believed beyond its limits is more dangerous than no result at all. The clinician who works with these strips needs to hold two ideas at once, that the test is an instrument of great power in the right hands and that it is a proxy for the disease rather than the disease itself. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Certain lethal possibilities must be named before the ordinary reasoning begins, because each is revealed by a finding that can be sought in the first minutes and each has a rapid test that can mislead. A patient who is confused, sweating, trembling, or unable to be roused may be hypoglycemic, and the finding that reveals it is a glucose measurement taken at once together with the response when the glucose is corrected, since the meter can read deceptively well in a patient whose brain is starving. A patient with fever who has been in a region where malaria is transmitted may have malaria, and the finding that reveals it is the parasite on a stained blood film or its product on a rapid strip, while a single negative strip proves far less than it appears to. A young woman with lower abdominal pain, a missed period, and vaginal bleeding may have a pregnancy that has implanted outside the uterus, and the finding that betrays it is a positive pregnancy test together with tenderness and signs of bleeding inside the abdomen, because this can kill within hours. A patient with chest discomfort may be having an acute myocardial infarction, and the finding that reveals it is a rise in the markers of heart muscle injury over time together with the trace on the electrocardiogram, or ECG, so that one early normal result excludes nothing. These are the presentations in which a strip read too confidently can cost the patient everything.

A rapid test works by fixing a reagent to a strip, a card, or a small cartridge and letting it react with something in a drop of blood, urine, or fluid. What it detects is almost never the disease itself but a proxy: an antigen shed by an organism, an antibody the patient has made against one, an enzyme that reports the presence of a sugar, or a protein released when cells are injured. That proxy travels imperfectly with the disease, appearing only after an interval, persisting after recovery, or appearing for reasons that have nothing to do with the illness in question. The conditions of storage matter as much as the chemistry, because heat, sunlight, moisture, and an expired date can destroy the reagent quietly, and a strip kept in a hot vehicle may fail without any warning on its face. The operator matters too, since too little sample, too much sample, a delayed reading, or a result read after the permitted interval all change the answer. The clinician should therefore ask of every device the same questions that would be asked of a laboratory: how was it kept, who performed it, and what does the maker say about its limits.

The value of a rapid test depends less on the strip than on the patient in front of the clinician, and this is the reasoning that separates a useful result from a misleading one. Every test has a probability of being positive when the disease is present and a probability of being positive when it is absent, and the meaning of a given result shifts with how likely the disease was before the test was performed. A positive result in a patient whose story already makes the disease very likely confirms a diagnosis, while the same positive result in a patient whose story makes it very unlikely is more often a false positive and should be checked rather than obeyed. A negative result in a patient whose story makes the disease very unlikely is reassuring, while the same negative result in a patient whose story makes it very likely should be treated as inconclusive and repeated or confirmed. This is why a clinician should state the probability before reaching for the strip, since that statement is what allows the result to be interpreted instead of merely recorded. The words sensitivity and specificity describe the test, but the question at the bedside is always what this result means for this patient, and the answer depends on both.

The glucose meter is the most widely used rapid test in the world and the one whose result is most often taken at face value. It measures the glucose in a drop of capillary blood by an enzymatic reaction that produces a small current or a color change, and it reports a value that is close to, but not identical with, the glucose measured in the laboratory on plasma. A reading of about 70 milligrams per deciliter is often taught as the line below which hypoglycemia should be assumed, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted boundary shifts with the patient, the sample, and the edition of the reference being used. The meter can mislead in both directions, since poor circulation, cold hands, dehydration, swelling, anemia, and a sugar that is changing quickly all distort the reading, and a strip that has been mishandled can report a value that has nothing to do with the patient. The lethal mistake is the patient who is hypoglycemic and whose meter reads a comfortable number, so that the clinician looks elsewhere while the brain is starved. The finding that should override the meter is the clinical picture of sweating, tremor, confusion, abnormal behavior, or a seizure in a patient at risk, and in that situation the sensible act is to treat and to recheck rather than to trust a single strip.

The same meter serves the opposite purpose, since a very high reading in a patient who is drowsy, breathing deeply, passing large volumes of urine, and vomiting may mean a metabolic emergency rather than simple poor control. A reading above about 250 milligrams per deciliter is a common reason to look further, and that cut-off, like every other number in this chapter, is a teaching illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the value at which a clinician should act depends on the patient, the meter, and the protocol in force. A strip that detects ketones in the urine or the blood adds a second piece of information, because it separates a patient who is merely high from one who is producing acid, and the two demand different decisions. The clinic without a laboratory can follow such a patient with repeated glucose readings, a record of urine output, and repeated examination of breathing, consciousness, and hydration, which together say more than any single number. The clinician should also remember that a reading taken from a fingertip in a cold, shut-down patient may underestimate a truly dangerous level, so the clinical picture keeps its authority. What the test changes is the timing of the decision, not the need for judgment.

The malaria rapid test detects an antigen released by the parasite, and it has changed the care of fever in places where microscopy is not available. Its great strength is speed, and its great danger is that a single negative result is treated as exclusion. In the early hours of an infection the number of parasites may be below the amount the strip can detect, so the first test is often negative in a patient who truly has the disease, and a strip that remains positive for weeks after successful treatment can mislead in the other direction. Some parasite populations do not produce the antigen the strip looks for, which produces a negative result in a genuine infection, and this is one reason the choice of test is tied to the region where it is used. The finding that must outweigh a negative strip is a patient who has been in a region where malaria is transmitted, who has a fever and looks unwell, and in whom no other cause has been found; such a patient needs the test repeated, a blood film where one can be made, and treatment on the clinical case if the diagnosis is likely and the patient is deteriorating. Any interval quoted for repeating the test is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the timing that matters depends on the assay, the species, and the setting.

The test for the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, detects antibodies that the body has made against the virus, and in many modern formats it also detects a part of the virus itself. Its difficulty is the interval between infection and the appearance of enough antibody to be detected, during which a person can be infected and infectious and still test negative. A negative result in that window therefore cannot be read as proof that the person is free of the virus, and a repeat after an interval is part of the reasoning rather than an admission of failure; confirm that interval against the current guidance where you work, because the length of the window depends on the generation of the assay and the protocol in use. A positive result also needs care, because cross-reacting antibodies, recent vaccination, pregnancy, and certain other conditions can produce a false positive on a screening strip, which is why a positive is confirmed by a second, different test before it is treated as final. The clinic that relies on the strip must protect confidentiality, offer the conversation that follows the result, and be honest with the patient about what the test can and cannot say. The lethal error is the missed diagnosis, since a person who is told wrongly that the result is negative may go untreated, and the second lethal error is the wrong positive, which carries a burden of its own.

The pregnancy test measures human chorionic gonadotropin, a hormone produced by the developing placenta, in urine or in blood. A positive result is strong evidence of pregnancy, and its most important use is not obstetric but urgent, because a young woman with abdominal pain, a missed period, and vaginal bleeding may have a pregnancy implanted outside the uterus, and that diagnosis can kill her within hours if it is missed. The finding that reveals it is a positive test together with tenderness in the lower abdomen, a soft and swollen belly, shoulder tip pain, dizziness, or signs of shock, and the finding that would make the clinician relax wrongly is a negative urine test in a patient whose story fits. A negative result can occur when the pregnancy is very early, when the urine is dilute, or when the level of the hormone is so high that the test behaves strangely, which happens in some abnormal pregnancies. A positive result without pregnancy can follow fertility treatment, some tumors, blood in the urine, or a pregnancy recently lost, so the test is read with the history rather than instead of it. Where a laboratory exists the blood level is measured and followed, and where it does not, the strip plus the examination decides whether the patient must travel now.

The urine dipstick is a row of small reagent pads on a plastic strip, and each pad asks a different question: protein, glucose, blood, ketones, bilirubin, the products of infection, and the acidity of the urine. Its virtue is that it costs almost nothing and takes very little time, and its vice is that it answers so many questions at once that a clinician may order more tests in response to the strip than the patient needed in the first place. A trace of blood is common after exercise, during menstruation, after sexual activity, and in a urinary infection, and following it with imaging and repeated samples may produce a cascade of findings that harm the patient without helping the diagnosis. A pad for nitrite and a pad for white cells are often used together to support a urinary infection, but neither a negative nor a positive result settles the question, because the test can be negative in a genuine infection and positive from contamination. Vitamin C in the urine can suppress several of the pads and make a real abnormality invisible, while a concentrated, heavily colored urine can produce readings that mean nothing. The finding that makes the whole strip uninterpretable is a contaminated or stale sample, and the remedy is a clean, fresh specimen rather than more testing.

Protein on the strip is the pad most often over-read, and its reasoning deserves a paragraph of its own. A positive result may reflect a fever, heavy exercise, a concentrated sample, or a urinary infection, and it may also reflect the harmless leakage that occurs in some people when they stand. The finding that makes protein meaningful is its persistence on repeated, properly collected specimens, together with a pressure that is raised, swelling of the legs, or a change in the urine volume, and where a laboratory exists the amount is measured over a day or compared with a substance in the blood. A dipstick that is positive in a patient with no other evidence of kidney disease should prompt a repeat rather than a diagnosis, because a single reading cannot separate the transient from the persistent. Ketones and bilirubin each add a specific piece of information, one about the metabolism of fat and the other about the liver, and each is interpretable only alongside the clinical picture. Every reference range attached to these pads is set by the maker and the laboratory, so confirm it against the current guideline and the local protocol before it changes a decision.

The cardiac troponin test measures a protein released from heart muscle when it is injured, and in a rapid format it can be performed beside the patient. It is the test that most invites a fatal oversimplification, because a single normal result early in the illness is taken as proof that the heart is not infarcting. The protein appears in the blood only after an interval from the onset of injury, and it rises over hours, so a test performed too early can be normal in a patient who is having an acute myocardial infarction at that very moment. The rise must be demonstrated by repeating the test over time, and that interval is an illustration of the reasoning that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the timing depends on the assay in use and the way the protocol defines a significant change. A raised value does not prove an infarction either, because the same protein leaks in kidney failure, in a clot in the lung, in severe infection, in a fast rhythm, and in a failing heart. The finding that keeps the clinician safe is a story of new or changing chest discomfort together with the ECG and the trend of the marker, and where no ECG and no laboratory exist, the decisive question is not whether the patient is having an infarction but whether the patient can reach a place that can answer the question now. A normal early test in a patient whose story is alarming changes nothing about the need to travel and to be observed.

A blood gas and electrolyte analyzer in a small format reports the acidity of the blood, the pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide, the bicarbonate, the salts, the lactate, and sometimes the hemoglobin, all from a small sample. It is a powerful instrument in a resuscitation room and a difficult one in a clinic, because the sample itself is easily spoiled, since air in the syringe, a delay before the reading, too little anticoagulant, or a sample drawn from a vein instead of an artery each produce a result that describes the error rather than the patient. The result is also a snapshot of one moment, and a patient who is deteriorating may need the measurement repeated rather than argued with. A lactate of about 2 millimoles per liter is often used to support the recognition of shock, but that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the boundary depends on the method, the site of sampling, and the population in which it was studied. Lactate rises in many conditions besides shock, including intense muscular activity, a seizure, some medicines, and liver disease, so the number supports a clinical impression rather than replacing it. Where a laboratory exists, the blood gas is confirmed and repeated there; where it does not, the clinician who can measure lactate has gained a signal about perfusion that the bedside examination alone might miss.

Rapid tests for infection now cover streptococcal throat infection, influenza, dengue, typhoid, tuberculosis, syphilis, hepatitis, and several markers of inflammation, and each carries the same lesson about what a proxy can and cannot say. A rapid streptococcal test is highly specific when positive but can be negative in genuine infection, so a negative result in a child with a classic picture does not by itself close the question. A test for inflammation such as C-reactive protein or procalcitonin reports the response of the body rather than the presence of an organism, and it may be raised in injury, in inflammation, and in many conditions that are not infectious, so it cannot separate bacterial from viral disease on its own. A urine test for a product of the tuberculosis organism helps in patients whose immune defenses are suppressed, but a negative result in that group excludes very little, and the diagnosis still rests on samples sent for culture or on molecular testing where it exists. A rapid test for dengue or typhoid may be negative early and positive later, and the timing of the sample matters as much as the choice of the test. The clinician who treats a number rather than a patient will miss the disease that the number was never able to see.

Tests of clotting in a rapid format allow a clinician to measure how long blood takes to clot and, in some devices, to estimate the international normalized ratio used to follow patients on blood-thinning treatment. These are the tests that matter most in trauma, in childbirth, and in any patient who is bleeding, because a failure of clotting turns a controllable hemorrhage into a fatal one. A bedside clotting time of about 20 minutes is sometimes quoted as a sign of trouble, and that figure, like all the others here, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the acceptable range depends on the method and the clinical situation. The measurement is operator-dependent, since the tube must be kept warm, observed continuously, and read at the right moment, and a result produced carelessly is worse than none. The test also says nothing about the strength of the clot or about the platelets, so a normal time does not exclude a bleeding disorder and an abnormal one does not name its cause. The decision that follows is whether the patient needs blood products, a medicine, or transfer, and that decision belongs to the clinician who can see the patient, the bleeding, and the whole picture rather than one number.

In a hospital where a laboratory exists, the rapid test has a different job, which is to shorten the interval between the question and a usable answer while the laboratory performs the definitive test. The bedside glucose is used to guide immediate care and the laboratory measurement confirms it, the rapid strip for an infection screens a patient while the culture grows, and the blood gas in the resuscitation room is followed by formal analysis. In this setting the rapid test must be subject to the same quality control as any other, with the device checked, the reagents stored properly, the results recorded, and the operator trained and reassessed. The clinician should also name the limits out loud in the notes, because a rapid result may be repeated in the laboratory and the two may disagree. A disagreement between a strip and a laboratory is never resolved by preferring the more convenient answer, and it should prompt a repeat and a review of the sample. What the hospital adds is confirmation and context, and what it must not add is the habit of treating the quick result as final simply because it arrived first.

In a clinic with no laboratory, the same tests are not an inferior copy of hospital practice but the laboratory itself, and the clinic must treat them with the seriousness that role deserves. The strips must be stored within the temperature the maker states, protected from light and damp, and checked against the expiry date before use, because a failed reagent produces a confident wrong answer. The device must be cleaned and checked as instructed, and the readings recorded in a register with the date, the time, the operator, and the action taken, so that the pattern over many patients becomes visible. Whenever a rapid test is stocked, someone must be responsible for the supply, the training, and the waste, since a test that cannot be repeated or replaced is a trap rather than a tool. The clinician must also know what the clinic cannot do and say so to the patient, rather than allowing the presence of a few strips to suggest a completeness that does not exist. The tests extend the reach of the examination, and they do not replace the history, the hands, the thermometer, or the torch, all of which remain the instruments that never expire.

A constructed illustration may make the discipline concrete, and it is a teaching device rather than a portrait of any real person. Imagine a patient brought in drowsy and sweating after a missed meal, whose glucose strip reads a number that seems acceptable, and whose clinician decides to treat for hypoglycemia anyway because the picture fits and the meter can be wrong; the patient wakes, and the diagnosis is confirmed by the response. Now imagine a traveler with a fever and a negative malaria strip, whose clinician repeats the test and looks for another cause while treating on the clinical case, because a single negative result was never able to exclude the disease. Neither patient is real, and neither story may be applied to a real person without a full assessment. What both share is the same move, which is to ask what finding would make the rapid result wrong and to act on the answer rather than on the strip alone. The clinician who names the dangerous diagnosis before reaching for the test, who states the probability first, and who records what the result changed will make fewer of the mistakes this chapter has described, because the reasoning was done in the right order.

To summarize, the tests that fit in a hand are questions asked at the bedside, and they are judged by what they measure, how often they are wrong, and what they change. The glucose meter can read deceptively in a patient who is hypoglycemic, the malaria strip can be negative at the first visit in a patient who truly has the disease, the pregnancy test can be negative in a patient with a pregnancy outside the uterus, the troponin can be normal early in an infarction, and the urine dipstick can generate a cascade of further testing from a single meaningless trace. Every strip is read with a probability formed before it was performed, a positive result in a low-probability patient is confirmed rather than believed, and a negative result in a high-probability patient is repeated or set aside on clinical grounds. In the clinic the tests are the laboratory, and they demand storage, training, records, and the honesty to state what remains unknown; in the hospital they shorten the interval to a definitive answer and never replace it. Every figure in this chapter, whether a glucose value, a lactate level, a clotting time, a reference range, or a cut-off, is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. A patient who looks unwell is helped first, and the test is used to sharpen the reasoning rather than to postpone it.

# Chapter 69 — Choosing and Interpreting Tests in Context

Every test in medicine is a question asked of the body, and the whole discipline of investigation lies in knowing what question is being asked before the sample is taken or the image is made. A result has no meaning by itself; it has meaning only against the probability that the patient already carried and against the decision that the clinician was about to make. This chapter is about that discipline, which governs laboratory tests, tracings, images, and the strip that changes color in a clinic with no laboratory at all. The organizing question is short and severe: what would I do differently if the result comes back positive, and what would I do differently if it comes back negative. If the answer to both is nothing, the test is not neutral; it is a harm with a cost, a risk, and a consequence. This material is educational and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Before anything else, the lethal possibilities that a reassuring test can hide must be named, because the most common fatal error in this chapter is not a wrong result but a right result misunderstood. A patient with a clot in the lung may have a normal chest radiograph and normal oxygen measurement, and the finding that reveals the danger is the story of sudden breathlessness with a swollen calf or a recent operation, together with a pulse and a breathing rate that stay high while the patient insists nothing is wrong. A patient with a dissection of the aorta may have a normal tracing of the heart's electricity, and the finding that betrays it is a tearing pain that moves between the chest and the back with a difference in pressure or pulse between the two arms. A patient with a severe infection of the bloodstream may have a white cell count inside the reference range, and the finding that reveals it is a change in behavior, a falling pressure, or a passage of urine that has shrunk. A patient with meningitis may be sent home because a single normal test was reassuring, and the finding that should have stopped that decision is a neck that resists flexion or a rash that does not fade when pressed. A patient in the earliest hours of a heart attack may have an unremarkable tracing, and the finding that reveals it is a discomfort that is new or that has changed its pattern in a patient who looks unwell. In every one of these, the test was not wrong; the mistake was to let a single result close a question that the story had opened. The clinician who keeps the lethal possibility in view while reading a normal result is doing the work that no test can do.

The first habit is to write the question down before the order is sent, in words that can be read later by the person who receives the result. A useful question names the finding, the patient, and the decision it will change, such as whether this breathless patient has a clot that would make treatment necessary tonight. A question that cannot be put in that form is usually a wish for reassurance rather than a diagnostic step, and reassurance is the weakest reason to test. The clinician should also decide in advance what a negative result would mean, because a test whose negative cannot be acted on is as useless as one whose positive cannot. When both outcomes lead to the same decision, the test has already been answered by the reasoning, and ordering it adds only the chance of confusion. The order that survives this scrutiny is short, targeted, and tied to a moment in the patient's care.

Every result is read against the probability that existed before it, and the same finding means different things in different patients. A positive result in a patient whose chance of disease was very low is more often a false positive than a true one, while a negative result in a patient whose chance was high rarely removes the diagnosis. This is why the history and the examination still carry the weight, and why a test cannot repair a clinician who has not formed a view. The clinician who estimates the probability honestly, in words such as unlikely, possible, or probable, has already decided how much a result can move it. The estimation is not arithmetic; it is the accumulated sense of how this patient's story compares with the stories of similar patients seen before. Writing that estimate down before the result arrives is the simplest defense against being led by the number.

A test is described by two behaviors that are worth understanding even when the arithmetic is never performed at the bedside. The first is how often it is positive in people who truly have the disease, and the second is how often it is negative in people who truly do not. A test that is positive in 9 of 10 people with the disease sounds impressive, but that proportion is measured in a particular group of patients, and such proportions vary with the population tested and with the laboratory, so confirm them against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than carrying a figure from a book. When a test is studied in patients who are already in hospital, it usually performs better than it will in a clinic where the disease is milder and earlier. The clinician who remembers that the study population is not the waiting room will be slower to trust a result that seems too clean.

Reference ranges deserve their own caution, because they are the numbers a listener is most tempted to memorize. A range is built from measurements taken in a group of people defined as healthy, and the boundary is drawn so that a proportion of that group falls outside it by design. A hemoglobin range such as 12 to 16 grams per deciliter is therefore a statement about a reference population rather than a rule about the person in front of the clinician, and it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because each laboratory sets its own limits on its own machines and in its own population. The patient's own usual value matters more than the printed range, which is why a result from last year is worth more than a general figure. A value just outside the range in a patient who looks and feels well is a question, not a diagnosis, and the reasoning should ask what else would be expected if the abnormality were real.

An unexpected result has a momentum of its own, and the cascade it begins is one of the most recognizable patterns in modern medicine. A minor abnormality on a scan leads to another image, which leads to a sample of tissue, which occasionally leads to a complication from the procedure itself, and the patient arrives at harm by a path that no one chose. The cascade usually starts with a test that was ordered without a question, because a result that no decision required has no natural stopping place. Breaking the cascade takes a deliberate act, which is to return to the patient and ask what the first result meant for this person, and whether pursuing it would change anything that matters. A clinician who says aloud that a small finding will be watched rather than chased is practicing medicine, not neglect. The record should carry the reasoning, so that the next clinician understands why the chain was stopped.

A false positive that is never corrected becomes a diagnosis, and that label is often harder to remove than it was to apply. The patient may be treated for a disease that was never present, the treatment may carry its own harms, and the label follows the patient into every future consultation. The error is compounded by anchoring, because once the diagnosis is written, later findings are read in its light and contradictory evidence is discounted. The remedy is a confirmatory test with a different basis, ordered before the label is fixed, and a willingness to state plainly when the first result proved to be wrong. Where two tests disagree, the clinician must decide which question each one answered rather than averaging them. A diagnosis made on a single imperfect result is a hypothesis, and it should be written as one.

Not every test is ordered for the patient, and honesty about that is part of the discipline. A test may be ordered to satisfy a family who cannot accept reassurance, a senior who expects a complete panel, an employer or an insurer who wants documentation, or the clinician's own fear of blame if something is missed. Defensive testing feels safe and is often the opposite, because every test carries a chance of a false result and a cascade that follows it. The clinician who recognizes whose anxiety the order serves can address that anxiety directly, with explanation, with a clear plan for review, and with the honesty to say that the test would not change the plan. That conversation is harder than writing the order and usually does more for the patient. A test ordered to protect the clinician rather than to help the patient should be named as such in the reasoning, even if it is ultimately sent.

Incidental findings are the price of looking, and the clinician should decide in advance how they will be handled. An image made for one question will sometimes answer another that was never asked, and the finding may be harmless, uncertain, or genuinely important. The response should be proportionate, which means asking whether the finding explains the patient's problem, whether it needs treatment, and whether knowing about it will help or only worry. Some findings are best watched over time rather than pursued, and that decision belongs to a clinician who knows the patient and can explain the choice. The patient must be told what was found and what will be done, because silence about an incidental finding is a breach of trust that no protocol can repair.

Ordering a test creates a duty to its result, and that duty is where systems fail most often. The result must reach the clinician who ordered it, be read against the question that was asked, be communicated to the patient in words the patient can use, and be acted on or deliberately set aside with a reason. A result that arrives after the clinician has gone off duty belongs to the service rather than to the individual, which is why handover must carry pending tests by name. The patient who was told that someone would call with the result must actually be called, and a result that is never followed up is a diagnosis lost in the space between people. A clinician who orders a test and does not own its result has done the easy half of the work.

Timing changes what a test means, and a value without its time is an incomplete result. A measurement taken at the wrong moment can be falsely reassuring, and the same measurement repeated later can be unmistakable, which is why serial results often carry more than any single one. A sample drawn after treatment has begun may no longer show what it would have shown before, so the order of drawing and treating is itself a clinical decision. The interval at which a test should be repeated is a figure that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because different services and different editions set different rhythms for the same measurement. The trend, read alongside the patient's condition, is usually more informative than the isolated number. A clinician who compares the patient today with the patient yesterday is using the laboratory well.

In a hospital the pressure runs toward more testing rather than less, because the machines are close, the results return quickly, and ordering feels like thoroughness. The daily panel drawn before the ward round, the repeated image ordered because the previous one was inconveniently timed, and the test added to the list because a colleague mentioned it are all familiar, and none of them is a question. The patient in the intensive care unit, known as the ICU, may have blood taken several times a day, and each sample has a cost in blood, in sleep, and in the chance of a spurious result that prompts another test. Availability is not an argument for use, and the clinician with the most tests at hand has the greatest need for restraint. In this setting the skill is to choose the one test that answers the question and to leave the others unasked. The patient who is unstable is treated on the clinical findings first, and the tests follow rather than lead.

Used well, the hospital turns uncertainty into evidence quickly, and the reasoning does not change because the tools improve. The clinician reviews the results already in the record before ordering anything new, because the answer is often there and the repeat adds nothing but delay. Each test is chosen for the decision it serves, and the clinician knows before the result arrives what would be done with either answer. The patient's own values, recorded over time, are read as a story rather than as isolated lines, and the clinician notices the direction in which they are moving. When a test cannot help, the clinician says so and offers the plan instead, whether that is observation, treatment, or discharge with clear instructions. A hospital that tests less and thinks more is not a poorer hospital; it is a safer one.

The cost of a test is not only money, though money is real and belongs in the reasoning. Every sample consumes the time of a person who could be doing something else, the reagent or the electricity that runs the machine, and the attention of the clinician who must interpret it. In a service where the laboratory is shared, a test ordered for no decision delays the test that someone else urgently needs. The harm is invisible because it falls on a patient the clinician never sees, and that invisibility is exactly why it must be named. A clinician who treats the laboratory as a free and infinite resource is spending someone else's scarcity. The same reasoning that justifies a test for the patient in front of the clinician should consider the patient who is waiting behind.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, scarcity performs the discipline that a hospital must impose on itself. A test must be justified twice, once by the question it answers and once by the journey or the money it costs the patient, and the clinician feels both. The scarcity does not lower the standard of reasoning; it raises it, because the history and the examination are the tests that are always available. The torch makes the throat, the ear, the eye, and the skin visible, the thermometer turns an impression into a repeatable figure, and the hands find the enlarged organ, the tender area, and the swelling that changes the plan. A breathing rate above 20 breaths per minute is worth recording rather than treating as a diagnosis, and that boundary must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because what counts as fast shifts with age, pregnancy, and fitness. Where a single rapid test exists, it is used for the one decision it can settle rather than as a general screen, and its limits are stated to the patient. The reasoning is the same reasoning, conducted with fewer instruments and the same duty.

Where the test cannot be done, the referral is the test, and it carries the same obligations. The decision to send the patient onward is a clinical judgment about probability and danger, and the clinician should state what is suspected and what finding would confirm it. The result of that referral must return, because a diagnosis made elsewhere is still the business of the clinician who sent the patient. If the patient does not go, or the appointment is missed, that is a result of the test, and it must be followed rather than forgotten. The record should show why the journey was thought necessary, so that the next clinician can see the reasoning rather than a bare request. A referral without a question is as unhelpful as a laboratory order without one.

The two worlds differ in their instruments and not in their logic, and the clinician should be able to move between them without changing the reasoning. The well-resourced clinician must ask the same question before ordering and must resist the pull of the available machine. The clinician in the clinic must own the result of the one test that was possible and must carry the referral to its conclusion. Both must remember that a test is a question and that the patient, not the result, is the subject of the work. When the same discipline is applied in both places, the patient receives the same quality of thought even when receiving very different technologies. The transferable part of medicine is the reasoning, and that is what this chapter is trying to protect.

A constructed illustration may make the contrast concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a patient in a large hospital who mentions a mild, intermittent discomfort in the abdomen, and whose scan is ordered to quiet the clinician's unease rather than to answer a question, and whose scan reveals a small, unrelated change that begins a chain of further images and a sample of tissue. Now imagine a patient in a clinic with a fever and a cough, in whom the clinician asks what the single available test would change, uses it for that one purpose, examines the chest carefully, and sends the patient home with a clear plan for review. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a living person without a full assessment. The difference between the two is not the machine; it is the question asked before the machine was touched.

The test must be explained to the patient before it is done and interpreted for the patient after, in language that carries the uncertainty honestly. The patient should know what the test is for, what it can and cannot show, and what will happen if the result is unclear. A false positive is far easier to accept when the possibility was mentioned in advance, and far more damaging when it appears as a surprise. The clinician should avoid the language of certainty, because very few tests deliver it, and should say plainly when a result does not settle the question. The conversation after a normal result is as important as the conversation after an abnormal one, since a normal result that is over-read becomes false reassurance. Consent for a test includes understanding its limits as well as its purpose.

A test whose result is pending creates a period of risk, and the plan for that period belongs in the record and in the patient's understanding. The patient should know which symptoms would mean returning before the result arrives, and how the result will be communicated if it is delayed or if the patient cannot be reached. A follow-up appointment arranged before the patient leaves is stronger than a promise to call, because it survives a lost telephone number and a busy week. The clinician should decide in advance what will be done if the patient does not return, rather than assuming that silence means recovery. Safety-netting is a diagnostic skill, and it is often the step that prevents a missed lethal diagnosis from becoming a death.

The record should show the question, the reasoning, and the plan, not only the result. A note that lists the tests ordered without saying why leaves the next clinician unable to interpret them and unable to stop. Writing the question beside the order is a small habit with a large effect, because it forces the clinician to have a question. The record should also show what was considered and set aside, and what the patient was told, so that the reasoning can be reviewed rather than reconstructed. A result that contradicts the working diagnosis must be recorded as a contradiction, not quietly omitted. The written record is the memory of the reasoning, and it is what the next shift inherits.

A test measures a surrogate rather than the patient, and the distinction matters when the two disagree. A number can be abnormal while the patient feels well, and a number can be normal while the patient is seriously ill, and both situations are common. The clinician should ask what the measurement represents in this person, and whether the usual interpretation applies to someone of this age, this pregnancy, this weight, or this illness. The patient's account of how they feel is data of a different kind, and it is not overruled by a result that does not fit. When the two conflict, the safest course is usually to repeat the observation and to watch the patient rather than to choose one and discard the other.

The most dangerous order in medicine is the one written to rule something out, because exclusion is a stronger claim than a test can usually support. A negative result lowers the probability in proportion to how often the test misses the disease, and it never reduces it to zero. The clinician who treats a negative result as proof of absence has mistaken a useful tool for a guarantee. This is especially true when the test was performed early, when it was performed on the wrong sample, or when the patient had already been treated. A rule-out order should therefore be paired with a statement of how much the negative changes the plan, and with a plan for what happens if the story continues. When the probability was high before the test, a negative result is a reason to reconsider the test rather than to relax.

The clinician's own mind is an instrument that needs checking, because a test can be ordered to confirm a belief rather than to test it. The habit that protects against this is to ask, before the result arrives, what finding would make the clinician abandon the working diagnosis. If no result could change the diagnosis, the diagnosis has stopped being a hypothesis and has become a commitment. A clinician should also notice when a test is ordered to answer the patient's theory rather than the clinical question, and should say so kindly. Seeking the result that would disprove the current view is not doubt for its own sake; it is the method that keeps the diagnosis honest. A diagnosis that has never been challenged is the one most likely to be wrong.

Over-testing has its own pathology, and it is a clinical error with consequences rather than a matter of etiquette. It produces anxiety in patients who were well, treatment for conditions that would never have caused harm, procedures that carry risk, and a diagnostic label that alters how a person is seen for the rest of their life. It consumes the attention of clinicians, so that the patient with a real problem waits behind a queue of investigations that no decision required. It also teaches patients that every symptom deserves a scan, which is a lesson that is difficult to unlearn. The correction is not a rule about numbers of tests but a habit of asking what the test will change. A clinician who can answer that question for every order is already practicing restraint.

Some of the most important decisions in medicine are made by not testing, and that decision deserves the same care as the decision to test. A patient with a clear, self-limiting illness and no danger signs may need an explanation and a plan rather than a sample. A patient whose symptoms are fully explained by a condition already known may need treatment for that condition rather than a search for another. The clinician who withholds a test should say why, so that the patient understands that the omission was a judgment rather than an oversight. Withholding is legitimate when the probability is low, when the result would not change the plan, and when the harm of the test outweighs its benefit. The clinician who can explain that reasoning has done more than the one who simply orders.

To summarize, every test is a question, and the discipline of investigation lies in asking it before the sample is taken, in deciding what either answer would change, and in owning the result until it has been acted on or deliberately set aside. The lethal possibilities that a reassuring result can hide are named at the bedside, among them the clot in the lung with a normal radiograph, the dissection with a normal tracing, and the severe infection with a normal white cell count. Over-testing is treated as the clinical error it is, with its cascades, its false positives that harden into diagnoses, its incidental findings, and its orders written for someone other than the patient. The hospital with its unlimited machines and the clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer share one question and one duty to the result, and the reasoning transfers between them unchanged. Every score, cut-off, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, or interval named in this chapter is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

# Chapter 70 — Scoring Systems and Rules

A score asks several questions in a fixed order and adds the answers, and a rule turns those answers into a decision. Both exist because judgment varies, memory is unreliable, and two competent clinicians can assess the same patient differently on the same afternoon. The reasoning that organizes this chapter is that a score is a formalization of somebody else's thinking rather than a substitute for the listener's own, fixing which findings were thought to matter, how heavily each was weighted, and what its authors feared most when they chose a line. The instruments used here as examples are the Wells score for the probability of a clot, the Curb sixty-five score for the severity of pneumonia, the Cha two D S two Vasc score for the risk of stroke in atrial fibrillation, the Ottawa rules for the decision about a radiograph after an injury, and the Centor criteria for the probability of streptococcal pharyngitis, and each is described by the reasoning it organizes rather than by its arithmetic. The arithmetic behind all of them changes with time and must be read from the current source and the local protocol rather than remembered from a lecture.

Before the mechanics of any rule, the causes that kill must be named where they appear, because a score never feels the patient. The patient whose probability of a clot is scored as low may still be dying of a clot that has traveled to the lung, and the finding that betrays it is a sudden dyspnea with a rapid pulse, sometimes with a swollen tender calf and sometimes with no leg signs at all. The patient whose pneumonia is scored as mild may be deteriorating while the form is completed, and the finding is a breathing rate that has climbed or a new confusion in an older person. The patient whose sore throat scores as likely streptococcal may instead have a deep infection of the neck that is closing the airway, and the findings are drooling, a muffled voice, difficulty swallowing, and a posture propped forward. The child who is scored as low risk may have meningitis or an infection of the bloodstream, and the finding is a rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed on it. A hemorrhage into the brain, a clot that travels to the brain, and an infection spreading through the blood outrank every number on a form.

Three questions should be asked before any rule is applied. The first is what decision the rule is meant to inform, because one built to decide whether to order a test behaves differently from one built to decide where a patient should be cared for. The second is the population in which it was derived and the one in which it has since been checked, since a rule tested in teaching hospitals may perform poorly in a rural clinic where the disease is rarer. The third is what the rule leaves out, which is usually the patient's own account, the ability to return if things worsen, the home circumstances, and the appearance that worries the clinician. Some scores predict, some stratify severity, some decide a test, and some merely record a state, and the Glasgow coma scale belongs to that last family because it summarizes consciousness without claiming to know the future. A rule not checked in a population like the one in front of the clinician is a hypothesis rather than a tool, and anyone using it should confirm the current figures against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A score produces a probability, and the same probability means different things in different rooms. A positive result that indicates serious illness on a ward where that illness is common may indicate a false alarm in a clinic where it is rare, because the meaning of a result depends on how many people in the room actually have the disease. This is why a rule can look excellent in the paper that derived it and disappointing in a new setting without any error by its authors. Prevalence changes with season, with the case mix of the clinic, and with the way patients are referred. A clinician who knows the local frequency of the disease is therefore better placed than one who knows only the score, and anyone who cannot estimate that frequency should treat the score as weak support and confirm the line in use against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Every cut-off is a choice about which mistake is worse. Moving the line in one direction catches more of the patients who have the disease and labels more of those who do not, while moving it the other way misses more true cases and raises fewer false alarms. The authors of a rule make that choice according to the danger of the illness and the harm of the action that follows, so a rule about a clot in the lung is built to miss as few clots as possible and accepts many false alarms, while a rule about a sore throat may accept missing some cases that would have settled anyway. A listener who knows which way a rule leans can use it intelligently, and the exact line in any published rule must be taken from the current source and the local protocol, because the same rule is often reproduced with a different threshold in a later edition.

This chapter will not recite the arithmetic of any score, and the restraint is deliberate. The items, the weights, and the line above which a result is called positive have changed between editions of the same rule, between countries, and between the specialties that use it. A listener who memorizes a number from a spoken chapter will carry it into a clinic where a different number is in force and will have no way to notice the error. What can be carried is the structure, which is the findings the rule considers, the direction in which each one pushes, and the decision the result is meant to support. A clinician who holds the structure can complete the arithmetic from the current source at the bedside, or can reason without it when no source can be reached, and where no source is available the honest course is to reason from first principles, record the uncertainty, and confirm the figures later against the local protocol.

The Wells score formalizes the reasoning about the probability of a clot in a deep vein or in the lung, and it is a good example of a rule built to guide a test rather than to make a diagnosis. Its items are the findings and risk factors that a thoughtful clinician would weigh anyway, among them a recent operation or a long period without moving, a cancer, a pregnancy or the weeks after birth, the use of hormones, a previous clot, a swollen tender calf, and a fast pulse. The reason the probability is estimated before anything is ordered is that the meaning of the next test depends on it. In a patient whose probability is low, a normal blood test for the product of clot breakdown makes the diagnosis very unlikely, and imaging can often be avoided, while in a patient whose probability is high the same blood test changes almost nothing and the decisive test is an ultrasound of the leg veins or a CT of the arteries of the lung. The cut-off that separates these groups is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the version in the original paper and the versions in use today do not draw the same line.

The Wells score was derived and refined in adults who came to emergency departments with a suspected clot, most of them able to walk, speak, and give a history. It performs less well in the groups that were thinly represented in those studies. In pregnancy the normal swelling and edema of the legs and the altered clotting of that state blur the findings the score counts, and the risk of a clot is genuinely higher, so the score is not the instrument to lean on. In the very old, in patients with cancer, and in those who have already had a clot, the baseline risk is high enough that a reassuring number means less than the arithmetic suggests, and in a patient already in hospital and unable to move the score was not designed for that situation at all. The greatest danger is the sentence in which a low number persuades a clinician that a breathless and frightened patient cannot have a clot. The findings that override any score are a sudden dyspnea, chest pain that worsens with a breath, a cough that brings blood, a fainting, or a swollen tender calf, and any of those should lead to a second look and a check against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The Curb sixty-five score formalizes the assessment of severity in a patient with pneumonia acquired in the community, and it answers a different question from the one that asked whether pneumonia is present. Its items are the signs that experience teaches a clinician to fear, among them confusion, a raised level of a waste product the kidney normally clears, a breathing rate that has climbed, a pressure that has fallen, and an age that reduces reserve. The result decides where the patient should be cared for and how closely watched, so it informs a decision about setting and urgency rather than diagnosis. The danger the score cannot see is the patient who looks comfortable and is quietly short of oxygen, whose breathing rate rises only when the patient walks, or whose confusion is mistaken for age. The finding that should override a comfortable score is a breathing rate that has increased between two observations, a new confusion, or a fall in oxygen that appears when the patient moves. The figures that separate the risk groups must be taken from the current guideline and the local protocol, because they have been revised and are applied differently in different services.

The Curb sixty-five score grew out of audits of adults admitted to hospital with community-acquired pneumonia in the United Kingdom, and that origin limits where it travels well. It was not designed for a young patient whose only abnormal finding is a low pressure, for a nursing home resident whose baseline state is already altered, or for a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed and who may carry a severe infection with few signs. It also depends on a measurement of kidney function that a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer cannot obtain, so there the rule can be started but not finished. The correct response is not to assume the missing item is normal, because that assumption converts an unknown into a falsely reassuring score. The clinician should complete what can be completed, name the missing part openly, and let the decision rest on what was measured together with the appearance of the patient. The threshold used locally must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the cut-offs and the actions attached to them differ between editions.

The Cha two D S two Vasc score formalizes the estimation of stroke risk in a patient with atrial fibrillation, and it exists to support one of the most consequential decisions in medicine, which is whether to treat such a patient with a medicine that reduces clotting. Its items are the conditions that raise the risk of a stroke, among them a previous stroke or a brief disturbance of brain function from a clot, an age above a certain line, a weakened pump, high pressure, diabetes, disease of the vessels, and being female. The reasoning it organizes is that risk is not the same for every patient with an irregular rhythm, and that the decision should follow the estimated risk rather than the rhythm alone. It does not settle the matter by itself, because the same decision must weigh the risk of bleeding, the patient's own values, and the ability to take a medicine reliably. The line above which treatment is recommended is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because guidelines in different countries have set it at different points and have changed it over time.

The Cha two D S two Vasc score was derived in people with atrial fibrillation that was not caused by disease of the mitral valve, most of them older adults in Europe and North America. It performs less reliably in patients with a mechanical or badly damaged valve, in those with moderate or severe narrowing of the mitral valve, and in people whose irregular rhythm comes and goes rather than persisting.
