Its power to predict is weaker in the very old, in people with severe kidney impairment, and in populations whose baseline risk of stroke differs from the one in which it was built. A score that predicts a population's risk cannot promise a particular patient's future, and a clinician who treats a low number as a guarantee is making a category error. The danger of the score replacing judgment is greatest when it is used to withhold treatment from a patient who has strong other reasons to receive it, or to give treatment to a patient whose bleeding risk has not been considered. Anyone relying on it should read the current version from its source and check the local protocol, because the items and their relative weight have been revised.

The Ottawa rules formalize a narrower and very practical decision, which is whether a patient who has injured an ankle, a foot, or a knee needs a radiograph. Their purpose is to reduce unnecessary imaging by identifying patients in whom the probability of a fracture is very low, and that purpose is different from finding every fracture. The reasoning behind them is that a small number of examination findings, taken together, can separate the patients who need an image from those who can be treated with support and advice, and using them well means accepting that they are designed to miss almost nothing while sending some patients for an image that turns out to be normal. The danger is not the fracture the rule occasionally allows through but the serious injury it was never built to detect, such as a dislocation that has already returned to place, an injury to a nerve or a vessel, or a wound that has opened the joint. The findings that demand attention regardless of the rule are a foot that is cold, pale, or pulseless, a limb that is numb or cannot be moved, a wound over the joint, and a deformity that returns as swelling settles. The interval after injury within which the rule was designed to be applied must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The Ottawa rules were derived in alert adults and older children who came to emergency departments soon after an injury, and their limits follow from that population. They were not built for a patient who is intoxicated, who cannot cooperate with an examination, who has a distracting injury elsewhere that masks the pain, or who arrives long after the event when swelling has changed the findings. In the very young child who cannot describe the pain, the examination is less reliable and the rules should not be used as though the child were an adult. In the multiply injured patient the question is not whether one joint needs an image but how the whole patient should be assessed. The greatest danger is the clinician who reads a negative rule as evidence that nothing serious has happened, when the rule was only ever about a fracture. The listener should confirm the version in use against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the items and the excluded groups have been restated in later publications.

The Centor criteria formalize the estimation of the probability that a sore throat is caused by the streptococcal organism, and they guide the decision about testing and treatment rather than make a diagnosis. The findings they gather are the ones a careful clinician would look for anyway, among them a fever, tender and enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, a white coating on the tonsils, and the absence of a cough. The reasoning is that these features together raise the probability enough to justify a test or a treatment decision, while their absence makes the infection less likely and supports another explanation. The danger that no score addresses is the sore throat that is not a sore throat, and every clinician should look for it before counting points. A deep infection of the neck, an infected collection beside the tonsil, or an infection of the flap that guards the airway can all present first as a sore throat, and the findings that reveal them are drooling, a muffled voice, difficulty swallowing, a stiff neck, or a patient who sits forward and refuses to lie down. The cut-off at which testing or treatment is recommended must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line and the recommended action vary between countries.

The Centor criteria were derived in adults who came to clinics and emergency departments with a sore throat, and they perform least well where that population is left behind. Children have a different pattern of illness and a different risk of complications, so an adult score applied to a child may mislead in both directions. In communities where rheumatic fever still occurs, the consequences of a missed streptococcal infection are far greater than where it has become rare, and the threshold for treatment is correspondingly different. In a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, the ordinary signs may be blunted and the score falsely reassuring. The most common error is not arithmetic but examination, since a clinician who counts the criteria without looking into the throat, feeling the neck, and checking that the airway is safe has used the rule to avoid the patient. The figures attached to each criterion must be read from the current source and the local protocol, because the criteria have been reproduced with different weights and different advice.

In a well-resourced hospital, scores are used mainly to organize urgency while more information is on its way. An early warning score built from the observations at the bedside tells the ward how often to look again and when to call for help, and its purpose is to make deterioration visible before it becomes irreversible. The quick sequential organ failure assessment formalizes the recognition of a patient whose infection is threatening the organs, using findings that any nurse can obtain, and the Glasgow coma scale records consciousness in a way that can be compared across shifts. None of these instruments diagnoses anything and none of them sees the patient, so a score that improves while the patient looks worse is a signal to trust the patient. The hospital's advantage is that the same measurements can be repeated often and placed beside laboratory results and images, which turns a single score into a trend. The danger is the ritual in which the form is completed, the number is filed, and the thinking stops, and every threshold used to trigger a call for help must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the same reasoning is available even when the same arithmetic is not. The breathing rate, the pulse, the temperature, the pressure, the level of consciousness, the ability to walk, the color of the skin, and the look of the throat can all be assessed with those three instruments and a watch, and those are the items most scores depend on. What cannot be obtained is a laboratory value, an image, or a measurement that needs a machine, and the clinician must judge how much that missing piece matters to the decision at hand. A score with a laboratory component cannot be completed here, and the honest course is to say so rather than treat the missing result as normal. The reasoning then becomes a referral decision, which is whether the patient can be watched here, whether treatment should begin on the clinical picture, and whether the journey to a hospital must start now. In this setting the appearance of the patient and the trend of the observations carry more weight than any instrument, and the figures printed in any rule must be compared with the current guideline and the local protocol, since a rule read in one clinic may have been revised before it is used in the next.

Scores built on adults require particular caution in children, in pregnant women, and in older adults, because normal values and the speed of deterioration differ. A child compensates for a falling circulation by raising the heart rate and keeping the pressure up, and then fails suddenly, so a score that waits for the pressure to fall will wait too long. The findings that should override any reassuring number in a child are a refusal to feed, a floppy body, a rash that does not fade when pressed, a breathing rate that is rising, and a parent who says the child is not right. In pregnancy the normal ranges of pulse, pressure, and breathing are altered and the risk of a clot is genuinely increased, so rules that ignore the pregnant state should not be leaned on. In the frail older patient a score may be normal while the patient has lost the ability to stand, to eat, or to think clearly, and those losses are the finding. Every age-specific threshold must be taken from the current guideline and the local protocol, since the lines that define abnormality in a child are drawn by age and differ between sources.

A score that is not written down has done only half its work, and a score written down without its reasoning can do harm. The note should record the findings that produced the number, not only the number, so that the next clinician can see what was examined and whether the findings have changed. When the score and the clinician's impression disagree, the disagreement should be documented rather than resolved silently in favor of the number. The deepest danger of a scoring culture is that it replaces the act of looking at the patient, so that a number computed at the door becomes an anchor that pulls every later observation toward its first verdict. A low number can license premature closure, so that the examination is finished before it has begun and the patient's own account is never heard, while a high number can begin treatment before the diagnosis has been questioned. The safeguard is to recalculate the score whenever the patient changes and to treat a patient who looks worse than the number as worse. Any figure copied into a record should carry the reminder that it must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A constructed illustration may make the discipline concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a middle-aged patient who arrives in a clinic with a swollen calf and a low score for the probability of a clot, whose score is recorded honestly, and who is sent onward because the clinician notices the swelling and a fast pulse despite the reassuring number. Imagine instead a child with a fever and a rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed on the skin, whose score for the severity of the illness is low, and whose clinician sets the score aside and arranges urgent transfer. Now imagine an older patient with an irregular pulse and a low score for the risk of stroke, in whom the decision about treatment is made after the bleeding risk and the patient's own wishes have been discussed rather than from the number alone. None of these patients is real, and none of these stories should be applied to a real person without a full assessment. What the three share is the move that matters, in which the clinician used the score to organize the questions and then let the patient decide the answer.

To summarize, a score is a formalization of clinical reasoning and never a substitute for the examination of the patient. The Wells score organizes the probability of a clot, the Curb sixty-five score organizes the severity of pneumonia, the Cha two D S two Vasc score organizes the risk of stroke in atrial fibrillation, the Ottawa rules organize the decision about imaging after an injury, and the Centor criteria organize the probability of streptococcal pharyngitis, and each was built in a particular population and leans in a particular direction. The lethal possibilities are named where they belong and outrank every number, among them the clot in the lung, the pneumonia that is deteriorating, the deep infection of the neck, the meningitis in a child, and the stroke that the risk score was meant to anticipate. The arithmetic is deliberately not spoken here, and every score, cut-off, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, and duration mentioned in this chapter, together with every figure attached to any instrument, must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen. A patient who looks worse than the score is a patient who is worse, and the clinician who keeps asking that question is using scores as they were meant to be used.

# Chapter 71 — Flowcharts and Algorithms

An algorithm is a route rather than an answer, and a flowchart is that route written down so that two different clinicians can walk it the same way. The subject of this chapter is the flowchart heard instead of seen, because nothing in this book can be shown and the listener has to follow the path by ear. The reasoning is straightforward, since a clinician under pressure does not need a list of every possible diagnosis but the next question, the finding that answers it, and the decision that follows, in the order in which time allows them to be asked. An algorithm supplies that order, and it does so best when the person using it understands why each step sits where it does. The dangerous possibilities are named first in every path worth following, which is the whole reason the path is written down at all. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Before any path is walked, the lethal possibilities deserve to be named, because each is revealed by a finding that can be sought within the first minutes. The febrile child who is drowsy, whose hands are cold, and who develops a rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed upon it may have an infection of the bloodstream, and that rash turns a routine fever into an emergency. The breathless adult who cannot finish a sentence, whose chest sounds silent when listened to, or who is visibly tiring may be close to failure of the breathing, and the silence of the chest and the effort of the shoulders reveal it. The patient with chest discomfort who sweats, vomits, and feels the pain move into the jaw or the arm may be having an acute myocardial infarction, and a normal examination does not exclude it, so the history and the electrocardiogram, or ECG, carry the decision together. The patient who collapses with a tearing pain that moves between the chest and the back, and whose pulses or pressures differ between the two arms, may have a dissection of the aorta. The patient who is pale, clammy, confused, and passing very little urine is in shock, whatever the cause, and shock is a decision to act rather than a diagnosis to complete.

Altered consciousness belongs in the same opening list, because several of its causes are reversible and one of them is fatal within hours if it is not recognized. A patient who is confused or unrousable may have a low level of sugar in the blood, and that is a question a meter answers in seconds, while a clinic without one must still treat the possibility as the first item on its path. The same patient may have a slow bleed inside the head, an infection of the brain or its coverings, a stroke, a poisoning, or a failure of the liver or the kidney, and the examination of the pupils, the limbs, the neck, and the smell of the breath narrows the field. The finding that most often changes the immediate plan is a difference between the two sides of the body, which speaks of a stroke, or a fever with a stiff neck, which speaks of infection. These are the patients for whom an algorithm is at its most useful and at its most dangerous, because the path has to be entered at the right door.

Algorithms exist because attention is finite and because the same mistake is made at the same point by one clinician after another. A well-made path puts the dangerous question before the comfortable one, forces the observations to be recorded rather than remembered, and makes the next step independent of the mood of the moment or the hour of the shift. It also makes care consistent, so that two clinicians handed the same patient would at least begin in the same place. The reasoning it formalizes is not new, because it is the sequence an experienced clinician follows without noticing, set down so that a tired one can follow it too. The cost of that clarity is rigidity, and much of this chapter is about holding the clarity without accepting the rigidity.

To hear a flowchart is to hear a series of questions with two or three exits, and the listener can hold the shape in mind if the structure is spoken plainly. Each step is a question followed by the answers that are possible and the place each answer leads, so the path unfolds as a route rather than as a picture. The walk ends when a step names an action instead of another question, and that action is almost always to treat now, to test, to watch, or to send the patient onward. A path learned this way is remembered as a journey through a building, with turns that can be pictured and repeated at the bedside. A listener who can say the path back to a colleague has learned it, while a listener who can only recognize it on a page has not.

Every algorithm assumes something about the patient in front of the clinician, and asking what it assumes is the discipline that keeps it safe. It assumes that the patient resembles the people in whom the path was studied, so a rule built for adults may mislead in a child and a rule built in one climate may mislead in another. It assumes that the first question can be answered, which is false when the patient cannot speak, when the family is absent, or when the record is missing. It assumes that every branch is available, so a path that forks toward a laboratory test is not the same path in a clinic that has none. It assumes that the finding it asks for means the same thing in every pair of hands, which is untrue of a murmur, a rash, or the feel of an abdomen. The clinician who names those assumptions aloud before starting has already improved on the chart.

The febrile child is the clearest example of a path that saves lives when it is followed and harms when it is abandoned halfway. The first question is the age of the child, because a fever in a newborn is handled as a serious illness until it is proved otherwise. The next is the general appearance, because a child who is alert, feeding, and playing is a different problem from a child who is limp, irritable, or inconsolable. The path then asks how the child is breathing and how the circulation is behaving, judged by the color of the skin, the warmth of the hands, and the speed with which the color returns after a finger is pressed. Any point that reaches a red exit sends the child for urgent help and treatment rather than for a period of waiting, and a rash that does not fade under pressure is one of those exits. Where the child looks well and no red exit is found, the path turns to the search for a focus, which is the examination of the throat, the ears, the chest, the abdomen, the skin, and the urine.

The edges of that path are where it misleads, and the clinician should know them before following it. A child in a region where malaria is transmitted may need the question about travel and exposure before any other, because the disease can kill within days and the examination can be deceptively calm. A child whose immune defenses are suppressed may never produce the appearance the path expects, and a child who has already received an antibiotic may look better than the illness warrants. Age shifts every line, since a fever that might be watched in a sturdy older child is treated at once in a baby of a few weeks, and the exact age at which that changes must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services draw the boundary in different places. In a clinic with no laboratory, the branches that ask for a blood count or a culture are replaced by the decision to treat on the clinical picture and to arrange the journey. A child who cannot be watched at home must travel even when the examination is reassuring, and that decision is part of the algorithm rather than a departure from it.

The breathless adult asks a different first question, which is whether the patient is about to fail. The path begins with the ability to speak, the rate and the effort of breathing, the use of the muscles of the neck and the spaces between the ribs, and the level of consciousness, because a patient who is tiring is treated before any cause is named. It then asks whether the breathlessness came suddenly or over days, because sudden onset sends the reasoning toward a clot in the lung, a collapsed lung, a rhythm that has failed, or fluid flooding the lungs. It asks about fever and cough, about chest pain, about swelling of the legs, and about the medicines the patient takes, since a common cause is a heart that has been pushed into failure. The examination listens to both lungs and to the heart, feels the pulse and the pressure, looks at the veins in the neck, and presses the legs. A patient who cannot lie flat is a patient whose lungs are congested until it is proved otherwise, and that single finding reorganizes the whole path.

Here the hospital and the clinic follow the same logic with different instruments. The hospital branch that asks for a chest radiograph, an ultrasound of the heart, a blood count, or a measurement of oxygen in the blood turns a good question into a picture, and the clinician must know which question each test is answering. The clinic branch cannot ask those questions, so it asks the same thing with the stethoscope, the thermometer, the watch, and the hands, and it reaches a decision about travel rather than a decision about a diagnosis. The error at the edge is to treat an unavailable test as though it had been performed and found normal, which is the same as declaring the clot absent because the scanner is far away. The correct move is to say plainly that a question could not be answered, to act as though the dangerous answer were possible, and to write down why.

Chest pain is the presentation where an algorithm earns its place most quickly, because the lethal causes are few and the time is short. The path asks first whether the patient is unstable, judged by consciousness, breathing, pulse, pressure, and the color of the skin, and an unstable patient is treated and moved rather than questioned further. It then asks what the discomfort is like, where it sits, where it travels, what brings it on, what relieves it, and how the pattern has changed, and the Socrates framework is a way of keeping that account complete. It asks about a tearing pain that moves to the back, about breathlessness and a swollen leg, about fever and a new murmur, and about the risk factors for a clot. Where an ECG exists it is performed early and repeated, because a single tracing can look innocent at the wrong moment, and where a laboratory exists the substances released by damaged heart muscle are measured in sequence. In the clinic with no ECG, the only safe exit for a new or changing chest discomfort is a journey to a place where the tracing can be done.

The edge of the chest pain path is the patient who does not look ill. An acute myocardial infarction can produce a normal examination, a normal pressure, and a normal pulse, and a clinician who waits for the picture to declare itself has already lost the time that mattered. The same is true of the young patient, in whom the path is often abandoned because the risk seems low, and of the older patient or the patient with diabetes, in whom the pain may be slight or absent and the presentation may be breathlessness, sweating, or vomiting instead. A dissection of the aorta is missed because the pain is attributed to something ordinary, and the finding that should stop the walk is a difference between the two arms in pulse or in pressure. The lesson is that the path must be entered on suspicion rather than on certainty, because the purpose of putting the dangerous question first is to ask it before the evidence is complete.

Shock is the clearest example of a presentation in which the algorithm is a sequence of actions rather than a sequence of thoughts. The path begins with the recognition that the circulation is failing, which is seen in a rapid pulse, a rapid breathing rate, cool or mottled skin, confusion, and a passage of urine that has shrunk, and every one of those lines shifts with age and with the usual state of the patient, so it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than carried in the head. The path then asks which broad pattern is present, whether blood loss, infection, failure of the pump, or loss of fluid through vomiting, diarrhea, or burns. It looks for the source of bleeding in the abdomen, the chest, the gut, and the pelvis, and for the signs of infection that make treatment urgent. It examines the heart for a murmur or a muffled sound, the lungs for crackles, the veins of the neck for their height, and the legs for swelling. The decision at the end is to restore the circulation and to call for senior help, and the diagnosis is settled while that is already happening.

Altered consciousness is the presentation where the algorithm must be entered at the fastest door, because several of its causes are reversible within minutes and one of them, a low level of sugar in the blood, is the reason every such patient is tested or treated for it first. The path then checks the airway, the breathing, and the circulation, because a patient who is not moving air or not moving blood will not improve whatever else is done. It asks about the speed of onset, about a fall or a blow to the head, about fever, about medicines and poisons, about alcohol, and about the illnesses the patient already carries, and it looks for a medicine list, a medical alert card, or a witness who can describe the hours before. The examination searches for a difference between the two sides of the body, for the size and the reaction of the pupils, for the stiffness of the neck, for the smell of the breath, and for any injury that does not fit the story. The Glasgow coma scale is one way of recording the level of consciousness by the response to voice, to pain, and to command, and the exact figure at which it should cause alarm belongs to the current source and the local protocol rather than to memory. A clinic with no meter must still treat the possibility of low sugar on the clinical picture, and a patient who does not return to normal must travel.

The danger at the edge of this path is the patient who is assumed to be drunk, tired, or simply old. A slow bleed inside the head, an infection, a stroke, and a disturbance of the body chemistry all present at the beginning as sleepiness, and the finding that should stop the walk is any asymmetry, any fever, any injury that does not fit the story, or any deterioration across successive observations. The clinician should also ask whether the usual state of this patient is known, because a family member's account of what is normal for this person is worth more than one examination. Where a medicine is the cause, the path turns toward reviewing what was prescribed and what was actually taken, and the decision that follows is a diagnostic one rather than a question of amounts. Where no cause is found and the patient is not returning to normal, the honest exit is referral, made before the period of observation has been stretched past what the setting can safely provide.

In a hospital with every option available, the algorithm grows longer, and the danger changes from missing a branch to losing the patient inside the machinery. Each test added to the path costs time, and a path that waits for a result before acting on an obvious emergency has replaced judgment with sequence. The hospital also rewards a habit the clinic cannot afford, which is to investigate an interesting question that would not change what is done, and the clinician must keep asking which decision each result would alter. The strength of the hospital is the ability to answer the questions the clinic had to leave open, so the path there should be read as a set of questions awaiting answers rather than as a single verdict. A clinician who carries the discipline of the clinic into the hospital, and who treats every test as a question rather than as an answer, uses both settings well.

The clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer cannot shorten the path, but it can translate it. The translation is made by asking what question each unavailable test was meant to answer and then finding another way to ask it. A test for anemia is replaced by looking at the color of the conjunctiva and the palms and by asking about bleeding. A test for dehydration is replaced by the state of the mouth, the skin, the pulse, and the urine, and a picture of the chest is replaced by the work of breathing, the symmetry of the breath sounds, and the history of what has changed. What cannot be translated at all becomes a referral decision, and that decision should be made explicitly rather than left to the judgment of the patient about how ill he or she is. The clinic also holds an instrument the hospital often forgets, which is time, because the same patient can be seen again and the comparison between visits is itself a test of great value.

An algorithm that has been translated in this way is no longer the published path, and the clinician should say so in the record rather than pretend otherwise. The record should show where the path was entered, which branch was taken, which branch could not be followed, and what was done instead, and the Soap notes format gives that account a familiar shape. That habit has three uses, because it makes the reasoning visible to the next clinician, it exposes the assumptions that were made, and it allows the path to be improved the next time the same problem is seen. It also protects the patient, since a documented plan for review is a promise that someone will look again. A path followed without any of this becomes a ritual, and a ritual is the form an algorithm takes when its reasoning has been forgotten.

An algorithm and a differential diagnosis are different tools, and confusing them is a common error. The algorithm orders the next few minutes, while the differential list widens the field so that nothing important is left out, and the Vindicate framework belongs to that second task. A clinician who uses only the path will handle the common presentation well and the unusual patient badly, because the path contains only the branches its authors thought of. A clinician who uses only the list will generate possibilities without deciding what to do first. The two work together when the list is written down and then narrowed by the path, and the reasoning is complete only when both have had their turn.

A constructed illustration may show the difference, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine an older patient brought to a clinic with a cough and a fever, breathing a little quickly, whose hands are warm, and in whom the path stops at the work of breathing and sends the patient onward instead of home with a diagnosis of a chest infection. Now imagine a child with a fever and a rash, whose mother says the rash does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, and in whom the path reaches its red exit in the first minute rather than after the throat has been examined. Neither patient is real, and neither story should be applied to a living person without a full assessment. What the two share is that the algorithm did not make the decision; it made sure the decision was faced in the right order.

An algorithm is also a language, and much of its practical value lies in the handover between clinicians. When the night team is told which branch was taken and which question remains unanswered, the next shift begins where the last one stopped instead of starting again. The same clarity serves the patient, who should be told what would bring them back rather than be given a diagnosis that may yet prove wrong. Safety-netting is the branch at the end of every path that says what to do if the patient does not improve, and a path without it is incomplete. The clinician should name the findings that would mean the plan was wrong and should write them where the patient or the family can see them. The algorithm does not remove uncertainty and should not pretend to, because its real gift is making uncertainty explicit enough to be managed.

To summarize, a flowchart is reasoning made audible, a route of questions whose exits lead to treatment, to testing, to watching, or to referral, and it is learned by walking it aloud rather than by looking at it. The dangerous causes are named at the entrance and not at the end, so the febrile child with a rash that does not fade, the breathless adult who is tiring, the patient with tearing chest pain and unequal pulses, the patient in shock, and the patient whose consciousness has changed are each met by the finding that reveals them. An algorithm clarifies the common path and misleads at the edges, and the discipline that keeps it safe is asking what it assumes about the patient in front of the clinician, which population it was built in, and which of its branches cannot be followed here. The same path is walked in a hospital with every option and in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, where an unavailable test becomes a question asked another way or a referral made deliberately rather than a result assumed to be normal. Every figure in this chapter, whether a rate, a pressure, a temperature, an age, or a duration, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and a patient who does not fit the path is a reason to leave it and think again rather than to force the patient into it.

# Chapter 72 — Red Flags and Referral Criteria

Every clinician carries two questions through a consultation, one about what the patient probably has and one about what the patient must not be allowed to have, and this chapter is about the second. The findings that answer it are called red flags, and the name misleads if it suggests a list to memorize, because a red flag is simply a finding that changes the next decision. When a symptom, a sign, or a number raises the probability of a cause that will injure or kill the patient if it is not dealt with soon, the plan stops being one of watching and becomes one of acting. The action may be treatment, a test at once, a telephone call, or a journey to another town, and the choice among them is the subject of referral. This chapter is educational material; it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it is not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or local protocol.

A red flag can come from any of the three instruments of the encounter, and a clinician who watches only one will miss the others. From the history come a sudden onset, the worst pain of a life, a pain that arrives at rest or wakes the patient from sleep, an unintended loss of weight, a bleed from a place that should not bleed, or a change in awareness the family noticed first. From the examination come a neck that resists bending, a rash that does not disappear under pressure from a clear glass, a cold mottled limb, a tender testis that has risen, a mass in the abdomen or breast, and a weakness on one side. From the vital signs, the cheapest measurements in medicine, come the numbers that describe a body losing its fight, and their direction over repeated observations matters more than any single reading. A red flag is therefore not a diagnosis; it is a change in the probability of a dangerous diagnosis large enough to change what happens next.

Because the dangerous causes must be named where the flags belong to them, this chapter names them now, each with the finding that reveals it. A fever with a stiff neck, a severe headache, a dislike of light, or a clouded consciousness may be meningitis, revealed by resistance when the neck is flexed and sometimes by a rash that does not fade under pressure. A headache that reaches full severity almost at once may be bleeding around the brain, revealed by neck stiffness, vomiting, and a brief loss of consciousness, while a normal examination is the trap that delays the diagnosis. A sudden scrotal pain may be a twisted testis, which destroys the organ quickly, revealed by a testis sitting high and crosswise with an absent reflex when the inner thigh is stroked. Blood in the urine without pain may be a tumor of the bladder or kidney, an unintended loss of weight may be tuberculosis or a cancer, and a new confusion in an older patient may be infection, a low sugar, or a stroke.

The logic of the red flag is a logic of costs rather than certainties, which is why a common harmless finding can be a flag while a rare frightening one is not. A finding deserves the name when the harm of missing the dangerous cause behind it is greater than the harm of acting on it, and that comparison depends on what acting costs where the patient lies. In a hospital with a scanner and a laboratory, acting may mean a test that settles the question within an hour, so the threshold is low. In a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, acting may mean a journey of hours and the loss of a day's work, so the threshold must still be set by the danger rather than by the inconvenience.

Three dispositions follow from the reasoning, and naming them plainly helps clinician and patient alike. The first is that the patient must go now, meaning the danger is present or cannot be excluded and the next hour changes the outcome; this covers the fever with a stiff neck, the headache that arrived like a blow, the sudden scrotal pain, the crushing chest pain, and the patient who is pale and cold after bleeding. The second is that the patient must be referred, meaning the danger is possible rather than immediate and the assessment needed lies elsewhere, so the journey may wait until transport is arranged. The third is that the patient may be watched with a safety net, meaning the dangerous causes have been considered and can be excluded by observation, and the patient or family can recognize the findings that should bring the patient back. The three are not degrees of one decision but different decisions, and a clinician who cannot say which applies has not finished the assessment.

The vital signs deserve their own place, because they are the red flags no history or examination can replace and because they can be obtained almost anywhere. The breathing rate is the measurement most often skipped and the one that most often reveals a deteriorating patient, since the body raises it before the pressure falls. A rate above 20 breaths per minute in an adult is often treated as the point of concern, though that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A pulse above 100 beats per minute at rest carries the same caution, and the figure that should prompt action is stated differently by different services, so it must be checked locally rather than recalled. A pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury, or a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius, belongs to the same family, and each must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the accepted value depends on the usual reading and the site of measurement. What matters most is the direction of travel, because a pulse that climbs, a pressure that falls, or a patient harder to rouse than an hour ago tells the clinician what absolute numbers cannot.

The history contributes red flags of a different kind, because they are descriptions rather than measurements, and the description that matters most is the shape of the symptom in time. A pain that reached full intensity at once is a different illness from one that grew over weeks, and a weakness that appeared while the patient watched differs from one that crept forward for months. The clinician therefore asks whether the onset was sudden, what the patient was doing, whether the symptom is the worst of the patient's life, and whether it has happened before. Other history flags include unintended weight loss, drenching night sweats, a cough bringing blood, bleeding after the menopause, a pregnancy with pain or bleeding, a recent operation, and a medicine or illness that suppresses the immune defenses. Each raises the probability of a dangerous cause and is worth writing down even when the examination that follows is normal.

A normal examination never removes a red flag from the history, and the clinician who allows it to do so makes the error that fills the case reviews. The sudden severe headache has often eased by the time the patient is seen, and the patient with a twisted testis may have no swelling in the first hour. A patient with bleeding around the brain may have a neck that bends freely, and a patient with a clot in the lung may have a quiet chest. The examination and the tests describe the present moment, while the history describes an event that has already happened, and an event is not undone by a quiet interval. That is why the clinician records what was found and what was absent, and decides on the history, the vital signs, and the trajectory together.

Fever with a stiff neck is the clearest flag in this chapter and the one most often softened by a reassuring explanation. The patient may have a headache, a dislike of light, vomiting, and a level of consciousness that is not quite right, and the examination looks for resistance when the chin is brought to the chest, for a rash that does not fade under pressure, and for any change in awareness. In a hospital the next steps are blood cultures drawn before treatment where that does not delay it, a lumbar puncture when it is safe, and help from the most senior clinician available. In a clinic with a thermometer and a torch, the same reasoning leads to treating on the clinical suspicion and arranging immediate transfer, because the illness can kill within hours and the journey must not wait for a test that does not exist. An older patient, a patient with diabetes, and a patient whose immune defenses are suppressed may have a neck that bends easily, and the absence of stiffness proves nothing in them.

Headache of sudden onset is the second flag, and the word sudden is the whole of it. The patient often describes a blow at the back of the head, a pain that reached its worst in seconds, vomiting, and sometimes a moment of lost consciousness or a strange sensation down the back of the neck. The interval within which the pain reaches its peak is a description rather than a measured threshold, so a figure a listener may have heard, whether one minute or five minutes, must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A normal examination after such an event is common and is not reassuring, since the bleeding may have stopped, and where a computed tomography scan, known as CT, exists it is performed early. In a clinic with nothing but a torch and a thermometer this description means an immediate journey, because a pain that has settled does not make the patient safe.

Sudden scrotal pain is a flag of a special kind, because the danger is not death but the loss of an organ, and the window in which it can be saved is short. The twisted testis turns on its cord and its blood supply is squeezed, and the patient is usually a boy or young man with a pain that came on quickly, sometimes waking him from sleep, often with nausea. The findings that support it are a testis sitting higher than its fellow and lying crosswise, a tender swollen scrotum, and an absent reflex when the skin of the inner thigh is stroked, though swelling may hide all of these early. In a hospital the diagnosis is pursued with an ultrasound where that can be obtained without delay, and with a surgical opinion regardless of the image, while in a clinic the decision is taken at once, because there is no test and no time.

Blood in the urine that causes no pain is the quietest flag in this chapter, because it does not hurt, it may come and go, and it is easy to attribute to an infection already treated. Visible blood, or blood found on testing in a patient with no symptoms, may be the first evidence of a tumor of the bladder, kidney, or prostate, and the risk is higher in an older patient, a smoker, or a person exposed to certain industrial substances. Infection and stones are far more common causes and are the ones a clinician considers first, which is exactly why the flag is missed, since treating an infection will often make the blood disappear while the tumor continues to grow. In a hospital the examination includes the microscopy of the urine, imaging of the urinary tract, and inspection of the inside of the bladder with a camera. In a clinic with a torch and no laboratory the finding is made by looking at the urine in good light, and the action is an urgent referral with a written note of what was seen. Only a proven and fully treated infection, with the blood gone on repeat examination, makes the referral unnecessary, and that proof must be obtained rather than assumed.

An unintended loss of weight is a flag that develops slowly and is often noticed by the family before the patient mentions it. The clinician asks how much weight has been lost, over what interval, whether the appetite has changed, and whether the loss was intended, and a loss the patient cannot explain deserves investigation whatever the patient weighs now. The causes that must not be missed are tuberculosis, a cancer, advanced infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, unrecognized diabetes, an overactive thyroid gland, and a disease of the bowel that prevents absorption of food, and night sweats, a cough lasting weeks, enlarged lymph nodes, and a mass felt anywhere all belong to the same search. The interval over which a loss becomes concerning cannot be fixed, since a figure such as 5 per cent of body weight over 6 months appears in some sources and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A new confusion in an older patient is a flag frequently attributed to age, to a change of surroundings, or to temperament, and each of those explanations can be right while a lethal cause is present. The important word is new, and the person who knows the patient's usual state, often a relative or caregiver, is the most reliable witness. Causes that can kill or maim include infection anywhere in the body, a low level of sugar, a low level of oxygen, a disturbance of the salts, a stroke, bleeding inside the head after a fall, and the effect of a medicine or of alcohol withdrawal. The quiet form, in which the patient is drowsy and slow rather than loud and restless, is the form most often missed and is just as dangerous, and the Glasgow coma scale is one way of recording the level of consciousness, though the figure at which it should cause alarm must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. In a clinic the measurement of sugar where a meter exists is the single most useful act, since a low sugar is reversible within minutes and imitates every other cause, and a patient with no meter and a new confusion must travel.

The examination contributes flags that must be sought deliberately, because a clinician who waits for them to announce themselves will miss them. A rash that does not fade under pressure may mean bleeding into the skin from an infection in the bloodstream, and a limb that is cold, pale, mottled, or pulseless may be losing its blood supply. A pulsating abdominal mass with back pain raises the possibility of a swelling of the aorta about to tear, and a rigid silent abdomen with severe pain, vomiting of blood, or black stool points to a problem needing surgical or endoscopic help. A chest pain that is new, comes at rest, or wakes the patient from sleep is treated as a possible heart attack until an electrocardiogram, known as ECG, and the history say otherwise, and a new weakness, a drooping face, or a sudden loss of vision is a stroke until proved otherwise, with the level of sugar measured at once because a low sugar imitates it. A child who is drowsy, cannot be roused, breathes with effort, drinks poorly, or has mottled skin needs immediate assessment, since serious illness in a child is often quiet rather than dramatic.

Referral is not a single act but a decision with criteria, and the criteria are clinical rather than administrative. The first is the nature of the suspected danger and the speed with which it can cause harm, since an illness that kills within hours and one that progresses over months call for different journeys. The second is the trajectory, because a finding that is stable, one that is improving, and one that is worsening are three different findings. The third is what can be done where the patient is now, and the fourth is the reliability of the observation that would follow if the patient stayed. The fifth is the distance and cost of the journey, not because they change the danger but because they change what must be done before the patient leaves.

The patient who must go now is the one in whom the danger is present or cannot be excluded and an hour or two changes the outcome. This covers the fever with a stiff neck, the headache that arrived like a blow, the sudden scrotal pain, the chest pain that is new or comes at rest, the sudden breathlessness, the stroke, the severe abdominal pain with a rigid abdomen, and bleeding that will not stop. The clinician does not require a completed diagnosis before sending such a patient and does not wait for a test hours away, because the delay is the harm. Help is summoned by the fastest means available, the receiving service is told what is coming and why, a note is written with the findings, times, reasoning, and any treatment given, and the patient is not sent alone. Where an unresponsive patient is not breathing, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, known as CPR, is begun at once, and where the receiving service is a telephone call away the clinician calls before the patient leaves and records who gave the advice and what was said. Only a demonstrated alternative cause that accounts for every abnormal finding and cannot itself deteriorate would change this disposition.

The patient who must be referred is the one in whom the danger is possible rather than immediate and the assessment that would settle it lies elsewhere. The flags that lead here are quieter: the painless blood in the urine, the unintended loss of weight, the lump in the breast or neck, the lymph node that has not settled after several weeks, the change in bowel habit in an older patient, and the heart murmur that was not there before. The interval within which such a referral should be seen depends on the suspected diagnosis and the service, and a figure such as 2 weeks must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since priority categories differ between systems. The finding that moves the patient into the group that must go now is any sign that the danger is no longer theoretical, such as severe pain, new bleeding, a rapidly growing mass, or a general deterioration.

Watching is a legitimate disposition and not a confession of uncertainty, but it requires that the dangerous causes have been considered and can be excluded by observation where the patient is. A patient with a mild fever, a clear source, stable vital signs, and a reliable person at home may be watched with a plan, and a patient with a twisted testis may not, whatever the hour. The safety net must be specific, because a patient cannot act on the advice to return if things worsen, which transfers no information and creates no plan, so the clinician names the findings that should bring the patient back and asks the patient or family to repeat them. A safety net that depends on a telephone that does not work, a journey the family cannot afford, or a literacy the patient does not have is not a safety net. The interval for review is decided by the illness, and a figure such as 24 hours is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, while any stated interval of days carries the same caution.

When referral is a telephone call, the clinician has a short structured conversation with a colleague who has not seen the patient, and the structure is what makes the call work. The opening states who is calling, from where, and whether the patient is in front of the caller, because a colleague who knows the patient is being described listens differently. The next part states the problem in one sentence, with the suspected danger and the finding that raised it, and it is better to say that a stiff neck and a fever are the reason for the call than to recite the whole history in order. The third part gives the observations, the times, and the treatment already given, and the fourth states plainly what is asked for, whether advice, a bed, an operating room, a scan, or a specialist review. Where the call cannot be completed, the clinician does not treat that as an answer and uses the next available route, which may be a second number, a radio, a message carried by a relative, or a journey begun without confirmation.

Where the referral is a journey of some hours, the reasoning changes, because the patient will be without a clinician for a long stretch and the danger will have that time to act. The patient should travel with a person who can watch and who carries a written note stating the diagnosis suspected, the findings and times, the treatment given, the results of any test, and a number that can be called. A patient who is bleeding, confused, unable to drink, or losing pressure should not travel unattended, and a patient whose condition is worsening may need the nearest facility even when that is not the intended destination. When no vehicle exists, the obligation does not end, and the reasoning is to find the nearest thing that can help, which may be a health post, a community health worker, a radio, or a neighbor with transport, and to keep responsibility until someone else has accepted it. In this setting the threshold for referral is lower rather than higher, because the clinician is trading the risk of an unnecessary journey against the certainty of being unable to observe the patient.

There will be occasions when the receiving service declines the patient, when the bed is full, when transport does not come, or when the family refuses to travel, and the duty of the clinician continues through each of them. The first response is to make the clinical case again, in the terms the receiving service needs, and to record what was said and by whom, because a refusal that is not documented cannot be reviewed. The second is to seek another route to the same help, and the third is to make the patient as safe as the local setting allows while the search continues, which may mean treatment begun on the clinical picture, observation at shorter intervals, or the involvement of a relative who can watch. If no help can be reached, the clinician says so in plain words, explains what is likely to happen and what can still be done, and continues whatever care is possible, because the absence of a facility does not create the option of abandonment.

The documentation of a red flag is part of the diagnosis rather than an administrative afterthought, because a clinician who does not write down why the patient was sent cannot explain it later, and the next clinician must begin again. The reasoning should be visible in a sentence such as the fact that a fever with a headache and a dislike of light was treated as possible meningitis and the patient sent at once, because that carries more than a list of numbers. The record should also show what was absent, since a neck that bends freely at one visit and resists a few hours later are two different observations, and the time of each should be given. A referral note should be legible, dated, timed, signed, and free of abbreviations only the writer understands, and where the record is electronic the same discipline applies, because a template describes a patient who may not be the one in the bed.

A constructed illustration may show how a red flag decides the plan, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a young man who arrives at a village clinic with a sudden scrotal pain that woke him in the night, who is nauseated, and whose right testis sits higher than the left. The clinician has no ultrasound and no surgeon within a day's walk, and the reasoning is not to watch, not to treat for infection, and not to wait for the pain to settle, but to arrange the fastest possible journey with a note of what was found and when. This patient is not real, and the story should not be applied to a real person without a full assessment. What it shows is the move that matters, which is that the clinician recognized the finding that had to decide the plan and let it decide before knowing the answer.

To summarize, a red flag is any finding from the history, the examination, or the vital signs that raises the probability of a cause which will injure or kill the patient soon enough to change what is done next, and the discipline is to let that finding govern the plan before the diagnosis is complete. The dangerous situations are named where the flags belong to them: the fever with a stiff neck, the headache that arrived like a blow, the sudden scrotal pain, the painless blood in the urine, the unintended loss of weight, and the new confusion in an older patient. The disposition is one of three decisions, whether the patient must go now, must be referred, or may be watched with a safety net that is specific, understood, and possible. The same criteria apply whether the referral is a telephone call or a journey of hours, and the journey itself is part of the care. Every figure in this chapter, whether a rate, a temperature, a pressure, a duration, a cut-off, or a score, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. A normal examination never cancels an alarming story, and a clinician who recognizes the flag, acts on it, and documents the reasoning has done the most important thing this book can teach.

# Chapter 73 — Follow-Up and Safety-Netting

Follow-up and safety-netting are the parts of the consultation that begin at the moment the clinician stops being certain, and they are as much a clinical skill as the examination that came before them. A working diagnosis is not a conclusion but a commitment: it is the best explanation the evidence allows today, together with a plan for testing that explanation over the hours and days that follow. The clinician who offers a diagnosis as a finished answer closes the door on the very information that would correct it. The clinician who names the uncertainty, says what is being watched for, and describes what should happen if the picture changes keeps the diagnosis open long enough to be right. This chapter is educational material, and it is not medical advice, not a protocol, and not a substitute for training, supervision, or the judgment of the clinician who is with the patient.

Failures of follow-up kill more often than the diseases that cause them, and each kind announces itself with a finding that can be described before the patient leaves the room. The patient with chest discomfort who is sent home from a clinic may be having an acute myocardial infarction, and the finding that reveals it is a pain that has come at rest, lasts longer than the patient's usual discomfort, or arrives with sweating and nausea, because a normal examination and a single normal tracing exclude nothing. The child sent home with a fever may have meningitis or an infection of the bloodstream, and the findings that betray it are drowsiness, a refusal to drink, breathing that is visibly too fast for the age, a rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed against it, and a passage of urine that has nearly stopped. The patient whose test result never arrived may be carrying an anemia, a failing kidney, or tuberculosis that was visible on an image weeks earlier, and the finding is not a symptom at all but a result sitting unread in a book or a system. Naming these dangers at the outset sets the standard for everything that follows, because a safety net exists precisely to catch a diagnosis that is still moving.

The first task is to explain what a working diagnosis is, in words a patient can carry home. A clinician who says that nothing is wrong has usually said more than the evidence supports, and a patient who hears that phrase returns late, if at all, because the illness has been declared unimportant. A more honest sentence names the leading possibility, the dangerous possibility that is thought unlikely but not excluded, and the specific change that would overturn the assessment. It is useful to speak of probability in the language of ordinary life, as likely, possible, or unlikely, rather than in figures the listener cannot weigh. The patient is not being asked to become a diagnostician; the patient is being given a reason to come back that does not depend on trusting a feeling.

A follow-up appointment and a safety net are different instruments, and both are needed. A follow-up appointment is a planned review at a stated time, arranged so that a question left open can be answered once the illness has had time to declare itself. A safety net is a set of specific findings, described in advance, that should bring the patient back sooner than that appointment, together with the route by which the patient can return. The appointment answers the question of when the clinician will look again, while the safety net answers the question of what the patient should do if something happens before then. A follow-up without a safety net leaves the interval unguarded, and a safety net without a follow-up leaves a slow worsening unnoticed. The clinician should be able to state both, to the patient and in the record, without looking anything up.

Vagueness is the most common way a safety net fails. An instruction to return if things get worse transfers the whole judgment back to a person who has no training and no baseline, and it is heard as a courtesy rather than as a plan. A usable safety net names the symptom, the change in it, the interval over which the change matters, and the person or place to go to. It also names what should not wait, because a patient deciding at midnight needs to know whether the decision can be postponed until morning. The clinician who has never said these words aloud should practice them, because they are harder to construct than they appear.

The words must survive the journey home, which means they must be short, concrete, and free of the phrases clinicians use among themselves. A patient who is told to watch for a change in the character of the pain may remember nothing, while a patient who is told to come back if the pain arrives while sitting still, or if it wakes him from sleep, has something to hold. The clinician asks the patient to repeat the instructions in his own words and listens for what has been lost rather than for what has been reproduced. Where a family member is present, that person is included in the conversation, because the patient may be the one least able to judge a change. The most reliable test of a safety net is not whether it was said but whether it can be said back.

A safety net that lists 20 symptoms is remembered as none of them, so the clinician chooses the few that would reveal the condition being watched for. For a child with a fever, those are drowsiness, a refusal to drink, breathing that is too fast, and a rash that does not fade when pressed. For a patient with chest discomfort, they are pain at rest, pain that lasts longer than usual, sweating, and breathlessness. For a patient whose result is pending, they are the symptoms of the illness the test was looking for, together with the instruction to ask for the result by name. A short list is not a compromise; it is the only form in which a spoken plan survives.

The safety net often contains a figure, and a figure spoken aloud needs its caution attached in the same breath. A review arranged within 1 day is a common teaching example, and the interval that is safe for a particular illness must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since such intervals are set differently in different services. A fever said to begin at 38 degrees Celsius is another illustration, and that boundary too must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line shifts with the site of measurement, the age of the patient, and the edition of the reference. The clinician should say what the number is for, because a figure without a purpose is remembered as a rule and applied to the wrong illness. The patient does not need the explanation of why the line moves; the clinician does.

Literacy changes the form of a safety net and not its content. A patient who cannot read a discharge paper can still be told the plan aloud, asked to repeat it, and given a card with a few large words and a drawing that a literate relative or a neighbor can read later. Where numbers are written down, they are written as the patient will speak them, and a telephone number is copied in digits rather than in words. The clinic may keep its own copy of the plan, so that the same instructions can be repeated at the next visit even if the card is lost. A safety net that exists only on paper the patient cannot read has not been given at all.

Where the telephone is unreliable, the safety net must be built on something that does not depend on it. A patient with no credit, no signal, no electricity, or no one at home to answer cannot be recalled, and a plan that assumes a call is a plan that assumes a working system. The alternatives are ordinary and effective: a named person in the household or the village who agrees to watch for the findings, a community health worker who visits, a return date written where it can be seen, and a transport plan made while the patient is still in front of the clinician. Where the patient must travel far, the clinician asks how the journey will be made, who will pay for it, and who will decide that it is necessary. The answer to those questions often changes the follow-up interval, because a review that cannot be attended is not a review.

The long journey deserves the same reasoning as any other clinical obstacle. A patient who lives many hours from the nearest hospital weighs every return against wages lost, the fare, the care of children, and the risk of traveling at night. The safety net is therefore made real by lowering its cost: choosing the nearest possible point of return, arranging the review on a day when transport already runs, giving the patient a letter that names the concern so that another clinician can act on it, and stating an interval short enough to be worth the journey yet long enough to be possible. Where onward travel is the plan, that letter is part of the diagnosis rather than an administrative courtesy, and it should carry the working diagnosis, the findings that matter, and the specific question being asked. A patient sent to a hospital without such a letter may be examined as a new problem and lose the very reasoning that prompted the journey.

The safety net belongs in the record, and what is written is what makes it auditable and transferable. The note should show the working diagnosis, the possibilities still open, the specific findings that were discussed, the name of the person who received the instructions, the language in which they were given, and the route back. Where the patient was asked to repeat the plan, that check is recorded as well, because it changes what the clinician can fairly assume. The Soap notes format accommodates this naturally, since the plan section is the place where the commitment to review is written down. A note that records only a diagnosis and a medicine has recorded the least useful part of the consultation.

The discharged chest pain is the first of the dangers named at the outset and the one most often revisited. A patient whose discomfort has settled, whose examination is normal, and whose single tracing is normal may still be having an acute myocardial infarction, because both the examination and the tracing can be untouched while the illness is under way. The finding that should keep the patient under observation is a pain that has changed its pattern, arriving at rest, lasting longer than the patient's usual episode, or returning with sweating, nausea, or breathlessness. Where repeated tracings and repeated measurement of the substances released by damaged heart muscle are available, they are used, because one sample taken too early decides nothing. Where they are not available, the question is not whether the diagnosis is certain but whether the patient can safely travel to a place where it can be settled, and the answer is usually that the journey begins now. The finding that would make discharge reasonable is a confirmed alternative cause that explains every feature of the story, and even then a review must be arranged.

The child sent home with a fever is the second danger, and it is missed more often because the child may look well at the moment of the visit. The findings that reveal serious illness are a change in behavior rather than the height of the temperature: drowsiness that is hard to wake, a refusal to drink, breathing that is visibly too fast for the age, a passage of urine that has nearly stopped, a rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed against it, and a neck that resists being flexed. The child who improves after a cooling measure and then worsens again has not turned the corner, and the parent who reports that the child is simply not himself should be taken seriously. In a clinic with a thermometer and a torch, the assessment is repeated rather than replaced, and the parent is asked to return at a stated interval even if the child seems better. That interval is a local decision rather than a fixed rule, and any figure used in teaching must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the safe period of observation differs with age, with the season, and with the diseases that are circulating. The parent is also given those few findings in the parent's own words and asked to repeat them.

The test result that never arrived is the third danger, and it is a failure of the system before it is a failure of knowledge. A sample that was taken, a result that was abnormal, and a patient who was never told form a chain whose break is invisible to everyone except the patient who does not improve. The findings that should trigger a search for a lost result are an illness that continues despite reassurance, a symptom that fits the test that was sent, and an admission by the patient that nobody explained what happened to the sample. The practices that prevent it are unglamorous: a log of samples sent, a named person responsible for checking results each working day, a rule that the clinician who ordered the test owns the result until it is acted upon, and a route for the patient to ask for it by name. Where the hospital keeps an electronic record, the pending list is reviewed rather than trusted, because a result filed in the wrong place is as invisible as one never entered. Where there is no electronic record, the paper book and the telephone, however unreliable, are the system, and they must be worked deliberately.

A related failure happens at the second visit, when the patient returns and is reassured because the first diagnosis still fits. The clinician who recognizes the patient, remembers the working diagnosis, and repeats the original reasoning may anchor on it and miss the change that has occurred in the interval. The remedy is to take the history again rather than to continue it, to examine the patient afresh, and to ask what is different from the last visit. A sign that was absent before and is present now is the most valuable information a review can produce. This is why a planned review is not an administrative task but a new act of diagnosis.

In a hospital, the safety net is built into the systems that surround the patient, and it fails when those systems are assumed to work. The early warning score formalizes the reasoning about deterioration by combining the breathing rate, the pulse, the pressure, the temperature, and the level of consciousness into a figure that triggers a review, and any trigger used for escalation is a local convention that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the components and the trigger differ between services. The patient discharged from an emergency area needs a written plan naming the working diagnosis, the results still pending, and the review that has been arranged, and that document must travel with the patient rather than remain in the building. The pending result is the most common safety net failure in hospital, and the clinician who orders a test owns the duty to see it acted upon. The handover between shifts is a safety net of its own, and it carries the same three elements: what is known, what is uncertain, and what should happen if the uncertainty resolves in the wrong direction. The patient who leaves the intensive care unit, or ICU, is especially vulnerable, because the illness that nearly killed has been treated while the cause may not yet be named.

In the clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, the safety net carries more weight because fewer tests will interrupt the story. The instruments still answer real questions: the stethoscope for the murmur or the crackles that change the plan, the torch for the throat, the ear, the pupil, and the rash, and the thermometer for a fever that can be recorded and compared rather than guessed. A watch turns the pulse and the breathing into numbers that can be followed across visits, and a measured walk along a corridor or to the gate is a test of the whole circulation that requires nothing at all. Where the clinic can hold a patient for a few hours, observation becomes a diagnostic instrument, and the patient who is unchanged after that interval is a different patient from the one who has improved. Where it cannot, the plan is the referral, and the referral letter is written as carefully as a discharge summary, because it is the only thread that will survive the journey. The clinic should keep its own register of patients under review, so that a person who does not return can be sought rather than merely noted as absent.

The safety net is agreed rather than imposed, and the agreement changes its shape. A patient who works far from home, cares for a dependent relative, or cannot afford a second journey will weigh the plan against those realities, and a clinician who ignores them will write a plan that is not followed. Asking what the patient is able to do, and what would make a return impossible, produces a net that is smaller but real. The patient's own priorities belong in the same conversation, because an illness matters differently to a person who is finishing a harvest or raising small children. The clinician should also say what the plan is designed to catch, so that the patient understands that the return visit is not a formality. Agreement does not transfer responsibility to the patient; it makes the responsibility shared and therefore more likely to be honored.

Some patients cannot carry a safety net at all, and for them it must be given to someone else. An infant, a young child, an older person with a failing memory, a patient who is confused or sedated, a person whose mental illness distorts the judgment of danger, and a patient who is isolated or imprisoned all depend on another person to notice the change and to act. In these situations the clinician identifies that person by name, speaks to them directly rather than to the patient alone, and records who was informed. Where no such person exists, the net must be built from services rather than from family, which may mean a scheduled visit, a community health worker, or an admission that would not otherwise have been necessary. The clinician who assumes that someone at home is watching, without asking who that someone is, has left the most vulnerable patient unguarded.

The patient is the second observer of the illness, and the safety net teaches that observer what to look for. Most of what happens between visits is invisible to the clinician and visible to the patient or the family, and the quality of that report depends on what was asked for in advance. A patient who has been given a baseline, such as how far he can walk, how many times he wakes at night, or how much he drinks and passes, can describe a change against that baseline rather than against a vague sense of feeling unwell. Recording those baseline observations at the visit costs a minute and repays it many times over. The clinician should say plainly that a change in the baseline is the reason to return, and that the patient will not be thought foolish for coming back.

The clinician's own uncertainty is part of the safety net, and it must be handled rather than hidden. There are moments when the right safety net is not a plan for the patient but a conversation with a senior colleague, a specialist, or a team that has seen the problem more often. Asking for that help early is a clinical act rather than an admission of failure, and it changes the plan before the patient is discharged rather than after. Where advice cannot be reached, the clinician records what was decided, why, and what would prompt a further attempt. A second opinion obtained while the patient is still present is worth more than one obtained by telephone the next day. The clinician who is alone with a worrying patient should say so in the record, because invisible uncertainty is the kind that harms.

Waiting is sometimes the correct plan, but only when it is a decision with a boundary rather than the absence of one. A patient with a self-limiting illness may be watched, provided the clinician has said what would end the watching and when the watching expires. The boundary may be a time, a symptom, or a test result, and it must be stated in the record as clearly as any treatment. The danger of unstructured waiting is that it quietly becomes abandonment, and the patient who was told to wait does not know when waiting has failed.
