A defined period of observation is a diagnostic instrument, because the trajectory of an illness carries information that no single visit contains. The clinician who names the limit of the wait has made a diagnosis by other means.

A patient whose diagnosis depends on a result that has not returned needs a plan for the interval, not only a promise of a call. The clinician should say what is being looked for, how long the answer is expected to take, what the patient should do if symptoms change before it arrives, and how the result will be communicated. Where the test is urgent, the patient stays until it is available rather than leaving and being recalled. Where it is not, the interval should be chosen so that a treatable disease will not progress beyond help while the answer is awaited. The expected interval for any test is a local matter, since laboratories differ in their methods and their queues, and the figure should be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than assumed. The patient should also be told that a result which is not communicated is not the same as a result which is normal.

A constructed illustration may make the whole chapter concrete, and it is a teaching device rather than a portrait of any real person. Imagine a man who comes to a clinic with a cough of several weeks, a low fever in the evenings, and a weight he cannot account for, whose sample is sent and whose abnormal result is filed in a place nobody looks at again. Imagine a different morning in the same clinic, in which a child with a fever is drowsy, refuses to drink, and has a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, and the clinician stops the examination, gives the parent the few findings to watch for, and arranges the journey before the child leaves the room. Now imagine a third room, in which a man with chest discomfort that came at rest is given a letter naming the working diagnosis and is sent with a relative to a place where a tracing can be done. None of these people is real, and none of these stories should be applied to a real patient without a full assessment. What the three share is that the diagnosis was left open and the plan was made before the door closed.

To summarize, follow-up and safety-netting begin where certainty ends, and a working diagnosis is a commitment to review rather than a conclusion. A follow-up appointment sets the time of the next look, while a safety net names the specific findings that should bring the patient back sooner and the route by which that return is possible. The words must be short, concrete, and repeatable at home, checked by asking the patient or the family to say them back, and they must be workable where the journey is long, the telephone is unreliable, and literacy is limited. The three dangers are named where they belong: the chest discomfort discharged from a clinic, the child sent home with a fever, and the patient whose test result never arrived. Every figure in this chapter, whether a temperature, a rate, a duration, an interval, a score, or a cut-off, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because these numbers differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. The safety net is a clinical intervention rather than a courtesy, and the patient who understands when to come back is a patient who has been treated.

# Chapter 74 — Case-Based Learning

Case-based learning is the habit of taking a clinical presentation apart so that the reasoning becomes visible instead of staying buried in the conclusion. Its subject is a method rather than a disease, and its organizing idea is the branch point, the place in the story where the reasoning could have gone one way and went another. A book of principles can tell a listener what ought to be done, while a worked case shows where the ought is lost in the noise of a real morning. Four failures carry most of the teaching, and they are the differential that was too narrow, the test that was ordered too early, the sign that was missed, and the diagnosis that was correct but reached by luck. Every case here is a constructed illustration rather than a portrait of any identifiable patient. The material is educational, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Before any case is opened, the lethal possibilities that recur across presentations should be named with the finding that reveals each. A patient with chest discomfort may be having an acute myocardial infarction, and the revealing finding is a tracing that shows injury or a rise in the substances released by damaged heart muscle, although a normal examination proves nothing. A patient with fever and a change in behavior may have meningitis, and the revealing finding is resistance when the neck is flexed, sometimes with a rash that does not fade under pressure. A woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain and a missed period may have a pregnancy outside the uterus, and the revealing finding is a positive pregnancy test together with evidence of blood in the abdomen. A patient who becomes suddenly breathless may have a clot in the lung, and the revealing finding may be a swollen calf, although the leg can look entirely normal. These causes are named early because a case is a rehearsal for a real encounter, and the rehearsal should rehearse the danger first.

Three decisions about method are worth stating before the cases begin. Every case below is a constructed illustration, assembled to make a point and not drawn from any identifiable patient, so no detail in it should be matched to a real person. Each case is read twice, once with the instruments of a well-resourced hospital and once with the stethoscope, the torch, and the thermometer of a small clinic, because the instruments change and the reasoning does not. The listener should also build cases of his own, since a clinician who can construct a plausible case learns to see the branch points in the patients he actually meets. In a real encounter the branch point is never labeled, and learning to see it in a case is the first step in seeing it while the patient is still talking.

The first constructed case concerns a man in his sixties who comes to a clinic because of a burning discomfort behind the breastbone that has troubled him on and off for weeks. He says it comes on when he hurries and goes away when he stops, and he has decided that it is his stomach, because it improves when he belches and because a friend told him that heartburn behaves in this way. He takes a tablet for his stomach from time to time and says that it helps a little. He does not mention that he has diabetes, that he smoked for many years, or that his father died suddenly at about his own age, because nobody has asked him a question that would bring those facts out. The first words of the presentation are therefore a story about the stomach, and the branch point is already present in the first minute. A clinician who is listening for the branch point hears the word burning and does not stop there.

The narrow differential is the failure here, and it is easy because the story is coherent. A clinician who accepts the word heartburn has closed the question before examining the patient, and ischemic heart disease is often described as burning rather than crushing, which is why the phrase is dangerous. The revealing findings concern pattern rather than severity, such as discomfort that comes with effort, travels to the jaw or the arm, arrives with sweating, and eases with rest. The dangerous cause is acute coronary ischemia, and it must be named at once, not after the stomach has been treated for weeks. One question separates the two stories, and it is asked before any test, which is what the patient does when the discomfort begins. The patient who stops and waits for it to pass is describing effort angina, and the patient who reaches for an antacid is describing what he believes. The Socrates framework takes that description in a fixed order so that nothing is left out.

In the well-resourced reading, the clinic has an electrocardiogram, or ECG, and a laboratory, and the man is moved to a monitored area rather than sent home. The tracing is performed early and repeated, and the substances released by damaged heart muscle are measured in sequence rather than once, because a single normal result in the first hours settles nothing. A discomfort that has lasted about 20 minutes at rest, or that is new and different from what the patient knows, is treated as acute until it is proved otherwise, and that interval is offered only as an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the timing that matters shifts with the definition in use. The decision to treat before the results return belongs to the clinician who is with the patient, and the finding that would make immediate treatment wrong is a clear alternative cause that explains every part of the story. Even then the patient is observed rather than discharged, because observation is a plan and not a delay.

In the low-resource reading, the man arrives at a clinic that has a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, and no tracing and no laboratory. The history carries more weight because there is nothing to correct it, and the effort relationship is established by asking the patient to walk while he is watched. The examination seeks the signs that change the plan, which are the pulse, the pressure, the sounds of the heart and lungs, the signs of heart failure, and the pulses in the feet. The decision is then not a diagnosis but a journey, and a man with a new or changing exertional discomfort who looks unwell, who is sweating, or whose pulse or pressure is abnormal must travel to a place where a tracing can be done. The finding that would make the journey unnecessary is a confirmed and fully explanatory alternative cause, and a clinician who writes down what was considered and why the patient was sent onward has done the whole of the work that the setting allows.

The second constructed case concerns a young woman who comes to an emergency department with pain in the lower abdomen that began suddenly on the previous evening. She describes it as sharp and one-sided, with some dizziness when she stands, and she has had a small amount of vaginal bleeding that she took for an early period. She is pale, her pulse is quick, and she says she feels as though she might faint. She does not volunteer that her period is late by several weeks, and the triage note records pain and bleeding and nothing else. The clinician who reads only the note begins to think of an infection of the urine or a problem of the bowel, and the dangerous possibility drifts further away with every minute that the wrong question is asked.

The test ordered too early is the failure here, and it is subtle because the test itself was not wrong. The clinician sent her for an ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder before asking whether she could be pregnant, and the scan showed a little free fluid that was called normal. The decisive step, a pregnancy test, came hours later, after her pressure had fallen, and the delay changed everything. The dangerous cause is a pregnancy outside the uterus, which can bleed into the abdomen and kill, and the revealing findings are a positive pregnancy test, an empty uterus on imaging, free fluid, and a falling blood count. The sequence of tests is itself a clinical decision, and the cheapest question that would reframe the assessment should come first. A test is never neutral, because it consumes time, shapes the thinking that follows, and can be believed more than the patient is. The right order is therefore whether she could be pregnant, then whether she is bleeding internally, and only then what else this might be.

In the well-resourced reading, the pregnancy test is performed at the first contact, a line is placed into a vein, the blood count and the blood group are sent, and an ultrasound of the pelvis is requested with the specific question of whether there is a pregnancy inside the uterus. The patient is observed where her pressure can be checked repeatedly, and the finding that would prompt immediate surgical help is a falling pressure, worsening pain, or a growing collection of blood in the abdomen. The finding that would allow a quieter path is a stable patient with a negative pregnancy test and an alternative explanation that accounts for every symptom. The hospital has no special insight into this young woman, only the ability to measure the direction of her illness minute by minute and to act on what it measures. That ability is wasted when the first question has not been asked.

In the low-resource reading, the clinic has no laboratory and no scanner, and the single most valuable instrument is a question asked without embarrassment. A pregnancy test, where one is available, is worth more than any other test in this situation, and where it is not available the reasoning rests on the missed period, the pain, the dizziness, the bleeding, and the signs of internal loss. The clinician looks for a rapid pulse, a pressure that falls when the patient sits up, pallor of the inner eyelids and the palms, tenderness in the lower abdomen, and pain felt when the cervix is moved. The decision that follows is not a diagnosis but an evacuation toward surgical care, begun before the diagnosis is certain, because a woman who may be bleeding into her abdomen has no time to spare. The finding that would change that decision is a clearly stable patient with a benign and fully explanatory cause, and even then the plan is review and a short leash.

The third constructed case concerns an older man brought to a hospital because of severe pain in the lower back that came on suddenly while he was lifting a box. He has felt unwell since, has vomited once, and is restless in a way that the nurse finds difficult to describe. His skin is clammy, his pulse is fast, and the pain is not changed by movement of the spine in the way that a muscular strain would be. He is given a medicine for the pain and is left to wait for a radiograph of the spine. The important finding was available at the bedside to anyone who placed a hand on his abdomen, and the clinician who orders the radiograph first has asked the machine a question that the hand could have answered sooner.

The missed sign is the failure here, and it is a pulsating, expansile mass in the middle of the abdomen, felt slightly left of the midline, with a murmur over it. The dangerous cause is a leaking aneurysm of the abdominal aorta, which can rupture and kill within minutes, and the revealing findings are that mass, pain running into the back, a falling pressure, and a difference between the pulses in the two legs. The diagnosis is made with the hands, and no image is needed to justify calling for senior help and surgical care at once. A clinician who attributes back pain in an older man to muscular strain without palpating the abdomen has not examined the patient, whatever was written down. Any older patient with sudden severe back pain, especially one who smokes or has high pressure, should be considered to have an arterial cause until the abdomen has been felt. The examination is gentle, with the flat of the hand, and the diagnosis is unlikely when the aorta feels soft and no wider than expected and the pain is reproduced by movement.

In the well-resourced reading, the man is moved to a resuscitation area, the pressure is measured in both arms, a line is placed into a vein, and blood is sent for the count and for matching while a bedside ultrasound and a computed tomography, or CT, of the aorta are arranged. A pressure below a figure such as 85 millimeters of mercury is treated as a warning that rupture may be under way, and that figure is only a teaching illustration and must be reconciled with the current guideline and the local protocol, since the pressure that should alarm depends on the patient's own usual value. The patient is kept still, and the surgical team is called before the imaging is complete, because the image confirms what the hands have found. The finding that would change the plan is a mass that is clearly not arterial, and the finding that would make a slower path safe is a stable patient with a normal aorta on imaging. Speed matters here, and it is speed in the right direction only when the right question has been asked.

In the low-resource reading, there is no scanner and no operating theater, and the reasoning compresses into a single decision about whether this patient needs to travel now and how he can travel without dying on the way. The abdomen is examined for the pulsatile mass, the pulses in the groin and the feet are compared, the pressure is taken sitting and lying, and the color and the level of consciousness are recorded. The absence of imaging does not weaken the case for transfer, and a clinician who waits for confirmation that will never arrive loses the patient. The finding that justifies immediate transfer is the pulsatile mass with pain and a fall in pressure, and the finding that would make watchful review reasonable is a soft aorta with a mechanical pain. The hand is the most portable instrument in medicine, and the clinic cannot see the aneurysm and does not need to see it in order to act on it.

The fourth constructed case concerns a young man who arrives at a clinic complaining of sudden breathlessness and pain on the right side of the chest that worsens when he breathes in. He is tall and thin, he smoked a little in the past, and he looks anxious but not unwell. The clinician recognizes the picture, remembers a lecture, and treats him for a clot in the lung before any test is done, and the treatment is given with confidence. He improves, and the clinician records the case as a success. The diagnosis may well have been right, and the reasoning that produced it was almost entirely absent.

The correct diagnosis reached by luck is the failure here, and it is the hardest of the four to see because the outcome was good. The same picture can be produced by a collapsed lung, and a tension pneumothorax is lethal within minutes, with the revealing findings of absent breath sounds and increased resonance on one side, a windpipe pushed away from the affected side, and distended veins in the neck. It can also be produced by a myocardial infarction, by an infection of the lung, by a fracture of a rib, and by anxiety alone, and each of those carries a different decision. A clinician who cannot say what would have made him change his mind has not made a diagnosis, because he has made a guess that happened to land. The remedy is to speak the reasoning aloud before treating, naming the diagnosis he is acting on, the finding that supports it, the alternatives that would demand different action, and the observation that would make him stop. A right answer is not evidence of a right process, and the two must be judged separately when a case is reviewed.

In the well-resourced reading, the tracing and the chest radiograph are performed early, the oxygen level in the blood is measured, and the substances released by heart muscle and the test for the breakdown products of a clot are used to answer specific questions. A clinician who has named his hypothesis already knows which result would change his plan, and he repeats the examination after treatment rather than assuming that improvement proves the diagnosis. The finding that would redirect the whole assessment is a lung that does not move air on one side, and the response to that finding is immediate and physical rather than pharmaceutical. The hospital's power lies in the speed with which it can test a thought, and that speed is wasted when there is no thought to test. The tests are servants of the reasoning, and they become masters when the reasoning is absent.

In the low-resource reading, the same young man is examined with the eyes, the hands, and the ear, and much of the decisive information comes without any instrument. The clinician watches both sides of the chest move, listens over each side while the patient breathes through the mouth, taps the chest to compare the note, and feels the windpipe above the breastbone. The breathing rate is counted over a full minute and compared with a later count, and a rate that climbs, such as one reaching 30 breaths per minute, is an illustration of the reasoning to be checked against the guideline in force and the protocol of the local service, since the line between a comfortable and an alarming rate shifts with age and fitness. The decision is whether to treat on the clinical picture or to send the patient onward, and a patient whose air entry is absent on one side travels at once. Where a trained clinician can place a needle safely and the picture is a tension pneumothorax, the decision to relieve it is made on the examination alone, because waiting for an image is waiting for permission that arrives too late.

The differential that was too narrow deserves a paragraph of its own, because it is the failure that most often follows a correct and confident first impression. Anchoring begins with a plausible explanation and then bends the subsequent history toward it, so that the question about smoking is never asked and the answer about the walk is never heard. The remedy is structural rather than moral, because the clinician writes down at least one alternative that would change the plan and asks at least one question whose answer could break his first idea. The Vindicate framework is a way of forcing the field open, since it walks through the vascular, infectious, neoplastic, degenerative, intoxication, congenital, autoimmune, traumatic, and endocrine possibilities in turn. Using it on a case after the fact shows how many doors were never opened, and using it at the bedside keeps them open. A differential is not a list to be admired but a set of plans, each of which would be different.

The sign that was missed is the third failure mode, and it is usually missed because it was never sought rather than because it was hidden. The remedy is to make the examination deliberately complete at least once, in a fixed order, so that the parts easy to forget are performed whether or not the story points to them. The neck, the abdomen, the groin, the back, the perineum, the pressure areas, and every line and tube placed in the body are examined directly, because these are the places where evidence waits without announcing itself. Palpating the abdomen of every older patient with back pain is not an excess of caution, but the difference between a diagnosis made with the hands and a diagnosis missed with them. The clinician should record the findings that were sought and not only the ones that were found, because a note that says the abdomen was soft and the aorta of normal width tells the next reader that the question was asked. A complete examination performed once, deliberately, is worth more than many partial ones performed in a hurry.

Reviewing one's own cases begins with a written record made at the time. The note should carry the reasoning and not only the findings, which means what the clinician thought the problem was, what else it might have been, what was looked for and not found, and what was expected to happen. Soap notes are one way of arranging the record so that reasoning sits beside the findings and the plan, and a note that states the working diagnosis and the findings that would overturn it becomes a lesson in a few lines. Return to the case after the outcome is known and reconstruct the branch points in order, asking at each one what information was available and what was done with it. The review is best done against fixed questions, because a question not asked in advance is answered by memory in whatever way flatters the reviewer. Was the dangerous possibility named at the bedside, what finding would have revealed it, and was the differential wide enough to include a plan that differed.

Constructing cases for teaching carries obligations, and they are the same obligations that govern any discussion of a patient. The case must be explicitly described as constructed, its details must be altered so that no individual can be recognized, and the clinical content must be plausible enough to be worth rehearsing. A case that depends on a bizarre detail teaches the listener to look for the bizarre, while a case built from ordinary material teaches the pattern that is actually met. The instructor should decide in advance which failure mode the case is meant to demonstrate, and should leave the branch point visible without pointing at it. When the case is discussed, the first question should be about the reasoning and not about the answer, because the answer is the least transferable part of the exercise. A teaching case that ends with a diagnosis and no branch points has taught a fact, and facts are not what this method exists to depend on.

Case review is also where the numbers used in practice should be examined, because a figure carried from a course into a clinic can do quiet harm. A score, a cut-off, a reference range, a pressure, a temperature, a rate, or a duration named in a discussion is an illustration of the reasoning, and the reviewer should ask where it came from and in which population it was derived. Check every such figure against the guideline currently in force and the protocol of the local service and laboratory, because the same measurement is reported differently from one country to the next and the editions do not agree. A number whose origin cannot be stated should not decide anything about a person. In a clinic with no laboratory the review is conducted from memory unless the clinician keeps a simple log, and a log is worth the effort. A few lines for each patient, written the same day, recording the presentation, the reasoning, the decision, and what happened, will after a year hold more teaching than many textbooks. The instrument is unimportant, and the regularity is not.

The limits of case-based learning should be stated as plainly as its uses, so that it is not mistaken for the whole of clinical education. A case is a reconstruction, and a reconstruction is cleaner than the event it describes, because the irrelevant details have been removed and the chronology tidied. The listener learns to reason about described patients, and the skill that remains is the one that cannot easily be described, which is being present with a person who is frightened, uncomfortable, or unable to explain. That skill is learned at the bedside under supervision, and no case can replace it. A clinician who wishes to review his own cases can begin with one habit, which is to write down the reasoning at the time and return to it after the outcome is known. He then asks where the branch points were, which failure mode appeared, and what he would do differently with the same information and no more. Done regularly, this turns every case into a lesson, and it is the only form of case-based learning that a clinician can practice alone.

To summarize, case-based learning is the deliberate reconstruction of an encounter so that the reasoning becomes visible, and its organizing idea is the branch point where the story could have turned. Four failure modes carry most of the teaching: the differential that was too narrow, the test ordered too early, the sign that was missed, and the diagnosis correct but reached by luck. The constructed cases here are illustrations only, never drawn from an identifiable patient, and each is read in a well-resourced hospital and in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, where the instruments change and the reasoning does not. The lethal possibilities are named where the presentation is described, with the finding that reveals each, because a rehearsal should rehearse the danger first. Every score, cut-off, range, pressure, temperature, rate, and duration mentioned here is an illustration rather than a rule, and each must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures vary between countries, editions, and laboratories. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

# Chapter 75 — Clinical Judgment Under Uncertainty

Most decisions a clinician makes are made before the diagnosis is known, and the skill this chapter describes is the skill of working well inside that gap. Uncertainty is not a failure of training or a sign that the history was taken badly, because the information available at the moment of decision is always incomplete and the patient cannot wait for it to become complete. The question is never whether uncertainty exists, but which uncertainty can be carried and which must be resolved first. A working diagnosis is the best current explanation, held with the honesty that it may be wrong, and a plan is the set of actions that follows from it together with the findings that would overturn it. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

The most dangerous position in medicine is not the dramatic presentation but the patient who is watched while something lethal is already under way. The greatest risk in this chapter is deterioration during observation, and the finding that reveals it is a change in the vital signs taken together rather than any single abnormal value. A breathing rate that has climbed, a pulse that has quickened, a pressure that has fallen, or an alertness that is no longer what it was all say more than one reading alone. A patient with an infection who is watched expectantly may be developing sepsis, and the earliest evidence is often the breathing rate written beside the pulse. A patient with fever and headache who is watched may be developing meningitis, and the finding that betrays it is resistance when the neck is flexed. A patient with abdominal pain who is watched may be developing a perforated bowel, revealed by a change in the character of the pain and an abdomen that has become rigid and tender. Watchful waiting is a plan only when it has a defined question, a defined interval, and a defined action if the answer is bad.

Uncertainty is tolerable when every explanation on the short list is benign enough to wait, when the patient is stable by every measure available, and when a clear path exists to reach the answer within a time the illness allows. Uncertainty demands action when any possibility on that list could kill or disable the patient within the interval that observation would consume. This distinction separates the clinician who waits well from the clinician who waits dangerously, and it is decided by the worst possibility rather than the most likely one. The reasoning is not a calculation of probability alone, because a rare catastrophe that can be prevented weighs more than a common illness that would settle by itself. A useful habit is to name the one finding that would make waiting unacceptable, and to commit to looking for it at a stated time.

Watchful waiting becomes a plan when it is written down in the same terms as any other decision. The plan names the working diagnosis, the question that observation is meant to answer, the findings that will be sought, and the interval at which the patient will be reviewed. An interval of 4 hours is often used for a patient whose condition could change quickly, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the safe interval depends on the illness, the setting, and the resources available. The plan also names the person responsible for the review, because an observation that belongs to nobody is an observation that will not happen. It names the action if the patient improves, if the patient is unchanged, and if the patient worsens. It names what the family should watch for, and how they will reach help. A plan without a trigger for action is simply a delay with better manners.

The working diagnosis is a tool rather than a verdict, and it must be held in a way that allows it to be discarded. Naming it honestly means saying to the team, and where appropriate to the patient, that this is the current best explanation and not a certainty. The clinician who writes probable pneumonia on a chart and then stops looking for anything else has converted a working diagnosis into a closed question. The honest form records what the explanation accounts for and what it leaves unexplained, and an unexplained finding is a signal that the working diagnosis may be wrong. A patient whose fever is explained by a chest infection but who also has a new weakness of one side has two problems until proven otherwise. The clinician who states the uncertainty aloud gives the next clinician permission to disagree, which is one of the most useful gifts one doctor can give another.

The discipline of saying aloud what would change the plan is the single most protective habit in the care of an uncertain patient, because it converts a vague intention to keep an eye on things into a set of observable conditions. The statement takes a simple form: if this finding appears, then we will do that. If the breathing rate rises above the level we have set, the patient goes to the intensive care unit. If the pain moves to the right lower abdomen and the abdomen becomes rigid, the surgeon is called. If the confusion does not clear when the infection is treated, imaging of the brain is arranged. Each condition is spoken in advance, so that the decision is made calmly rather than at the moment of crisis, and so that any member of the team can act on it. A plan that exists only in one clinician's head dies when that clinician goes off duty.

Every diagnosis rests on assumptions about the patient, and those assumptions must be revisited whenever the patient changes. The assumption that the patient is normally independent may fail when a relative describes a slow decline over months. The assumption that the patient can give a reliable history may fail when the patient is confused, intoxicated, or speaking a language the clinician does not share. The assumption that the patient will return if worse may fail when the clinic is far away or the family has no transport. The assumption that the fever is infectious may fail when the patient has been taking a new medicine for several weeks. Reviewing these assumptions at each encounter catches the error that repetition would otherwise hide, and also catches the opposite error in which an early hypothesis is abandoned too readily because it once seemed uncertain.

Time is itself a diagnostic instrument, and in many presentations it is the only one that resolves the question. The abdomen that is soft at the first examination and rigid an hour later has told the clinician more than any single test could. A fever that settles over 2 days may belong to a self-limiting illness, while a fever unchanged after that interval asks a different question, and any such interval is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the expected course differs with the cause and with the patient. The clinician should record the time at which each finding was found, so that trajectory can be read from the record. The patient who is improving and the patient who is not are separated by the direction of change rather than by any single set of numbers. Where resources allow, the examination is repeated by the same clinician, because a comparison between two observers is weaker than one made by a single pair of eyes.

A short list of lethal possibilities deserves to be held in mind whenever a patient is observed without a diagnosis, because each can progress while the clinician waits. Sepsis is revealed by a rising breathing rate, a falling pressure, mottled skin, and a shrinking passage of urine. Meningitis is revealed by a stiff neck, a dislike of light, and a rash that does not fade when pressed. A pregnancy outside the uterus is revealed by lower abdominal pain, a missed period, and tenderness on internal examination, and in a clinic without imaging the possibility alone should prompt urgent referral. A clot in the lung is revealed by sudden breathlessness, a fast pulse, and a swollen tender calf, although the leg may look entirely normal. A tear in the aorta gives pain that moves between the chest and the back together with a difference in pressure between the two arms. A heart attack is revealed by chest discomfort with sweating and nausea, and the electrocardiogram, or ECG, together with the history carries the decision. A stroke is revealed by sudden weakness of the face, arm, or leg on one side with a change in speech.

In a well-resourced hospital, uncertainty is managed with instruments of measurement and with the people who can be gathered around the patient. The pressure, the pulse, the breathing rate, the temperature, and the level of alertness are recorded at intervals, and the trend is read rather than any single figure. Laboratory tests, an ECG, a chest radiograph, ultrasound, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging can be arranged within hours, and each is chosen because its result would change what is done next. The hospital can also bring the patient back for review, admit for observation, and call a colleague from another specialty for a second opinion. The advantage is not that uncertainty disappears but that it can be reduced faster and that deterioration can be detected earlier. The risk of the hospital is that the monitors are trusted more than the patient, so that a machine reading a normal number is believed while the patient is visibly worse, and alarms silenced repeatedly have allowed patients to deteriorate unnoticed in well-equipped wards. The clinician who looks at the patient before looking at the screen keeps the instrument in its proper place.

In a clinic that has a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, uncertainty is not abolished but it is managed with the same reasoning. The history is taken more carefully rather than less, because it is the instrument that never runs out, and the examination is performed completely because it may not be repeated. The torch makes the throat, the eardrum, the skin, the eyes, and the mouth visible, and the thermometer turns an impression into a number that can be compared at the next visit. The stethoscope carries the sounds of the heart, the lungs, and the abdomen, and a watch allows the pulse and the breathing rate to be counted rather than guessed. The clinician then builds a plan for the patient to carry home, and that plan is the treatment of uncertainty in this setting. The limitation of this setting is real and should be stated plainly to the patient rather than hidden, because the patient who knows the limit can help to compensate for it. Where the reasoning concludes that the answer cannot be reached without a test, the decision is not to guess but to send the patient where the test exists.

Of the two settings, observation at home holds the greater risk, and the reason lies in the distance between the patient and help. A patient in a hospital bed who worsens is seen within minutes, while a patient at home may spend hours or a day before anyone notices. The home setting also holds fewer instruments, fewer observers, and often a family who cannot judge whether a change is serious. The risk is greatest for the very young, the very old, the pregnant patient, the patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, and the patient who lives alone or far from care. The clinician should therefore raise the threshold for sending a patient home rather than lower it, because caution is the correct response to the greater hazard.

Mitigation begins with a safety net that the patient and the family can actually use. The clinician states in plain words the findings that should bring the patient back, and writes them down so that they are not lost. The patient is asked to repeat those findings in his or her own words, which is the only reliable test that the message was understood. The clinician checks that the patient can reach the clinic or the hospital, that someone at home can recognize a change, and that a telephone number works. A named person is given responsibility, whether a relative, a community health worker, or the clinician on the next shift. A review is arranged at a definite time rather than left to the patient's judgment, and where the journey to help is long the threshold for return is set lower and said explicitly. A safety net that has never been tested is a hope rather than a plan.

Some patients should not be observed at home at all, and the clinician who recognizes them prevents the most serious failure. The patient who looks unwell despite normal numbers, the patient whose vital signs are already abnormal, and the patient whose pain is severe or worsening all need more than a home plan. The patient with signs of organ failure, the patient with a stiff neck and a rash that does not fade, and the patient who is confused or difficult to rouse need treatment and senior help at once. The pregnant patient with abdominal pain or bleeding needs urgent assessment, because a pregnancy outside the uterus can bleed catastrophically. The patient whose immune defenses are suppressed, the patient with a device or a line in the body, and the infant who is feeding poorly should be referred even when the examination seems reassuring. The patient who cannot describe symptoms, who lives alone, or who has no means of returning should be admitted where that is possible. The decision to refer is a diagnostic decision, made on the reasoning rather than on a single measurement.

The patient who is watched for too long is the central failure this chapter exists to prevent. It does not happen because the clinician is careless, but because a working diagnosis has quietly become a belief. The clinician sees the patient improve in one respect and fails to weigh the finding that has become worse. The plan drifts from an interval into a hope, and the review promised at 4 hours is postponed until the next morning, and even that interval must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because what is safe in one service is not safe in another. The patient who is watched too long often has a normal early examination, and that normal examination is exactly what makes the delay feel safe. The remedy is a fixed trigger that does not depend on the clinician's impression at the end of a long shift, so that when the trigger is met the action happens without further deliberation. A clinician who notices the delay and escalates late has still done the right thing and should never be discouraged from doing it.

There comes a point in every uncertain case where the patient needs treatment before the diagnosis is settled, and choosing that point is part of the reasoning. Treatment before diagnosis is right when the patient looks seriously ill, when a dangerous treatable cause is strongly suspected, or when the harm of waiting exceeds the harm of treating something that turns out not to be present. It is also right when the patient's immune defenses are suppressed, because the usual signs may not appear and the illness can move faster than the tests. Treatment before diagnosis is wrong when a clear non-infectious cause explains the picture, when the patient is stable enough to allow the diagnosis to be completed safely, and when treating first would destroy the samples on which the diagnosis depends. The clinician should take the samples that can be taken without delaying treatment, and should record what was given and when. The finding that would justify treatment and the finding that would forbid it are more useful to name than any particular medicine, because the reasoning travels between settings while the available drugs do not. This book names the decision and never the amount, and nothing in it should be used as a prescription.

Tests are used differently under uncertainty, and the difference lies in what a result is expected to do. A test that can rule a dangerous condition in is worth doing early even when the suspicion is low. A test that can only rule a dangerous condition out is worth doing when a negative result would genuinely allow a safe plan. A normal result in a patient who is visibly unwell is not reassurance but a reason to reconsider the working diagnosis. A test whose result will not change the plan should not be ordered, because every test carries a cost, a delay, and the risk of a false result that sends the patient down a wrong path. Where the test does not exist, the clinician must ask whether the reasoning can proceed without it, and if it cannot, the patient must travel. Sending a patient away for a test that will not change management consumes a journey that might be needed later for a real one.

A time-limited trial is a useful device when the diagnosis cannot be settled and some decision must still be made. The clinician defines the finding that will be judged, the interval over which it will be judged, and the action that will follow either improvement or failure. An interval of 48 hours is sometimes used for such a trial, and that figure is an illustration of the reasoning that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the appropriate interval depends on the illness and on the setting. If the patient improves in the expected way, the working diagnosis is supported but not proven. If the patient does not improve, it is abandoned and the reasoning begins again. The trial protects the patient from indefinite treatment based on a hypothesis that has never been tested, and it protects against changing course too often because the interval is fixed in advance.

Some patients leave the clinic with a symptom but without a diagnosis, and that outcome can be safe if it is handled deliberately. The clinician states what has been excluded, what remains possible, and what the course of the illness has been so far. A review is arranged, and the patient is told that the absence of a name does not mean the absence of a plan. The clinician watches for the appearance of a new finding, because a diagnosis often declares itself over weeks rather than in one encounter. The temptation to give a harmless label in order to end the consultation should be resisted, because a false label can delay a true one for a long time. Where the patient is anxious, the anxiety should be acknowledged without letting it become the diagnosis. The record should make clear that the question remains open, so that the next clinician does not read the absence of a diagnosis as the absence of a problem.

Uncertainty belongs to the patient as much as to the clinician, and it should be explained in words that neither frighten nor deceive. The clinician can say that there are several possible explanations, that the most likely is one of them, and that the plan is designed to catch the others if they appear. The patient should hear what is being done and why, and should know what the plan will be if the first explanation turns out to be wrong. Saying that we do not know yet is honest and is usually better received than a confident answer that later collapses. The explanation should leave room for the patient's own knowledge, because the patient may know which symptom came first or which medicine was started recently. A family who understands the plan is a second observer and a partner in the safety net, while the clinician who shares uncertainty without sharing a plan has transferred anxiety rather than information.

Uncertainty handled alone is heavier and more error-prone than uncertainty handled by a team. Saying aloud to a colleague that the diagnosis does not fit is not an admission of weakness but a recognized method of reducing error. A second clinician often sees the finding that the first had stopped noticing, because attention narrows when a hypothesis forms. The team also allows the plan to be handed over safely, with the working diagnosis, the trigger for action, and the interval of review all stated. A handover that says only that the patient is stable, without saying what would make the patient unstable, has lost the reasoning. Escalation to a senior clinician is a diagnostic act, and the threshold for it should be low when the patient is uncertain rather than high.

The record of an uncertain case should contain the thinking and not only the findings. It should state the working diagnosis, the alternatives that remain possible, and the reasoning that ranked them. It should state the plan, the interval of review, the findings that would trigger action, and who is responsible. It should record what the patient was told, and in what words the safety net was given. The record should also show what was considered and set aside, and why, because that reasoning is what makes the next review faster. Soap notes are a familiar structure for this writing, and the assessment and the plan are the parts that carry the uncertainty. A record that shows only a diagnosis and a treatment leaves the next clinician unable to see how close the patient is to changing course.

A constructed illustration may make these habits concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a middle-aged patient brought to a hospital with fever and a cough, whose chest radiograph suggests an infection, and who is admitted with a working diagnosis of pneumonia. The breathing rate is recorded at 30 breaths per minute, which is faster than expected, and that figure is an illustration of reasoning and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the expected range depends on age and on the reference being used. The team writes a plan that names the trigger, which is a further rise in the breathing rate, a fall in the pressure, or a new confusion, and names the intensive care unit as the action if the trigger is met. Overnight the pressure begins to fall and the patient becomes drowsy, and the trigger is recognized by the nurse on the next shift because it was written down. The working diagnosis was reasonable, and the outcome was decided not by its correctness but by the plan attached to it, and neither the patient nor the hospital is real.

Now imagine the same reasoning in a clinic that has a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer. A young patient comes with lower abdominal pain, a missed period, and a pulse of 110 beats per minute, and that rate is another illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since what is normal varies with age, pregnancy, and fitness. The clinician cannot test for pregnancy and cannot image the pelvis, but the reasoning does not require either, because a missed period, lower abdominal pain, and a racing pulse together raise the possibility of a pregnancy outside the uterus. The dangerous cause is named at the bedside, the patient is not sent home to be watched, and the journey to a hospital begins immediately with a companion and a note that states the suspicion. The clinician also explains why the journey cannot wait, which is part of the treatment of uncertainty rather than an addition to it. In this case the plan was decided by what could not be excluded rather than by what was most likely, and again the patient is constructed and the situation is described for teaching only. The reasoning transfers between the two settings even when the instruments do not, and that is the argument of this whole book.

To summarize, uncertainty is the ordinary condition of clinical work rather than a failure, and the task is to decide which uncertainty can be carried and which demands action before anything else is done. The dangerous possibility is named early, and the presentation this chapter warns about most strongly is the patient who is watched while something lethal is already under way. The finding that reveals it is a change in the vital signs taken together, particularly the direction of the breathing rate, the pulse, the pressure, and the level of alertness. Watchful waiting is a plan only when it names the question, the interval, the trigger for action, and the person responsible, and a working diagnosis is held honestly as the best current explanation rather than as a verdict. Assumptions about the patient must be revisited each time the patient changes, and the clinician must say aloud what would change the plan. Observation at home carries the greater risk because help is further away, and it is mitigated by a safety net that is written, taught back, tested for transport and contact, and reviewed at a stated time. Every score, cut-off, interval, rate, pressure, and temperature named in this chapter is an illustration of reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because those figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and the clinician is not required to be certain but is required to be honest, to plan, and to act when the plan says act.

# Chapter 76 — Ethics and Patient-Centered Diagnosis

A diagnosis lands on a person's life as much as on a disease, and the two are never separated in the room where the news is given. This book reasons from findings and probabilities, but those findings come from someone with a body, a family, a language, a fear, and a right to be told what is happening. This chapter places that person at the center and asks three questions of every consultation: what does this patient understand, what has this patient agreed to, and what does this patient want done. The subject is not politeness added to diagnosis, but the same reasoning carried out with the patient as a participant rather than a specimen. This is educational material, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Several dangers belong at the beginning, because each grows out of how a diagnosis is conducted rather than out of the disease itself. The first is the treatable illness missed because the consultation closed politely and quickly, before the patient's real concern was spoken aloud. The finding that reveals it is the answer to one open question about what the patient feared most, together with a vital sign that was never repeated. The second danger is the error known and not disclosed, since a decision made on a hidden mistake rests on false information. The third is the test accepted without understanding, which leaves the patient unable to recognize the harm it causes. Each is exposed by something that costs nothing: an open question, a pause, and a note that records the reasoning.

Patient-centered diagnosis is a method rather than a manner, and it can be described as moves another clinician could repeat. The clinician asks for the patient's agenda before imposing a structure, listens for what the symptom means to this person, explains the reasoning in words the patient can hold, and then checks that the explanation has landed. Every patient also arrives with an explanation of what has happened, and that explanation belongs in the history rather than standing in its way. The patient may blame a fall, a curse, a food, a stress, a medicine, or a spiritual cause, and each belief shapes what is reported and withheld. Asking what the patient thinks is wrong, and what the patient fears, is a diagnostic act with a real yield.

The consultation opens with an invitation rather than an interrogation, and the first minute belongs to the patient. A question such as what made you come today, asked without a list attached, lets the patient begin where the alarm is greatest. The clinician lets the story run and notes the structure to be imposed later, because the Oldcarts framework is a discipline applied after the account has been heard. Silence is an instrument here, since the sentence added after a pause often carries the diagnosis. The clinician who cannot tolerate a pause collects the ordinary parts of the story and loses the dangerous one.

A patient can look well and be dying, and the ethics of diagnosis include the duty to look again when the appearance does not match the numbers. The febrile patient who has sat upright all night, the patient whose breathing rate has climbed without complaint, and the older patient who has grown quiet and stopped eating may all be released too early. The finding that reveals each is a set of vital signs taken together, repeated after an interval, and compared with what they were before. The clinician who notices the mismatch owes the patient an explanation of why the plan is changing, because a patient who does not understand may refuse and leave. Naming the dangerous possibility aloud, to the patient and to the next clinician, is part of treating the patient.

The examination is an intrusion the patient permits, and its manner teaches the patient whether to trust the clinician with the body as well as the history. The clinician says what is about to be done before touching, asks permission at each step, and keeps the patient covered except for the part being examined. A chaperone should be offered where the examination may feel exposing, and the order of the examination should be explained, because a patient who knows what comes next can relax against it. Teaching uses the same body as a place of learning, and that use requires a consent of its own. A patient who agrees to be seen has not agreed to be examined by a student or watched by learners, and a patient who refuses loses nothing in care.

Consent is a conversation that ends in a decision, not a signature that ends a conversation, and the form only records that the conversation happened. For consent to be real, the patient must understand and weigh the information, must be given what a reasonable person would want to know, and must be free to refuse without punishment or abandonment. The information that matters is the purpose of the test, what it involves, what it may find, what would happen if nothing were done, and what the alternatives are. The clinician should describe the uncertainty honestly, including the chance that a test settles nothing and leads only to another test. Consent taken as a formality produces a patient who has signed and has not agreed.

Capacity is the ability to make this decision at this moment, and it is assumed rather than withdrawn until there is reason to question it. The clinician tests it by asking the patient to say back what has been explained, to weigh the options in the patient's own terms, and to show that a choice follows from reasons the patient can give. A patient who refuses treatment the clinician believes is necessary has not thereby proved incapacity, and a patient who agrees with everything has not thereby proved capacity. Capacity can fluctuate with delirium, with pain, with exhaustion, and with a medicine given shortly before, so the assessment may need to be repeated. Where capacity is absent, the decision passes to the person whom the law and the local protocol designate, and that framework must be confirmed against the law of the place of practice.

The patient may also refuse, and the clinician's duty then shifts from persuading to protecting. A refusal is a decision to be understood rather than a problem to be overcome, so the clinician asks what the patient fears, corrects any misunderstanding, and records what was offered and what was decided. A patient with capacity who refuses admission for a condition that may kill has the right to do so, and the clinician's obligation is to make that refusal informed and to arrange the best possible follow-up rather than abandon the patient at the door. Safety-netting must then be explicit: the signs that should bring the patient back, the person who will check, and the time by which the check will happen. Any such interval must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because expectations differ between services and editions. A refusal is not a discharge, and the patient who refuses remains the clinician's patient.

Some consent is implicit in the arrangement, and the clinician should tell the difference between what the setting implies and what must be asked in words. A patient who joins a queue at a clinic has agreed to be seen, and a patient who rolls up a sleeve has agreed to have a pressure taken, but neither has agreed to an examination of the body. A queue is a place where patients are often examined in view of others, and the fact that everyone else is examined the same way is not a reason to skip the question. A brief sentence, spoken quietly, asking whether the clinician may look and naming what will be looked at, turns a public examination into a permitted one. Explicit consent belongs to everything invasive and everything uncertain, and a lumbar puncture, a biopsy, a sedated procedure, a photograph, a recording, or the storage of tissue for research each require their own conversation.

A test is an intervention, and ordering one is a clinical decision as serious as any other. Every investigation has a purpose, a burden, a chance of being wrong in either direction, and a chance of finding something that was never asked about. The clinician should be able to say what would be done differently for each possible result. An incidental finding can set off a chain of further tests whose harms may exceed the illness being sought, so the conversation before the test should mention the possibility of the unexpected result. A test ordered because it is available, because the clinician is uneasy, or because the patient expects something to be done is a test whose result is unlikely to be used well.

Telling a patient the diagnosis and explaining it are different acts, and both are owed. Telling is the short sentence that names the condition in words the patient already knows or can learn, with nothing hidden behind a phrase only a clinician understands. Explaining connects the name to what the patient will experience, what is known and unknown about the cause, what the options are, and what happens next. The order matters, because news delivered before the patient has somewhere to put it will not be retained, and a flood of detail delivered with the news is heard as noise. The clinician should therefore tell, stop, and let the patient respond before explaining, since the response shows how much can be carried at this visit.

The setting in which news is given is part of the news itself, because a patient told in a corridor hears the words as a verdict delivered in passing. A short warning sentence before the news allows the patient a moment to prepare, and the pause that follows belongs to the patient rather than to the clinician's need to fill it. The diagnosis should be repeated at the end of the visit and again at the next, because shock interferes with memory. Asking the patient to say the plan back in their own words is worth more than asking whether everything is clear. Where the diagnosis is uncertain, that uncertainty is part of the news and is better told plainly than buried under a comfortable guess.

Language is not a detail of the encounter but the encounter itself, and a diagnosis delivered through a relative who edits it is a diagnosis the patient may not receive at all. The clinician should use an interpreter where one is available and should speak to the patient rather than about the patient, because a person described in the third person becomes an object in their own consultation. A family's request to keep the diagnosis from the patient is common and should be handled as a question about the patient's own preference, since many patients said to be too fragile to know already know or wish to be told. Confidentiality within a family is not one rule but a series of decisions, and the patient's consent decides who may be told what. A relative who asks for information about a patient who has not agreed to share it should receive an explanation rather than the information itself.

Honesty and hope are not opposites, and the clinician who withholds the truth to protect hope usually damages both. Hope is best understood as a direction rather than a forecast, since hope for comfort, for time, for a particular event, or for a dignified death remains available even when a cure does not. The clinician therefore tells what is known, states plainly what is not known, and then turns to what can still be done, which is never nothing at all. A promise not to abandon the patient is the sentence most often remembered from a difficult consultation. The patient also has the right not to be told, and that right is respected without abandoning the duty of care, though the limits appear where the patient must know something in order to consent or to act.

Shared decision-making belongs where the reasonable options are genuinely balanced and the choice turns on what the patient values. When one option is clearly better on the evidence, the clinician owes the patient a recommendation rather than a menu, and offering a false balance abandons the patient to a decision the clinician is better placed to frame. When the options are balanced, the clinician lays out what each offers and what each costs in terms the patient lives with, including work, family, sleep, pain, travel, and the chance of being present for a particular event. The patient's values then decide, and the clinician's task is to make sure those values are informed rather than to make the choice instead of the patient. Recording who was present, what was explained, and what the patient chose turns a conversation into a plan.

Uncertainty is the ordinary condition of diagnosis, and admitting it is a skill rather than a confession. A clinician who says plainly that the evidence does not yet separate the possibilities, and then states what will be done to narrow them, gives the patient something solid to hold. A confident answer that later collapses destroys the trust that honesty would have protected. A working diagnosis should be named as working, and its replacement should be explained when the evidence moves rather than quietly abandoned. Uncertainty that is communicated becomes a shared plan, while uncertainty that is hidden becomes a private worry for the clinician and a surprise for the patient.

Diagnostic error is not an unusual event but a predictable feature of a process that depends on incomplete information, limited time, and human attention. Errors arise from a missed finding, a wrong weighting of evidence, an interrupted handover, a test that was never followed up, or a shortcut in reasoning that closed the question too early. The clinician's own mind contributes through the biases that make a first impression sticky, and the system contributes through fatigue, understaffing, and a queue that allows no second look. Naming the source honestly matters, because a purely personal account produces shame and concealment while a purely systemic account produces an excuse. Both are true at once, and both must be addressed if the same error is not to reach the next patient.

When an error is recognized, the duty to disclose it is owed to the patient, and it does not depend on whether the patient would otherwise find out. Disclosure means telling the patient in plain words what happened, what is known about the consequences, what will be done to correct the situation, and what the patient can expect next. The conversation should include what changes in the patient's care as a result, because a disclosure that ends with nothing is heard as an apology for a problem that is still present. An apology is owed as well, and it names the harm, accepts responsibility for the part that belongs to the clinician or the service, and expresses regret. Honesty after an error is an obligation rather than a technique, and it is owed whether or not it repairs the relationship.

The duty created by an error reaches past the patient who suffered it, because the next patient has not yet been harmed and can still be protected. The clinician records what happened in terms that make the system visible, reports it through the channel the service provides, and takes part in the review that asks how the same error could happen again. A review that ends with a name and a warning accomplishes little, while a review that ends with a change in the handover, the follow-up, or the way results are tracked protects patients who will never know it. The record itself is an ethical instrument rather than a diary of impressions, and it should show what was found, what was considered and set aside, what was explained, what the patient chose, and the plan for the next review. Statements that judge the patient's character or record a colleague's error in a way that invites blame should not enter the record, because the record follows the patient and may be read by the patient.

Confidentiality protects more than privacy, because it protects the patient's willingness to return and to speak. A diagnosis of infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, known as HIV, of a mental illness, of a sexually transmitted infection, or of an addiction carries a social cost the clinician must anticipate. The corridor, the shared waiting area, and the open ward are places where that cost is imposed, so the clinician should ask before speaking in front of a relative and should avoid naming a diagnosis where others may hear. An infectious disease that must be reported, a partner who may be at risk, or a driver whose condition may endanger others raises a conflict between confidentiality and the protection of third parties. The clinician should not resolve that conflict alone and silently, and the requirement differs between countries and must be confirmed against the current law and the local protocol.

A consultation with neither time nor privacy is not excused from the ethical essentials, and the essentials are fewer than they appear. The patient must be greeted and given the chance to say what brought them, must be told what is being done and asked before it is done, must be told what has been found and what the plan is, and must be told what should bring them back. A short consultation can still have a structure, in which the clinician sits if there is a seat, opens with an invitation, and asks permission before touching. After the examination, the clinician says what has been found, what remains uncertain, and which symptoms should bring the patient back sooner, and then asks the patient to repeat the plan. The clinician who preserves these essentials in the hardest setting is practicing the same medicine as the clinician in the private room.

A constructed illustration may make the contrast concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a hospital clinic where a man is told that the shadow on his chest radiograph is a tumor, in a room with a door, a chair for his wife, and a clinician who has put the telephone aside. The clinician gives the warning sentence, waits, names the diagnosis in plain words, and then explains what is known and what will be tested. Now imagine the same conversation in a district clinic whose waiting area is a bench under a tree, where the clinician calls the patient to the far end of the veranda and sits beside him rather than across from him. The news is given in the same order, shortened to what the patient can hold, and the warning sentence, the pause, the name of the illness, and the promise not to abandon him are all preserved. Both patients are invented, and the point of placing them together is that the ethical content of the two consultations is the same while the resources are not.

Children require a different arrangement, since the decision usually rests with a parent while the child remains a person with a view. The clinician should explain at the child's level, should ask the child's assent before an examination or a test where the child can give it, and should treat distress as information rather than as an obstacle. A patient who cannot speak, hear, see, or remember is owed more effort rather than less, because the usual route to the history is closed. The clinician should use whatever channel remains, whether writing, gesture, a familiar person, or a quiet room where speech can be heard, and a patient with aphasia should be given simple questions answerable with yes or no. The age at which a young person may consent alone differs between jurisdictions and must be confirmed against the law and the protocol of the place of practice.

A test that will not change comfort, that requires a journey the patient cannot make, or that consumes time the patient could spend with family should not be ordered simply because it exists. The clinician should explain why the question is being closed and what will take its place, because a patient who hears only that nothing more will be done may hear abandonment. A diagnosis is transferred between clinicians many times, and each transfer is an ethical moment as well as a clinical one. The clinician who hands over a patient should say what is known, what is suspected, what has been excluded, what is awaited, and what would change the plan, because a handover that lists only the diagnosis transfers the conclusion and loses the reasoning. A result that is awaited must be tracked by a named person, because the result nobody owns is the one that is missed.

Safety-netting belongs to the same duty, and the patient should be told which symptoms would mean the working diagnosis was wrong or the illness had changed, when to return, whom to contact, and what to do if that person cannot be reached. The clinician should check that the patient can repeat the plan and has the means to act on it, which may include money for travel or a telephone that works. Where the risk is high the net should be tighter, with an interval confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services set their expectations differently. Treating a colleague, a friend, or a relative brings pressures that damage judgment, and the clinician may skip the examination that would be embarrassing or order a test to be reassuring rather than informative. The best arrangement is usually to hand the care to someone else while remaining a support, and to say clearly why that is being done.

The record belongs to the patient in a moral sense even where the law assigns it to the institution, and a patient who asks to see it should be met with help rather than resistance. Reading it can correct a misunderstanding, reveal an error, and allow the patient to take part in the next decision, so the record should be written in the knowledge that the patient may read it. The ethical failures of diagnosis are often produced by the conditions in which diagnosis is done, and a queue that allows no second look, a shift that runs past the point of safe attention, and a handover in a corridor all shape the decisions that follow. The clinician should use whatever authority exists to protect the time a difficult conversation requires, and where the system cannot be changed the honest response is to say what it prevented in the record. Patient-centered diagnosis is not a separate subject from good diagnosis but the condition under which good diagnosis happens.

The clinician who holds both the reasoning and the person in view makes fewer errors, is told more, and is trusted with the truth when the truth is bad. A diagnosis that is technically correct and delivered without consent, without explanation, or without a plan has failed at the level that matters most to the person who received it. The whole of this book, from the first look at the patient to the last decision about follow-up, is carried out on someone whose life the diagnosis will change. The discipline is to remember that in every consultation, including the ones that are too short, too public, and too sad. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

To summarize, a diagnosis belongs to the person who receives it as much as to the clinician who makes it, and the ethical work is part of the diagnostic work rather than an addition to it. The dangerous failures of the process are named early: the treatable illness missed because the consultation closed before the patient's concern was spoken, the error known and not disclosed, the test done without understanding, and the patient sent home without a net. Telling and explaining are distinct acts, consent is a conversation rather than a signature, and the consent implied by a queue does not cover an examination of the body, a procedure, or a use of the patient for teaching. Where the options are balanced the patient's values decide, where they are not the clinician owes a recommendation, and uncertainty is stated plainly because hidden uncertainty becomes a private worry and a public surprise. The duty created by an error reaches past the patient who suffered it, through disclosure and apology to the record, the review, and the next patient. Every score, cut-off, reference range, pressure, temperature, rate, interval, or duration mentioned in this chapter is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. The essentials of dignity, consent, disclosure, and follow-up can be preserved in a private room and in a clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer, and the clinician who preserves them in the harder setting has understood the point.

# Chapter 77 — Teaching and Self-Assessment

The reasoning this book has described is not absorbed by hearing it once, and it does not stay with the clinician who learned it quickly and then stopped. What keeps it is a set of habits deliberately built: practice on real patients, a commitment to a diagnosis made before the result arrives, feedback that is sought rather than awaited, errors reviewed without shame, and a practice audited against what happened to its patients. A manual can describe reasoning, but only practice keeps it alive, which is why this chapter is about learning and teaching rather than about one more disease. The material is educational and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen. It is offered to the student at the bedside, to the clinician who works alone, and to the teacher who must draw the reasoning out of someone else.
