The dangerous possibility this chapter keeps in view is not one disease but the missed diagnosis of anything that kills within hours, and the finding that most often reveals it is the direction of the observations across time rather than any single reading. One constructed patient arrives with a new chest discomfort and a fast pulse, the discomfort settles with rest, and the clinician sends the patient home after recording the improvement, while the electrocardiogram, or ECG, that the danger required was never obtained. Another constructed patient has a breathing rate that climbs from one recording to the next while the plan in the notes stays the same, and that mismatch betrays a deterioration nobody noticed. A breathing rate of 20 breaths per minute is often quoted as the line above which concern should rise, but that figure is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line moves with age, with pregnancy, and with the edition of the reference in use. Such misses come not from ignorance of a disease but from a reasoning habit never examined, which is why this subject belongs to safety rather than to academic polish.

Learning to reason begins when the learner stops reading about diagnosis and starts making diagnoses that can be checked. Deliberate practice has three parts: work at the edge of present ability, immediate feedback on how the work turned out, and repetition of the same kind of problem until the reasoning becomes reliable. In diagnosis the edge of ability is a real patient whose presentation is not quite clear, the feedback is the result of a test or the later course of the illness, and the repetition is the next patient with a similar story. The teacher's task is therefore not to supply information but to arrange the conditions in which reasoning is practiced and corrected.

Every chapter read and every lecture heard leaves a comfortable illusion of having understood something that has not yet been used. Recognition is not recall, and recall is not reasoning, so a clinician may recognize a disease on a page and still fail to consider it while the patient is talking. The remedy is to make the reasoning visible while it happens, by saying it aloud, writing it in the note, or answering a question before the answer is known. A learner who says that this looks like an infection of the lungs because the fever is high and the breathing is fast has produced something that can be examined and corrected, while a learner who nods at the same facts has produced nothing.

The most useful discipline in self-assessment is to commit to a diagnosis before the result that will settle it arrives. The commitment should be written down with the reasoning behind it and a rough statement of confidence, because a judgment kept only in the mind is revised by memory to fit whatever happens next. When the result arrives, the clinician compares it with the commitment, and the comparison teaches what no result can teach alone: whether the reasoning was sound, sound but unlucky, or whether a finding was available and ignored. In a hospital the commitment can be a line before the scan, and in a place with no scan it can be a line before the referral, stating what is expected and why.

In a clinic where no test will arrive, the commitment takes the form of the plan written before the patient leaves. The clinician states the working diagnosis, the finding that supports it, the findings that would overturn it, and the signs that should bring the patient back. That plan is tested by the follow-up visit, which is the only laboratory the clinic possesses, and a plan that names what would change it is a hypothesis rather than a habit. The clinician who reviews the plans of the past period against what happened to those patients is doing audit at the smallest scale, and it costs nothing but attention.

Reviewing one's own reasoning is hard because the mind rewrites the past to make the present seem inevitable. Once a diagnosis is known, every earlier finding appears to have pointed toward it, and the moment when several possibilities were equally open is forgotten. This is why the original record matters, and why a note containing only a conclusion cannot be reviewed at all; the clinician who wrote that the illness was probably viral but that the neck was stiff has left a trace that a bare diagnosis destroys. Reconstructing what was known at the time, rather than what is known now, is what turns a mistake into a lesson.

The review of one's own errors must be conducted without humiliation, because humiliation produces concealment and concealment produces the next error. An error is information about the system that produced it, which includes the clinician, the team, the record, the equipment, and the time available. A bad outcome is not the same as an error, and a sound decision made with the information at hand can end badly, so confusing the two destroys careful clinicians and flatters the lucky ones. The useful question is not who is at fault but what made the wrong path look reasonable and what would have made the right path visible.

A method helps, and it can be a few questions asked in order. What did I think was happening, and which finding supported that thought? What else could have explained the picture, and on what grounds did I set it aside? What would have changed my plan, and at what moment could that change still have been made? The answers belong in a private register of the cases that surprised the clinician, which becomes the most personal textbook the clinician will ever own and reveals, across many cases, the presentations habitually dismissed and the findings habitually not sought.

Feedback on reasoning rarely arrives by itself, because the patient who recovers does not return to say the diagnosis was right, and the patient who does badly often goes elsewhere. The silence after a consultation is therefore not evidence of success, and the clinician who waits for feedback will wait a long time. What works is to ask for it directly, at the moment when the person who can answer is still present. A question that asks what the other person would have done differently produces more than one that asks whether everything was all right, because the first invites a description and the second a reassurance.

In a hospital the colleague is close at hand, and the habit is the informal second opinion asked before a decision hardens rather than after it fails. In a clinic with one clinician, the colleague may be a distant voice on a telephone, a periodic supervisor, or a group of peers who meet over cases they have each seen. What matters is not the seniority of the person asked but the freshness of the eye, because a clinician who has already decided is least able to see the alternative. The question to ask is narrow: here is the story, here is what I think, and here is what I may be missing.

The record makes all of this possible, and it must be written for the reviewer rather than for the bill. A note showing the reasoning, the alternatives considered, the findings sought and not found, and the plan with its review conditions can be audited by the clinician who wrote it and by anyone who follows. A note showing only a diagnosis cannot be audited, taught from, or used to protect the patient at the next visit. The Soap notes framework, which separates the subjective account, the objective findings, the assessment, and the plan, keeps those elements from dissolving into one another, and it is a scaffold for thought as much as a format for writing.

Audit compares what a practice does with what happens to the patients it serves, and it can be done anywhere. The clinician who keeps a register of every patient sent home with chest pain, referred with a fever, or returned unwell soon afterwards, and who then looks at what became of them, is conducting an audit. The purpose is not a report for someone else but a view of one's own patterns, and the most valuable finding is usually a group of patients who were not followed up at all. The standard a service adopts for follow-up, and the interval at which it is applied, must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because what counts as adequate follow-up differs between settings and editions.

Many services hold a meeting that reviews a death or a serious complication, and its value depends on how it is conducted. A meeting that searches for a person to blame will receive fewer and less honest cases each time, until it receives none, while a meeting that asks what the team knew, what the record shows, and what would have made the outcome different will produce lasting change. The clinician whose patient died should speak first and at length, without being interrupted by a defense. The conclusions should name both the reasoning that could improve and the resources that were missing, because a broken thermometer and a missed diagnosis can belong to the same story.

The teacher's central skill is the question that draws reasoning out rather than the question that tests recall. A question asking for a fact can be answered with a word or a number and teaches nothing about how the answer was reached, while a question asking why this finding matters, what else might produce it, what would change the plan, and what the clinician would do without the test forces a chain of thought into the open. The teacher should wait after asking, because the silence that follows a good question is where thinking happens, and filling it destroys the exercise. The learner should commit before the teacher comments, since a comment made first only replaces the learner's reasoning with the teacher's.

Questioning must not become an interrogation, and the difference is whether the learner is helped to think or shown to be wrong. A chain of questions designed to arrive at a predetermined answer is recall testing in disguise, and the learner only guesses what the teacher wants. A better pattern is to ask for the working diagnosis and its reasoning, then for the finding that would overturn it, then for what the learner will actually do. When the reasoning is faulty, the correction should aim at the step that failed rather than at the person, which is the same discipline the clinician owes his or her own errors.

The examination is taught by demonstration, then supervised repetition, then independent performance with a report. The teacher should watch the learner rather than the patient for part of every encounter, because the commonest fault is not a missed sign but a step never performed at all. The learner should say what is being sought before the hand moves, so the maneuver is connected to a question rather than performed as a ritual. Where the examination is normal, the teacher should ask what that normality excludes and what it does not, because the meaning of a normal finding is the part most often left unlearned.

Frameworks such as Socrates for the pain story, Oldcarts for the history of the present illness, and Vindicate for the differential diagnosis are taught as scaffolds, and they should be presented that way. They prevent the omission that comes from enthusiasm, and they are most useful to the beginner and to the clinician who is tired or interrupted. They diagnose nothing, and a clinician who fills in every letter and then names the first disease that fits has used the framework as a substitute for thought. The teacher should show where the framework ends, which is where this particular patient differs from the general pattern.

In a well-resourced hospital the learner has instruments that a book can only describe, and each should test reasoning rather than replace it. The ECG library allows tracings to be read against the clinical story, and the learner should predict the tracing before it is shown, while imaging by ultrasound, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging lets anatomical reasoning be checked against what the image shows. The intensive care unit, or ICU, records trajectories of pulse, pressure, breathing, and urine output continuously, which makes it the best classroom for learning what a trend means. A systolic pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the point at which shock must be assumed, and that figure is likewise an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the pressure that matters depends on the patient's usual value, age, and pregnancy.

Simulation is valuable and has a limit that should be stated to learners. A mannequin does not look at the clinician with fear, does not answer a question in a way that changes the story, and does not have a family in the corridor. Communication and the reading of a person's face are practiced only on people, and they are as diagnostic as any test, so a learner comfortable in a simulated emergency and uncomfortable beside a frightened patient has practiced half the task. The teacher should therefore pair every simulated exercise with a real encounter in which the learner speaks to the patient and then reports what was said.

The clinic with a stethoscope, a torch, and a thermometer is not a lesser school, and some of its lessons cannot be learned elsewhere. There the reasoning is fully exposed, because nothing can be ordered and the decision must come from the history and the examination alone, and a patient with a fever and no laboratory teaches the value of the repeated temperature and the honest naming of uncertainty. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is often taught as the line above which fever is present, and that figure too is an illustration whose exact value must be verified against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold depends on where the temperature is taken and on which edition of the reference is followed. The torch makes the throat, the ear, the skin, and the eye visible, the thermometer turns an impression into a record, and a watch turns a guess about the pulse into a measurement.

In a clinic where patients wait and time is short, teaching still happens, though it must be small. The teacher can ask one question after the consultation about the finding that decided the plan or the possibility set aside, and the learner can commit to a diagnosis in writing before the patient leaves. A case can be discussed with the patient's agreement in a few sentences, without identifying anyone, as educational material rather than advice about that person. The teacher should not let the teaching replace the care, because a patient waiting while two clinicians reason is still waiting.

Self-assessment becomes real when given a form, and several are available to the clinician who works alone. A logbook of cases, with the diagnosis made and the outcome where it is known, is the simplest and most durable, while a personal list of the cases that surprised the clinician shows the patterns of thought that need attention. A plan naming two or three specific weaknesses and the cases that will address them is more useful than a general intention to read more. A review of the referrals made, and of the patients who returned unwell, is an audit in miniature and needs only a notebook.

Calibration is the match between a clinician's confidence and that clinician's accuracy, and it can be assessed without statistics. A clinician certain of every diagnosis and often wrong is dangerous, and so is one uncertain of every diagnosis who treats nobody. Stating confidence in words and then comparing it with what happened is the practical way to correct either fault, because the clinician who notices that confidence is always high in one kind of presentation that proves innocent has found a bias worth knowing. Neither correction requires a course, only attention and a record.

Expertise in diagnosis is maintained rather than acquired, and the clinician who stops examining his own judgment is the one who will be surprised by it. Knowledge learned well enough to pass an examination fades unless it is used, and habits learned at the bedside drift unless they are watched. A clinician who has not changed a diagnosis in years has either an unusual practice or a closed mind, and the second is more common. The protection is to remain a learner deliberately, to ask for feedback when it is uncomfortable, and to keep teaching, because nothing exposes a gap in one's own reasoning as quickly as explaining it to someone else.

Teaching is therefore not a duty that follows expertise but one of the practices that preserves it. A clinician who must explain why a finding matters, and who must answer a learner's question about the alternative, revisits ground that habit had made automatic. The teacher also learns the shape of his or her own reasoning, including the parts that were never conscious and the parts that do not survive being stated. A team that teaches together develops a shared vocabulary for uncertainty, which lets one member say that something does not fit without being thought incompetent, and the patient benefits because a concern that can be spoken can be acted upon.

The two settings differ in their instruments and not in their reasoning, and a teaching program should say so. In the hospital the learner can check judgment against an ECG, an image, and a laboratory result, so the feedback loop closes quickly, while in the clinic it may close only at the follow-up visit or when the patient returns worse. The hospital teaches the natural history of severe disease, and the clinic teaches the early and the ordinary, which is where most diagnoses are actually made. The clinician who moves between them should expect the instruments to change and should not expect the reasoning to change with them.

A constructed illustration may make the shape of a teaching encounter concrete, and it is offered as a teaching device rather than as a portrait of any real person. Imagine a learner who presents a patient with a shortness of breath and says the diagnosis is an infection of the lungs. The teacher does not correct the diagnosis but asks what finding supports it, what else could produce the same picture, and what the learner would do if the fever were absent. The learner then notices that the heart rate has climbed to 110 beats per minute and that the pressure has fallen, and the diagnosis changes to a failing circulation, with the lung findings explained differently; the rate that should alarm a particular patient is not fixed, and this figure is a teaching illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since fitness, age, and medicines all shift the line. That patient is not real, and the story should not be applied to any real person without a full assessment.

What the clinician writes about his or her own learning matters as much as what is written about patients. A brief entry after a difficult case, recording what was thought, what was found, and what would be done differently, is enough. The entry should be honest about emotion as well as reasoning, because fear, hurry, and irritation cause errors that a purely clinical note will never show. The register should be reviewed deliberately, and its patterns turned into the two or three specific aims already mentioned.

The patient is the ultimate source of feedback, and the clinician who asks can receive it directly. A patient who understood the plan, who knows what to watch for, and who knows when to return has become a partner in the diagnosis rather than a passive recipient of it. A patient who did not understand, who was not asked about the medicine already being taken, or who left without knowing when to come back has revealed a gap that no test result will show. Asking the patient to repeat the plan back is a form of assessment that costs nothing and catches errors before they leave the room.

A culture that supports this work is one in which uncertainty can be spoken and error reported without punishment. That culture is built by small acts: a senior who admits not knowing, a team that thanks the person who raises a concern, a meeting that changes a process rather than a reputation. It is destroyed by the same acts in reverse, and the destruction is faster than the building. The learner watches how errors are handled more closely than he or she listens to any lecture about safety.

Senior clinicians therefore teach most by what they do with uncertainty in front of others. A consultant who says the diagnosis is not yet clear, and who states what would settle it, teaches more than one who produces a confident label to end the discussion. A trainee who sees a senior ask for help learns that asking is a professional act rather than a failure, and a trainee who sees a mistake concealed learns to conceal the next one. The teaching of diagnosis is thus inseparable from the conduct of the team, and the two improve or decay together.

Some of what a clinician must review is not reasoning at all but the conditions in which the reasoning was done. A torch with a failing battery, a thermometer that has not been checked, a queue that does not allow a patient to be undressed, and a record system that loses the last note are sources of diagnostic error in their own right. A practice that audits itself will find these causes beside the cognitive ones, and will often find them easier to fix. Naming the system cause does not excuse the reasoning error, and naming the reasoning error does not excuse the broken equipment; both are examined and both are addressed.

If reasoning is what matters, then the assessment of learners should measure reasoning rather than recall. A question that presents a short story and asks for the next step, the dangerous possibility, and the finding that would change the plan tests something a factual question cannot. A commitment recorded before a result is known, and reviewed afterwards, tests calibration rather than knowledge, and a simulated deterioration in which the learner must notice a trend tests the habit of repeated observation. The examination that rewards the recitation of a list will produce clinicians who recite lists.

The loop closes when what was learned is put back into the next patient's care. The clinician who has identified a habitual omission asks a different question at the next consultation and watches whether the answer changes anything, the teacher who has found that a question works refines it, and the practice that has found a gap in follow-up changes how it arranges the next appointment. Without that return, self-assessment becomes introspection, which is pleasant and useless. The measure of whether the learning was real is not what the clinician felt during the review but what the next patient experienced. The habits described here are meant to be practiced within training, supervision, clinical judgment, and the protocol of the service, and not in place of them.

To summarize, the reasoning of this book is kept by practice on real cases, by committing to a diagnosis before the result arrives, by seeking feedback rather than waiting for it, by reviewing one's own errors without humiliation, and by auditing the practice against what happened to the patients it served. The lethal possibility kept in view is the missed diagnosis of a condition that kills within hours, and the finding that most often reveals it is the direction of the observations across time rather than any single reading. Every figure in this chapter, whether a rate, a pressure, a temperature, a score, or an interval, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, between editions, and between laboratories. The teacher's work is to ask questions that draw reasoning out rather than questions that test recall, and the clinician's work is to keep asking those questions of himself or herself. Expertise is maintained rather than acquired, and the clinician who stops examining his own judgment is the one who will be surprised by it. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service.

# Appendix A — Examination Checklists by System

This appendix gathers the examinations of the body into sequences that can be run from memory, one system at a time, in the order the hands and eyes actually move. A checklist is not a form to be completed and not a substitute for thought, which is why it is written as a sequence of observations rather than as a set of headings that cannot be spoken at the bedside. The order carries the reasoning, so the clinician who inspects before touching, and who listens before palpating in the abdomen, is following the logic of the body rather than a ritual. This appendix is meant to be returned to rather than heard from beginning to end, and it is written for the student, the house officer on the ward round, and the clinician in a clinic with a stethoscope and a torch. It is educational material, it is not medical advice, it is not a protocol, and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the local protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Several habits run through every checklist that follows and are worth stating once rather than repeating with each system. The first is comparison, because almost every sign is judged against the other side of the body or against the patient's earlier state, and a symmetrical finding is described differently from one that is not. The second is the patient's account, since the examination is a conversation as much as an inspection, and a sign that appears while the patient speaks of it means more than one found in silence. The third is the record, because a finding not written down cannot be compared at the next visit, and the words used should describe what was seen rather than the diagnosis it suggests. A clinician who runs these sequences in the same order every time will eventually run them without thinking, which is the purpose of a checklist, to free the mind by making the hands reliable. No sequence here is a screening program, and each is performed only with consent, privacy, and a chaperone where the examination requires one.

The examination of any patient begins before a hand is laid on the skin, with a general inspection that no checklist may omit in any setting. The clinician looks at alertness, posture, and movement, at whether the patient lies flat comfortably or is propped up and fighting for each breath, and at the color of the face, the lips, and the visible skin. The hands are examined next, because they show clubbing, pallor, tremor, coolness, and staining of the fingertips, and the eyes for jaundice and pallor. Hydration and nutrition are judged from the skin, the tongue, and the shape of the body. The vital signs belong here as the first quantitative observations, so the pulse and the breathing are counted over a stated interval, the temperature is taken by a stated route, and the pressure is measured with a cuff that fits the arm, while weight and height give the body mass index, spelled out in full because the short form has no place at the bedside. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius is the figure many textbooks print as the line above which fever is recorded, and that figure is an illustration of the reasoning that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted threshold shifts with the route of measurement, the age of the patient, and the edition in use. A general inspection takes less time than the telling of it, and it is the part of the examination least often recorded and most often decisive.

The cardiovascular examination begins with the hands, examined for temperature, capillary refill, and the changes that speak of infection on a valve, and it then moves to the pulse. The pulse is felt at the wrist for its rate, rhythm, volume, and the character of its rise, and then at the other wrist and down the leg, because a pulse absent or delayed in one place changes the whole assessment. The pressure is measured in both arms when a dissection is possible, and with the patient standing when fainting is part of the story. The neck is inspected for the height and character of the jugular venous pulse, judged with the patient lying at an angle and light falling across the neck. The chest is inspected for the apex beat and for surgical scars, and the heart is then listened to over the valve areas with the patient turned, sitting, and holding the breath as each position requires. A systolic pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the point at which shock must be assumed, and that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the pressure that matters depends on the patient's usual value, age, and pregnancy. The legs are pressed for swelling, the abdomen is examined for an enlarged or tender liver, and the eyes for the retinal vessels. The examination is not finished until the patient has been watched standing or walking where that is safe, since pressure and pulse may be ordinary lying and abnormal on rising.

The respiratory examination begins with the hands, where clubbing, a fine tremor, and a bluish tinge of the nail beds are sought, and with the chest, inspected for its shape, symmetry, and movement. Breathing rate, depth, and effort are observed before the chest is touched, and the use of the neck muscles and the drawing in between the ribs belong to inspection rather than to the ears. The trachea is felt for its position, because a shift tells which side is losing volume and which is under pressure. The chest is then felt for expansion and for the vibration of the voice, and percussed from top to base, with the note compared side against side. Listening follows, over the front and the back, and the clinician deliberately listens to the same spot on both sides before moving, so that a difference is heard rather than remembered. Breath sounds are described for quality, added sounds for timing and character, and voice sounds for the change that indicates solid lung beneath. A silent chest, a stridor heard without a stethoscope, and a trachea pushed to one side may never be omitted in any setting, because each signals a threat to the airway or the circulation.

The abdominal examination is the one in which the order of the hands changes what is found, so the sequence is strict. The patient lies flat with the knees bent and the arms at the sides, the clinician stands on the right, and the hands are warmed before they touch the skin. The abdomen is inspected for shape, movement with breathing, scars, visible veins, and the bulges that appear when the patient coughs. Listening comes before touching, since the sound of the bowel is altered by the pressure of a hand. Palpation begins lightly and away from the place the patient says hurts, then becomes deeper, with the liver, spleen, kidneys, and bladder sought by name and the aorta felt for its width and its pulse. Guarding, rigidity, and the pain that returns when a hand is withdrawn quickly are sought last, and tenderness out of proportion to the pressure applied is taken seriously rather than explained away. The examination is not complete until the hernial openings, the back, the perineum, and the external genitalia have been inspected, and until a rectal or pelvic examination has been considered and either performed or deliberately omitted with a reason.

The neurological examination is long when done in full and short when done well, and it begins with the level of consciousness. The response to voice, to a command, and to a painful stimulus is recorded using the Glasgow coma scale, whose exact contents and whose alarming figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the version in common use differs between services and editions. The pupils are examined for size, symmetry, and reaction to light, and eye movements are checked in all directions. Power is tested group by group in the arms and legs, tone is felt at the wrists and knees, and the reflexes are struck and recorded, with the plantar response sought by stroking the sole. Coordination is judged by finger to nose and heel to shin movements, sensation is tested for light touch, pinprick, vibration, and position, and speech is heard for fluency and clarity. The neck is flexed and the meningeal signs sought in any patient with headache, fever, or a change in consciousness, and the back is examined for a midline defect or a tender spot. The examination ends with the patient standing and walking where it is safe, and sudden weakness of one side, a pupil that is fixed and wide, or a neck that will not bend may never be postponed.

The musculoskeletal examination asks first how the patient moves rather than where it hurts. Gait is watched from the front, the back, and the side, posture and the shape of the spine are inspected, and the patient is asked to perform the movements of daily life that the complaint has made difficult. Each symptomatic joint is inspected for swelling, redness, warmth, and deformity, felt for tenderness and fluid, and moved through its range by the patient and then by the examiner, because a movement the examiner can perform but the patient cannot differs from one blocked in both. Strength is tested against resistance, the joint above and the joint below are examined, and the other side is examined for comparison. The spine is inspected and its movements tested in the neck and lower back, the sacroiliac joints are stressed, and the muscles around the joint are examined for wasting and tenderness. A hot, swollen joint the patient will not move is treated as an infection until proved otherwise, and a limb that is cold, pale, and pulseless after an injury is an emergency that stops the checklist.

The examination of the head and neck gathers the senses and the structures that admit air, food, and speech, and it is performed with a light and a torch everywhere. The head is inspected for shape, scars, symmetry, and the movement of the face, and the scalp is parted with the fingers so that the skin beneath the hair is seen rather than assumed. The ears are examined outside and, where an instrument exists, inside, the nose is inspected for deformity, discharge, and bleeding, and the sinuses are pressed for tenderness. The mouth is opened with a light, and the lips, gums, teeth, tongue, palate, and back of the throat are inspected in turn, because a dental abscess or hidden ulcer can explain a fever nothing else explains. The neck is inspected for swelling and for the position of the trachea, and felt for lymph nodes in each region, for the thyroid gland, and for the movement of the larynx with swallowing. A patient with drooling, a muffled voice, a stiff neck, or difficulty swallowing is examined for a threatened airway and referred at once, and a fixed, hard lymph node in the neck of an adult is investigated rather than observed. The short form ear, nose, and throat, or ENT, is used here only for convenience, and the examination itself is always the same set of observations.

The skin is examined from the scalp to the soles, in good light, with the surface uncovered in stages so that the patient is not exposed more than necessary. The clinician notes color, moisture, temperature, and texture, then looks deliberately at the places usually hidden, which include the scalp, behind the ears, the armpits, the groin, the perineum, the buttocks, and between the toes. The nails and the mucous membranes of the mouth and eyes are part of the same examination, since pallor and small bleeding spots are often seen first in the mouth. Any rash is described by its distribution, shape, border, color, and whether it fades when a clear glass is pressed against it, and a rash that does not fade is treated as an emergency until a cause is found. The hair and scalp are inspected for loss, scaling, and infestation, and the lymph nodes draining the area of any skin lesion are felt in the neck, the armpits, and the groins. A skin examination in a patient with fever is not complete until the whole surface has been seen, because the finding that changes the diagnosis is often a single lesion the patient cannot see.

The examination of the genitourinary system and of the breast requires the most care with consent, privacy, and the presence of a chaperone, and it is performed only when the history or general examination gives it a reason. The breasts are inspected with the patient sitting and then lying with the arms raised, and each is examined in a fixed sequence that covers all of its tissue, with the armpit and the area above the collarbone felt in the same sitting. The clinician notes any lump by its size, shape, firmness, and movement within the tissue, and looks for a change in the skin, a retraction of the nipple, or a discharge. In the male patient the external genitalia are inspected and the testicles felt for size, tenderness, and a lump, and a sudden severe pain in a testis with a high-riding organ is treated as a twisted testis until proved otherwise. The groin is examined for hernia and enlarged lymph nodes, and the prostate is felt through the rectal wall where that examination is indicated. In the female patient a speculum and pelvic examination are performed only by a clinician trained and consented to do them, and the external genitalia, the urethral opening, and the perineum are inspected in every patient whose complaint could arise there. A pregnant patient with bleeding or pain is not examined in a way that delays her journey to obstetric care, and the finding that changes the plan is often the pressure, the pulse, and the abdominal examination rather than the pelvic one.

The mental state examination begins as soon as the clinician meets the patient and continues through every other system. Appearance, dress, posture, and cooperation are noticed, behavior and movement are observed, and speech is heard for its rate, volume, coherence, and direction. Mood is asked about directly and judged from what is said and shown, and the content of thought is explored for worry, for fixed false beliefs, and for the intention to harm the self or another. Perception is tested by asking whether the patient hears or sees anything that others do not, and insight is judged by what the patient believes about the illness. Cognition is examined by testing attention, orientation, memory, and the ability to follow a simple command, and the difference between a clouded attention that fluctuates and a memory that has failed over months is one of the most useful distinctions in medicine. The history is completed with an account from a relative or caregiver, because a patient with failing memory may describe a life that no longer matches the one the family sees.

Some parts of these sequences may be omitted when the patient is dying in front of the clinician, and some may never be. In an emergency the fine special tests of the joints, the formal testing of cognition, and the examination of the breast and the pelvis are postponed until the immediate threat has been handled. What may never be omitted is the general inspection, the assessment of the airway and the breathing, the pulse and the pressure, the level of consciousness, the skin for a rash that does not fade, the neck for stiffness, and the response of the pupils, because each decides whether the patient is treated now or observed. The examination of the abdomen in a patient with pain may never be abandoned in favor of a machine, since the hand that finds rigidity is often ahead of any image. In the clinic with a stethoscope and a torch, the same sequences run in the same order with fewer instruments, so the torch replaces the lamp, the watch replaces the monitor, and careful comparison of one side with the other replaces the imaging that is not available. What changes is the depth of the testing and the certainty of the diagnosis, not the reasoning, and the clinician who records what could not be examined has told the truth about the limits of the assessment. A checklist followed rigidly in a patient who is deteriorating is itself a danger, and the rule that governs all of them is that the patient sets the order.

Constructed illustrations may show how the sequences behave when used rather than recited, and both are teaching devices rather than portraits of any real person. Imagine first a patient brought in unresponsive: the general inspection notes breathing and color, the pulse and pressure are taken, the pupils are examined, the neck is flexed, and the skin is checked for a rash, while the joints and the formal mental state wait. Now imagine a patient in a clinic with a swollen ankle and no fever: the gait is watched, both ankles are compared, the pulses of the foot are felt, the skin is inspected, and the joints above are examined, because a swollen ankle is sometimes the first sign of a problem that began elsewhere. What both share is that no part of the sequence was chosen at random, and that the finding which changed the plan came from an observation a hurried clinician might have skipped. A checklist used this way is a memory aid and not a replacement for the patient in front of the clinician, and the clinician who senses that something is wrong should return to the beginning rather than push to the end.

To summarize, this appendix sets out the examination of each system as a sequence of observations that can be run from memory at the bedside, beginning with the general inspection and moving through the cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, neurological, musculoskeletal, head and neck, skin, genitourinary and breast, and mental state examinations. The order carries the reasoning, which is what is looked at before what is touched and what is listened to before what is pressed. The items that may be postponed in an emergency and those that may never be omitted are both named, so that each is chosen deliberately. Every figure here, whether a temperature or a pressure, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between countries, editions, and laboratories. This appendix is educational material and it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and no checklist, however carefully followed, substitutes for the patient in front of the clinician.

# Appendix B — Differential Diagnosis Tables by Symptom

This appendix gathers the differential diagnosis of the common presentations into spoken form, so that a clinician who is stuck can run through the possibilities in the order the patient's story deserves. The order applies one principle twice: first by likelihood, so the ordinary explanation is tested early, and then by danger, so the killing diagnosis is named before it is comfortable to do so. Each presentation opens with its can't-miss entry, the diagnosis that must be set aside before any other is settled, and the finding that reveals it is named in the same breath. What follows is a sequence of possibilities rather than an exhaustive list, each attached to the finding that moves it up or down, because a diagnosis without a discriminating finding is only a name. This appendix is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is seen.

Fever most often arrives without a focus, and the first question is whether the patient is stable enough to be investigated at leisure. The can't-miss entries are meningitis, infection of the bloodstream, malaria in a patient who has traveled, and infection on a heart valve, and each announces itself through a finding rather than through the height of the temperature. A temperature such as 38 degrees Celsius is often taught as the line above which fever is recorded, but that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted threshold depends on the site of measurement, the age of the patient, and the edition in use. A stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under pressure, a new murmur, and a recent journey move those dangerous entries upward. The bedside can tell an alert, hydrated patient from one who is drowsy, mottled, or breathing quickly, while the test that names the organism and the referral that provides it belong to a hospital.

Chest pain is a presentation in which the danger is not proportional to the severity, and the can't-miss entries are an acute myocardial infarction, a dissection of the aorta, a clot in the lung, and a tear of the esophagus. Discomfort that is new, comes at rest, or has changed its pattern moves infarction upward, and a normal examination does nothing to remove it from the list. A tearing pain that travels between the chest and the back, with a difference between the pulses or pressures in the two arms, moves dissection upward. Sudden breathlessness with a swollen calf moves a clot in the lung upward, and vomiting after a violent retch moves a tear of the esophagus upward. At the bedside the clinician can compare the arms, feel the pulses, listen to the heart and lungs, and press the chest wall; the tracing of the heart, the enzyme the laboratory measures, and the imaging of the aorta belong to a hospital.

Dyspnea and cough ask whether the problem lies in the lungs, the heart, the airway, or the blood, and the can't-miss entries are a clot in the lung, a severe infection, a collapsed lung, an airway that is closing, and pulmonary edema. A sudden onset in a patient with recent immobility, surgery, cancer, or a previous clot moves a clot upward. High fever with crackles and dullness moves infection upward, sudden breathlessness with reduced breath sounds and a shifted windpipe moves collapse upward, and stridor with a change in the voice, or swelling of the face and tongue, moves a closing airway to the top at once. The patient who cannot lie flat and coughs frothy, blood-stained sputum moves pulmonary edema upward, and a raised pressure in the neck veins with swollen ankles supports it.

Headache and dizziness divide into the sudden and the gradual, and the sudden onset carries the danger. The can't-miss entries are a subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, a stroke or bleeding into the brain, raised pressure inside the skull from a tumor, and the headache of carbon monoxide poisoning or very high blood pressure. A headache that reaches full intensity almost at once, often described as a blow to the back of the head, moves a subarachnoid hemorrhage to the front, and it must be treated as that diagnosis until a test excludes it, because the first examination is often normal. Fever with a stiff neck moves meningitis upward, a headache with weakness or disturbed speech or vision moves a vascular event upward, and a headache worse on waking, with coughing, or lying flat moves raised pressure upward. Dizziness that truly spins suggests the inner ear, while dizziness that is faintness suggests the circulation, and asking what the patient means separates the two. The bedside can examine the eyes, vision, power, and balance; imaging of the brain and examination of the fluid around it belong to a hospital.

Abdominal pain is where the can't-miss entries change with age, sex, and the possibility of pregnancy, and where dangerous diagnoses hide behind a soft, unimpressive abdomen. The can't-miss entries are a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, a leaking or ruptured aortic aneurysm, a perforated hollow organ, a strangulated hernia, whose blood supply has been cut off, a twisted ovary or testis, and mesenteric ischemia, a loss of blood supply to the bowel. In any woman of childbearing age pregnancy is settled first, because a positive test moves a ruptured ectopic pregnancy to the top at once. Pain out of proportion to the examination, in an older patient with an irregular pulse or known aneurysm, moves a vascular catastrophe upward, while a tender hernia that cannot be reduced, pain that settled before returning worse, and a rigid abdomen move perforation and strangulation upward. The bedside can inspect, palpate, percuss, and listen, and can examine the hernial openings and the testes; ultrasound for free fluid, the pregnancy test, and imaging of the bowel and vessels require a hospital, and a deteriorating patient must travel rather than wait.

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation are usually self-limiting, and they are dangerous in the few patients who are dehydrated, bleeding, obstructed, or poisoned. The can't-miss entries are dehydration with failing kidneys, obstruction of the bowel, bleeding from the gut, an infection that has spread to the bloodstream, and a metabolic cause such as diabetic ketoacidosis, the accumulation of acid when insulin is lacking. Vomiting that is bile-stained or feculent, abdominal distension, and the absence of stool and gas move obstruction upward, and a high-pitched or absent bowel sound supports it. Blood in the vomit or stool moves bleeding upward, while a dry mouth, weak pulse, and shrinking urine move dehydration upward, and deep, rapid breathing with a smell of acetone moves ketoacidosis upward. A patient who cannot keep fluids down, has lost weight quickly, or has severe pain is not one for watchful waiting.

Bleeding from the gut and jaundice are signs rather than diseases. The can't-miss entries for bleeding are a burst varicose vein in the esophagus, a bleeding ulcer, a tear where the esophagus meets the stomach, and a cancer of the gut; for jaundice they are obstruction of the bile duct, infection of the bile ducts, a failing liver, a cancer of the pancreas, and the destruction of red cells, called hemolysis. Black, tarry stool and vomit like coffee grounds move bleeding from the upper gut upward, fresh red blood from the back passage moves bleeding from the lower gut upward, and a falling pressure with a rising pulse means active bleeding whatever the color of the stool. Jaundice with fever, right upper abdominal pain, and a tender liver is an emergency from infected bile ducts, while painless, progressive jaundice moves a cancer upward. The bedside can look at the color of eyes and skin, feel the liver and spleen, and examine the back passage; the blood count, liver and clotting tests, endoscopy, and imaging belong to a hospital. A hemoglobin such as 70 grams per liter is the kind of figure a laboratory may report after bleeding, and the range against which it is judged belongs to that laboratory and the population it serves, so read it with the local report and the current guideline rather than from memory.

Palpitations and collapse ask two questions at once, whether the heart is the cause and whether the circulation has failed. The can't-miss entries are a rhythm that has made the circulation fail, a clot in the lung, bleeding from the gut, a ruptured aneurysm, an ectopic pregnancy, and a seizure mistaken for a faint. Collapse during effort, with chest pain, or with a family history of sudden death moves a dangerous rhythm upward, and the electrocardiogram, or ECG, answers that question where it exists. A pulse that is very slow, such as fewer than 40 beats per minute, very fast, or irregular without pattern must be recorded and acted upon, but the rate at which a particular patient becomes unstable depends on the heart and the patient, so that figure must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than applied as a rule. The bedside can measure pulse and pressure lying and standing, listen to the heart, and ask what the patient remembers; the ECG and monitoring of the rhythm belong to a hospital.

Back pain is common and mostly mechanical, and the task is to find the few patients in whom it is not. The can't-miss entries are compression of the spinal cord, infection of the spine, a cancer that has spread to the spine, a fracture, and a leaking aortic aneurysm or kidney stone presenting as back pain. Compression of the cord declares itself through weakness of the legs, numbness around the back passage and inner thighs, and difficulty passing urine or holding stool, and it is an emergency that requires referral before the diagnosis is complete. Fever, a history of injecting drugs, a recent spinal procedure, or a suppressed immune defense moves infection upward, while constant pain, worse at night and unrelieved by rest, moves a cancer upward, especially with a known tumor or unexplained weight loss. The bedside can inspect the spine, test power and sensation in the legs, examine the back passage, and check the groin pulses; imaging of the spine and inflammatory markers in the blood require a hospital.

Unintentional weight loss and fatigue are often diagnosed from the history, because the patient's own account of what has changed carries most of the information. The can't-miss entries are a cancer, tuberculosis, infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, or HIV, diabetes, an overactive thyroid gland, depression, and a chronic infection or inflammation. A weight loss of about 5 per cent of the body weight over 6 months is one way its significance is described, but the figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the threshold depends on the patient's starting weight and the reference consulted. Night sweats, an enlarged lymph node, a cough that will not settle, and an evening fever move tuberculosis and cancer upward, while thirst, large volumes of urine, and blurred vision move diabetes upward. A fast pulse, heat intolerance, tremor, and a swelling in the neck move an overactive thyroid upward.

Swelling and lumps divide into the generalized and the local, and a local lump raises the question of cancer. The can't-miss entries are a cancer of the breast or another organ presenting as a lump, an infected collection of pus, a clot in a deep vein, and the swelling of heart, kidney, or liver failure. A lump that is hard, fixed, irregular, and painless demands an answer, and any lump in the breast, neck, armpit, or groin should be examined with the whole region and the opposite side for comparison. Swelling of both legs with breathlessness and a raised pressure in the neck veins moves heart failure upward, while swelling beginning in the face and spreading downward suggests a kidney cause, and swelling with jaundice and a swollen abdomen suggests the liver. A single warm, tender calf moves a clot upward, and a hot, red, painful area with fever moves infection upward.

Urinary symptoms and blood in the urine are separated first by whether the patient is passing urine easily and whether the blood is visible. The can't-miss entries are a cancer of the kidney, bladder, or prostate, an infection of the kidney, an obstruction such as a stone, and a serious injury to the urinary tract after trauma. Visible blood, especially in an older patient and especially when painless, moves a cancer upward and must be investigated rather than attributed to infection, because infection and cancer can exist together. Fever, flank pain, and tenderness over the kidney move infection upward, while colicky pain traveling from the flank to the groin moves a stone upward. A poor stream, difficulty starting, and a feeling of incomplete emptying move an obstruction of the outlet upward, and a patient who cannot pass urine at all with a tender, distended lower abdomen needs relief now. The bedside can inspect the abdomen, percuss the bladder, examine the back, and dip the urine where a dipstick exists; microscopy of the urine and imaging of the urinary tract belong to a hospital.

A change in consciousness gives the clinician the least time and needs the widest list, because the causes come from every system at once. The can't-miss entries are a low sugar in the blood, a low oxygen, an infection of the brain or its covering, a stroke or bleeding into the brain, a poisoning or withdrawal from alcohol, a head injury, and a seizure that is continuing or recurring. The bedside can measure the sugar where a meter exists and can assess the airway, breathing, and circulation, and those three are addressed before the cause is named. Fever with a stiff neck moves infection of the covering of the brain upward, while sudden weakness on one side, disturbed speech, or unequal pupils move a vascular event upward. A seizure that has not stopped, or that returns without the patient waking, is an emergency requiring treatment and referral at once. The bedside can look for a rash, a bitten tongue, a head wound, and the smell of the breath; salts and sugar in the blood, imaging of the brain, and examination of the fluid around it belong to a hospital, and a patient who cannot protect the airway needs the intensive care unit, or ICU.

A rash is read by its distribution, shape, color, and whether it fades when pressed, and those four questions separate most dangerous entries from ordinary ones. The can't-miss entries are a rash that does not fade under pressure, which may mean bleeding into the skin from an infection in the bloodstream, a drug reaction that is peeling the skin, a severe reaction with fever and involvement of the mouth and eyes, and the rash of a serious illness such as measles in a vulnerable patient. A purple rash that does not fade when a clear glass is pressed against it must be acted upon before it is explained, and skin peeling or coming away in sheets requires referral at once. A rash beginning after a new medicine, with fever and a rising pulse, moves a drug reaction upward, while a rash with fever, a runny nose, and a cough in an unvaccinated child moves measles upward. The bedside can examine the whole skin in good light, including palms, soles, scalp, and mouth, and can ask what the patient has taken, eaten, or touched; a skin sample, a swab, and blood tests belong to a hospital. A severe skin reaction may need the protective measures of a burns unit rather than an ordinary ward.

Bleeding, bruising, and anemia are grouped because they may share one cause, a failure of clotting, a shortage of red cells, or a loss of blood that has not been seen. The can't-miss entries are a cancer of the gut or the blood, a failure of the bone marrow, the tissue inside bone where blood cells are made, a shortage of platelets, the small cells that help the blood to clot, a clotting disorder, and serious bleeding from an unreported injury. A patient with leukemia, a cancer of the blood-forming cells, may present with bruising, infections, and fatigue before any blood test is taken. Bruising without cause, bleeding gums or nose, blood in the stool, and tiny red spots move a disorder of the blood or clotting upward, while a diet poor in iron, heavy menstrual loss, and chronic loss from the gut move an iron shortage upward.

Used well, this appendix is a discipline rather than a catalogue, and its value depends on the order in which the clinician speaks the possibilities. The habit is to commit to a leading diagnosis and a can't-miss diagnosis before any test is ordered, then to ask what finding would change the ranking, because a test that cannot change it was not worth sending. A framework organizes memory and can also close the mind, so the entries are a prompt and never a fence. Where no test exists, the same sequence still works, and the decision that replaces the diagnosis is a plan: watch and review, begin treatment on the clinical picture, or travel now. The population in which a rule was derived matters, and a pattern learned in one setting can mislead in another, so local experience and local protocol are part of the reasoning. The record should show which entries were considered, which were set aside, and on what finding, because the next clinician will read the reasoning and not the conclusion alone.

To summarize, this appendix offers the differential diagnosis of the common presentations as a sequence of possibilities rather than a list, each opened by the can't-miss entry and each attached to the finding that moves it up or down. The order is likelihood first and danger always, the bedside questions are separated from the tests and the referrals, and a deteriorating patient is treated and moved before the diagnosis is complete. Every figure here, whether a temperature, a rate, a pressure, a proportion, or a concentration, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between editions, and between the laboratory and the ward. No table organizes memory into a diagnosis, and no sequence of possibilities examines the patient, so the clinician who holds the list lightly and looks at the person in front of them will use it best. This appendix is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service. The entries are meant to be returned to at the bedside and rehearsed until they come without effort, and the patient, not the framework, is always the final authority.

# Appendix C — Normal Values and Reference Ranges

A reference range is a promise a laboratory makes about a measurement, and it is made for a particular method, a particular population, and a particular place. When a report says that a result lies between two figures, it means that most of the healthy people studied fell inside them, not that a value outside them is a disease. The range belongs to the machine, the units, and the people from whom it was drawn, so a range carried from one country to a patient in another is a guess dressed as a fact. This appendix gathers values met most often in the adult, the child, and the pregnant patient, and it gives them only as illustrations of the kind of figure a report may contain. Every one of them must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because reference intervals differ between laboratories, between countries, and between editions. This appendix is educational material, not medical advice, not a protocol, and not a substitute for training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and no patient described in it is real.

The vital signs are the measurements a clinician makes rather than orders, and they are the ones most often compared against memory instead of a record. In a resting adult the temperature is often given as 36 to 38 degrees Celsius, the pulse as 60 to 100 beats per minute, and the breathing rate as 12 to 20 breaths per minute. The pressure is commonly written as a pair of figures such as 120 over 80 millimeters of mercury, and oxygen saturation at sea level in a healthy adult is usually stated as 95 to 100 per cent. Each of these is a teaching illustration and each must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted boundaries shift with the method, the age, and the edition consulted. The breathing rate is the sign least often counted properly and most often informative, and pulse and pressure together say more than either alone.

Children are not small adults, and their normal values move with age in a way that surprises anyone who learned only adult figures. A newborn's pulse may sit between 100 and 160 beats per minute and falls gradually through infancy and childhood toward the adult range, and the breathing rate follows the same descent. The pressure is lower in childhood and climbs with growth, so a figure unremarkable in an adult may be a warning in a small child, and one alarming in an adult may be ordinary in an infant. Hemoglobin and the red cell indices change in the first months of life, and the white cell count is higher in the newborn than it will ever be again. Because these boundaries are set locally and revised from time to time, confirm every pediatric figure against the current guideline and the local protocol, and read the child's own previous results whenever they exist.

Pregnancy changes almost every measurement a laboratory makes, and a range taken from a non-pregnant adult will mislead in a woman who is expecting. The pulse rises a little and the pressure tends to fall in the middle months before returning toward its old level near term, so a low reading may be entirely physiological. The blood is diluted by the extra plasma, so the hemoglobin falls even though the total red cell mass has increased, and a value suggesting anemia outside pregnancy may be expected here. The kidneys filter more, so creatinine and urea fall, the thyroid hormones shift in a pattern that can mimic disease, and clotting factors rise so that a swollen calf is never dismissed. Gestational age and the laboratory's own trimester-specific ranges change the answer, so take these figures to the current guideline and the local protocol before you interpret them.

The blood count is the most frequently ordered set of numbers in medicine and the one most often read without its context. Hemoglobin in a healthy adult man is often given as 13 to 17 grams per deciliter and in a woman as 12 to 15 grams per deciliter, while the white cell count commonly falls between 4 and 11 thousand cells per microliter and the platelet count between 150 and 400 thousand per microliter. The hematocrit is the proportion of blood occupied by red cells, and the red cell indices describe the size and the color of the cells rather than their number. A low hemoglobin with small pale cells suggests a different problem from a low hemoglobin with large cells, and the indices make that distinction rather than the hemoglobin alone. These intervals are illustrations printed by one laboratory for one population and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since units, methods, and boundaries vary between services and editions.

The chemistry panel answers questions about the salts, the sugar, and the waste products, and each of its figures belongs to its own population. Sodium is often quoted as 135 to 145 millimoles per liter, potassium as 3.5 to 5.0 millimoles per liter, bicarbonate as 22 to 28 millimoles per liter, and chloride as 98 to 107 millimoles per liter. Fasting glucose is commonly given as 4 to 6 millimoles per liter, calcium as 2.2 to 2.6 millimoles per liter, and magnesium as 0.7 to 1.0 millimoles per liter, although the units used for sugar and calcium differ between countries. A potassium at the edge of its range matters more than a sodium at the edge, because the heart tolerates a mild disturbance of sodium far better than a mild disturbance of potassium. Every one of these intervals is an illustration and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the figures, the units, and the analytic methods are not the same everywhere.

The kidney values are read together rather than singly, because no one of them describes filtration on its own. Creatinine is often reported as 60 to 110 micromoles per liter, and the estimated glomerular filtration rate, calculated from creatinine with age and sex, is commonly given as above 90 milliliters per minute for each 1.73 square meters of body surface area. Urea is usually quoted as 2.5 to 7.0 millimoles per liter, and creatinine depends on muscle, so a frail older patient may have a reassuring value while filtration is poor. A rise in creatinine over days is more alarming than the same value reached slowly over years, and the rate of change most often decides the urgency. Because the equations and the units differ between laboratories and are revised between editions, confirm every kidney figure against the current guideline and the local protocol, and read the trend alongside the value.

The liver values divide into those that speak of injury and those that speak of function, and the two do not always move together. Bilirubin is often reported as 5 to 20 micromoles per liter, albumin as 35 to 50 grams per liter, and total protein as 60 to 80 grams per liter. The enzymes alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase are commonly quoted with an upper boundary near 40 units per liter, alkaline phosphatase with one near 120 units per liter, and gamma-glutamyl transferase with one that differs between men and women. The clotting tests, the prothrombin time and the international normalized ratio, describe what the liver can still make, and they worsen when function fails rather than when cells are merely injured. All of these boundaries vary with the method and the population, so take them to the current guideline and the local protocol rather than relying on memory.

The inflammatory markers are the least specific numbers in the laboratory and the easiest to over-read. C-reactive protein is often described with a boundary near 5 milligrams per liter, the erythrocyte sedimentation rate with a boundary that rises with age and differs between men and women, and procalcitonin with a boundary some services use to support a decision about infection. Ferritin is both an iron store and an inflammatory marker, so a raised value may speak of inflammation as readily as of overload. None of these substances names a cause, since they say that something is happening while the history and the examination say what, and a marker that climbs in a patient who looks worse is a reason to hunt for a collection of pus. Because assays and boundaries are set locally and revised between editions, confirm every one of these figures against the current guideline and the local protocol, and never treat a single result as a diagnosis.

The blood gas describes how well the lungs and the kidneys are keeping the blood in balance, and it is meaningless without the sample it came from. Arterial blood in a healthy adult is often given a pH between 7.35 and 7.45, a partial pressure of oxygen between 80 and 100 millimeters of mercury, and a partial pressure of carbon dioxide between 35 and 45 millimeters of mercury, with bicarbonate between 22 and 26 millimoles per liter. Venous blood gives different figures, and a sample from a vein cannot be judged against arterial boundaries. Altitude lowers the oxygen figure in a healthy person, age lowers it a little, and a low oxygen with a high carbon dioxide tells a different story from a low oxygen with a normal one. Take every figure here to the current guideline and the local protocol, because the boundaries differ between laboratories and between the editions on which they rely.

The urine is the specimen a clinic can obtain without a needle, and its values depend on the method as much as any in medicine. The specific gravity of a normal urine is often given as 1.005 to 1.030, and the reaction is usually acidic, between 4.5 and 8.0, depending on the diet. A dipstick may report protein, glucose, ketones, blood, leukocyte esterase, and nitrite, and microscopy may report white cells, red cells, casts, crystals, and organisms, each with a locally set boundary. A collection over 24 hours measures how much protein or how much of a substance leaves the body in a day, and it is uninterpretable if the collection was incomplete, while a positive dipstick for blood means little in a menstruating woman or after exercise. Because strip chemistry, microscopy, and units vary between services, confirm each figure against the current guideline and the local protocol, and read the urine with the history rather than apart from it.

The endocrine values are the ones most often misread, because the hormone is interpreted without the gland and the patient it serves. Thyroid stimulating hormone is often quoted as 0.4 to 4.0 milliunits per liter, with free thyroxine reported in a range each laboratory sets around its own method. Glycated hemoglobin, which reflects the average sugar over the previous weeks, is commonly described with a boundary near 6.5 per cent, and a fasting glucose with one near 7 millimoles per liter, although the units and the boundaries differ between countries. Cortisol moves through the day, so a single value cannot be judged without the hour it was taken, and in acute illness almost every hormone can be disturbed without glandular disease. Confirm all of these boundaries against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the assays are not standardized between laboratories and the same patient can appear to change simply by changing the hospital.

The clotting tests describe how quickly blood forms a clot in a test tube and how well the liver and the platelets are doing their work. The prothrombin time is often given as 11 to 14 seconds, the activated partial thromboplastin time as 25 to 35 seconds, and fibrinogen as 2 to 4 grams per liter, while the international normalized ratio is commonly quoted as 0.8 to 1.2 in a person not taking a blood-thinning medicine. The platelet count belongs with these figures, because a normal clotting time in a patient with very few platelets is not reassuring. A clot that forms slowly may mean a deficiency of one factor, a blood-thinning medicine, liver disease, or consumption of clotting factors during severe illness, and the pattern across the tests separates them. Since each of these intervals is set by the reagent and the analyzer that performs it, take them to the current guideline and the local protocol before you act, and never compare a result from one hospital with a boundary printed in another.

Some values are reported by the laboratory but belong to the heart, and they are read with the tracing rather than alone. Troponin is released by injured heart muscle, and each laboratory sets its own boundary and its own way of deciding what counts as a rise, so a result is interpreted against the interval printed by the laboratory that produced it. A natriuretic peptide reflects the stretch of a failing heart, and its boundary is set locally and shifts with age and kidney function. On the electrocardiogram, or ECG, the duration of each part of the tracing is an approximate figure whose boundaries move with the rate, the age of the patient, and the machine that recorded it. A single normal marker never excludes a heart attack and a single abnormal marker never proves one, so confirm every one of these figures against the current guideline and the local protocol, since assays, units, and accepted boundaries are revised repeatedly.

Three influences move more reference ranges than any others, and they are age, pregnancy, and altitude. Age changes the pulse, the breathing rate, the pressure, the hemoglobin, the white cell count, and the kidney figures, and it changes them in different directions, so a value ordinary at 1 year may be abnormal at 40 and unremarkable again at 80. Pregnancy changes the blood count, the clotting, the kidney values, the thyroid, and the pressure, and it requires ranges stated by trimester. Altitude raises hemoglobin and red cells and lowers the oxygen figure in the blood gas, and the change takes days to weeks to settle, while illness itself moves many values through inflammation, dehydration, fever, and medicines. Because these influences are handled differently in different services, confirm any range you use against the current guideline and the local protocol, and prefer the interval your own laboratory prints for the population it serves.

Most of the numbers in this appendix are worth more as a trend than as a single reading, and the reason is biological variation. The same substance in the same healthy person moves during the day, changes with meals and sleep, and differs from one sample to the next by more than a clinician expects. A change smaller than that ordinary variation may be noise, while a small change in the same direction across three samples may be real. The patient's own previous results are therefore the best comparison available, and the direction of travel usually matters more than the distance from the printed boundary. The report itself should be read with its units, its method, and its reference interval, since a value quoted without those is a number without a meaning. Read the trend against the current guideline and the local protocol as well, because the interval and the units may have changed between the two occasions you are comparing.

A constructed illustration may show how these habits work, and it is invented for teaching rather than drawn from any real person. Imagine a woman in late pregnancy whose hemoglobin sits at the lower edge of the non-pregnant range, whose platelet count has drifted down a little, and whose creatinine has fallen, since none of these is disease and all follow from the physiology of pregnancy. Now imagine an older man, thin and frail, whose creatinine lies comfortably inside the printed interval while his kidney function has silently declined, and whose only clue is a climb from his own previous result. Neither patient exists, and neither story should be applied to a real person without a full assessment. Take each figure in such a case to the current guideline and the local protocol, because the interval that helped one hospital may mislead in another.

Where there is no laboratory, the ranges in this appendix do not lose their value, but they change their role. They become the background against which a clinician judges what can be measured by hand, among them the pulse, the breathing rate, the temperature, the pressure, the color of the skin, the passage of urine, and the trend of the patient's appearance over hours. A clinic that can do a urine dipstick and count a pulse still holds two of the most useful measurements in medicine. The decision that follows is rarely a diagnosis but a plan, and the plan asks whether the patient can be watched, whether treatment should begin on the clinical picture, and whether the journey to a hospital must start now. The reasoning survives the loss of the machine, so every figure you remember from this appendix must still be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

To summarize, a reference range belongs to a laboratory, a method, and a population, and it illustrates reasoning rather than settling a diagnosis. The values here are gathered by system, from the vital signs and the blood count through the chemistry, the liver and kidney figures, the inflammatory markers, the blood gas, and the urine, with the changes that age, pregnancy, and altitude produce noted as they arise. Each is offered only as the sort of number a report may contain, and each must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the interval is local to the laboratory and the edition in use varies from service to service. Most are more useful as a trend in one patient than as a single measurement compared with a printed boundary, and the patient's own previous results are the best comparison available. This appendix is educational material, it does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the protocol of your own service, and no patient described in it is real. A number is a question to be answered in the light of the patient, never an answer on its own.

# Appendix D — Red-Flag Summary Cards

A red flag is not a diagnosis; it is one finding that changes the order of what happens next. Ordinary reasoning weighs probabilities, but a red flag demands action before the explanation is complete.
